title: Cain and Abel
text:
Adam and Eve had two sons. Cain, the elder, worked the soil. Abel kept flocks. In the course of time, Cain brought some of the fruits of the ground as an offering to the Lord, and Abel brought the fat portions of the firstborn of his flock.

The Lord looked with favor on Abel and his offering, but not on Cain and his. Cain was furious, and his face fell. The Lord spoke to him: why was he angry? If he did what was right, would he not be accepted? But if not, sin was crouching at the door; it desired to have him, but he must rule over it.

Cain did not master it. He said to his brother, "Let us go out to the field." And while they were in the field, Cain attacked Abel and killed him.

The Lord asked Cain where his brother was. "I do not know," Cain answered. "Am I my brother's keeper?" The Lord said that his brother's blood was crying out from the ground. Cain was cursed: the earth would no longer yield its strength to him, and he would be a restless wanderer. Cain protested that his punishment was more than he could bear, and that whoever found him would kill him. So the Lord put a mark on Cain, so that no one would kill him, and he went away and lived in the land of Nod, east of Eden.
lesson: Envy between siblings is natural, but it must be mastered before it masters us. Notice resentment early and deal with it while it is still small.
people: Cain, Abel, Adam, Eve
source: Genesis 4:1-16

title: The Workers Who Built the Pyramids
text:
For centuries people imagined the Great Pyramid being raised by vast gangs of slaves under the whip. Herodotus, writing two thousand years after it was built, said a hundred thousand men worked in shifts of three months. Excavations at Giza since the late twentieth century have given a different picture.

From 1990 the Egyptian archaeologist Zahi Hawass excavated a cemetery of the pyramid builders on the slope south of the monuments. The workers had been buried with honor near the kings they served, with bread and beer for the afterlife, and some tombs carried the titles of gang supervisors and skilled craftsmen. Skeletons showed the strain of heavy labor, but also healed fractures and evidence of medical care.

Nearby, a team led by the American archaeologist Mark Lehner uncovered a large settlement often called the Lost City of the Pyramid Builders: bakeries, breweries, storerooms and long galleries that probably housed rotating crews. Animal bones showed that the workers were fed large amounts of meat, including beef.

Inscriptions and graffiti suggest how the labor was organized. Crews had names, such as Friends of Khufu or Drunkards of Menkaure, and were divided into smaller groups that competed and worked in rotation. A permanent core of skilled craftsmen was joined by larger numbers of laborers drawn from villages across Egypt for periods of service. They were not free volunteers in the modern sense, but neither were they slaves.
lesson: Great works are built by organized teams with names, pride and care for each other. Treat people as members of a crew, not as tools.
people: Mark Lehner, Zahi Hawass, pyramid builders of Giza
source: Mark Lehner, The Complete Pyramids (1997); Zahi Hawass and Mark Lehner, excavation reports of the Giza Plateau Mapping Project and the workers' cemetery
caveat: Labor was probably rotating compulsory service owed to the state, so the line between paid work and obligation remains debated.

title: The Eloquent Peasant
text:
A peasant named Khunanup loaded his donkeys with goods from his home in the Field of Salt and set off for Egypt's valley to trade them for food for his family. On the way he had to pass the estate of Nemtynakht, a man in the service of the high steward Rensi. Nemtynakht coveted the donkeys. He spread a cloth across the narrow public path so that the peasant had to steer his animals along the edge of a barley field. When one donkey snatched a mouthful of barley, Nemtynakht seized all the donkeys and beat their owner.

Khunanup took his case to Rensi himself. He spoke so beautifully that Rensi reported it to King Nebkaure, who was delighted. The king ordered Rensi to give no answer, so that the peasant would keep speaking and his words could be written down. In secret, the king had food sent to the peasant and to his wife and children.

Khunanup returned again and again, nine times in all, each time more desperate and more eloquent, reminding the steward that an official is meant to be a rudder for the helpless and a balance that does not tilt. After the ninth speech, Rensi had the petitions read to the king. The peasant's goods were restored, and Nemtynakht's property was given to him.
lesson: Officials owe a fair hearing to people with no power at all. And if you are the one being wronged, keep stating your case clearly and persistently, because persistence is sometimes what finally gets justice done.
people: Khunanup, the high steward Rensi, Nemtynakht, King Nebkaure
source: The Tale of the Eloquent Peasant, Middle Kingdom Egyptian text (Berlin papyri)

title: Abraham and the Three Strangers
text:
Abraham was sitting at the entrance of his tent by the oaks of Mamre in the heat of the day when he looked up and saw three men standing nearby. He did not wait for them to approach. He ran from the tent to meet them, bowed to the ground and begged them not to pass by. "Let a little water be brought so you can wash your feet and rest under the tree," he said, "and I will fetch a bite of bread so you can refresh yourselves."

The bite of bread turned into a feast. Abraham hurried into the tent and told Sarah to quickly knead fine flour and bake cakes. He ran to the herd himself, chose a tender calf and gave it to a servant to prepare. Then he set curds, milk and the meat before his guests and stood near them under the tree while they ate.

"Where is your wife Sarah?" they asked. "In the tent." Then one of them said, "I will surely return to you about this time next year, and Sarah your wife will have a son." Sarah, listening at the tent door, laughed to herself, because she and Abraham were very old. The visitor asked why she had laughed, and whether anything was too hard for the Lord.

The guests, Genesis makes clear, were messengers of God. A year later Sarah gave birth to Isaac.
lesson: Welcome people warmly and generously before you know who they are or what they can do for you. Hospitality reveals character.
people: Abraham, Sarah, three visitors

title: Jacob and Esau Reconcile
text:
Twenty years earlier, Jacob had cheated his twin brother Esau twice: first buying his birthright for a bowl of stew, then tricking their blind father Isaac into giving him the blessing meant for Esau. Esau swore he would kill him, and Jacob fled to his uncle Laban in Haran.

Now Jacob was coming home with wives, children and flocks, and messengers brought word that Esau was coming to meet him with four hundred men. Jacob was terrified. He divided his household into two camps, prayed, and sent ahead wave after wave of gifts: goats, sheep, camels, cows and donkeys, hundreds of animals, with servants instructed to tell Esau they were a present from his servant Jacob.

That night, alone by the ford of the Jabbok, Jacob wrestled with a mysterious man until dawn and came away limping, with a new name, Israel.

In the morning he saw Esau approaching. Jacob went ahead of his family and bowed to the ground seven times as he approached his brother. But Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, threw his arms around his neck and kissed him, and they wept. Esau at first refused the gifts: "I have enough, my brother." Jacob pressed him, saying that seeing his face was like seeing the face of God, now that Esau had received him so kindly. Esau accepted, and the two brothers parted in peace.
lesson: Old wrongs between siblings can be healed if one comes humbly and the other chooses generosity. Make the first move, even if you are afraid.
people: Jacob, Esau
source: Genesis 25, 27 and 32 to 33

title: Joseph Forgives His Brothers
text:
Jacob loved his son Joseph more than his other sons and gave him a richly ornamented robe. Joseph told his brothers about dreams in which they bowed down to him. They hated him for it. One day, far from home, they seized him, threw him into a dry pit, and sold him to traders bound for Egypt. They dipped his robe in goat's blood and let their father believe a wild animal had killed him.

In Egypt, Joseph was a slave, then a prisoner, and finally, after interpreting Pharaoh's dreams, governor of the whole land, in charge of storing grain for a coming famine.

When the famine struck, his brothers came to Egypt to buy grain and bowed before him. They did not recognize him. Joseph tested them: he accused them of spying, kept one brother hostage, and demanded they bring the youngest, Benjamin. When they returned with him, Joseph had his silver cup hidden in Benjamin's sack and declared that Benjamin would be his slave. Judah stepped forward and begged to be taken instead, because losing Benjamin would kill their father.

Joseph could no longer control himself. He sent everyone else out and wept so loudly the Egyptians heard. "I am Joseph," he said. He told them not to be distressed or angry with themselves: God had sent him ahead to save lives. He kissed his brothers and wept over them, and sent for his father Jacob to come to Egypt.
lesson: Forgiveness can follow even deep betrayal, especially when it meets real change in those who did wrong. Look for the change before you test, and then let the test end.
people: Joseph, his brothers, Judah, Benjamin, Jacob
source: Genesis 37 to 45

title: Joseph and the Seven Years of Plenty
text:
Pharaoh had two dreams in one night. In the first, seven fat, healthy cows came up out of the Nile, followed by seven gaunt, ugly cows, which ate the fat ones. In the second, seven full ears of grain grew on one stalk, and then seven thin ears, scorched by the east wind, swallowed them up. None of Egypt's wise men could explain the dreams.

Then Pharaoh's chief cupbearer remembered a young Hebrew he had met in prison, who had correctly explained his own dream. Joseph was brought out, shaved and dressed, and stood before Pharaoh. It was not in him, he said, but God would give Pharaoh an answer. The two dreams were one: seven years of great plenty were coming to Egypt, followed by seven years of famine so severe that the plenty would be forgotten.

Then he gave advice. Pharaoh should appoint a wise and discerning man over the land, set officials to collect a fifth of the harvest during the good years, and store the grain in the cities as a reserve for the famine.

Pharaoh put Joseph himself in charge. For seven years he gathered grain until it was like the sand of the sea and they stopped measuring it. When the famine came and spread across all lands, there was bread in Egypt, and people from every country came there to buy grain.
lesson: Good years are when you prepare for bad ones. Set aside a fixed share in times of plenty, before you need it, because when the famine comes, it is too late to start saving.
people: Joseph, Pharaoh, the chief cupbearer
source: Genesis 41
caveat: The story belongs to the patriarchal narratives of Genesis, whose historicity is not established by outside evidence.

title: The Egyptian-Hittite Peace Treaty
text:
Around 1274 BC the armies of Ramesses II of Egypt and the Hittite king Muwatalli II fought a great chariot battle at Kadesh, in Syria. Ramesses was nearly destroyed in an ambush and fought his way out. Both kings claimed victory, and Ramesses covered temple walls with his version. In fact neither side had won, and the struggle for Syria dragged on for years.

About sixteen years later, around 1259 BC, Ramesses II and the Hittite king Hattusili III, Muwatalli's brother, concluded a formal peace treaty. It is one of the earliest peace treaties whose text survives from both sides. The Egyptian version was carved in hieroglyphs on temple walls at Karnak and the Ramesseum in Thebes. The Hittite version, written in Akkadian, the diplomatic language of the time, was found on clay tablets in the Hittite capital, Hattusa.

The two kings promised never to attack each other, to come to each other's aid against foreign enemies and rebels, and to hand back fugitives, with a clause requiring that returned fugitives not be punished. Both versions call on the gods of both lands as witnesses.

The peace held for the rest of the Hittite empire's existence. The royal families exchanged letters, and Ramesses later married a Hittite princess. A copy of the treaty is displayed at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
lesson: When neither side can win, the strongest move may be to make the stalemate official and turn a rival into a partner. Both sides can claim honor in peace.
people: Ramesses II, Hattusili III, Muwatalli II
source: The Egyptian text at Karnak and the Ramesseum; the Akkadian tablets from Hattusa
caveat: The exact dates depend on the chronology used for the reign of Ramesses II.

title: Aaron and Hur Hold Up Moses' Arms
text:
In the Book of Exodus, soon after the Israelites left Egypt, the people of Amalek attacked them at Rephidim. Moses told Joshua to choose men and go out to fight. He himself would stand on top of the hill with the staff of God in his hand.

The next day Joshua led the fighting in the valley, and Moses climbed the hill with his brother Aaron and with Hur. As long as Moses held up his hands, Israel prevailed. Whenever he lowered them, Amalek prevailed.

But as the hours went on, Moses' arms grew heavy. He could not keep them raised. So Aaron and Hur took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it. Then they stood on either side of him, one on one side and one on the other, and held up his hands. His hands stayed steady until the sun went down.

In the valley below, Joshua's men defeated Amalek.
lesson: Even the strongest leader tires, and no one can hold the line alone all day. Good teammates notice when someone is flagging and quietly hold up their arms.
people: Moses, Aaron, Hur, Joshua
source: Exodus 17:8-13

title: Jethro Advises Moses to Delegate
text:
After the Israelites left Egypt, Moses' father-in-law Jethro, a priest of Midian, came to visit him in the wilderness, bringing Moses' wife and sons. The two men greeted each other warmly, and Moses told him everything that had happened.

The next day Jethro watched Moses at work. Moses sat to judge the people, and they stood around him from morning until evening, waiting for him to settle their disputes and tell them God's laws. Jethro asked him why he sat alone with everyone standing around him all day. Moses explained that the people came to him to inquire of God and to have their cases decided.

Jethro told him plainly that what he was doing was not good. He would surely wear himself out, and the people with him. The task was too heavy for one man. He advised Moses to keep the role of teaching the law and bringing the hardest matters before God, but to choose capable men who feared God, were trustworthy and hated bribes, and appoint them over groups of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens. They would judge the small cases and bring only the great ones to Moses.

Moses listened and did everything Jethro said. Then Jethro went home to his own country.
lesson: If everything must pass through you, you have become the bottleneck. Choose trustworthy people, give them real authority, and keep for yourself only the decisions only you can make.
people: Moses, Jethro
source: Hebrew Bible, Exodus 18

title: Moses and the Runaway Young Goat
text:
Before he led Israel out of Egypt, Moses was a shepherd in Midian, tending the flock of his father-in-law Jethro. The rabbis tell what happened one day in the wilderness.

A young goat broke away from the flock and ran off. Moses went after it. It ran until it came to a shaded spot where there was a pool of water, and there it stopped and began to drink.

When Moses caught up, he understood. "I did not know you were running because you were thirsty," he said. "You must be tired." He lifted the little animal onto his shoulders and carried it back to the flock.

The midrash says that God then declared: "You have shown such compassion in leading the flock of a mere mortal. By your life, you shall shepherd My flock, Israel." Soon afterward, Moses came upon the burning bush.
lesson: When someone strays or falls behind, find out why before you judge. How you treat the weakest member of a group is the best evidence of whether you can be trusted with the whole.
people: Moses
source: Exodus Rabbah 2:2
caveat: The midrash speaks of a young goat (kid), though popular retellings often make it a lamb.

title: Nachshon Enters the Sea
text:
The book of Exodus tells how the Israelites, fleeing Egypt, were trapped between the sea and Pharaoh's approaching army, and how the waters parted before them. The rabbis of the Talmud asked a question the Bible does not answer: who went into the water first?

Rabbi Meir taught that the tribes competed for the honor and the tribe of Benjamin jumped in first. Rabbi Yehuda told it differently. Each tribe, he said, held back and said it would not be the first to go into the sea. Then Nachshon, the son of Aminadav and prince of the tribe of Judah, stepped forward and walked into the water, and his tribe followed him.

At that moment, in Rabbi Yehuda's telling, Moses was standing in long prayer. God told him that this was no time for long prayers, while His beloved ones were drowning in the sea. Later midrashic tradition adds that Nachshon kept walking until the water reached his nose, and only then did the sea split.

The Talmud says that because of this act, the tribe of Judah was given royal leadership in Israel.
lesson: Some situations will not change until someone commits before the way is clear. Leadership often means being the first to step in while everyone else waits to see what happens.
people: Nachshon ben Aminadav, the tribe of Judah, Moses
source: Babylonian Talmud, Sotah 36b to 37a; Mekhilta de-Rabbi Ishmael, Beshallach
caveat: This is a rabbinic legend that expands the biblical account, and the rabbis themselves recorded competing versions.

title: The People Bring More Than Enough
text:
In the Book of Exodus, after the Israelites camped at Mount Sinai, Moses told them that a sanctuary was to be built, a portable tent of meeting called the tabernacle. He did not order a tax. He asked everyone whose heart moved them to bring an offering.

The people came. Men and women brought gold earrings and rings and brooches, silver and bronze, blue and purple and scarlet yarn, fine linen, goat hair, ram skins, acacia wood, oil, spices and precious stones. Women who were skilled spun yarn with their own hands. Others spun goat hair. The leaders brought onyx and gems for the priest's garments.

Moses appointed Bezalel and Oholiab, master craftsmen, to lead the work, along with every skilled person who was willing. Each morning the people kept bringing more gifts.

After a while the craftsmen left their tasks and came to Moses. The people are bringing much more than enough, they said, more than the work requires. So Moses had a message carried through the camp: no man or woman should make anything more as an offering. And the people were restrained from bringing any more, because what they had brought was already more than enough to finish the work.
lesson: People give generously to a shared project when they are invited rather than ordered. Pair willing contributors with skilled leaders and know when to say you have enough.
people: Moses, Bezalel, Oholiab, the Israelites
source: Exodus 35:4 to 36:7

title: Gilgamesh and Enkidu
text:
Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, was two parts god and one part man, and he was a tyrant. He wore out the young men of the city and took what he wanted, and the people cried out to the gods. So the gods made a match for him: Enkidu, a wild man who lived among the animals on the steppe. Through the woman Shamhat, Enkidu learned to eat bread, drink beer and live among people, and he came to Uruk.

When Gilgamesh came to enter a wedding house, Enkidu blocked the door with his foot. The two grappled like bulls, smashing the doorposts and shaking the walls. At last Gilgamesh threw him, and as his anger cooled, the two became the closest of friends.

Together they went to the Cedar Forest and killed its guardian Humbaba, and back in Uruk they slew the Bull of Heaven. But the gods decreed that one of them must die for these deeds, and it was Enkidu. He fell ill and died after twelve days.

Gilgamesh refused to let him be buried. He wept over him for seven days and seven nights, until a worm fell from his friend's nose. Then, terrified of death, he put on a lion skin and wandered the wilderness, searching for a way to live forever.
lesson: A real friend can turn rivalry into partnership and change who you are. Value such people while they are with you, because their loss reshapes your life.
people: Gilgamesh, Enkidu, Shamhat
source: Epic of Gilgamesh, Standard Babylonian version, Tablets I to X

title: The Tale of Two Brothers
text:
Two brothers lived together in ancient Egypt. Anpu, the elder, had a house and a wife. Bata, the younger, lived with them and worked the fields and the cattle, and the story says there was no one as strong in all the land.

One day Anpu's wife tried to seduce Bata. He refused, angry, and promised to say nothing of it. But she, afraid, made herself look as if she had been beaten and told her husband that Bata had attacked her. Anpu sharpened his spear and hid behind the stable door to kill his brother when he came home.

The cows warned Bata. He fled, and the sun god placed a stretch of water full of crocodiles between the brothers. Across it, Bata told Anpu the truth and swore a terrible oath of innocence. Anpu believed him and wept, but Bata would not come back. He went to the distant Valley of the Cedar, telling Anpu that if his beer ever foamed, it would mean Bata was in danger. Anpu went home and killed his wife.

Years later Anpu's beer foamed. He set out at once, searched for years, found his brother's heart and brought him back to life. In the end Bata became king of Egypt, and Anpu succeeded him.
lesson: A false accusation inside a family can do damage that takes years to repair. Listen to both sides before acting in anger, and be ready to do hard work to make it right.
people: Anpu (Anubis), Bata
source: The Tale of Two Brothers, Papyrus D'Orbiney (British Museum EA 10183), 19th Dynasty

title: Gideon's Three Hundred
text:
The Midianites and their allies had been raiding Israel for years, and now their vast army lay camped in the valley of Jezreel. Gideon gathered thirty two thousand men against them. But, the book of Judges says, God told him the army was too large: if they won, Israel would boast that it had saved itself.

So Gideon announced that anyone who was afraid could go home. Twenty two thousand left. Ten thousand remained, still too many. Gideon led them down to the water to drink. Most knelt and put their faces to the water. Three hundred scooped up water with their hands and lapped it. Those three hundred he kept, and he sent the rest home.

That night Gideon crept down to the edge of the enemy camp with his servant Purah and overheard a soldier telling a dream about a loaf of barley bread that tumbled into the camp and knocked a tent flat. His comrade said it could only mean Gideon's sword.

Gideon divided his men into three companies and gave each man a ram's horn trumpet and an empty jar with a torch hidden inside. In the middle of the night they surrounded the camp. At his signal they blew the horns, smashed the jars, held up the blazing torches and shouted. In the dark and confusion, the Midianites turned their swords on each other and fled.
lesson: A smaller, committed team can beat a larger one when it chooses the moment, uses surprise and makes the enemy's own size and confusion work against it.
people: Gideon, Purah, the Midianites
date: ancient Israelite tradition, set c. 12th century BC
source: Judges 7
caveat: The account is from the book of Judges, whose stories are not independently attested.

title: Jotham's Fable of the Trees
text:
Abimelech, a son of the judge Gideon, wanted to rule over Shechem. With money from the local temple he hired men, went to his father's house and killed his brothers, seventy of them, on a single stone. Only the youngest, Jotham, escaped by hiding. The citizens of Shechem then made Abimelech king.

When Jotham heard, he climbed to the top of Mount Gerizim above the town and called down a fable. Once the trees went out to anoint a king. They asked the olive tree, but it said it would not give up its oil, which honored gods and men, just to sway over the trees. They asked the fig tree, which would not leave its sweet fruit, and the vine, which would not leave the wine that cheered gods and men. Finally they asked the bramble. The bramble accepted and said: come and take shelter in my shade, and if not, let fire come out of the bramble and burn up the cedars of Lebanon.

Jotham told the Shechemites that if they had acted in good faith, they could rejoice in their king, and if not, fire would come from Abimelech and consume them. Then he fled. Three years later Abimelech and Shechem turned on each other, he destroyed the town, and he died besieging another.
lesson: When capable people refuse responsibility because they are comfortable, it often falls to whoever wants it most. Ask who is eager for power and why, and do not leave the field to them.
people: Jotham, Abimelech, the citizens of Shechem
source: Hebrew Bible, Judges 9:1-57

title: Ruth and Naomi
text:
During a famine in the days of the judges, Elimelech of Bethlehem took his wife Naomi and their two sons to the land of Moab. There the sons married Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. Then Elimelech died, and about ten years later both sons died too. Naomi was left with no husband and no children, only two foreign daughters-in-law.

When she heard that there was food again in Judah, she set out for home and urged the young women to go back to their mothers' houses and find new husbands. Orpah kissed her and went. But Ruth clung to her. "Where you go, I will go; where you lodge, I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried."

The two widows reached Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest. Ruth went out to glean the leftover grain behind the reapers, and by chance came to the field of Boaz, a relative of Elimelech. He had heard of her loyalty to Naomi and told his workers to let extra grain fall for her.

Guided by Naomi, Ruth asked Boaz to act as the family redeemer. He did so properly before the elders at the town gate, and married her. They had a son, Obed, and the women of Bethlehem placed the baby in Naomi's lap, saying that Ruth was better to her than seven sons. Obed became the grandfather of King David.
lesson: Family can be made by loyalty as well as by blood. Standing by an in-law in hard times can create bonds as deep as any.
people: Ruth, Naomi, Orpah, Boaz
date: ancient Israelite tradition (period of the judges)
source: Book of Ruth 1 to 4

title: David and Jonathan
text:
After the young shepherd David killed Goliath, Jonathan, the son of King Saul and heir to the throne, loved him as his own soul. He made a covenant with David and gave him his own robe, his armor, his sword, his bow and his belt.

But as David's fame grew, Saul grew jealous and began trying to kill him. Jonathan spoke up for his friend and for a time persuaded his father to relent. When the danger returned, David hid in the countryside, and the two friends agreed on a signal. At the feast of the New Moon Jonathan would test his father's mood, then go out to the field where David was hiding and shoot arrows. If he called to the boy fetching them that they were beyond him, David must flee.

At the feast Saul noticed David's empty seat, and when Jonathan defended him, the king raged that as long as David lived, Jonathan would never be king. He even hurled his spear at his own son. The next morning Jonathan went to the field and shot the arrows, crying out that they were beyond the boy. Then he sent the boy home.

David came out of hiding. The two friends kissed each other and wept together, David most of all. "Go in peace," Jonathan told him, "for we have both sworn friendship in the name of the Lord."
lesson: A true friend wants good things for you even when your success costs him something. Be loyal in ways that are inconvenient, not only in ways that are easy.
people: David, Jonathan, Saul
source: 1 Samuel 18 to 20

title: David Spares Saul in the Cave
text:
King Saul, jealous of the young warrior David, was hunting him to kill him. With three thousand chosen men, Saul pursued David into the wild country around En Gedi, near the Dead Sea. On the way, Saul went alone into a cave to relieve himself. He did not know that David and his men were hiding deep in the same cave.

David's men whispered that this was the day God had promised: his enemy had been delivered into his hand. David crept forward and quietly cut off the corner of Saul's robe. Even that troubled his conscience. He told his men that God forbid he should lift his hand against the Lord's anointed, and he would not let them attack Saul.

Saul left the cave and went on his way. David came out after him and called: "My lord the king!" When Saul looked back, David bowed to the ground and held up the piece of the robe. Today, he said, you have seen that the Lord put you into my hand in the cave, and I would not harm you. Let the Lord judge between us.

Saul wept aloud. "Is that your voice, my son David?" he said. "You are more righteous than I. You have repaid me with good, while I have repaid you with evil." Saul went home, and David and his men went back up to their stronghold.
lesson: Having the power to strike a rival is not the same as having the right. Restraint at that moment shows others what kind of leader you will be, and can disarm an enemy better than force.
people: David, Saul, David's men
location: En Gedi, near the Dead Sea (modern Israel)
source: Hebrew Bible, 1 Samuel 24

title: David and Goliath
text:
The armies of Israel and the Philistines faced each other across the valley of Elah. Every morning and evening for forty days, a Philistine champion named Goliath came out and challenged Israel to send a man to fight him in single combat. He was a giant, armored in bronze from head to foot, with a spear whose shaft was like a weaver's beam. No Israelite dared face him.

David, a young shepherd, had come to the camp only to bring food to his older brothers. He heard the challenge and offered to fight. King Saul doubted him: he was just a boy. David replied that he had protected his father's sheep from lions and bears and killed them.

Saul dressed David in his own armor and gave him his sword. David took a few steps and took them off again. He was not used to them. Instead he went down to the stream, picked out five smooth stones, put them in his shepherd's bag, and walked out with his staff and his sling.

Goliath scorned the boy. David ran toward him, put a stone in the sling and let it fly. It struck the giant in the forehead and sank in, and Goliath fell face down. David ran over, took Goliath's own sword and killed him with it. When the Philistines saw their champion was dead, they fled.
lesson: Do not fight a stronger opponent on his terms or in borrowed armor. Use the skills you have actually practiced, at the distance where they work.
people: David, Goliath, King Saul
date: ancient Israelite tradition, set c. 1000 BC
source: 1 Samuel 17
caveat: Another verse, 2 Samuel 21:19, credits a man named Elhanan with killing Goliath, and scholars debate the history behind the story.

title: David Pours Out the Water from Bethlehem
text:
During the wars with the Philistines, David was at his stronghold near the cave of Adullam, while a Philistine garrison held his home town of Bethlehem and their army was camped in the valley of Rephaim. It was harvest time.

David, homesick and thirsty, spoke a wish aloud: "Oh, that someone would give me a drink of water from the well of Bethlehem, which is by the gate!" It was not an order, only a longing.

Three of his mighty warriors heard him. They broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well by Bethlehem's gate, and carried it back to David.

David would not drink it. Instead he poured it out on the ground as an offering to the Lord. "Far be it from me, O Lord, that I should do this," he said. "Is this not the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?" And he refused to drink it.
lesson: People will sometimes take real risks just to please you. Treat their effort as precious, and never enjoy a privilege that others have paid for with danger as if it were your due.
people: David, his three mighty men
source: Hebrew Bible, 2 Samuel 23:13-17; also 1 Chronicles 11:15-19

title: The Tower of Babel
text:
The Book of Genesis says that after the great flood, the whole earth had one language and one way of speaking. As people moved east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there.

They said to one another: come, let us make bricks and bake them hard. They used brick instead of stone and bitumen for mortar. Then they said: let us build ourselves a city, and a tower with its top in the heavens, and make a name for ourselves, so that we will not be scattered over the face of the whole earth. And they set to work together.

The Lord came down to see the city and the tower. The text has him observe that they were one people with one language, and that this was only the beginning of what they would do. Nothing they planned would now be impossible for them. So the Lord confused their language, so that they could no longer understand one another's speech.

Unable to understand each other, they stopped building the city. The Lord scattered them from there over all the earth, which was exactly what they had feared. The city was called Babel, the text explains, because there the language of the whole earth was confused.
lesson: A shared language is one of a group's greatest powers. When people stop understanding each other, even a great common project falls apart and the group scatters.
people: The builders of Babel
source: Genesis 11:1-9

title: Nathan's Parable of the Ewe Lamb
text:
King David had taken Bathsheba, the wife of his soldier Uriah, and when she became pregnant he arranged for Uriah to be killed in battle. Then he married her. No one dared to confront the king.

The prophet Nathan came to David with what sounded like a legal case. There were two men in a city, he said, one rich and one poor. The rich man had a great many flocks and herds. The poor man had nothing but one little ewe lamb that he had bought and raised. It grew up with his children, ate from his plate, drank from his cup and slept in his arms. It was like a daughter to him. When a traveler came to visit the rich man, he did not want to take an animal from his own flocks, so he took the poor man's lamb and cooked it for his guest.

David burned with anger. He swore that the man who had done this deserved to die, and that he must repay the lamb four times over, because he had done it without pity.

Nathan said to David: "You are the man." He went on to name what David had done to Uriah. David answered: "I have sinned against the Lord."
lesson: It is easy to see injustice in others and hard to see it in yourself, especially when no one can challenge you. If you have power, value the people who find a way to show you your own conduct.
people: Nathan, King David, Bathsheba, Uriah
source: Hebrew Bible, 2 Samuel 11 to 12:14

title: Solomon Asks for Wisdom
text:
Early in his reign, young King Solomon went to Gibeon, the great high place, and offered a thousand burnt offerings there. That night God appeared to him in a dream and said: "Ask what I shall give you."

Solomon began by remembering the kindness God had shown his father David. Then he spoke about himself. He was king in his father's place, he said, but he was only a little child who did not know how to go out or come in. He was in the middle of a great people, too many to be counted. So he asked for one thing: an understanding heart to judge the people and to tell good from bad. Otherwise, he asked, who could govern so great a people?

The request pleased God. Because Solomon had not asked for long life, or riches, or the death of his enemies, but for understanding to do justice, he would receive a wise and discerning heart, greater than anyone's before or after him. And he would also receive what he had not asked for: riches and honor beyond any other king of his time.

Solomon woke and knew it had been a dream. He returned to Jerusalem, stood before the Ark of the Covenant, offered sacrifices, and held a feast for all his servants.
lesson: When you take on responsibility for others, admit what you do not know and ask first for the ability to do the job well. Status and rewards tend to follow competence, not the reverse.
people: Solomon
source: Hebrew Bible, 1 Kings 3:3-15

title: The Judgment of Solomon
text:
Two women came before King Solomon with a baby. They lived together in the same house, and each had given birth to a son, three days apart. There had been no one else in the house.

The first woman told the king what had happened. During the night, the other woman's baby had died, because she had lain on him in her sleep. She had then got up at midnight, taken the first woman's living son from beside her, and put her dead child in his place. In the morning, when the first woman went to nurse her baby, she found him dead, but looking closely, she saw it was not her son. The second woman insisted it was a lie: the living child was hers. They argued back and forth in front of the king.

Solomon called for a sword. When it was brought, he gave his order: cut the living child in two, and give half to one woman and half to the other.

At once the real mother, overwhelmed with love for her son, cried out to the king to give the baby to the other woman, and not to kill him. The other woman said: let him be neither mine nor yours. Cut him in two.

The king then ruled: give the living baby to the first woman. Do not kill him. She is his mother. When all Israel heard the verdict, they held the king in awe.
lesson: When stories conflict and evidence is missing, design a choice that only the honest party would make. How people react under pressure reveals what they truly want.
people: King Solomon, two mothers
date: ancient Israelite tradition, set c. 10th century BC
caveat: The story is part of the biblical account of Solomon and is not independently attested.

title: Rehoboam Rejects the Elders
text:
When King Solomon died, his son Rehoboam went to Shechem, where all Israel had gathered to make him king. The people, led by Jeroboam, came to him with a request. Solomon had laid a heavy yoke on them with taxes and forced labor. If Rehoboam lightened it, they would serve him. He told them to come back in three days.

First he consulted the elders who had served his father. They advised him: if today you will be a servant to this people and answer them with kind words, they will be your servants forever.

Then he consulted the young men he had grown up with. They told him to answer: "My little finger is thicker than my father's loins. My father laid a heavy yoke on you, and I will add to it. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions."

Rehoboam followed the young men's advice and said exactly that. The people answered: "What share do we have in David? To your tents, O Israel!" When Rehoboam sent his official in charge of forced labor to them, they stoned him to death, and the king had to flee to Jerusalem in his chariot. Ten of the tribes made Jeroboam their king, and the kingdom was never united again.
lesson: When people ask you for relief, a show of toughness may feel strong but can break the very loyalty you rely on. Listen to experienced advisers, not just to the ones who tell you what you want to hear.
people: Rehoboam, the elders, the young advisers, Jeroboam, Adoram
source: Hebrew Bible, 1 Kings 12:1-20

title: Achilles and Priam
text:
Achilles had killed Hector, the greatest warrior of Troy, to avenge his friend Patroclus. For days he dragged Hector's body behind his chariot around Patroclus's tomb. The gods protected the body from decay, and at last Zeus sent word that Achilles must give it back.

Old King Priam, Hector's father, set out at night with a wagon of treasure for the ransom. Guided by the god Hermes, he passed unseen through the Greek camp and walked into Achilles's hut. He fell at Achilles's knees and kissed his hands, the terrible hands that had killed so many of his sons.

"Remember your own father," Priam said, "an old man like me." He told Achilles that he had done what no man on earth had done before: kissed the hands of the man who killed his son.

The words moved Achilles. He took the old man's hand, and the two of them wept together, Priam for Hector, Achilles for his father and for Patroclus. Then Achilles lifted Priam up, had Hector's body washed and wrapped, and himself laid it on the wagon. They ate together and looked at each other in wonder. Achilles promised a truce of eleven days for Hector's funeral, and the Iliad ends with the burial of Hector, tamer of horses.
lesson: Shared grief can break through even deep hostility. When you are in conflict, remember that the other side has fathers, sons and losses too.
people: Achilles, Priam, Hermes
source: Homer, Iliad, Book 24

title: Diomedes and Glaucus Exchange Armor
text:
In the middle of a battle before Troy, the Greek hero Diomedes found himself facing Glaucus, a leader of the Lycians fighting for the Trojans. Before attacking, Diomedes asked who he was, in case he might be a god.

Glaucus answered with a famous reflection: the generations of men are like leaves, scattered on the ground by the wind and growing again in spring. Then he told his family history. His grandfather was the hero Bellerophon, who had come to Lycia, killed the Chimera, and married a king's daughter.

When Diomedes heard the name, he was delighted. He drove his spear into the earth. His own grandfather Oeneus, he said, had once welcomed Bellerophon as a guest for twenty days, and the two had exchanged gifts of friendship. That made Glaucus and Diomedes guest friends by inheritance. There were plenty of other enemies to fight, he said, so they should avoid each other in battle, and exchange armor so that everyone could see their bond.

They leapt from their chariots, clasped hands and pledged friendship. Then they swapped armor. Homer notes wryly that Zeus must have taken away Glaucus's wits, for he gave gold armor worth a hundred oxen for bronze worth nine.
lesson: Old bonds of friendship and hospitality deserve to be honored even when circumstances put you on opposite sides. Look for what connects you before you fight.
people: Diomedes, Glaucus
source: Homer, Iliad, Book 6

title: Hector's Farewell to Andromache
text:
During the Trojan War, Hector, Troy's greatest warrior, came back from the battlefield into the city. He looked for his wife Andromache at home, but she had gone to the walls with their baby son Astyanax to watch the fighting. He found her near the Scaean Gate.

She took his hand and pleaded with him. Achilles had killed her father and her seven brothers, she said; her mother was dead too. Hector was now father, mother, brother and husband to her. She begged him to stay on the walls and not make her a widow and their son an orphan.

Hector answered that he would be ashamed before the Trojans if he hung back like a coward. He knew in his heart that Troy would fall, and what grieved him most was not his own death but the thought of her being led away as a slave.

He reached out for his son. But the baby shrank back, crying, frightened by the bronze helmet and its nodding horsehair crest. Hector and Andromache both laughed. Hector took off the helmet and set it on the ground, kissed his son and rocked him in his arms, and prayed that the boy would one day be greater than his father. Then he handed him back to his wife, who smiled through her tears, and went out to the war.
lesson: Duty can pull us away from the people we love, but in the moments we have, take off the helmet. Children need to see the person, not the armor.
people: Hector, Andromache, Astyanax
source: Homer, Iliad, Book 6

title: The Wrath of Achilles
text:
In the tenth year of the siege of Troy, Chryses, a priest of Apollo, came to the Greek camp with a rich ransom for his daughter Chryseis, whom Agamemnon, the commander in chief, had taken as a prize of war. Agamemnon sent him away with insults. Apollo answered his priest's prayer with a plague, and for nine days the funeral pyres burned.

Achilles, the greatest of the Greek warriors, called an assembly. The seer Calchas revealed the cause, and Agamemnon was forced to give the girl back. But he would not go without a prize while others kept theirs. He announced that he would take Briseis, the woman Achilles had been awarded by the army.

Achilles was so enraged that he began to draw his sword, and only the goddess Athena, seizing him by the hair, held him back. Instead he swore that the Greeks would one day long for him when they were falling in hundreds before Hector, and he withdrew to his ships with his men. Agamemnon's heralds took Briseis from his tent.

Achilles then asked his mother, the sea goddess Thetis, to persuade Zeus to give the Trojans victory until the Greeks honored him. Zeus agreed. In the fighting that followed, the Greeks were driven back to their ships, and Achilles' dearest friend Patroclus was killed.
lesson: Insulting your best people to protect your own pride can cost far more than the prize you keep. When you are wrong in front of everyone, give way gracefully instead of making someone else pay.
people: Agamemnon, Achilles, Chryses, Calchas, Briseis
source: Homer, Iliad, Book 1

title: My Name Is Nobody
text:
On his way home from Troy, Odysseus and twelve of his men entered a huge cave full of cheeses and lambs. Its owner, the one eyed giant Polyphemus, came home with his flocks, rolled an enormous stone across the entrance, and ate two of the men for supper. Odysseus wanted to kill him as he slept, but realized that they could never move the stone themselves. They would die trapped inside.

So he made a plan. His men sharpened a long stake of olive wood and hardened its point in the fire. Odysseus offered the giant strong wine he had brought, and Polyphemus drank bowl after bowl. He asked the stranger's name. Odysseus told him it was Nobody. The giant promised, as a favor, to eat Nobody last, and fell into a drunken sleep. The men heated the stake and drove it into his eye.

Polyphemus roared for help, and the other Cyclopes came to the cave and asked who was hurting him. Nobody is killing me, he cried. Then nothing is wrong, they said, and went away. In the morning the men escaped by clinging under the bellies of his sheep as he let them out to graze.

But once safely on the ship, Odysseus could not resist shouting back his real name. The blinded giant prayed to his father, Poseidon, and the rest of Odysseus's journey home became years of disaster.
lesson: Plan around the obstacle you cannot move, not just the enemy in front of you. And once you have won, resist the urge to boast; it can hand your enemy the means to strike back.
people: Odysseus, Polyphemus, Odysseus's men
source: Homer, Odyssey, Book 9

title: Odysseus and the Sirens
text:
Before Odysseus left her island, the goddess Circe warned him about the Sirens. They sat in a meadow by the sea, surrounded by the bones of men, and sang so beautifully that any sailor who heard them steered toward them and never came home.

Odysseus made a plan. As the ship approached, he softened beeswax and pressed it into the ears of each of his men, so they could hear nothing. Then he had them tie him upright to the mast, hand and foot, so that he alone would hear the song. He gave them strict orders: if he begged or commanded to be set free, they must tie him tighter.

The wind dropped and the crew rowed toward the island. The Sirens saw the ship and began to sing. They called to Odysseus by name and promised him knowledge of everything that had happened at Troy and everything that happens on the earth.

Odysseus longed to go to them. He frowned and nodded at his men to untie him. Instead, two of them, Perimedes and Eurylochus, rose and bound him with more ropes, and the others rowed harder. Only when the song had faded behind them did the men take the wax out of their ears and untie their captain.
lesson: If you know a temptation will overpower your judgment in the moment, decide in advance and make it hard for your future self to give in.
people: Odysseus, his crew, the Sirens, Circe
source: Homer, Odyssey, Book 12

title: The Trojan Horse
text:
For ten years the Greeks besieged Troy and could not take it. At last, on the advice of Odysseus, the craftsman Epeius built an enormous wooden horse. The best Greek warriors climbed inside it, and the rest of the army burned their camp and sailed away, though only as far as a nearby island, where they hid.

In the morning the Trojans found the beach empty and the great horse standing on it. Virgil's Aeneid tells how they argued over what to do. The priest Laocoon warned them that he feared the Greeks even when they brought gifts, and threw a spear into the horse's side. Then a Greek named Sinon, who had stayed behind on purpose, let himself be captured and told a convincing story: the horse was an offering to the goddess Athena, built so huge that the Trojans could not bring it into their city and win her favor. When two great serpents rose from the sea and killed Laocoon and his sons, the Trojans took it as a sign.

They pulled down part of their own walls to drag the horse inside and spent the night celebrating. While the city slept, Sinon let the warriors out. They opened the gates to the returning Greek army, and Troy was taken and burned.
lesson: When a direct assault fails for years, change the question from how to break in to how to be invited in. And be wary of gifts that require you to open your walls.
people: Odysseus, Epeius, Sinon, Laocoon, the Trojans
source: Homer, Odyssey, Books 4 and 8; Virgil, Aeneid, Book 2
caveat: Homer mentions the horse only briefly; the fuller story of Sinon and Laocoon comes from Virgil and other later poets.

title: When Two Go Together
text:
In Book 10 of Homer's Iliad, the Greeks were in a desperate situation. The Trojans were camped on the plain right next to the Greek ships, their fires burning in the dark, and the Greek leaders could not sleep. Old Nestor asked whether anyone would dare to slip into the Trojan camp at night and find out what the enemy planned.

Diomedes, one of the bravest of the Greeks, volunteered at once. But he said he wanted a companion. When two go together, he explained, one may notice an opportunity before the other, while a man alone thinks less quickly and his judgment is thinner. Many offered to go with him, and he was told to choose whomever he liked. He chose Odysseus, the cleverest of the Greeks, because he was resourceful and the goddess Athena favored him.

The two set out into the darkness. They caught a Trojan scout named Dolon, who was on his way to spy on the Greek ships, and made him tell them where the enemy's newly arrived allies were camped. They found the Thracian king Rhesus asleep with his men. Diomedes did the killing, while Odysseus pulled the bodies aside so the horses would not shy at them. Then they drove the king's famous white horses back to the Greek camp.
lesson: For a hard job, pick a partner who sees what you miss. Two people with complementary strengths notice more and recover faster than one person alone.
people: Diomedes, Odysseus, Nestor, Dolon, Rhesus
location: Ancient Greece (story set at Troy, modern Turkey)
source: Homer, Iliad, Book 10
caveat: Many scholars think Book 10 was added to the Iliad later than the rest of the poem.

title: The Bag of Winds
text:
In Homer's Odyssey, on his long voyage home from Troy, Odysseus came with his twelve ships to the floating island of Aeolus, keeper of the winds. Aeolus treated them kindly for a month, and when they left, he gave Odysseus a remarkable gift: a bag of oxhide, tied shut with a silver cord, in which he had shut up all the stormy winds. Only the gentle West Wind was left free, to blow the ships straight home.

For nine days and nights they sailed, and Odysseus himself held the sail's rope the whole time, trusting it to no one. On the tenth day they came so close to Ithaca that they could see men tending fires on the shore. Then, worn out at last, Odysseus fell asleep.

His crew began to talk. Everywhere their captain went, people gave him treasure, and now this bag. It must be full of gold and silver, and he was keeping it for himself while they came home with nothing. They untied the bag to see.

The winds burst out all at once. A storm tore the ships away from Ithaca and drove them all the way back to Aeolus's island. When Odysseus begged for help again, Aeolus drove him away, saying that a man so hated by the gods would get no more help from him.
lesson: Suspicion inside a team can destroy a success that is almost won. Leaders who keep their crew in the dark invite rumors, and crews that act on rumors can lose everything.
people: Odysseus, Aeolus, Odysseus's crew
source: Homer, Odyssey, Book 10

title: Penelope Tests Odysseus with the Bed
text:
After twenty years away, ten at the war in Troy and ten more wandering, Odysseus came home disguised as a beggar, killed the suitors who had been taking over his house, and revealed himself. But his wife Penelope did not run to him. She sat across the hall, looking at him in silence. Their son Telemachus scolded her for her hard heart. She answered that if this truly was Odysseus, they had their own secret signs.

Odysseus bathed and dressed in fine clothes, and still she held back. So he complained that she must have a heart of iron, and told the old nurse to make him a bed alone.

Then Penelope tested him. She told the nurse to move the great bed out of their bedroom and make it up for him outside.

Odysseus burst out in anger. Who had moved his bed? It could not be moved. He had built it himself: there had been an olive tree growing in the courtyard, and he had built the bedroom around it, cut off the trunk, and shaped the bedpost from the living tree. No one else knew.

At that, Penelope's knees gave way. She ran to him, threw her arms around his neck, and wept, and explained that she had feared being deceived by some impostor.
lesson: A long marriage is built on things only the two partners know and share. Those private foundations are what let trust survive long separations.
people: Penelope, Odysseus, Telemachus, the nurse Eurycleia
source: Homer, Odyssey, Book 23

title: Bao Shuya Understood Guan Zhong
text:
In the 7th century BC, in the state of Qi, two young men named Guan Zhong and Bao Shuya were close friends. Sima Qian preserves Guan Zhong's own memory of that friendship. When they traded together, Guan took the larger share of the profits, and Bao did not call him greedy, because he knew Guan was poor. When Guan's plans failed, Bao did not call him foolish, because he knew timing could be against him. When Guan fled from battle three times, Bao did not call him a coward, because he knew Guan had an old mother to support.

Later the two served rival princes in a struggle for the throne of Qi. Guan Zhong even shot an arrow at Bao's master, Prince Xiaobai, and hit his belt buckle. Xiaobai won and became Duke Huan. Guan was captured and seemed sure to die.

Instead Bao Shuya urged the duke to make Guan Zhong his chief minister, and took the lower place himself. Under Guan's government Qi became the leading power among the states. Guan Zhong said: "My parents gave me life, but it is Bao who understood me." The phrase "the friendship of Guan and Bao" is still used in Chinese for a true friendship.
lesson: Judge a friend by his circumstances and his abilities, not by his worst moments. Speaking up for someone's talent, even at your own expense, can change his life.
people: Guan Zhong, Bao Shuya, Duke Huan of Qi
source: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), chapter 62, Biographies of Guan Zhong and Yan Ying

title: Satyakama and His Mother's Truth
text:
A boy named Satyakama wanted to become a student of the Vedas. A student had to give the name of his family line, so he asked his mother, Jabala, what his lineage was.

She told him honestly that she did not know. When she was young, she said, she had worked as a servant and moved about a great deal, and she had conceived him then. All she could tell him was that her name was Jabala and his was Satyakama. He should simply call himself Satyakama Jabala.

The boy went to the teacher Haridrumata Gautama and asked to be accepted. When Gautama asked about his family, Satyakama repeated exactly what his mother had said, without hiding anything.

Gautama answered that no one but a true brahmin could speak so plainly. "Bring the firewood, my son. I will initiate you, because you have not departed from the truth." He then gave the boy four hundred thin, weak cows and sent him off to tend them. Satyakama vowed not to return until they had become a thousand. He spent years in the wilderness, and by the time he came back with the herd, the Upanishad says, his face shone with knowledge.
lesson: Honesty about awkward family facts is a strength, not a shame. A child who can tell the truth plainly has learned what matters most.
people: Satyakama, his mother Jabala, the teacher Haridrumata Gautama
source: Chandogya Upanishad 4.4 to 4.9

title: Uddalaka and the Salt in the Water
text:
Shvetaketu, son of the sage Uddalaka Aruni, went away to study at the age of twelve. He came home at twenty four, having learned all the Vedas, and he was conceited, sure of his learning and proud of himself.

His father asked him whether he had learned the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard and the unknown becomes known. Shvetaketu had to admit that his teachers had never taught him that. So his father began to teach him, not with lectures but with simple tasks.

One evening he told his son to put a lump of salt into a pot of water and bring it back in the morning. In the morning he said, "Bring me the salt." Shvetaketu felt around in the water but could not find it; it had dissolved.

"Sip from the top," his father said. "How does it taste?" "Salty." "Sip from the middle." "Salty." "Sip from the bottom." "Salty." The salt was everywhere in the water, though it could not be seen.

In the same way, Uddalaka explained, there is a subtle essence in everything that cannot be seen but is present throughout. "That is the truth. That is the self. And you are that, Shvetaketu."
lesson: A proud learner rarely accepts correction in words. Let them discover the gap for themselves with something they can see and taste.
people: Uddalaka Aruni, his son Shvetaketu
source: Chandogya Upanishad 6.1 and 6.13

title: Duke Mu Gives Wine to the Horse Thieves
text:
Duke Mu of Qin ruled in the 7th century BC in what is now western China. According to the Lushi Chunqiu, compiled in the 3rd century BC, one day some of his fine horses broke loose and wandered off. Local country people at the foot of Mount Qi caught them and ate them, about three hundred men in all.

The duke's officials arrested them and expected them to be executed. Duke Mu said a gentleman should not harm people for the sake of an animal. He added that he had heard eating horse meat without drinking wine was bad for the health, so he gave the men wine to drink and let them go.

Some years later, in 645 BC, Qin went to war with the state of Jin at Han. In the battle Duke Mu was surrounded, his chariot was in danger and he was wounded. Suddenly a band of about three hundred men burst through the Jin ranks and fought fiercely to rescue him. They were the men who had eaten his horses. Qin won the battle and captured the ruler of Jin. Sima Qian tells the same story in his Records of the Grand Historian.
lesson: Generosity toward small offenders costs little and is often remembered. Those you treat kindly when you have the power to punish may stand by you when you need them most.
people: Duke Mu of Qin
source: Lushi Chunqiu, book 8; Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), Basic Annals of Qin
caveat: The story is a traditional anecdote whose details, like the number of men, may be embellished.

title: The King of Chu and the Torn Hat Tassels
text:
King Zhuang of Chu, who ruled from 613 to 591 BC, once gave a banquet for his officers that went on into the night. According to the Han dynasty collection Shuo Yuan, compiled by Liu Xiang, a gust of wind blew out the candles. In the darkness one of the guests, drunk, tugged at the clothing of the king's favored lady.

She snatched the tassel off the man's hat and told the king. If he had the lamps relit, she said, he could find the offender by his broken hat and punish him.

The king refused. He had given the men wine, he said, and it was his own fault if they behaved badly when drunk. How could he shame a loyal officer to display a woman's virtue? Before the lights came back, he ordered every guest to tear the tassels off their hats so that all were alike. Then the party went on happily.

Some years later Chu fought the state of Jin. One officer kept charging at the front of the army, fighting with reckless courage until the enemy broke. The king asked why he had risked his life so readily. The man answered that he was the one whose tassel had been torn off that night.
lesson: Sparing someone public humiliation for a small, foolish mistake can earn their devotion for life. Shame rarely improves people; quiet mercy often does.
people: King Zhuang of Chu
source: Liu Xiang, Shuo Yuan (Garden of Stories), chapter Fu En (Returning Kindness)
caveat: The story is a traditional moral anecdote and cannot be confirmed by earlier records.

title: Demeter and Persephone
text:
Persephone, daughter of Demeter the goddess of grain, was picking flowers in a meadow with her friends when she reached for a wonderful narcissus. At that moment the earth split open, and Hades, lord of the dead, rose in a golden chariot and carried her off to the underworld. Zeus, her father, had agreed to it without telling her mother.

Demeter heard her daughter's cry and searched the earth for nine days, carrying torches and refusing to eat or bathe. When she learned the truth from the Sun, she abandoned Olympus in anger. Disguised as an old woman, she went to Eleusis, where she served as nursemaid in a royal household.

Then she made the earth barren. Seed would not sprout and the fields produced nothing. People began to starve, and the gods received no offerings. Zeus sent one god after another to persuade her, but she refused to let anything grow until she saw her daughter again.

At last Zeus sent Hermes to bring Persephone back. Before she left, Hades gave her a pomegranate seed to eat. Mother and daughter were reunited with great joy. But because she had eaten food of the dead, Persephone had to return below for a third of every year. When she comes up again, the fields grow green and the earth flowers.
lesson: When a family must share a child between two homes, the arrangement may be painful but can still let everyone live. Grief and reunion can take turns.
people: Demeter, Persephone, Hades, Zeus, Hermes
source: Homeric Hymn to Demeter

title: Solon Leaves Athens for Ten Years
text:
Around 594 BC Athens was close to civil war. Poor farmers were sinking into debt and many had been enslaved for it, while the wealthy held the land and power. The Athenians gave Solon, a poet and merchant trusted by both sides, special authority to reform the city.

Solon cancelled debts secured on people's freedom, banned enslavement for debt, freed those who had been sold, reorganized the political classes by wealth instead of birth, and wrote a new code of laws. Neither side got everything it wanted. Many urged him to make himself tyrant, and he refused.

Then, according to Herodotus, he did something unusual. The Athenians had sworn to keep his laws for ten years, and Solon left the city for ten years, saying he wanted to see the world. Herodotus says the real reason was to avoid being forced to repeal any of the laws he had made. Plutarch adds that people were pestering him every day with complaints and requests to explain or change his laws, and that he left to let them stand on their own.

He traveled to Egypt, Cyprus and, according to tradition, Lydia, before returning to Athens.
lesson: If you build a system, let it work without you. Stepping away can be the best way to show that rules, not people, are in charge.
people: Solon
source: Herodotus, Histories, Book 1, chapter 29; Plutarch, Life of Solon, chapters 15 to 26

title: Thales Corners the Olive Presses
text:
Thales of Miletus, often called the first Greek philosopher, lived in the 6th century BC. Aristotle, in his Politics, tells a story about him that was already old in Aristotle's time.

People mocked Thales for his poverty, saying it proved that philosophy was useless. According to the story, Thales used his knowledge of the heavens to foresee, while it was still winter, that the coming olive harvest would be exceptionally large. With the little money he had, he paid small deposits to rent all the olive presses in Miletus and on the island of Chios. Because it was winter and no one else was bidding, he got them cheaply.

When harvest time came, everyone suddenly needed presses at once. Thales controlled them all and rented them out on whatever terms he chose. He made a large sum of money. Aristotle says Thales thus showed that it is easy for philosophers to become rich if they want to, but that wealth is not what they care about.

Aristotle himself adds a dry comment: the method was not really a matter of special wisdom but a general principle of making money, which is to create a monopoly. Some cities, he notes, used the same trick when they needed funds.
lesson: Foresight pays most when you act on it early and cheaply, before others see what you see. Secure your position while it costs little.
people: Thales of Miletus
source: Aristotle, Politics 1.11 (1259a)
caveat: Aristotle presents it as a traditional story about Thales, so it may be legend.

title: Cleobis and Biton Pull Their Mother's Cart
text:
Herodotus tells how Solon, the wise lawgiver of Athens, visited Croesus, the fabulously rich king of Lydia. Croesus showed him his treasures and asked who was the happiest man Solon had ever seen, expecting to hear his own name. Solon first named an Athenian, Tellus, who had lived well and died bravely for his city. Croesus then asked who came second. Solon named two young men of Argos, the brothers Cleobis and Biton.

They were strong young men, both winners of athletic prizes. On the day of the festival of Hera, their mother had to be taken to the goddess's temple by ox cart (later writers say she was Hera's priestess). The oxen had not come back from the fields in time. So the brothers put themselves under the yoke and pulled the cart, with their mother on it, about forty-five stades, some eight kilometers, all the way to the temple.

The crowd at the festival praised them, the men for their strength and the women for the mother who had such sons. Overjoyed, the mother stood before the statue of Hera and prayed that the goddess would give her sons the best thing that can happen to a human being. After the sacrifice and the feast, the young men lay down to sleep in the temple and never woke up.

The Argives, Herodotus says, made statues of them and dedicated them at Delphi as men who had been the best of men.
lesson: Devotion to our parents is a form of greatness that ordinary people recognize at once. A good life is measured by its love and honor, not its wealth.
people: Cleobis, Biton, their mother (Cydippe in later sources), Solon, Croesus
source: Herodotus, Histories 1.31
caveat: Herodotus presents the tale as told by Solon; it is a legend, and the conversation between Solon and Croesus is chronologically doubtful.

title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
text:
All through the long summer the ants worked. They carried grains of wheat and barley from the threshing floors, one by one, and stored them in their nest under the ground. It was slow, hot, dull work, and they kept at it every day while the fields were full.

The grasshopper watched them and laughed. Why toil in such fine weather? He spent his days in the grass, singing and enjoying the sun, and he told the ants they were wasting the best part of the year.

Then autumn passed and winter came. Snow covered the fields, and there was nothing left to eat. The grasshopper, weak with hunger, came to the ants' door and begged them for a little of the grain they had dried and stored.

The ants asked him what he had been doing all summer, when he could have gathered food for himself. He told them he had been too busy singing. Then, the ants answered, since he had sung all summer, he could dance all winter. They shut the door, and the grasshopper went away hungry into the cold.
lesson: Good times do not last, so use them to build reserves. The effort you put in while things are easy is what carries you through the season when they are not.
people: An ant, a grasshopper
source: Aesop's Fables

title: The Ass and the Lapdog
text:
A farmer kept an ass and a little lapdog. The ass lived in the stable, had plenty of hay and oats, and worked hard: he turned the mill, carried wood from the forest, and hauled loads from the fields. The lapdog lived in the house. He knew clever tricks, sat on his master's knee, and whenever the master dined out, he came home with a treat for his dog.

The ass watched all this and grew bitter. Why should that useless little animal be petted while he did all the work? He decided that if he behaved like the lapdog, he would be loved the same way.

One day he broke his halter and galloped into the house. He kicked up his heels and tried to jump around his master just as he had seen the dog do. He smashed the table and the dishes, and then he tried to climb onto his master's lap. The servants, hearing the shouts, rushed in with sticks, beat the ass soundly, and drove him back to the stable, where he lay bruised and sore.
lesson: Every role on a team has its value and its costs. Copying someone else's role out of envy usually means doing it badly and losing respect for the one you had.
people: An ass, a lapdog, their master
source: Aesop's Fables, The Ass and the Lapdog

title: The Ass and His Purchaser
text:
A man who wanted to buy a donkey went to the market and found one he liked. Before paying, he asked the seller whether he could take the animal home for a short trial, and the seller agreed.

At home the man led the new donkey into his yard, where his own donkeys were standing, and let it go to see what it would do. The newcomer looked around at all of them. Then it walked past the strong, steady workers and went to stand right beside the laziest and greediest donkey in the yard, the one that did the least work and ate the most.

The man did not wait to see any more. He put a halter on the donkey, led it straight back to the market and handed it to the seller.

The seller was surprised. "Surely you have not tested him properly in so short a time," he said. "I do not need any more of a test," replied the man. "I can see what sort of animal he is from the companion he chose for himself."
lesson: The people you choose to spend your time with shape you and tell others who you are. Choose companions you would be glad to resemble.
people: A buyer, an ass
source: Aesop's Fables

title: The Ass Carrying the Image
text:
A donkey was given an important job. It was to carry a famous wooden statue of a god through the streets of a city to the temple where the image would be installed.

As the procession passed, crowds lined the streets. People bowed low, knelt and pressed their hands together in reverence. The donkey looked around and drew its own conclusion: all this respect was for him. He lifted his head, swelled with importance and soon decided that a creature so honored should not have to keep walking. He planted his hooves and refused to take another step.

The driver did not share his view. He brought the stick down hard on the donkey's back and told him plainly that people had not yet started worshipping donkeys. The bows were for the god he was carrying. The donkey, sore and corrected, went on to the temple.
lesson: When people defer to you because of your position, the respect belongs to the role, not to you. Keep carrying the load, and you will be less surprised on the day the role passes to someone else.
people: A donkey, its driver, the crowd
source: Aesop's Fables

title: The Bear and the Two Travelers
text:
Two men were traveling together along a forest road, and they had promised each other to stand together whatever danger they met. Suddenly a bear came out of the trees in front of them.

One of the men was quick and light. Without a word to his companion he ran to the nearest tree, scrambled up into the branches and hid there. The other man was too slow to follow. Seeing that he could neither escape nor fight, he threw himself flat on the ground, held his breath and lay as still as a corpse, because he had heard that bears will not touch a dead body.

The bear came up, sniffed at him, put its muzzle to his ear and nosed around his face. The man did not move. After a while the bear decided he was dead and lumbered off into the forest.

When it was safe, the first man climbed down and asked with a laugh what the bear had whispered in his ear. "It gave me some good advice," said his companion. "It told me never again to travel with a friend who deserts you at the first sign of danger."
lesson: Watch how people act when trouble comes, not what they promise in good times. Choose friends whose loyalty has been tested, and be that kind of friend yourself.
people: Two travelers, a bear
source: Aesop's Fables (Perry Index 65)

title: The Boy and the Filberts
text:
A boy found a jar full of filberts, the sweet hazelnuts he loved, and pushed his hand down through its narrow neck to take some.

He did not want just a few. He closed his fist around as many nuts as his hand could possibly hold and began to pull it out. But his fist, stuffed with nuts, was now much wider than the neck of the jar, and his hand would not come through.

He pulled and twisted and shook the jar. Nothing worked. He was not willing to let go of a single nut, and he could not get his hand out while he held them all. At last he burst into tears, stuck fast and furious at his bad luck.

A man who had been watching came over and gave him some simple advice. If the boy would be content with half as many nuts, he said, his hand would come out easily, and he could always reach in again for more.

The boy let go of half, slid his hand free, and had his nuts after all.
lesson: When you are stuck, check whether you are trying to grab too much at once. Taking a smaller piece now and coming back for the rest often works better.
people: A boy, a bystander
source: Aesop's Fables

title: The Boy Who Cried Wolf
text:
A shepherd boy watched the village sheep on a hillside not far from the houses. The days were long and dull, and one afternoon, to amuse himself, he ran toward the village shouting, "Wolf! Wolf! A wolf is after the sheep!"

The villagers dropped their work and rushed up the hill with sticks and pitchforks. There was no wolf. The boy laughed at their worried faces, and they went back down grumbling. A few days later he did it again, and again the villagers came running, and again they found only the boy laughing.

Then one evening a wolf really did come out of the forest and fell upon the flock. The boy ran toward the village and screamed, "Wolf! Wolf! Please come, it is real this time!" The villagers heard him, but they shook their heads and went on with their work. They were not going to be fooled a third time.

Nobody came. The wolf killed sheep after sheep at its leisure, and in some versions of the tale it also ate the boy.
lesson: Every lie spends trust, and trust is slow to rebuild. Be truthful in small things so that people believe you when it matters.
people: Shepherd boy, villagers
source: Aesop's Fables (Perry Index 210)

title: The Bundle of Sticks
text:
An old farmer had several sons who could not stop quarreling. They argued over the work, over the land and over every small slight, and nothing he said made any difference. He had pleaded with them and scolded them, and still the house was full of their bickering.

One day he told them to bring him a bundle of sticks, tied tightly together. He handed it to the eldest and asked him to break it. The young man strained until his face went red, but the bundle would not give. Each brother tried in turn, and each one failed.

Then the father untied the cord and gave every son a single stick. They snapped them easily, almost without effort.

"You see," he said, "as long as you stand together, no enemy can harm you. But if you are divided among yourselves, you will be broken as easily as these sticks."
lesson: Family members who stand together can weather almost anything. Divided by petty quarrels, each of them becomes easy to break.
people: An old father, his quarreling sons
source: Aesop's Fables (Perry 53)

title: The Cock, the Dog and the Fox
text:
A dog and a cock were good friends, and they decided to travel together. When night fell they were in a thick wood. The cock flew up and perched on a high branch, and the dog curled up to sleep in the hollow at the foot of the same tree.

At dawn the cock crowed as he always did. A fox heard him and came running, already thinking of breakfast. He stood under the branch and called up in his sweetest voice. What a magnificent singer, he said. He longed to meet the owner of such a voice. Would the cock please come down so they could become friends?

The cock saw through him. He answered that he would be delighted, but first the fox should go around to the trunk and wake the porter, who would open the door to let him in.

The fox, pleased, went to the hollow and called out. The dog sprang out at once, seized him, and that was the end of the fox.
lesson: Know what your partners can do and use it. A threat to one member can be met by another member whose strengths fit it better.
people: A cock, a dog, a fox
source: Aesop's Fables, The Dog, the Cock and the Fox

title: The Crab and Its Mother
text:
A mother crab was watching her young one scuttle across the wet sand. It moved the way all crabs move, sideways, dragging its legs at an angle and twisting its body as it went.

"Why do you walk so crookedly, child?" she said. "It is far more becoming to walk straight ahead. Hold yourself properly and go forward like a respectable creature."
