The young crab stopped and looked at her. "I would be glad to, Mother," it said. "Just show me how. Walk straight in front of me, and I promise I will follow your steps exactly."

The mother crab set out to demonstrate. She lifted one leg and then another, pushed forward, and found herself sliding off sideways just as her child had done. She tried again and again, and every time the result was the same.

In the end she gave up, and said nothing more to her child about the way it walked.
lesson: Children copy what we do far more than what we say. Before correcting a habit in them, check whether they learned it from you.
people: A mother crab, her child
source: Aesop's Fables (Perry 322)

title: The Crow and the Pitcher
text:
In a dry season a crow was nearly dying of thirst. Flying over the fields, she spotted a pitcher standing on the ground and swooped down to it, hoping for water.

There was water inside, but only a little, lying at the very bottom. The neck of the pitcher was narrow and the water was low, and however far she pushed her head in and stretched her beak, she could not reach it. She tried to tip the pitcher over, but it was too heavy for her to move.

She was close to giving up when she noticed the small pebbles scattered on the ground nearby. She picked one up in her beak and dropped it into the pitcher. Then she brought another, and another. With each stone, the water rose a little.

It was slow work, and she was tired and parched, but she did not stop. Pebble by pebble, the water climbed up the inside of the pitcher, until at last it came within reach of her beak. The crow drank her fill and flew away.
lesson: When force does not work, look at what is lying around you. Patient, small steps applied with a bit of thought can solve a problem that seemed impossible.
people: A crow
source: Aesop's Fables

title: The Dog and Its Reflection
text:
A dog had got hold of a fine piece of meat, perhaps from a butcher's shop, and was carrying it home in his mouth to eat in peace. On the way he had to cross a narrow plank laid over a stream.

Halfway across he glanced down at the water. There below him he saw another dog, holding another piece of meat in its jaws, and to his eyes that piece looked twice as big as his own.

He did not stop to think. He wanted that bigger piece, and he meant to take it. He snarled and snapped at the dog in the water, opening his mouth wide to seize the meat.

As soon as his jaws opened, his own piece of meat fell out, splashed into the stream and was carried away by the current. The other dog vanished too, because it had only ever been his own reflection.

The dog stood dripping on the plank with nothing at all, having lost the real meat while grabbing at a shadow.
lesson: Before you chase something that looks bigger, check that it is real and count what you risk to get it. Grasping for more can cost you what you already hold.
people: A dog
source: Aesop's Fables

title: The Dog in the Manger
text:
A dog was looking for a comfortable place to sleep and found one in the stable, lying in the manger on the soft hay that had been put there for the cattle.

In the evening an ox came in from a long day of work in the fields, tired and hungry, and went to the manger to eat. The dog woke up, jumped to its feet and snarled. Every time the ox came close, the dog barked and snapped at its nose, so that the poor animal could not take a single mouthful.

The dog had no use for the hay. It could not eat it, and it did not even need to sleep there; the stable had other corners. Yet it would not let the ox have what the ox needed.

At last the ox gave up and turned away. "What a spiteful creature," it said. "It cannot eat the hay itself, and it will not let those eat it who can."
lesson: Notice when you are holding on to something only so that someone else cannot have it. Letting go of what you do not need costs you nothing and earns goodwill.
people: Dog, ox
source: Aesop's Fables (Perry Index 702)
caveat: The fable is attributed to Aesop by tradition but appears only in later collections, not in the oldest Greek ones.

title: The Dove and the Ant
text:
On a hot day an ant went down to a spring to drink. As it leaned over the edge, it slipped and fell into the water. The current carried it away, and the little creature struggled hopelessly to keep from drowning.

A dove was sitting on a branch above the stream and saw what was happening. She broke off a leaf with her beak and let it fall onto the water just beside the ant. The ant climbed onto the leaf, floated safely to the bank and crawled out onto dry ground.

Not long afterward a bird catcher came to the spot. He saw the dove resting in the tree and quietly began to set up his snare, or in some versions to raise his limed rods, to catch her. The dove had no idea she was in danger.

But the ant had seen him. It ran up and bit him hard on the foot. The man cried out in pain and jerked, his trap was spoiled, and the noise warned the dove, who flew away to safety.
lesson: Small kindnesses are worth doing even when you expect nothing back. Help travels in both directions, often from people you thought could never return it.
people: Dove, Ant, a fowler
source: Aesop's Fables (Perry Index 235)

title: The Farmer and His Sons
text:
A farmer who knew he was dying worried about his sons. They were idle young men, and he feared that once he was gone they would let the farm go to ruin.

He called them to his bedside. "My sons," he said, "I am about to leave this world. Everything I have to give you is in the vineyard. Search there and you will find it." Then he died without saying more.

Convinced their father had buried a treasure, the sons went out with spades and mattocks. They dug up every corner of the vineyard. They turned the soil row by row, deep and thoroughly, again and again. They found no pot of gold, no hidden chest, nothing at all.

But the vines, with their roots so well loosened and the earth so well worked, produced a harvest richer than any the farm had seen in years. When the sons sold the grapes, they finally understood what their father had left them. The treasure was the work itself.

La Fontaine retold the fable in 1668, with an old ploughman telling his children that a treasure lies hidden in the field.
lesson: The most valuable inheritance is not money but the habit of steady work. Give children reasons to put their hands to something that grows.
people: A dying farmer, his sons
source: Aesop's Fables (Perry 42); Jean de La Fontaine, Fables, Book V, 9 (Le Laboureur et ses Enfants)

title: The Farmer and the Viper
text:
One bitter winter day a farmer was walking home across his frozen fields when he saw a snake lying on the ground, stiff and almost dead from the cold.

He knew perfectly well what kind of snake it was. Even so he felt sorry for it. He picked it up, opened his coat and put it against his chest to warm it with his own body, and carried it home.

As the warmth soaked into the snake, it began to stir. Its strength came back, and with it its nature. It raised its head and bit the man who had saved it.

The farmer knew the bite was fatal. As he sank down he said, "I deserve this, for showing pity to a creature that was wicked from the start."
lesson: Compassion is good, but it is not the same as naive trust. Before you take someone close, look at how they have treated others.
people: Farmer, viper
source: Aesop's Fables (Perry Index 176)

title: The Father and His Two Daughters
text:
A man had two daughters. One had married a gardener, the other a man who made tiles and bricks. Some time after the weddings, the father set out to see how they were getting on.

He went first to the gardener's house. His daughter told him that everything was going well and that she had only one wish: a good heavy rain, so that the plants would be well watered and the crops would thrive.

A little later he visited the daughter married to the tile maker. She, too, said she wanted for nothing. Her one wish was for the dry weather to last, with a hot bright sun, so that the bricks and tiles laid out in the yard would bake hard.

The father went home thinking about the two answers. If one daughter wanted rain and the other wanted sunshine, he said to himself, which of them was he supposed to join in praying for?
lesson: Children who build different lives will want different things. A parent cannot take every side at once, and sometimes the best course is to love both without choosing.
people: A father, a gardener's wife, a potter's wife
source: Aesop's Fables (Perry 299)

title: The Fisherman and the Little Fish
text:
A fisherman who lived on what his nets brought in had a bad day. After hours of work he pulled in his net and found only one fish in it, and a very small one at that.

The little fish gasped and flapped and begged for its life. What use was it to him? It was hardly a mouthful. It was not yet grown. If he would only throw it back into the sea, it would soon grow into a big fish, fit for the tables of rich people. Then he could come back, catch it again, and sell it for a good price.

The fisherman listened and then shook his head. He would be a fool, he said, to give up a gain he had in his hand for the hope of a bigger one that might never come. The sea was wide and the fish might swim anywhere, or be caught by someone else, or never be seen again.

He put the little fish in his basket and took it home.
lesson: Weigh a certain small gain against an uncertain larger one honestly. Promises of more later, especially from someone who wants to escape, are worth less than what is already in your hands.
people: A fisherman, a little fish
source: Aesop's Fables

title: The Four Oxen and the Lion
text:
Four oxen grazed together in the same field. A lion had watched them for a long time and wanted very much to eat them, but whenever he crept close, the oxen turned their tails together and faced outward, so that from every side he met a row of horns. He could not find a way in, and he went away hungry again and again.

The lion changed his method. Instead of attacking, he began to talk. He visited one ox and hinted what the others were saying about him behind his back. He visited the next and did the same. Little by little suspicion grew among the four, until they quarreled and stopped feeding together. Each went off to graze alone in a separate corner of the field.

That was all the lion had been waiting for. He attacked them one at a time, and one at a time, with no horns guarding their backs, they fell to him until none was left.
lesson: A group that stands together is hard to beat, which is why rivals often try to divide it first. Treat whispered stories about your teammates with suspicion.
people: Four oxen, a lion
source: Aesop's Fables, The Lion and the Four Bulls (also The Lion and the Three Bulls); Avianus, Fables

title: The Fox and the Crow
text:
A crow found a piece of cheese, or in older versions a piece of meat, and flew up to a branch to eat it in peace. A fox passing below caught the smell and stopped. He wanted that cheese, and he knew he could not climb the tree to take it.

So he looked up admiringly. "What a beautiful bird," he said. "Such glossy feathers, such a graceful neck, such bright eyes. Surely a bird so handsome must also have a lovely voice. If only I could hear you sing just once, I would know you were the queen of all the birds."

The crow was delighted. Nobody had ever praised her like that, and she wanted to prove the fox right. She lifted her head, opened her beak wide and gave her loudest caw.

The cheese fell straight down. The fox snapped it up before it touched the ground. "Your voice is fine," he said as he trotted away. "What you are missing is sense."
lesson: When someone praises you lavishly, ask what they want from you. Enjoy sincere compliments, but do not let flattery make your decisions.
people: Fox, Crow
source: Aesop's Fables (Perry Index 124); La Fontaine, Fables I.2

title: The Fox and the Goat in the Well
text:
A fox fell into a deep well and could not climb out. The walls were steep and smooth, and he was stuck there, with no idea how he would escape.

After a while a thirsty goat came to the edge of the well and looked down. Seeing the fox, he asked if the water was good. The fox hid his trouble and praised the water to the skies: it was the sweetest he had ever tasted, and the goat should come down and try it for himself.

The goat, thinking only of his thirst, jumped straight in and drank. Then the fox told him the truth: they were both trapped. But he had a plan. If the goat stood up with his front feet against the wall and lowered his horns, the fox would climb up his back, get out, and then pull the goat up after him.

The goat agreed. The fox ran up his back, sprang off his horns and was out of the well in a moment. Then he trotted away. When the goat shouted after him about his promise, the fox called back that if the goat had as much sense as he had beard, he would never have gone down without first seeing how to get up again.
lesson: Before you commit to anything, know your exit. And be wary of anyone who urges you into a situation they are desperate to get out of.
people: A fox, a goat
source: Aesop's Fables

title: The Fox and the Grapes
text:
A hungry fox was trotting along a country road when he saw a vine climbing over a high trellis. From it hung bunches of grapes, dark, ripe and heavy with juice. His mouth watered at the sight.

He backed up, ran and leaped for the nearest bunch, but his jaws snapped shut on empty air a little below it. He tried again, jumping higher, and again he missed. He tried from a different angle, and then from a running start, and then again and again, until he was panting and his legs ached. The grapes still hung just out of reach.

At last he gave up. He sat down, caught his breath, and looked up at the vine with a sniff. Those grapes, he said to himself, were plainly sour. Nobody with any sense would want them. He was glad he had not wasted any more effort on such poor fruit.

Then he put his nose in the air and walked off down the road, telling himself that he had never really wanted them at all.
lesson: When you fail to get something, notice if you suddenly decide it was worthless. Rationalizing a loss feels better, but it stops you from learning why you failed or whether to try another way.
people: A fox
source: Aesop's Fables

title: The Fox and the Stork
text:
A fox and a stork were on friendly terms, and one day the fox invited the stork to dinner. As a joke, he served the meal as a thin soup poured into a wide, shallow dish. The fox lapped it up easily. The stork, with her long narrow beak, could only wet the tip of it and went home as hungry as she had come. The fox said he was sorry she had not enjoyed the soup.

The stork did not complain. A few days later she invited the fox to dine with her in return. When he arrived, hungry and pleased with himself, a delicious smell of food filled the air. But the stork served it in a tall jar with a long, narrow neck.

The stork put her beak into the jar and ate comfortably. The fox could only lick the outside of the jar and sniff at the rim. He had to go home with an empty stomach. He could not even protest, because he knew exactly where the idea had come from.
lesson: The way you treat people is the way you teach them to treat you. A cheap trick played on someone usually comes back to you in the same form.
people: Fox, Stork
source: Aesop's Fables (Perry Index 426); La Fontaine, Fables I.18

title: The Fox Without a Tail
text:
A fox was caught in a trap. He struggled and twisted and finally tore himself free, but he left his fine bushy tail behind in the iron jaws. When he limped home, he realized how ridiculous he looked, and he dreaded the laughter of the other foxes.

So he made a plan. He called all the foxes to a meeting and gave a serious speech. Tails, he told them, were a nuisance. They were heavy, they dragged in the mud, they got caught in brambles, and they gave hounds something to grab. He had lately tried living without one, and he could honestly say he had never felt lighter or freer. He urged them all to cut off their tails at once.

The foxes listened politely. Then an old fox at the back spoke up. If you still had your own tail, he said, I doubt you would be giving us this advice. The meeting ended in laughter, and every fox kept its tail.
lesson: When someone urges the whole group to adopt a change, ask what that person gains from it. Advice that would spread someone's own loss to everyone deserves a second look.
people: A fox, his fellow foxes
source: Aesop's Fables, The Fox Who Had Lost His Tail

title: The Frogs Who Desired a King
text:
The frogs of a quiet pond grew tired of living without a ruler. They sent a delegation to Jupiter and begged him to give them a king. Jupiter, amused by their simplicity, dropped a large log into the water.

The splash sent every frog diving to the bottom in terror. For a long while none dared to look. At last a brave one peeped out and saw that the new king never moved. Soon the frogs swam up to it, climbed onto it, sat on its back and treated it with open contempt. A king who did nothing, they decided, was no king at all, and they went back to Jupiter to demand a real one.

This time Jupiter lost patience. In the version told by the Roman poet Phaedrus he sent them a water snake, and in later retellings a stork. The new ruler was anything but idle. It stalked along the bank and began to seize and eat the frogs one by one. The frogs cried out to Jupiter to take it away, but he refused. They had asked for a king who would act, and now they had one.
lesson: Before you demand a stronger hand in charge, ask what that strength will be used for. A dull but harmless authority can be far better than an energetic and cruel one.
people: The frogs, Jupiter, King Log, King Stork
source: Aesop's Fables; Phaedrus, Fables 1.2

title: The Goose That Laid the Golden Eggs
text:
A poor farmer and his wife owned a goose. One morning the farmer went to the nest and found an egg that was yellow and heavy and glittered in the light. He thought someone was playing a trick on him, but when he took it to be tested, it turned out to be solid gold.

The next morning the goose laid another golden egg, and the next morning another. Each day there was one, and the couple soon began to grow rich. They bought land and fine things and lived better than they ever had.

But as their wealth grew, so did their impatience. One egg a day began to seem too slow. If the goose could make gold, they reasoned, she must be full of it inside. Why wait day after day, when they could have all of it at once?

So they killed the goose and cut her open. Inside they found nothing but an ordinary goose, no different from any other. There was no hoard of gold, and now there would be no more eggs. The couple had destroyed the only thing that had made them rich.
lesson: Protect whatever produces your steady gains, whether it is a business, a relationship or your own health. Squeezing it for everything at once can leave you with nothing.
people: A farmer and his wife, a goose
source: Aesop's Fables

title: The Hawk and the Pigeons
text:
A flock of pigeons lived in fear of a kite. Every so often it swooped on the dovecote and carried one of them off, and the pigeons could find no way to stop it.

At last they had an idea. The hawk was stronger than the kite and could drive it away. They went to the hawk and asked him to be their defender. He agreed at once, with every appearance of goodwill, and they opened the dovecote and invited him in.

The arrangement did keep the kite away. But once the hawk was inside, he began to feed on the pigeons himself, and he was far hungrier and far closer than the kite had ever been. In a single day, the fable says, he killed more of them than the kite had managed to take in a whole year. The pigeons had found their protector, and he was the worst thing that had ever happened to them.
lesson: When you are afraid, be careful whom you invite in to make the fear go away. Judge a protector by what he will do once he is inside, not by the danger he promises to remove.
people: The pigeons, a kite, a hawk
source: Aesop's Fables, The Hawk, the Kite, and the Pigeons

title: The Horse and the Overloaded Ass
text:
A man set out on a journey with a horse and an ass. He put the whole load on the ass, and the horse trotted along carrying nothing at all.

The ass struggled under the weight. After a while he begged the horse to take part of the load. It would be nothing much for you, he said, and it might save my life. The horse refused. The load was not his business, and he had no intention of tiring himself.

The ass staggered on a little farther, then collapsed on the road and died. Their master did not leave the goods behind. He moved the entire load onto the horse, and on top of it he added the skin of the dead ass.

The horse groaned under the burden. Now he understood. He had refused to carry a small share when it was offered, and as a result he was carrying all of it, and the hide of his companion besides.
lesson: Helping a struggling colleague with part of the load is often cheaper than refusing. When one member of a team breaks down, the work falls on those who are left.
people: A horse, an ass, their master
source: Aesop's Fables, The Horse and the Loaded Ass (Perry 181)

title: The Horse and the Stag
text:
Long ago the horse had a meadow all to himself and grazed it freely. Then a stag came along and began to feed in the same pasture, trampling the grass and eating his share.

The horse was furious and wanted revenge, but he could not drive the stag away on his own. So he went to a man and asked for help in punishing the intruder.

The man agreed, on one condition. The horse would have to let him put a bit in his mouth and a saddle on his back, and carry him. Then the man would take his weapons and deal with the stag.

The horse accepted the bargain. The man mounted him, and together they chased the stag out of the pasture. The horse had his revenge.

But when it was over, the man did not take the bit out of the horse's mouth or climb down. He rode him home, tied him in a stable, and kept him working. From that day on the horse was no longer free. To get even with the stag, he had made himself the servant of man.
lesson: Before asking a stronger party to fight your battle, ask what they will want afterward. The price of help can be your independence.
people: A horse, a stag, a man
source: Aesop's Fables

title: Jupiter and the Monkey's Baby
text:
Jupiter, king of the gods, announced a contest among the animals. Every creature was to bring its offspring before his throne, and he would give a prize to the one judged the most beautiful.

The animals came in a long procession: the birds with their chicks, the deer with their fawns, the lions with their cubs. Among them came a monkey, carrying her baby in her arms with all a mother's tenderness. It was a flat-nosed, hairless, scrawny little creature.

When the monkey presented it, the gods burst out laughing. The mother monkey held her child closer and was not in the least embarrassed.

"Jupiter may give the prize to whomever he likes," she said. "But I know that in my own eyes this is the dearest, handsomest and most beautiful of all."
lesson: Every parent sees their own child through love. It is a good thing at home, but remember that others see with different eyes.
people: Jupiter, a monkey mother
source: Aesop's Fables (Perry 364)

title: The Lark and Her Young Ones
text:
A lark built her nest in a field of young wheat in early spring. By summer her chicks were nearly ready to fly, and the wheat around them had ripened.

One day the farmer came with his son to look at the crop. It was time to harvest, he said; he would ask his neighbors to come and help reap it. The young larks heard this and told their mother in alarm. Where should they go? She told them there was no need to move yet. A man who leaves the work to his neighbors is not really in earnest.

A few days later the farmer returned. The grain was overripe and beginning to fall. This time he said he would send for his relatives and friends to help. Again the chicks were frightened, and again their mother calmed them. Relatives and friends have their own fields to see to.

Then the farmer came a third time and saw the crop spoiling. Tomorrow, he said, he and his son would come themselves at dawn, with whatever workers they could hire, and cut the wheat. When the lark heard that, she gathered her young and moved them out that very night. Now, she said, the man meant it.
lesson: To judge whether something will really happen, ask who is actually going to do it. Plans that depend on others are often just talk; plans someone owns get done.
people: A lark, her chicks, a farmer and his son
source: Aesop's Fables
caveat: Versions differ in the number of visits and who the farmer first relies on.

title: The Lion and the Boar
text:
It was a scorching summer day, and every animal was desperate for water. A lion and a boar reached a small spring at exactly the same moment. Neither would let the other drink first. They argued, then charged, and soon they were locked in a savage fight, tearing at each other with claws and tusks.

After a while both were bleeding and exhausted, and they broke apart to catch their breath before going at it again. As they stood panting, they happened to look up. On the rocks and branches around the spring sat a row of vultures, waiting patiently. The birds did not care which one won. They were only waiting to see which would fall first, so they could eat him.

The lion and the boar looked at the vultures and then at each other. They agreed at once to stop. It was better, they said, to be friends than to become food for vultures. Then they drank, side by side.
lesson: Before a dispute with a colleague goes too far, look around at who benefits from the fight. Often it is someone who wants you both weakened.
people: A lion, a boar, vultures
source: Aesop's Fables, The Lion and the Boar

title: The Lion and the Mouse
text:
A lion lay asleep in the shade when a little mouse, running across the ground, scampered over his face and woke him. The lion clapped a huge paw down on the mouse and opened his jaws to swallow it.

The mouse begged for its life. "Let me go," it squeaked, "and one day I may be able to repay you." The lion found the idea so funny that a mouse could ever help the king of beasts that he laughed, lifted his paw and let it run off.

Some time later hunters set a trap in the forest, and the lion walked straight into it. A net of thick ropes dropped over him, and the more he struggled, the tighter it held. His roars of rage and fear echoed through the trees.

The mouse recognized the voice and ran toward it. Finding the lion tangled and helpless, it set to work with its sharp little teeth and gnawed through one rope after another until a hole opened in the net. The lion pushed his way out and went free. "You laughed at me," said the mouse, "but now you know that even a mouse can help a lion."
lesson: Treat people kindly whatever their size or status. You cannot know today who will be the one able to help you tomorrow.
people: Lion, Mouse
source: Aesop's Fables (Perry Index 150)

title: The Lion's Share
text:
A lion once made a hunting partnership with a few weaker animals. In the version Phaedrus tells, they were a cow, a goat and a sheep. They agreed to hunt together and share whatever they caught.

Together they brought down a large stag. The lion took charge of the division and carefully cut the carcass into four parts. Then he explained the arrangement. "The first part is mine because I am called the lion. The second you will grant me because I am brave. The third comes to me because I am the strongest. And as for the fourth, woe to anyone who touches it."

The other animals looked at the four portions, then at the lion's teeth and claws. None of them moved. They had done their share of the running and the work, and they went home with nothing. The lion dragged the whole stag away, and the phrase "the lion's share" has meant the biggest piece, taken by force, ever since.
lesson: Before you join a partnership, look at who will divide the results and what will hold them to the deal. A promise of fairness from someone far stronger than you is only as good as their character.
people: The lion, his hunting partners
source: Aesop's Fables; Phaedrus, Fables 1.5

title: The Mice and the Weasels
text:
The mice and the weasels were at war, and the weasels kept winning. After one defeat too many, the mice held a council and decided that the problem was organization. They had no proper commanders, so they fought as a disorderly crowd.

They chose generals from the most distinguished families and the bravest fighters, and divided the army into troops and regiments. To make sure everyone could tell them apart, the new generals fastened tall decorations to their heads, straws or horns that stood up proudly above the ranks. A herald declared war, and the mice marched out in good order.

The battle went badly almost at once. The ordinary mice turned and ran, and each one darted safely into its hole. The generals ran too, but their splendid headgear would not fit through the narrow openings. They were stuck outside, and the weasels caught and ate every one of them.
lesson: Titles and symbols of rank do not make anyone a leader, and they can become a burden when things go wrong. Invest in what helps the people you lead, not in what makes you stand out.
people: The mice and their generals, the weasels
source: Aesop's Fables; Phaedrus, Fables 4.6

title: The North Wind and the Sun
text:
The North Wind and the Sun once argued about which of them was the stronger. Neither would give way, so they agreed on a test. A traveler was walking along the road below, wrapped in a cloak. Whoever could make him take it off would be the winner.

The North Wind went first. He blew a cold blast that tugged at the cloak and whipped it around the man's legs. The traveler only pulled it tighter. The Wind blew harder and harder, howling and hurling gusts until the trees bent, but the harder he blew, the more firmly the man held his cloak closed and hunched against the cold. At last the Wind gave up.

Then the Sun came out from behind a cloud and simply shone. The air grew mild, and the traveler loosened his grip. The Sun shone a little warmer, and the man opened the cloak. Soon the heat was so pleasant and then so strong that he took the cloak off entirely, and finally, overcome by the heat, he stripped further and went to bathe in a nearby stream.

The Sun had won without any struggle at all.
lesson: Pressure makes people dig in. When you want someone to change, warmth, patience and good reasons usually work far better than force.
people: North Wind, Sun, a traveler
source: Aesop's Fables (Perry Index 46)

title: The Sick Lion and the Fox
text:
A lion had grown old and weak and could no longer hunt by strength. So he decided to hunt by cunning. He went into his cave, lay down, and let it be known throughout the forest that he was very ill.

The other animals felt sorry for him. One after another they came to the cave to pay their respects and ask how he was. Each one went in, and the lion, lying in wait in the dark, seized and ate it. In this way he fed well without ever having to leave his den.

After many animals had gone missing, the fox came by. He did not go in. He stood outside the entrance, at a respectful distance, and politely asked the king how he was feeling.

The lion answered that he was very poorly and invited the fox to step inside so they could talk more comfortably. The fox thanked him but declined. He had noticed, he said, a great many footprints leading into the cave, and not a single one coming out. Then he went on his way.
lesson: Before you accept an invitation, look at the evidence of what happened to those who accepted before you. The track record says more than the host.
people: A lion, a fox
source: Aesop's Fables

title: The Stag at the Pool
text:
On a hot day a stag came to a spring to drink. As he bent his head, he saw his reflection in the still water and stopped to admire it. His antlers were magnificent, tall and wide and branching. He was proud of them.

Then his eyes fell on his legs, and he frowned. They were so thin and spindly, so plain compared with the splendid crown on his head. He wished they were more handsome.

While he stood there admiring and complaining, a lion crept up to the pool and crouched to spring. The stag saw it just in time and bolted. On the open plain his slender legs carried him easily ahead of the lion, and he kept a safe distance as long as the ground was clear.

But then he ran into a wood, and his great antlers caught in the low branches. He twisted and pulled, but he could not free himself. The lion came up and seized him. As he died, the stag cried out that he had despised the legs that would have saved him and taken pride in the antlers that had destroyed him.
lesson: Take a hard look at what you value in yourself or your organization. The plain, useful strengths are often the ones that save you, while the showy ones can trap you.
people: A stag, a lion
source: Aesop's Fables

title: The Swallow and the Other Birds
text:
In spring a swallow saw a farmer sowing seed in a field and recognized it: hemp, or in some versions flax. She gathered the other birds and warned them. That seed, she said, would grow into the plant men twist into cord and weave into the nets they use to catch birds. Now, while it lay on the ground, they should pick up every grain and eat it.

The other birds laughed at her. It was only a few seeds in the dirt, and there was plenty of other food. Why should they bother?

The seed sprouted and the plants came up green. The swallow warned them again: pull up the young shoots now, before it is too late. Again they ignored her.

The crop ripened and was harvested, and from its fibers men made cords and nets. Soon birds that had mocked the swallow were being caught in snares made from that very field. The swallow left the open country and went to live near people's houses, under their eaves, where she was safe. The other birds stayed in the fields and were trapped.
lesson: Small threats are cheapest to deal with when they first appear. Waiting until a danger is fully grown means facing it when it is strongest.
people: A swallow, other birds
source: Aesop's Fables
caveat: Versions differ on the bird and the plant: some give the warning to an owl or name flax instead of hemp.

title: The Thief and His Mother
text:
A schoolboy stole a writing tablet from a classmate and carried it home to his mother. She did not punish him or send him back with it. Instead she praised him for his cleverness.

Encouraged, he next brought home a cloak he had taken, and again she approved. As he grew into a young man his thefts grew with him, from small things to things of real value, until at last he was caught in the act. His hands were bound behind his back and he was led away to be executed.

His mother followed in the crowd, weeping and beating her breast. The young man asked the guards to let him say something to her in private. When she leaned close, he seized her ear in his teeth and bit it hard.

She cried out that he was a monster of a son. He answered that if she had punished him the first time he brought home that stolen tablet, he would never have ended where he was now, being led to a shameful death.
lesson: Small wrongs that a child gets away with become habits. Correcting them early, even when it is unpleasant, is a kindness to the adult they will become.
people: A boy thief, his mother
source: Aesop's Fables (Perry 200)

title: The Tortoise and the Hare
text:
The hare was proud of his speed and liked to mock the tortoise for his short legs and slow, heavy steps. One day the tortoise had heard enough. He laughed and said that, fast as the hare might be, he would beat him in a race.

The hare thought this was the funniest thing he had ever heard and agreed at once. They agreed that the fox should choose the course and set the finishing post.

When the race began, the hare shot off and was out of sight in moments. Looking back and seeing no sign of his rival, he decided there was no hurry. It was warm, the grass was soft, and he lay down by the road for a short rest. Soon he was fast asleep.

The tortoise never stopped. He did not run, because he could not, but he kept putting one foot in front of the other, mile after mile, past the sleeping hare and on toward the post.

When the hare finally woke and dashed for the finish, he was too late. The tortoise was already there, resting comfortably at the end of the course.
lesson: Talent that coasts loses to effort that keeps going. Do not judge a contest by who starts fastest, and never assume a slower rival will stop because you did.
people: A tortoise, a hare
source: Aesop's Fables

title: The Trees and the Axe
text:
A man walked into a forest carrying an axe head with no handle. He went to the trees and asked them politely for a piece of wood to make one. It seemed a small request, and the great trees talked it over and agreed. They chose a young ash tree, one of the least important among them, and gave it to him.

The man shaped the ash into a strong handle and fitted it to his axe. Then he set to work. He did not stop at a sapling or two. Stroke after stroke, he cut down the oldest and noblest trees of the forest, the giants that had stood there for centuries.

As the man moved through the wood, an old oak watched its companions fall. It turned to a cedar standing nearby and said that their first step had ruined them all. If they had stood up for the ash, they might all have stood for ages. By handing over the weakest of their number, they had given the enemy the very tool that brought them down.
lesson: Do not sacrifice a weaker member of your group to buy peace. What you hand over to an opponent can become the tool used against everyone.
people: The trees, a woodsman
source: Aesop's Fables, The Trees and the Axe

title: The Trumpeter Taken Prisoner
text:
In the middle of a battle, a trumpeter who had been sounding the charge and urging his side forward was cut off and captured by the enemy.

He pleaded for his life. He told his captors that he had done them no harm at all. He had not killed a single one of their men. He carried no sword or spear, nothing but his brass trumpet, so it would be unjust to put him to death.

The soldiers were not moved. That, they told him, was exactly why he deserved to die. He might never strike a blow himself, but every time he raised the trumpet to his lips he sent others rushing in to strike for him. A man who stirs up a whole army is more dangerous than any single fighter in it.
lesson: Words that move others to act carry responsibility for what those others do. If you rally people, you own the results of the rally, even if your own hands stay clean.
people: A trumpeter, his captors
source: Aesop's Fables

title: The Two Travelers and the Axe
text:
Two men were walking together along a road. One of them spotted an axe lying in the dust, picked it up, and called out happily, "I have found an axe!"

His companion corrected him. Since they were traveling together, he said, it would be better to say that we have found an axe. The first man shrugged and kept the axe for himself.

They had not gone far when they heard shouting behind them. The owner of the axe had discovered his loss and was running after them with some of his neighbors, looking for the thief. The man holding the axe went pale. "We are lost," he said.

His companion did not move closer. No, he answered, keep to what you said before. You found the axe, so say: I am lost. When the find was good news, you did not want to share it, so do not expect to share the trouble now.
lesson: If you claim the rewards alone, you cannot expect your partners to share the risks. People stand with you in trouble when you stood with them in success.
people: Two travelers
source: Aesop's Fables, The Two Travelers and the Axe

title: The Wolf and the Lamb
text:
A wolf came to drink at a stream and saw a lamb drinking a little way below him. He wanted to eat it, but he also wanted a reason that would make the meal look just.

"Why are you muddying the water I drink?" he growled. The lamb answered gently that this was impossible: the stream flowed from the wolf down to her, so she could not foul his water. The wolf tried again. "Then it was you who insulted me six months ago." The lamb replied that six months ago she had not even been born.

The wolf was not bothered by being proved wrong twice. "If it was not you, it was your father," he said, and he sprang on the lamb and ate her.

The lamb had won every argument. It made no difference, because the wolf had decided what he would do before he opened his mouth, and the accusations were only there to dress up the decision.
lesson: When someone with power keeps changing the charge after each one is answered, the charges are not the real issue. Recognize a pretext early and stop expecting good arguments alone to protect you.
people: The wolf, the lamb
source: Aesop's Fables; Phaedrus, Fables 1.1

title: The Wolves and the Sheep
text:
For a long time the wolves and the sheep had been at war, and the wolves were always losing their prey because of the dogs that guarded the flock. So the wolves sent envoys to the sheep with a proposal for peace.

Why, the wolves asked, should there be all this fear and bloodshed between them? It was the dogs who caused all the trouble. They barked whenever a wolf came near and attacked before any harm had been done. If the sheep would only send the dogs away, the wolves and sheep could live together in friendship.

The sheep listened. They were tired of fear and liked the sound of peace, and the offer seemed reasonable enough. They agreed to the treaty and sent their dogs away.

As soon as the dogs were gone, the wolves came down on the flock. With no one left to defend them, the sheep were torn apart one after another, and the wolves ate as many as they pleased.
lesson: Be very suspicious when an opponent's price for peace is that you give up your defenses. Those who ask you to disarm are often the ones who benefit most.
people: Wolves, sheep, sheepdogs
source: Aesop's Fables

title: Croesus on the Pyre Calls Out Solon's Name
text:
Croesus, king of Lydia, was famous for his wealth. Herodotus says that years earlier the Athenian lawgiver Solon had visited him and refused to call him the happiest of men, saying no one should be called happy until his life had ended well.

Around 546 BC the Persian king Cyrus captured Croesus's capital, Sardis. According to Herodotus, Cyrus had a great pyre built and placed Croesus on it in chains with fourteen Lydian boys. Standing there, Croesus remembered Solon's words and groaned his name three times.

Cyrus had interpreters ask him whom he was calling. At first Croesus would not answer. Then he told the story of Solon's visit. Cyrus, Herodotus says, reflected that he too was a man, about to burn alive another man who had once been as fortunate as himself, and that nothing human is secure. He ordered the fire put out, but it had taken hold. Croesus prayed to Apollo, and a sudden storm quenched the flames.

Cyrus freed him and kept him as an adviser. Croesus's first counsel was to stop the soldiers plundering Sardis, since it was now Cyrus's own city they were looting.
lesson: When you have the upper hand, remember that fortune turns. Treating the defeated as you would want to be treated is both decent and wise.
people: Cyrus the Great, Croesus, Solon
source: Herodotus, Histories, Book 1, chapters 29 to 33 and 86 to 88
caveat: Solon's visit is chronologically unlikely, and other ancient sources give different accounts of Croesus's fate.

title: Sun Tzu Drills the King's Concubines
text:
Sima Qian tells how Sun Wu, known as Sun Tzu, a native of Qi, came to King Helu of Wu with his thirteen chapters on the art of war. The king said he had read them all and asked whether Sun Wu could give a small test of his methods, using women. Sun Wu agreed.

One hundred and eighty women from the palace were brought out. Sun Wu divided them into two companies, put one of the king's two favorite concubines at the head of each, and gave everyone a halberd. He explained the commands carefully: front, back, left and right, signaled by the drum. Then he gave the order to face right. The women burst out laughing.

Sun Wu said that if the orders are not clear, it is the general's fault. He explained them again, several times, and gave the order to face left. Again they laughed. Now, he said, the orders were clear, and if they were not carried out, it was the fault of the officers. He ordered the two captains beheaded. The king, watching from a terrace, sent word begging him to spare them. Sun Wu replied that a general in command does not accept every order of his ruler, and had them executed.

He appointed the next women as captains. This time the drill was carried out perfectly, in silence. The king made him a general.
lesson: Make your expectations unmistakably clear first. Then enforce them consistently, including for people close to power, or the rules mean nothing.
people: Sun Wu (Sun Tzu), King Helu of Wu
source: Sima Qian, Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), chapter 65
caveat: Many historians doubt this story, and even whether Sun Wu existed as Sima Qian describes him.

title: Bo Ya and Zhong Ziqi
text:
Bo Ya was a master of the qin, the Chinese zither. Zhong Ziqi was a woodcutter, or in some versions simply a man of no special rank, who was a gifted listener.

When Bo Ya played with his mind on climbing high mountains, Zhong Ziqi would say, "Wonderful! Towering like Mount Tai!" When Bo Ya's thoughts were on flowing water, Zhong Ziqi would say, "Wonderful! Vast and rolling like the great rivers!" Whatever Bo Ya had in his mind as he played, Zhong Ziqi heard it.

Once, the Liezi says, they were caught by a sudden storm and sheltered under a cliff. Bo Ya, feeling melancholy, took up his instrument and played, first a melody of steady rain, then of crashing mountains. With every piece, Zhong Ziqi understood exactly what he meant. Bo Ya put down his qin and sighed that his friend heard what was in his heart, so that nothing he played could escape him.

When Zhong Ziqi died, Bo Ya broke his qin and cut its strings, and he never played again for the rest of his life. He felt there was no one left in the world worth playing for. From this story Chinese has the word zhiyin, "one who knows the tone", for a true friend.
lesson: A friend who truly understands you is rare and precious. Tell such people what they mean to you, and try to be that kind of listener for others.
people: Bo Ya, Zhong Ziqi
source: Liezi, Chapter 5 (Tang Wen); Lushi Chunqiu, Book 14 (Ben Wei)

title: What Confucius Taught His Own Son
text:
Confucius had one son, Kong Li, known as Boyu. Since Confucius taught many disciples, some of them wondered whether he kept special teachings for his own family. The Analects record what happened when a man named Chen Kang put the question directly.

Chen Kang asked Boyu whether he had heard any lessons from his father different from what the other students heard. Boyu said no. Once, he said, his father was standing alone when Boyu hurried past through the courtyard. Confucius asked whether he had studied the Book of Odes. When Boyu said not yet, his father told him that without the Odes he would have nothing to say in conversation, so Boyu went and studied them. Another day, in the same way, Confucius asked whether he had studied the rites. When Boyu said not yet, his father told him that without the rites he would have no ground to stand on. So he studied the rites. Those two things, Boyu said, were all he had heard.

Chen Kang went away delighted. He had asked about one thing, he said, and learned three: about the Odes, about the rites, and that a gentleman keeps a certain distance from his own son.

Boyu died before his father. Elsewhere the Analects record that Confucius gave him a plain burial, as his means and position allowed.
lesson: Children deserve the same honest teaching as everyone else, not secret favors. Sometimes the most useful thing a parent does is ask a simple question at the right moment.
people: Confucius, Kong Li (Boyu), Chen Kang
source: Confucius, Analects 16.13 and 11.8, trans. James Legge

title: Harsh Government Is Fiercer Than a Tiger
text:
Confucius was traveling past the side of Mount Tai with some of his disciples when he came upon a woman weeping bitterly beside a grave. He listened to her for a while, then sent his disciple Zilu to ask what had happened.

Zilu said to her that she wept like someone who had suffered sorrow upon sorrow. She told him it was so. Some years ago her husband's father had been killed by a tiger in this place. Then her husband had been killed by a tiger. And now her son had died the same way.

Confucius asked why she did not simply leave such a dangerous place. She answered: "Here there is no harsh government."

Confucius turned to his disciples and said: "Remember this, my children. Harsh government is fiercer than a tiger."
lesson: People will put up with real danger to escape constant oppression. If those you manage prefer hardship elsewhere to working under you, look at how you govern before you blame them.
people: Confucius, Zilu, a grieving woman
source: Book of Rites (Liji), Tangong II

title: The Tilting Vessel
text:
Confucius once visited the ancestral temple of Duke Huan of Lu and noticed a strange vessel set at an angle. He asked the temple keeper what it was. The keeper told him it was a vessel kept at the right side of the seat as a warning.

Confucius said he had heard of such vessels: when empty they tilt, when filled halfway they stand upright, and when full they overturn. He told his disciples to pour water into it. They did. Halfway full, it stood straight. When they filled it to the top, it tipped over and spilled. When it was empty, it leaned again.

Confucius sighed and said: "Ah! Is there anything that is full and does not overturn?"

His disciple Zilu asked whether there was a way to hold on to fullness. Confucius said that intelligence should be guarded with an air of simplicity, great achievement with modesty, courage with caution, and wealth with humility. This, he said, is the way to draw water out before the vessel overflows.
lesson: Success is the moment of greatest risk, because it tempts you to keep filling. When things go best, add humility and caution on purpose instead of more ambition.
people: Confucius, Zilu, the temple keeper
source: Xunzi, Chapter 28 (Youzuo)

title: Laolaizi Plays the Child
text:
Laolaizi was a recluse of the state of Chu who, according to tradition, cared for his parents with great devotion. Even when he himself was seventy years old, his parents were still alive, and he worried that seeing their son grown old would remind them of their own age and sadden them.

So he never spoke of being old. He dressed in brightly colored clothes like a little child and played on the floor in front of them, making childish noises to amuse them.

Once, carrying water into the hall for his parents, he slipped and fell. Rather than let them worry that he had hurt himself, or be reminded of his age, he lay on the ground and wailed like a baby, and his parents laughed at the sight.

The story became one of the Twenty Four Filial Exemplars, the collection of tales of devotion to parents that was read and illustrated across China, Korea and Japan for centuries. Pictures of the white-haired man in bright child's clothing, tumbling in front of his parents, were among the most familiar images in the series.
lesson: Caring for elderly parents is not only about meeting needs. It also means protecting their spirits, and sometimes setting aside your own dignity to make them laugh.
people: Laolaizi, his parents
source: Guo Jujing, The Twenty Four Filial Exemplars (Ershisi Xiao), Yuan dynasty; earlier in Liu Xiang's Lienu zhuan
caveat: Laolaizi is a semi-legendary figure and the episode is a traditional tale.

title: Lord Ye Loves Dragons
text:
Lord Ye, a nobleman of the state of She, was famous for his love of dragons. He had dragons carved on his belt hooks and wine vessels and painted on the walls and beams of his house. Everyone knew that no one adored dragons more than he did.

A real dragon in heaven heard about this and was touched. It flew down to visit its admirer. It put its head in through Lord Ye's window and let its tail trail through the hall. When Lord Ye saw it, he turned pale, lost his wits and ran away in terror. What he loved, the story concludes, was not dragons at all but things that looked like dragons.

In the collection where Liu Xiang preserved the tale, it is told by Zizhang, a disciple of Confucius. He had traveled far to visit Duke Ai of Lu, who was known to praise scholars, and had waited seven days without being received. Leaving, he sent the duke this story, saying that the duke loved men who resembled scholars, not real ones.
lesson: Saying you want independent thinkers or bold ideas is easy. Notice how you react when one actually shows up in your office, and whether you welcome it or retreat.
people: Lord Ye (Zigao) of She, Zizhang, Duke Ai of Lu
source: Liu Xiang, Xinxu (New Prefaces), compiled 1st century BC

title: The Belly and the Members
text:
Once the parts of the body held a meeting and made a complaint. The hands worked from morning to night, the feet walked everywhere, the mouth chewed and the teeth ground, and all of it went to the belly, which lay at the center doing nothing but receiving. Why, they asked, should they slave for a lazy master?

So they went on strike. The hands stopped carrying food, the mouth refused to open, and the teeth would not chew. For a day or two the members felt pleased with themselves. Then the hands grew weak, the legs began to shake, and the eyes went dim. The whole body was wasting away, and the members discovered too late that the belly, quiet as it seemed, had been turning their food into the strength that kept every one of them alive.

The Roman historian Livy tells how this fable was put to use. In 494 BC the common people of Rome, angry at the patricians, walked out of the city and camped on a hill. The senate sent Menenius Agrippa, a man the people trusted, and he told them only this story. According to Livy, the comparison worked: the people saw that the city and its classes depended on one another, and talks began that brought them back.
lesson: Before you decide that a quieter part of your team contributes nothing, find out what it actually does. Pulling out of a shared effort usually hurts you too.
people: The belly and the members; Menenius Agrippa
date: c. 6th century BC; told in Rome in 494 BC according to Livy
source: Aesop's Fables, The Belly and the Members; Livy, History of Rome (Ab Urbe Condita) 2.32
caveat: Livy wrote about four centuries after the secession, and the scene with Menenius may be a later embellishment.

title: Gou Jian Tastes the Gall
text:
In 494 BC King Gou Jian of Yue was crushed by King Fu Chai of Wu and trapped with his last troops on Mount Kuaiji. On the advice of his ministers he surrendered, and according to tradition he and his wife went to Wu to serve its king in humiliation before being allowed to return home. Sima Qian himself says little about this captivity.

Back in Yue, Gou Jian did not forget. Sima Qian writes that he hung a gall bladder where he sat and tasted its bitterness before eating or lying down, asking himself whether he had forgotten the shame of Kuaiji. He worked in the fields with his own hands, his wife wove her own cloth, he ate simple food, and he treated the people and talented men generously. With his ministers Fan Li and Wen Zhong he spent years building up the population, the economy and the army, while sending gifts to Wu and appearing loyal.

Fu Chai, meanwhile, turned to wars with northern states and ignored warnings about Yue. When Wu's army was far away, Yue struck. After years of further fighting, in 473 BC Yue besieged the Wu capital. Fu Chai asked for terms, as Gou Jian once had, but was refused, and he killed himself. The later idiom "sleeping on brushwood and tasting gall" became the Chinese expression for enduring hardship to prepare a comeback.
lesson: A defeat need not be the end if you keep the memory sharp and use the years well. Patient, quiet rebuilding can reverse a loss.
people: Gou Jian of Yue, Fu Chai of Wu, Fan Li, Wen Zhong
location: Yue and Wu (modern Zhejiang and Jiangsu, China)
source: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), chapter 41
caveat: The detail of sleeping on brushwood was added in later retellings; Sima Qian mentions only the gall.

title: Confucius and Yan Hui's Rice
text:
Confucius and his disciples were once stranded between the states of Chen and Cai. For seven days they had no cooked food and lived on wild greens. At last his favorite disciple, Yan Hui, managed to obtain some rice and set it to cook.

As the rice was nearly done, Confucius glanced over and saw Yan Hui reach into the pot, take some of the rice with his hand and eat it. Confucius was disappointed, but he pretended not to have seen.

When the rice was ready and Yan Hui brought it to him, Confucius got up and said he had just dreamed of his late father and wanted first to offer some clean rice to the ancestors. Yan Hui answered at once that this was impossible. Some soot had fallen into the pot while it was cooking, he explained. It seemed wrong to throw away the spoiled food, so he had taken out the dirty part and eaten it himself.

Confucius sighed. "We trust our eyes, and yet our eyes are not to be trusted. We rely on our hearts, and yet our hearts are not enough. Remember this, my disciples: it is not easy to know a person."
lesson: Even what you see with your own eyes may not tell you why someone acted. Ask before you conclude, especially about people who have earned your trust.
people: Confucius, Yan Hui
location: Between the states of Chen and Cai (modern Henan, China)
source: Lushi Chunqiu, Book 17 (Ren Shu)
caveat: The hardship in Chen and Cai is historical tradition, but this particular episode appears only in later texts and is likely legendary.

title: Coriolanus Turned Back by His Mother
text:
Gnaeus Marcius, called Coriolanus for his courage at the capture of Corioli, was driven out of Rome by the people he had scorned. According to the tradition preserved by Livy and Plutarch, he went over to the Volscians, Rome's enemies, and led their army to within a few miles of the city. Rome sent envoys, then priests. He sent them all away.

Then the women of Rome went out to his camp. At their head walked his aged mother, with his wife and his small sons. Livy calls the mother Veturia and the wife Volumnia; Plutarch gives the mother the name Volumnia. Coriolanus rushed to embrace his mother, but she stopped him and asked whether she had come to an enemy or to a son, and whether she was a captive in his camp. She told him that if she had never borne a son, Rome would not now be under attack.

The man who had refused every embassy broke down. Plutarch records his answer: "O mother, what have you done to me?" He said she had won a victory that saved Rome and ruined her son. He withdrew the Volscian army. The traditions disagree on his end: some say the Volscians killed him, others that he lived on in exile. Rome, Livy says, built a temple to Fortuna Muliebris, the Fortune of Women, in memory of the day.
lesson: The people who raised us often reach us when no argument can. When someone is set on a destructive course, the voice that matters may be the one closest to home.
people: Gnaeus Marcius Coriolanus, Veturia, Volumnia
source: Livy, History of Rome 2.39 to 2.40; Plutarch, Life of Coriolanus 33 to 36
caveat: The story belongs to Rome's early legendary history, and even the names of the women differ between Livy and Plutarch.

title: Themistocles Turns Silver Into Ships
text:
In the 480s BC the Athenians struck a rich new vein of silver in the state mines at Laurion, in southern Attica. The revenue was large, and the popular plan was to share it out among the citizens, about ten drachmas each.

Herodotus says that Themistocles persuaded the assembly to do something else. Instead of dividing the money, Athens should use it to build two hundred warships. His argument was not about Persia, which seemed distant, but about Aegina, the nearby island with which Athens was then at war and whose navy dominated the local waters. That was an enemy every citizen could see.

The assembly agreed, and the ships were built. A few years later, in 480 BC, Xerxes invaded Greece with a vast army and fleet. Athens had the largest navy among the Greeks, and those triremes formed the core of the fleet that fought at Artemisium and won at Salamis. Herodotus judged that the war with Aegina saved Greece by forcing Athens to become a sea power, and the navy built from the Laurion silver became the base of Athenian power for the rest of the century.
lesson: A windfall is a chance to build lasting strength rather than to spend for comfort today. Frame a long-term investment in terms people can feel now.
people: Themistocles
source: Herodotus, Histories 7.144; Plutarch, Life of Themistocles 4
caveat: Plutarch gives one hundred ships instead of the two hundred in Herodotus.

title: Aristides Writes His Own Name
text:
In classical Athens citizens could vote once a year to send one prominent man into exile for ten years. Each voter scratched a name on a piece of broken pottery, an ostrakon. Around 482 BC the vote turned against Aristides, a statesman so famous for his honesty that he was called "the Just".

Plutarch tells what happened on the day of the vote. An illiterate farmer, who did not know Aristides by sight, handed him his potsherd and asked him to write the name Aristides on it. Surprised, Aristides asked whether Aristides had ever done him any harm. The man said no, he did not even know him, but he was tired of hearing him called the Just everywhere.

Aristides said nothing, wrote his own name on the shard, and gave it back.

He was ostracized. As he left the city, Plutarch says, he prayed that Athens would never face a crisis that would make the people remember him. Two years later, with the Persians invading, Athens recalled its exiles, and Aristides fought at Salamis and commanded the Athenians at Plataea.
lesson: Keep acting honestly even toward people who are working against you. Your integrity is yours to keep, whatever they do.
people: Aristides the Just
source: Plutarch, Life of Aristides, chapter 7

title: Leonidas at Thermopylae
text:
In 480 BC the Persian king Xerxes invaded Greece with an enormous army. A small Greek force of a few thousand men, led by the Spartan king Leonidas with his bodyguard of three hundred Spartans, took position at Thermopylae, a narrow pass between the mountains and the sea.

Herodotus tells how for two days the Greeks held the pass against wave after wave of attacks, including the king's elite troops. Then a local man, Ephialtes, showed the Persians a mountain path that led around behind the Greek position.

When Leonidas learned he was about to be surrounded, he sent most of the allied contingents away. Herodotus says Leonidas stayed with his three hundred Spartans, the seven hundred Thespians who refused to leave, and a contingent of Thebans. Herodotus adds that an oracle had told the Spartans that either Sparta would be destroyed or a Spartan king would die.

On the third day the remaining Greeks fought in the open until they were overwhelmed. Leonidas was killed, and they fought over his body. The Spartans and Thespians died almost to a man; the Thebans, Herodotus says, surrendered. An epitaph later set up there asked the passerby to tell the Spartans that their men lay there, obedient to their orders.
lesson: Standing by a hard commitment, and releasing others who need not share it, can give your example a meaning that lasts for generations.
people: Leonidas I of Sparta, Xerxes, Ephialtes
source: Herodotus, Histories, Book 7, chapters 201 to 228
caveat: Herodotus's figures for the Persian army are impossibly large, and his account of the Thebans' role is disputed.

title: Rivals Themistocles and Aristides Unite at Salamis
text:
Themistocles and Aristides had been the bitterest rivals in Athenian politics. In 482 BC Themistocles' faction had Aristides ostracized, sent into exile for ten years. But when Xerxes invaded Greece in 480, Athens recalled its exiles.

In September the Greek fleet lay at Salamis, and the allied commanders were quarreling over whether to retreat to the Isthmus. Themistocles wanted to fight in the narrow strait. That night the Persian fleet moved to block both ends of the channel.

Herodotus says Aristides crossed from Aegina, slipped past the enemy ships, and called Themistocles out of the council. He told him that they should always be rivals, but now especially, over which of them could do more good for their country. Then he reported that the Greeks were surrounded. Themistocles was delighted: the Persians had done exactly what he had tricked them into doing. He asked Aristides to tell the other commanders himself, since they would not believe Themistocles.

Plutarch adds that Aristides proposed they lay aside their "vain and childish contention" and compete only in saving Greece, and that when a Corinthian sneered that Aristides was silent in council, he replied that he would not be silent if Themistocles were not giving the best advice. In the battle that followed, the Greeks won, and Aristides led a force that cleared the Persians off the islet of Psyttaleia in the strait.
lesson: Rivals can still be teammates. When the stakes are shared, compete only over who contributes more, and back a good idea even when it comes from your opponent.
people: Themistocles, Aristides
source: Herodotus, Histories 8.79 to 8.82 and 8.95; Plutarch, Life of Aristides 8 to 9

title: Themistocles Sends a Secret Message
text:
In September 480 BC the Greek fleet lay at Salamis, near Athens, which the Persians had just burned. Many Greek commanders wanted to sail back to the Isthmus of Corinth to defend the Peloponnese. Themistocles of Athens believed the only chance was to fight in the narrow strait, where the larger Persian fleet could not use its numbers. He was losing the argument.

Herodotus tells how he forced the issue. He slipped out of the council and sent his trusted slave Sicinnus, the tutor of his children, by boat to the Persian camp. Sicinnus told the Persian commanders that Themistocles secretly favored the king, that the Greeks were terrified and about to flee, and that if the Persians attacked now the Greeks would fight each other instead of them.

Xerxes believed it. During the night Persian ships moved to block both exits from the strait. When the Greek captains learned that they were surrounded, the debate was over: they had to fight where they were.

The next day the Persian ships, crowded in the narrows, fouled each other and were badly beaten while Xerxes watched from the shore. Soon after, he withdrew with much of his army to Asia. Herodotus adds that Themistocles later made Sicinnus a citizen of Thespiae and a rich man.
lesson: Choosing the ground of a contest can matter more than the size of the forces. Sometimes you must arrange the situation so that the right decision is the only one left.
people: Themistocles, Sicinnus, Xerxes
source: Herodotus, Histories 8.75 to 8.96; Plutarch, Life of Themistocles 12

title: Esther Goes Before the King
text:
Esther, a young Jewish woman raised by her cousin Mordecai, had become queen to Ahasuerus, king of Persia, without revealing her people. Then the king's chief minister Haman, enraged that Mordecai would not bow to him, obtained a royal decree to destroy all the Jews of the empire on a single day.

Mordecai sent word to Esther that she must go to the king and plead for her people. She answered that anyone who went to the king in the inner court without being summoned was put to death, unless the king held out his golden scepter, and she had not been called for thirty days. Mordecai replied that she should not think she would escape in the palace. If she kept silent, help would come from somewhere else, but she and her family would perish. "And who knows," he added, "whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"

Esther asked all the Jews of Susa to fast for her for three days, as she would. "Then I will go to the king, though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish."

On the third day she stood in the inner court. The king held out the scepter. She invited him and Haman to a banquet, and then to a second. There she revealed who she was and named Haman as the enemy who sought her people's death. The king had Haman hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai.
lesson: A position of access or influence is not only a privilege, it is a responsibility. When those who depend on you are in danger, the comfort of your position is not a reason to stay silent.
people: Esther, Mordecai, Ahasuerus, Haman
date: Ancient Jewish tradition, set in the 5th century BC
source: Hebrew Bible, Book of Esther 3 to 7

title: Fan Li Leaves at the Peak
text:
Fan Li was one of the two chief ministers who helped King Gou Jian of Yue recover from defeat and finally destroy the rival state of Wu in 473 BC. At the moment of triumph he was among the most honored men in the kingdom.

Sima Qian says that Fan Li then decided to leave. He judged that great fame makes a man hard to keep safe, and that Gou Jian was a ruler with whom one could share hardship but not good fortune. He departed by boat with his family and possessions. From abroad he wrote to his colleague Wen Zhong a warning that became proverbial: when the birds are all shot, the good bow is put away; when the cunning hare is dead, the hunting dog is cooked. He urged Wen Zhong to leave too.

Wen Zhong stayed, though he began to stay away from court claiming illness. Before long he was accused of plotting rebellion, and Gou Jian sent him a sword, the signal to kill himself, which he did.

Fan Li, meanwhile, settled in Qi under another name, farmed and traded, and grew rich. Later he moved to Tao, a busy trading center, and as Tao Zhu Gong became so famous for his wealth that his name was a byword for a successful merchant. Sima Qian adds that he gave much of his fortune away and made it again.
lesson: Knowing when to step away is part of strategy. Read the people you serve, and do not assume that what you were valued for in a struggle will protect you after it.
people: Fan Li, Wen Zhong, Gou Jian of Yue
location: Yue (modern Zhejiang), Qi and Tao (modern Shandong), China
source: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), chapters 41 and 129

title: Castor and Pollux Share Immortality
text:
Castor and Polydeuces (Pollux to the Romans) were twin brothers who never left each other's side. But they did not share the same father. Polydeuces was the son of Zeus and immortal. Castor was the son of a mortal man and would one day die.

In a quarrel with two other brothers, Idas and Lynceus, Castor was killed by Idas's spear. Polydeuces chased down the killers; Zeus struck Idas with a thunderbolt. Then Polydeuces returned to find his brother dying.

Weeping, he called out to his father Zeus and asked to die with Castor. Without his brother, he said, life had no honor.

Zeus came to him and gave him a choice. He could live forever on Olympus among the gods, untouched by age or death. Or he could share his immortality with his brother: half their days they would spend beneath the earth, and half in the golden homes of heaven.

Polydeuces did not hesitate. He chose to share. Zeus opened the eyes of Castor, who had been dead, and freed his voice. From then on, according to Pindar, the two brothers alternate between the world below and the home of the gods, never apart.
lesson: Loyalty between siblings can mean choosing to share losses as well as gifts. What is given up for a brother or sister is rarely regretted.
people: Castor, Polydeuces (Pollux), Zeus, Idas, Lynceus
source: Pindar, Nemean Ode 10

title: Cincinnatus Returns to His Plow
text:
In 458 BC, according to the Roman historian Livy, a Roman army under the consul Minucius was trapped by the Aequi in a mountain valley. The Senate decided the city needed a dictator, a temporary ruler with near-absolute power, and chose Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus, a former consul who was then working a small farm of about four acres across the Tiber.

Livy says the envoys found him at work in the field, digging or plowing. He asked his wife Racilia to bring his toga from the cottage, wiped off the dust and sweat, and put it on to hear the Senate's message. He was saluted as dictator and taken into the city.

He acted quickly. He ordered every man of military age to assemble before sunset with food and stakes, marched through the night, and surrounded the enemy who were surrounding the Romans. The Aequi surrendered and were made to pass under a yoke of spears.

The dictatorship could legally last six months. Livy reports that Cincinnatus resigned it after sixteen days and went back to his farm.
lesson: Authority given for a task should be returned when the task is done. Holding power only as long as it is needed earns more trust than any title.
people: Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus
location: Rome and the Alban Hills (modern Italy)
source: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita, Book 3, chapters 26 to 29
caveat: Early Roman history in Livy mixes tradition and legend, and the details of this episode cannot be verified.

title: The Poisoned Arrow
text:
A monk named Malunkyaputta was troubled because the Buddha had never answered certain great questions. Was the world eternal or not? Was it finite or infinite? Were the soul and the body the same thing or different? Did an enlightened one exist after death or not? He went to the Buddha and declared that unless these questions were answered, he would give up his training and return to ordinary life.

The Buddha replied with a story. Suppose a man were struck by an arrow smeared thickly with poison. His friends and family bring a surgeon to treat him. But the wounded man says: I will not let this arrow be pulled out until I know who shot me, whether he was a noble or a priest or a merchant or a worker, what his name and clan are, whether he was tall or short or of medium height, what his skin was like, where he lived. And I want to know what kind of bow he used, what the string was made of, what feathers were on the shaft, and what kind of arrowhead it was.

That man, the Buddha said, would die before he learned any of it. In the same way, he had left those questions unanswered because they did not lead to the end of suffering. What he taught was suffering, its cause, its end and the path to its end.
lesson: When you are in trouble, deal with the wound before the theory. Sort questions by whether answering them changes what you must do now.
people: The Buddha, Malunkyaputta
location: Jeta's Grove, Savatthi (modern Uttar Pradesh, India)
source: Majjhima Nikaya 63 (Cula Malunkyovada Sutta)

title: The Buddha Tends the Sick Monk
text:
According to the monastic rules of early Buddhism, the Buddha was once walking through the lodgings of a monastery with his attendant Ananda when they found a monk lying sick with dysentery. He was too weak to get up and lay in his own filth. Nobody was looking after him.

The Buddha asked him why no one cared for him. The monk answered that he had been of no use to the other monks, so they did not attend to him.

The Buddha sent Ananda for water. Together they washed the man, the Buddha holding his head and Ananda his feet, and laid him on a bed.

Then the Buddha called the monks together and asked whether there was a sick monk in that place and why nobody tended him. They gave the same answer: he had done nothing for them. The Buddha reminded them that they had left their families and had no mother or father to care for them. If they did not look after one another, who would? And he told them that whoever wished to tend him should tend the sick. From then on, caring for a sick member became a duty of the community.
lesson: A community proves itself in how it treats members who cannot repay it. Looking after the weakest is not charity on the side, it is part of the work.
people: The Buddha, Ananda, a sick monk
source: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga 8.26

title: The Gift That Is Not Accepted
text:
A brahmin of the Bharadvaja clan was furious when he heard that one of his clan had left home to become a monk under the Buddha. He went to find the Buddha and abused him to his face with rude and harsh words.

The Buddha waited until he had finished. Then he asked a question. "Brahmin, do friends and relatives come to visit you as guests?" "Yes, sometimes." "And do you offer them food and refreshments?" "Yes, I do." "And if they do not accept them, to whom do those things belong?" "If they do not accept them, they remain mine."

"In the same way," said the Buddha, "you have abused me, who does not abuse, and scolded me, who does not scold. I do not accept it. It is all yours, brahmin, it belongs to you." He explained that one who answers abuse with abuse is like a guest sharing the meal, while one who does not repay anger with anger wins a battle hard to win.

The brahmin was taken aback. According to the sutta, he asked to become a monk himself, was accepted, and in time reached the goal of the holy life.
lesson: Insults only hurt you if you take them in. You can decline to pick up someone's anger and let it stay with them.
people: The Buddha, the brahmin Akkosaka Bharadvaja
source: Samyutta Nikaya 7.2 (Akkosa Sutta)

title: Kisa Gotami and the Mustard Seed
text:
Kisa Gotami was a young woman of Savatthi whose only son died when he was just old enough to run about. Unable to accept it, she carried the small body on her hip from house to house, asking everyone for medicine that would cure him. People thought she had lost her mind.

At last a wise man sent her to the Buddha. She begged him for a remedy. He told her he could help, but first she must bring him a few mustard seeds from a house in which no one had ever died.

Mustard seed was common, and she set off with hope. At the first door they gladly offered her some, but when she asked whether anyone had died there, they said, "The living are few, and the dead are many." It was the same at the next house, and the next. In one a father had died, in another a child, in another a wife.

By evening she understood. Death had come to every family in the city. She took her son to the cremation ground and laid him down. Then she returned to the Buddha, became a nun, and later was honored as one of his wise disciples.
lesson: Grief isolates us, as if loss had singled us out. Hearing how others have lost and survived can begin to bring us back to the living.
people: Kisa Gotami, the Buddha
source: Dhammapada Commentary (Dhammapada-atthakatha) on verse 114; Therigatha Commentary
caveat: The story comes from commentaries written down many centuries after the Buddha's time.
