title: The Blind Men and the Elephant
text:
Some monks came to the Buddha after their alms round in Savatthi. They had seen teachers of rival sects arguing in the town, each insisting that his own view was the only truth and wounding the others with sharp words. The Buddha answered with a story.

Long ago, he said, a king of that same city ordered all the men born blind to be gathered together. Then he had an elephant brought before them. One blind man was led to touch its head, another its ear, others the tusk, the trunk, the body, a leg, the back, the tail and the tuft at the end of the tail.

Then the king asked each of them what an elephant was like. The one who had felt the head said it was like a water pot. The one who had touched the ear said a winnowing basket. The tusk was a plowshare, the trunk a plow pole, the body a storeroom, the leg a pillar, the back a mortar, the tail a pestle, the tuft a broom.

Each was sure he was right. They began to shout, "An elephant is like this!" "No, it is not!" until they were hitting each other with their fists, while the king looked on and laughed.
lesson: Your experience of a problem is real but partial. Before arguing, ask what the other person has touched that you have not.
people: The Buddha, a king, blind men
source: Udana 6.4 (Tittha Sutta)

title: Zeng Zi Keeps His Wife's Promise
text:
Zeng Zi was one of the most respected disciples of Confucius, known above all for his devotion to his parents and his scrupulous honesty. The philosopher Han Feizi, writing in the third century BC, preserved a story about him that Chinese children still learn.

One day Zeng Zi's wife was setting out for the market, and their small son followed her, crying to go along. To get rid of him she said: go back home, and when I return I will kill the pig for you. Pork was a rare treat.

When she came back from the market, she found Zeng Zi getting ready to catch the pig and kill it. She stopped him, saying that she had only been joking with the child.

Zeng Zi answered that one must not joke with a child in that way. A child, he said, knows nothing by himself; he learns from his parents and follows their teaching. If you deceive him now, you are teaching him to deceive. And if a mother deceives her son, the son will no longer trust his mother. That is not the way to raise a child. Then he killed the pig and cooked it for the boy.

The phrase "Zeng Zi kills the pig" became a Chinese saying for keeping one's word, especially to children.
lesson: Children learn honesty from the promises we keep, even casual ones. If we would not keep a promise, it is better not to make it.
people: Zeng Zi (Zeng Shen), his wife and son
source: Han Feizi, chapter 32 (Outer Collection of Explanations, Upper Left)
caveat: The story is told by Han Feizi about two centuries after Zeng Zi's lifetime.

title: Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall
text:
According to the Book of Nehemiah, Nehemiah was cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes when he heard that the walls of Jerusalem still lay in ruins and its gates were burned. He asked the king's permission to go and rebuild them, and the king sent him with letters and supplies.

In Jerusalem, Nehemiah first rode out quietly at night to inspect the broken walls. Then he gathered the people and divided the work. Chapter 3 of the book lists who built what: the high priest and his fellow priests rebuilt the Sheep Gate, the men of Jericho built the next stretch, a goldsmith and a perfumer each repaired a section, a man and his daughters built another. Many families repaired the part of the wall directly in front of their own houses. The text even notes that the nobles of one town would not bend their necks to the work.

Local enemies mocked them, saying that even a fox would knock their stone wall down, and then they threatened to attack. Nehemiah set guards and organized the people so that half worked and half stood ready with spears, while every builder kept a sword at his side. A trumpeter stayed with him to call everyone together if an attack came.

The book says the wall was finished in fifty-two days.
lesson: Large projects move fast when each group owns a clear piece, especially one close to home. Keep both building and guarding in view when people want the work to fail.
people: Nehemiah, the people of Jerusalem, Sanballat, Tobiah
source: Book of Nehemiah, chapters 2 to 4 and 6:15

title: Creon and Antigone
text:
After the brothers Eteocles and Polynices killed each other in a war for the throne of Thebes, their uncle Creon became king. He decreed that Eteocles, who had defended the city, would be buried with honor, while Polynices, who had attacked it, would be left unburied for the dogs and birds. Anyone who buried him would die.

Their sister Antigone defied him. She covered her brother's body with dust and performed the rites, declaring that the unwritten laws of the gods outranked any king's decree. Creon condemned her to be shut up alive in a rocky tomb.

Creon's son Haemon, who was engaged to Antigone, pleaded with his father. He told him the city was quietly on her side, and that a wise man knows how to bend, like the trees that bend in a flood and survive, while the rigid ones are torn out by the roots. Creon called him a slave of a woman. Then the blind prophet Tiresias warned him that the gods were angry and that he would pay with his own family. Creon insulted him too, but after he left, frightened, he finally gave way.

It was too late. When he reached the tomb, Antigone had hanged herself. Haemon attacked his father, then killed himself. When the news reached the palace, Creon's wife Eurydice killed herself as well. Creon was left alone.
lesson: Firmness becomes a fault when it stops you from hearing those who love you. If everyone around you is warning you, change course before events make the decision for you.
people: Creon, Antigone, Haemon, Tiresias, Eurydice
source: Sophocles, Antigone

title: Mozi Stops a War on a Tabletop
text:
In the 5th century BC the master craftsman Gongshu Ban built new siege ladders, called cloud ladders, for the powerful state of Chu, which planned to use them against the small state of Song. The philosopher Mozi, who taught universal love and opposed wars of aggression, heard of it. The book that bears his name says he set out at once and walked ten days and ten nights to the Chu capital.

Mozi first argued with Gongshu Ban, then with the king of Chu, pointing out that attacking Song was unjust and that Chu, already rich, gained nothing worth the wrong. Both admitted he was right, but the king said that since Gongshu Ban had built the ladders, he would still take Song.

So Mozi proposed a demonstration. He took off his belt and laid it out as a city wall and used small wooden tablets as machines. Gongshu Ban attacked nine times with nine different devices, and Mozi repelled every attack, with defenses still to spare. Gongshu Ban said he knew a way to beat Mozi but would not say it. Mozi said he knew what it was: to kill him. But, he added, his disciple Qin Guli and three hundred students were already on the walls of Song with his defensive devices. Killing him would change nothing.

The king called off the attack. The text adds that on his way home Mozi passed through Song in the rain and was refused shelter at its gate.
lesson: The best way to stop an attack can be to show, calmly and concretely, that it will fail. Prepare your defenses so that your opponent's decision makes itself.
people: Mozi, Gongshu Ban, King of Chu, Qin Guli
location: Ying, capital of Chu (modern Hubei, China)
source: Mozi, chapter 50 (Gongshu)

title: Pericles' Funeral Oration
text:
In the winter of 431 to 430 BC, after the first year of the Peloponnesian War against Sparta, Athens held its traditional public funeral for the citizens who had died in battle. The bones of the dead were carried in cypress coffins, one for each tribe, and buried in the public cemetery outside the walls. The city chose Pericles, its leading statesman, to give the speech.

The version recorded by the historian Thucydides is not mainly about the dead. Pericles spoke instead about the city they had died for. He described a democracy in which power was in the hands of the many, where people were advanced by merit rather than class, where citizens were free in their private lives yet obeyed the laws, and where people loved beauty without extravagance and wisdom without softness. Athens, he said, was an education to Greece.

Only then did he turn to the fallen, saying they had made the city's greatness their own, and to the families, offering comfort and practical advice.

Thucydides follows the speech immediately with the plague that struck Athens the next summer, which killed a large part of the population. Pericles himself died of it in 429 BC.
lesson: People bear sacrifice better when they understand what it is for. A leader's job includes saying clearly what is worth defending.
people: Pericles
source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, Book 2, chapters 34 to 46
caveat: Thucydides admits his speeches give the general sense of what was said, not the exact words.

title: Socrates Refuses to Arrest Leon of Salamis
text:
In 404 BC Athens lost the Peloponnesian War, and a Spartan-backed oligarchy, later called the Thirty Tyrants, took control of the city. The Thirty executed many of their opponents and seized the property of wealthy citizens and foreign residents.

They also tried to make as many Athenians as possible complicit in their crimes. In Plato's Apology, Socrates tells the jury at his trial in 399 BC what happened to him. The Thirty summoned him and four other men to the Tholos, their headquarters, and ordered them to go to Salamis and bring back Leon, a citizen they had decided to put to death.

The other four went to Salamis and brought Leon back, and he was executed. Socrates, by his own account, simply went home. He told the jury that he had shown, not in words but in action, that he did not care at all about death, but cared above all about doing nothing unjust or impious. He added that he might well have been killed for it, had the Thirty not fallen soon afterward.

In the same speech he recalled an earlier time, under the democracy, when he alone of the presiding committee had opposed an illegal trial.
lesson: Even when you cannot stop an injustice, you can refuse to take part in it. Quiet refusal is still a choice, and it counts.
people: Socrates, the Thirty Tyrants, Leon of Salamis
source: Plato, Apology 32b to 32e; Xenophon, Memorabilia, Book 4, chapter 4

title: Xenophon Leads the Ten Thousand Home
text:
In 401 BC more than ten thousand Greek mercenaries marched deep into the Persian Empire for Cyrus the Younger, who was trying to overthrow his brother, King Artaxerxes. At Cunaxa, near Babylon, the Greeks won their part of the battle, but Cyrus was killed. They were stranded in the heart of a hostile empire, far from the sea.

Soon after, the Persian satrap Tissaphernes invited the Greek generals to a parley and had them seized and later executed. Xenophon, a young Athenian who had come along as a guest without any command, describes in his Anabasis how the army sank into despair that night. He could not sleep. He got up, called together the officers of his murdered friend Proxenus, and told them that waiting would mean death and that they must act at once and choose new leaders.

The army elected new generals, Xenophon among them. They burned their extra baggage, formed a hollow square, and fought their way north through the mountains of Kurdistan and the snows of Armenia. Months later, from a mountain, the vanguard saw the Black Sea and shouted "The sea! The sea!" Most of the army survived.
lesson: When the people in charge are gone and everyone is frozen, the one who speaks up with a plan becomes the leader.
people: Xenophon, Cyrus the Younger, Tissaphernes
location: From Cunaxa (modern Iraq) to Trapezus (modern Trabzon, Turkey)
source: Xenophon, Anabasis, especially Books 1 to 4
caveat: Xenophon's account is the main source and naturally presents his own role favorably.

title: Bian Que and Duke Huan of Cai
text:
The legendary physician Bian Que came to see Duke Huan of Cai. After standing before him for a while, he said: "My lord, you have an illness in the skin. If it is not treated, it will go deeper." The duke replied that he was perfectly well. When Bian Que left, the duke remarked that doctors like to treat healthy people so they can take credit for curing them.

Ten days later Bian Que came again and said the illness had reached the flesh. The duke did not answer and was displeased. Ten days after that Bian Que said it had reached the stomach and intestines. Again the duke ignored him.

After another ten days, Bian Que caught sight of the duke, turned and walked away. The duke sent someone to ask why. Bian Que explained that an illness in the skin can be reached with poultices, in the flesh with needles, and in the stomach with herbal broths. But now it was in the marrow of the bones, where it belonged to the god of fate, and nothing could be done, so he had nothing more to say.

Five days later the duke felt pain all through his body. He sent for Bian Que, who had already fled to the state of Qin. The duke died.
lesson: Problems are cheapest to fix when they are still small and easy to deny. Listen most carefully to the warnings that arrive while you still feel fine.
people: Bian Que, Duke Huan of Cai
source: Han Feizi, Yu Lao (Illustrations of Laozi)
caveat: Bian Que is a semi-legendary figure, and the Shiji tells a similar story with a duke of Qi.

title: The Seven Conditions of the Vajjis
text:
King Ajatasattu of Magadha wanted to conquer the Vajjis, a confederation of clans ruled by assemblies rather than a single king. Before marching, he sent his chief minister, Vassakara, to the Buddha to ask what the outcome would be.

The Buddha did not answer the minister directly. He turned to Ananda, who was fanning him, and asked a series of questions. Did the Vajjis meet often and in full numbers? Did they meet in harmony, end their meetings in harmony and carry out their business in harmony? Did they keep to their established laws rather than inventing new ones on a whim? Did they honor and listen to their elders, protect their women, maintain their shrines, and look after holy men who came to them? To each question Ananda answered yes.

As long as the Vajjis kept to these seven things, the Buddha said, they could be expected to prosper and not decline. Vassakara drew the conclusion himself: the Vajjis could not be beaten in war, except through bribery or by breaking up their unity. Then he left. The Buddha later gathered his monks and applied the same conditions to their own community.
lesson: Groups that meet regularly, decide together and carry out decisions in unity are hard to defeat. Watch for the first signs of division, because that is where outsiders get in.
people: The Buddha, Ananda, the minister Vassakara, King Ajatasattu
source: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), opening section

title: Dhritarashtra's Blind Love
text:
Dhritarashtra, the blind king of the Kurus, loved his eldest son Duryodhana beyond reason. When the boy was born, there were terrible omens, and the king's wise half brother Vidura advised him to give up the child for the sake of the family. Dhritarashtra could not do it.

As Duryodhana grew up, his jealousy of his cousins, the five Pandava brothers, grew with him. He tried to poison Bhima and later to burn all the Pandavas alive in a house built of lacquer. Each time Dhritarashtra was told, and each time he found reasons not to act.

When Duryodhana schemed to win the Pandavas' kingdom through a rigged game of dice, Vidura begged the king to stop it. Gandhari, Duryodhana's own mother, urged him to restrain their son. Dhritarashtra agreed that it was wrong, then allowed it anyway, because he could not bear to refuse his son. The Pandavas lost everything, and their wife Draupadi was dragged before the court and humiliated.

Years later, when Krishna came to negotiate peace, Duryodhana refused to give the Pandavas even five villages. Dhritarashtra again failed to overrule him. The great war at Kurukshetra followed, and all of Dhritarashtra's hundred sons were killed.
lesson: Loving a child sometimes means saying no and enforcing it. A parent who cannot refuse a favorite child can let a small fault grow into a disaster for everyone.
people: Dhritarashtra, Duryodhana, Vidura, Gandhari
source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sabha Parva and Udyoga Parva

title: Kunti Meets Karna
text:
Long before her marriage, while still a girl, Kunti had borne a son to the sun god Surya. Afraid of disgrace, she put the baby in a basket and set him adrift on a river. A charioteer and his wife found him and raised him as their own. They named him Karna.

Karna grew into a great warrior, but because people believed he was a charioteer's son, he was mocked by the princes, and the only one who honored him was Duryodhana. Karna became his loyal friend, and so an enemy of the Pandavas, Kunti's five younger sons.

On the eve of the great war, Kunti went to Karna as he stood praying by the Ganges. She told him the truth: he was her firstborn and the Pandavas were his brothers. She begged him to join them.

Karna answered that she had abandoned him when he most needed a mother, and that Duryodhana had stood by him when no one else would. He would not betray his friend now. But he gave her a promise: he would not kill any of her sons except Arjuna. Whatever happened, she would still have five sons.

In the war, Arjuna killed Karna. Only afterward did the Pandavas learn they had killed their own elder brother.
lesson: Family secrets do not stay small. A truth kept hidden for years can do more harm when it finally comes out than it would have done if told early.
people: Kunti, Karna
source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva

title: Rama Accepts Exile
text:
King Dasharatha of Ayodhya, growing old, decided to crown his eldest son Rama as heir. The city rejoiced. But his young queen Kaikeyi, stirred up by her maid Manthara, reminded the king of two boons he had promised her long ago when she saved his life in battle.

Now she named them: her own son Bharata must be crowned instead, and Rama must be sent into the forest for fourteen years. Dasharatha begged her to choose anything else, but he had given his word and could not take it back.

When Rama was summoned, he saw his father's grief and heard the demand from Kaikeyi. He did not argue or protest. He said he would go gladly so that his father would not break his promise. His wife Sita insisted on going with him, and his brother Lakshmana would not be left behind either. The three set out in bark clothing, while the people of Ayodhya followed weeping.

Soon after they left, Dasharatha died of grief. Bharata, returning home, refused the throne and went to the forest to beg Rama to come back. Rama still refused, so Bharata took his brother's sandals, set them on the throne, and ruled only as Rama's deputy until his return.
lesson: Keeping faith with family can cost a great deal. Honoring a commitment, even one you did not make, can hold a family together when everything else is pulling it apart.
people: Rama, Dasharatha, Kaikeyi, Sita, Lakshmana, Bharata
date: c. 5th century BC to 3rd century AD
source: Valmiki, Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda

title: Savitri and Satyavan
text:
Savitri, daughter of King Ashvapati, chose as her husband Satyavan, the son of a blind king who had lost his throne and lived in exile in the forest. The sage Narada warned her that Satyavan had every virtue but would die exactly one year from that day. Savitri refused to change her choice, and married him.

She kept the prophecy to herself. As the fatal day approached, she fasted for three days and nights, and on the morning itself she insisted on going with Satyavan into the woods to cut firewood. There he felt a sudden pain in his head and lay down with it in her lap. Yama, the lord of death, appeared and drew out his life.

When Yama set off southward, Savitri followed. He told her to turn back, but she kept walking and spoke to him so wisely about virtue and friendship that he offered her a boon, anything except her husband's life. She asked for her father-in-law's sight, then his kingdom, then sons for her own father. Each time she kept following.

Finally Yama granted her a hundred sons by Satyavan. She pointed out that this was impossible unless her husband lived. Caught by his own promise, and pleased with her, Yama released Satyavan, who woke in her lap as if from sleep.
lesson: Persistence works best when joined to clear thinking. Keep showing up for the people you love, and look for the honest argument that changes the situation.
people: Savitri, Satyavan, Yama, Narada
source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), Pativrata Mahatmya

title: Wu Qi and the Soldier's Wound
text:
Wu Qi was a famous general of the Warring States period in China, who served the states of Lu, Wei and Chu around the late fifth and early fourth centuries BC. Sima Qian describes his way of commanding.

As a general, Wu Qi ate and dressed the same as the lowest-ranking soldiers. When he slept he did not use a mat. On the march he did not ride, and he carried his own rations. He shared all the hardships of his men.

Once a soldier had an abscess, and Wu Qi himself sucked out the pus. When the soldier's mother heard about it, she wept. Someone asked her why she was crying, since her son was only a soldier and the general himself had sucked his wound.

She answered that years before, Wu Qi had done the same for her son's father. Her husband had followed him into battle without ever turning back, and had died at the hands of the enemy. Now that the general had sucked her son's wound, she said, she did not know where her son would die. That was why she wept.
lesson: Care for your people because it is right, and be honest with yourself about what loyalty you are asking for in return.
people: Wu Qi
source: Sima Qian, Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), chapter 65

title: Yudhishthira Chooses Nakula
text:
During their exile in the forest, the five Pandava brothers grew desperately thirsty. Nakula went looking for water and found a clear lake. A voice warned him not to drink until he had answered its questions. He ignored it, drank, and fell dead. Sahadeva, Arjuna and Bhima followed one by one and met the same fate.

Last came Yudhishthira, the eldest. He found his four brothers lying lifeless at the water's edge. The voice, a yaksha, a nature spirit, posed its riddles, and Yudhishthira answered every one patiently and wisely: what is faster than the wind (the mind), what is the greatest wonder (that people see others die every day and still act as if they will live forever).

Pleased, the yaksha offered to bring back one brother. Yudhishthira chose Nakula. The yaksha was astonished: why not mighty Bhima or the great archer Arjuna, on whom he would depend in war?

Yudhishthira explained that his father had two wives, Kunti and Madri. He himself was Kunti's son and still alive. If Nakula lived, Madri too would have a son left. He would not favor his own mother's line. The yaksha then revealed himself as the god Dharma, Yudhishthira's own father, and restored all four brothers to life.
lesson: Fairness means looking after the people who have the least standing, even when favoring your own side would be easier or more useful.
people: Yudhishthira, the Yaksha (Dharma), Nakula, Bhima, Arjuna, Sahadeva
source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), the Yaksha Prashna episode

title: Camillus and the Treacherous Schoolmaster
text:
In 394 BC, according to Roman tradition, the general Marcus Furius Camillus was besieging Falerii, a town of the Faliscans north of Rome. The siege was dragging on, and the town was well defended.

Livy and Plutarch tell the story. The Faliscans entrusted the education of the children of their leading families to a schoolmaster, who took them out of the town each day for walks and exercise. In the time of war he kept doing so, taking them a little farther each day. One day he led them all the way into the Roman camp, brought them before Camillus, and offered them as hostages: with these children in Roman hands, he said, the town would have to surrender.

Camillus refused. Plutarch has him say that even in war good men observe certain laws, and that a great general should rely on his own virtue and not on other men's vices. He ordered the schoolmaster stripped and his hands bound behind his back, gave the boys rods, and told them to drive their teacher back to the town, whipping him as they went.

The Faliscans, who had been in despair over the loss of their children, saw them return, whipping the traitor. Moved by the Roman general's honesty, the town decided that it would rather trust Rome's justice than keep fighting. They sent envoys and surrendered to Camillus on terms.
lesson: Refusing an unfair advantage can win more than taking it. A reputation for integrity can persuade an opponent to trust you when force alone could not.
people: Marcus Furius Camillus
source: Livy, History of Rome 5.27; Plutarch, Life of Camillus 10
caveat: The story belongs to the early Roman tradition and is probably more moral legend than history.

title: The Ring of Gyges
text:
In Plato's Republic, Glaucon challenges Socrates to prove that justice is worth having for its own sake. To make his case, he tells a story about Gyges, a shepherd in the service of the king of Lydia.

One day, after a storm and an earthquake, the ground split open where Gyges was grazing his flock. He went down into the chasm and found a hollow bronze horse with little doors. Inside lay the body of a man larger than human size, wearing nothing but a gold ring. Gyges took the ring and went back up.

At the monthly meeting of the shepherds, he happened to turn the setting of the ring toward the inside of his hand and found that the others began talking about him as if he had gone. He turned it back and became visible again. Once he was sure of its power, he arranged to be one of the messengers sent to the king. At the palace he seduced the queen, plotted with her, killed the king and took the throne.

Glaucon's argument is that if there were two such rings, one worn by a just man and one by an unjust man, both would end up doing the same. People are just, he says, only because they fear being caught. Socrates spends much of the rest of the Republic trying to prove him wrong.
lesson: Ask yourself what you would do if no one could ever find out. Character is built in exactly those moments, especially as you gain power and fewer people can check you.
people: Gyges, Glaucon, Socrates
location: Athens, Greece (story set in Lydia, modern Turkey)
source: Plato, Republic, Book II, 359c to 360d

title: The Ship of State
text:
In Book VI of Plato's Republic, Socrates explains why the best qualified people are rarely the ones in charge of a city. He uses an image of a ship.

The owner of the ship is bigger and stronger than anyone on board, but he is a little deaf, somewhat short-sighted, and knows little about sailing. The sailors quarrel with each other over who should steer. None of them has ever learned navigation, and they insist it cannot even be taught, and they are ready to tear to pieces anyone who says it can. They crowd around the owner, begging him to hand them the helm. When others win his favor, they kill them or throw them overboard. Then they drug or intoxicate the owner, take control of the ship, help themselves to the cargo, and sail along drinking and feasting.

They praise as a fine navigator anyone who helps them get control, and call anyone who does not useless. They have no idea that a true navigator must study the seasons, the sky, the stars and the winds. If such a person were on board, they would call him a stargazer and a babbler, good for nothing.

Socrates' point is that philosophers are scorned in cities for the same reason: the people who should steer are dismissed by those who only know how to win the owner's favor.
lesson: Being good at getting the job and being good at doing it are different skills. When you choose who steers, weigh real expertise over charm, loyalty and noise.
people: Socrates, Adeimantus, the shipowner, the sailors, the true navigator
source: Plato, Republic, Book VI, 488a to 489a

title: The Sacred Band of Thebes
text:
In the 370s BC Thebes formed an elite unit of three hundred chosen soldiers, kept and trained at public expense. Plutarch, in his Life of Pelopidas, says it was first organized by Gorgidas, and that it was made up of pairs of lovers. He quotes the Theban general Pammenes, who said Homer was wrong to group soldiers by tribe and family: men of the same clan care little for each other in danger, but a band bound by love will not break, because each man is ashamed to act basely in front of the one he loves.

At first Gorgidas spread the Band thinly across the front ranks of the army. Pelopidas, after seeing them fight alone and win against a larger Spartan force at Tegyra in 375 BC, never divided them again. He kept them together as one body and gave them the hardest assignments in the great battles. Plutarch compares them to horses that run faster harnessed together than alone, each spurring the others on. They played a key part in the Theban victory over Sparta at Leuctra in 371 BC.

Plutarch says the Band was never defeated until the battle of Chaeronea in 338 BC, when Philip of Macedon crushed Thebes and Athens. Walking over the field afterward, Philip found the three hundred lying dead together where they had faced his phalanx. Told who they were, he wept and said: "Perish any man who suspects that these men either did or suffered anything that was base."
lesson: Units hold under pressure when members care about each other personally, not just about the mission. Keep close teams together rather than scattering them.
people: Gorgidas, Pelopidas, Philip II of Macedon
source: Plutarch, Life of Pelopidas 18 to 19
caveat: Ancient authors give the Band only brief mention, and some details of its composition rest on Plutarch alone.

title: Epaminondas Honors the Lowliest Office
text:
Epaminondas was the Theban general who broke Sparta's military power at Leuctra in 371 BC and became one of the most admired men in Greece. He also had enemies at home in Thebes who resented his influence.

Plutarch, in his essay of advice to politicians known as Precepts of Statecraft, tells how those rivals once tried to humiliate him. Out of envy and as an insult, they had him elected telmarch, a minor city official whose job was to keep the alleys clear of dung and to see that rainwater drained away from the streets. It was a post no one of standing would want.

Epaminondas did not refuse it or treat it with contempt. He took it on and did the work seriously. Plutarch says that he remarked that it is not only the office that shows what kind of man holds it, but also the man who shows what the office is. By the way he carried out the job, he raised the telmarchy, which until then had been nothing but a sort of supervision of street cleaning, to a position of dignity.

Plutarch offers the story to men entering public life, as a model for taking small duties seriously.
lesson: Do the small job you are given as if it mattered. The way you fill a role can raise the role, whatever others meant by giving it to you.
people: Epaminondas
source: Plutarch, Moralia, Precepts of Statecraft (Praecepta gerendae reipublicae), 811b

title: Damon Stands Surety for Pythias
text:
The story was told by Aristoxenus, who said he heard it from Dionysius himself, the tyrant of Syracuse, after his fall. Damon and Phintias (later called Pythias) were two followers of Pythagoras living in Syracuse in the 4th century BC. Courtiers of Dionysius, wanting to test how far the famous loyalty of the Pythagoreans went, had Phintias accused of plotting against the tyrant and condemned to death.

Phintias asked for the rest of the day to settle his affairs and those of Damon, his friend and partner. He offered Damon as surety. Damon agreed to stay in his place and die if Phintias did not come back. The courtiers laughed and expected that Damon had been made a fool.

As evening approached, Phintias returned to face his execution. Dionysius was so struck that he released both men and asked to be admitted as a third member of their friendship. According to the account, they declined. Cicero, Diodorus and Iamblichus all repeated the story, and Damon and Pythias became the classic pair of faithful friends in later literature.
lesson: Keep your word to a friend even when breaking it would save you. That kind of faithfulness is rare enough to move even people who believe no one can be trusted.
people: Damon, Phintias (Pythias), Dionysius of Syracuse
source: Aristoxenus, quoted in Iamblichus, Life of Pythagoras 33; Cicero, De Officiis 3.45; Diodorus Siculus, Library 10.4
caveat: Ancient versions differ on which Dionysius was involved and on details of the test, and the story may be partly embellished.

title: Mencius's Mother Cuts the Weaving
text:
When Mencius was a boy, his widowed mother supported the household by weaving. She worked hard to give her son an education.

One day the young Mencius came home from his studies early. His mother was at her loom. She asked him how far he had got with his lessons. He answered casually that he was about where he had been before.

Without a word she took a knife and cut through the cloth on her loom, ruining all the work she had done. Mencius was frightened and asked her why.

She told him that his abandoning his studies was just like her cutting the weaving. A scholar studies to make a name and to gain broad knowledge, so that he can live in peace and stay clear of harm. If he gave up now, he would end up as a servant or a thief, unable to escape trouble. Leaving learning halfway, she said, was like a woman who stops weaving cloth halfway: the family would have nothing to wear or eat.

Mencius was shaken. From then on he studied morning and evening without slacking, and he went on to become one of the greatest Confucian thinkers.
lesson: A dramatic, concrete demonstration can teach what many lectures cannot. Abandoning a commitment halfway often wastes everything already put into it.
people: Mencius, his mother
source: Liu Xiang, Lienu zhuan (Biographies of Exemplary Women), 1.11
caveat: The story was recorded by Liu Xiang in the 1st century BC, centuries after Mencius, and is best treated as a traditional anecdote.

title: Shang Yang Pays the Man Who Moved the Log
text:
In the fourth century BC Shang Yang, a minister serving Duke Xiao of Qin, prepared a sweeping set of new laws meant to make Qin strong: rewards for farming and for military merit, punishments for idleness, and a strict system of mutual responsibility.

Sima Qian tells how, before announcing the laws, Shang Yang worried that the people would not believe the government meant what it said. So he had a wooden pole about three zhang long, roughly seven meters, set up at the south gate of the capital's market. He announced that anyone who moved it to the north gate would receive ten pieces of gold.

People thought it strange, and no one dared to move it. Shang Yang raised the reward to fifty. One man carried the pole to the north gate, and Shang Yang immediately paid him the fifty pieces of gold, to show that he did not deceive. Only then did he proclaim the new laws.

The laws were enforced harshly, even against the crown prince's tutors when the prince broke them. Qin grew powerful. After Duke Xiao died, Shang Yang's enemies turned on him, and he was killed in 338 BC.
lesson: Before asking people to follow your rules, show them you keep your word. Credibility is built with small promises kept exactly.
people: Shang Yang, Duke Xiao of Qin
location: Yueyang, capital of Qin (modern Shaanxi, China)
source: Sima Qian, Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), chapter 68

title: Tian Ji Wins the Horse Race
text:
In the state of Qi in the 4th century BC, the general Tian Ji often raced horses against King Wei and the princes for large wagers. Each side entered three horses, one from each of three grades: top, middle and lowest. The king's horses in each grade were a little better than Tian Ji's, so Tian Ji kept losing.

Sima Qian tells that Tian Ji had recently taken in Sun Bin, a strategist who had been crippled and branded by a jealous rival in the state of Wei and smuggled out to Qi. Sun Bin watched the races and noticed that the horses of each grade were not very far apart. He told Tian Ji to bet heavily, promising him victory.

His plan changed only the order. Tian Ji would run his lowest horse against the king's best, his best against the king's middle horse, and his middle horse against the king's lowest. Tian Ji followed the advice. He lost the first race badly but won the other two, and with them a thousand pieces of gold.

Impressed, Tian Ji introduced Sun Bin to King Wei. The king questioned him on the art of war and made him his military adviser.
lesson: You do not have to be stronger everywhere to win. Decide where to concede and where to concentrate, and match your strengths against the other side's weaker points.
people: Tian Ji, Sun Bin, King Wei of Qi
source: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), chapter 65

title: Besiege Wei to Rescue Zhao
text:
In 354 BC the state of Wei sent its army against Zhao and besieged the Zhao capital, Handan. Zhao begged Qi for help. King Wei of Qi wanted to make Sun Bin commander, but Sun Bin declined because he had been mutilated and branded as a criminal, so Tian Ji led the army and Sun Bin rode along in a covered cart as adviser.

Tian Ji meant to march straight to Handan and fight the Wei army there. Sima Qian records Sun Bin's objection: to untangle a snarled thread you do not pull at it with your fists, and to break up a fight you do not join the blows. Wei's best troops, he argued, were all at Handan, leaving only the old and weak at home. Qi should march on the Wei capital, Daliang, and seize its roads. Wei would have to abandon the siege to save itself.

Tian Ji agreed. When the Wei army heard that its capital was threatened, it left Handan and hurried home. Exhausted after the long march, it met the Qi army at Guiling and was heavily defeated. The phrase "besiege Wei to rescue Zhao" became one of the classic Chinese strategic sayings.
lesson: Instead of meeting a problem where it is strongest, look for the place the other side must protect. Pressure there can resolve the original fight without fighting it.
people: Sun Bin, Tian Ji, Pang Juan
location: Handan and Guiling (modern Hebei and Henan, China)
source: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), chapter 65

title: Mencius's Mother Moves House Three Times
text:
Mencius, the great Confucian thinker of the fourth century BC, lost his father when he was small and was raised by his mother. Liu Xiang, a scholar of the Han dynasty, collected her story in his Biographies of Exemplary Women.

At first they lived near a cemetery. The boy played at funerals, digging and wailing like the mourners. His mother decided this was no place to raise a son and moved near a market. Now he played at buying and selling, imitating the hawkers' cries. She moved again, this time next to a school. There the boy began to imitate the rituals of the students and teachers, bowing, yielding and practicing ceremony. His mother said that this was a place fit for her son, and they stayed.

Mencius grew up to become, in later Chinese memory, the second sage after Confucius. "Mencius's mother moved three times" became a Chinese proverb for the care a parent takes over a child's surroundings.
lesson: Children absorb their surroundings long before they absorb our advice. Choosing where and among whom they grow up may be one of the most important things a parent decides.
people: Mencius, his mother (traditionally surnamed Zhang)
source: Liu Xiang, Lienu Zhuan (Biographies of Exemplary Women), Book 1, The Mother of Meng Ke
caveat: The story was written down about three centuries after Mencius lived and is best read as tradition.

title: Philip Watches Alexander Tame Bucephalus
text:
Plutarch tells this story in his Life of Alexander. A horse dealer from Thessaly named Philonicus brought a horse called Bucephalus to King Philip of Macedon, asking thirteen talents for him, an enormous price. When they took him out to the field to try him, the horse was wild. He reared up and would not let any of the king's men mount him or even speak to him. They were leading him away as useless.

The young Alexander, standing by, kept saying what a fine horse they were losing for lack of skill and nerve. At first Philip ignored him. Then he asked whether Alexander was criticizing his elders as if he knew better. Alexander said he could handle this horse better than they had. Philip asked what he would forfeit if he failed. The price of the horse, said Alexander, and everyone laughed.

Alexander had noticed that the horse was frightened of his own shadow. He turned him to face the sun, stroked him, let him run forward a little, then quietly slipped off his cloak and leapt onto his back. Without whip or spur, he let him go at full speed, and brought him back in triumph. The company cheered. Philip, Plutarch says, wept with joy and kissed his son, saying: "My son, seek a kingdom equal to yourself, for Macedonia is too small for you."

Plutarch adds that Philip, seeing his son could be led by reason but not forced, then sent for Aristotle to teach him.
lesson: Watching closely what a child can do, and recognizing it, gives confidence nothing else can. Children who can be reasoned with should be persuaded, not commanded.
people: Philip II of Macedon, Alexander the Great, Philonicus
source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 6 to 7

title: Sun Bin Reduces the Campfires
text:
Years after his rival Pang Juan had him mutilated, Sun Bin faced him again. In about 342 BC the state of Wei attacked Han, and Qi sent an army under Tian Ji with Sun Bin as strategist. As before, they marched toward the Wei capital, and Pang Juan turned back to chase them.

According to Sima Qian, Sun Bin knew the Wei soldiers despised the men of Qi as cowards. He ordered that on the first night the camp should show cooking fires for a hundred thousand men, on the second for fifty thousand, and on the third for thirty thousand. Pang Juan counted the fire pits and concluded that Qi's troops were deserting in droves. He left his infantry behind and raced ahead with light troops.

Sun Bin calculated where Pang Juan would arrive at nightfall: Maling, where the road ran through a narrow pass. He had a large tree stripped of bark and wrote on the bare wood that Pang Juan would die under this tree. He hid ten thousand crossbowmen along the road with orders to shoot when they saw a light.

Pang Juan arrived in the dark, saw writing on the tree and lit a torch to read it. The crossbows fired at once, his army broke, and Pang Juan cut his own throat. Qi destroyed the Wei army and captured the Wei crown prince.
lesson: People read evidence through what they already believe. Give a confident opponent the signs he expects to see and he may rush into the place you have prepared.
people: Sun Bin, Pang Juan, Tian Ji
source: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), chapter 65
caveat: The exact year and site of Maling are debated, and the details of the inscribed tree may be embellished.

title: The Fox Borrows the Tiger's Might
text:
King Xuan of Chu once asked his ministers why the states to the north were so afraid of his general Zhao Xixu. One of them, Jiang Yi, answered with a story.

A tiger hunting for food caught a fox. Before it could eat him, the fox said: "You dare not eat me. The Lord of Heaven has made me the leader of all the animals. If you eat me, you defy his command. If you don't believe me, walk behind me and see whether any animal fails to run when I appear."

The tiger agreed and followed the fox through the forest. Every creature that saw them fled in panic. The tiger, not realizing that it was he whom they feared, believed the fox.

Jiang Yi then made his point. The king's realm was five thousand li across and his armies numbered a million men, and he had placed them under Zhao Xixu. The northern states, he said, did not fear the general. They feared the king's own armed might, just as the animals feared the tiger and not the fox.
lesson: When people defer to someone who reports to you, check whether they respect that person or only the power you lent them. And if you are the fox, remember whose strength you are walking with.
people: Jiang Yi, King Xuan of Chu, Zhao Xixu
source: Zhanguo Ce (Strategies of the Warring States), Chu

title: Alexander and the Gordian Knot
text:
In the spring of 333 BC, Alexander reached Gordium, the old capital of Phrygia, on his march into Asia. In the citadel stood an ancient ox cart said to have belonged to Gordius, the peasant who became king, or to his son Midas. Its yoke was tied to the pole with a knot of cornel bark so tangled that no one could find where it began or ended. A prophecy said that whoever untied it would rule Asia.

Alexander could not walk away from such a test with his army watching. Arrian reports two versions of what happened. In the more famous one, Alexander, unable to find the ends, drew his sword and cut through the knot. Aristobulus, who served on the campaign, said instead that he pulled out the peg that held the yoke to the pole and slid the yoke free. Plutarch repeats both accounts.

Either way, Alexander declared the prophecy fulfilled, and Arrian adds that thunder and lightning that night were taken as a sign of the gods' approval. He offered sacrifices and moved on. Within a few years he had defeated Darius and ruled the Persian Empire from Egypt to the Indus.
lesson: When a problem is defined by rules that make it unsolvable, ask whether the rules are really binding. A fresh angle can turn an impossible puzzle into a simple task.
people: Alexander the Great
source: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 2.3; Plutarch, Life of Alexander 18
caveat: The ancient sources disagree on whether Alexander cut the knot or removed the pole pin, and the prophecy itself is legend.

title: Alexander Drinks the Suspect Medicine
text:
In 333 BC, as Alexander the Great marched through Cilicia toward the Persian king Darius, he fell dangerously ill. Some said he caught a chill bathing in the icy river Cydnus. According to Plutarch, his physicians thought the case so desperate that none dared treat him, fearing the anger of the Macedonians if he died in their care.

Only Philip of Acarnania, an old friend, agreed to try a strong purge. Just then a letter arrived from the general Parmenion warning Alexander that Philip had been bribed by Darius to poison him, with money and the promise of the king's daughter in marriage. Alexander read it and slipped it under his pillow without showing it to anyone.

When Philip came in with the cup, Alexander handed him the letter and drank the medicine while Philip read. Plutarch describes the scene: the king calm and cheerful, the doctor horrified, raising his hands to heaven and begging Alexander to trust him. The drug at first left Alexander weak and nearly speechless, but Philip nursed him back, and within days he showed himself to his army again. Arrian tells the same story.
lesson: When you have good reason to trust someone, show it openly at the moment it counts. Visible confidence can bind people to you more firmly than suspicion protects you.
people: Alexander the Great, Philip of Acarnania, Parmenion
source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 19; Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 2.4

title: Porus Asks to Be Treated Like a King
text:
In 326 BC Alexander the Great crossed the Hydaspes River in the Punjab and met the army of the Indian king Porus. It was one of Alexander's hardest battles. Porus fought from a huge war elephant at the center of his line and kept fighting after his army had broken, though badly wounded.

Plutarch says historians agreed Porus was very tall, and that his elephant protected him through the battle, kneeling gently when he weakened. When Porus was finally brought before Alexander, the conqueror asked him how he wished to be treated. Porus answered: "As a king." Alexander asked whether he had nothing more to say. Porus replied that everything was contained in that word. Arrian, writing from earlier sources, gives the same exchange.

Alexander was impressed by his courage and dignity. He gave Porus back his kingdom to rule as his ally and added to it territory of neighboring peoples. Porus remained loyal to Alexander afterward.
lesson: Keep your dignity in defeat. People who keep their self-respect when they have lost tend to win the respect of the one who beat them.
people: Porus, Alexander the Great
source: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 5.19; Plutarch, Life of Alexander 60

title: Alexander Pours Out the Water in the Desert
text:
In 325 BC Alexander the Great led part of his army back from India through the Gedrosian desert, in what is now southern Iran and Pakistan. The march was a disaster. Men and animals died of heat and thirst, and the army moved at night to escape the sun.

Arrian, writing in the second century AD from earlier sources, tells a story he places on this march. The army was suffering badly from thirst, and Alexander, on foot like his men, was leading the column. Some light-armed soldiers who had gone searching found a little water in a shallow gully. They collected it with difficulty, poured it into a helmet, and brought it to the king.

Alexander thanked them, took the helmet, and in full view of the army poured the water out on the ground. Arrian says the whole army was so heartened by this that it was as if every man had drunk what Alexander poured away.

Arrian notes that some writers placed the incident elsewhere, but he praised the act itself as proof of Alexander's endurance and his skill as a general.
lesson: When you lead people through hardship, refusing a comfort they cannot share is often worth more than the comfort itself.
people: Alexander the Great
source: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander, Book 6, chapter 26
caveat: Arrian himself notes that other writers placed this story elsewhere in Alexander's campaigns.

title: Drawing a Snake and Adding Feet
text:
A nobleman of Chu, after making a sacrifice, gave his retainers a jug of wine. There was not enough for all of them, but it was too much for one. So they agreed on a contest: each would draw a snake on the ground, and whoever finished first would drink the whole jug.

One man finished his snake quickly. He picked up the jug and was about to drink, but seeing that the others were still drawing, he held the wine in his left hand and with his right began to add feet to his snake, to show how fast and clever he was.

Before he had finished the feet, another man completed his snake and snatched the jug from him. A snake has no feet, he said. How can you give it feet? And he drank the wine. The man who drew the feet lost the prize.

The adviser Chen Zhen told this story to Zhao Yang, a Chu general who had just won a great victory over Wei and was now preparing to attack Qi. He already held the highest rank, Chen argued. A new war could add nothing to it, but defeat could take away everything he had won. Zhao Yang saw the point, and withdrew his army.
lesson: Once you have won, know when to stop. Extra flourishes after the job is done add risk without adding value, and can cost you the victory.
people: Chen Zhen, Zhao Yang, retainers of a Chu nobleman
source: Zhanguo Ce (Strategies of the Warring States), Qi section

title: Chanakya and the Hot Porridge
text:
Chanakya, also called Kautilya, is remembered in Indian tradition as the brilliant and ruthless Brahmin who helped the young Chandragupta Maurya overthrow the Nanda dynasty of Magadha and found the Maurya empire in the late 4th century BC. Many legends gathered around him, preserved in later Buddhist and Jain writings.

One of the best known appears in the Jain poet Hemachandra's account and, in a somewhat different form, in a Buddhist commentary on the chronicle of Sri Lanka. In Hemachandra's version, Chanakya and Chandragupta first attacked the Nanda capital directly and were badly beaten. They had to flee and wandered the country in disguise.

One day they were in a village and overheard a mother scolding her child. The boy had been given a bowl of hot rice porridge and had put his fingers straight into the middle, burning himself. The mother told him that he was as foolish as Chanakya, who attacked the center of the kingdom first. Eat from the edges, she said, where it has cooled, and work your way inward.

Chanakya took the lesson. Instead of striking the capital, he and Chandragupta built up their forces by winning over the frontier regions first, then advanced step by step. In the legend, they closed in on the Nanda center only when the outer lands were theirs, and Chandragupta became king.
lesson: When the center of a problem is too hot to handle, start at the edges. Build strength where resistance is weakest and close in once you have a base.
people: Chanakya (Kautilya), Chandragupta Maurya
source: Hemachandra, Parishishtaparvan, canto 8; Vamsatthappakasini (Pali commentary on the Mahavamsa)
caveat: The story is a legend preserved in sources written many centuries after the events.

title: Fifty Steps Laughing at a Hundred
text:
King Hui of Liang told Mencius that he did his utmost for his people. When famine struck the region inside the river bend, he moved people to the east bank and sent grain to those who stayed, and when it struck the east he did the same in reverse. None of the neighboring rulers took such care. Yet their populations did not shrink and his did not grow. Why?

Mencius answered with an image from war, since the king loved war. The drums sound, the weapons clash, and some soldiers throw away their armor and flee, dragging their weapons. One runs a hundred paces before stopping, another fifty. What if the man who ran fifty paces laughed at the one who ran a hundred?

"He has no right to," said the king. "He only did not run a hundred paces. He ran away all the same."

"If Your Majesty understands that," said Mencius, "then do not expect your people to be more numerous than your neighbors'." He went on to describe real care: do not take farmers away in the busy seasons, let the forests and fish recover, and make sure no one dies of hunger in the roads while dogs and pigs eat food meant for people.
lesson: Being slightly better than poor competitors is not the same as doing well. Measure yourself against what the people you serve actually need, not against the worst around you.
people: Mencius, King Hui of Liang
source: Mencius, Book 1A, Chapter 3

title: Pulling Up Seedlings to Help Them Grow
text:
Mencius told this story to explain how a person should cultivate character, and it has been repeated in China ever since.

There was a man of Song who was worried that the young shoots of his grain were not growing fast enough. Every day he went out to the field to look at them, and every day they seemed no taller. At last he could not stand it any longer. He went into the field and, one by one, pulled each seedling up a little, to make it taller.

He came home in the evening completely exhausted and told his family that he was worn out, because he had spent the whole day helping the seedlings grow. His son, alarmed, ran out to the field to look. All the seedlings had withered.

Mencius drew the lesson himself. Few people in the world, he said, do not try to help their seedlings grow this way. Some think nothing can be done and neglect them, never bothering to weed. Others try to force them, pulling them up. Neglecting does no good, but forcing does positive harm.
lesson: Growth in people, skills and projects needs steady care, not force. Pushing for results before their time can kill what you are trying to help.
people: A man of Song, his son, Mencius
source: Mencius, Book 2A, Chapter 2

title: Zhuangzi Drums on a Pot After His Wife's Death
text:
When Zhuangzi's wife died, his friend Huizi came to offer condolences. He found Zhuangzi sitting with his legs sprawled out, drumming on an earthenware basin and singing.

Huizi was shocked. "You lived with her," he said. "She raised your children and grew old with you. It would be enough not to weep now that she is dead. But to beat on a pot and sing, isn't that going too far?"

Zhuangzi said it was not like that. When she first died, how could he not have grieved? But then he thought back to before her beginning. There was a time when she had no life, and before that no form, and before that not even breath. In the midst of the jumble of things, a change took place and there was breath; breath changed and there was form; form changed and there was life. Now there had been another change, and she was dead. It was like the turning of the four seasons, spring to summer, autumn to winter.

She was lying peacefully in the great room of the world. If he went on sobbing and wailing, he said, it would show that he did not understand anything about fate. So he stopped.
lesson: Grief is natural, but seeing a death as part of the larger pattern of life can loosen its grip over time. Mourning and acceptance can follow one another.
people: Zhuangzi, Huizi
source: Zhuangzi, Chapter 18 (Zhi Le, Perfect Happiness)

title: The King Who Spared the Ox
text:
King Xuan of Qi asked Mencius whether someone like him could become a true king who protects his people. Mencius said yes, and gave a reason. He had heard that the king, sitting in his hall, once saw an ox being led past. The animal was to be killed so its blood could consecrate a new bell. The king could not bear to watch it trembling like an innocent man going to execution, and ordered it released and a sheep used instead.

The king admitted it was true. His people, he said, thought he had done it out of stinginess, swapping a big animal for a small one. Mencius said he knew better: the king had seen the ox and not the sheep. The feeling that moved him was real compassion, and that feeling was enough to make a true king.

Then Mencius pressed his point. The king's kindness was enough to reach animals, yet its benefits did not reach his people. A man who could lift a heavy weight but claimed he could not lift a feather was not unable, only unwilling. The king's failure to care for his people was the same: not that he could not, but that he did not. He needed only to extend the heart he already had from the ox in front of him to everyone in his kingdom.
lesson: Most of us already feel care for the people right in front of us. The work of leadership is to extend that same care to those you do not see every day.
people: Mencius, King Xuan of Qi
source: Mencius, Book 1A, Chapter 7

title: Buying the Bones of a Fine Horse
text:
King Zhao of Yan came to the throne of a state that had just been ravaged by its neighbor Qi. He wanted to attract able men to help him rebuild and take revenge, and he asked the scholar Guo Wei how to do it. Guo Wei answered with a story.

A ruler of old offered a thousand pieces of gold for a horse that could run a thousand li in a day. Three years passed and no such horse was found. One of his attendants asked to try. Within three months he found one, but it had already died. He bought its head for five hundred pieces of gold and brought it back.

The ruler was furious at paying so much for a dead horse. The attendant explained that if the king would pay five hundred for a dead one, the world would conclude he would pay far more for a live one, and the horses would come. Within a year, three horses of a thousand li were brought to him.

"If Your Majesty truly wants to attract talent," Guo Wei said, "begin with me. If even I am honored, how much more will better men come." The king built a residence for Guo Wei and treated him as his teacher. Soon able men, among them the general Yue Yi, came to Yan from other states.
lesson: People decide whether to join you by watching how you treat those already with you. Visible respect for modest contributors is the best advertisement for attracting great ones.
people: Guo Wei, King Zhao of Yan, Yue Yi
source: Zhanguo Ce (Strategies of the Warring States), Yan

title: Mr. Nanguo and the Yu Ensemble
text:
The philosopher Han Fei tells this story. King Xuan of Qi loved music played on the yu, a mouth organ made of bamboo pipes, and he especially loved to hear it played by a great ensemble. He kept three hundred players, who always performed together.

A man called Mr. Nanguo asked to join. He could not play the yu at all, but he saw that among three hundred musicians, nobody would notice one who only pretended. The king was pleased to have another player and gave him the same pay and rations as the rest, which were generous. For years Mr. Nanguo sat with the ensemble, holding his instrument to his lips, swaying in time and collecting his wages.

Then King Xuan died, and his son, King Min, came to the throne. The new king also loved the yu, but he had different taste. He preferred to hear the players one at a time, each performing for him alone.

When Mr. Nanguo heard of the new arrangement, he slipped away and fled before his turn came.
lesson: A large group can hide someone who does not contribute, but only until each person's work is seen on its own. Make individual contributions visible.
people: Mr. Nanguo, King Xuan of Qi, King Min of Qi
source: Han Feizi, Inner Collections of Sayings, Upper Series (Nei Chu Shuo Shang)

title: The Foolish Old Man Who Moved the Mountains
text:
North of two great mountains, Taihang and Wangwu, lived a man called Yu Gong, the Foolish Old Man, who was nearly ninety. The mountains blocked the way from his house to the south, and every journey meant a long detour.

He gathered his family and proposed that they level the mountains. His wife doubted it: he could not even flatten a small hill, and where would they put all the earth and stones? The family decided to carry them to the shore of the Bohai Sea. Yu Gong, his sons and grandsons began breaking rocks and digging soil and hauling it away in baskets. A neighbor's young son, a boy of seven or eight, skipped along to help. A round trip took a whole season.

A man known as the Wise Old Man of the River Bend laughed at him. At his age, he said, he could not even pull up a blade of grass on the mountain.

Yu Gong sighed. "When I die, my sons will carry on. They will have sons, and those sons will have sons, without end. But the mountains will not grow any higher. Why can't they be leveled?" The wise man had no answer.

According to the story, the spirit of the mountains heard this and reported it to the Lord of Heaven, who was so moved that he had the two mountains carried away.
lesson: Work that is too big for one lifetime can still be done by a family that shares the goal across generations. Start the work, and teach the next generation why it matters.
people: Yu Gong, his family, Zhisou (the Wise Old Man of the River Bend)
date: c. 4th century BC to 4th century AD
source: Liezi, Chapter 5 (Tang Wen)
caveat: The Liezi's date is disputed, with many scholars placing its compilation around the 4th century AD.

title: Cook Ding Carves the Ox
text:
Cook Ding was cutting up an ox for Lord Wenhui. Every movement of his hand, every push of his shoulder, every step and every press of his knee was in rhythm, and his knife slid through with a sound like music, as if he were performing an ancient dance. Lord Wenhui was amazed and praised his skill.

Cook Ding put down his knife and said that what he cared about was the Way, which goes beyond skill. When he first began cutting up oxen, all he could see was the whole ox. After three years, he no longer saw the whole ox. Now he met it with his spirit rather than his eyes. He followed the natural structure, slipping his blade through the big gaps and along the hollows, never touching a ligament, let alone a bone.

A good cook changes his knife once a year, because he cuts. An ordinary cook changes it once a month, because he hacks. Ding had used his knife for nineteen years and cut up thousands of oxen, and its edge was as fresh as if it had just come from the whetstone. Still, whenever he came to a difficult knot, he slowed down, looked carefully, and moved his blade very lightly until the meat fell apart like a clod of earth.

Lord Wenhui said that, hearing the cook, he had learned how to care for life.
lesson: Study the structure of a problem until you can work along its natural joints. Effort spent fighting the grain wears you out; effort that follows it lasts for years.
people: Cook Ding, Lord Wenhui
source: Zhuangzi, Chapter 3 (The Secret of Caring for Life)

title: The Frog in the Well
text:
A frog lived in an old, broken down well. One day a great turtle from the Eastern Sea passed by, and the frog called up to him, delighted to show off his home.

How happy I am here, the frog said. I can hop up onto the edge of the well and rest in the gaps of the broken bricks. I can swim in the water up to my armpits, and wade in the mud up to my ankles. Look at the crabs and tadpoles: none of them can match me. I am master of all this water and all this well. Why not come in and see for yourself?

The turtle tried. But before his left foot was even in, his right knee was already stuck fast in the narrow opening. He backed out carefully and told the frog about the sea.

Its width, he said, could not be measured in a thousand miles, nor its depth in a thousand fathoms. In the time of the great Yu there were floods nine years out of ten, and the sea did not rise. In the time of Tang there were droughts seven years out of eight, and it did not sink. That was the joy of the Eastern Sea.

When the frog heard this, he was struck dumb with astonishment and felt very small indeed.
lesson: What you can see from where you stand is not the whole world. Before declaring yourself the best or calling something impossible, find out what lies outside your well.
people: A frog, a turtle of the Eastern Sea
source: Zhuangzi, Chapter 17 (Autumn Floods)

title: Three in the Morning
text:
A man who kept monkeys fed them chestnuts every day. When food grew short, he went to the monkeys and announced a new arrangement: from now on they would get three chestnuts in the morning and four in the evening.

The monkeys were furious. They screamed and jumped about in protest.

So the keeper changed the offer. All right, he said, you can have four in the morning and three in the evening.

The monkeys were delighted and calmed down at once.

Nothing real had changed. They were getting seven chestnuts a day either way. But their anger had turned to joy simply because the same amount was presented in a different order. The keeper had gone along with what the monkeys wanted, and it cost him nothing.

Zhuangzi uses the story to make a point about argument. People wear themselves out insisting that things must be one way, without seeing that the matter is the same underneath. The wise person, he says, lets disputes rest in balance, accepts the monkeys' view where it does no harm, and walks two roads at once.
lesson: People react to how a deal is framed, not only to what it contains. When the substance is the same, letting the other side choose the framing can settle a fight at no cost.
people: A monkey keeper, his monkeys
source: Zhuangzi, Chapter 2 (Discussion on Making All Things Equal)
caveat: A version of the same story also appears in the Liezi, where the keeper is a man of Song.

title: Wheelwright Pian and Duke Huan
text:
Duke Huan was reading a book up in his hall, while below, in the courtyard, a wheelwright named Pian was chiseling a wheel. Pian put down his tools, went up the steps and asked the duke what he was reading.

"The words of the sages," said the duke. "Are the sages still alive?" asked Pian. "They are dead." "Then what you are reading is only the dregs of the ancients."

The duke was angry. How dare a wheelwright comment on his reading? "If you can explain yourself, well and good. If not, you die."

Pian answered from his own trade. When he cut a wheel, if he worked too slowly the chisel slid and did not bite, and if he worked too fast it jammed and stuck. Not too slow and not too fast: he got it in his hand and felt it in his heart. He could not put it into words. There was a knack to it, but he could not teach it even to his own son, and his son could not learn it from him. That was why, at seventy, he was still making wheels himself. The ancients, he said, died along with what they could not pass on, so what the duke was reading was only their dregs.
lesson: Books and reports cannot give you the judgment that comes from doing the work. If you lead people who make things, spend time where the work happens and learn from those whose hands know it.
people: Duke Huan, Wheelwright Pian
source: Zhuangzi, Chapter 13 (The Way of Heaven)

title: Feng Xuan Buys Righteousness
text:
Lord Mengchang of Qi, in the 3rd century BC, kept thousands of retainers in his household. One of them, Feng Xuan, arrived poor and seemed to have no talents. The Strategies of the Warring States says he kept complaining by singing to his sword about having no fish to eat, no carriage and no means to support his mother, and Lord Mengchang provided each.

One day the lord needed someone to collect the debts owed to him by the people of his fief at Xue. Feng Xuan volunteered and asked what he should buy with the money. Lord Mengchang told him to buy whatever his household lacked. At Xue, Feng Xuan called together the debtors and checked their tallies. Then he announced, in his lord's name, that all the debts were forgiven, and he burned the tallies. The people cheered the lord's name.

Feng Xuan returned empty handed and explained that the lord's house had treasures, horses and beautiful women but lacked righteousness, so he had bought him some. Lord Mengchang was displeased.

A year later the king of Qi dismissed Lord Mengchang, and his retainers deserted him. He retired to Xue. While he was still a long way off, the people came out on the road, old and young, to welcome him. Lord Mengchang turned to Feng Xuan and said that now he saw the righteousness he had been bought.
lesson: Goodwill is an investment that pays when you need it most. Generosity given without immediate return can become your safest refuge.
people: Feng Xuan, Lord Mengchang (Tian Wen)
source: Strategies of the Warring States (Zhanguo Ce), Strategies of Qi; also Sima Qian, Shiji, chapter 75 (as Feng Huan)

title: The Snipe and the Clam
text:
The state of Zhao was preparing to attack its neighbor Yan. The adviser Su Dai traveled to the court of Zhao and told King Huiwen a story.

On the way here, he said, as I crossed the Yi River, I saw a clam lying open on the bank, sunning itself. A snipe came along and pecked at its flesh. The clam snapped its shell shut and caught the bird's beak.

The snipe said: if it does not rain today, and does not rain tomorrow, there will be a dead clam. The clam answered: if I do not let you out today, and do not let you out tomorrow, there will be a dead snipe. Neither would give way. Then a fisherman came along and took them both.

Now, Su Dai said, Zhao is about to attack Yan. If the two states wear each other down in a long war, I fear that powerful Qin will be the fisherman. He asked the king to think carefully.

King Huiwen agreed that he was right, and called off the attack.
lesson: Before locking yourself into a fight with a rival, look around for the third party who gains when you both exhaust yourselves.
people: Su Dai, King Huiwen of Zhao
location: States of Zhao and Yan, Ancient China
source: Zhanguo Ce (Strategies of the Warring States), Yan section

title: Lian Po Carries Thorns to Lin Xiangru
text:
In the 3rd century BC, in the kingdom of Zhao, Lian Po was a famous general. Lin Xiangru had begun as a household retainer, but he twice outfaced the powerful king of Qin in diplomacy, once by bringing the precious He jade back safely and once at the meeting at Mianchi. King Huiwen rewarded him with a rank above Lian Po.

Sima Qian records that Lian Po was furious. He had won his rank fighting, he said, while this upstart had only used his tongue, and he swore to humiliate Lin if they met. Lin Xiangru avoided him. He pleaded illness to skip court, and once turned his carriage aside when he saw Lian Po coming. His own followers felt ashamed and wanted to leave him.

Lin explained that he had not feared the king of Qin, so he did not fear Lian Po. But Qin left Zhao alone only because the two of them were there; if they fought, Qin would profit. He put the state first and private grudges last. When Lian Po heard this, he bared his back, carried a bundle of thorny branches, and went to Lin's gate to beg punishment. The two became friends ready to die for each other.
lesson: When a rival attacks your pride, ask what the fight would cost the people you both serve. And when you realize you were wrong, apologize openly and in person.
people: Lian Po, Lin Xiangru, King Huiwen of Zhao
location: Handan, State of Zhao (modern Hebei, China)
source: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), chapter 81, Biographies of Lian Po and Lin Xiangru

title: Pyrrhus and the Costly Victory
text:
In 280 BC King Pyrrhus of Epirus, one of the finest generals of his age, crossed to Italy to help the Greek city of Tarentum against Rome. He brought a professional army trained in the Macedonian style, together with war elephants, which the Romans had never faced. He beat the Romans at Heraclea, but at heavy cost.

In 279 BC the two sides met again near Asculum in Apulia. Plutarch says that the fighting went on over two days. On the first day the wooded, broken ground hampered Pyrrhus's cavalry and elephants. On the second he seized level ground, and his phalanx and elephants finally drove the Romans back to their camp. Plutarch cites figures of six thousand Roman dead, while Pyrrhus's own records admitted about 3,500 of his men.

The numbers favored Pyrrhus, but the arithmetic did not. Plutarch reports that when someone congratulated him on the victory, Pyrrhus replied that one more such victory would utterly undo him. He had lost a large part of the army he had brought from Greece, along with most of his friends and chief commanders, and he could not replace them. Rome, by contrast, refilled its legions quickly from its large manpower, as if from a fountain, and its anger only grew.

Pyrrhus soon left for Sicily, and in 275 BC he returned to Greece. His name became a word for a victory that costs more than it gains.
lesson: Count the cost of winning, not only the result. A victory that drains resources you cannot replace may set you up to lose the larger contest.
people: Pyrrhus of Epirus
source: Plutarch, Life of Pyrrhus 21

title: Fabricius Warns Pyrrhus of Poison
text:
In 280 and 279 BC King Pyrrhus of Epirus invaded Italy to help the Greek city of Tarentum against Rome, and won two costly battles. Plutarch says the Roman envoy Gaius Fabricius impressed Pyrrhus deeply: he refused the king's offers of gold and could not be startled even when Pyrrhus had an elephant suddenly trumpet behind him.

The next year Fabricius was consul. According to Plutarch, a man came to the Roman camp with a letter from the king's own physician, offering to poison Pyrrhus and end the war if Rome paid him well. Fabricius was disgusted. With his fellow consul he wrote to Pyrrhus to warn him. The letter told the king he seemed to judge badly both his friends and his enemies, since he was at war with honest men and trusted villains. The Romans added that they were not telling him out of favor, but so that no one could say Rome had won by treachery because it could not win by force.

Pyrrhus investigated, punished the physician and sent his Roman prisoners home without ransom. Rome, not wanting to be in his debt, freed an equal number of his allies' prisoners in return.
lesson: Win honestly, even against an enemy. Refusing a dirty shortcut protects your own name, and decency can earn more from an opponent than betrayal ever would.
people: Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, Quintus Aemilius Papus, Pyrrhus of Epirus
source: Plutarch, Life of Pyrrhus 20 to 21
caveat: Ancient writers tell different versions of the plot and the traitor's identity.

title: Mending the Pen After the Sheep Are Lost
text:
Zhuang Xin, a minister of Chu, warned King Xiang that the court was in danger. The king surrounded himself with flattering favorites, lived in luxury and ignored the affairs of state, while the powerful state of Qin was watching. If this went on, Zhuang Xin said, Chu would fall.

The king was offended. He asked whether the old man had gone senile, or was trying to spread evil omens about the kingdom. Zhuang Xin replied that he was only saying what he saw, and asked permission to withdraw to the state of Zhao to wait and watch. The king let him go.

Within months, Qin attacked. The armies of Qin captured city after city, including Ying, the capital of Chu, and the king was forced to flee. In exile, he remembered the warning and sent for Zhuang Xin, asking him what could still be done.

Zhuang Xin answered with a saying. To see the hare and then turn to call the dog is not too late. To lose the sheep and then mend the pen is not too late. Chu, he said, had lost a great deal, but it still held thousands of miles of land. If the king mended his ways now, the state could still be saved.
lesson: After a first loss, do not despair and do not pretend nothing happened. Fix the weakness that caused it while you still have something left to protect.
people: Zhuang Xin, King Xiang of Chu
source: Zhanguo Ce (Strategies of the Warring States), Chu section
caveat: The dialogue comes from the Zhanguo Ce, a collection of persuasion stories whose details are not always reliable history.

title: Ashoka's Remorse After Kalinga
text:
Around 261 BC, eight years after his coronation, the Mauryan emperor Ashoka conquered Kalinga, a kingdom on the east coast of India in what is now Odisha. It was the only major war of his reign, and he won it.

We know what he felt about it because he said so himself, in an inscription carved on rock and set up in many parts of his empire, known as Rock Edict XIII. In it Ashoka states that 150,000 people were carried away from Kalinga, 100,000 were killed, and many times that number died. He writes that he felt deep remorse, because conquering an unconquered country meant killing, death and the deportation of people, and that this weighed heavily on him. He grieved also for the good people, priests and families caught up in it.

The edict announces that the only conquest he now valued was conquest by dhamma, a moral law of compassion, honesty and respect for all. In the years that followed Ashoka issued edicts promoting tolerance between religious groups, care for the sick, wells and shade trees along roads, and restraint in killing animals. He did not launch another war of conquest.
lesson: Look honestly at the full cost of your wins, including who paid it. What you learn may change how you choose to use your power.
people: Ashoka
source: Ashoka, Rock Edict XIII
