title: The Voyage of the Argonauts
text:
In the epic by Apollonius of Rhodes, Jason was sent by his uncle, King Pelias, to fetch the Golden Fleece from Colchis, at the far eastern end of the Black Sea. He could not do it alone, so he gathered the greatest heroes of Greece to sail with him on the Argo, a ship built by Argus with the help of the goddess Athena.

The crew was chosen for its gifts as much as its courage. Tiphys was the helmsman. Lynceus could see farther than any other man. Orpheus played music that calmed the sea and set the rowers' rhythm. Zetes and Calais, the winged sons of the North Wind, chased off the Harpies who were tormenting the blind prophet Phineus. Polydeuces, the boxer, beat a brutal king who challenged every stranger to a fight.

In return Phineus told them how to pass the Clashing Rocks: release a dove first, and if it got through, row with everything they had. They did, and the Argo made it through, losing only the tip of its stern. Even the strongest of them, Heracles, was left behind early on, when he went searching for his lost companion Hylas and the ship sailed without him. The voyage went on without its greatest fighter, carried by everyone else.
lesson: A strong crew is built from different gifts, each used at the right moment. No single star, however strong, is indispensable if the rest of the team works as one.
people: Jason, Tiphys, Lynceus, Orpheus, Zetes, Calais, Polydeuces, Heracles, Phineus
location: Alexandria (Egypt); voyage from Greece to Colchis (modern Georgia)
source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica, Books 1 and 2

title: Waiting by the Stump for a Hare
text:
In the state of Song there was a farmer who had a tree stump standing in the middle of his field. One day, while he was working, a hare came racing across the field, ran headlong into the stump, broke its neck and died.

The farmer picked it up and took it home. It was a free meal, gained without any effort at all. It seemed to him a much better way to get food than plowing.

So he put down his plow and stopped working the field. Every day he sat beside the stump and waited for another hare to come running into it. Days passed, then weeks. No hare came. His field went to weeds, and he became the laughingstock of the whole state of Song.

The philosopher Han Fei, who told this story in the third century BC, used it against the rulers of his day who wanted to govern by copying the methods of the ancient sage kings. Times had changed, he argued. Hoping that the old ways would work again because they once worked was exactly like waiting by the stump for another hare.
lesson: Do not build a strategy on a single lucky outcome. What worked once by chance, or in a different age, needs to be tested again before you bet on it.
people: A farmer of Song
source: Han Feizi, Chapter 49 (The Five Vermin)

title: The Banyan Deer King
text:
The king of Benares loved hunting deer so much that he forced his subjects to leave their fields to drive game for him. To free themselves, the people built a great enclosure in the royal park and herded two whole herds of deer into it. One herd was led by the Banyan Deer, the future Buddha, and the other by the Branch Deer. The king spared both leaders but hunted the rest, and many deer were wounded in the chase.

To end the needless suffering, the two deer kings agreed that each day one deer would go by lot to the chopping block, taken in turn from each herd. One day the lot fell on a pregnant doe from the Branch Deer's herd. She asked to wait until her fawn was born, but her leader refused. She went to the Banyan Deer, who told her to go back to her herd. Then he walked to the block himself and laid his head on it.

The cook ran to the king, who came and asked why the deer king he had spared was there. The Banyan Deer explained. The king, moved, granted life to him and the doe. The Banyan Deer then asked for the same for the rest of the deer, and step by step for all four-footed creatures, birds and fish, until the king had granted protection to all of them.
lesson: Rules that sacrifice the weakest are easy to accept until someone with standing refuses to. A leader willing to take the cost personally can change what those above him consider normal.
people: The Bodhisatta as the Banyan Deer king, the Branch Deer, a pregnant doe, the king of Benares
source: Jataka 12 (Nigrodhamiga Jataka)

title: The Hare in the Moon
text:
In this tale of one of the Buddha's earlier lives, he was born as a wise hare living in a forest with three friends: a monkey, a jackal and an otter. The hare taught them to keep the holy days and to give food to anyone who asked.

On one holy day each friend went looking for something to give. The otter found fish left on a river bank, the jackal found some meat and a pot of curds, and the monkey picked mangoes. The hare had only grass, and nobody eats grass. So he decided that if a beggar came, he would give his own body.

Sakka, king of the gods, heard of this resolve and came down disguised as a hungry brahmin. The others gave him their food. When he reached the hare, the hare told him to light a fire. Then the hare shook himself three times so that no small creature in his fur would die with him, and leapt into the flames.

The fire did not burn him; it felt cool as snow. Sakka revealed himself and, so that the hare's goodness would be remembered for an age, pressed a mountain to squeeze out its essence and drew the outline of a hare on the face of the moon.
lesson: Generosity is measured by what it costs the giver, not by the size of the gift. Give what you truly have, even if it seems small.
people: The Bodhisatta as a hare, Sakka
source: Jataka 316 (Sasa Jataka)

title: The Jackal and the Otters
text:
Two otters were hunting along a river. One of them, swimming in deep water, seized a huge fish, so big and strong that it began to drag him under. He called to his partner, and together they wrestled the fish to the bank and killed it.

Then the trouble began. Each otter said the fish was his. One had caught it, the other had saved it. They quarrelled loudly and could not agree how to divide it.

Just then a jackal came down to the river to drink. The otters asked him to settle their dispute. The jackal sat down with a judicious air and gave his verdict. To the otter who had swum along the bank he gave the tail. To the one who had gone into the deep water he gave the head. "And the middle," he said, "goes to the judge for his fee." He picked up the whole fat body of the fish and trotted off with it.

The two otters sat looking at a head and a tail. They admitted that had they not quarrelled, the whole fish would have fed them both for days.
lesson: When partners fight over shares, an outsider often ends up with the best part. Settle disagreements between yourselves before you need someone else to do it.
people: Two otters, a jackal
source: Jataka 400 (Dabbhapuppha Jataka)

title: The Monkey Gardeners
text:
In the royal park at Benares, a festival was announced, and the king's gardener wanted to go and enjoy it with everyone else. But the young trees in the park needed watering. So he went to the monkeys who lived there and asked their king if his monkeys would water the saplings while he was gone. The monkey king agreed.

When the gardener had left, the monkey king gave his orders. Water was precious, he said, so they must not waste it. Before watering each tree, they should pull it up and look at its roots. Trees with long roots need a lot of water, and trees with short roots need only a little.

The monkeys set to work with great diligence. They pulled up every sapling, examined the roots, gave each one carefully measured water, and planted it again.

A wise man passing through the park saw what they were doing and asked why. When they explained, he remarked that fools who try to do good end up doing harm. The young trees, uprooted one by one, withered and died.
lesson: Following a sensible rule without understanding its purpose can wreck the thing it was meant to protect. Make sure the people carrying out your plan understand what it is for.
people: Monkeys and their king, the king's gardener, the Bodhisatta
source: Jataka 46 (Aramadusaka Jataka)

title: The Monkey King's Bridge
text:
In this Jataka tale the future Buddha was born as the king of a troop of eighty thousand monkeys. They lived in a great mango tree on the bank of the Ganges, whose fruit was so sweet that the monkey king had them strip every mango from the branches over the water, so none would float downstream and reveal the tree to men. One fruit was missed.

It drifted down to Benares, where King Brahmadatta tasted it and set out with his men to find the tree. They surrounded it at night, planning to shoot the monkeys at dawn. The monkey king leapt across the river, tied one end of a long cane to a tree on the far bank and the other around his own waist, and jumped back. The cane fell short. So he gripped a branch of the mango tree and stretched his own body to complete the bridge, and the whole troop ran across his back to safety.

The last to cross was a jealous monkey, the future Devadatta, who leapt down hard on his back and dealt him a mortal blow. King Brahmadatta had watched the whole night. He had the dying monkey king lowered gently, cared for him, and asked why he had done it. The monkey king said that a ruler must seek the welfare of those he rules, and he died content.
lesson: Leadership is tested when the plan falls short and someone has to close the gap personally. People follow, and even opponents respect, the person who takes the strain so others can cross.
people: The Bodhisatta as monkey king, King Brahmadatta of Benares, Devadatta
source: Jataka 407 (Mahakapi Jataka)

title: The Partridge, the Monkey and the Elephant
text:
Near a great banyan tree in the Himalayan foothills lived three friends: a partridge, a monkey and an elephant. They often fell out, and none treated the others with respect. At last they decided that life would go better if they agreed to honor the eldest among them. But who was the eldest?

The elephant spoke first. When he was a young calf, he said, this banyan was only a bush, and as he walked over it, its top branches brushed his belly. The monkey said that when he was a baby, he sat on the ground and nibbled the shoots at the very top of the young tree. The partridge then explained that long ago there had been another great banyan elsewhere. He had eaten its fruit and dropped a seed here, and from that seed this very tree had grown.

So the partridge was the oldest. The monkey and the elephant honored him and followed his advice, and the three lived together in harmony from then on. In the Jataka, the Buddha tells this story to his monks when they fail to give their senior members proper lodging.
lesson: Groups argue less when they agree in advance on a fair rule for who decides. A clear, shared order of respect can settle disputes before they start.
people: A partridge, a monkey, an elephant
source: Jataka 37 (Tittira Jataka); Vinaya, Cullavagga 6.6

title: The Quarreling Quails
text:
The Jataka tells that the future Buddha was once born as a quail and led a large flock in the forest. A fowler had learned to imitate the call of quails. When the birds gathered at his call, he threw his net over them, stuffed them in his basket, and sold them.

The leader of the flock taught the others a defense. When the net fell, each quail should push its head through a mesh, and then all should fly up together, carrying the net, and drop it on a thornbush. They could then slip out underneath. It worked. Day after day the fowler threw his net and watched it fly away, and he came home empty-handed and had to free it from the thorns.

Then one day, as the quails landed to feed, one bird accidentally stepped on another's head. The second bird snapped at him, and soon they were arguing over who lifted the net and who did not. The leader saw what this meant and took the wise birds away with him to another place. The next time the fowler cast his net, the quarreling quails each waited for the others to lift it. He gathered them all up and carried them off.
lesson: A team's best method only works while its members still trust one another. Quarrels about who does the most can destroy the cooperation that keeps everyone safe.
people: The Bodhisatta as a quail, the quail flock, a fowler
source: Jataka 33 (Sammodamana Jataka)

title: Sama Cares for His Blind Parents
text:
In the forest near the Migasammata river lived two ascetics, husband and wife, with their only son, Sama. When Sama was still a boy, his parents were caught in a rainstorm and took shelter under a tree on top of an anthill. Water dripping from their bodies fell on a snake below, and its angry breath blinded them both.

From then on Sama looked after them completely. He fetched water and fruit, cleaned their hut, and stretched ropes between the hut and the river so that his parents could find their way. He was so gentle that the deer of the forest walked with him.

One day, as he filled his water jar, Piliyakkha, the king of Benares, out hunting, shot him with a poisoned arrow. As he lay dying, Sama's only concern was for his parents: who would care for them now? Stricken with remorse, the king went to the hut himself, told them what had happened, and promised to serve them as their son had.

The parents asked to be led to Sama's body. There they made a solemn act of truth, declaring his goodness to his parents. A goddess who had loved Sama in an earlier life added her own. The poison left him, Sama rose alive, and his parents' sight was restored.
lesson: Caring for aging parents is not a burden to hide but one of the most honorable things a person can do. Steady, daily care matters more than grand gestures.
people: Sama, his blind parents Dukulaka and Parika, King Piliyakkha
source: Jataka 540 (Sama Jataka, also called Suvannasama Jataka)
caveat: The collection was written down centuries after the Buddha, and the dating of individual tales is uncertain.

title: The Man Who Lost His Axe
text:
A man in ancient China lost his axe and could not find it anywhere. He began to suspect his neighbor's son.

Once the thought had come to him, he watched the boy closely. The way the boy walked looked like the walk of a man who had stolen an axe. His expression looked like the expression of a man who had stolen an axe. The way he spoke sounded exactly like the way a thief speaks. Everything the boy did, every gesture and every look, seemed to show that he was the one who had taken it.

Some time later the man was digging in his own garden, or in some versions clearing a ditch in his own valley, and his spade struck metal. It was his axe, lying where he himself had dropped it.

The next day he saw the neighbor's son again. Now nothing about the boy's walk, his face or his manner looked in the least like a thief.
lesson: Once you suspect someone, you start reading every small sign as proof. Check the facts before you let a suspicion color how you see a person.
people: A man, his neighbor's son
date: c. 4th century BC to 4th century AD
source: Liezi, Chapter 8 (Shuo Fu); a version also in the Lushi Chunqiu
caveat: The dating of the Liezi is disputed; parts of it may have been compiled as late as the 4th century AD.

title: Regulus Returns to Carthage
text:
During the First Punic War the Roman general Marcus Atilius Regulus invaded Africa and was defeated and captured by the Carthaginians in 255 BC.

According to the story told by Cicero and later Roman writers, some years later the Carthaginians sent him to Rome with their envoys to arrange an exchange of prisoners, after making him swear that he would return to Carthage if the exchange failed. In Rome, Cicero says, Regulus refused to speak in the Senate as a citizen at first, since he considered himself a prisoner. Then he argued against the exchange. The Carthaginian prisoners were young and capable commanders, he said, while he was old and worn out. Returning them would harm Rome.

The Senate followed his advice. His family and friends begged him to stay. Regulus kept his oath and went back to Carthage, where, the story says, he was put to death by cruel tortures.

Cicero held him up in On Duties as the model of a man who kept his word to an enemy because an oath is an oath. The poet Horace describes him pushing through the crowd of relatives who tried to hold him back.
lesson: Keep your word even when breaking it would be easy and no one could force you. Promises kept at a cost are what make trust possible.
people: Marcus Atilius Regulus
source: Cicero, De Officiis, Book 3, chapters 99 to 115; Horace, Odes, Book 3, Ode 5
caveat: Polybius does not mention the embassy or the torture, and many historians consider them Roman legend.

title: Eratosthenes Measures the Earth
text:
Around 240 BC Eratosthenes, librarian of the great library at Alexandria, set out to measure the size of the Earth without leaving Egypt. Greek scholars already accepted that the Earth was a sphere. The question was how big.

The method is described by the later astronomer Cleomedes. Eratosthenes had learned that at Syene, in the south of Egypt, on the day of the summer solstice the noon sun shone straight down, so that upright objects cast no shadow. On the same day at noon in Alexandria, farther north, a vertical pointer in a bowl-shaped sundial did cast a short shadow. He measured the angle of that shadow at about one fiftieth of a full circle.

Assuming that the sun was so far away that its rays arrive parallel, and that Syene lay due south of Alexandria, the angle of the shadow equals the angle between the two cities at the center of the Earth. So the distance between them must be one fiftieth of the Earth's circumference. Taking that distance as 5,000 stadia, he multiplied by fifty and arrived at 250,000 stadia.

We do not know exactly which stadium length he used, so his precise accuracy is debated. But depending on the conversion, his figure falls fairly close to the true circumference, an astonishing result from a shadow, a distance and a piece of geometry.
lesson: A problem that seems too large to handle directly can often be solved by finding a small, measurable piece connected to it by sound reasoning.
people: Eratosthenes of Cyrene
source: Cleomedes, On the Circular Motions of the Celestial Bodies 1.7
caveat: The length of the stadium Eratosthenes used is uncertain, so claims about how accurate he was vary.

title: Marking the Boat to Find the Sword
text:
A man from the state of Chu was crossing a river by boat. Partway across, his sword slipped from its scabbard and fell over the side into the water.

He did not panic. Instead, he took out a knife and carefully cut a notch in the side of the boat, at the exact place where the sword had gone over. That, he said, is where my sword fell.

The boat sailed on and came to land on the far bank. Then the man went to the notch he had made, jumped into the water at that spot, and began searching the riverbed for his sword.

Of course he did not find it. The boat had moved; the sword had not. Looking for it this way, the text remarks, was surely a muddle.

The compilers of the Lushi Chunqiu, writing for the court of Qin in the third century BC, put this story in a chapter arguing that a ruler must examine the present instead of slavishly copying the laws of former kings. Governing a state with the old laws, they wrote, is just like this. The times have moved on, but the laws have not, and to govern that way is very difficult.
lesson: When circumstances change, your reference points change with them. Do not keep searching for answers where they used to be.
people: A man of Chu
source: Lushi Chunqiu, chapter Cha Jin (Examining the Present)

title: Fabius the Delayer
text:
In 217 BC Hannibal destroyed a Roman army at Lake Trasimene, and Rome in panic named Quintus Fabius Maximus dictator. Fabius decided not to fight Hannibal in open battle at all. Instead he followed the Carthaginian army along the hills, camping on high ground, cutting off foragers and stragglers, and denying Hannibal the decisive victory he needed. Hannibal was far from home, and every month without a battle wore his army down.

The strategy made Fabius hated. Plutarch says the soldiers called him Hannibal's pedagogue, the slave who trails after a child, and his own master of horse, Minucius, mocked him as a coward. Hannibal made it worse by sparing Fabius's estates while burning everything around them, to make him look like a traitor. The people gave Minucius equal command. Minucius soon attacked rashly and was trapped, and Fabius came down from the hills and saved him. Plutarch reports that Minucius then called Fabius father and put himself under his command again.

When Fabius's term ended, Rome returned to pitched battle, and in 216 BC lost a huge army at Cannae. After that disaster the Romans went back to his method of avoiding battle with Hannibal while wearing him down. The poet Ennius later wrote that one man, by delaying, restored the state, and Fabius kept the nickname Cunctator, the Delayer.
lesson: Against a stronger opponent who needs a quick win, refusing the fight he wants can be your best move. Expect to be called timid while it works.
people: Quintus Fabius Maximus, Marcus Minucius Rufus, Hannibal
source: Plutarch, Life of Fabius Maximus 5 to 13; Livy, History of Rome, book 22

title: Hannibal's Trap at Cannae
text:
On 2 August 216 BC, near the village of Cannae in southern Italy, the largest army Rome had ever fielded faced Hannibal. The Romans, under the consuls Varro and Aemilius Paullus, had roughly eighty thousand men. Hannibal had about fifty thousand, but more and better cavalry.

Polybius describes Hannibal's deployment. He placed his Gallic and Spanish infantry in the center in a line that bulged forward toward the Romans. On each side of them, set back, stood his veteran African infantry. His cavalry held the wings. The Romans, trusting in weight, packed their legions deep and narrow and pushed straight at the center.

The bulge gave ground slowly as planned, bending back into a hollow. The Roman mass followed it in, pressing tighter. Then the African infantry on either side turned inward and attacked the Roman flanks. Meanwhile Hannibal's cavalry, under Hasdrubal, had routed the Roman horse and swung around to strike the Roman rear. The Romans were surrounded and so crowded that many could not use their weapons.

Polybius says about seventy thousand Romans died, including Paullus, while Hannibal lost under six thousand. Cannae became the textbook example of encirclement, studied by generals for two thousand years.
lesson: Let an opponent's strength carry him where you want him. A part that yields on purpose can be the hinge of the whole plan.
people: Hannibal Barca, Hasdrubal, Gaius Terentius Varro, Lucius Aemilius Paullus
source: Polybius, Histories 3.107 to 3.117; Livy, History of Rome, book 22
caveat: Ancient casualty figures for Cannae are likely inflated; modern estimates vary.

title: Archimedes Defends Syracuse
text:
In 214 BC the Roman general Marcellus attacked Syracuse, the great Greek city of Sicily, by land and sea. He expected a quick success. Instead, Polybius and Plutarch say, he met the machines of Archimedes, the city's aged mathematician.

Catapults of different ranges threw stones and missiles, so that ships were struck at every distance as they approached. When Roman ships came close under the sea walls, cranes swung out and dropped heavy weights on them. Other machines lowered an iron grip, often called the claw, that hooked a ship's prow, lifted it out of the water and let it fall, so that it capsized or was smashed. Marcellus's floating siege tower on lashed ships was wrecked. On land, attackers were struck by missiles through small openings in the walls.

Plutarch writes that the Romans became so frightened that if they saw a rope or a beam projecting over the wall, they turned and fled, shouting that Archimedes was about to use some engine on them. Marcellus gave up assault and settled down to a blockade.

The city held out for more than two years. In 212 BC the Romans took part of it by surprise during a festival, and the rest fell soon after. In the sack, Archimedes was killed by a Roman soldier, reportedly while absorbed in a geometric problem. Plutarch says Marcellus was grieved by his death.
lesson: Ingenuity can multiply the strength of a small side, but it buys time rather than certainty. Use the time it buys to solve the larger problem.
people: Archimedes, Marcus Claudius Marcellus
source: Polybius, Histories 8.3 to 8.7; Plutarch, Life of Marcellus 14 to 19
caveat: The story that Archimedes burned Roman ships with mirrors appears only in much later writers and is probably legend.

title: The First Emperor Burns the Books
text:
In 221 BC the king of Qin conquered the last of his rivals and became Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor of a unified China. His chancellor, Li Si, helped him replace the old feudal states with a centralized system of provinces.

In 213 BC, according to the historian Sima Qian, a scholar named Chunyu Yue spoke at a court banquet and urged the emperor to follow the ancient model of granting fiefs to his sons, warning that anything not modeled on antiquity would not last. Li Si answered that scholars who used the past to criticize the present were confusing the people. He proposed that the histories of the other states be burned, that private copies of the classic Book of Songs and Book of Documents be handed over and burned, and that anyone who discussed them or used the past to criticize the present be executed. Books on medicine, divination and agriculture were spared. The emperor approved.

The next year, Sima Qian says, the emperor had more than four hundred and sixty scholars put to death for criticizing him.

The dynasty did not last. The First Emperor died in 210 BC, Li Si was executed in a court intrigue, and the Qin collapsed in 206 BC.
lesson: Silencing critics removes the warnings you most need. A leader who cannot bear to hear the past questioned cannot see the future coming.
people: Qin Shi Huang, Li Si, Chunyu Yue
source: Sima Qian, Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), chapters 6 and 87
caveat: Some historians think Han writers exaggerated the scale of the burning and the killing of scholars to discredit the Qin.

title: The Continence of Scipio
text:
In 209 BC the young Roman general Publius Cornelius Scipio captured New Carthage, the Carthaginian base in Spain. Among the prisoners, Livy says, his soldiers brought him a young woman of extraordinary beauty.

Scipio learned that she was engaged to a young Celtiberian chieftain named Allucius, who loved her deeply. He sent for her parents and her fiance. He told Allucius that she had been kept as carefully as if she were in her own parents' house, and that she was returned to him untouched. All he asked in return was that Allucius be a friend to the Roman people.

Her parents had brought a large sum of gold to ransom her. They begged Scipio to accept it as a gift. He had the gold laid at his feet, then gave it to Allucius as a wedding present.

Allucius went home and praised Scipio to his people as a godlike young man. A few days later, according to Livy, he returned to the Roman camp with fourteen hundred horsemen to serve under him. The historian Polybius tells a simpler version of the same story, without names. The scene was painted by many later artists as The Continence of Scipio.
lesson: Generosity toward the defeated can win loyalty that force never could. People remember how you treated them when you held all the power.
people: Scipio Africanus, Allucius
source: Livy, History of Rome 26.50; Polybius, Histories 10.19
caveat: The episode may have been polished by Roman writers to glorify Scipio.

title: Calling a Deer a Horse
text:
After the First Emperor of Qin died in 210 BC, the eunuch Zhao Gao helped put a weak younger son on the throne as the Second Emperor. Zhao Gao gradually made himself the real power at court, eliminating rivals, including the chancellor Li Si.

Sima Qian tells how, in 207 BC, Zhao Gao decided to find out which officials would dare oppose him. He brought a deer to court, presented it to the Second Emperor and said it was a horse.

The emperor laughed and said that the chancellor must be mistaken, calling a deer a horse. He asked the officials around him. Some kept silent. Some said it was a horse, to please Zhao Gao. Some said it was a deer. Afterward, Zhao Gao found ways to have those who had said "deer" punished under the law. From then on, Sima Qian says, every official at court feared him.

With no one willing to tell him the truth, the Second Emperor did not learn how serious the rebellions in the empire had become. Within months Zhao Gao forced him to commit suicide, and the Qin dynasty fell soon after. "Pointing at a deer and calling it a horse" became a Chinese idiom.
lesson: When people are punished for stating the obvious, everyone stops telling you the truth. Make it safe to say "that is a deer".
people: Zhao Gao, Qin Er Shi (the Second Emperor)
source: Sima Qian, Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), chapter 6

title: Han Xin's Army With Its Back to the River
text:
In 204 BC, during the war that founded the Han dynasty, the general Han Xin marched against the kingdom of Zhao through the Jingxing pass. Zhao's commander Chen Yu waited with a far larger army and ignored an adviser who urged him to cut Han Xin's supply line in the narrow pass.

Sima Qian describes what Han Xin did next. At night he sent two thousand light horsemen, each carrying a red Han banner, to hide in the hills near the Zhao camp. He then placed ten thousand men with their backs to a river, a position every manual condemned. The Zhao officers laughed when they saw it.

At dawn Han Xin advanced with his own flags and drums, fought, then fell back to the troops at the river. The Zhao army poured out of its camp to finish him off. But with the river behind them, Han Xin's soldiers had nowhere to run and fought desperately. Meanwhile his hidden cavalry rode into the empty Zhao camp, tore down the Zhao flags and raised two thousand red banners. Seeing them, the Zhao troops believed their camp and king were taken and broke. Chen Yu was killed and the king of Zhao captured.

Asked afterward, Han Xin cited the military classics: put soldiers on deadly ground and they will survive.
lesson: Keeping an easy way out can weaken commitment. Sometimes the best way to get full effort from yourself or a team is to remove the fallback.
people: Han Xin, Chen Yu
source: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), chapter 92
caveat: Sima Qian's figures for the size of the Zhao army are probably exaggerated.

title: Han Xin Repays the Washerwoman
text:
As a young man in Huaiyin, in the late 3rd century BC, Han Xin was poor, idle and widely despised. He could not earn a living and often lived off other people. Sima Qian records that he went fishing under the city walls, where some old women were washing silk floss in the river. One of them saw he was starving and shared her food with him every day for several weeks until the washing was done.

Han Xin was delighted and promised he would repay her richly one day. She was angry. A grown man who could not feed himself, she said: she had fed him out of pity, not in hope of any reward.

Years later Han Xin had become one of the greatest generals in Chinese history, the man who won the wars that founded the Han dynasty. He was made King of Chu, ruling his home region. When he returned, he sought out the old washerwoman and gave her a thousand pieces of gold.
lesson: Remember who helped you when you had nothing and could offer nothing back. Repaying old kindness when you are able is one of the surest marks of character.
people: Han Xin
source: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), chapter 92, Biography of the Marquis of Huaiyin

title: Jambavan Reminds Hanuman of His Strength
text:
In the Ramayana, the monkey army was searching the south for Sita, Rama's wife, who had been carried off by the demon king Ravana. At last they reached the shore of the ocean and learned that she was held in Lanka, an island a hundred leagues across the sea. Nobody could see how to get there.

The leaders gathered on the beach, and one after another they said how far they could leap. One could manage ten leagues, another twenty, another more. Prince Angada thought he could reach Lanka but was unsure he could return. None of them was enough. Through all this, Hanuman sat apart and said nothing.

The old bear Jambavan, the wisest of the company, went over to him. He reminded Hanuman who he was: the son of the wind god, a match for the eagle Garuda in speed. He reminded him how, as a child, he had leaped into the sky to grab the rising sun, thinking it was a ripe fruit. Why, Jambavan asked, was he sitting silent when he alone could do this?

As Hanuman listened, he began to grow. He climbed Mount Mahendra, gathered his strength, and with the army cheering below, sprang out over the ocean toward Lanka.
lesson: Sometimes the person a team needs most does not know their own ability. Reminding a colleague what they have already done can unlock what the whole group needs.
people: Jambavan, Hanuman, Angada, the monkey army
date: c. 5th century BC to 3rd century AD (text)
source: Valmiki, Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda, cantos 65 to 67

title: The Brahmin's Wife and the Mongoose
text:
A brahmin and his wife had a baby son. On the same day a mongoose in the house had a young one, and the wife, who loved small creatures, raised the little mongoose alongside her child, feeding it milk and caring for it like a second son. Yet in her heart she never fully trusted it. It was a wild animal, she thought, and might one day turn on the baby.

One morning she needed to fetch water. She left the baby sleeping, told her husband to keep watch, and went out. But the brahmin soon went off to beg for alms and left the house empty.

While they were gone, a black snake slid out of a hole toward the cradle. The mongoose saw it, attacked, and after a fierce fight tore it to pieces. Proud of what it had done, it ran out to meet the mother, its mouth and paws smeared with blood.

When she saw the blood, she was sure it had killed her son. Without stopping to think, she threw her heavy water pot down on the mongoose and killed it. Then she ran inside, found her baby sleeping safely and the torn body of the snake beside the cradle, and broke down in grief over the loyal animal she had destroyed.
lesson: Fear and haste make us strike before we look. When something alarms you, take a moment to check what really happened before you act.
people: A brahmin's wife, her baby, a mongoose, a snake
source: Panchatantra, Book V (Aparikshitakarakam), frame story
caveat: The Panchatantra's date is uncertain, and versions differ on whether the brahmin or his wife kills the mongoose.

title: "These Are My Jewels"
text:
Cornelia was the daughter of Scipio Africanus, the general who defeated Hannibal. Widowed young, she refused to remarry (Plutarch says she even turned down a proposal from a king of Egypt) and devoted herself to raising her children. Of twelve, only three survived to adulthood, among them Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, who later became famous as reforming tribunes of the people.

Valerius Maximus, who collected memorable deeds and sayings for Roman readers in the first century AD, tells how a wealthy woman from Campania once stayed as a guest in Cornelia's house. The visitor showed off her jewelry, which was the most beautiful of its time. Cornelia kept her talking until her sons came home from school. Then she pointed to them and said: "These are my jewels."

Cornelia was known in Rome for her education and her letters, and Cicero and Quintilian both said her sons owed their fine speech to her. Plutarch writes that she took care to raise them so well that they were thought to owe their virtue more to their education than to their birth. After both sons were killed in political violence, she lived on at Misenum, receiving visitors and speaking of her sons without tears, Plutarch says, as she would speak of the heroes of old.
lesson: What we pour into our children's character is worth more than anything we can display. Time and attention spent on their education is an investment no jewel can match.
people: Cornelia, Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus
source: Valerius Maximus, Memorable Deeds and Sayings 4.4 (preface); Plutarch, Life of Tiberius Gracchus 1 and Life of Gaius Gracchus 19

title: The Old Man Who Lost His Horse
text:
Near China's northern frontier lived an old man skilled in reading signs. One day his horse ran away across the border into the land of the nomads. His neighbors came to console him. The old man said: how do you know this will not turn out to be good fortune?

Some months later the horse came back, bringing with it a fine nomad stallion. The neighbors came to congratulate him. The old man said: how do you know this will not turn out to be a misfortune?

Now there was a good horse in the family, and the old man's son loved to ride. One day he fell from the new horse and broke his hip, and he was left lame. The neighbors came to console him again. The old man said: how do you know this will not turn out to be good fortune?

A year later the nomads invaded in force. Every able bodied young man was called up to fight, and of those who went to the frontier, nine out of ten died. Because the son was lame, he was not taken, and father and son both survived.
lesson: Judge events slowly. A setback can open a door and a windfall can carry a hidden cost, so keep your balance and wait to see how things unfold.
people: An old man of the frontier (Sai Weng), his son
source: Huainanzi, Chapter 18 (In the World of Men)
caveat: The Huainanzi was compiled around 139 BC; the frontier man is a figure of the parable, not a recorded individual.

title: Zhang Qian's Thirteen-Year Mission
text:
Around 138 BC Emperor Wu of Han wanted allies against the Xiongnu, the nomadic empire that raided China's northern frontier. He had heard that a people called the Yuezhi, driven west by the Xiongnu, wanted revenge. He asked for volunteers to find them. Zhang Qian, a palace official, set out with more than a hundred men and a guide named Ganfu.

Sima Qian records what happened. Crossing Xiongnu territory, Zhang Qian was captured. He was held for more than ten years and given a Xiongnu wife, with whom he had a son. But he kept the staff that marked him as the Han emperor's envoy, and finally he escaped and continued west.

He passed through Dayuan, in the Ferghana valley, and Kangju, and found the Yuezhi settled in rich lands near Bactria. They no longer wanted war with the Xiongnu. His mission had failed. On the way home he was captured by the Xiongnu again, and held for more than a year before escaping in a time of turmoil.

In 126 BC he reached China with only Ganfu of the original party. His reports on the kingdoms, horses and trade routes of Central Asia led to Han expansion westward and the opening of the routes later called the Silk Road.
lesson: Stay loyal to your purpose through setbacks you cannot control. Even a mission that fails at its first goal can change the world through what you bring back.
people: Zhang Qian, Emperor Wu of Han, Ganfu
location: From Chang'an (modern Xi'an, China) to Central Asia
source: Sima Qian, Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), chapter 123; Ban Gu, Han Shu, chapter 61

title: Sima Qian Completes His Father's History
text:
Sima Tan was Grand Astrologer at the court of the Han emperor Wu, an office that also kept records. He had begun to compile a history of China from the earliest times. In 110 BC, when the emperor performed the great sacrifice at Mount Tai, Sima Tan fell ill and was left behind at Luoyang. His son Sima Qian found him dying there.

Sima Qian recorded the scene in the last chapter of his history. His father took his hand, wept, and charged him to become Grand Astrologer in his turn and to complete the history, so that the deeds of rulers and worthy men would not be forgotten. Sima Qian bowed and promised.

He took up his father's office. Then, in 99 BC, he spoke up at court in defense of a general, Li Ling, who had surrendered to the Xiongnu. The emperor was enraged, and Sima Qian was sentenced to death. He could have chosen death with honor. Instead he accepted castration, the most shameful punishment, so that he could live to finish the work.

In a letter to his friend Ren An, he explained that every man must die, but that some deaths weigh more than Mount Tai and others less than a feather. He could not die with his work unfinished. The result, the Records of the Grand Historian, became the model for Chinese history writing for two thousand years.
lesson: A promise to a parent can give strength to endure what seems unbearable. Some work is worth finishing because of whom we are finishing it for.
people: Sima Qian, Sima Tan, Emperor Wu of Han
source: Sima Qian, Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), chapter 130; Letter to Ren An (Han Shu 62)

title: Bharata Rules with Rama's Sandals
text:
King Dasharatha of Ayodhya had promised his queen Kaikeyi two wishes. When he prepared to crown his eldest son Rama, she asked that Rama be exiled to the forest for fourteen years and that her own son Bharata be made king instead. Bound by his word, the king agreed, and soon after he died of grief.

Bharata had been away. When he returned and learned what his mother had done, he was horrified. He refused the throne and set out with the army, the royal family and the citizens to find Rama in the forest and bring him back. He found him at Chitrakuta and begged him to return and rule.

Rama refused. He would not break their father's word. When nothing could move him, Bharata asked for Rama's sandals. He carried them back on his head, placed them on the throne, and governed in Rama's name from the village of Nandigrama outside the capital, living simply, dressed like a hermit, and reporting every matter to the sandals as if to the king.

When Rama returned after fourteen years, Bharata handed back the kingdom.
lesson: Sometimes you are given power you did not earn and should not keep. Hold it as a trustee: run things well, take nothing for yourself, and be ready to hand it back.
people: Bharata, Rama, Kaikeyi, Dasharatha
date: c. 5th century BC to 3rd century AD
source: Valmiki, Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda

title: Vibhishana's Counsel to Ravana
text:
Ravana, the king of Lanka, had carried off Sita, the wife of Rama. Now Rama had found where she was held, and an army of monkeys and bears stood on the shore ready to cross to the island. Ravana called his council. His ministers and generals flattered him and boasted that they would destroy Rama easily.

Only his younger brother Vibhishana spoke against the mood of the room. He reminded Ravana of the bad omens in the city and of what Hanuman, a single messenger, had already done when he set Lanka on fire. Taking another man's wife was a wrong, he said, and the way to save the kingdom was to return Sita to Rama.

Ravana's son Indrajit mocked Vibhishana as a coward. Ravana himself grew furious. He accused his brother of envying him and of siding with the enemy, and said that if anyone else had spoken like that he would have killed him on the spot. Vibhishana rose, told Ravana he had spoken only for his good, and left Lanka with four companions. He crossed to Rama, who welcomed him.

In the war that followed, Ravana's sons and brothers fell one by one, and finally Ravana himself. Vibhishana was crowned king of Lanka.
lesson: The people who disagree with you in the meeting are often the ones looking out for you. If you punish honest counsel, you will soon hear only what you want to hear.
people: Vibhishana, Ravana, Indrajit, Rama
date: c. 5th century BC to 3rd century AD
source: Valmiki, Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda

title: Honi and the Carob Tree
text:
The Talmud tells that Honi the Circle Maker was troubled by a verse in the Psalms about the return from exile: "We were like dreamers." Seventy years of exile, he wondered; can a person really dream for seventy years?

One day, walking along the road, he saw a man planting a carob tree. Honi asked him how long it would take for the tree to bear fruit. "Seventy years," the man said. Honi asked whether he really expected to live seventy years to eat from it.

The man answered that he had found the world full of carob trees. His ancestors had planted them for him, and he was planting this one for his own children.

Honi sat down to eat his bread, and sleep came over him. A rock formed around him, hiding him from sight, and he slept for seventy years. When he woke, he saw a man gathering fruit from the carob tree. He asked whether he was the one who had planted it. "I am his grandson," the man said.

Honi went home and to the study house, but no one believed he was Honi, and no one treated him with the respect he was used to. Grieving, he prayed for death, and died.
lesson: Much of what we enjoy was planted by people who never saw it bear fruit. Do something today for grandchildren you may never meet.
people: Honi the Circle Maker, an old man planting
source: Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 23a

title: Cicero and His Friend Atticus
text:
Marcus Tullius Cicero spent his life in the thick of Roman politics: consul, orator, exile, and in the end an enemy of Mark Antony. His closest friend, Titus Pomponius Atticus, chose the opposite path. A wealthy knight, Atticus lived in Athens for about twenty years to avoid Rome's civil strife, refused all public office, and kept friendly relations with men on every side.

He was the one person Cicero told everything. More than four hundred of Cicero's letters to Atticus survive, written from 68 to 44 BC. In them Cicero confesses doubts, vanity, fear and grief he showed to no one else. Atticus managed Cicero's money, had copyists produce and circulate his books, looked after his family, sent him help during his exile in 58 BC, and stood by him when his beloved daughter Tullia died in 45 BC.

Atticus's own replies are lost, but Cicero's side shows how much he leaned on him. When Antony's men killed Cicero in 43 BC, Atticus survived the purges, because over the years he had helped people in every faction, including Antony's family. His friend Cornelius Nepos wrote his biography.
lesson: A friend who stays outside your battles can be your steadiest support. Value the person you can tell everything to, and be that person for someone else.
people: Marcus Tullius Cicero, Titus Pomponius Atticus
source: Cicero, Letters to Atticus; Cornelius Nepos, Life of Atticus

title: Caesar's Double Wall at Alesia
text:
In 52 BC most of Gaul rose against Rome under the Arvernian chief Vercingetorix. After a failed battle he withdrew with a large army into Alesia, a hilltop town in eastern Gaul, and sent his cavalry out to summon help from every tribe.

Caesar, in his own Commentaries, describes his answer. Rather than storm the hill, he surrounded it with a siege line about eleven Roman miles long: ditches, a rampart with towers, and fields of hidden stakes and pits in front. Knowing that a relief army was coming, he then built a second, outer line facing outward, about fourteen miles around, so that his legions sat in a ring between two walls. He stored food and fodder to last for a month.

Inside, food ran low. The Gauls expelled the local Mandubii people, women and children included, but Caesar refused to let them through, and they were trapped between the lines. Then the relief army arrived, which Caesar puts at a quarter of a million men, and attacked the outer wall while Vercingetorix attacked the inner one. For several days the Romans fought on both fronts. In the final assault Caesar, recognizable by his scarlet cloak, led reserves to the critical point, and his cavalry struck the attackers from behind. The relief army broke.

The next day Vercingetorix surrendered. The revolt collapsed, and Gaul remained Roman.
lesson: When pressure may come from two sides at once, prepare for both before either arrives. Securing your own position can matter as much as attacking.
people: Julius Caesar, Vercingetorix
source: Julius Caesar, Commentaries on the Gallic War 7.68 to 7.89
caveat: Caesar's figures for the Gallic armies are almost certainly inflated.

title: Caesar Calls His Mutinous Soldiers "Citizens"
text:
In 47 BC, during the civil war, Julius Caesar's veteran legions in Italy mutinied. Among them was the Tenth, his most trusted legion. They had served for years, they had not received the rewards they were promised, and they refused to sail for the next campaign in Africa. They marched on Rome, demanding their discharge and their money.

According to Suetonius and Appian, Caesar went out to meet them in person and asked what they wanted. They demanded to be discharged, expecting that he needed them too much to agree. Caesar replied at once that he discharged them. He promised that they would receive everything owed to them, after he had won the war with other soldiers and celebrated his triumph.

The decisive moment, both writers say, was the way he addressed them. Instead of calling them "soldiers" or "comrades", he called them "Quirites", the word for civilians.

The effect was immediate. The veterans shouted that they were his soldiers and begged him to take them back and to punish the ringleaders. Caesar relented, and the veterans followed him to Africa, where the Tenth fought at Thapsus.
lesson: People often value belonging more than their demands. Showing calmly that you can do without them may remind them what they would lose.
people: Julius Caesar, the Tenth Legion
source: Suetonius, Life of the Deified Julius, chapter 70; Appian, Civil Wars, Book 2, chapters 92 to 94

title: Cicero Mourns His Daughter Tullia
text:
Marcus Tullius Cicero, orator and statesman, loved his daughter Tullia more than anyone. His letters call her his darling and his delight. Her marriages were unlucky. Her third husband, Dolabella, was unfaithful and spendthrift, and they divorced. In January 45 BC she gave birth to a son, and a month later, in February, she died at Cicero's villa at Tusculum.

Cicero was shattered. He retreated alone to his villa at Astura on the coast, where he spent his days walking in the woods and reading every book of consolation he could find. He wrote a consolation addressed to himself, the first of its kind, and made plans to build a shrine in her memory. In his letters to his friend Atticus he admitted that nothing helped: reading and writing calmed him only for a time.

His friend Servius Sulpicius sent him a famous letter of comfort from Greece. Sailing from Aegina towards Megara, he wrote, he had looked around at Aegina, Megara, Piraeus and Corinth, once flourishing cities now lying in ruins, and asked himself how short-lived humans could protest when one of them died. He reminded Cicero that Tullia had lived as long as life had anything to give her.

Cicero replied gratefully but honestly. Before, he wrote, when public life went badly, he found refuge at home with his daughter. Now he had no refuge at all.
lesson: Grief for a child does not yield to arguments, even a philosopher's. A friend's words help most when they keep us company rather than ask us to stop grieving.
people: Marcus Tullius Cicero, Tullia, Servius Sulpicius Rufus, Atticus
source: Cicero, Letters to Atticus, book 12; Letters to Friends 4.5 (Sulpicius) and 4.6 (Cicero's reply)

title: Hillel and the Man on One Foot
text:
The Talmud tells of a gentile who came to the great teacher Shammai with a challenge. "Convert me," he said, "on condition that you teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot."

Shammai was a strict man and took this as mockery. He pushed the man away with the builder's measuring rod he was holding.

The man then went to Hillel and made the same demand. Hillel did not get angry. He accepted him and said, "What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow. That is the whole Torah. The rest is commentary. Now go and learn it."

The Talmud places this story among several in which impatient or provocative would-be converts were sent away by Shammai and received by Hillel. Later, it says, these converts met and agreed that Shammai's strictness had nearly driven them from the world, while Hillel's patience had brought them under the wings of the divine presence.
lesson: A hard question deserves a patient answer. And when you are unsure how to treat someone, start with what you would not want done to you.
people: Hillel, Shammai, a would-be convert
source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a

title: The Wager to Anger Hillel
text:
The Talmud tells of two men who made a bet of four hundred zuz, a large sum. One of them claimed he could make Hillel lose his temper, and the other said it could not be done.

The challenger chose his moment carefully: a Friday afternoon, when Hillel was washing his hair to prepare for the Sabbath. He walked past the door shouting, "Who here is Hillel? Who here is Hillel?" Hillel wrapped himself in a cloak and came out. "My son, what do you need?" "I have a question. Why are the heads of the Babylonians round?" Hillel answered patiently that it was because they lacked skilled midwives.

The man went away, waited, and came back shouting again, this time asking why the people of Palmyra had bleary eyes. Hillel came out again and answered: because they live among the sands. A third time he came, asking why the Africans had wide feet. Because they live in marshy land, Hillel said.

At last the man said, "I have many more questions, but I am afraid you will get angry." Hillel sat down. "Ask them all." Instead the man burst out, "May there not be many like you in Israel! I have lost four hundred zuz because of you." Hillel replied that he should watch his temper: Hillel was worth his losing four hundred zuz and four hundred more, and Hillel would still not get angry.
lesson: Answer tiresome or provocative people from your own calm, not from their tone. Patience costs little and usually wins more than irritation does.
people: Hillel, a man who bet he could anger him
source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 30b to 31a

title: Aeneas Carries Anchises from Troy
text:
On the night Troy fell, the Greeks poured out of the wooden horse and the city was burning. The Trojan prince Aeneas fought until he saw it was hopeless. His mother, the goddess Venus, showed him the gods themselves tearing down the walls, and told him to go home and save his family.

But at home his old father Anchises refused to leave. He would not outlive Troy, he said. Aeneas, desperate, prepared to go back and die fighting rather than abandon him. Then a soft flame appeared around the head of his little son Ascanius, flickering harmlessly in his hair. Anchises asked Jupiter for a confirming sign; there was a crack of thunder and a shooting star blazed over the city. The old man gave way.

Aeneas told his father to climb on his shoulders and to carry the household gods, since his own hands were stained with blood. He took his son by the hand, and his wife Creusa followed behind. They hurried through the dark, burning streets.

At the meeting place outside the city, Creusa was missing. Aeneas ran back through the ruins calling her name. Her ghost appeared to him, told him that the gods had other plans for her, and asked him to love their son. He tried three times to embrace her, and three times his arms closed on air. He returned and led the survivors to the mountains.
lesson: In a crisis, a family is carried on shoulders and led by the hand. Care for the old and the young together, even when it slows you down.
people: Aeneas, Anchises, Ascanius (Iulus), Creusa, Venus
location: Troy (modern Turkey, myth); written in Rome, Italy
source: Virgil, Aeneid, Book 2

title: Augustus Exiles His Daughter Julia
text:
Julia was the only child of the emperor Augustus. He used her as a tool of dynastic policy. At fourteen she was married to her cousin Marcellus, who died two years later. Then she was married to Agrippa, Augustus's closest general, a man a generation older, and bore him five children. When Agrippa died, Augustus made his stepson Tiberius divorce a wife he loved in order to marry Julia. The marriage was unhappy, and Tiberius withdrew to Rhodes.

In 2 BC Augustus learned, or was persuaded, that his daughter had taken lovers among the young nobles of Rome, among them a son of Mark Antony. According to Suetonius, he sent an account of the matter to the senate in writing, being too ashamed to appear, and banished her to the tiny island of Pandateria. Her mother, Scribonia, whom Augustus had divorced on the day Julia was born, chose to go into exile with her.

Suetonius says that Augustus forbade Julia wine and every comfort, and allowed no man to visit her without his permission, after a detailed description of the visitor's appearance. When the people of Rome begged him to bring her back, he refused. He used to quote a line of Homer, wishing he had never married and had died without children, and called Julia, his granddaughter and his grandson his three running sores. Even in his will he forbade that she be buried in his tomb.
lesson: Children used as instruments of ambition may never find a way home. A parent who treats a child as a policy loses the child.
people: Augustus, Julia the Elder, Scribonia, Tiberius
source: Suetonius, Life of Augustus 63 to 65 and 101; Cassius Dio, Roman History 55.10
caveat: Some historians think the adultery charges covered a political conspiracy.

title: Abhimanyu in the Chakravyuha
text:
On the thirteenth day of the great war at Kurukshetra, Drona, commanding the Kaurava army, arranged his troops in the chakravyuha, a formation of rings within rings that few warriors knew how to break. Arjuna, who did know, had been drawn away to fight elsewhere on the field.

Yudhishthira turned to Arjuna's young son Abhimanyu, a brilliant fighter, and asked him to break the formation. Abhimanyu answered that he knew how to force his way into it, but if trouble came, he did not know how to get out. Yudhishthira and Bhima promised to follow right behind him through the breach and protect him.

Abhimanyu charged, and he broke into the circle. But as the Pandava warriors rushed to follow, Jayadratha, king of the Sindhus, held the gap and drove them back. Abhimanyu was alone inside.

He fought with astonishing courage, killing many warriors. Finally several great fighters attacked him together. They broke his bow, killed his horses and his charioteer, and destroyed his chariot. He fought on with a sword and then with a chariot wheel. At last, exhausted and surrounded, he was struck down and killed.
lesson: Before you commit to a bold move, plan your way out as carefully as your way in, and do not rely on support that someone else must break through to deliver.
people: Abhimanyu, Yudhishthira, Drona, Jayadratha, the Kaurava warriors
source: Mahabharata, Drona Parva

title: Arjuna and the Wooden Bird
text:
Drona, the teacher of arms to the young princes of the Kuru family, wanted to test which of his pupils was truly ready. He had an artificial bird made and set it high in the top of a tree. Then he called the princes together and told them that each, in turn, would aim at the bird's head.

He began with Yudhishthira, the eldest. When the prince had taken aim, Drona asked him what he saw. Yudhishthira said he saw the tree, the bird, his teacher and his brothers. Drona asked him again, and he gave the same answer. Drona told him to step aside without shooting. He put the same question to the other princes one after another, and each described the tree, the bird, the people around him. Each was sent away.

Then it was Arjuna's turn. He drew his bow and Drona asked what he saw. Arjuna said he saw only the bird; not the tree, not his teacher. Drona asked him to describe the bird. Arjuna replied that he saw only its head, not its body.

Drona, delighted, told him to shoot. Arjuna released the arrow and cut off the bird's head, and it fell to the ground.
lesson: Before you act on a goal, narrow your attention until only the target remains. Everything else in view is a distraction you have chosen to keep.
people: Drona, Arjuna, Yudhishthira and the other pupils
source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva
caveat: In the Sanskrit text Arjuna sees only the bird's head; popular retellings say he saw only its eye.

title: Krishna's Peace Mission and the Five Villages
text:
After their thirteen years of exile, the five Pandava brothers asked their cousin Duryodhana to return the half of the kingdom that had been taken from them in a rigged game of dice. Duryodhana refused. War between the two branches of the family seemed certain.

The eldest Pandava, Yudhishthira, made one last offer to avoid bloodshed. He would give up the claim to half the kingdom and accept just five villages, one for each brother. Krishna himself traveled to the Kaurava court at Hastinapura as envoy to plead for peace. The elders of the court, Bhishma, Drona and Duryodhana's own father, the blind king Dhritarashtra, all urged Duryodhana to accept.

Duryodhana would not. He declared that he would not give the Pandavas even as much land as could be pierced by the point of a needle. He even tried to have Krishna seized, and Krishna revealed his divine form to the court before he left.

The war that followed on the field of Kurukshetra lasted eighteen days. Almost every warrior on both sides was killed, including Duryodhana and all his brothers.
lesson: When the other side asks for very little, refusing out of pride can cost you everything. Know what you can afford to give before a dispute becomes a fight no one wins.
people: Krishna, Duryodhana, Yudhishthira, the Pandavas, Dhritarashtra
source: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva

title: Ekalavya's Thumb
text:
Drona was the great teacher of archery to the princes of the Kuru royal house, and Arjuna was his favorite pupil. Drona had promised Arjuna that no archer in the world would ever be his equal.

One day a young man named Ekalavya, the son of a chief of the Nishadas, a forest tribe, came and asked to be Drona's student. Drona refused him because of his low birth. Ekalavya went back into the forest, made a clay image of Drona, and practiced in front of it every day as if before his teacher. He became an astonishing archer.

Later the princes went hunting, and their dog barked at Ekalavya. Before it could close its mouth, he shot seven arrows into it, filling its mouth without killing it. The princes were amazed and found him. Asked who his teacher was, he named Drona. Arjuna went to Drona and reminded him of his promise.

Drona went to the forest. Ekalavya welcomed him with deep respect. Drona then claimed the fee a pupil owes his teacher, and he asked for the young man's right thumb. Without hesitation Ekalavya cut it off and gave it to him. When he shot again, he was no longer as quick as before, and Arjuna was the greatest archer once more.
lesson: People with the power to open or close doors can use it to protect favorites at the cost of real talent. Watch whether your own rules and standards are serving the work or only those you prefer.
people: Ekalavya, Drona, Arjuna
source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva

title: King Shibi and the Dove
text:
King Shibi was known through the world for his righteousness. To test him, the gods took animal form: Agni as a dove and Indra as a hawk. The dove, chased by the hawk, flew into the king's lap and begged for protection. Shibi promised it.

The hawk then spoke. It said the dove was its rightful food, that it was starving, and that a king who took away a creature's food was doing it a wrong too. Shibi offered the hawk any other meat it wanted, a bull or a boar, anything except the bird who had come to him for refuge. The hawk refused. It would accept only one thing: flesh from the king's own body, equal in weight to the dove.

Shibi agreed. A pair of scales was brought, and he put the dove on one side and began cutting flesh from his own body and placing it on the other. However much he cut, the dove remained heavier. At last the king climbed onto the scale himself, offering his whole body. At that the two gods revealed themselves, praised his steadfastness, and restored him.
lesson: A promise to protect someone is tested exactly when keeping it becomes expensive. If you are not willing to pay the cost, do not make the promise.
people: King Shibi, Agni as a dove, Indra as a hawk
source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva)
caveat: The Mahabharata contains more than one version of the tale, with different gods and details.

title: The Mongoose with the Half Golden Body
text:
After the great war, King Yudhishthira performed a magnificent horse sacrifice. Gold, food and gifts poured out to priests and the poor. When it was over, a mongoose appeared on the sacrificial ground. Half of its body shone like gold. It rolled in the ground, then declared in a human voice that this whole sacrifice was not equal to a handful of barley flour given by a poor brahmin of Kurukshetra.

Asked to explain, the mongoose told its story. During a famine a brahmin lived with his wife, son and daughter-in-law by gleaning grain. After days of hunger they had gathered just enough barley to make four small portions. As they were about to eat, a hungry guest arrived. The brahmin gave him his share. The guest was still hungry, so the wife gave hers, then the son, then the daughter-in-law.

The guest then revealed himself as Dharma, and the family was taken up to heaven. The mongoose came out of its hole, rolled in the flour that had fallen, and wherever it touched, its fur turned to gold.

Ever since, it had searched for a sacrifice that could gild its other half. Yudhishthira's had not done it.
lesson: A gift's worth lies in what it costs the giver and the spirit behind it. Sharing your little in a hard time can mean more than giving plenty from abundance.
people: A mongoose, Yudhishthira, a poor brahmin family
source: Mahabharata, Ashvamedhika Parva

title: The Two-Headed Bird
text:
By a lake there lived a strange bird called a Bharunda. It had one body and one stomach, but two necks and two heads.

One day, as the bird walked along the shore, one of its heads came upon a fruit that had washed up on the bank. It tasted wonderful, sweet as nectar, and the head ate it all. The second head asked for a taste. The first refused. They shared one stomach, it said, so what difference did it make which mouth ate the fruit?

The second head said nothing, but it brooded. Some days later it found a poisonous fruit. The first head saw it and begged it not to eat, since the poison would kill them both. The second head reminded it of the nectar fruit and ate the poison anyway.

The poison went into the stomach they shared, and the bird died.
lesson: Members of a team who share one fate cannot win by spiting each other. Small slights left unresolved can grow into revenge that ruins everyone.
people: The Bharunda bird with two heads
source: Panchatantra, Book V (Ill-Considered Action)

title: The Blue Jackal
text:
A hungry jackal named Chandarava wandered into a town looking for food. The town dogs chased him, and in his panic he leapt into a large vat of indigo dye in a dyer's yard. When he crawled out and escaped into the forest, his fur was a deep, strange blue.

The forest animals had never seen anything like him. Lions, tigers, elephants and leopards all drew back in fear. The jackal saw his chance. He announced that the creator had made him in this unusual color and sent him to be king of the beasts. The animals believed him and served him. He made the lion his minister, the tiger his chamberlain, and gave other high posts to the great animals. His own kind, the jackals, he drove out in contempt so no one would recognize him.

One evening a pack of jackals began to howl in the distance. Chandarava's nature was stronger than his disguise. Without thinking, he threw back his head and howled in answer. The lion and the tiger looked at each other, understood that their king was only a jackal, and tore him to pieces.
lesson: Authority built on an image, rather than on who you really are, lasts only until a moment of pressure reveals you. It is safer to lead as yourself and to stay loyal to the people you came from.
people: Chandarava the jackal, the forest animals
source: Panchatantra, Book I

title: The Brahmin and the Three Rogues
text:
A brahmin went to a nearby village to get an animal for a sacrifice. He came back with a fat goat, slung it over his shoulders and set off home through the forest.

Three rogues saw him and wanted the goat. They agreed on a plan and placed themselves at different points along his path.

The first stepped out in front of him and said, in a shocked voice, that he was amazed to see a holy man carrying a dog on his shoulders. Dogs were unclean; how could a brahmin touch one? The brahmin told him angrily that he was blind; it was a goat for a sacrifice. He walked on.

Further on, the second rogue stopped him and asked, just as shocked, why a brahmin was carrying a dead calf on his shoulders. The brahmin began to wonder. He put the goat down, looked at it carefully, picked it up again and went on, now uneasy.

Then the third rogue met him and asked, with disgust, why a holy man was carrying a donkey, an animal no brahmin should touch. Now the brahmin was sure that he was mistaken, or that some demon had bewitched him. Three men could not all be wrong. He threw the goat down, hurried off to bathe and purify himself, and the rogues took the goat home and ate it.
lesson: Trust your own evidence. When several people repeat the same claim, check whether they are independent witnesses or one interest speaking with several voices.
people: A brahmin, three rogues, a goat
source: Panchatantra, Book III
caveat: In the Panchatantra the rogues call the goat a dog, a dead calf and a donkey; in the Hitopadesha version all three call it a dog.

title: The Camel and the Lion's Courtiers
text:
A camel that had strayed from a caravan wandered into a forest ruled by a lion. The lion's three attendants, a crow, a jackal and a leopard, brought the stranger before their king. The lion questioned him kindly, promised him safety, and let him live in the forest. The camel grazed in peace and grew fat.

Then the lion was badly wounded fighting an elephant and could no longer hunt. He and his courtiers began to starve. The three attendants looked at the camel and saw a meal, but the lion refused: he had given his word, and killing a guest who trusted him would be a great sin.

So the courtiers arranged a little play. They went before the lion together, and one by one each offered his own body to save the king. Each offer was turned down on some pretext or other, the crow, for example, being too small to make a meal. The camel, watching, thought it would look loyal to make the same offer and expected to be refused like the rest. The moment he spoke, the leopard and the jackal declared that the offer was noble and must be accepted. They tore him apart, and the lion ate.
lesson: A promise is broken just as surely when you let others find a clever way around it. If you rely on advisers to do what you would not do openly, the dishonor is still yours.
people: A lion, a crow, a jackal, a leopard, a camel
source: Panchatantra, Book I

title: The War of the Crows and the Owls
text:
The crows and the owls were bitter enemies. The owl king attacked the crows night after night, when owls can see and crows cannot, and killed many of them. The crow king asked his ministers what to do. The oldest of them, Sthirajivin, proposed a trick.

The crows staged a quarrel. In front of owl spies, Sthirajivin was attacked by his own side, smeared with blood and left lying under a tree. When the owls found him, he told them that he had advised his king to make peace with the owls and had been beaten for it. Now he wanted to serve the owl king and help him take revenge.

The owl king consulted his ministers. One of them, Raktaksha, warned that a defector from the enemy should never be trusted and urged the king to kill him. The others argued that a beaten and helpless crow could do no harm and that refugees should be protected. The king listened to them, and Raktaksha left in disgust.

The old crow was given a place near the entrance of the owls' cave. Day by day he collected sticks there, as if making a nest. One morning, while the owls were blind in daylight, the crows brought burning brands. Sthirajivin set the pile alight, the cave filled with fire and smoke, and the owls inside were destroyed.
lesson: Be careful with anyone who switches sides too conveniently, and listen to the adviser who asks the uncomfortable question. A warm welcome without scrutiny can let the enemy in.
people: Sthirajivin the old crow, the crow king, the owl king, the owl minister Raktaksha
source: Panchatantra, Book III

title: The Crows and the Serpent
text:
A pair of crows lived in a great tree. Every time they hatched chicks, a black serpent that lived in a hollow at the foot of the tree climbed up and ate them. The crows grieved but were too small to fight a snake.

They went to their friend, a jackal, for advice. The jackal told them that what could not be done by force could be done by cleverness. He told them where to find a weapon.

The crows flew to a lake where the women of the royal household were bathing. They had left their clothes and jewelry on the bank. The female crow swooped down, seized a gold chain, and flew slowly off with it, making sure she was seen. The palace guards and servants ran after her with sticks.

She led them straight to the tree and dropped the chain into the serpent's hole. When the servants came to recover it, they found the snake inside, coiled and hissing. They beat it to death, took back the chain and went home. The crows raised their next brood in peace.
lesson: If you cannot defeat a problem with your own strength, find a stronger force that has its own reason to act, and lead it there.
people: A crow couple, a black serpent, the queen's servants
source: Panchatantra, Book I
caveat: Details differ between versions of the Panchatantra; in some the jewel is taken from a prince or king rather than the queen's women.

title: The Doves Who Flew Away with the Net
text:
A flock of doves was led by a king named Chitragriva. One day, flying over a forest, they saw grains of rice scattered on the ground, a fine meal for hungry birds. They swooped down to eat, and a hunter's net, hidden under the grain, fell over them all.

The doves panicked, each beating its wings and pulling in a different direction, which only tangled them further. Chitragriva called out to stop. Struggling alone, he said, no one would escape. But if they all rose together at the same moment, they could carry the net with them. On his signal the whole flock lifted off at once, and the net rose into the air with them while the hunter on the ground ran after them until he lost sight of the flock.

Chitragriva led them to his friend Hiranyaka, a mouse who lived nearby. The mouse wanted to free the king first, but Chitragriva refused and asked him to free his followers before him, in case the mouse grew tired. Hiranyaka gnawed through the cords one by one until every dove was free, and the flock flew home.
lesson: A trap that holds individuals can often be overcome by a group acting at the same moment. A good leader makes sure his people are safe before himself.
people: Chitragriva the dove king, the doves, Hiranyaka the mouse
source: Panchatantra, Book II (The Winning of Friends)

title: The Elephants and the Mice
text:
A great colony of mice lived in the ruins of an old abandoned town near a lake. A herd of elephants, on their way to drink, began to take a path to the lake that ran straight through the mouse town. Every time the herd passed, huge feet crushed burrows and killed many mice.

The king of the mice went to the king of the elephants and asked politely whether the herd could take a different route. Then he added that if the elephants ever needed help, the mice would remember the favor. The elephant king was amused that such tiny creatures could ever help him, but he agreed and led his herd by another path.

Some time later a king sent trappers to capture elephants. They caught the elephant king and many of his herd in a trap and tied the animals fast with thick ropes to strong trees in the forest. The captive elephant king thought of the mice and sent one of his elephants that had escaped the trap to ask their king for help.

The mice came out in thousands. They swarmed over the ropes and gnawed through every one of them, and the elephants walked free.
lesson: Use your strength considerately, and listen when someone weaker asks for fair treatment. Goodwill you build when you hold the power may save you later.
people: Elephant king, mice
source: Panchatantra, Book II (The Winning of Friends)

title: The Crow, the Mouse, the Tortoise and the Deer
text:
A crow named Laghupatanaka watched a mouse named Hiranyaka gnaw through a hunter's net and free a flock of trapped doves. Admiring such a useful friend, the crow asked for the mouse's friendship. The mouse was wary at first, since crows eat mice, but the crow won him over, and when hard times came the crow carried the mouse to a lake where his old friend, the tortoise Mantharaka, lived. Later a frightened deer named Chitranga, fleeing hunters, joined the three.

One day the deer was caught in a snare. The crow spotted him from the air and flew to fetch the mouse, who chewed through the cords. But the slow tortoise had followed them out of worry, and when the hunter returned and found the deer gone, he caught the tortoise instead, tied him to his bow and set off home.

The friends made a plan. The deer ran ahead and lay down by a pond as if dead, and the crow perched on him, pretending to peck. The hunter dropped the tortoise and hurried toward the easy prize. While he was away, the mouse cut the tortoise's bonds and the tortoise slipped into the water. As the hunter approached, the crow flew up and the deer bounded away, and the hunter went home with nothing.
lesson: Friends with different strengths can rescue one another from situations none could escape alone. Value people for what they bring that you lack.
people: Laghupatanaka the crow, Hiranyaka the mouse, Mantharaka the tortoise, Chitranga the deer
source: Panchatantra, Book II (The Winning of Friends), frame story

title: The Heron and the Crab
text:
An old heron lived beside a pond full of fish. He had grown too old and slow to catch them easily, so he thought of a trick. He stood at the edge of the water looking miserable and refused to eat.

A crab asked him what was wrong. The heron said he had heard terrible news: fishermen were coming soon to drain the pond and catch everything in it. He was sad because he would lose his food and his neighbors would die.

The fish panicked and begged the heron to save them. He offered to carry them, one at a time, to a large lake nearby where they would be safe. They eagerly agreed. Each day he took a fish in his beak, flew off to a flat rock out of sight, ate it, and came back for the next. The fish fought over whose turn was next.
