One day the crab asked to go. The heron, wanting a change of diet, picked him up. As they flew, the crab saw the rock covered in fish bones and understood. He gripped the heron's neck in his claws and squeezed until the heron's head came off. Then he crawled back to the pond and told the remaining fish the truth.
lesson: When a predator offers to rescue you, ask who gains from the rescue. Check where the others who accepted ended up before you go yourself.
people: A heron, the fish of a pond, a crab
source: Panchatantra, Book I

title: The King and the Foolish Monkey Guard
text:
A king kept a pet monkey that he loved dearly. The monkey had the run of the palace, went everywhere at the king's side, and was trusted completely. Because he was so devoted, the king gave him a special duty: to stand guard over him while he slept.

One hot afternoon the king lay down for a nap, and the monkey took up his post beside the bed, holding a sword to protect his master. Soon a bee, or in some tellings a fly, came buzzing in and settled on the king's chest. The monkey waved it away. It flew off and came back. He chased it again, and again it returned and landed in the same place.

The monkey grew furious. Determined to finish the pest once and for all, he raised the sword and brought it down with all his strength on the insect. The insect flew away unharmed. The blow split the sleeping king's chest, and he died.

The story is told in the Panchatantra to make a single point: a wise enemy is better than a foolish friend.
lesson: Loyalty is not the same as judgment. When you hand someone power over things that matter, make sure they understand the job, not only that they love you.
people: A king, his pet monkey
source: Panchatantra, The King and the Foolish Monkey

title: The Lion, the Bull and the Jackal
text:
Pingalaka, the lion king of a forest, once heard a tremendous bellow and was secretly terrified. The sound came from Sanjivaka, a bull who had been abandoned by a merchant and was now grazing by the river. Damanaka, an ambitious jackal who had lost favor at court, saw an opening. He went to the bull, brought him before the king, and arranged a friendship between them.

The friendship worked too well. Lion and bull became inseparable. Sanjivaka taught the king calm and wisdom, and Pingalaka spent his days in conversation and stopped hunting, so his courtiers, the jackals among them, went hungry and lost influence.

Damanaka decided to undo what he had built. He went to the lion and whispered that the bull was plotting to seize the throne. Then he went to the bull and whispered that the lion planned to kill and eat him. Each was told to watch for signs in the other's manner. When they next met, each saw what he had been told to expect. They fought, and the lion killed his friend. Only afterward did Pingalaka grieve for what he had done, and the jackal took the post of chief minister.
lesson: When someone brings you private warnings about a trusted colleague, ask what the messenger stands to gain. Talk directly to the person accused before you act on a story you heard secondhand.
people: Pingalaka the lion, Sanjivaka the bull, Damanaka and Karataka the jackals
source: Panchatantra, Book I (frame story)

title: The Lion and the Clever Hare
text:
In a forest lived a mighty lion named Bhasuraka who killed animals without end, far more than he could eat. At last the animals went to him with a proposal. If he would stay in his den, they would send him one animal every day for his meal. He agreed, and from then on the animals drew lots each day to choose who would go.

One day the lot fell to a hare. He knew he was going to die, but he took his time on the way, thinking hard. He arrived very late, and the lion, starving and angry, roared at him.

The hare bowed and explained. Other hares had set out with him, he said, but on the way another lion had stopped them, claimed the forest as his own, and eaten his companions. He alone had been allowed to go and report.

Bhasuraka was enraged. He demanded to be shown this rival at once. The hare led him to a deep well and pointed down. The lion looked in and saw a lion glaring up at him from the water. He roared, and the well roared back. In his fury he leaped down to attack the rival and drowned. The hare went home and told the animals they were free.
lesson: A more powerful opponent can often be beaten through his own pride and temper. Find what he cannot resist reacting to, and let him defeat himself.
people: Bhasuraka the lion, a hare
source: Panchatantra, Book I

title: The Lion Makers
text:
In a town there lived four young brahmins who were close friends. Three of them had studied for years and mastered many learned sciences, but they had little common sense. The fourth had no great learning, but he had plenty of sense. They decided to travel together to seek their fortune with their knowledge.

On the road through a forest they came upon the bones of a dead lion. The three scholars saw a chance to show what they could do. The first said he could put the bones back together into a skeleton. The second said he could cover it with skin, flesh and blood. The third said he could give it life.

The fourth friend begged them to stop. If they brought a lion to life, he said, it would kill them all. They scorned him as an ignorant man. So he asked them to wait a moment, and climbed a tall tree.

The first scholar assembled the skeleton. The second gave it flesh and skin. The third breathed life into it. The lion rose, saw three men standing in front of it, and killed them. When it had gone, the man with common sense climbed down from the tree and went home alone.
lesson: Technical skill tells you what you can do; judgment tells you whether you should. Listen to the person asking what happens next, even if they know less than you.
people: Four brahmins
source: Panchatantra, Book V

title: The Monkey and the Crocodile
text:
A monkey lived in a rose apple tree on the bank of a river. One day a crocodile came out of the water to rest beneath it, and the monkey threw him some of the sweet fruit. The two became friends. Every day the crocodile came to talk, and every day he took some fruit home to his wife.

The wife, however, grew jealous of the hours her husband spent away, and she reasoned that a monkey who ate such sweet fruit every day must have a very sweet heart. She told her husband she would only be happy if she could eat it. After much nagging, the crocodile gave in.

He invited the monkey to visit his home and carried him across the river on his back. In the middle of the water, feeling safe, he told the monkey the truth. The monkey kept calm. "Friend, why did you not say so earlier?" he said. "I keep my heart up in the rose apple tree. Take me back and I will fetch it for your wife."

The foolish crocodile swam back to the bank. The monkey leapt into his tree, climbed high out of reach and told the crocodile that their friendship was over.
lesson: Keep a cool head when someone you trusted turns on you; calm thinking can get you out of danger. And never let another person talk you into betraying a friend.
people: Monkey, crocodile, the crocodile's wife
source: Panchatantra, Book IV (Loss of What Was Gained), frame story

title: The Monkey and the Wedge
text:
Near a town, carpenters were building a temple. They were sawing a great log lengthwise, and when the saw had gone halfway down, they hammered a wooden wedge into the split to hold it open. Then, at midday, they went off to eat, leaving their tools and the half split log behind.

A troop of monkeys came down from the trees and began to play around the building site, climbing over the timber and poking at everything. One monkey, whose fate was near, was especially curious about the wedge. He climbed onto the log and sat right over the open split, with his legs and body hanging into the gap, and began to tug at the wedge with both hands, wondering what it was for.

He pulled and wiggled until it suddenly came free. The moment it did, the two halves of the log snapped shut on him. He was caught fast in the crack and died there.

When the carpenters came back from their meal, they found the wedge on the ground and the monkey dead in the closed log.
lesson: Before you pull on something you do not understand, find out what it is holding apart. Meddling in matters outside your knowledge can trap you in the consequences.
people: A monkey, carpenters
source: Panchatantra, Book I

title: The Sparrow and the Elephant
text:
A pair of sparrows had built their nest in a tree and laid their eggs. One day a wild elephant, wandering in the heat, broke the branch to shade himself. The nest fell and every egg was smashed. The mother sparrow grieved, and she swore to destroy the elephant.

What could a sparrow do against an elephant? She went to her friend the woodpecker, and together they asked for the help of a gnat and a frog. They made a plan in which each would do only one small thing.

At noon the gnat flew to the elephant's ear and hummed a soft, sweet tune. The elephant closed his eyes with pleasure. At that moment the woodpecker darted in and pecked out his eyes. Blind and in pain, the elephant grew desperately thirsty as the day wore on. Then the frog sat at the edge of a deep pit and croaked. Hearing a frog, the elephant believed there must be water there. He stumbled toward the sound, fell into the pit, and died.
lesson: No single small ally may be able to win, but several with different skills, each doing one part at the right moment, can overcome a much stronger opponent.
people: A sparrow, a woodpecker, a gnat, a frog, an elephant
source: Panchatantra, Book I (The Loss of Friends)

title: The Three Fish
text:
In a pond lived three large fish. One was called Forethought, one Ready Wit, and one Whatever Will Be.

One evening some fishermen walked past the pond and stopped to look at it. It was full of fish, they said, and the water was low. Tomorrow they would come back with their nets and catch the lot.

Forethought heard them and called the others together. They should leave tonight, he said, through the stream that led to another lake, while they still could. Ready Wit said there was no need to flee yet; if trouble came, he would think of something. Whatever Will Be said he would not leave the pond where he was born because of some passing talk. What was fated would happen anyway.

So Forethought left that night with his family. The next morning the fishermen came and dragged their nets through the pond. Ready Wit was caught, but he lay perfectly still and pretended to be dead. The fishermen tossed him aside onto the bank, and when no one was watching, he flipped back into the water and escaped. Whatever Will Be thrashed about in the net until the fishermen killed him.
lesson: The best plan is to act before trouble arrives; the next best is to keep your head when it does. Leaving everything to fate is not a strategy.
people: Three fish named Forethought, Ready Wit and Whatever Will Be, fishermen
source: Panchatantra, Book I

title: The Talkative Tortoise
text:
A tortoise lived in a lake with two geese who were her close friends. Then came a drought. The lake shrank day by day, and the geese decided to fly to another lake that still had plenty of water. The tortoise begged them not to leave her behind to die in the mud.

The geese came up with a plan. They found a stout stick. The tortoise would grip the middle of it firmly in her mouth, and the two geese would each take one end in their beaks and carry her through the air. There was only one condition: whatever happened, she must not open her mouth. She promised.

So they rose into the sky and flew over the countryside. As they passed above a town, people below looked up, pointed and laughed. Look, they shouted, the geese are carrying a tortoise on a stick! What a strange sight!

The tortoise was annoyed. She wanted to tell them it was none of their business. She opened her mouth to answer, let go of the stick, fell to the ground, and was killed. In the Jataka version, the story is told to a king who could not stop talking, and he took the hint.
lesson: A good plan can be ruined by one moment of indiscipline. When you have committed to staying quiet or patient, do not let someone's mockery provoke you into letting go.
people: A tortoise, two geese
source: Panchatantra, Book I; Jataka 215 (Kacchapa Jataka)

title: The Pandavas in Disguise at Virata's Court
text:
In the Mahabharata, the five Pandava brothers and their wife Draupadi lost a rigged game of dice. As part of their punishment they had to spend twelve years in the forest and a thirteenth year in hiding. If anyone discovered them during that final year, they would have to begin the whole exile again.

They decided to hide at the court of King Virata, and each chose a disguise that matched a real skill. Yudhishthira, the eldest, who loved dice, became the king's companion and gaming partner under the name Kanka. Bhima, the strongest and the greatest eater, became the royal cook and a wrestler. Arjuna, the great archer, disguised himself as Brihannala, a eunuch who taught music and dance to the princess. Nakula, who understood horses, took charge of the royal stables, and Sahadeva, who knew cattle, became a herdsman. Draupadi became a maid to the queen.

The year was full of danger. Bhima had to kill the queen's brother Kichaka secretly to protect Draupadi, and at the very end Arjuna fought off an invading army. But they kept their secret until the year was over, and then revealed themselves to an astonished king.
lesson: A team can survive a hard stretch when each person takes on the role that fits a real strength. Hiding well is easier when you play a part you already know how to do.
people: Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula, Sahadeva, Draupadi, King Virata
source: Mahabharata, Virata Parva

title: The Churning of the Ocean
text:
In Hindu tradition, the gods, the devas, had lost their strength and were losing their long war against their rivals, the asuras. The god Vishnu told them that they could regain their power by drinking amrita, the nectar of immortality, which lay hidden at the bottom of the cosmic ocean of milk. But the ocean had to be churned to bring it up, and that task was too great for the gods alone. They would have to work with their enemies.

So devas and asuras made a truce. They uprooted Mount Mandara to use as a churning rod and wrapped the great serpent Vasuki around it as a rope. The asuras held one end and the devas the other, and they pulled back and forth. When the mountain began to sink into the ocean, Vishnu took the form of a giant tortoise and held it up on his back.

The churning brought up wonders, and also a deadly poison that threatened to destroy the world. Shiva drank it and held it in his throat, which turned blue. At last the physician of the gods rose with the pot of amrita. The asuras seized it, but Vishnu, disguised as the enchanting Mohini, distracted them and served the nectar to the devas.
lesson: Some goals are too large for any one side, and reaching them may require working with people you distrust. Agree in advance how the results will be shared, or the cooperation will end in a fight.
people: The devas, the asuras, Vishnu, Shiva, the serpent Vasuki
source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Astika Parva); Bhagavata Purana, Book 8; Vishnu Purana

title: Yudhishthira and the Dog
text:
At the end of their lives, after the great war and many years of rule, the five Pandava brothers and their wife Draupadi gave up their kingdom and set out on a final journey toward the Himalayas, heading for the mountain of the gods. A dog joined them at the start and followed them all the way.

One by one, the travelers fell on the road and died: first Draupadi, then the twins Sahadeva and Nakula, then Arjuna, then Bhima. Yudhishthira walked on without looking back, and only the dog stayed with him.

At last the god Indra appeared in his chariot to carry Yudhishthira to heaven in his own body. Yudhishthira asked to bring the dog, which had been devoted to him. Indra refused: there was no place in heaven for dogs, and Yudhishthira should simply leave it behind. Yudhishthira said that abandoning one who was devoted to him, frightened and without other protection, was a grave sin, and he would not do it even to gain heaven.

The dog then changed shape. It was Dharma, the god of righteousness and Yudhishthira's own divine father, testing him. Praising his steadfastness, Dharma and Indra took him to heaven.
lesson: The way you treat those who depend on you, especially when you are about to move on to something better, shows what you really are. Do not trade loyalty for advancement.
people: Yudhishthira, a dog (Dharma), Indra
source: Mahabharata, Mahaprasthanika Parva

title: Augustus Pardons the Conspirator Cinna
text:
Seneca, writing to the young emperor Nero about mercy, tells a story about Augustus. The emperor learned that Gnaeus Cornelius Cinna, a grandson of Pompey, was plotting to kill him. Augustus spent a restless night, torn between punishing Cinna and sickened by the thought of yet more executions, since earlier conspiracies had been crushed and new ones kept appearing.

Seneca says his wife Livia advised him to do what doctors do: when the usual remedies fail, try the opposite. Severity had not worked, so he should try clemency.

Augustus summoned Cinna alone, told him to listen without interrupting, and then spoke for more than two hours, reminding Cinna of the favors he had received and laying out every detail of the plot. Cinna was speechless. Augustus then told him that he was giving him his life a second time, once as an enemy and now as a plotter, and proposed they become friends.

Later he made Cinna consul. Seneca says Cinna became one of his most loyal friends and left him as his heir, and that no one plotted against Augustus again.
lesson: When punishment keeps producing new enemies, try a different approach. Mercy offered from strength can turn an opponent into an ally.
people: Augustus, Gnaeus Cornelius Cinna
date: Late 1st century BC or AD 4 (sources differ)
source: Seneca, De Clementia, Book 1, chapter 9; Cassius Dio, Roman History, Book 55, chapters 14 to 22
caveat: Seneca and Cassius Dio disagree about the date and setting, and the long speeches are literary reconstructions.

title: Atalanta and the Golden Apples
text:
Atalanta was faster than any man alive. An oracle had warned her against marriage, so she set a hard condition for her many suitors: each must race her. Whoever won would marry her, but whoever lost would die. Many tried, and all lost their lives.

Hippomenes came to watch one of these races, meaning to laugh at the fools who risked death for a bride. But when he saw Atalanta run, he fell in love and decided to challenge her himself. Before the race, he prayed to Venus for help. The goddess brought him three golden apples from her sacred garden on Cyprus and told him how to use them.

The race began, and Atalanta soon drew ahead. Hippomenes rolled the first golden apple across her path. Dazzled, she turned aside to pick it up, and he passed her. She caught up again. He threw the second, and again she stopped for it and lost ground, and again she overtook him.

Near the end, with the finish line close, Hippomenes threw the last apple off to the side of the course, with all his strength. Atalanta hesitated, then ran after it, and Venus made the apple heavier to slow her down. Hippomenes crossed the line first and won his bride.
lesson: A stronger competitor can be beaten by pulling them off course. Watch for shiny distractions that cost you the race you are actually running.
people: Atalanta, Hippomenes, Venus
source: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book 10

title: Baucis and Philemon
text:
Jupiter and Mercury once came down to earth disguised as weary travelers, to see how people in the hill country of Phrygia treated strangers. They knocked at a thousand doors, and a thousand doors were bolted against them.

At last they reached a tiny cottage thatched with reeds. There lived Baucis and Philemon, an old couple who had married young, grown old together, and made their poverty bearable by accepting it. They took the strangers in at once. Baucis blew the embers into a fire. Philemon brought in a cabbage from the garden and took down a side of smoked bacon. They washed the guests' feet, set out olives, cheese, eggs and wine, and apologized for the humble meal.

Then they noticed that the wine bowl kept refilling itself. Frightened, they realized who their guests were, and tried to catch their only goose to serve it. The gods stopped them, revealed themselves, and led them up the hill. Below, the whole valley was drowned in a flood. Only their cottage remained, and it turned into a temple of marble and gold.

Jupiter asked what they wished for. After a quiet word with his wife, Philemon asked that they might be priests of the temple, and since they had lived together in harmony, that they might die in the same hour, so that neither would see the other's grave. Many years later, standing before the temple, each saw the other putting out leaves. They said farewell together, and became an oak and a linden, growing side by side.
lesson: A good marriage shows itself in ordinary generosity, shared together. The best wish may be not riches but simply to stay together to the end.
people: Baucis, Philemon, Jupiter, Mercury
location: Phrygia (modern Turkey); written in Rome, Italy
source: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book 8

title: Daedalus and Icarus
text:
Daedalus, the great craftsman of Athens, was trapped on Crete by King Minos, who would not let him leave. Land and sea were guarded, but the sky was not. So Daedalus set to work making wings. He laid feathers in rows from small to large, tied them with thread at the middle and fixed them with wax at the base, and bent them gently to curve like a bird's.

His young son Icarus stood beside him, laughing, catching at floating feathers and pressing the soft wax with his thumb, getting in his father's way.

When the wings were ready, Daedalus fitted them to the boy and gave him careful instructions: fly the middle course. If you fly too low, the spray of the sea will weigh down your wings; if you fly too high, the sun will burn them. Follow me. His cheeks were wet as he spoke, and his hands trembled.

They rose into the air. Fishermen and shepherds below stared up at them, taking them for gods. But Icarus began to delight in the flight and left his father behind, soaring higher toward the sky. The heat of the sun softened the wax. The feathers fell away, and Icarus, flapping bare arms, fell into the sea calling his father's name. Daedalus found the feathers on the waves and buried his son.
lesson: Giving children freedom means trusting them with limits they may ignore. Explain the reasons for the middle course, then fly close enough to help.
people: Daedalus, Icarus
source: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book 8

title: King Midas and the Golden Touch
text:
Silenus, the old companion of the god Bacchus, wandered off drunk and was found by Phrygian peasants, who brought him to their king, Midas. Midas welcomed him with ten days of feasting and then returned him safely to Bacchus. Grateful, the god offered Midas any reward he wished.

Midas asked that everything he touched should turn to gold. Bacchus granted it, though he was sorry Midas had not asked for something better.

Midas hurried off to test his gift. He broke a twig from an oak, and it turned to gold. He picked up a stone and a clod of earth, and they turned to gold. He plucked ears of grain and an apple, and they shone like treasure. He was overjoyed.

Then his servants set a meal before him. When he touched the bread, it hardened into gold. When he bit into meat, his teeth met gold. When he mixed wine with water and raised it to his lips, molten gold ran into his mouth. Rich and miserable, starving and parched, he raised his shining arms to the sky and begged Bacchus to take back the gift.

The god told him to go to the source of the river Pactolus and wash himself in it. Midas did, and the power passed from his body into the water. Ever since, the sands of that river have glittered with gold.
lesson: Before you ask for something, think through what it would mean to have it in every part of your life. An outcome that sounds perfect can carry costs you never pictured.
people: Midas, Bacchus (Dionysus), Silenus
source: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book 11

title: Orpheus and Eurydice
text:
Orpheus, the finest singer and lyre player who ever lived, married Eurydice. Soon after the wedding, as she walked in a meadow, she was bitten on the ankle by a snake and died.

Orpheus mourned her above ground until he could bear it no longer. Then he did what no living man should do: he went down through the gate of the underworld, past the ghosts of the dead, and stood before Hades and Persephone. He played his lyre and sang. He asked only that Eurydice be given back to him for the span of a natural life; she would come back to them in time anyway. His song was so moving that the ghosts wept, Tantalus forgot his thirst, and for the first time, it was said, the cheeks of the Furies were wet with tears.

The rulers of the dead could not refuse. Eurydice could go, on one condition: Orpheus must not look back at her until they had left the underworld.

They climbed the steep, dark, silent path. They were almost at the edge of the upper world when Orpheus, afraid she might be faltering and longing to see her, turned around. At once she slipped back. She reached out to him, and he to her, but he caught only the air. She did not reproach him, Ovid says; what could she complain of, except that she had been loved? With a faint farewell, she was gone.
lesson: Love can attempt almost anything, but grief eventually asks us to trust and let go. Holding on too tightly can lose what we are trying to keep.
people: Orpheus, Eurydice, Hades, Persephone
location: Thrace (Greek myth); written in Rome, Italy
source: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book 10; Virgil, Georgics, Book 4

title: Phaethon and the Chariot of the Sun
text:
Phaethon's mother had told him that his father was the Sun. When a friend mocked him for believing it, Phaethon traveled to the far east to the Sun's palace to find out for himself.

His father welcomed him, took off his blazing crown so the boy could come close, and confirmed that he was his son. To prove it, he swore by the river Styx, an oath the gods cannot break, to grant Phaethon any wish.

Phaethon asked to drive the chariot of the Sun across the sky for one day. His father regretted his promise at once. Not even Jupiter could drive those horses, he said. He begged his son to choose anything else. But Phaethon insisted, and the oath held.

The fiery horses felt the light weight in the chariot and ran wild. They left their road, plunged near the earth and scorched it: mountains burned, rivers boiled away, cities and peoples turned to ash. The Earth herself cried out to Jupiter. To save the world, he struck Phaethon with a thunderbolt. The boy fell blazing like a falling star into the river Eridanus. His sisters wept over his grave until they were turned into poplar trees, their tears hardening into amber.
lesson: Love that tries to prove itself by granting anything can do great harm. A parent's real gift is sometimes the refusal.
people: Phaethon, Sol (Helios), Clymene, Jupiter
location: Greek myth; written in Rome, Italy
source: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Books 1 and 2

title: Ariadne's Thread
text:
King Minos of Crete had defeated Athens and demanded a cruel tribute: every few years the Athenians had to send seven young men and seven young women to Crete. There they were sent into the Labyrinth, the vast maze built by the craftsman Daedalus, where the Minotaur, a monster with the body of a man and the head of a bull, lived. None ever came out.

Theseus, son of the king of Athens, volunteered to go with the victims. In Crete, Minos's daughter Ariadne saw him and fell in love. She knew that even if Theseus could kill the Minotaur, he would never find his way out of the Labyrinth, whose passages were made to confuse anyone who entered. So she gave him a ball of thread.

Theseus tied one end of the thread at the entrance and unwound it as he went deeper and deeper into the maze. In its depths he found the Minotaur and killed it. Then, instead of wandering lost among the endless turns, he simply followed the thread back the way he had come and walked out into the daylight, leading the young Athenians with him.

He sailed away with Ariadne, though, in the best known version, he left her behind on the island of Naxos.
lesson: Before you go into a complicated situation, secure your way back out. A simple line to retrace is worth more than strength once you are lost.
people: Theseus, Ariadne, Minos, the Minotaur
date: Greek myth; Ovid 8 AD, Plutarch c. 100 AD
source: Plutarch, Life of Theseus; Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book 8
caveat: Ancient authors give several versions of the myth; Plutarch himself records conflicting accounts.

title: Liu Xiu Burns the Letters
text:
In the chaos that followed the fall of Wang Mang's short-lived dynasty, several men fought to restore or replace the Han. In 24 AD Liu Xiu, a member of the Han imperial clan, besieged the city of Handan, held by his rival Wang Lang, a pretender who claimed to be a Han prince.

When Handan fell and Wang Lang was killed, Liu Xiu's men seized the enemy's archives. Among them, according to the official History of the Later Han, were thousands of letters from officials and officers on Liu Xiu's own side, writing to Wang Lang to curry favor with him or to slander Liu Xiu while the outcome was uncertain.

Liu Xiu did not read them. He gathered his generals, had the letters burned in front of them, and said it was so that those who were uneasy could set their minds at rest.

No one was punished for what he had once written. The following year Liu Xiu proclaimed himself emperor as Guangwu of Han. He reunited China and is remembered as one of the most capable and generous founders of a Chinese dynasty.
lesson: Sometimes the wisest thing is not to look for every past disloyalty. Letting people put a moment of weakness behind them can earn their lasting loyalty.
people: Liu Xiu (Emperor Guangwu of Han), Wang Lang
source: Fan Ye, Book of the Later Han (Hou Hanshu), Annals of Emperor Guangwu

title: Counting the Cost of the Tower
text:
Large crowds were following Jesus, and he turned and spoke to them about what it would really cost to be his disciple. He did not want followers who started out with enthusiasm and gave up halfway. To make the point, he told two short stories.

Suppose one of you wants to build a tower, he said. Would you not first sit down and estimate the cost, to see whether you have enough money to finish it? Otherwise, you might lay the foundation and then be unable to complete the work. Then everyone who saw the bare foundation would mock you, saying: this man began to build and was not able to finish.

Or suppose a king is about to go to war against another king. Will he not first sit down and consider whether, with ten thousand men, he can stand against an enemy coming at him with twenty thousand? If he cannot, then while the other king is still a long way off, he will send envoys and ask for terms of peace.

In both cases, the sensible person sits down before acting, counts honestly, and decides on that basis whether to begin at all.
lesson: Before starting a project or a fight, sit down and add up what it will truly take. If you cannot finish, it is wiser to negotiate early than to leave a monument to your misjudgment.
people: Jesus, a builder, a king going to war
location: Galilee and Judea (modern Israel and Palestinian territories)
source: Gospel of Luke 14:28-32

title: The Good Samaritan
text:
An expert in the law asked Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life. Love God, and love your neighbor as yourself, came the answer. The lawyer, wanting to justify himself, asked, "And who is my neighbor?" Jesus replied with a story.

A man was going down the steep road from Jerusalem to Jericho when he fell among robbers. They stripped him, beat him and left him half dead by the road. A priest happened to come that way, saw him, and passed by on the other side. A Levite, an assistant at the Temple, did the same.

Then a Samaritan came along, a member of a people the Jews of that time despised. When he saw the man, he was moved with pity. He went to him, poured oil and wine on his wounds and bandaged them. He put him on his own animal, brought him to an inn and took care of him. The next day he gave the innkeeper two silver coins and said, "Look after him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back."

"Which of these three," Jesus asked, "was a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?" The lawyer said, "The one who showed him mercy." Jesus told him, "Go and do likewise."
lesson: Do not ask who deserves your help; ask who needs it in front of you. Kindness that crosses group lines is the kind that counts.
people: A traveler, a priest, a Levite, a Samaritan
location: Road from Jerusalem to Jericho, Judea (modern Israel and West Bank)
source: Gospel of Luke 10:25-37

title: Jesus Washes the Disciples' Feet
text:
On the evening before his arrest, Jesus was at supper with his disciples. In that time and place, guests' dusty feet were washed when they arrived, a task for the lowest servant of the house.

During the meal, Jesus got up from the table, took off his outer garment and tied a towel around his waist. He poured water into a basin and began to wash his disciples' feet and dry them with the towel.

When he came to Simon Peter, Peter protested: "Lord, are you going to wash my feet? You shall never wash my feet." Jesus answered that if he did not wash him, Peter had no part with him. Then Peter swung to the other extreme: "Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head!"

When he had finished, Jesus put his garment back on, returned to his place and asked them whether they understood what he had done. "You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am. If I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet. For I have given you an example, that you should do as I have done to you."
lesson: Authority is most convincing when it is used to serve. If there is a humble task nobody wants, doing it yourself teaches your team more than any speech about values.
people: Jesus, Simon Peter, the disciples
source: New Testament, Gospel of John 13:1-17

title: The Nets Begin to Break
text:
In the Gospel of Luke, Jesus was standing by the Lake of Gennesaret, with a crowd pressing in to hear him. He saw two boats at the shore, where the fishermen had stepped out and were washing their nets. He got into one, which belonged to Simon, and asked him to push out a little from the land. Then he sat down and taught the crowd from the boat.

When he finished speaking, he told Simon to put out into deep water and let down the nets for a catch. Simon answered that they had worked hard all night and caught nothing. But because Jesus said so, he would let down the nets.

They did, and they caught such a great number of fish that their nets began to break. So they signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. The partners came, and they filled both boats so full that the boats began to sink.

Simon fell at Jesus' knees, overwhelmed, and so were his partners, James and John, the sons of Zebedee. Jesus told Simon not to be afraid: from now on he would be catching people. And when they brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him.
lesson: When a success is too big for you to handle alone, call your partners right away rather than letting the nets break. Good fortune also needs a team.
people: Jesus, Simon Peter, James, John
location: Lake of Gennesaret (Sea of Galilee, modern Israel)
source: Gospel of Luke 5:1-11

title: The Parable of the Talents
text:
Jesus told of a man who was going on a long journey. Before he left, he called his servants and entrusted his property to them. To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one, each according to his ability. A talent was a very large sum of money, worth many years of a laborer's wages.

The servant with five talents went at once and traded with them and made five more. The one with two did the same and gained two more. But the one who had received one talent dug a hole in the ground and hid his master's money.

After a long time the master returned and settled accounts. The first two servants brought their gains, and to each he said: "Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much."

Then the third came. "Master," he said, "I knew you to be a hard man, reaping where you did not sow. So I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent in the ground. Here is what is yours." The master called him wicked and lazy. If that was what he believed, he should at least have put the money with the bankers, so it would have earned interest. He had the talent taken from him and given to the servant who had ten, and the useless servant was thrown out.
lesson: When you are trusted with resources, doing nothing out of fear is also a choice, and usually a poor one. Put what you have been given to work and own the risk.
people: A master, three servants
source: New Testament, Gospel of Matthew 25:14-30

title: The Two Sons
text:
In the temple courts in Jerusalem, the chief priests and elders challenged Jesus about his authority. According to Matthew's Gospel, he answered them with a short parable.

A man had two sons. He went to the first and said, "Son, go and work in the vineyard today." The son answered, "I will not." But later he changed his mind and went.

Then the father went to the second son and said the same thing. That son answered, "I will, sir," but he did not go.

Jesus asked his listeners which of the two did what his father wanted. "The first," they said.

Jesus then applied the story to them. Tax collectors and prostitutes, he said, were entering the kingdom of God ahead of them. John the Baptist had come showing them the way of righteousness, and they had not believed him, while the tax collectors and prostitutes did. Even after seeing that, they had not changed their minds and believed.
lesson: What a child does matters more than what he promises. The same is true of adults: a polite yes followed by nothing is worse than an honest no that turns into action.
people: A father, two sons, Jesus, the chief priests and elders
source: Gospel of Matthew 21:28-32

title: Four Friends Lower the Paralytic Through the Roof
text:
In the Gospel of Mark, Jesus came back to Capernaum, and word spread that he was at home. So many people gathered that the house was full and there was no room left, not even around the door. He was speaking to them.

Four men arrived carrying a friend who was paralyzed, lying on a mat. They could not get near Jesus because of the crowd. So they climbed onto the flat roof. They dug through the roof above the place where Jesus was, made an opening, and lowered the mat with the paralyzed man on it down into the room.

When Jesus saw their faith, Mark says, he said to the paralyzed man that his sins were forgiven. Some scribes who were sitting there grumbled to themselves that only God could forgive sins. Jesus asked them which was easier, to say "your sins are forgiven" or to say "get up, take your mat and walk." To show them, he told the man to get up, pick up his mat and go home.

The man got up, picked up his mat at once and walked out in front of them all. The crowd was amazed and praised God, saying they had never seen anything like it.
lesson: Friends who share the weight of a burden can find a way through when the front door is blocked. Sometimes helping means carrying someone and refusing to give up.
people: Jesus, a paralyzed man, his four friends, the scribes
source: Gospel of Mark 2:1-12

title: The Prodigal Son
text:
In a parable recorded by Luke, Jesus told of a man who had two sons. The younger one asked his father for his share of the inheritance at once, before his father's death. The father divided his property, and a few days later the younger son packed everything and left for a distant country, where he squandered it all on reckless living.

Then a severe famine struck. With nothing left, he hired himself out to a farmer who sent him to feed pigs, and he was so hungry that he longed to eat the pods the pigs were eating. At last he came to his senses. His father's hired workers had food to spare, he thought, while he was starving. He would go home and say he was no longer worthy to be called a son; he would ask to be taken on as a hired hand.

While he was still a long way off, his father saw him, was filled with compassion, ran to him, threw his arms around him and kissed him. Before the son could finish his speech, the father called for the best robe, a ring and sandals, and ordered the fattened calf killed for a feast.

The elder son, coming in from the fields, heard music and refused to go in. He had served his father faithfully for years and never been given even a goat. The father went out and pleaded with him: "You are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate, because your brother was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found."
lesson: A parent's door can stay open to a child who strays. The harder lesson may be the elder brother's: to rejoice when someone undeserving is welcomed home.
people: A father, his younger son, his elder son
source: Gospel of Luke 15:11-32

title: The Rich Fool
text:
A man in the crowd called out to Jesus and asked him to tell his brother to share the family inheritance with him. Jesus refused to act as a judge between them. Instead he warned the crowd to guard against every kind of greed, because a person's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions. Then he told a story.

There was a rich man whose land produced an exceptional harvest. He thought to himself: what shall I do? I have no place to store all my crops. Then he decided. He would tear down his barns and build bigger ones, and store all his grain and goods there. Then he would say to himself: you have plenty laid up for many years. Take life easy. Eat, drink and be merry.

But God said to him: you fool. This very night your life will be demanded from you. Then who will get what you have prepared for yourself?

Jesus concluded that this is how it will be for anyone who stores up things for himself but is not rich toward God.
lesson: Planning for the future is wise, but no plan controls how much time you have. Make sure what you are building is worth having even if tonight is your last night.
people: Jesus, a man from the crowd, a rich man
location: Galilee and Judea (modern Israel and Palestinian territories)
source: Gospel of Luke 12:13-21

title: The Ten Virgins
text:
Jesus compared the kingdom of heaven to ten young women who took their lamps and went out at night to meet a bridegroom and escort him to the wedding feast. Five of them were foolish and five were wise. The foolish ones took their lamps but no extra oil. The wise ones took flasks of oil along with their lamps.

The bridegroom was delayed. The hours went by, and all ten grew drowsy and fell asleep.

At midnight a cry went up: the bridegroom is coming, go out to meet him! The women woke and trimmed their lamps. The foolish ones found that theirs were going out, and they asked the wise ones to give them some oil. The wise refused: there might not be enough for both, they said. Better to go to the sellers and buy some for yourselves.

While the five foolish women were away buying oil, the bridegroom arrived. Those who were ready went in with him to the wedding feast, and the door was shut. Later the others came back and called out, asking to be let in. He answered that he did not know them. Jesus ended: keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.
lesson: Expect delays and pack for them. Some kinds of preparation cannot be borrowed from others at the last minute, and the moment you are away scrambling may be the moment that matters.
people: Ten bridesmaids, a bridegroom
location: Galilee and Judea (modern Israel and Palestinian territories)
source: Gospel of Matthew 25:1-13

title: The Unforgiving Servant
text:
Peter asked Jesus how often he should forgive someone who wronged him. As many as seven times? Not seven times, Jesus said, but seventy-seven times, and he told a story.

A king decided to settle accounts with his servants. One of them owed him ten thousand talents, a sum so vast he could never repay it. The king ordered that the man, his wife, his children and everything he owned be sold. The servant fell on his knees and begged, "Be patient with me, and I will pay you everything." The king took pity on him, released him and cancelled the entire debt.

That same servant went out and met a fellow servant who owed him a hundred denarii, a small amount. He seized him by the throat and demanded, "Pay what you owe!" The fellow servant fell down and begged in the very same words, "Be patient with me, and I will pay you." But he refused and had the man thrown into prison until he could pay.

The other servants were deeply troubled and told the king. The king summoned the man. "You wicked servant," he said. "I forgave you all that debt because you begged me. Should you not have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?" In anger he handed him over to the jailers until he should pay back all he owed.
lesson: Remember how often you have been forgiven and given second chances. Let that memory shape how you treat people who owe or have wronged you.
people: A king, a servant, a fellow servant
source: Gospel of Matthew 18:21-35

title: The Wise and Foolish Builders
text:
At the end of the long teaching known as the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus finished with a short story about two men who each built a house.

The first was a wise man. He built his house on rock. Then the rain came down, the streams rose and flooded, and the winds blew and beat against the house. But it did not fall, because its foundation was on the rock.

The second was a foolish man. He built his house on sand. To look at, it may have seemed just as good, and it was certainly easier and quicker to build. Then the same rain came down, the streams rose, and the winds blew and beat against that house. It fell, and its fall was great.

Jesus said that whoever heard his words and put them into practice was like the wise builder, and whoever heard them but did not act on them was like the foolish one. Matthew records that when he finished speaking, the crowds were astonished at his teaching, because he taught as one who had authority. In Luke's shorter version of the same story, the wise builder digs deep before laying his foundation.
lesson: Storms will test every plan, career and relationship. Put the slow, unseen work into foundations now, because by the time the flood comes, it is too late to dig.
people: Jesus, two builders
location: Galilee and Judea (modern Israel and Palestinian territories)
source: Gospel of Matthew 7:24-27

title: Let Him Who Is Without Sin
text:
Early one morning Jesus was teaching in the Temple courts when the scribes and Pharisees brought in a woman who had been caught in adultery. They made her stand before everyone. "Teacher," they said, "this woman was caught in the act. In the law Moses commanded us to stone such women. What do you say?" They were setting a trap: whatever he answered could be used against him.

Jesus bent down and began to write on the ground with his finger. They kept pressing him for an answer. At last he straightened up and said, "Let any one of you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her." Then he bent down again and went on writing.

One by one the accusers went away, beginning with the eldest, until Jesus was left alone with the woman standing there.

He looked up and asked her, "Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you?" "No one, sir," she said. "Neither do I condemn you," Jesus answered. "Go, and from now on do not sin again."
lesson: Before you condemn someone, take an honest look at your own record. You can hold a high standard and still offer people a way forward.
people: Jesus, a woman, scribes and Pharisees
source: Gospel of John 7:53 to 8:11
caveat: The passage is missing from the earliest surviving manuscripts of John and is widely thought to be a later insertion of an older tradition.

title: The Workers in the Vineyard
text:
Jesus told of a landowner who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. He agreed to pay them a denarius for the day, the usual daily wage, and sent them to work.

At about nine o'clock he went out again and saw others standing idle in the marketplace. He sent them into the vineyard too, promising to pay whatever was right. He did the same at noon and at three. At about five, an hour before the end of the day, he found still others standing around. When they told him no one had hired them, he sent them into the vineyard as well.

In the evening he told his manager to call the workers and pay them, beginning with the last. Those hired at five o'clock each received a full denarius. When those hired first came, they expected more. But they also received a denarius. They grumbled that the last had worked a single hour, and he had made them equal to those who had borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat.

The landowner answered one of them: "Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what belongs to you and go. Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or do you begrudge my generosity?"
lesson: Be fair first: keep every promise you made. Then you are free to be generous, and those who received exactly what they agreed to have no real grievance when others receive more.
people: A landowner, laborers hired at different hours
source: New Testament, Gospel of Matthew 20:1-16

title: The Bees, the Drones and the Wasp
text:
Some bees had built their honeycombs high in an oak tree. A group of lazy drones came along and claimed the combs were theirs. The bees protested, and since neither side would give way, the case was brought before a judge: the wasp.

The wasp knew both kinds of creature well, and she saw at once that they looked much alike and buzzed with the same color and sound. Appearances would not decide this. So she proposed a simple test. Each side should take an empty hive and build new combs and fill them with honey. Then she would compare the shape of the cells and the taste of the honey with what was in the oak, and the true makers would be obvious.

The bees agreed immediately. The drones refused. They had no intention of building anything, because they could not.

That refusal was enough for the wasp. She gave her verdict on the spot: the drones had shown that they were not the makers, and the honey belonged to the bees.
lesson: When people argue over who deserves credit, ask each to show the work again. Those who did it are usually glad to, and those who did not find reasons to refuse.
people: Bees, drones, a wasp as judge
source: Phaedrus, Fables, Book III, 13 (Apes et Fuci Vespa Iudice)

title: Arria: "Paetus, It Does Not Hurt"
text:
Pliny the Younger heard this story from Fannia, Arria's granddaughter, and wrote it down in one of his letters. He said that Arria's most famous deed was not her greatest.

Once her husband, Caecina Paetus, and their son were both seriously ill. The son died. He was a young man of rare beauty and goodness. Arria arranged the funeral so quietly that her husband did not know. Whenever she entered his room, she spoke as if their son were alive and getting better, and when he asked how the boy was, she said he had slept well and eaten with appetite. When she could no longer hold back her tears, she left the room, wept, and came back with dry eyes.

In 42 AD Paetus took part in a failed revolt against the emperor Claudius and was brought to Rome as a prisoner by ship. Arria begged to be allowed to go with him as a servant. When she was refused, she hired a small fishing boat and followed the ship. Her son-in-law Thrasea tried to persuade her not to die with her husband. To prove she was determined, she struck her head against a wall.

When Paetus was condemned to die, Arria took the dagger, plunged it into her own breast, drew it out and handed it to him, saying: "Paetus, it does not hurt."
lesson: In marriage, courage can be the gift we give each other at the worst moment. Sometimes the bravest love is the quiet kind no one sees.
people: Arria the Elder, Caecina Paetus, Fannia, Thrasea Paetus
source: Pliny the Younger, Letters 3.16

title: Seneca Consoles His Mother from Exile
text:
In 41 AD the emperor Claudius exiled the philosopher Seneca to the island of Corsica on a charge of adultery with the emperor's niece. Seneca was in his forties, at the height of his career. His mother, Helvia, was left in Rome, and he knew the news had struck her hard.

So, around 42, Seneca did something unusual: he wrote a consolation to his mother for his own misfortune. He began by admitting that he had hesitated, since a man still suffering should not try to heal another. Then he reminded her of all she had already endured. Her own mother had died giving birth to her. She had lost an uncle she loved and her husband. Less than twenty days after Seneca's own young son died in her arms, she heard that Seneca had been exiled.

Exile, he argued, was only a change of place. Nature had given every human being the same sky, and a mind that was sound could be at home anywhere. He was not unhappy, he assured her, and asked her not to grieve for him. He pointed her toward the comforts she still had: his brothers, her grandchildren, her devoted sister. Above all, he urged her to turn to philosophy, and regretted that his father's old-fashioned strictness had not allowed her to study more deeply.

Seneca remained in Corsica for eight years. He was recalled in 49 to become tutor to the young Nero.
lesson: Sometimes the best way to comfort a worried parent is to show them how we are bearing up. Care can flow from child to parent too.
people: Seneca the Younger, Helvia
source: Seneca, To Helvia on Consolation (Ad Helviam Matrem de Consolatione), Dialogues 12

title: Kamtza and Bar Kamtza
text:
The Talmud says Jerusalem was destroyed because of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza. A man in the city had a friend named Kamtza and an enemy named Bar Kamtza. He gave a feast and told his servant to invite Kamtza, but the servant brought Bar Kamtza instead.

When the host found his enemy at the table, he ordered him to leave. Bar Kamtza, mortified, offered to pay for whatever he ate if he could stay. The host refused. He offered to pay half the cost of the feast, then the whole of it. The host refused, took him by the hand and threw him out. Leading rabbis were among the guests, and none of them said a word.

Bar Kamtza decided that their silence meant they approved, and he went to the Roman emperor to accuse the Jews of rebellion. As proof, he said, send them a sacrifice and see if they will offer it. The emperor sent a fine calf, and on the way Bar Kamtza made a small cut in its lip, a blemish that disqualified it under Jewish law but not under Roman custom.

The rabbis debated offering it anyway for the sake of peace, or even killing Bar Kamtza, but Rabbi Zechariah ben Avkulas talked them out of both. The offering was refused, and in the Talmud's telling this set in motion the war that ended with the Temple in flames.
lesson: Humiliating someone in public, and staying silent while it happens, can set off consequences far beyond the moment. Speak up when you see someone shamed.
people: A host, Bar Kamtza, Rabbi Zechariah ben Avkulas, the rabbis
date: 1st century, as told in the Talmud
source: Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 55b to 56a
caveat: This is a rabbinic moral narrative, not a historical account of the causes of the Jewish War of 66 to 70 AD.

title: Yochanan Ben Zakkai Leaves in a Coffin
text:
During the Roman siege of Jerusalem around 70 AD, the city was controlled by zealot factions determined to fight to the end. The Babylonian Talmud tells a story about Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, the leading sage of the time, who believed the city could not hold.

According to the Talmud, the zealots had burned the city's stores of food to force the population to fight, and no one was allowed to leave. Yochanan asked his nephew, a zealot leader, for help. The nephew suggested he pretend to be ill and then dead, since only corpses were carried out of the city for burial. His disciples Eliezer and Joshua carried him out in a coffin, past the guards at the gate.

Once outside, Yochanan went to the Roman commander Vespasian and greeted him as king. Vespasian objected that he was not a king, but at that moment, the story says, a messenger arrived from Rome to tell him he had been made emperor. Vespasian, pleased, offered Yochanan a request. He did not ask Vespasian to spare Jerusalem, which he judged impossible. He asked for the town of Yavneh and its sages, protection for the family of the patriarch Gamaliel, and a physician to heal the starving Rabbi Tzadok.

Jerusalem and the Temple were destroyed. At Yavneh, Yochanan's academy became the center from which rabbinic Judaism was rebuilt without the Temple.
lesson: When you cannot save everything, decide what is truly essential and secure that. A modest, achievable request can preserve the future.
people: Yochanan ben Zakkai, Vespasian, Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, Joshua ben Hananiah
source: Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 56a to 56b; also Avot de-Rabbi Natan, version A, chapter 4
caveat: The story is a rabbinic legend: Vespasian was proclaimed emperor in 69 and had left Judea before the city fell.

title: Pliny the Elder Sails Toward Vesuvius
text:
In August 79 AD, Pliny the Elder, the great naturalist and author of the Natural History, commanded the Roman fleet at Misenum, on the Bay of Naples. His widowed sister and her son, the seventeen-year-old Pliny the Younger, were staying with him. Years later the nephew described what happened in two letters to the historian Tacitus.

Early one afternoon his mother pointed out a huge cloud rising over the bay, shaped like an umbrella pine. The scholar in Pliny the Elder wanted to see it more closely, and he ordered a boat. He invited his nephew along, but the young man replied that he would rather keep studying. Then a message came from a woman whose villa lay at the foot of Vesuvius, begging for rescue. Pliny turned his scientific trip into a rescue mission, launched warships, and steered straight toward the danger while others fled.

Unable to land, he went on to Stabiae, where he calmed his frightened friend Pomponianus by bathing, dining cheerfully and going to sleep. In the night, as ash piled up, they fled to the shore with pillows tied to their heads. There Pliny collapsed and died.

At Misenum, the nephew lived through his own night of terror. As they fled, his mother begged him to leave her behind, since she was old and slow and he could escape alone. He refused, took her hand and made her walk faster. Both survived.
lesson: Courage and duty can be passed from one generation to the next by example. In a crisis, the people we refuse to leave behind define who we are.
people: Pliny the Elder, Pliny the Younger, his mother Plinia, Pomponianus
location: Misenum and Stabiae, Bay of Naples, Italy
source: Pliny the Younger, Letters 6.16 and 6.20
caveat: The traditional date of 24 August has been questioned, and some scholars place the eruption in the autumn.

title: Akiva and the Water on the Stone
text:
According to the tradition preserved in Avot de-Rabbi Natan, Akiva had reached the age of forty without learning anything. He was an unlettered man, and it seemed far too late for him to begin the study of the Torah, which scholars spent their whole lives mastering.

One day he was standing by a well and noticed a stone at its mouth with a deep hollow worn into it. He asked who had carved it. He was told that it was the water, which fell on it constantly, drop by drop, day after day.

Akiva thought about this. If something as soft as water could carve its way into something as hard as stone, how much more could the words of the Torah, which are as hard as iron, carve their way into his heart, which was only flesh and blood.

He went straight off to study. With his young son, he sat with the children at a teacher's side and began with the alphabet, writing the letters on a tablet. He went on, letter by letter and teaching by teaching, until he had learned the whole Torah. Rabbi Akiva became one of the greatest scholars in Jewish history.
lesson: It is rarely too late to start. Small efforts repeated every day can wear through what looks impossibly hard.
people: Rabbi Akiva
source: Avot de-Rabbi Natan, Version A, Chapter 6
caveat: This account of Akiva's beginnings is a traditional story from rabbinic literature compiled centuries after his death.

title: Rabban Gamliel Is Removed from Office
text:
Rabban Gamliel was head of the academy at Yavneh. The Talmud tells that a student once asked Rabbi Yehoshua whether the evening prayer was obligatory, and he said it was optional. The student then asked Rabban Gamliel, who said it was obligatory, and added that Rabbi Yehoshua had told him otherwise.

Rabban Gamliel waited until the scholars were assembled. Then the question was raised in public, and he asked whether anyone disagreed. Rabbi Yehoshua said no. Rabban Gamliel told him that the opposite had been reported in his name, and ordered him to stand up so the witness could testify against him. Rabbi Yehoshua stood. Rabban Gamliel went on teaching and left him standing, until the assembly began to murmur and told the speaker to stop. It was not the first time Rabban Gamliel had humiliated Rabbi Yehoshua this way, they said, and they removed him from office. In his place they appointed the young Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah. That day the guard at the door was removed, and so many new students came that hundreds of benches had to be added.

Rabban Gamliel went to Rabbi Yehoshua's house to apologize. Seeing its blackened walls, he learned that Rabbi Yehoshua earned his living as a smith or charcoal maker. Rabbi Yehoshua told him that a generation led by someone who did not know how scholars struggled to live was to be pitied. Rabban Gamliel asked his forgiveness, and received it. In the end, the sages arranged for him to share the leadership with Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah.
lesson: Winning an argument by humiliating a colleague can cost you the trust that holds your position up. When you have done harm, go yourself, admit it and ask to be forgiven.
people: Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah
source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 27b to 28a

title: Ban Zhao Finishes Her Brother's History
text:
Ban Biao, a scholar of the first century AD, began writing a continuation of Sima Qian's great history of China. When he died, his son Ban Gu took over and reshaped the work into a history of the Former Han dynasty, the Book of Han. Ban Gu's twin brother, Ban Chao, became a famous general in Central Asia. Their younger sister, Ban Zhao, was married at fourteen, widowed young, and devoted herself to study.

In 92 AD Ban Gu was caught up in the fall of a powerful patron, the general Dou Xian. He was imprisoned and died there, leaving the Book of Han unfinished. According to her biography in the History of the Later Han, the emperor ordered Ban Zhao to complete it, giving her access to the imperial library. She finished the eight tables and, with the help of the scholar Ma Xu, the treatise on astronomy.

The book was so difficult that many readers could not follow it. The scholar Ma Rong, later one of the most famous classicists of the age, was sent to study it under her. Ban Zhao also served as teacher to the empress and the palace ladies, and wrote Lessons for Women, advice to her daughters. When she died, the empress dowager wore mourning for her.

The Book of Han, the work of a father, a son and a daughter, became the model for all later Chinese dynastic histories.
lesson: Family work can pass from one generation to the next, and to whoever is most able to carry it. Talent in a family should not be overlooked because of who holds it.
people: Ban Zhao, Ban Gu, Ban Biao, Ban Chao
source: Fan Ye, Hou Hanshu (History of the Later Han), biography of the wife of Cao Shishu (Ban Zhao)

title: Rabbi Akiva and Rachel
text:
Akiva was an unlearned shepherd working for Kalba Savua, one of the richest men in Jerusalem. Kalba Savua's daughter saw that he was modest and good, and asked him: if she betrothed herself to him, would he go and study Torah? He said yes. They married secretly. When her father found out, he threw her out of the house and vowed that she would get nothing from his property.

The Talmud says they were so poor in the winter that they slept on straw, and Akiva would pick the straw from her hair. He told her that if he could, he would give her a "Jerusalem of gold," a golden crown engraved with the city.

She sent him off to study. After twelve years he came home with twelve thousand students. As he approached, he overheard an old man mocking her for living as a widow while her husband was away. She answered that if he listened to her, he would study twelve more years. Hearing this, Akiva turned around and went back.

He returned after another twelve years with twenty four thousand students. She went out to meet him, in shabby clothes, and fell at his feet. His students tried to push her away, but Akiva stopped them: "What is mine and what is yours is hers." Kalba Savua, hearing of the great scholar, came to have his vow annulled and gave them half his wealth.
lesson: One partner's belief and sacrifice can make the other's achievement possible. When success comes, honor the person who made it possible.
people: Rabbi Akiva, his wife (traditionally called Rachel), Kalba Savua
source: Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 62b to 63a; Nedarim 50a
caveat: The Talmudic accounts are legendary and differ in details, and the name Rachel comes from later tradition.

title: Hercules Cleans the Augean Stables
text:
For his fifth labor, King Eurystheus ordered Hercules to carry out all the dung from the cattle yards of Augeas, king of Elis, in a single day. Augeas owned enormous herds, and the filth had piled up for years. It was a task meant to be both impossible and humiliating.

Hercules went to Augeas without mentioning that he was acting on Eurystheus's orders. He offered to clear out all the dung in one day in return for a tenth of the king's cattle. Augeas did not believe it could be done and agreed, and his son Phyleus witnessed the promise.

Hercules did not pick up a shovel. Two rivers, the Alpheus and the Peneus, flowed nearby. He broke an opening through the foundations of the cattle yard, cut channels to turn both rivers into it, and made another opening on the far side for the water to flow out. The torrent swept through and carried all the filth away.

Augeas then learned that the work had been ordered by Eurystheus and refused to pay, denying he had ever promised anything. When the dispute came before judges, Phyleus testified against his own father, and Augeas angrily banished them both. Eurystheus, for his part, refused to count the labor, because Hercules had done it for pay.
lesson: When a job looks impossible by hand, look for a larger force already flowing nearby that you can redirect. And get agreements in a form that will hold when the other side wants out.
people: Hercules (Heracles), King Augeas, Phyleus, Eurystheus
date: Greek myth; Apollodorus, 1st or 2nd century AD
source: Apollodorus, Library 2.5.5
caveat: Other ancient authors tell the story with different details.

title: Hercules, Iolaus and the Hydra
text:
The second labor that King Eurystheus set for Heracles was to kill the Hydra, a monstrous serpent living in the swamps of Lerna. According to the mythographer Apollodorus, it had nine heads, and the middle one could not die.

Heracles drove to Lerna in a chariot with his nephew Iolaus at the reins. He forced the Hydra out of its lair with burning arrows and grappled with it. But every time he smashed one of its heads with his club, two new ones grew in its place. To make things worse, a giant crab came out of the swamp to help the Hydra and bit him on the foot. He killed the crab, but he was making no progress against the monster.

So Heracles called to Iolaus for help. Iolaus set fire to part of a nearby wood, and each time Heracles cut off a head, Iolaus seared the stump with a burning branch so that no new heads could sprout. Working together, they destroyed the heads one after another. At last Heracles cut off the immortal head, buried it under a heavy rock, and dipped his arrows in the Hydra's poisonous gall.

Eurystheus later refused to count this labor, because Heracles had not done it alone.
lesson: Some problems multiply faster than one person can handle them and need a partner who deals with what you cannot. Do not let anyone shame you for having had help.
people: Heracles (Hercules), Iolaus, Eurystheus
date: Ancient Greek myth; text 1st or 2nd century AD
source: Apollodorus, Library (Bibliotheca) 2.5.2

title: The Oven of Akhnai
text:
The Babylonian Talmud tells of a debate among the sages over a clay oven built in separate rings with sand between them. Was it subject to the laws of ritual impurity? Rabbi Eliezer said it was not. All the other sages disagreed.

Rabbi Eliezer brought every argument he could, and they did not accept them. So he said: if the law is as I say, let this carob tree prove it. The carob tree uprooted itself and moved a hundred cubits. The sages said one does not bring proof from a carob tree. Let the stream prove it, he said, and the water flowed backward. Let the walls of the study house prove it, and the walls began to lean. Rabbi Yehoshua rebuked the walls, and out of respect for him they did not fall, and out of respect for Rabbi Eliezer they did not straighten. They are still leaning, the Talmud says.

Finally Rabbi Eliezer called on heaven itself, and a heavenly voice declared that the law was as he said. Rabbi Yehoshua stood up and quoted Deuteronomy: "It is not in heaven." The Torah had been given to people, and the law follows the majority.

The Talmud adds that the prophet Elijah later reported God's reaction: God smiled and said, "My children have defeated me." The sages then ruled against Rabbi Eliezer and placed him under a ban.
lesson: A group that agrees on how decisions are made must hold to that process, even when someone has a striking argument from outside it. And winning a vote does not excuse wounding a colleague.
people: Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananiah, the sages
date: Late 1st to early 2nd century (set); text c. 6th century
source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 59a to 59b

title: The Road That Is Short but Long
text:
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananiah was one of the great sages of his generation, famous for his learning and quick wit. Yet he liked to say that only three people had ever got the better of him: a woman, a little girl and a little boy. This is the story of the boy.

He was traveling and came to a crossroads where a child was sitting. He asked the boy which road led to the city. The child pointed: this one is short and long, he said, and that one is long and short.

The rabbi, naturally, took the short road. Soon he could see the city ahead of him. But when he came close, he found that it was ringed by gardens and orchards, with walls and hedges, and there was no way through to the town. He had to turn around and walk all the way back to the crossroads.

There he found the boy again and said: my son, did you not tell me this road was short? The child answered: and did I not also tell you it was long?

Rabbi Yehoshua kissed him on the head and said: happy are you, Israel, for all of you are wise, from the greatest to the smallest.
lesson: The route that looks quickest is not always the fastest way to your actual goal. Listen to the full answer, including the part you would rather not hear.
people: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananiah, a child
source: Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 53b

title: Two Travelers and One Flask
text:
The Talmud records a hard case that the sages argued about. Two people are walking through the desert, far from any town. Only one of them has a flask of water. If both of them drink from it, both will die before they reach a settlement. If only one drinks, that one will reach a settlement alive.

The sage Ben Petura taught that it is better for both to drink and die, so that neither should have to watch the death of his companion. The water should be shared, whatever it costs.

Then Rabbi Akiva came and taught differently. He pointed to a verse in Leviticus about helping a brother in need: "that your brother may live with you." With you, Akiva said, means that your own life comes first. The one who owns the water should drink it.

The Talmud gives Akiva's view as the conclusion, and the passage has been studied and argued over ever since.
lesson: Caring for others does not require you to destroy yourself. Look after your own life so that you can go on helping, and take hard dilemmas seriously instead of pretending they are easy.
people: Ben Petura, Rabbi Akiva
source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 62a

title: "Then Stop Being Emperor"
text:
The Roman emperor Hadrian, who ruled from 117 to 138, spent much of his reign traveling around the empire, inspecting provinces and armies and meeting the people he governed.

The historian Cassius Dio, writing about a century later, tells a short story about one of these journeys. As Hadrian was passing along a road, a woman came up and asked him to hear a request. He was busy and told her that he had no time. She called after him: "Then stop being emperor." Hadrian turned around, Dio says, and gave her a hearing.

Dio tells the story as an example of the emperor's attention to ordinary subjects. He also mentions that Hadrian took care over the administration of justice, sat with advisers when he judged cases, and dealt with many matters personally. The woman's sharp answer survived because the emperor took it as a fair rebuke rather than an insult.
lesson: If you hold a position of responsibility, listening to the people it affects is the job, not an interruption of it.
people: Emperor Hadrian
source: Cassius Dio, Roman History, Book 69, chapter 6
caveat: A very similar story is told of earlier kings, such as Philip II of Macedon, so it may be a traveling anecdote.

title: Androcles and the Lion
text:
The Roman writer Aulus Gellius retold this story from the scholar Apion, who claimed to have seen its ending in Rome. A slave named Androcles ran away from a cruel master, a Roman official in Africa. He hid in a desert cave, and soon a lion limped in, groaning, and held out a swollen paw. Androcles found a large thorn buried in it, pulled it out, pressed out the pus and bound the wound.

For three years man and lion shared the cave, and the lion brought him the best parts of its kills. At last Androcles grew tired of that wild life and left. He was captured by soldiers, sent back to Rome and condemned to be thrown to the beasts in the Circus Maximus.

On the day of the games a huge lion was released against him. It ran at him, then stopped short, approached slowly, and began to wag its tail and lick his hands and feet. The crowd was astonished. When the emperor asked for an explanation, Androcles told his story, and it spread through the stands on written tablets. The people demanded that he be freed and given the lion. Afterward, Apion says, Androcles led the lion through the city on a light leash, and people gave him money and threw flowers on the lion.
lesson: Help given freely, even to a creature that cannot thank you in words, can come back when you least expect it. Gratitude is a strong bond.
people: Androcles, a lion
date: 2nd century AD (set in the 1st century AD)
source: Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 5.14, after Apion
caveat: Apion claimed to be an eyewitness, but the tale is generally treated as a legend rather than a historical event.

title: Beruriah and the Troublesome Neighbors
text:
Rabbi Meir was one of the great sages of the second century, and his wife Beruriah was famous in her own right for her learning, which is unusual in the records of that age.

In their neighborhood lived some hoodlums who caused Rabbi Meir a great deal of grief. They harassed him so much that he began to pray that they would die.

Beruriah heard him and objected. "What are you thinking?" she asked. "Is it because it is written in the Psalms, 'Let sins cease from the earth'? It does not say 'sinners', it says 'sins'. And look at the end of the same verse: 'and the wicked will be no more.' Once the sins have ended, there will be no more wicked people. Pray for them instead, that they turn back from their ways, and then they will be wicked no longer."

Rabbi Meir took her advice. He prayed for them to change rather than to perish, and the Talmud reports that they repented.
lesson: When someone is making your life hard, aim at ending the harmful behavior, not at destroying the person. People can change, and enemies can become neighbors again.
people: Rabbi Meir, Beruriah
source: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 10a

title: Beruriah and the Returned Jewels
text:
A Jewish midrash tells that Rabbi Meir was teaching in the house of study one Sabbath afternoon. While he was away, his two sons died at home. His wife Beruriah laid them on a bed and covered them with a sheet.

When Rabbi Meir came home after the Sabbath ended, he asked where his sons were. She said they had gone to the study house. He said he had looked for them there and not seen them. She brought him the cup for the blessing that ends the Sabbath, and he made it. Again he asked about his sons. She said they had gone somewhere and would come soon, and she gave him food.

When he had eaten, she said: "Rabbi, I have a question. Some time ago a man gave me something to keep for him. Now he has come back to claim it. Should I return it or not?" Meir said that of course a person must return a deposit to its owner.

She said she would not have returned it without his knowledge. Then she took him by the hand, led him up to the room and drew back the sheet. Meir began to weep: "My sons, my sons." Beruriah reminded him of his own words: did he not say a deposit must be returned to its owner? "The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away."
lesson: Hard news can be given gently and in its time. Preparing someone you love for grief is itself an act of care.
people: Beruriah, Rabbi Meir, their two sons
source: Midrash Mishlei (Midrash on Proverbs) 31
caveat: The midrash is a late compilation, and the story is a pious legend rather than a historical record.

title: Kong Rong Gives Up the Larger Pears
text:
Kong Rong, who lived in the late Han dynasty and was a descendant of Confucius, was one of several brothers. When he was four years old, the family was given a plate of pears.
