The boys were allowed to choose. Kong Rong did not grab for the biggest one, as small children usually do. He reached for the smallest pear on the plate.

The adults asked why he had chosen it. He answered that he was a small boy, so he ought to take the small one. Older brothers should have the larger pears.

The story was told about him throughout his family and later throughout China. Kong Rong grew up to be a well known scholar and official, but he is remembered above all for this one small act. Many centuries later the episode was placed in the Three Character Classic, the rhyming primer from which generations of Chinese children learned to read: "Rong at four could yield the pears."
lesson: Children learn generosity in small daily choices like who gets the bigger share. Notice and praise the moment a child chooses to give way.
people: Kong Rong, his brothers
source: Hou Hanshu, biography of Kong Rong, with commentary citing the Rong Biezhuan; Three Character Classic
caveat: The anecdote comes from a commentary rather than the main historical record and is a traditional story.

title: Marcus Aurelius Auctions the Palace Treasures
text:
In the late 160s the Roman Empire was in crisis. A plague brought back by the army from the east was killing large numbers of people, and Germanic peoples were crossing the Danube frontier. The emperor Marcus Aurelius needed money for a long war, and the treasury was empty.

According to the Historia Augusta, a collection of imperial biographies written later, Marcus refused to impose new taxes on the provinces. Instead he held a public auction in the Forum of Trajan in Rome. He sold the imperial furnishings: gold and crystal cups, vessels fit for kings, statues and paintings by great artists, and even his wife's silk and gold-embroidered robes and the jewels he found in a private treasury of the emperor Hadrian. The sale went on for two months, the biography says.

It raised enough to carry on the war. Afterward, the biography adds, Marcus let it be known that anyone who wished to return what they had bought could do so and get the price back, but he did not pressure those who chose to keep their purchases. The historian Eutropius tells the same story.
lesson: Before asking others to give something up, give up something of your own first. People notice who pays.
people: Marcus Aurelius
source: Historia Augusta, Life of Marcus Aurelius, chapters 17 and 21; Eutropius, Breviarium, Book 8, chapter 13
caveat: The Historia Augusta is often unreliable, though Eutropius independently reports the auction.

title: Marcus Aurelius and His Son Commodus
text:
For most of the second century, Roman emperors chose their successors by adoption, picking capable adult men. Marcus Aurelius had himself been adopted in this way, and trained for years before taking power in 161. He was a philosopher on the throne, whose private notebook, the Meditations, is still read today. But unlike his predecessors, he had a surviving son of his own: Commodus, born in 161.

Marcus gave the boy the best teachers available and raised him to rule. In 177, when Commodus was fifteen, his father made him co-emperor. Commodus accompanied Marcus on his long campaigns against the Germanic tribes along the Danube. In March 180 Marcus died in his camp, and Commodus, now eighteen, became sole emperor.

He quickly made peace with the tribes and returned to the pleasures of Rome. The historian Cassius Dio, who was a senator at the time, wrote that Commodus was not naturally wicked but simple and easily led by bad companions. His reign turned into a series of plots and executions. He handed government to favorites, renamed Rome after himself and fought as a gladiator in the arena before the horrified senate. On the last day of 192 he was strangled by a wrestler on the orders of his own household.

Dio wrote that with the death of Marcus, Roman history descended from a kingdom of gold to one of iron and rust.
lesson: Even the wisest parent cannot guarantee a child's character, and love can blind us to a child's unfitness. Handing someone power is different from preparing them for it.
people: Marcus Aurelius, Commodus, Cassius Dio
source: Cassius Dio, Roman History 72 (71).34 to 73 (72).22; Historia Augusta, Life of Commodus

title: The Oath in the Peach Garden
text:
The Romance of the Three Kingdoms, the great fourteenth century Chinese novel attributed to Luo Guanzhong, opens in 184, as the Han dynasty totters and the Yellow Turban rebellion spreads.

In the county of Zhuo a notice goes up calling for volunteers to fight the rebels. Liu Bei, a poor man who sells straw sandals and mats but claims descent from the imperial house, reads it and sighs. Zhang Fei, a butcher and wine seller with a booming voice, scolds him for sighing instead of acting. In a tavern they meet Guan Yu, a tall, red-faced man with a long beard, on the run after killing a local bully.

The three find they share the same hopes. In the peach garden behind Zhang Fei's house, among the blossoms, they sacrifice a black ox and a white horse and swear brotherhood before Heaven and Earth. They vow to help each other and the people, and declare that though they were not born on the same day, they wish to die on the same day. Liu Bei becomes the eldest brother, Guan Yu the second, Zhang Fei the third.

The novel follows their loyalty through decades of war, until Liu Bei founds the kingdom of Shu. The historical record, Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms, does not mention any oath, but it does say that Liu Bei treated Guan Yu and Zhang Fei with the affection of brothers and that they followed him through every hardship.
lesson: A small group bound by clear, mutual commitment can hold together through long years of setbacks. Say out loud what you owe each other.
people: Liu Bei, Guan Yu, Zhang Fei
source: Luo Guanzhong, Romance of the Three Kingdoms, chapter 1; Chen Shou, Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguozhi), biography of Guan Yu
caveat: The oath is a literary invention of the novel; the history records only that the three were close as brothers.

title: Cao Cao Punishes Himself for Trampling Crops
text:
Cao Cao was the most powerful warlord of late Han China at the end of the second century, and the founder of what became the kingdom of Wei. He was known both as a brilliant general and administrator and, in later tradition, as a cunning schemer.

A story about him survives in a work called the Cao Man Zhuan, quoted by Pei Songzhi in his fifth-century commentary on the Records of the Three Kingdoms. Once, on campaign, Cao Cao ordered that no soldier should trample the growing wheat, on pain of death. Cavalrymen dismounted and led their horses carefully through the fields.

Then Cao Cao's own horse was startled and plunged into the wheat. He called the army's registrar and asked him to decide his punishment. The registrar cited the old principle that punishments are not applied to those of the highest rank. Cao Cao answered that if he made a law and broke it himself, how could he command his men. But as the commander he could not kill himself, so he drew his sword, cut off his hair and threw it on the ground as a substitute for his head.

In that era cutting one's hair was a real disgrace, and the gesture made the point to the whole army.
lesson: The rules you set for others bind you too. When you break one, take the consequence visibly, or your rules lose their force.
people: Cao Cao
source: Cao Man Zhuan, quoted by Pei Songzhi in his commentary on Chen Shou, Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguozhi), Biography of Cao Cao
caveat: The Cao Man Zhuan was a hostile source from the rival state of Wu, which told the story to show Cao Cao's craftiness.

title: The Blind Man and the Lame Man in the Orchard
text:
The Talmud records a conversation between the Roman Antoninus and Rabbi Judah the Prince. Antoninus argued that body and soul could each escape judgment. The body could say that it was the soul that sinned, since once the soul left, the body lay still like a stone. The soul could say that it was the body that sinned, since without the body it flew through the air like a bird.

Rabbi Judah answered with a parable. A king had a beautiful orchard with fine early figs. He set two watchmen to guard it, one lame and one blind. The lame man said to the blind man that he could see wonderful figs in the orchard. Come, he said, let me ride on your shoulders and we will get them and eat them. The blind man carried the lame man, and together they picked the figs and ate them.

Some time later the king came and asked where his figs had gone. The lame man said: do I have legs to walk to them? The blind man said: do I have eyes to see them? So the king set the lame man on the blind man's shoulders and judged them as one. In the same way, Rabbi Judah said, God puts the soul back into the body and judges them together.
lesson: When partners achieve something together, they share responsibility for it together. Neither can claim the gain and then blame the other for the harm.
people: Antoninus, Rabbi Judah the Prince
source: Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 91a to 91b

title: Liu Bei Visits Zhuge Liang Three Times
text:
Around 207 Liu Bei was a warlord without a secure base, sheltering under another lord in Jing province in central China. He was in his forties and had spent twenty years fighting and losing. An adviser, Xu Shu, told him about a young scholar living in retirement at Longzhong, Zhuge Liang, and said he was a "sleeping dragon". Liu Bei asked Xu Shu to bring him. Xu Shu answered that such a man could be visited, but not summoned.

So Liu Bei went himself. According to Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms, he went three times before he was received. Zhuge Liang was then about twenty-six.

When they finally met, Zhuge Liang laid out a long-term plan: take Jing and Yi provinces, make alliances with the southern peoples and with Sun Quan in the east, and wait for the right moment to strike north. Liu Bei followed it, and it shaped the founding of the Shu Han kingdom.

Twenty years later, in his famous memorial to Liu Bei's son, Zhuge Liang recalled that the late emperor had not thought him too humble and had come three times to his thatched cottage.
lesson: If you want exceptional people to join you, go to them and keep going. Humility and persistence in asking show what you value.
people: Liu Bei, Zhuge Liang, Xu Shu
source: Chen Shou, Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguozhi), Biography of Zhuge Liang; Zhuge Liang, Chu Shi Biao (227)

title: Fire Ships at Red Cliffs
text:
In the winter of 208, the warlord Cao Cao, master of northern China, came down the Yangtze with a huge army and fleet to finish off his southern rivals. Sun Quan and Liu Bei joined forces against him, with Sun Quan's general Zhou Yu in command. They were heavily outnumbered.

Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms says that Zhou Yu's officer Huang Gai noticed something about the enemy fleet: Cao Cao's ships were moored close together, bow to stern, and could be burned. Huang Gai sent Cao Cao a letter offering to defect with his ships. He then prepared a squadron of vessels packed with dry reeds and brushwood soaked in oil, covered with curtains and decked with flags, each towing a small fast boat behind it.

Huang Gai sailed toward Cao Cao's fleet with the wind behind him. Cao Cao's men came out to watch, thinking he was surrendering. Close to the line, his crews set the ships on fire and escaped in the small boats. The blazing ships drove into the packed fleet, and the fire spread to the camps on the shore. Many of Cao Cao's men burned or drowned. Weakened also by sickness in his army, Cao Cao retreated north. The battle ended his hope of uniting China and led to the division into three kingdoms.
lesson: A larger force often has a structural weakness that comes with its size. Find what makes the opponent strong and ask how that same feature could be turned against him.
people: Zhou Yu, Huang Gai, Cao Cao, Sun Quan, Liu Bei
location: Red Cliffs on the Yangtze (modern Hubei, China)
source: Chen Shou, Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguozhi), biography of Zhou Yu
caveat: The exact site of the battle is disputed, and the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms added many famous details not in the history.

title: Cao Zhi's Seven-Step Poem
text:
Cao Cao, the great warlord of the end of the Han dynasty, had several talented sons. For a time he seemed to favor Cao Zhi, a brilliant poet, as his heir, but in the end he chose the elder, Cao Pi. When Cao Cao died in 220, Cao Pi took the throne as the first emperor of Wei. He never trusted his gifted brother.

The New Account of Tales of the World, a collection of anecdotes compiled in the fifth century by Liu Yiqing, tells what happened next. The emperor ordered Cao Zhi to compose a poem in the time it took to walk seven steps. If he failed, he would be put to death.

Cao Zhi walked and composed. His poem compared the two brothers to beans and beanstalks. The beans are boiled to make a soup, he said, while the stalks burn under the pot; the beans weep in the pot. We sprang from the same root, so why are you in such a hurry to cook me?

According to the story, the emperor was deeply ashamed. Cao Zhi's life was spared. He spent the rest of it moved from one fief to another under close watch, kept away from any real power, and died in 232 at forty. The line about "the same root" became a proverb, used ever since to plead against quarrels between brothers and kin.
lesson: Rivalry between siblings can be shamed by a reminder of what they share. Before attacking family, remember that you grew from the same root.
people: Cao Pi (Emperor Wen of Wei), Cao Zhi
source: Liu Yiqing, Shishuo Xinyu (A New Account of Tales of the World), Literature section 66
caveat: The story appears centuries later and historians doubt it happened; the poem may not be Cao Zhi's own.

title: Zhuge Liang's Empty Fort
text:
One of the most famous stories of the Three Kingdoms is a bluff. The oldest version survives because the historian Pei Songzhi, in the 5th century, quoted it in his commentary on Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms, attributing it to an earlier writer, Guo Chong.

In Guo Chong's account, Zhuge Liang, chancellor of Shu, was at Yangping with only a small force after sending most of his troops away. The Wei general Sima Yi approached with a large army. Zhuge Liang's officers were terrified. Instead of fleeing or barricading the walls, Zhuge Liang ordered the flags lowered and the drums silenced, and had the city gates thrown open with men sweeping the ground in front of them. Sima Yi, who knew Zhuge Liang as a careful commander who never took needless risks, suspected a hidden ambush and withdrew his army.

Pei Songzhi himself doubted the story. He pointed out that Sima Yi was serving far away at the time and that the details did not fit the known record. Centuries later the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms moved the scene to a town called Xicheng and added the most famous image: Zhuge Liang sitting calmly on the wall, playing the zither, while the enemy army hesitated below.
lesson: A reputation for caution can make a bold move believable. Know what your opponent expects of you, because his expectations can be used as much as your resources.
people: Zhuge Liang, Sima Yi
location: Yangping (modern Shaanxi, China) in the earliest version
source: Guo Chong, quoted by Pei Songzhi in his commentary on Chen Shou, Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguozhi); Luo Guanzhong, Romance of the Three Kingdoms, chapter 95
caveat: Already in the 5th century Pei Songzhi judged the episode untrue, and the zither scene is fiction from the novel.

title: Zhuge Liang Executes Ma Su in Tears
text:
In 228 Zhuge Liang, chancellor of the Shu Han kingdom, launched his first northern campaign against the rival kingdom of Wei. For the key post of Jieting, guarding his army's flank, he chose Ma Su, a talented young officer he valued highly, over more experienced generals. Before his death, the Shu founder Liu Bei had warned Zhuge Liang that Ma Su's words exceeded his real abilities.

At Jieting Ma Su ignored Zhuge Liang's instructions and the advice of his deputy Wang Ping. He left the road and camped on a hill away from water. The Wei general Zhang He cut off his water supply and routed his army. The loss of Jieting forced Zhuge Liang to abandon the whole campaign.

Ma Su was condemned to death. Chen Shou's history records his death, and later sources cited in Pei Songzhi's commentary say that Zhuge Liang wept for him and took care of his family.

Zhuge Liang also blamed himself. He wrote to the emperor that the defeat came from his own poor choice of commander and asked to be demoted three grades. The request was granted, though he kept his duties.
lesson: Hold people accountable even when you like them, and own your part in putting them where they failed.
people: Zhuge Liang, Ma Su, Wang Ping
source: Chen Shou, Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguozhi), Biographies of Zhuge Liang and Ma Su, with Pei Songzhi's commentary
caveat: One passage in the Sanguozhi says Ma Su died in prison rather than by execution.

title: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
text:
One day Rabbi Yochanan was bathing in the Jordan when Resh Lakish, then a bandit and gladiator of enormous strength, leapt into the river after him. Yochanan said, "Your strength should be for Torah." Resh Lakish answered, "Your beauty should be for women." Yochanan offered him his sister, more beautiful than himself, if he would change his life. Resh Lakish agreed. Yochanan taught him, and he became one of the greatest scholars of his generation, Yochanan's study partner and brother-in-law.

Years later, in the study hall, they disagreed about when weapons such as swords and knives become finished objects in law. Yochanan said one thing, Resh Lakish another. Then Yochanan snapped, "A bandit knows his trade." Resh Lakish was deeply hurt by the reminder of his past. Yochanan was hurt in turn, Resh Lakish fell ill, and Yochanan refused even his sister's pleas to pray for him. Resh Lakish died.

Yochanan sank into grief. The sages sent him a brilliant scholar, Elazar ben Pedat, who supported every statement Yochanan made with a source. "Are you like the son of Lakish?" Yochanan cried. "When I said something, he raised twenty-four objections, I gave twenty-four answers, and the law became clear." He went about tearing his clothes and weeping, "Where are you, son of Lakish?" until he lost his mind, and the sages prayed for his death.
lesson: In a close friendship, one contemptuous remark about the other's past can cut deeper than any argument. Value the friend who challenges you, and repair hurts while you still can.
people: Rabbi Yochanan, Resh Lakish
source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 84a

title: Abba Moses and the Leaking Jug
text:
Abba Moses, called the Ethiopian or the Black, had been a slave and, by tradition, the leader of a band of robbers before he became a monk in the Egyptian desert of Scetis. In time he was one of its most respected elders.

Once a brother at Scetis committed a fault. The monks called a council to judge him and sent for Abba Moses, but he would not come. Then the priest sent someone to tell him, "Come, everyone is waiting for you."

So Moses got up and went. He took a jug that leaked, filled it with water and carried it with him. In later retellings it is a basket full of sand that ran out through the holes as he walked.

The brothers came out to meet him and asked, "What is this, Father?" The old man said, "My sins are running out behind me, and I do not see them. And today I am coming to judge the faults of someone else."

When they heard this, they said nothing more to the brother and forgave him.
lesson: When you feel ready to judge someone, remember the faults you no longer notice in yourself. Humility makes forgiveness easier.
people: Abba Moses the Ethiopian, the monks of Scetis
source: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Apophthegmata Patrum), alphabetical collection, Moses 2

title: Ambrose Makes the Emperor Do Penance
text:
In 390 a riot broke out in Thessalonica, in Greece, and the crowd killed Butheric, the commander of the local garrison. The emperor Theodosius I, furious, ordered a reprisal. Soldiers trapped the people of the city in the circus and massacred them. Theodoret, a church historian of the next century, puts the dead at seven thousand.

Ambrose, the bishop of Milan where Theodosius was then residing, wrote the emperor a private letter, which survives. He told him that he could not offer the Eucharist in his presence until he had repented, and urged him to do public penance, as King David had done.

Theodoret later dramatized the scene, describing Ambrose meeting the emperor at the church door and barring his way. Whatever the exact form, Theodosius submitted. He laid aside his imperial ornaments and did public penance for some months before he was readmitted to communion around Christmas. Theodoret adds that he also passed a law requiring a delay of thirty days between a sentence of death and its execution, so that anger would not decide such matters.
lesson: No position puts you above answering for harm done in anger. Building a pause between rage and action protects everyone, including yourself.
people: Emperor Theodosius I, Ambrose of Milan
source: Ambrose, Letter 51 to Theodosius; Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History, Book 5, chapters 17 and 18
caveat: Theodoret's scene at the church door and his death toll are probably embellished; Ambrose's own letter is the reliable source.

title: The Man Who Drilled Under His Own Seat
text:
The rabbinic collection Leviticus Rabbah preserves a short parable taught in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai.

Some people were sitting together in a boat, out on the water. One of them took a drill and began boring a hole in the floor under his own seat.

The others stared at him. What are you doing? they asked.

What business is it of yours? he answered. Am I not drilling under my own place?

They replied that it was very much their business. When the water came up through his hole, it would not stay under his seat. It would flood the boat for all of them.

The rabbis used the parable to explain how one person's wrongdoing affects a whole community. The passage applies it to a verse from the Book of Job, where Job's friend complains that Job's error does not stay with him alone. A community is like that boat: what one member does to his own corner, everyone else will share.
lesson: In a shared enterprise, no one's choices are purely private. Speak up early when someone's action threatens the whole boat, even if it looks like his own business.
people: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, passengers on a boat
source: Leviticus Rabbah (Vayikra Rabbah) 4:6

title: Pope Leo Goes to Meet Attila
text:
In 452 Attila, king of the Huns, invaded northern Italy. He destroyed the city of Aquileia and took Milan and other cities of the Po valley. The Western Roman Empire seemed helpless, and Rome itself appeared to lie open before him.

The emperor Valentinian III sent an embassy to Attila. It was led by Pope Leo I, together with two senior Roman officials, the former consul Gennadius Avienus and the former prefect Trigetius. They met the king near the Mincio River, close to Mantua.

The chronicler Prosper of Aquitaine, a contemporary who knew Leo, wrote that Attila received the embassy and was so pleased by the presence of the high priest that he ordered his army to stop and withdrew beyond the Danube, promising peace. Attila died the next year.

Later legend added that the apostles Peter and Paul appeared behind Leo with drawn swords, threatening Attila, a scene Raphael painted in the Vatican. Historians point to more practical reasons as well: Attila's army was suffering from famine and disease, and the Eastern Roman emperor had sent troops against the Huns' homeland.
lesson: Going in person to face someone who threatens you can achieve what force cannot. Courage and dignity at the table are a form of power.
people: Pope Leo I, Attila, Gennadius Avienus, Trigetius
location: Near the Mincio River, Mantua, Italy
source: Prosper of Aquitaine, Epitoma Chronicon, year 452; Jordanes, Getica 42
caveat: Other factors, including disease and famine in the Hun army and Eastern Roman attacks, probably weighed as much as Leo's persuasion.

title: The Ballad of Mulan
text:
Mulan sat at her loom, but instead of the click of the shuttle there were only her sighs. The night before, she had seen the army notices. The Khan was calling up troops, and the conscription lists, twelve scrolls of them, all carried her father's name. Her father had no grown son, and she had no older brother.

So she decided to go in his place. She bought a fine horse in the east market, a saddle in the west market, a bridle in the south and a long whip in the north. At dawn she left her parents, and by evening she was camped by the Yellow River, hearing not her father and mother calling her but the rushing of the water.

She served for years, through cold nights on the frontier and many battles. When the army returned victorious, the Son of Heaven offered her high office and rich rewards. Mulan asked only for a swift camel to carry her home.

Her parents came out to meet her, her older sister put on her finest makeup, her little brother sharpened a knife to kill a pig and a sheep for a feast. Mulan changed back into her old dress, did her hair before the mirror and went out to greet her comrades. They were astonished. In twelve years together they had never known she was a woman.
lesson: Love for family can call out courage nobody suspected. When the moment passes, the greatest reward may simply be coming home.
people: Mulan, her father, her family
source: The Ballad of Mulan (Mulan Shi), anonymous, preserved in Guo Maoqian, Yuefu Shiji (12th century)
caveat: Mulan is a figure of legend and poetry, and there is no reliable evidence that she was a historical person.

title: The Rule of Saint Benedict
text:
In the early sixth century, Benedict of Nursia, an Italian who had once lived as a hermit, founded a monastery at Monte Cassino, south of Rome. Around 530 to 540 he wrote a short rule, in 73 chapters, to govern the daily life of his monks. He called it "a little rule for beginners."

The Rule set out a balanced day of communal prayer, manual work and reading. It limited food and drink to moderate portions, allowed for the sick, the old and the very young, and asked the abbot to adapt demands to the strength of each monk. The abbot, elected by the community, held real authority, but was to act like a father and would answer to God for every soul in his care.

One chapter tells the abbot to call the whole community together for any important decision and to hear everyone's advice. Benedict explains that all should be called because God often reveals what is better to the youngest. The abbot then decides, but only after listening.

The Rule spread across Western Europe and, after Charlemagne's time, became the standard rule for most monasteries there. For centuries Benedictine communities preserved books, cleared land, ran schools and kept learning alive. Benedictine monks and nuns still live by the same rule today, nearly fifteen hundred years after it was written.
lesson: A community lasts when its rules are clear, moderate and humane. Ask everyone for their view before big decisions, including the youngest.
people: Benedict of Nursia
source: The Rule of Saint Benedict, especially chapters 2, 3 and 48; Gregory the Great, Dialogues, book 2

title: Theodora Refuses to Flee
text:
In January 532 the rival chariot-racing factions of Constantinople, the Blues and the Greens, united against the emperor Justinian. What began as anger over executions and taxes became the Nika riot, named after the rioters' cry, "Conquer!" For days the crowds burned large parts of the city, including the great church of Hagia Sophia, and proclaimed a new emperor, Hypatius.

The historian Procopius, who was in the city, says that Justinian and his advisers met in the palace to decide whether to escape by ship. The empress Theodora then spoke. She said that this was not the time to argue whether a woman should speak among men. Flight, even if it brought safety, was not to be chosen; anyone born must die, but one who had been an emperor should not become a fugitive. If the emperor wished to save himself, there was the sea and there were the ships. As for her, she held to an old saying that royalty is a good burial shroud.

Justinian stayed. His generals Belisarius and Mundus led troops into the Hippodrome, where the rebels had gathered, and massacred them. Procopius says more than thirty thousand died. Hypatius was executed, and Justinian ruled for another thirty-three years.
lesson: In a moment of panic, one steady voice that refuses to run can change everyone's decision. Calm resolve is contagious.
people: Empress Theodora, Justinian I, Belisarius
source: Procopius, History of the Wars, Book 1, chapter 24
caveat: Procopius probably shaped Theodora's speech in a literary way, and his death toll is likely exaggerated.

title: Hatim Tai and His Horse
text:
Hatim al-Tai was a poet and chief of the Arab tribe of Tayy who lived in the generation before Islam, and his generosity became proverbial across the Arab and Persian world. Many stories are told of him. One of the best known concerns his horse.

Hatim owned a horse of rare beauty and speed, famous far and wide. A powerful ruler, in many versions the Byzantine emperor, heard both of the horse and of Hatim's generosity and decided to test the second by asking for the first. He sent envoys across the desert to request it.

They arrived at Hatim's tent late, in a time of drought, and he had no food to set before his guests. Rather than let them go hungry, he slaughtered the only animal he had at hand, roasted it and served it to them.

In the morning the envoys explained their mission and asked for the famous horse. Hatim told them, with sorrow, that they had eaten it the night before. He could not let guests go hungry under his roof, he said, and the horse was all he had left to give. The envoys returned and reported what had happened, and the ruler declared that Hatim's reputation fell short of the truth.
lesson: Real hospitality gives the best you have to the person in front of you, now. Do not save generosity for convenient moments.
people: Hatim al-Tai, envoys of a ruler
source: Arabic and Persian tradition on Hatim al-Tai
caveat: Hatim was a real person, but this story is a legend that exists in several versions with different rulers and details.

title: Kongo Gumi: A Family Firm for Fourteen Centuries
text:
In 578, according to the company's records, Prince Shotoku of Japan brought skilled carpenters from the Korean kingdom of Baekje to build Shitenno-ji, a great Buddhist temple in what is now Osaka. One of them, Shigemitsu Kongo, stayed on. His family founded Kongo Gumi, a construction company that went on to build and repair temples for more than fourteen hundred years, longer than any other known company.

The family kept the business alive through wars, fires and the rise and fall of dynasties. One of its customs was that the leadership did not automatically pass to the eldest son. The family chose the most capable heir, and when no son was suitable, a talented son-in-law could be adopted into the family and take the Kongo name. In the 1930s, when the 37th leader died, his widow Yoshie Kongo took charge, the first woman to lead the firm. During the Second World War, when no one was building temples, the company survived by making wooden coffins.

In the 1980s Kongo Gumi borrowed heavily to invest in property during Japan's bubble economy. When land prices collapsed, the debts became too much. In 2006, after some forty generations of family ownership, its assets were taken over by the Takamatsu Construction Group, which kept it running as a subsidiary. The family scrolls tracing its lineage survive.
lesson: A family enterprise lasts by choosing successors for ability, not birth order. Even fourteen centuries of care can be undone by one generation's reckless borrowing.
people: Shigemitsu Kongo, the Kongo family, Yoshie Kongo
source: Kongo Gumi company records; reporting on the 2006 takeover (Bloomberg Businessweek, 2007)
caveat: The founding date and early history come from the company's own traditional records.

title: Khadija Comforts Muhammad
text:
Khadija bint Khuwaylid was a wealthy merchant of Mecca. According to the early biography of Ibn Ishaq, she hired a young man named Muhammad to take her goods to Syria, was impressed by his honesty, and proposed marriage to him herself. Tradition says he was twenty-five and she was about forty.

Around 610, when Muhammad was forty, he used to retreat to a cave on Mount Hira, outside Mecca, to meditate. There, according to Islamic tradition, the angel Gabriel appeared to him and commanded him to recite. Muhammad came home shaking with fear. The account preserved in the hadith collection of al-Bukhari says he went to Khadija and asked her to cover him, and she wrapped him up until his fear left him. Then he told her what had happened and said he feared for himself.

Khadija answered that God would never disgrace him. She reminded him that he kept good relations with his family, helped the weak, gave to the poor, honored his guests and stood by those struck by misfortune. Then she took him to her cousin, Waraqa ibn Nawfal, an old Christian scholar, who told Muhammad that what had come to him was the same messenger that had come to Moses.

Khadija is remembered in Islam as the first person to believe in Muhammad's message. They remained married until her death in 619, which tradition calls the Year of Sorrow.
lesson: When someone we love is frightened, reminding them of who they are can give them the courage to go on. A spouse's faith can steady us at our weakest moment.
people: Khadija bint Khuwaylid, Muhammad, Waraqa ibn Nawfal
source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Revelation, hadith 3; Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, trans. A. Guillaume
caveat: The account is traditional, and Khadija's age at marriage is reported differently by some early sources.

title: The Negus Shelters the Muslim Refugees
text:
Around 615, the early followers of Muhammad in Mecca were being persecuted by the leaders of the Quraysh. Muhammad advised some of them to flee across the Red Sea to the Christian kingdom of Aksum, whose king, the Negus, called al-Najashi in Arabic, was known as a just ruler. A small group, including the Prophet's cousin Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, made the crossing.

According to Ibn Ishaq's biography of the Prophet, the Quraysh sent two envoys, one of them Amr ibn al-As, with rich gifts of leather for the king and his generals. They asked him to hand over the refugees, saying they had abandoned their people's religion without adopting his.

The Negus refused to give anyone up without hearing them. He called the Muslims before him and his bishops. Ja'far spoke for them, describing how they had lived before and what their new faith taught, and at the king's request he recited a passage from the Quran about Mary and the birth of Jesus. The Negus wept until his beard was wet. He said that this and what Jesus had brought came from the same source. He returned the gifts and told the refugees they could live safely in his land.
lesson: Give people a fair hearing before you judge them, especially when powerful voices demand that you turn them away. Justice begins with listening.
people: Al-Najashi (Ashama or Armah), Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, Amr ibn al-As
source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, as edited by Ibn Hisham
caveat: The account is traditional, written down more than a century later, and the king's exact identity is uncertain.

title: Digging the Trench at Medina
text:
In 627 a coalition of the Quraysh of Mecca and their tribal allies, by far the largest army the Muslims had faced, marched on Medina. The Muslim community was small, and Medina had no walls.

According to the early biography of the Prophet by Ibn Ishaq, as edited by Ibn Hisham, it was Salman the Persian, a former Zoroastrian who had converted to Islam, who proposed a solution unknown to the Arabs: dig a trench across the open northern approach to the town, as was done in Persia. The rest of Medina was protected by lava fields, rocky ground and walled orchards.

Ibn Ishaq says the whole community dug, and that Muhammad himself worked alongside them, carrying earth. The diggers sang verses as they worked. When they struck a rock they could not break, they called the Prophet, who broke it. A later tradition says the emigrants from Mecca and the Medinans each claimed Salman as one of their own, until Muhammad said that Salman belonged to his own household.

When the confederate army arrived, its cavalry could not cross the trench. The siege dragged on for weeks. Supplies ran low, the allies distrusted each other, and a fierce cold wind battered their camp. In the end they broke up and went home. Medina was saved, and the Meccans never again attacked the town.
lesson: A good idea can come from the newest member of a team. It works best when everyone, including the leader, takes up the shovel together.
people: Muhammad, Salman the Persian
source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (Life of the Messenger of God), as edited by Ibn Hisham; translated by A. Guillaume (1955)
caveat: The details come from biographical traditions written down more than a century after the events.

title: The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah
text:
In 628 the Prophet Muhammad set out from Medina toward Mecca with about fourteen hundred followers, dressed as pilgrims for the lesser pilgrimage rather than armed for war. Mecca's ruling tribe, the Quraysh, with whom the Muslims had fought several battles, would not let them enter. The Muslims stopped at a place called Hudaybiyyah, outside the sacred territory, and envoys went back and forth.

The early biography by Ibn Ishaq describes the talks with the Quraysh envoy Suhayl ibn Amr. The terms seemed one-sided. The Muslims would go home without making the pilgrimage that year and could return the next year for three days. There would be a truce for ten years. Anyone from Quraysh who went over to Muhammad without his guardian's permission would be sent back, but anyone who left Muhammad for Quraysh would not. Suhayl even objected to the wording of the document, and Muhammad agreed to sign simply as Muhammad son of Abdullah rather than as the Messenger of God.

Many of the companions were dismayed, Umar among them. But the truce allowed people to travel and talk freely between the two sides, and in the following two years many more people joined Islam than before. In 629 the Muslims made their pilgrimage. When allies of Quraysh attacked a tribe allied with Muhammad, the truce was broken, and in 630 Muhammad marched on Mecca with a large army. The city surrendered with very little fighting.
lesson: A deal that looks like a concession can be a win if it secures what matters most: time, peace and the freedom to grow. Judge agreements by where they lead.
people: Muhammad, Suhayl ibn Amr, Umar ibn al-Khattab
source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, in the recension of Ibn Hisham (translated by A. Guillaume as The Life of Muhammad, 1955)

title: The Woman Who Gave Water to a Dog
text:
Among the sayings of the Prophet Muhammad collected by al-Bukhari is a short story about a woman of the Children of Israel. She was a prostitute, the kind of person respectable people looked down on.

One hot day she came upon a dog walking around and around a well. Its tongue was hanging out and it was so close to dying of thirst that it was licking the damp earth. There was no bucket, and the water lay far below.

The woman took off her leather shoe, tied it with her head scarf, and lowered it into the well. She drew up water and gave it to the dog to drink, again and again, until it had had enough.

The Prophet said that because of this act, God forgave her. In a parallel saying about a man who did the same for a thirsty dog, his companions asked whether there was really a reward for kindness to animals. He answered that there is a reward for kindness to every living creature.
lesson: Never think a small act of mercy is too small to matter, and never assume someone's reputation tells you all of who they are.
people: A woman of the Children of Israel, a thirsty dog
source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Prophets (hadith 3467); the parallel story of a man is in the Book of Distribution of Water

title: The Amnesty at the Conquest of Mecca
text:
For years the Quraysh, the ruling tribe of Mecca, had persecuted the Prophet Muhammad and his followers, driven them out of the city, and fought them in a series of wars. In January 630, after the Quraysh's allies broke a truce, Muhammad marched on Mecca with an army of about ten thousand.

The city barely resisted. According to Ibn Ishaq's biography, preserved in the edition of Ibn Hisham, Muhammad had announced beforehand that anyone who stayed in their own house with the door closed, took refuge in the house of the Meccan leader Abu Sufyan, or entered the sacred mosque would be safe.

After entering the city and clearing the idols from the Kaaba, he stood at its door and addressed the assembled Quraysh, many of whom had fought him for years. Ibn Ishaq reports that he asked them what they thought he would do with them. They answered that they expected good from a generous brother and the son of a generous brother. He told them: "Go, you are free."

A small number of individuals were excluded from the amnesty, and some of them were later pardoned too. Many former enemies, including Abu Sufyan, became Muslims and leaders in the community.
lesson: The moment you have power over old enemies is the moment generosity counts most. Forgiveness then can turn opponents into allies.
people: Muhammad, Abu Sufyan, the Quraysh
source: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, as edited by Ibn Hisham

title: Tie Your Camel
text:
In early Islam, trust in God, called tawakkul, was among the virtues most praised. A believer was to rely on God for his sustenance and safety, not on his own cleverness. But how far should that trust go?

The collection of hadith compiled by al-Tirmidhi preserves a short exchange on this question, reported by Anas ibn Malik, a companion of the Prophet. A man came to the Prophet with his camel. For a desert people, a camel was a means of travel, a store of wealth and sometimes the difference between life and death, and an animal left loose could easily wander off or be stolen.

The man asked what he should do. Should he tie up his camel and trust in God? Or should he leave it untied and trust in God?

The Prophet answered: tie her, and trust.

The answer was short, and it has traveled far. It is quoted across the Muslim world and beyond, often in the form "Trust in God, but tie your camel," as a reminder that faith and good sense are not opposites. Doing everything sensible within your power is part of trusting, not a sign of doubt.
lesson: Hope and faith are no substitute for basic precautions. Do your part fully, lock the door and check the plan, and then let go of what is outside your control.
people: The Prophet Muhammad, a man with a camel
source: Al-Tirmidhi, Jami (Sunan) al-Tirmidhi, Book of the Description of the Day of Judgment, hadith 2517, narrated by Anas ibn Malik
caveat: Al-Tirmidhi himself called this hadith unusual (gharib); later scholars differ on how strong its chain of transmission is.

title: Emperor Taizong Lets the Condemned Go Home
text:
In the year 632 Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty, reviewing the cases of prisoners condemned to death, was moved by pity. According to the Chinese histories, he ordered that 390 of them be sent home to their families. They were to return to the capital on a set day the following autumn to be executed.

No guards went with them. When the appointed day came in 633, every one of the 390 returned of their own accord to face death. The emperor was so impressed that he pardoned them all.

The story was retold for centuries as proof of how a ruler's virtue could transform even criminals. In the 11th century the Song statesman and historian Ouyang Xiu wrote a famous essay, On Releasing Prisoners, questioning it. He argued that the emperor released them expecting them to return so he could pardon them, and the prisoners returned expecting to be pardoned, so each side was performing for the other. Good rule, he said, depended on steady laws, not on gestures that could not be repeated.
lesson: Trust given openly can call out trustworthiness in others. But ask whether a gesture builds a lasting system or only a good story.
people: Emperor Taizong of Tang, Ouyang Xiu
source: Sima Guang, Zizhi Tongjian, chapter 194; Ouyang Xiu, "On Releasing Prisoners" (Zong Qiu Lun)
caveat: Ouyang Xiu and later critics suspected the episode was staged for political effect.

title: Umar Declines to Pray in the Church
text:
In 637 or 638 Jerusalem surrendered to the Arab armies after a long siege. The Patriarch Sophronius is said to have insisted on surrendering only to the caliph himself, so Umar ibn al-Khattab traveled from Medina to accept the city. Muslim and Christian traditions agree that he came simply dressed and that the city was taken without a sack.

The Egyptian Christian historian Eutychius (Said ibn Batriq), writing in the tenth century, tells what happened next. Sophronius was showing Umar around the Church of the Holy Sepulchre when the time for prayer came. The patriarch invited him to pray there. Umar declined. He explained that if he prayed inside the church, Muslims after him would claim it as a place where Umar had prayed and take it from the Christians. He went outside and prayed on the steps alone.

Eutychius adds that Umar then gave the patriarch a written document forbidding Muslims to pray on those steps in congregation. The church remained in Christian hands, and a mosque named after Umar was later built nearby.
lesson: In victory, think about what your followers will do with your example after you. Limiting your own claims can protect others for generations.
people: Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab, Patriarch Sophronius
source: Eutychius (Said ibn Batriq), Annals
caveat: The story is recorded about three centuries after the events and cannot be confirmed from contemporary sources.

title: Taizong Loses His Mirror
text:
Emperor Taizong, who ruled Tang China from 626 to 649, had come to power by killing two of his brothers. One of the advisers he inherited from his murdered elder brother was Wei Zheng, a minister who had once urged that Taizong be dealt with. Taizong kept him and made him a senior official.

Wei Zheng became famous for criticizing the emperor to his face. Historical records describe him submitting hundreds of remonstrances, against costly building projects, hunting trips, harsh punishments and the emperor's moods. Taizong often grew angry, but he usually accepted the advice.

When Wei Zheng died in 643, Taizong mourned him deeply. According to the Old Book of Tang, he said that with bronze as a mirror one can straighten one's clothes, with history as a mirror one can understand the rise and fall of states, and with people as a mirror one can see one's own successes and mistakes. He had kept all three mirrors, he said, and now one of them was lost.
lesson: Keep near you at least one person who will tell you plainly when you are wrong, and protect them when it stings.
people: Emperor Taizong of Tang, Wei Zheng
source: Old Book of Tang (Jiu Tang Shu), Biography of Wei Zheng; Wu Jing, Zhenguan Zhengyao

title: Return As Far As You Can
text:
A rabbinic parable, told to explain the prophet's call "Return to me, and I will return to you," speaks of a king whose son had gone astray. The son had drifted far from his father, in distance and in spirit, a journey of a hundred days away.

His friends urged him to go home to his father. He said he could not; the distance was too great, and he did not have the strength for the journey. He was ashamed of how far he had gone and how long he had stayed away, and the road home looked endless.

So his father, the king, sent him a message. "Return as far as you are able," he said, "and I will come to you the rest of the way."

In the same way, the parable concludes, God says to Israel, "Return to me, and I will return to you."
lesson: When a relationship is broken, do not wait for the other person to cover the whole distance. Take whatever steps you can, and go out to meet them.
people: A king, his estranged son
source: Pesikta Rabbati 44:9; Malachi 3:7

title: No Work, No Food
text:
Hyakujo, the Chinese Zen master known in China as Baizhang, kept working alongside his pupils even when he was eighty years old. Every day he went out with them to trim the gardens, clean the grounds and prune the trees.

The pupils felt sorry to see the old teacher working so hard. They knew he would not listen if they told him to stop, so they hid his tools.

That day the master did not eat. The next day he did not eat, nor the day after. The pupils began to worry. Perhaps he was angry that they had hidden his tools. They decided they had better put them back.

The day they returned the tools, the master worked and ate the same as before. In the evening he explained to them: "No work, no food."
lesson: Asking others to work while exempting yourself teaches them that work is for lesser people. Doing your share, even when you could skip it, makes your standards believable.
people: Hyakujo (Baizhang Huaihai), his pupils
source: 101 Zen Stories, compiled by Nyogen Senzaki and Paul Reps (1919)
caveat: The saying "a day without work is a day without food" is traditionally attributed to Baizhang, but the anecdote comes from later Zen literature.

title: An Elephant for Charlemagne
text:
Around 797 Charlemagne, king of the Franks, sent an embassy to Harun al-Rashid, the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, ruler of the richest empire of the age. The mission included two Frankish nobles and a Jewish merchant named Isaac, probably chosen for his languages and knowledge of the routes. The journey took years. Both noblemen died along the way.

According to the Royal Frankish Annals, Isaac returned in 801 with gifts from the caliph, among them an elephant named Abul-Abbas. Getting it to Europe was a feat: he brought it across North Africa, over the sea to Italy, and in the spring of 802 over the Alps. It arrived at Charlemagne's court in Aachen in July 802, the first elephant seen in northern Europe in centuries, and lived there until 810.

The exchanges continued. In 807 Harun's envoys brought more gifts, including a splendid tent and a brass water clock that marked the hours by dropping little balls onto a bell, with mechanical horsemen that appeared at each hour. Charlemagne's court had never seen such a device. Einhard, Charlemagne's biographer, says Harun valued Charlemagne's friendship above that of all other kings.
lesson: Goodwill between distant parties is often built with patient gestures and thoughtful gifts. Respect shown across great differences can open relations that force never could.
people: Harun al-Rashid, Charlemagne, Isaac the Jew
source: Royal Frankish Annals, years 801, 802 and 807; Einhard, Life of Charlemagne 16
caveat: Einhard's claims about the warmth of Harun's friendship are not confirmed by Arabic sources, which do not mention the embassies.

title: Harun al-Rashid's Sons Go to War
text:
Harun al-Rashid, the most famous caliph of the Abbasid dynasty, had two sons born months apart, in 786 and 787. Abdallah, later called al-Mamun, was the elder, but his mother was a Persian slave concubine. Muhammad, later called al-Amin, was the son of Zubayda, Harun's wife and herself a granddaughter of a caliph.

Harun tried to settle the succession in advance. In 802, on pilgrimage to Mecca, he made both sons swear to an agreement. Al-Amin would be caliph in Baghdad, while al-Mamun would govern the vast eastern province of Khurasan and succeed his brother. The documents were hung inside the Kaaba itself, to make them sacred.

Harun died in 809. Within a year al-Amin, urged on by his advisers, moved to break the agreement, removing his brother from the succession in favor of his own young son. Al-Mamun, supported by Khurasan, refused. In 811 war broke out. Al-Mamun's general Tahir ibn Husayn defeated the caliph's much larger army and advanced on Baghdad. The great city was besieged for more than a year, and whole quarters were destroyed. In September 813 al-Amin was captured while trying to escape and was killed.

Al-Mamun became caliph and later presided over a golden age of learning. The historian al-Tabari recorded the war in detail.
lesson: A parent can divide an inheritance on paper, but only goodwill between children keeps the peace. Agreements that leave rivals equally powerful invite conflict.
people: Harun al-Rashid, al-Amin, al-Mamun, Zubayda, Tahir ibn Husayn
source: Al-Tabari, History of the Prophets and Kings, vols. 30 to 31 (English trans. SUNY)

title: The House of Wisdom Translators
text:
In the eighth and ninth centuries, the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad and the wealthy families around them paid for one of history's great translation efforts: putting Greek works of philosophy, medicine, mathematics and astronomy into Arabic. The caliph al-Mamun, who ruled from 813 to 833, was among its keenest patrons, and the palace library known as the House of Wisdom, Bayt al-Hikma, became linked to the movement in later memory.

The translators came from many backgrounds. The best known, Hunayn ibn Ishaq, was a Nestorian Christian physician from al-Hira who knew Greek, Syriac and Arabic. He worked with his son Ishaq and his nephew Hubaysh as a kind of workshop. Hunayn described how he hunted for multiple Greek manuscripts of a work, compared them to establish a correct text, and only then translated, often first into Syriac and then into Arabic. He translated most of the works of the Greek physician Galen. Another leading translator was Thabit ibn Qurra, a Sabian from Harran, and Muslim scholars such as the mathematician al-Khwarizmi built new work on what was translated.

The tenth century bookseller Ibn al-Nadim, in his catalog the Fihrist, records a story that al-Mamun was moved to support translation after dreaming of Aristotle.

The works they translated were studied, criticized and extended by scholars across the Islamic world. Centuries later many reached Europe through Latin translations from Arabic.
lesson: Knowledge grows fastest when people of different languages and faiths work together on a shared goal. Careful method and openness to outsiders both matter.
people: Caliph al-Mamun, Hunayn ibn Ishaq, Thabit ibn Qurra, al-Khwarizmi
source: Ibn al-Nadim, Kitab al-Fihrist (987); Dimitri Gutas, Greek Thought, Arabic Culture (1998)
caveat: Historians such as Dimitri Gutas argue the House of Wisdom was mainly a library and that the translation movement was much broader than one institution.

title: Fatima al-Fihri Builds a Mosque in Fez
text:
In the early ninth century, a merchant named Muhammad al-Fihri left Kairouan, in what is now Tunisia, and settled with his family in Fez, a new city in Morocco then ruled by the Idrisid dynasty. He prospered. When he died, his two daughters, Fatima and Maryam, inherited his wealth.

According to the fourteenth century chronicle known as the Rawd al-Qirtas, the sisters decided to spend their inheritance on something lasting for their community. In 859 Fatima began building a mosque in the quarter where the families from Kairouan lived, and Maryam built another across the river, in the Andalusian quarter. The chronicle says Fatima bought the land, had the workers use clay and stone from the site itself, and fasted every day until the building was finished.

The Qarawiyyin mosque, named after the people of Kairouan, grew over the centuries into one of the great centers of learning in the Muslim world. Scholars came to teach law, theology, grammar, astronomy and medicine, and its library collected precious manuscripts. Later rulers enlarged the building many times.

Today the University of al-Qarawiyyin is often described as the oldest existing educational institution that still operates, though it became a modern state university only in the twentieth century.
lesson: An inheritance spent on the common good can outlast every private fortune. What a family builds for its community may be remembered for a thousand years.
people: Fatima al-Fihri, Maryam al-Fihri, Muhammad al-Fihri
source: Ibn Abi Zar, Rawd al-Qirtas (14th century)
caveat: The main source was written five centuries later, and the claim that it was the oldest university depends on how a university is defined.

title: Alfred Burns the Cakes
text:
In January 878 the Danish army under Guthrum made a surprise attack on Chippenham, where Alfred, king of Wessex, was spending the winter. Most of Wessex submitted to the Danes. Alfred escaped with a small band and hid in the marshes of Somerset, at a place called Athelney. For a few months the last independent English king was a fugitive.

A story told later, first written down in a Life of St Neot about a century after Alfred's death, describes his time in hiding. He took shelter, unrecognized, in the cottage of a swineherd. One day the swineherd's wife put some loaves on the fire to bake and asked the stranger to watch them. Alfred, absorbed in his own troubles, let them burn. The woman came back and scolded him for being glad enough to eat her bread but too lazy to mind it. The king took the rebuke meekly.

What followed is history, not legend. In the spring Alfred gathered the men of Somerset, Wiltshire and Hampshire, and in May he defeated Guthrum at the Battle of Edington. Guthrum accepted baptism with Alfred as his godfather, and Wessex survived.
lesson: A setback can humble you without defeating you. Accept the rebuke, learn from the low point, and use the time to regroup.
people: Alfred the Great, Guthrum
source: Life of St Neot (late 10th or 11th century); Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 878
caveat: The burning of the cakes is a legend recorded long after Alfred's lifetime; the flight to Athelney and the victory at Edington are historical.

title: The Ass, the Ox and the Farmer
text:
At the start of the Thousand and One Nights, before Shahrazad went to the king, her father the vizier tried to warn her with a story.

A rich farmer had been given the gift of understanding animals, on condition that he never revealed what he heard. One evening he overheard his ox complaining to his ass. The ox plowed all day while the ass, who was rarely ridden, rested in a clean stall. The ass gave him advice: tonight, refuse your fodder and lie down as if you were sick, and they will leave you alone.

The ox did exactly that. In the morning the plowman reported that the ox was ill, and the farmer, who had heard everything, smiled and said: then yoke the ass in his place. The ass spent the whole day dragging the plow.

That night, aching and sore, the ass realized his advice had cost him dearly. He told the ox, with great concern, that he had heard the master say that if the ox stayed sick, he would be slaughtered and his hide sold. The frightened ox ate all his fodder, and the next morning he went eagerly to the plow, while the farmer, who had understood every word, laughed out loud.
lesson: Teaching a colleague to dodge work rarely ends well, since someone has to do it, and it may be you. Be careful what shortcuts you recommend to others.
people: An ass, an ox, a farmer who understood animals
date: Medieval; frame story of the collection
source: One Thousand and One Nights, frame story, The Tale of the Ox and the Ass, told by the vizier to Shahrazad

title: The Fisherman and the Jinni
text:
A poor old fisherman went down to the sea every day and cast his net exactly four times. One day the first three casts brought up a dead donkey, a jar full of mud and a heap of broken pots. On the fourth cast he pulled up a copper jar, sealed with lead and stamped with the seal of King Solomon.

He opened it, hoping to sell it, and smoke poured out and rose to the sky, then gathered into a gigantic jinni. The jinni told the fisherman to choose how he wanted to die. Solomon had shut him in that jar centuries ago, he explained. During the first hundred years he had sworn to make his rescuer rich. During the next he swore to open the treasures of the earth for him. Then he swore to grant three wishes. When no one came, he grew furious and vowed to kill whoever freed him.

The fisherman thought quickly. He said he simply could not believe that such an enormous being had ever fit inside such a small jar. He would never believe it unless he saw it with his own eyes.

Stung, the jinni turned back into smoke and poured himself into the jar to prove it. At once the fisherman jammed the lead stopper back on. Now it was the jinni who pleaded, and he was freed again only after swearing an oath to do the fisherman no harm.
lesson: A powerful opponent's pride can be his weak point. Questioning what someone boasts about can lead him to step right into the trap.
people: A fisherman, a jinni
location: Medieval Middle East (Persian and Arabic tradition)
source: One Thousand and One Nights
caveat: Details of the first three casts and of the ending differ between versions.

title: Scheherazade's Thousand Nights
text:
King Shahryar discovered that his wife had betrayed him, and the shock turned him cruel. He had her executed, and then decided that no woman could be trusted. Every day he married a young woman, and every morning he had her put to death. Families fled the city with their daughters, and fear spread through the kingdom.

Shahrazad, the clever and well read daughter of the king's vizier, told her father she would marry the king. He begged her not to, but she had a plan. On her wedding night she arranged for her younger sister, Dunyazad, to be brought to the room and to ask her for a story.

Shahrazad began a tale, and the king listened. When dawn broke, the story was not finished, and she stopped. It was nothing, she said, compared with what she could tell the next night, if the king let her live. He wanted to hear the end, so he spared her for one more day.

The next night she finished that story and began another, which also broke off at dawn. So it went on, night after night, with tales nested inside tales, for a thousand and one nights. By the end, the king had changed. He gave up his vow, and Shahrazad became his queen.
lesson: When you cannot win an argument head on, change the situation one step at a time. Keeping the other side curious about what comes next buys time for minds to change.
people: Shahrazad, King Shahryar, Dunyazad
location: Medieval Middle East (Persian and Arabic tradition)
source: One Thousand and One Nights, frame story
caveat: Endings differ between manuscripts and editions; in some, Shahrazad has borne the king children by the end.

title: The Seventeen Camels
text:
An old man died and left seventeen camels to his three sons. His will said that the eldest should have half of the camels, the second son a third, and the youngest a ninth.

The brothers set to work and quickly ran into trouble. Half of seventeen is eight and a half. A third is five and two thirds. A ninth is not quite two. No one wanted to cut up a camel, and each brother suspected the others of trying to get more than his share. The argument grew bitter, and the family seemed about to fall apart.

At last they went to a wise man and asked for help. He listened, thought for a while, and then said he would lend them one of his own camels. Now there were eighteen.

Half of eighteen is nine, so the eldest took nine camels. A third of eighteen is six, so the second son took six. A ninth of eighteen is two, so the youngest took two. Nine and six and two make seventeen. One camel was left over: the wise man's own. He took it back and went home, and the brothers were satisfied.
lesson: When a negotiation is stuck, look for something you can add to the table, even temporarily, that lets everyone see a solution that was there all along.
people: Three brothers, a wise man
source: Middle Eastern folk tradition
caveat: The tale's origin is uncertain; it works because the father's fractions add up to only seventeen eighteenths of the herd.

title: The Fall of Jamshid
text:
Jamshid was one of the greatest kings in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh. Blessed with the divine glory, the farr, he ruled for centuries over a golden age. He taught people to forge weapons and armor, to spin and weave, to build with brick, to work gems and make perfumes and medicines. He organized society into its classes. The demons served him, and he had them raise him on a jeweled throne into the sky. The day he rose up was celebrated as the first Nowruz, the new year.

Under him, the poem says, there was no death or disease, and the world was at peace. But as the years passed, Jamshid came to see all of it as his own work. He gathered the nobles and priests and told them that he alone had brought all this into being, that he knew no king in the world but himself, and that they should call him the creator of the world.

The nobles bowed their heads in silence. At that moment the divine glory left him. His nobles began to drift away, and in time his army deserted him for Zahhak, the usurper from the west. Jamshid fled and hid for a hundred years before Zahhak found him and had him sawn in two.
lesson: Success built with many hands and some luck is easy to start calling your own. The moment you claim all the credit is often the moment people stop following you.
people: Jamshid, Zahhak
source: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh, the reign of Jamshid

title: Kaveh the Blacksmith
text:
In the Shahnameh, the tyrant Zahhak ruled Iran with two serpents growing from his shoulders. Each day the serpents had to be fed the brains of two young men, and the kingdom paid in sons. Haunted by a dream that a young man named Fereydun would overthrow him, Zahhak decided to protect his name. He had a document drawn up declaring him a just and generous king, and he made the nobles sign it. Out of fear, they all did.

At that moment a blacksmith named Kaveh burst into the court, crying out for justice. He had had eighteen sons, and seventeen had already been taken for the serpents. Now the last one had been seized. Zahhak, wanting to look merciful, returned the boy and asked Kaveh to add his name to the declaration.

Kaveh read it, turned on the nobles and called them shameless for signing, then tore the document to pieces and walked out. In the market he raised his leather blacksmith's apron on the point of a spear and called on the people to follow him. Crowds gathered behind the apron, and Kaveh led them to Fereydun.

Fereydun covered the apron with jewels and made it his royal banner. With that army he defeated Zahhak and chained him inside Mount Damavand.
lesson: Unjust power often depends on respectable people signing what they know is false. Refusing to lend your name to a lie can be the act that gives others the courage to stand up.
people: Kaveh, Zahhak, Fereydun
source: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh, the reign of Zahhak

title: Ouyang Xiu's Mother Writes in the Sand
text:
Ouyang Xiu, born in 1007, became one of the greatest writers and statesmen of the Song dynasty: a master of prose and poetry, a reforming official and the author of two official histories. He started life with almost nothing.

His father, a minor official, died when the boy was about three, leaving the family poor. His mother, whose family name was Zheng, took him to live near an uncle in Suizhou. According to his biography in the official History of Song, the family was so poor that she could not afford paper and brush. Instead she cut the stems of reeds and used them to trace characters on the ground, teaching her son to write in the earth.

The boy proved a quick and devoted student. Since the family had few books, he borrowed them from wealthier neighbors and copied them out, and he found an old edition of the essays of the Tang writer Han Yu, which he studied with passion. He passed the highest civil examination in 1030 and went on to a long career at court, where he championed a plain, clear prose style and helped discover talented younger writers such as Su Shi.

The image of his mother teaching with reeds became a Chinese byword for a parent's devotion to a child's education against poverty.
lesson: Lack of money does not have to mean lack of learning. A determined parent can teach with whatever is at hand.
people: Ouyang Xiu, his mother (Lady Zheng)
source: History of Song (Song Shi), biography of Ouyang Xiu

title: Rostam and Sohrab
text:
The great hero Rostam, hunting near the borders of Turan, lost his horse Rakhsh and followed its tracks to the city of Samangan. There he spent a night with Tahmineh, the king's daughter, and they married. In the morning he left, giving her a token to fasten on the arm of their child, if a child came.

A son was born, Sohrab. He grew quickly into a young warrior of extraordinary strength. When his mother told him who his father was, he decided to lead an army into Iran, overthrow its king and place Rostam on the throne. The ruler of Turan, Afrasiab, eager to set father and son against each other, gave him troops and saw to it that he would not learn which of the Iranian champions was Rostam.

So the two met on the battlefield as strangers. Sohrab sensed something and asked his opponent directly whether he was Rostam. Rostam denied it. They fought for days. Sohrab threw Rostam once and spared him; on the next day Rostam threw Sohrab and drove his dagger into his chest.

Dying, Sohrab warned that his father Rostam would avenge him. Rostam tore open his armor and saw the token on his arm. He begged the king for a healing potion, but it came too late. Sohrab died in his father's arms.
lesson: Distance and pride can make family members strangers to each other. Ask the direct question, and answer it honestly, before it is too late.
people: Rostam, Sohrab, Tahmineh, Afrasiab, Kay Kavus
location: Persia (Iran and Turan, ancient epic geography)
source: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh, the story of Rostam and Sohrab

title: King Canute and the Tide
text:
Cnut, often called Canute, was a Danish prince who conquered England in 1016 and went on to rule Denmark and Norway too. He was one of the most powerful kings in Europe.

About a hundred years after his death the English chronicler Henry of Huntingdon told a story about him. At the height of his power, Cnut had his chair placed on the shore as the tide was rising. He said to the sea that it was subject to him, and that the land on which he sat was his, and he commanded the water not to rise onto his land or wet his clothes or limbs.

The tide came in as usual and soaked his feet and legs. The king jumped back and said, in Henry's account, that everyone should know how empty and worthless is the power of kings, for no one deserves the name of king except the one whom heaven, earth and sea obey by eternal laws.

Henry adds that Cnut never wore his golden crown again, but placed it on a crucifix. The story is often remembered backwards, as a tale of royal arrogance. In the original, the king staged it to teach humility.
lesson: Know the limits of your power and do not let flattery hide them from you. Sometimes it helps to show others those limits plainly.
people: Cnut the Great
location: England (shore not named; later tradition suggests Southampton or Bosham)
source: Henry of Huntingdon, Historia Anglorum, Book 6
caveat: The story is first recorded about a century after Cnut's death and may be a moral tale rather than a real event.

title: First to Worry, Last to Rejoice
text:
Fan Zhongyan was a Song dynasty statesman who rose from a poor childhood through the civil service examinations. In the early 1040s he led an ambitious program of government reforms, known as the Qingli Reforms, meant to curb favoritism and make officials more capable. Powerful opponents brought them down within about two years, and Fan and his allies were sent away from the capital to provincial posts.

In 1046 his friend Teng Zijing, who had also been demoted and posted to Yuezhou on Lake Dongting, rebuilt the famous Yueyang Tower there and asked Fan to write an essay to commemorate it.

Fan's short essay describes how visitors to the tower feel gloomy when the lake is dark with storms and joyful when it shines in spring sunshine. Then he turns to the people of old who were truly virtuous. They were not made happy by things or sad on their own account. In high office they worried about the people; far from court they worried about their ruler. Such people, he wrote, would be the first to worry about the world's troubles and the last to enjoy its pleasures.

The line became one of the best-known statements of the ideal of public service in China. Fan later used his own income to found a charitable estate supporting his clan.
lesson: A leader's place is to worry before others and to enjoy rewards after them. Ask whether your comforts come before or after your people's.
people: Fan Zhongyan, Teng Zijing
source: Fan Zhongyan, Record of Yueyang Tower (Yueyang Lou Ji), 1046

title: The Feigned Retreats at Hastings
text:
On 14 October 1066 Duke William of Normandy faced King Harold of England on a ridge near Hastings. Harold's army, only weeks after defeating a Norwegian invasion at Stamford Bridge, formed a dense shield wall along the crest. The Normans, with archers, infantry and mounted knights, had to attack uphill.

The morning attacks failed. The English line held, and at one point the Norman left, made up largely of Bretons, broke and fled downhill, pursued by some of the English. A rumor spread that William had been killed. According to William of Poitiers, the duke's chaplain, he rode among his men, pushed back his helmet to show his face, and rallied them. The Normans turned on the English who had chased them down the slope and cut them down in the open.

William of Poitiers then reports that the Normans used this experience deliberately. Twice more they pretended to flee, drawing groups of Englishmen out of the shield wall to pursue them, then wheeled their horses and destroyed them. Each time the English line grew thinner. Late in the day, after hours of attack with archers and cavalry, the line finally gave way. Harold was killed, along with his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine, and the English army collapsed.

William was crowned king of England at Westminster on Christmas Day 1066.
lesson: A disciplined opponent can be beaten by tempting him to break his own formation. Do not let an apparent success pull you away from the position that protects you.
people: William of Normandy, Harold Godwinson
source: William of Poitiers, Gesta Guillelmi; the Bayeux Tapestry
caveat: Historians debate whether the later feigned retreats were truly deliberate or a flattering interpretation of real routs.

title: Henry IV at Canossa
text:
In 1076 the struggle between the young German king Henry IV and Pope Gregory VII over who could appoint bishops came to a head. Henry and his bishops declared the pope deposed. Gregory answered by excommunicating Henry and releasing his subjects from their oaths of loyalty.

The German princes, many of whom resented Henry, seized their chance. They declared that if he was not freed from excommunication within a year he would lose his throne, and they invited the pope to come to Germany early in 1077 to judge the matter. A meeting between the pope and the rebellious princes would almost certainly have ended Henry's reign.

Henry moved first. In midwinter he crossed the Alps with his wife, his young son and a small following and went to meet the pope, who had stopped at the castle of Canossa in northern Italy, the fortress of Countess Matilda of Tuscany. According to the chronicler Lampert of Hersfeld and Gregory's own letter, Henry stood outside the castle gate as a penitent, barefoot and in woolen clothes, for three days in January 1077, asking for forgiveness. As a priest, Gregory could hardly refuse a penitent, and after three days he absolved him.

The humiliation became legendary, but it achieved its purpose: the princes lost their main argument. They elected a rival king anyway, but Henry fought a civil war and survived. In 1084 he took Rome, and Gregory died in exile the next year.
lesson: Sometimes the strongest move is to give your opponent what he cannot refuse. A public act of humility can disarm a coalition that was waiting to judge you.
people: Henry IV, Pope Gregory VII, Matilda of Tuscany
source: Gregory VII, letter to the German princes (1077); Lampert of Hersfeld, Annals
caveat: Lampert's vivid details of Henry's suffering in the snow may be exaggerated.

title: Su Shi Visits His Old Opponent Wang Anshi
text:
In 11th century Song China, Wang Anshi was the chief minister behind the sweeping reforms known as the New Policies. The poet and official Su Shi was one of their fiercest critics. The conflict divided the court for years, and Su's sharp tongue and pen made him enemies. In 1079 he was arrested over poems said to mock the government, nearly executed, and then exiled to Huangzhou.

By 1084 Wang Anshi had long since retired from power and was living quietly at Jinling, today Nanjing. That year Su Shi, given permission to move nearer the capital, traveled down the Yangtze and stopped there. According to Song accounts, the old statesman rode out on a donkey to meet him at the river. The two spent many days together, walking in the hills, discussing poetry and Buddhism, and writing poems to each other.

In one of the poems he wrote in reply to Wang, Su Shi said that the old man had urged him to buy a small plot of land and settle nearby, and that he now felt he had come to follow him ten years too late. Wang died two years later.
lesson: Political opponents can still recognize each other's worth once the fight is over. Do not let a past contest stop you from honoring a gifted adversary.
people: Su Shi (Su Dongpo), Wang Anshi
source: Su Shi, poems written in reply to Wang Anshi at Jinling (1084); Song period anecdotal accounts
caveat: Some anecdotes about their meeting, including the warmth of their words, come from later collections and may be embellished.

title: He Who Would Be Chief, Let Him Be a Bridge
text:
In the Welsh tale of Branwen, Bran the Blessed was king of the Island of the Mighty, as Britain is called in the story, and a giant so huge that no house could hold him. He gave his sister Branwen in marriage to Matholwch, king of Ireland. In Ireland she was mistreated: she was made to work in the kitchen, and the butcher came each day to box her ears. She tamed a starling, taught it to speak, and sent it across the sea with a letter to her brother.

Bran gathered an army and crossed to Ireland. The ships sailed, and Bran, too big for any ship, waded through the sea. The Irish retreated across a river and broke down the bridge behind them. The river could not be crossed by ship or by any bridge they could build.

Bran's men asked him what they should do. He answered with words that became a Welsh proverb: "A fo ben, bid bont," he who would be chief, let him be a bridge. He lay down across the river. Hurdles were laid on his body, and his whole army crossed over on him.
