lesson: Leading people across a hard place sometimes means carrying the weight yourself. The leader's job is to make the crossing possible, not to cross first.
people: Bran the Blessed, Branwen, Matholwch, the men of the Island of the Mighty
date: Medieval Welsh, written down c. 11th to 12th century
source: Mabinogion, Second Branch: Branwen Daughter of Llyr

title: Cu Chulainn and Ferdiad at the Ford
text:
Cu Chulainn and Ferdiad had trained together as youths under the warrior woman Scathach. They were foster brothers in arms and had sworn friendship. But when Queen Medb of Connacht invaded Ulster in the Cattle Raid of Cooley, Cu Chulainn alone held the fords against her army, and Medb, running out of champions, turned to Ferdiad. With rich gifts, her daughter's hand and the threat that her poets would shame him with satire, she persuaded him to fight his friend.

The two met at a ford and fought for three days. Each evening, when the fighting stopped, they threw their arms around each other and kissed. Their horses shared a paddock and their charioteers a fire. Cu Chulainn sent Ferdiad healing herbs for his wounds, and Ferdiad sent Cu Chulainn a share of his food.

On the fourth day the fighting turned desperate. When Ferdiad gained the upper hand, Cu Chulainn called for the gae bolga, his terrible barbed spear, and with it struck Ferdiad a mortal blow.

Cu Chulainn carried his friend's body across the ford to the Ulster side, then collapsed beside it. He grieved over him in a famous lament, crying that all the fighting before had been play compared to this. The ford was named after Ferdiad.
lesson: Do not let others turn you against a friend with bribes or pressure. Even in real disagreement, you can keep respect and decency toward the people you care about.
people: Cu Chulainn, Ferdiad, Queen Medb
source: Tain Bo Cuailnge (The Cattle Raid of Cooley), Book of Leinster recension

title: The Words on Yue Fei's Back
text:
Yue Fei was a general of the Southern Song dynasty who fought the Jurchen Jin invaders who had overrun northern China in the 1120s. He rose from a poor farming family to command one of the most effective armies of the age, and won a series of victories that brought him close to recovering lost territory.

At court, however, the chief minister Qin Hui favored peace with the Jin. In 1140 Yue Fei was recalled from the front by a series of urgent orders. He was arrested, charged with treason on flimsy grounds, and put to death in prison in 1142, at thirty-nine.

The official History of Song records that when he was interrogated, Yue Fei tore open his robe to show his interrogators four characters deeply tattooed across his back: "Serve the country with utmost loyalty."

Later tradition, most fully in popular novels and plays written centuries afterward, explains the tattoo with a story about his mother. As her son prepared to go to war, she is said to have pricked the words into his skin with a needle and ink so that he would never forget his duty. The scene of the mother tattooing her son became one of the best known images in Chinese culture. Yue Fei was rehabilitated twenty years after his death and is honored at a temple beside West Lake in Hangzhou.
lesson: Parents give children values to carry long after they leave home. What we teach them to hold dear can guide them in their hardest hour.
people: Yue Fei, his mother (Lady Yao)
source: History of Song (Song Shi), biography of Yue Fei; later popular tradition
caveat: The tattoo is recorded in the official history, but the story that his mother made it comes from later tradition.

title: The Letters of Abelard and Heloise
text:
Peter Abelard was the most brilliant and famous teacher in Paris in the early twelfth century. Around 1116 he became tutor to Heloise, the young niece of a canon of Notre-Dame named Fulbert. Heloise was already known for her learning. Teacher and pupil fell in love. When she became pregnant, Abelard took her to his family in Brittany, where she gave birth to a son they called Astrolabe.

To appease her uncle, Abelard proposed marriage. Heloise argued against it, saying a marriage would harm his career and that she preferred love freely given. They married secretly anyway. Fulbert, believing Abelard meant to abandon her, sent men who attacked him at night and castrated him. Both then entered religious life, Heloise as a nun and later abbess of the Paraclete, a convent Abelard had founded.

Years later, around 1132, Abelard wrote a long account of his misfortunes. Heloise read it and wrote to him, beginning a series of letters that still survive. She told him, with stunning frankness, that she had entered the convent for him, not for God, that she would rather be called his mistress than an empress, and that she could not repent of her love. He answered as a monk and spiritual guide, urging her to turn her love to Christ.

Abelard died in 1142, and his body was brought to the Paraclete. When Heloise died two decades later, she was buried beside him.
lesson: Love that is written down honestly can survive loss and separation. Telling the truth about our feelings, even when it is unwelcome, is a form of fidelity.
people: Peter Abelard, Heloise, Fulbert
location: Paris and the Paraclete, Champagne, France
source: Abelard, Historia Calamitatum; The Letters of Abelard and Heloise, trans. Betty Radice (1974)
caveat: A minority of scholars have questioned whether all the letters are authentic.

title: The Women of Weinsberg Carry Out Their Husbands
text:
In 1140 the German king Conrad III, of the Hohenstaufen family, was at war with the rival Welf dynasty. In December of that year he besieged the castle and town of Weinsberg, in Swabia, which was held for the Welfs. After the Welf relief army was defeated, the defenders had to surrender.

According to the Royal Chronicle of Cologne, written at the time, Conrad granted the women of the town permission to leave freely and to take with them whatever they could carry on their shoulders. The women came out through the gate carrying their husbands on their backs. The men had expected to be killed or imprisoned.

The later tellings add that Conrad's followers protested that this was not what the king had meant. Conrad is said to have answered that a king's word should not be twisted, and he let the men go. He was reportedly amused by the women's cleverness.

The ruined castle above Weinsberg has been known ever since as Weibertreu, "women's faithfulness." The story became a favorite in German literature, retold in a ballad by Gottfried August Burger, and the town still celebrates it.
lesson: Loyalty finds a way when the rules seem to leave none. Reading an offer carefully, and taking it at its word, can save what matters most.
people: Conrad III, the women of Weinsberg
source: Chronica regia Coloniensis (Royal Chronicle of Cologne), year 1140
caveat: The surrender is historical and the women's ruse is reported by a contemporary chronicle, but the dialogue and some details come from later retellings.

title: The Donkey Who Played Watchdog
text:
In the city of Varanasi lived a washerman who kept a donkey to carry his loads and a dog to guard his house. One night, after a long day, he was sleeping soundly when a thief crept into the yard.

The donkey saw the thief and nudged the dog. Bark, he said, that is your job. The dog refused. Our master has neglected me, he complained. He feeds me badly and takes me for granted. Let him lose something, and then he will remember what I am worth.

The donkey was outraged. A servant, he said, should not bargain in an emergency. If the dog would not do his duty, the donkey would do it for him. He lifted his head and brayed as loudly as he could.

The washerman woke with a start, furious at being disturbed. He saw no thief, only his donkey making a racket in the middle of the night. He picked up a stick and beat the donkey hard, then went back to sleep.
lesson: Each role on a team exists for a reason. Doing another person's job out of indignation, without the means to do it well, can bring trouble on you instead of solving the problem.
people: A washerman, his donkey, his dog, a thief
source: Narayana, Hitopadesha, Book II

title: The Old Tiger and the Gold Bracelet
text:
An old tiger lived beside a lake. He had become too weak to hunt, so he sat on the bank after bathing, holding a gold bracelet in his paw, and called out to passing travelers that he would give it away as an act of charity.

A traveler heard him and was tempted, but he was not a fool. It was a fine bracelet, but its owner was a tiger. He asked how he could trust a creature that killed people.

The tiger had an answer ready. In his youth, he admitted, he had done many wicked things and killed many men and cattle. But he had lost his wife and children, and a holy man had taught him to give alms and live righteously. Now he was old, his claws were worn and his teeth had fallen out. Who could fear him? He only wished to give the bracelet to a worthy man. But first the traveler must bathe in the lake, as was proper before receiving a gift.

The traveler, convinced, waded into the lake. He sank deep into the mud and could not get out. The tiger said he would come and help him, walked over, and seized him. As he was being killed, the traveler reflected that he had trusted a tiger.
lesson: Tempting offers from people with a known record of harm deserve the most skepticism, especially when the offer comes with a story of reform and conditions that put you in their reach.
people: An old tiger, a traveler
source: Narayana, Hitopadesha, Book I

title: The Round Table
text:
The Norman poet Wace, writing his verse history of the kings of Britain around 1155, is the first writer known to mention King Arthur's Round Table.

According to Wace, Arthur's court was full of noble barons, and every one of them believed himself the best. None would accept a lower place than the others, and questions of who sat where at the king's table were a constant source of jealousy and quarrels. So Arthur had a round table made. At a round table there was no head and no foot. Every knight sat in an equal place, all were served alike, and no one could boast that he sat higher than his companions.

A few decades later the English poet Layamon expanded the story in his own Brut. In his version, a quarrel over seating at a Christmas feast turned into a bloody brawl in the king's hall. Arthur put down the fight harshly, and afterward a craftsman offered to build him a table at which a great many men could sit without any one of them being above the others.

The Round Table became the symbol of Arthur's knights, a fellowship of equals bound to the same king.
lesson: Fights over rank can poison a group of able people. Arrangements that make members visibly equal can remove the reason to quarrel.
people: King Arthur, his knights
source: Wace, Roman de Brut (c. 1155); Layamon, Brut (c. 1200)
caveat: Arthur and his table are legendary, and the origin story was told differently by later writers.

title: Henry II, Becket and the Angry Words
text:
Thomas Becket rose to power as the friend and chancellor of King Henry II of England. The two hunted, worked and feasted together. In 1162 Henry made him Archbishop of Canterbury, expecting a loyal ally at the head of the English Church. Instead Becket became a fierce defender of the Church's rights against the king. Their friendship turned to bitter enmity, and Becket spent six years in exile.

In 1170 a fragile peace allowed Becket to return. Almost at once he excommunicated bishops who had supported the king. News reached Henry at his court in Normandy at Christmas. Contemporary chroniclers report that he flew into a rage and cried out against the men he had fed and promoted who let him be mocked by a low-born clerk. The famous line about a "turbulent priest" comes from later retellings.

Four knights took his words as a command. They crossed to England and on December 29, 1170, killed Becket in Canterbury Cathedral. The monk Edward Grim, who tried to protect him and was wounded, wrote an eyewitness account. Europe was horrified. Becket was made a saint in 1173, and in 1174 Henry did public penance at his tomb.
lesson: Words spoken in anger by someone with power can be taken as orders. If people act on what you say, choose your words as if they will.
people: Henry II of England, Thomas Becket, Edward Grim
source: Edward Grim, Life of St. Thomas; contemporary chroniclers including William FitzStephen
caveat: The king's exact words are uncertain, and whether he truly meant to order the killing is debated.

title: Hoelun Raises Her Sons Alone on the Steppe
text:
The Secret History of the Mongols, written in the thirteenth century, tells the early life of Temujin, later Genghis Khan. His mother, Hoelun, had been carried off by his father, Yesugei, from her Merkit bridegroom. When Temujin was about nine, Yesugei was poisoned by Tatars on his way home.

The clan that had followed Yesugei, the Tayichiud, saw no future in a widow with young children. One spring they broke camp and left the family behind. Hoelun seized the clan standard, mounted her horse, and rode after them, shaming some into turning back, but they did not stay. She was left with her sons and the family of Yesugei's second wife, with almost nothing.

The Secret History describes how she tied up her skirts and went up and down the banks of the Onon river, digging wild roots and gathering fruit and onions to feed the children. The boys learned to fish and hunt small game. They grew up hungry and hard.

When Temujin and his brother Qasar killed their half-brother Begter in a quarrel over a fish, Hoelun was furious. She told them they had no friends but their own shadows and no whips but their horses' tails, and that they should be uniting against their enemies, not killing each other. Temujin later united the Mongol tribes. He kept his mother close and valued her counsel.
lesson: A parent's strength in the worst times becomes the child's first lesson in survival. Holding a family together sometimes means feeding it and scolding it with equal force.
people: Hoelun, Temujin (Genghis Khan), Qasar, Begter
source: The Secret History of the Mongols, sections 73 to 78, trans. Igor de Rachewiltz (2004)
caveat: The Secret History mixes history with legend, and its dates are uncertain.

title: Henry II's Sons Rise Against Him
text:
Henry II of England ruled an empire stretching from Scotland's border to the Pyrenees, much of it through his wife, Eleanor of Aquitaine. They had four sons who survived to adulthood. Henry gave them titles but kept the power. His eldest, also Henry, was crowned king in 1170 during his father's lifetime, yet had no lands to rule and little money.

In 1173 the Young King fled to the court of his father-in-law, King Louis VII of France. His brothers Richard and Geoffrey joined him, and so did their mother, Eleanor. It was an extraordinary alliance: a queen and three princes in arms against the king, backed by France, Scotland and rebellious barons. Contemporary chroniclers record that Eleanor was captured while trying to reach France, and one says she was dressed in men's clothing.

Henry fought back hard. In July 1174 he did penance at the tomb of Thomas Becket in Canterbury, and that same week the king of Scotland was captured. The rebellion collapsed. Henry forgave his sons, but he kept Eleanor a prisoner for the rest of his reign, about fifteen years.

The family never healed. His sons rebelled again in the following years. In 1189, ill and defeated by Richard and the French king, Henry learned that his favorite son, John, had also gone over to the enemy. He died at Chinon days later.
lesson: Parents who hold back trust and play their children against each other may see them unite against the parents. Real responsibility given early can prevent a revolt later.
people: Henry II, Eleanor of Aquitaine, Henry the Young King, Richard, Geoffrey, John
source: Roger of Howden, Chronica; Ralph of Diceto, Ymagines Historiarum; Gervase of Canterbury, Chronicle; W. L. Warren, Henry II (1973)

title: The Lombard League at Legnano
text:
In the mid-twelfth century the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa set out to restore imperial authority over the wealthy, self-governing cities of northern Italy. The cities were bitter rivals, often at war with each other, and some sided with him. In 1162, after a long siege, he took Milan and had much of it destroyed.

His harshness pushed the rivals together. In 1167 a number of cities formed the Lombard League, swearing to defend each other and their liberties. They helped rebuild Milan and founded a new fortified city, named Alessandria after Pope Alexander III, who supported them.

On 29 May 1176, near Legnano, northwest of Milan, Barbarossa's army met the League's forces. The emperor's knights scattered the League's cavalry, then charged the Milanese infantry, who had gathered around the carroccio, a great ox-drawn wagon carrying the city's banner and an altar. The foot soldiers held their ground around it. The League's cavalry, reinforced, returned and struck the imperial army, which broke. Frederick was unhorsed in the fighting and for days was believed dead.

The defeat forced the emperor to negotiate. A truce followed at Venice in 1177, and in the Peace of Constance in 1183 he recognized the cities' right to govern themselves under nominal imperial authority. Before long, though, the cities were again quarreling among themselves.
lesson: Rivals who unite against a common threat can defeat a far stronger power. Holding together after the victory is often the harder test.
people: Frederick Barbarossa, cities of the Lombard League, Pope Alexander III
source: Contemporary chronicles and letters; Gianluca Raccagni, The Lombard League, 1167 to 1225 (2010)
caveat: Popular details such as the 'Company of Death' and its leader Alberto da Giussano come from later legend.

title: The Conference of the Birds
text:
In this Persian poem by Farid ud-Din Attar, the birds of the world gathered because they had no king. The hoopoe, the wisest among them, told them they did have one, the Simurgh, who lived far away beyond the mountains of Qaf. The journey to reach him was long and terrible, but they should go.

At first the birds were eager, and then each found an excuse. The nightingale could not leave its love for the rose. The parrot wanted immortality rather than a king. The peacock longed for paradise, the duck could not leave the water, the hawk was content serving earthly kings, and so on. The hoopoe answered each one with a story.

At last a great flock set out. They had to cross seven valleys: of the quest, of love, of understanding, of detachment, of unity, of bewilderment, and of poverty and annihilation. Many birds died or turned back along the way.

Only thirty birds finally reached the Simurgh's court. When the veil was lifted, they looked upon the Simurgh, and in it they saw themselves. In Persian, si murgh means thirty birds. What they had traveled so far to find was what they had become together.
lesson: A group sometimes discovers that the strength it was looking for outside was in its own members all along, but only after they have gone through the hard road together.
people: The hoopoe, the birds, the Simurgh
source: Farid ud-Din Attar, The Conference of the Birds (Mantiq al-Tayr)

title: Saladin's Trap at Hattin
text:
In the summer of 1187 Saladin, sultan of Egypt and Syria, invaded the crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem with a large army. King Guy of Lusignan gathered nearly all the kingdom's fighting men at the springs of Sephoria, a strong position with plenty of water. Saladin wanted a battle on his own terms, so he attacked the town of Tiberias on the Sea of Galilee, where the wife of Count Raymond of Tripoli was besieged in the citadel.

At the council of war, according to the Frankish chroniclers, Raymond advised Guy to stay where he was, even though his own wife was at risk: the summer heat and lack of water on the road to Tiberias would ruin the army. Other barons, led by the Master of the Templars, Gerard of Ridefort, accused Raymond of cowardice and treachery. Guy changed his mind and ordered the march.

On 3 July the army set out across the dry plateau in burning heat. Saladin's horse archers harassed it constantly, and it failed to reach water. That night the Franks camped without water near the twin hill called the Horns of Hattin. Saladin's men set the dry grass on fire, sending smoke over the camp. On 4 July the parched army broke apart. Guy was captured and the relic of the True Cross was lost. Within months Saladin had taken most of the kingdom, and Jerusalem surrendered in October.
lesson: Do not let an opponent choose the ground for you. Pressure to look brave can push a leader into the very move his adversary planned.
people: Saladin, Guy of Lusignan, Raymond III of Tripoli, Gerard of Ridefort
source: Imad ad-Din al-Isfahani; Ibn al-Athir, The Complete History; the Old French Continuation of William of Tyre

title: Saladin Takes Jerusalem Without a Massacre
text:
In July 1187 the Muslim ruler Saladin destroyed the army of the crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem at the Battle of Hattin. In September he besieged Jerusalem itself. The city was crowded with refugees and had few knights. Its defense was led by Balian of Ibelin, a nobleman who had escaped from Hattin.

When the walls were breached, Balian went to negotiate. According to the Arab chronicler Ibn al-Athir, he warned Saladin that if no terms were given, the defenders would kill their Muslim prisoners, destroy the Dome of the Rock and the holy places, kill their own families, and fight to the death. Saladin, who had earlier sworn to take the city by the sword as the crusaders had done in 1099, agreed to terms.

The inhabitants could leave in safety after paying a ransom: ten dinars for a man, five for a woman, two for a child. Saladin entered the city on October 2, 1187. There was no massacre. According to chroniclers on both sides, Saladin and his brother al-Adil released thousands of poor people without ransom.

Many who could not pay were still enslaved. But the contrast with the bloodshed of 1099 made Saladin's name respected even in Christian Europe.
lesson: How you behave at the moment of victory shapes your reputation long after. Restraint can win the respect even of those you defeated.
people: Saladin, Balian of Ibelin, al-Adil
source: Imad ad-Din al-Isfahani; Ibn al-Athir, The Complete History; Old French Continuation of William of Tyre (Ernoul)
caveat: The numbers freed without ransom, and enslaved, differ greatly between the Muslim and Christian chroniclers.

title: Saladin Sends Horses to Richard at Jaffa
text:
In the summer of 1192, during the Third Crusade, Saladin made a surprise attack on the port of Jaffa, recently taken by the crusaders. Richard I of England sailed down the coast, waded ashore with a small force and drove the attackers out of the town. A few days later, on August 5, Saladin's army attacked his little camp outside the walls.

Richard had only a handful of horses. According to the crusader chronicle known as the Itinerarium, during the fighting Saladin's brother al-Adil sent him two fine horses as a gift, so that a king would not fight on foot. Richard used them in the battle, and his outnumbered spearmen and crossbowmen held their ground until the attack broke off.

The two sides had long mixed war with courtesy. Envoys passed back and forth, al-Adil and Richard had met and exchanged gifts, and negotiations never fully stopped. A month later, exhausted and with Richard ill, they agreed the Treaty of Jaffa: a three year truce that left the coast to the crusaders and allowed Christian pilgrims to visit Jerusalem.
lesson: Respect toward an opponent does not weaken you in a hard contest. It keeps your honor intact and leaves the door open for the agreement that usually has to come.
people: Saladin, al-Adil, Richard I of England
source: Itinerarium Peregrinorum et Gesta Regis Ricardi, Book 6; Baha ad-Din ibn Shaddad, The Rare and Excellent History of Saladin
caveat: The gift of horses is reported by the crusader chronicle; Muslim sources describe the battle and the courtesies between the leaders but not all its details.

title: Blondel Searches for King Richard
text:
In December 1192, returning from the Third Crusade, King Richard I of England was shipwrecked and tried to cross central Europe in disguise. Near Vienna he was recognized and seized by Duke Leopold of Austria, whom he had insulted at Acre. Richard was handed over to the Holy Roman Emperor Henry VI, who held him for a huge ransom. These facts are history.

A legend first written down in the 13th century, in the collection known as the Tales of a Minstrel of Reims, adds a story. Richard's minstrel Blondel, it says, did not know where his master was held, and set out to find him. He wandered from castle to castle across Germany and Austria. At each one he sang beneath the walls a song that he and Richard had composed together.

At last, at one castle, he sang the first verse and heard a voice from a high window answer with the second. It was the king. Blondel hurried home with the news, and Richard was soon ransomed.

In reality, Richard's whereabouts were soon widely known, and he was released in 1194 after England paid an enormous ransom.
lesson: Loyalty that keeps searching for a lost friend, even without a map, is a kind of love worth remembering. Do not give up on people who have vanished from view.
people: Blondel de Nesle, Richard I of England
source: Recits d'un menestrel de Reims (c. 1260)
caveat: The Blondel episode is a legend; the capture and ransom of Richard are historical.

title: Belling the Cat
text:
The mice lived in terror of the cat. It moved so quietly that it was on top of them before they knew it, and every week another mouse disappeared. At last they called a council to decide what to do.

Many ideas were put forward and rejected. Then a young mouse stood up with a plan that seemed brilliant. The danger, he said, was that they never heard the cat coming. So they should hang a bell around its neck. Whenever the cat moved, the bell would ring, and every mouse would have time to run to its hole.

The council cheered. The plan was simple and clever, and everyone agreed it would save them all. In the middle of the applause an old mouse, who had said nothing so far, got up and asked one question: which of them was going to put the bell on the cat?

The room went silent. The mice looked at one another, and then at the floor. Nobody volunteered, and the meeting broke up with the cat still unbelled.
lesson: A plan everyone applauds is worth nothing until someone has agreed to carry out the hardest step. Ask who will do it before you celebrate the idea.
people: The mice, an old mouse
date: Medieval fable tradition, attributed to Aesop
source: Aesop's Fables, The Mice in Council; Odo of Cheriton, Fabulae
caveat: Although usually listed with Aesop, the fable is first found in medieval collections such as that of Odo of Cheriton.

title: The Sword in the Stone
text:
When King Uther Pendragon died, he left no acknowledged heir, and the barons of Britain could not agree who should rule. At Christmas they gathered in the church in the great city to pray for a sign. When they came out after Mass, they found a block of stone with an anvil on it, and a sword stuck through the anvil. Letters on the sword said that whoever pulled it out would be king by God's choice.

The great lords tried one after another, and none could move it. Then young Arthur, whom everyone took to be the son of the knight Sir Ector and the younger brother of Kay, was sent to fetch a sword for Kay. Unable to find one, he pulled the sword from the stone with ease and brought it to his brother.

The barons were outraged that a boy of no known family should be their king. They demanded more time, and the test was repeated at Candlemas, at Easter and at Pentecost. Each time the lords failed and Arthur drew the sword. In the version by Robert de Boron, Arthur agreed patiently to every delay, and when the lords tested him with rich gifts, he gave them away generously and wisely. At last the common people cried out that they would have Arthur and no other, and he was crowned.
lesson: A position given to you is not the same as authority. When people doubt you, patience and visible fairness can earn what the appointment alone cannot.
people: Arthur, Sir Kay, Sir Ector, the barons, Merlin
source: Robert de Boron, Merlin (c. 1200); Thomas Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book I (1485)
caveat: Arthur is a figure of legend, and the sword in the stone appears first in Robert de Boron, not in earlier Welsh or Latin sources.

title: The Mountain Where Elders Were Left
text:
A Japanese folk tale tells of a province ruled by a harsh lord, where food was so scarce that the old were said to be carried into the mountains and left there to die once they could no longer work.

A poor farmer's mother reached that age. With a heavy heart he lifted her onto his back and climbed into the mountains. As they went deeper into the forest, he noticed that his mother was reaching out and breaking off small twigs from the branches they passed, dropping them along the path.

He thought she meant to find her way back. But when they reached the place where he had to leave her, she told him why she had done it. The path was steep and confusing, she said, and she did not want her son to lose his way going home in the dark. She had marked the trail for him.

The son was overcome. Even as he was abandoning her, her only thought was for his safety. He could not leave her. He carried her back down the mountain in the night and hid her at home, caring for her in secret. In some tellings her wisdom later helped him solve impossible riddles set by the lord, who then abolished the cruel custom.
lesson: A parent's love does not stop to calculate what it gets back. Remembering what our parents gave us can change how we treat them when they become a burden.
people: A son, his old mother
source: Japanese folktale (Ubasute or Obasute legend); early versions of the abandonment theme in the Yamato Monogatari and Konjaku Monogatari
caveat: Ubasute is a legend; there is no firm historical evidence that it was ever a common practice.

title: Genghis Khan Spares the Archer Who Shot His Horse
text:
Around 1201 the young Mongol leader Temujin, not yet called Genghis Khan, fought a battle against the Tayichiud, a rival clan. During the fighting an archer on a hillside shot an arrow that hit Temujin's horse, a prized war horse, in the neck.

The Secret History of the Mongols, the Mongols' own thirteenth-century account, tells what happened after Temujin won. A young man named Jirgoadai, who had fought for the Tayichiud, came to submit. Temujin asked who had shot his horse from the hill.

Jirgoadai answered that he had. If the khan chose to kill him, he said, he would rot on a patch of ground the size of a palm. If he spared him, he would ride ahead in his service and break through deep water and shatter hard stones for him. Temujin said that an enemy usually hides what he has done and lies about it, but this man had told the truth. Such a man was worth having as a companion. He gave him a new name, Jebe, meaning "arrow" or "weapon".

Jebe became one of the greatest Mongol generals, leading campaigns from China to Central Asia and across the Caucasus.
lesson: Value honesty, even when it is uncomfortable to hear. People who tell you the truth about their mistakes are worth keeping close.
people: Temujin (Genghis Khan), Jebe (Jirgoadai)
source: The Secret History of the Mongols, sections 145 to 147

title: Temujin and Jamukha, Sworn Brothers
text:
The Secret History of the Mongols, written in the 13th century, tells how the boy Temujin, later Genghis Khan, met another boy, Jamukha, on the frozen Onon River. They became anda, sworn brothers, exchanging knucklebones for playing games and later arrowheads. As young men they renewed the oath.

When Temujin's wife Borte was kidnapped by the Merkits, Jamukha joined the war that rescued her. Afterward the two camped together for about a year and a half and were inseparable. Then one day, as the camp moved, Jamukha said something ambiguous about where they should pitch their tents. Temujin, on Borte's advice, read it as a sign that Jamukha wanted him under his command, and he moved on through the night. Many followers came with him.

The friends became rivals for leadership of the steppe. Jamukha was proclaimed gurkhan by a coalition and fought Temujin for years. In 1205, defeated and on the run, he was betrayed by his own companions, who handed him over. Temujin had the traitors executed for betraying their lord. According to the Secret History, he offered Jamukha friendship again. Jamukha refused, saying that he would only trouble Temujin like a louse in his collar or a thorn in his lapel, and asked to be put to death without shedding his blood. Temujin granted his request.
lesson: Friendships need shared aims to survive ambition. When paths split, part honestly, because rivalry between old friends can become the hardest kind.
people: Temujin (Genghis Khan), Jamukha, Borte
source: The Secret History of the Mongols, chapters 3 to 8
caveat: The Secret History mixes history with literary storytelling, and Jamukha's last speech in particular may be shaped by the author.

title: The Mongol Decimal Army
text:
When Temujin was proclaimed Chinggis Khan in 1206, he united steppe peoples who had spent generations raiding and betraying each other. To hold them together, he reorganized his whole people on a decimal system.

Men were grouped in units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and, at the largest scale, ten thousand, each with its own commander. According to the Secret History of the Mongols, Chinggis named the commanders of ninety-five units of a thousand, rewarding loyal companions rather than old tribal chiefs. Crucially, many units were deliberately formed by mixing men from different clans and tribes, including defeated enemies. Loyalty shifted from the tribe to the unit and to the khan.

The units lived, traveled and fought together, and their members were bound to one another. The Franciscan friar John of Plano Carpini, who visited the Mongols in the 1240s, reported harsh rules of collective responsibility: if one or two men of a group of ten fled in battle, all ten were put to death, and if a man was captured and his comrades did not try to free him, they too were punished.

Promotion was based on ability and loyalty. Chinggis also created an elite guard drawn from the sons of commanders, which served as both a training school and a check on the units. With this structure, a people of perhaps a million built the largest contiguous land empire in history.
lesson: Small units with shared responsibility create strong bonds. Organizing people around the team rather than old loyalties can unify a divided group.
people: Chinggis Khan (Genghis Khan), John of Plano Carpini
source: The Secret History of the Mongols (13th century); John of Plano Carpini, History of the Mongols (c. 1247)
caveat: Population estimates for the early Mongol nation are rough; Carpini's account of collective punishment is an outsider's report.

title: King John Seals Magna Carta
text:
By 1215 King John of England had lost most of his family's lands in France, including Normandy, and his attempt to win them back had ended in defeat at Bouvines in 1214. To pay for his wars he had squeezed his barons with heavy taxes, arbitrary fines and seizures, and he used the courts and hostages to keep them in line.

In the spring of 1215 a group of barons rebelled and took control of London. John was forced to negotiate. On June 15, 1215, at Runnymede, a meadow by the Thames near Windsor, he accepted the terms of a charter worked out with the help of Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury.

The charter dealt with many specific grievances, about inheritance, widows, debts and forests. But some clauses reached further. No free man was to be arrested, imprisoned, stripped of his rights or property, or outlawed except by the lawful judgment of his peers or by the law of the land. To no one would the king sell, deny or delay justice. A council of twenty-five barons was to enforce the charter.

The peace did not last. Within weeks John asked Pope Innocent III to annul the charter, which he did in August, and civil war followed. But after John's death in 1216 the charter was reissued in revised form, and it became a lasting foundation of the idea that rulers are bound by law.
lesson: Power used without limits tends to provoke the limits it tried to avoid. Rules that bind leaders protect everyone, including the leaders.
people: King John, the barons, Stephen Langton
source: Magna Carta (1215), clauses 39, 40 and 61; contemporary chroniclers including Roger of Wendover

title: Francis of Assisi Meets the Sultan
text:
In 1219, during the Fifth Crusade, a crusader army was besieging the Egyptian port of Damietta, held by the Ayyubid sultan al-Malik al-Kamil, nephew of Saladin. Francis of Assisi, founder of the Franciscan friars, arrived in the crusader camp. He was dismayed by the soldiers' conduct and warned them against attacking.

Then, with a single companion, he crossed the lines unarmed and walked toward the Muslim camp. He was seized by guards, beaten according to some accounts, and brought before the sultan. Francis had come to preach Christianity to him.

The French bishop Jacques de Vitry, who was in the crusader camp, wrote that the sultan listened attentively to Francis for several days. Al-Kamil did not convert, but he treated Francis with courtesy, and according to Jacques de Vitry he asked Francis to pray for him that God would show him the faith most pleasing to Him. Then the sultan sent him back safely to the Christian camp.

Damietta fell to the crusaders that November, but the crusade ended in failure two years later. Al-Kamil later negotiated the peaceful return of Jerusalem to the Christians with Emperor Frederick II in 1229.
lesson: Even in the middle of a bitter conflict, two people can meet with courtesy and actually listen. Going in person to the other side takes courage, and it is rarely wasted.
people: Francis of Assisi, Sultan al-Malik al-Kamil, Jacques de Vitry
source: Jacques de Vitry, letter of 1220 and Historia Occidentalis; Thomas of Celano, First Life of St. Francis
caveat: Later Franciscan accounts added embellishments, such as an offer to walk through fire, that are not in the earliest sources.

title: Frigg's Oath for Baldr
text:
Baldr, son of Odin and Frigg, was the best loved of all the gods, so fair and bright that light seemed to shine from him. One night he began to have terrible dreams that his life was in danger. When he told the other gods, they decided to protect him.

His mother Frigg traveled through all the worlds and took oaths from everything to do Baldr no harm: fire and water, iron and every metal, stones, earth, trees, sicknesses, beasts, birds, poisons and serpents. Afterward the gods made a game of it. Baldr would stand in the middle of their assembly while they threw things at him, shot arrows and struck at him with swords, and nothing hurt him.

Loki did not like this. Disguised as an old woman, he visited Frigg and asked whether everything had sworn. Frigg said yes, except a young shoot west of Valhalla called mistletoe; it seemed too young to ask. Loki went and pulled it up.

At the assembly he found Baldr's blind brother Hod standing apart. Loki gave him the mistletoe and guided his aim. Hod threw, and Baldr fell dead. The gods were struck speechless. Frigg sent a messenger to the goddess of the dead, Hel, who promised to release Baldr if everything in the world would weep for him. Everything did, except one giantess, believed to be Loki in disguise. So Baldr stayed with Hel.
lesson: No protection is total, and the small thing we overlook can matter most. Care for children by preparing them, not only by trying to shield them from everything.
people: Frigg, Baldr, Loki, Hod (Hodr), Odin, Hel
source: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 49

title: Saint Francis and the Wolf of Gubbio
text:
According to The Little Flowers of Saint Francis, a huge wolf once terrorized the town of Gubbio in Umbria. It devoured animals and even people, and the townsfolk were so afraid that they went out armed, as if to war, and many would not leave the walls at all.

Francis, who was staying there, went out to find the wolf despite everyone's warnings. When it ran at him with open jaws, he made the sign of the cross and called it Brother Wolf. The wolf closed its mouth and lay down at his feet.

Francis spoke to it plainly. It had done great harm and deserved punishment, he said, but he wanted to make peace between it and the town. He knew it had done these things out of hunger. If the people promised to feed it every day, would it promise never to hurt man or beast again? The wolf bowed its head and placed its paw in his hand as a pledge.

Francis led it into the market square and repeated the pact before the whole town, and again the wolf gave its paw. For two years it lived in Gubbio, going from door to door and being fed, and the dogs did not even bark at it. When it died of old age, the people mourned it.
lesson: Many conflicts end only when you understand what is driving the other side and meet that need. A fair agreement, kept by both, can turn a threat into a neighbor.
people: Francis of Assisi, the wolf, the townspeople
source: The Little Flowers of Saint Francis (Fioretti), Chapter 21
caveat: The story is a legend first written down about 150 years after Francis's death.

title: Thor in the Hall of Utgarda Loki
text:
Thor, the strongest of the gods, traveled to the giants' stronghold of Utgard with Loki and his young servant Thjalfi. The giant king, Utgarda Loki, received them with contempt and told them no one could stay unless he excelled at something.

Loki said he could eat faster than anyone, and was matched against a man named Logi. Both ate from a trough of meat, but while Loki ate the meat, Logi ate the meat, the bones and the trough. Thjalfi raced a youth named Hugi three times and was beaten badly each time. Thor was given a drinking horn and told that a good drinker emptied it in one draught. After three huge gulps, the level had barely dropped. He was told to lift the king's cat, and managed to raise only one paw. Then he wrestled the king's old nurse, Elli, and was forced down onto one knee. They went to bed humiliated.

In the morning, as he saw them off, Utgarda Loki told them the truth. Logi was fire itself, which consumes everything. Hugi was the king's own thought, which no one can outrun. The end of the horn reached the sea, and Thor's drinking had lowered the ocean. The cat was the World Serpent that encircles the earth. Elli was old age, which brings everyone down. Thor raised his hammer in fury, but the king and his castle had vanished.
lesson: Before judging a defeat, find out what you were really up against. Sometimes a narrow loss means you nearly moved the sea.
people: Thor, Loki, Thjalfi, Utgarda Loki
source: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning

title: Tyr and the Binding of Fenrir
text:
In the Prose Edda, Snorri Sturluson tells how the gods raised the wolf Fenrir, a child of Loki, in their own home. He grew so fast and so fierce that only the god Tyr had the courage to go near him and feed him. Prophecies warned that the wolf would bring them ruin, so the gods decided to bind him.

Twice they brought chains, and twice Fenrir broke them with ease. Then dwarves made a fetter called Gleipnir from impossible things: the sound of a cat's footfall, the beard of a woman, the roots of a mountain, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish and the spittle of a bird. It was as smooth and soft as a silk ribbon.

The gods brought Fenrir to an island and invited him to test his strength against it. The wolf suspected a trick. He would let them bind him only if one of the gods placed a hand in his mouth as a pledge that there was no deceit. The gods looked at each other. No one wanted to lose a hand. Then Tyr stepped forward and put his right hand between the wolf's jaws.

The gods bound Fenrir. The harder he struggled, the tighter Gleipnir held. All the gods laughed, except Tyr. He lost his hand.
lesson: When a plan requires someone to pay a personal price, the leader should be the one to offer. Trust is built by those who put themselves on the line, not by those who only make the plan.
people: Tyr, Fenrir, the gods (Aesir)
source: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning

title: Blanche of Castile Raises a King
text:
When King Louis VIII of France died in November 1226, his son and heir, Louis IX, was only twelve. His mother, Blanche of Castile, a granddaughter of Eleanor of Aquitaine, took charge as regent. Powerful barons, thinking a foreign-born woman and a child easy prey, rose in revolt. Blanche outmaneuvered them with armies and diplomacy and held the kingdom together until her son came of age.

She raised Louis herself, with great strictness and piety. His friend and biographer Jean de Joinville, who knew him well, records what she used to say to him: that she loved him more than any mortal, but that she would rather see him dead than know he had committed a mortal sin. Louis remembered these words all his life, and became famous for his justice and devotion. After his death he was canonized as Saint Louis.

Blanche's love was also possessive. Joinville tells that she was so jealous of Louis's young wife, Margaret of Provence, that the couple had to meet secretly on a staircase in the castle at Pontoise between their two rooms, with servants posted to warn them when the queen mother was coming.

When Louis left on crusade in 1248, he again left the kingdom in his mother's hands. She governed until her death in 1252. Louis heard the news in the Holy Land, and Joinville says he mourned her deeply.
lesson: Firm principles given in childhood can shape a whole life. But even a devoted parent must learn to let a grown child have a life of his own.
people: Blanche of Castile, Louis IX (Saint Louis), Margaret of Provence, Jean de Joinville
source: Jean de Joinville, Life of Saint Louis

title: Rumi Meets Shams of Tabriz
text:
In 1244 Jalal ad-Din Rumi was a respected religious scholar and teacher in Konya, in Anatolia, with many students. That autumn a wandering dervish in his sixties arrived in the city: Shams-i Tabrizi, a restless, outspoken mystic who had spent his life searching for a companion who could bear his company.

Accounts of their first meeting, collected later, differ in the details, but all agree on what followed. Rumi and Shams became inseparable. They spent weeks and months together in conversation, and Rumi neglected his classes. The scholar became a poet and began to recite verses and dance to music. His students and family were bewildered and jealous of the stranger.

Around 1246 Shams left abruptly. Rumi was devastated and sent his son Sultan Walad to find him in Damascus and bring him back. Shams returned, but the hostility around him grew, and around 1247 he vanished for good. Some later accounts say he was murdered; others that he simply left.

Rumi searched for him and then turned his grief into poetry. Thousands of his lyric poems are signed with Shams's name instead of his own, and he went on to write the Masnavi, among the greatest works of Persian literature.
lesson: A single friendship can transform a life. Even when it is lost, what it awakened in you can keep growing and become your best work.
people: Jalal ad-Din Rumi, Shams-i Tabrizi, Sultan Walad
source: Sultan Walad, Ibtidanama; Shams al-Din Aflaki, Manaqib al-Arifin
caveat: Much of the story comes from hagiographic sources written decades later, and the end of Shams is unknown.

title: Eat, My Coat, Eat
text:
Nasreddin Hodja was invited to a wedding feast. He came straight from working in his fields, dressed in his old, patched and dusty clothes.

Nobody paid any attention to him. The servants seated him at the far end, the host did not greet him, and the dishes of rice and meat passed by without reaching him. After a while Nasreddin got up quietly and slipped out.

He hurried home, washed, and put on his finest fur coat and a fresh turban. Then he walked back to the feast. This time the host rushed to welcome him at the door, led him to the place of honor, and pressed the best food upon him.

Nasreddin took the sleeve of his splendid coat and dipped it into the soup. "Eat, my coat, eat," he said, pushing it toward the plates. The other guests stared at him. The host asked what on earth he was doing.

"When I came in my old clothes, nobody offered me a thing," said Nasreddin. "Now I am wearing this coat, and everything is given to it. So it seems only right that the coat should eat."
lesson: Notice whether you treat people according to their clothes, title or status. The person is the same whatever they wear, and so should your respect be.
people: Nasreddin Hodja, a host and guests
source: Nasreddin Hodja tales (Turkish and wider Middle Eastern folk tradition)
caveat: Nasreddin is a folk figure, and the stories attached to him were collected over centuries.

title: The Pot That Gave Birth
text:
Nasreddin Hodja borrowed a large cooking pot from his neighbor. A few days later he brought it back, and inside it sat a small pot.

The neighbor asked what the little pot was doing there. Congratulations, said Nasreddin. While your pot was at my house, it gave birth. Since the mother is yours, the child is yours too.

The neighbor thought this was nonsense, but he was not about to argue his way out of a free pot. He thanked Nasreddin warmly and took both pots inside.

Some time later Nasreddin came to borrow the big pot again. The neighbor lent it gladly, perhaps hoping for another little one. Days passed, then weeks, and the pot did not come back. At last the neighbor went to Nasreddin's house to ask for it.

Nasreddin looked very sad. I am sorry to tell you, he said, that your pot has died.

The neighbor was outraged. Died? How can a pot die? Who ever heard of such a thing?

Nasreddin shrugged. You believed it could give birth, he said. Why can you not believe it could die?
lesson: If you accept a convenient falsehood because it benefits you, you lose the right to object when the same logic turns against you. Hold to the same standard in gains and losses.
people: Nasreddin Hodja, his neighbor
source: Nasreddin Hodja tales
caveat: Nasreddin is a figure of folklore; stories attributed to him were collected and added over centuries.

title: You Are Right Too
text:
Nasreddin Hodja was once serving as the village judge. Two neighbors came before him with a quarrel that had been dragging on for weeks, and a small crowd gathered to watch.

The first man told his side of the story at length, with feeling and many details. Nasreddin listened carefully, nodded and said, "You are right."

Then the second man spoke. He told the same events in a completely different way, just as earnestly, explaining why his neighbor was to blame. Nasreddin listened carefully again, nodded and said, "You are right."

Nasreddin's wife had been listening from the next room. She came in, astonished. "Husband, what kind of judgment is this?" she said. "They cannot both be right!"

Nasreddin thought about this for a moment. Then he nodded to her as well. "You know, wife," he said, "you are right too."
lesson: Almost every account sounds convincing when you hear it alone. Before you take sides in a conflict, hear everyone involved, and stay humble about what you know.
people: Nasreddin Hodja as judge, two litigants, his wife
source: Nasreddin Hodja tales (Turkish and wider Middle Eastern folk tradition)
caveat: Nasreddin is a folk figure, and this joke is also told of other characters and rabbis.

title: The Dutch Water Boards
text:
Much of the western Netherlands lies at or below sea level. From the Middle Ages, as people drained peat bogs and marshes to farm them, the land sank, and the sea and rivers constantly threatened to flood it. No single farmer could hold back the water alone. A dike is only as strong as its weakest stretch, and a breach on one man's land drowns his neighbors too.

So communities organized. Landowners in each area were made responsible for maintaining sections of dikes and ditches, and inspectors walked the dikes to check that each had done his part. Over the thirteenth century these local arrangements grew into regional water boards, the waterschappen, with their own officials, led by a dike reeve. The Hoogheemraadschap van Rijnland, one of the oldest, traces its origins to the middle of the thirteenth century.

The boards worked on a simple principle often summarized as interest, payment, say: those who benefited from protection paid for it, and in return had a voice in how the board was run. They could levy taxes, make rules and punish people who neglected their dikes. Their authority rested on the shared danger, which everyone understood.

Water boards still exist in the Netherlands, now fewer and larger, and their members are still elected by local residents. They are among the oldest democratic institutions in the country, and many Dutch people trace their habit of consultation and compromise, sometimes called the polder model, to the long need to manage water together.
lesson: A common threat can teach neighbors to govern together. When everyone depends on everyone else's part, shared rules and a shared say keep the team strong.
people: Dutch landowners, dike reeves and water board members
source: Water board charters; William H. TeBrake, Medieval Frontier: Culture and Ecology in Rijnland (1985)
caveat: The link between medieval water boards and modern Dutch consensus politics is a popular interpretation rather than an established fact.

title: Anushirvan Pays for the Salt
text:
In his Gulistan, the Persian poet Saadi tells a story about Anushirvan the Just, the Sasanian king remembered in Persian tradition as the model of a fair ruler.

Anushirvan was out hunting, and his servants were roasting game for him at the hunting ground. They discovered that they had no salt. A servant was sent to a nearby village to fetch some. As he left, the king called after him to pay for the salt, so that it would not become a custom and the village be ruined.

His companions were puzzled. What harm could come from a pinch of salt? Anushirvan answered that oppression in the world had begun small. Everyone who came after added a little to it, until it reached its present size.

Saadi then adds his own verses to drive the point home. If the king eats a single apple from a peasant's orchard, his servants will pull up the tree by the roots. If the sultan allows five eggs to be taken by force, his soldiers will put a thousand chickens on the spit.
lesson: People below you copy what you allow yourself, and they copy it larger. Keep your own small habits clean, because they set the limit for everyone else.
people: Anushirvan the Just (Khosrow I), his servants
source: Saadi, Gulistan, Chapter 1 (On the Manners of Kings)

title: The Kind Lie
text:
The first story of Saadi's Gulistan tells of a king who ordered a prisoner to be put to death. Knowing he had nothing left to lose, the man began to curse the king in his own language, saying every abusive thing that came to him.

The king did not understand the words and asked his ministers what the prisoner was saying. One minister, a kind man, answered: "He is saying, 'Those who restrain their anger and forgive people are loved by God.'" The king was moved. He took pity on the prisoner and spared his life.

A second minister, a rival of the first, objected. "It is not right for men of our rank to speak anything but the truth in the king's presence," he said. "This man was cursing the king and insulting him."

The king frowned. "His lie pleases me more than the truth you have told," he said. "His was meant to do good, and yours was meant to do harm." Saadi adds the line for which the story is famous: a well meant falsehood is better than a truth that stirs up trouble.
lesson: Being right is not the only thing that matters in what you say. Ask whether your words will heal or harm before you speak them.
people: A king, a condemned prisoner, two ministers
source: Saadi, Gulistan (The Rose Garden), Chapter 1, Story 1

title: Moses and the Shepherd
text:
In Rumi's poem, Moses was walking in the countryside when he heard a shepherd praying aloud. "O God, where are you, so that I can serve you? I would mend your shoes and comb your hair. I would wash your clothes and pick the lice from them. I would bring you milk, kiss your little hands and rub your little feet, and sweep your sleeping place at bedtime."

Moses was shocked. "Who are you talking to?" he demanded. "This is blasphemy! God has no need of shoes or milk. Stuff cotton in your mouth before your nonsense sets the world on fire." The shepherd was crushed. He tore his clothes, sighed, and wandered off into the desert.

Then a revelation came to Moses from God. "You have driven my servant away from me. You were sent to bring people close, not to cut them off. I have given each one his own way of praising me. I do not look at the words and the speech; I look at the heart and the inner state."

Moses ran into the desert, followed the shepherd's tracks and finally caught up with him. "Good news," he said. "You have permission. Say whatever your heart wants to say." But the shepherd answered that he had already moved beyond that place.
lesson: Do not mock or correct the way others express sincere feelings just because it is not your way. Look at the heart behind the words.
people: Moses, a shepherd
source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi, Book II

title: The Pied Piper of Hamelin
text:
The legend says that in 1284 the town of Hamelin in Lower Saxony was overrun by rats and mice. A stranger appeared in a coat of many colors and offered to rid the town of them for a fee. The townspeople agreed. He took out a pipe and began to play, and the rats came pouring out of every house and followed him to the river Weser, where they waded in and drowned.

With the rats gone, the townspeople refused to pay him. In Browning's poem the mayor offers fifty guilders instead of the agreed thousand and treats the piper as a joke. The piper left, angry.

On the feast of Saints John and Paul, June 26, he came back, dressed as a hunter, and played a different tune in the streets. This time the children came running out to follow him, a hundred and thirty of them according to the old account. He led them out of the town gate and into a mountain, and they were never seen again. In the Grimms' account, two children straggled back, one blind and one mute, and could tell only part of what happened. In Browning's poem, a lame boy was left behind.
lesson: A promise made under pressure must still be kept once the pressure is gone. Cheating someone who solved your problem is the surest way to create a worse one.
people: The piper, the mayor and council of Hamelin, the children of Hamelin
source: Brothers Grimm, Deutsche Sagen (1816); Robert Browning, The Pied Piper of Hamelin (1842)
caveat: Town records suggest some real loss of Hamelin's children in 1284, but the rat catching was added to the legend only in the 16th century.

title: The Rutli Oath and the Swiss Alliance
text:
In early August 1291, the men of three valley communities around Lake Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz and Nidwalden, drew up a charter in Latin. They promised to help one another with all their power, inside and outside their valleys, against anyone who attacked them. They also agreed not to accept any judge who had bought his office or who was not a native of their valleys, and set rules for settling disputes among themselves. The document, known as the Federal Charter of 1291, survives in an archive in Schwyz.

Around this sober document a famous legend grew up. Written down in the fifteenth century in the White Book of Sarnen, and later polished by the chronicler Aegidius Tschudi, it tells of three men, Walter Furst of Uri, Werner Stauffacher of Schwyz and Arnold of Melchtal from Unterwalden, who met secretly on the Rutli, a meadow above the lake, and swore an oath to free their valleys from harsh Habsburg bailiffs. The same tradition includes the tale of William Tell.

The alliance itself was real and lasting. In 1315 the confederates defeated a Habsburg army at Morgarten, and in the following centuries other towns and valleys joined, until the confederation grew into modern Switzerland.

In the nineteenth century the Swiss adopted 1 August as their national day, and the Rutli meadow remains a national symbol, visited every year by people from across the country.
lesson: Small communities that pledge to defend one another can stand up to far greater powers. A clear written promise outlasts the heroes of the story.
people: Uri, Schwyz, Nidwalden (Unterwalden); legendary figures Walter Furst, Werner Stauffacher, Arnold of Melchtal
source: Federal Charter of 1291 (Bundesbrief), Schwyz; White Book of Sarnen (c. 1470); Aegidius Tschudi, Chronicon Helveticum
caveat: The charter is authentic, but the Rutli oath scene and its three heroes are later legend.

title: Robert the Bruce and the Spider
text:
In 1306 Robert the Bruce had himself crowned King of Scots in defiance of Edward I of England. Within months he was beaten at Methven and again at Dalrigh. His supporters were killed or captured, his wife and daughter were taken prisoner, and three of his brothers were later executed. Bruce went into hiding, probably on the western isles or in Ireland, through the winter.

A well-known story, which Walter Scott retold for children in his Tales of a Grandfather in 1828, comes from this period. Lying in a poor hut and wondering whether to give up the struggle, Bruce watched a spider trying to swing from one roof beam to another to fix its web. It tried six times and failed six times. Bruce reflected that he too had fought six times against the English and failed. He decided that if the spider tried a seventh time and succeeded, he would try again. The spider succeeded.

Whatever its origin, Bruce did return in 1307. He fought a long guerrilla war, took back castle after castle, and in 1314 defeated the English army at Bannockburn.
lesson: Repeated failure is not a verdict. Small reminders of persistence can carry you through the moment when quitting seems reasonable.
people: Robert the Bruce
location: Scotland (traditionally a cave or hut in the west)
source: Walter Scott, Tales of a Grandfather (1828), from earlier Scottish tradition
caveat: The spider story first appears centuries later, and a similar tale was told of Bruce's companion James Douglas.

title: Mansa Musa's Gold in Cairo
text:
In 1324 Mansa Musa, ruler of the empire of Mali in West Africa, set out on the pilgrimage to Mecca. His caravan crossed the Sahara with a huge following and a great quantity of gold, which came from the mines of the West African interior. When he reached Cairo, then the largest city of the Islamic world, his visit became legendary.

The Egyptian official and scholar al-Umari, who wrote some years later and interviewed people who had met the king, reports what happened. Mansa Musa and his entourage spent and gave away gold lavishly, to officials, to the sultan's court and in the markets. So much gold entered the city that its value fell. Al-Umari says that the price of gold in Egypt had been high before, but it dropped after the visit and had still not recovered twelve years later.

The chroniclers also record a sequel. On his way home, Mansa Musa's party had spent so much that he had to borrow money from Cairo merchants at high rates. The visit made Mali famous across the Mediterranean, and a few decades later European mapmakers drew Mansa Musa enthroned in the middle of Africa, holding a nugget of gold.
lesson: What is scarce is valuable; flood a market with it and its worth drops. Abundance spent without thought can undermine the very wealth it displays.
people: Mansa Musa, Shihab al-Din al-Umari
source: Ibn Fadl Allah al-Umari, Masalik al-Absar fi Mamalik al-Amsar; translated in N. Levtzion and J. F. P. Hopkins, Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History (1981)
caveat: The size of Mansa Musa's caravan and the amounts of gold are uncertain and often exaggerated in modern retellings.

title: The Dean of Santiago and Don Illan
text:
In a tale told by the Spanish prince Don Juan Manuel, the dean of Santiago came to Toledo to learn magic from the famous master Don Illan. Don Illan was reluctant. Men who rose to high places, he said, soon forgot those who had helped them. The dean swore he would never forget, and he would grant Don Illan whatever he asked. Don Illan quietly told his housekeeper to get partridges ready for dinner but not to cook them until he gave the order.

Then messengers arrived. The dean's uncle, the archbishop of Santiago, was ill, then dead, and the dean was elected in his place. Don Illan asked that his son receive the vacant deanship. The new archbishop gave it to his own brother instead, promising something better later. Soon he was made bishop of Toulouse, then cardinal, then pope. Each time Don Illan asked for something for his son, and each time the post went to a relative or friend, with fresh promises.

At last, as pope, he told Don Illan to stop asking or he would throw him in prison as a heretic and sorcerer. Don Illan replied that since there was nothing for him, he would just have to eat the partridges he had ordered for dinner.

At that moment the dean found himself back in Toledo, still a dean, in Don Illan's house. Everything had been an illusion. Don Illan sent him home ashamed, without even sharing the partridges.
lesson: Notice how people treat you when they no longer need you, ideally before you have given them everything. And keep your own promises once you rise.
people: Don Illan of Toledo, the dean of Santiago
source: Don Juan Manuel, El Conde Lucanor, Exemplo 11

title: "Let the Boy Win His Spurs"
text:
On 26 August 1346, near the village of Crecy in northern France, the English army of King Edward III faced a much larger French army. The king's eldest son, Edward of Woodstock, later called the Black Prince, was sixteen. His father had given him nominal command of one of the three divisions, the one in the front line, surrounded by experienced knights to guide him.

The chronicler Jean Froissart tells that as the battle grew fierce, the prince's division came under heavy attack from the French and their allies. The knights around him grew worried and sent a messenger to the king, who was watching from a windmill on a hill above, asking him to send help.

According to Froissart, the king asked whether his son was dead, or struck down, or so badly wounded that he could not fight on. The messenger said no, but that he was in a hard fight. Then, said the king, go back to those who sent you and tell them not to send for me again as long as my son is alive. Let the boy win his spurs, he said, for if God wills it, I want the day and the honor to be his and those around him.

The prince's division held, and the English won a crushing victory. Froissart says that afterwards the king embraced his son and told him he had acquitted himself well, and the prince bowed low before his father.
lesson: Letting a child face real difficulty, while staying close enough to help, builds confidence no rescue can. Sometimes the best support is trusting them to finish the fight.
people: Edward III, Edward the Black Prince
source: Jean Froissart, Chronicles, book 1
caveat: Froissart wrote years later and dramatized his battle scenes, so the exact words are uncertain.

title: The Burghers of Calais
text:
In 1346, after his victory at Crecy, Edward III of England laid siege to the French port of Calais. The town held out for eleven months, until its people were starving. When it finally offered to surrender, Edward, angry at the long resistance, at first wanted to put everyone to the sword.

The chronicler Jean Froissart tells how, after his advisers urged mercy, Edward set a condition. He would spare the town if six of its leading citizens came out bareheaded and barefoot, with ropes around their necks, carrying the keys of the town and castle, to be put to death.

When the terms were read out in the market square, Eustache de Saint-Pierre, one of the richest men in Calais, stepped forward first and offered himself. Five others followed.

The six came out to the English camp as required, and Edward ordered them beheaded. His knights pleaded for them, and Edward refused. Then Queen Philippa, who was pregnant, knelt before him and begged him, for her sake, to spare them. Froissart says the king looked at her for a while in silence, and then gave the men to her. She had them clothed and fed and sent them away safe.
lesson: Leadership can mean offering yourself first when your community is in danger. Mercy, too, takes courage when anger is in charge.
people: Edward III, Queen Philippa of Hainault, Eustache de Saint-Pierre
source: Jean Froissart, Chronicles, Book 1
caveat: Some historians think the scene was a planned ritual of submission rather than a real threat of execution.

title: Federigo's Falcon
text:
Federigo degli Alberighi was a young nobleman of Florence who fell in love with Monna Giovanna, a married lady. To win her he held feasts and tournaments and spent his whole fortune, but she, being virtuous, paid him no attention. Ruined, he retired to a little farm outside the city, where he lived poorly. The only thing of value he had left was a magnificent falcon.

Giovanna's husband died, and she spent the summer at a country house near Federigo's farm with her young son. The boy became friends with Federigo and fell in love with the falcon. Then he fell seriously ill and told his mother that if he could have the falcon, he would get well.

Giovanna went to ask for it, embarrassed. Federigo, overjoyed at her visit, wanted to give her a meal, but there was nothing in the house. Without hesitating, he killed his fine falcon, had it roasted and served it to her. After dinner she made her request. Federigo burst into tears and told her she had just eaten it.

She was sorry for the falcon but moved by his greatness of soul. Her son died a few days later. When her brothers pressed her to remarry, she chose Federigo, saying she would rather have a man who lacked money than money that lacked a man. He married her and from then on managed his wealth wisely.
lesson: Character shows most clearly when someone gives freely with nothing left over. Look for generosity of spirit in people, not only for what they own.
people: Federigo degli Alberighi, Monna Giovanna, her son
source: Giovanni Boccaccio, Decameron, Day 5, Story 9

title: The Parable of the Three Rings
text:
In Boccaccio's Decameron, Saladin, the sultan of Egypt, needed money and summoned Melchizedek, a wealthy Jewish moneylender of Alexandria. Hoping to trap him, he asked which of the three laws was the true one: the Jewish, the Muslim or the Christian.

Melchizedek saw the danger and answered with a story. A rich man once owned a beautiful and precious ring and declared that whichever son received it would be his heir and head of the family. The ring passed down through generations until it came to a father who loved his three sons equally and could not choose among them. He secretly had a master craftsman make two copies so perfect that even he could not tell them apart, and before he died he gave each son a ring in private.

After his death each son claimed the inheritance and produced his ring. The rings were identical, and the question of which was the true heir, said Melchizedek, is still pending. So it is with the three laws given by God to three peoples.

Saladin saw how skillfully he had escaped the snare, told him openly what he needed, and Melchizedek lent the money. Saladin repaid it in full, honored him with gifts and kept him as a friend. Four centuries later Lessing retold the parable in Nathan the Wise, adding a judge who tells each son to prove his ring by the goodness of his life.
lesson: When people disagree on questions no one can settle, respect and good conduct do more than winning the argument. Let your actions make your case.
people: Saladin, Melchizedek (Boccaccio), Nathan (Lessing)
location: Florence (modern Italy); set in Alexandria and Cairo (modern Egypt)
source: Giovanni Boccaccio, Decameron, Day 1, Story 3; Gotthold Ephraim Lessing, Nathan the Wise (1779), Act III

title: The Hanseatic League
text:
In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, German merchants trading across the North Sea and the Baltic faced pirates, unpredictable foreign rulers and little protection from their own distant emperor. They responded by banding together. Merchants from the same towns traveled in groups, and in foreign trading centers they formed associations, or hansas, to defend their rights.

Over time the towns themselves cooperated. Led by Lubeck, dozens of cities, including Hamburg, Bremen, Cologne, Danzig, Riga and Visby, formed a loose league. Its merchants ran trading posts in London, Bruges, Bergen and Novgorod, where they lived under their own rules. From the fourteenth century, delegates of the member towns met in a general assembly, the Hanseatic Diet, usually in Lubeck.

The league had no permanent army, no common treasury and few officials. Its chief weapon was collective action. If a ruler or a city broke its agreements, the league could impose a trade embargo, and a member town that refused to cooperate could be expelled. When King Valdemar IV of Denmark captured Visby and threatened the league's trade, the towns allied, went to war, and in the Treaty of Stralsund of 1370 forced Denmark to grant them trading privileges and control of fortresses on the Danish coast for fifteen years.

The league declined from the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, as strong territorial states and new trade routes arose. Its last diet met in 1669. Hamburg, Bremen and Lubeck still call themselves Hanseatic cities.
lesson: Independent members can achieve great power by acting together under shared rules. A credible commitment to collective action can replace an army.
people: Merchants and towns of the Hanseatic League, Valdemar IV of Denmark
location: North Sea and Baltic coasts (Germany, Poland, the Baltic states, Sweden and beyond)
source: Philippe Dollinger, The German Hansa (1964; English translation 1970)

title: Borrowing Arrows with Straw Boats
text:
In the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms, the allied armies of Liu Bei and Sun Quan faced Cao Cao's huge force across the Yangtze. Zhou Yu, the brilliant commander of Wu, was jealous of Zhuge Liang, the strategist of his ally, and looked for a way to ruin him. He asked Zhuge Liang to produce one hundred thousand arrows for the coming battle within ten days.

To his surprise, Zhuge Liang said three days would be enough, and signed a pledge to accept punishment if he failed. He then asked Lu Su, a friendly officer, for twenty boats, each with a crew of soldiers, covered with cloth screens and lined with bundles of straw. For two days he did nothing at all.

On the third night a thick fog rolled over the river. Before dawn, Zhuge Liang had the boats tied together and rowed toward Cao Cao's camp, with the crews beating drums and shouting as if attacking. Cao Cao, unable to see anything in the fog and fearing a trap, ordered his archers to shoot rather than sail out. Arrows rained down on the straw. Zhuge Liang turned the boats to load the other side evenly.

As the fog lifted, the boats rowed away bristling with arrows, more than a hundred thousand of them. Zhuge Liang told the astonished Lu Su that he had read the weather three days before.
lesson: Know the conditions and your opponent's habits well enough, and you can make a rival's caution supply what you lack.
people: Zhuge Liang, Zhou Yu, Lu Su, Cao Cao
location: Yangtze River near Red Cliffs, China
source: Luo Guanzhong, Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Chapter 46
caveat: The episode is fiction; the historical records give no such feat to Zhuge Liang, though a similar tale is told of Sun Quan.

title: Chanticleer and the Fox
text:
In a poor widow's farmyard lived a splendid rooster named Chanticleer, the finest crower in the land, with his favorite hen, Pertelote. One night he dreamed of a reddish beast that tried to seize him. Pertelote scolded him for being afraid of dreams and told him to take a laxative. He argued long and learnedly that dreams can be warnings, but in the end he forgot his fear and strutted about the yard.

A fox named Russell had slipped into the garden and lay hidden among the herbs. When Chanticleer spotted him and was about to flee, the fox spoke kindly. He had only come, he said, to hear Chanticleer sing. He had known his father, whose singing was magnificent: he used to close his eyes, stand on tiptoe and stretch out his neck to crow. Could the son do as well?

Chanticleer, flattered, shut his eyes and stretched his neck, and the fox seized him by the throat and ran for the woods. The widow, her daughters, the dogs and the whole farm chased after them, shouting.

In the fox's jaws, Chanticleer had an idea. He suggested that the fox turn and taunt his pursuers. The fox liked the idea and opened his mouth to speak. Chanticleer broke free and flew up into a tree. The fox tried flattery again, but the rooster had learned his lesson and stayed where he was.
lesson: Flattery works best when you are tired of being careful. If someone praises you into closing your eyes, open them. And an opponent's own vanity can be your way out.
people: Chanticleer, Pertelote, Russell the fox
source: Geoffrey Chaucer, The Canterbury Tales, The Nun's Priest's Tale

title: The Pardoner's Tale
text:
In Chaucer's Canterbury Tales, the Pardoner told of three young rioters drinking in a tavern in Flanders early one morning during a time of plague. They heard a bell as a corpse was carried past and learned that it was an old friend of theirs, killed in the night by a thief called Death, who had slain a thousand people in the area.

Drunk and furious, the three swore an oath to be brothers to one another and to find and kill Death. On the road they met a poor old man and roughly demanded to know where Death was. He told them that they would find him under an oak tree at the end of a crooked path.

Under the tree they found a heap of gold coins. They forgot all about Death. They decided to wait until night to carry the gold away safely, and they drew lots to send one to town for bread and wine. The youngest went.

While he was gone, the other two agreed to kill him when he returned and split the gold two ways. Meanwhile, the youngest bought poison and put it into two of the three bottles of wine, so that he could keep the gold for himself. When he came back, the two stabbed him. Then they sat down and drank the wine. And so all three found Death under the tree.
lesson: A group bound only by greed has no real loyalty, and each member is a threat to the others the moment there is something to divide. Build partnerships on more than shared gain.
people: Three rioters, an old man
location: England (tale set in Flanders, modern Belgium)
