source: Geoffrey Chaucer, The Canterbury Tales, The Pardoner's Tale

title: What Women Most Desire
text:
In the days of King Arthur, a young knight of the court came upon a girl walking alone and raped her. The outcry was so great that he was sentenced to death. But the queen and her ladies begged the king to let them decide his fate. The queen told the knight she would spare his life if, within a year and a day, he could tell her what women desire most.

He wandered from place to place asking. Some said wealth, some honor, some fine clothes, some flattery, some to be free. No two agreed. As the year ran out, he came upon an ugly old woman sitting on a green at the edge of a forest. She promised him the true answer if he would grant the next thing she asked.

At court, he gave her answer: what women most desire is sovereignty, to have mastery over their husbands and over their own lives. No lady there could deny it, and his life was spared. Then the old woman claimed her reward: he must marry her.

On their wedding night he lay miserable beside her. She offered him a choice: she could be ugly and old and faithful, or young and beautiful and take her chances with other men. He thought, sighed, and said that she should choose whatever was best for them both. Since he had given her the mastery, she said, she would be both beautiful and faithful. He looked and saw a lovely young woman.
lesson: A marriage changes when one partner stops trying to control and gives the other real choice. Respect for the other's judgment can transform the relationship.
people: A knight, an old woman, the queen, King Arthur
source: Geoffrey Chaucer, The Canterbury Tales, The Wife of Bath's Tale
caveat: The tale opens with a rape that the story treats as the knight's crime; it is a medieval text with medieval assumptions.

title: Christine de Pizan Writes to Feed Her Family
text:
Christine de Pizan was born in Venice in 1364. Her father, a physician and astrologer, was called to the court of King Charles V of France and brought his family to Paris. Unusually for a girl, Christine was allowed to pick up learning at home. At fifteen she married Etienne du Castel, a royal secretary, and the marriage was happy.

Then, within a few years, her world collapsed. Her father died, and in 1390 her husband died suddenly in an epidemic. At twenty-five she was left with three young children, her widowed mother and a niece to support, and with debts she had known nothing about. She spent years in lawsuits trying to recover money owed to her husband's estate, and wrote later of the humiliation of being made to wait in courts and offices.

She decided to live by her pen. She began with poems of love and mourning, which found readers at court, and then moved on to history, politics and moral works. Rich patrons, among them the dukes of Burgundy and Berry, paid for copies, and she supervised the production of her manuscripts herself. She is often called the first professional woman writer in Europe. In The Book of the City of Ladies, in 1405, she defended women against the scorn of male authors.

In her Book of the Mutability of Fortune, she wrote that misfortune had changed her from a woman into a man, able to take the helm of her family's ship.
lesson: Loss can force us to discover abilities we never knew we had. Providing for those who depend on us can turn grief into purpose.
people: Christine de Pizan, Etienne du Castel
source: Christine de Pizan, Lavision-Christine (1405); The Book of the City of Ladies (1405); The Book of the Mutability of Fortune (1403)

title: Brunelleschi and the Egg
text:
By the early 1400s Florence's cathedral stood unfinished, with a vast octagonal hole where its dome should be. The space was so wide that no one knew how to vault it, since the usual wooden scaffolding to support a dome during construction would have needed more timber than could be found. In 1418 the cathedral authorities held a competition for ideas.

Giorgio Vasari, writing his Lives of the Artists more than a century later, tells how Filippo Brunelleschi handled it. Architects and masters gathered and proposed all sorts of schemes, from columns in the middle to filling the space with earth mixed with coins so that the poor would carry it away afterward. Brunelleschi said he could build the dome without any supporting framework but refused to show his model or explain how, fearing that others would steal the idea.

The others demanded proof. Vasari says Brunelleschi proposed that whoever could make an egg stand upright on a flat marble surface should build the dome, since that would show his ingenuity. Each master tried and failed. Brunelleschi then tapped the egg on the marble, crushing its end, and stood it up. The others protested that they could have done that too. Brunelleschi answered that they would also have known how to vault the dome if they had seen his model.

He received the commission, at first shared with Lorenzo Ghiberti. The dome was completed in 1436 and is still the largest masonry dome in the world.
lesson: An idea explained too early is easy to copy and easy to dismiss. Show what you can do in a way that proves your competence without giving away the method.
people: Filippo Brunelleschi, Lorenzo Ghiberti
source: Giorgio Vasari, Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors and Architects, Life of Filippo Brunelleschi
caveat: The egg story is probably apocryphal; a similar tale was later told about Columbus.

title: Joan of Arc at Orleans
text:
In 1429 France was losing the Hundred Years War. The English and their Burgundian allies held Paris and the north, and since October 1428 the English had been besieging Orleans, the key city on the Loire. The heir to the French throne, Charles, had not even been crowned.

That winter a peasant girl of about seventeen from Domremy, in Lorraine, reached Charles at Chinon. Joan said that voices from God had told her to raise the siege and lead him to be crowned at Reims. After examination by churchmen, Charles sent her with a relief convoy to Orleans. She entered the city at the end of April.

Over the next days the French, with Joan riding at the front with her banner, attacked the English forts around the city one after another. On May 7, at the fortress of Les Tourelles, she was hit by an arrow between the neck and shoulder. Witnesses at her later rehabilitation trial said she had the wound treated and returned to the fight, and the fort fell that evening.

The next day the English abandoned the siege. In July Charles was crowned at Reims with Joan beside him.
lesson: Visible conviction and courage at the front can give heart to people who have grown used to losing.
people: Joan of Arc, Charles VII
source: Records of Joan's trial (1431) and rehabilitation trial (1450 to 1456)

title: The Children of Lir
text:
Lir, a lord of the Tuatha De Danann, had four children: a daughter, Fionnuala, and three sons, Aed, Fiachra and Conn. When their mother died, Lir married her sister Aoife. At first she loved the children, but she grew jealous of how much their father and everyone else loved them.

One day she took them to Lough Derravaragh. While they bathed, she struck them with a druid's wand and turned them into four white swans. They kept their human voices and minds. She doomed them to spend three hundred years on that lake, three hundred on the stormy Sea of Moyle between Ireland and Scotland, and three hundred more on the western sea off Inis Gluaire. When Lir learned what had happened, Aoife was punished, but the spell could not be undone.

The nine hundred years were bitter. On the Sea of Moyle the storms were fierce and the cold so harsh that their feet froze to the rocks. Through it all Fionnuala sheltered her brothers: Conn under her right wing, Fiachra under her left, and Aed under the feathers of her breast. She sang to comfort them.

When the spell finally ended, the swans heard a Christian bell. They became human again, but now they were withered, ancient people. A holy man baptized them before they died, and the four were buried together in one grave, as Fionnuala had asked.
lesson: Siblings can carry each other through long hardship. One person who keeps the family together, even in exile, can make it bearable for all.
people: Lir, Aoife, Fionnuala, Aed, Fiachra, Conn
date: late medieval Irish (manuscripts from the 15th century)
source: Oidheadh Chlainne Lir (The Fate of the Children of Lir)

title: The Peacemaker Unites the Five Nations
text:
Haudenosaunee tradition tells of a time when the nations south of Lake Ontario were locked in endless revenge killings. Into this world came a man known as the Peacemaker, who carried a message of peace, power and righteousness.

His first great ally was Hiawatha, a man so stricken with grief after his daughters died that he wandered alone in the forest. The Peacemaker found him, and with strings of shell beads spoke words to wipe away his tears and clear his mind. That ritual, in the tradition, became the condolence ceremony still used to raise up new chiefs.

Together they went from nation to nation. The Mohawk, Oneida, Cayuga and Seneca agreed to the peace. The hardest to win was Tadodaho of the Onondaga, a fearsome leader said to have snakes twisting in his hair. In the end they combed the snakes out and made him the keeper of the council fire, with the Onondaga hosting the great council.

The Peacemaker planted a white pine as the Tree of Peace. The leaders threw their weapons into a hole beneath its roots, and an eagle was set on top to watch for danger. In one version he showed them that a single arrow snaps easily, while five bound together cannot be broken. The Five Nations became a confederacy governed by the Great Law of Peace, and in the early eighteenth century the Tuscarora joined as a sixth nation.
lesson: Former enemies can unite when grief is acknowledged and the strongest holdout is given an honored role. A bundle of arrows is stronger than any single one.
people: The Peacemaker (Deganawida), Hiawatha, Tadodaho
location: Haudenosaunee homelands, New York State, USA
source: Haudenosaunee oral tradition of the Great Law of Peace (Kaianere'ko:wa); Arthur C. Parker, The Constitution of the Five Nations (1916)
caveat: This is a traditional account; scholars date the founding of the confederacy anywhere from the twelfth to the sixteenth century.

title: The Pastons Defend Their Home
text:
The Pastons were a gentry family in Norfolk, in eastern England, who rose from peasant origins to wealth in the fifteenth century. They kept their letters, and about a thousand of them survive, an unmatched record of an ordinary family's life during the Wars of the Roses.

The men were often away in London, fighting lawsuits over land. At home, the wives ran the estates. In 1448 Margaret Paston, wife of John Paston, was living in a house at Gresham, a manor claimed by a powerful neighbor, Lord Moleyns. In January 1450, according to the family's own complaint, Moleyns's men, a large armed force, broke into the house while she was inside, undermined the walls and carried her out. Earlier, as the threat grew, Margaret had written to her husband with practical requests: crossbows, poleaxes and almonds and sugar.

The family kept fighting through the courts. In 1459 John inherited Caister Castle from the old soldier Sir John Fastolf, and the inheritance was challenged. In 1469 the Duke of Norfolk besieged Caister with a small army. The young John Paston held out for weeks with a handful of men. Margaret wrote urgently to her eldest son, warning that the defenders were short of gunpowder and arrows and that his brother's life was in danger. The castle was surrendered, but the family eventually got it back.

The letters show a family bound together by duty, quarrels, money and stubborn courage.
lesson: Ordinary families have always had to defend what is theirs, and the steady person at home often does the hardest part. Keeping records and keeping together are both forms of strength.
people: Margaret Paston, John Paston I, John Paston II, John Paston III, Lord Moleyns
source: The Paston Letters, ed. James Gairdner (1904); Norman Davis, Paston Letters and Papers of the Fifteenth Century (1971 to 1976)

title: Mehmed Moves His Fleet Over the Hill
text:
In the spring of 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II besieged Constantinople. The city was protected on its land side by massive walls and on its north by the Golden Horn, a deep harbor whose entrance the Byzantines had closed with a great floating chain. Behind the chain, Byzantine and Italian ships kept the harbor safe, so the defenders did not have to man the weaker sea walls along it. Ottoman attempts to break through the chain failed.

Mehmed found another way. On the far side of the Golden Horn, behind the Genoese town of Galata, his engineers prepared a road over the hill from the Bosphorus to the upper harbor, laid with greased wooden runners. On 22 April 1453, according to the Greek historian Kritovoulos and the Venetian ship's doctor Nicolo Barbaro, who was inside the city, teams of men and oxen hauled dozens of ships up and over the ridge and slid them down into the Golden Horn, behind the chain. Accounts say some ships went over with sails raised and crews aboard.

The defenders woke to see an Ottoman fleet inside their harbor. An attempt to burn it failed. Now they had to spread their few soldiers along the sea walls of the Golden Horn as well as the land walls. On 29 May 1453 the Ottomans stormed the city, and the Byzantine Empire came to an end.
lesson: When the obvious path is blocked, the solution may lie in a route everyone considers impossible. Changing the field can stretch a defense past its limit.
people: Mehmed II, Constantine XI
source: Kritovoulos, History of Mehmed the Conqueror; Nicolo Barbaro, Diary of the Siege of Constantinople
caveat: The number of ships carried over is given differently in the sources, roughly between seventy and eighty.

title: Isabella and Ferdinand Marry in Secret
text:
In 1468 Isabella, half-sister of King Henry IV of Castile, was recognized as heir to the throne. Henry wanted her to marry the king of Portugal or a French prince, matches that would serve his own policy. Isabella, eighteen, chose for herself: her cousin Ferdinand, heir to the crown of Aragon.

Henry opposed the match, and Ferdinand had to cross hostile territory to reach her. According to the chroniclers, he traveled in disguise in October 1469 with a few companions, posing as a servant of merchants, and waited on the others at the inns. The couple met for the first time at Valladolid and were married there on 19 October 1469, with a papal dispensation for their kinship that was of doubtful validity.

When Henry died in 1474, Isabella proclaimed herself queen of Castile. Ferdinand's supporters argued that he, as a man, should rule. The question was settled in 1475 by an agreement at Segovia that defined their shared authority. They issued laws, coins and documents in both names. Later generations summed up the arrangement with a popular saying built on Ferdinand's personal motto, Tanto monta: each counted as much as the other.

Ruling together, the Catholic Monarchs united the crowns of Castile and Aragon, completed the conquest of Granada in 1492 and sponsored Columbus. Their reign also brought the Inquisition and the expulsion of the Jews, part of their joint legacy.
lesson: A marriage of equals works when power is shared openly and its terms are agreed. Partners who choose each other freely can achieve more together.
people: Isabella I of Castile, Ferdinand II of Aragon, Henry IV of Castile
source: Fernando del Pulgar, Cronica de los Reyes Catolicos; Concord of Segovia (1475); Peggy K. Liss, Isabel the Queen (1992)

title: Lorenzo de Medici Sails to Naples
text:
In April 1478 conspirators backed by the Pazzi family and supported by Pope Sixtus IV attacked Lorenzo de Medici and his brother Giuliano during Mass in Florence cathedral. Giuliano was killed; Lorenzo escaped wounded. Florence executed the conspirators, including an archbishop, and the pope responded by excommunicating Lorenzo and placing the city under interdict. With King Ferrante of Naples as his ally, Sixtus made war on Florence.

The war went badly for Florence. Its troops were beaten, its territory raided, and its own allies were unreliable. By late 1479 the city was exhausted, and some Florentines were beginning to blame Lorenzo, since the enemies said they fought him, not the city.

In December 1479 Lorenzo made an extraordinary decision. Without a guarantee of safety, he sailed from Pisa to Naples to put himself in the hands of the enemy king. The risk was real: Ferrante had a reputation for treachery and had once had a visiting commander arrested and killed despite a safe conduct. Lorenzo wrote to the Florentine government that, since he was the one the enemy wanted, he would go himself.

Lorenzo spent about three months at Ferrante's court. He argued that a strong Florence was a better friend to Naples than an ambitious papacy, and he charmed the court. In March 1480 a peace was agreed. Lorenzo returned to Florence to great acclaim, his position stronger than ever.
lesson: Sometimes the direct, personal approach to an adversary can achieve what force cannot. Understand what he really wants and show him that his interests lie with you.
people: Lorenzo de Medici, Ferrante of Naples, Pope Sixtus IV
source: Lorenzo de Medici's letter to the Signoria of Florence (December 1479); Niccolo Machiavelli, Florentine Histories, book 8

title: The Chasqui Relay Runners
text:
The Inca Empire, which in the early sixteenth century stretched along the Andes from modern Ecuador to Chile, had no horses, no wheeled vehicles and no alphabet. Yet its rulers in Cusco received news from distant provinces with remarkable speed. They did it with teams of relay runners called chasquis.

Along the great network of Inca roads stood small huts at short intervals. In each one, runners waited in shifts. When a chasqui came up the road, he called out or blew a conch shell to warn the next station. A fresh runner joined him, ran alongside while the message was repeated, took any knotted cord records, called khipu, and set off at full speed toward the next post. No single man ran more than a short stage, so each could run flat out.

The Spanish chronicler Pedro Cieza de Leon, who traveled in Peru in the 1540s, described the system with admiration. He wrote that messages traveled along the roads faster than they could have been carried by riders on horseback, and that the posts were maintained by the surrounding communities as part of their labor duty to the state.

The system tied together an empire of millions of people across some of the most difficult terrain on Earth. It collapsed with the Spanish conquest, but parts of the roads it ran on can still be walked today.
lesson: A relay of people, each doing a short stage at full effort, can outrun any lone hero. Design work so that handoffs are quick and no one has to carry everything.
people: Chasqui runners of the Inca Empire
source: Pedro Cieza de Leon, Chronicle of Peru, part 2 (c. 1550)

title: The Squirrel at Rama's Bridge
text:
In the Ramayana, Rama's army of monkeys and bears built a bridge across the sea to Lanka to rescue Sita. A story told across India adds a small figure to that great work.

The monkeys were hauling huge boulders and whole trees and throwing them into the water. Among them, a little squirrel was also at work. Again and again it rolled in the wet sand on the shore, ran onto the half-built bridge, and shook the sand off its fur into the gaps between the stones. Then it ran back for more.

Some of the monkeys found this ridiculous. One of them laughed and pushed the squirrel aside, or in some tellings flung it away, telling it to stop getting under the feet of those doing real work.

Rama saw what happened. He picked the squirrel up gently and told the monkeys that it was helping as much as it was able, and that its few grains of sand filled the cracks between their great stones. Then he stroked its back with three fingers. Ever since, the tellers say, Indian palm squirrels have carried three pale stripes down their backs, the marks of Rama's hand.
lesson: Do not measure contributions only by their size. The person filling the small gaps may be what holds the larger work together, and they deserve thanks.
people: Rama, a squirrel, the monkey army
source: Indian folk tradition and regional Ramayana retellings
caveat: The squirrel episode is not in Valmiki's Ramayana and comes from later regional and folk tradition.

title: Columbus and the Eclipse
text:
On his fourth voyage, in June 1503, Christopher Columbus was stranded on the north coast of Jamaica. His two remaining ships were so riddled by shipworm that he had them run aground. A few of his men set off by canoe to seek help from Hispaniola, but months passed without rescue.

At first the local Taino people traded food for trinkets. As time went on, they grew tired of feeding a hundred hungry strangers, and some of Columbus's men mutinied and robbed villages. The supplies dwindled.

Columbus's son Ferdinand, who was with him, describes what happened next. Columbus had an astronomical almanac which predicted a total lunar eclipse for the night of 29 February 1504. He called the local chiefs together and told them that God was angry at their refusal to feed his people and would show it by a sign in the sky that night. As the moon rose, it darkened and turned red. The Taino, frightened, begged Columbus to intercede. He withdrew to his cabin, timed the eclipse, and shortly before it ended, announced that God had forgiven them on condition that they supply food. The moon returned to normal.

From then on, Ferdinand writes, the Taino provided food willingly. A rescue ship finally arrived in June 1504, and Columbus returned to Spain.
lesson: Knowledge others lack is a form of power. Notice how easily it can be used to manipulate, and judge such tricks by who benefits and at whose expense.
people: Christopher Columbus, Ferdinand Columbus
source: Ferdinand Columbus, The Life of the Admiral Christopher Columbus by His Son Ferdinand

title: Cortes Runs His Ships Aground
text:
In 1519 Hernan Cortes landed on the Gulf coast of Mexico with about five hundred Spaniards. He had sailed against the orders of Diego Velazquez, the governor of Cuba, and many of his men were Velazquez loyalists who wanted to go home. After Cortes founded the town of Veracruz, some of them plotted to seize a ship and sail back to Cuba. Cortes discovered the plot and punished the leaders.

Bernal Diaz del Castillo, a soldier on the expedition, describes what followed. Cortes had the anchors, sails, rigging and iron taken off the ships and then had the hulls run aground and wrecked, keeping only a small boat or two. Diaz says the ship masters declared the vessels unseaworthy, and that the decision was presented as agreed with the soldiers. Whatever the form, the effect was plain: no one could retreat to Cuba, and the sailors joined the land force.

Cortes then marched inland toward the Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, gathering indigenous allies, above all the Tlaxcalans. The campaign brought disaster as well as success, including the bloody flight from the city in 1520, but in August 1521 Tenochtitlan fell after a long siege, with enormous loss of life among its people.
lesson: Removing your own escape routes can force full commitment from a wavering group. Be sure the goal is worth it, because the same move also removes your chance to correct course.
people: Hernan Cortes, Diego Velazquez
source: Bernal Diaz del Castillo, The True History of the Conquest of New Spain
caveat: The popular image of Cortes burning his ships is a later embellishment: the sources say they were stripped and run aground.

title: Jakob Fugger Buys an Election
text:
When Emperor Maximilian died in January 1519, seven German electors had to choose his successor as Holy Roman Emperor. The two main candidates were Maximilian's grandson Charles, already king of Spain, and Francis I of France. Both sides knew the vote would go to whoever paid the electors most, and the bribes had to be in cash or reliable credit.

Jakob Fugger of Augsburg, the richest banker of his age, had long financed the Habsburgs. He backed Charles and refused to provide money for the French. Fugger's house supplied the larger part of the roughly 850,000 florins Charles spent on the election, with other bankers providing the rest. In June 1519 the electors unanimously chose Charles, who became Emperor Charles V.

Charles was slow to repay. In 1523 Fugger wrote him a famous letter. He reminded the emperor that it was well known that without Fugger's help he could not have obtained the imperial crown, and that the electors' own letters proved it. He asked politely but firmly for his money with interest. Charles arranged repayment, partly by granting the Fuggers rights to income from Spanish mines and lands. The family's fortunes remained bound to the Habsburgs for decades.
lesson: Timing makes money powerful: support given when someone needs it most buys lasting leverage. Remember that the same dependence can tie the lender to the borrower.
people: Jakob Fugger, Charles V, Francis I
source: Jakob Fugger, letter to Charles V (April 1523); Greg Steinmetz, The Richest Man Who Ever Lived (2015)

title: King Afonso Protests to the King of Portugal
text:
Afonso I, called Nzinga Mbemba before his baptism, ruled the Kingdom of Kongo in west central Africa from about 1509 to the early 1540s. He was a Christian, literate in Portuguese, and an ally of Portugal. He welcomed Portuguese priests, teachers and craftsmen, sent young Kongolese nobles to study in Lisbon, and traded with Portuguese merchants.

That trade increasingly meant slaves. In 1526 Afonso wrote several letters to King Joao III of Portugal, which survive in the Portuguese archives. He complained that Portuguese merchants were flooding his kingdom with goods, encouraging his own subjects to defy him, and seizing free people, even nobles and members of the royal family, to sell them overseas. He wrote that the country was being depopulated. He asked the Portuguese king to send no more merchants or goods, only priests and teachers and what was needed for the church.

Afonso then set up a commission of officials to inspect every captive before export and to free anyone who had been taken illegally. He did not end the trade, which he too took part in under those rules, and Portugal ignored his request to stop it.
lesson: A leader must be willing to name a harm that enriches powerful people around him, even when he cannot stop it alone.
people: Afonso I of Kongo (Nzinga Mbemba), Joao III of Portugal
location: Mbanza Kongo, Kingdom of Kongo (modern Angola)
source: Letters of Afonso I to Joao III, 1526, Portuguese archives (published in Antonio Brasio, Monumenta Missionaria Africana)

title: Babur Offers His Life for His Son
text:
In 1530 Humayun, the eldest son of Babur, founder of the Mughal empire, fell gravely ill. He was brought to Agra, and the doctors could do nothing for him. His sister Gulbadan Begum, who was a child at the time, later wrote the story in her memoir of her brother's reign, the Humayun-nama.

According to her account, those around the emperor suggested that he give away something of great value, in the hope that God would accept it in exchange for his son's life. Babur answered that nothing he owned was as valuable as his own life, and that he would give that. He walked three times around Humayun's bed, praying that the illness pass from his son to himself.

Gulbadan writes that from that day Humayun began to recover, while Babur himself fell ill. His condition worsened over the following months. He gathered his nobles, named Humayun as his successor, and asked them to be loyal to him. Babur died at Agra in December 1530, at forty-seven.

Humayun's reign proved difficult. He lost the empire to Sher Shah Suri and spent fifteen years in exile, but he reconquered Delhi shortly before his death, and his son Akbar became the greatest of the Mughals.
lesson: Many parents would take a child's suffering upon themselves if they could. That love is real even when it cannot change what happens.
people: Babur, Humayun, Gulbadan Begum
source: Gulbadan Begum, Humayun-nama (Ahval-i Humayun Badshah), trans. Annette Beveridge (1902)
caveat: The account comes from Babur's daughter, writing decades later; historians note Babur may already have been in poor health.

title: Atahualpa's Ransom at Cajamarca
text:
In November 1532 Francisco Pizarro led about 170 Spaniards into the Andean town of Cajamarca. Atahualpa, the Inca ruler, was camped nearby with a huge army, fresh from victory in a civil war against his brother Huascar. He knew the strangers were few and seems to have regarded them as a curiosity rather than a threat. He agreed to meet Pizarro in the town square.

The Spaniards hid their horsemen, foot soldiers and small cannon in the buildings around the square. Late on 16 November Atahualpa arrived, carried on a litter and accompanied by thousands of attendants who were largely unarmed. According to the accounts of Pizarro's secretary Francisco de Xerez and his cousin Pedro Pizarro, the friar Vicente de Valverde approached with a breviary or Bible and demanded that Atahualpa submit to the Christian faith and the Spanish king. Atahualpa examined the book and threw it to the ground. At a signal the Spaniards opened fire and charged. In the panic, thousands of Inca attendants were killed, and Pizarro seized Atahualpa himself.

From captivity Atahualpa offered a ransom: to fill a large room once with gold and twice with silver. The Spaniards accepted, and over the following months treasure poured in from across the empire and was melted down. But once the ransom was gathered, Pizarro's men, fearing a rescue attempt, put Atahualpa on trial and executed him in July 1533. The leaderless empire was then conquered piece by piece.
lesson: Never let contempt for a weaker party lower your guard, and do not hand your fate to someone who has already shown he will betray you. A promise from a captor is not security.
people: Francisco Pizarro, Atahualpa, Vicente de Valverde
source: Francisco de Xerez, True Account of the Conquest of Peru (1534); Pedro Pizarro, Relation of the Discovery and Conquest of the Kingdoms of Peru (1571)

title: Thomas More and His Daughter Margaret
text:
Thomas More, lawyer, author of Utopia and later Lord Chancellor of England, ran a household school at his home for his children. In an age when few women learned more than to read, he insisted his daughters be educated as thoroughly as his son: Latin, Greek, logic, philosophy, astronomy. His eldest daughter, Margaret, became one of the most learned women in England. Erasmus admired her, and she translated one of his works from Latin into English.

More wrote her affectionate letters praising her writing. She married William Roper, who later wrote More's biography.

When More refused to swear the oath recognizing Henry VIII's new marriage and break with Rome, he was imprisoned in the Tower of London in 1534. Margaret was allowed to visit him and tried, with all her learning, to persuade him to take the oath and save his life. He would not, but their letters from this time are full of tenderness.

According to William Roper's account, after More was condemned in July 1535, Margaret forced her way through the guards on the Tower wharf to embrace and kiss her father in front of everyone. On the eve of his execution, More wrote her a final letter with a piece of coal. He was beheaded on 6 July 1535. Tradition says Margaret recovered his head from London Bridge and kept it until her own death.
lesson: Educating daughters as fully as sons is a gift that can outlast a parent's life. Loving someone does not mean agreeing with every choice they make.
people: Thomas More, Margaret Roper, William Roper, Erasmus
location: Chelsea and the Tower of London, England (UK)
source: William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More (c. 1556); The Correspondence of Sir Thomas More
caveat: The story of the head comes from later tradition.

title: Thomas More Refuses the Oath
text:
Thomas More was a lawyer, scholar and author of Utopia, and from 1529 he was Lord Chancellor of England, the highest office under the king. When Henry VIII broke with the pope to end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon and marry Anne Boleyn, More could not agree. In 1532 he resigned and retired into private life.

In 1534 Parliament passed the Act of Succession, and all leading subjects were required to swear an oath that accepted Anne's children as heirs and rejected the authority of the pope. More was willing to accept the succession itself, which he said Parliament could settle, but he would not swear the oath as written. He refused to explain his reasons in detail, so as not to give the king grounds to charge him. He was sent to the Tower of London in April 1534.

After more than a year in prison he was tried for treason on July 1, 1535, convicted largely on the testimony of Richard Rich, which More said was false. He was beheaded on July 6. A contemporary report says he told the crowd he died the king's good servant, but God's first.
lesson: Integrity sometimes means refusing to say what you do not believe, even when saying it would be easy and refusing costs everything.
people: Thomas More, Henry VIII, Richard Rich
source: Records of More's trial; William Roper, The Life of Sir Thomas More; the Paris News Letter account of his execution

title: The Eight Immortals Cross the Sea
text:
The Eight Immortals of Chinese legend were eight very different figures who had each attained immortality: a beggar with an iron crutch and a gourd, a general with a fan, an old man who rode his donkey backward, a scholar with a sword, a young woman with a lotus, a musician with a flute, a wandering singer with a basket of flowers, and a nobleman with castanets.

In the best-known story, they were traveling home from a celestial banquet when they came to the Eastern Sea. They could simply have ridden clouds across. Instead, one of them proposed that each should cross using only his or her own particular magic. So the iron-crutch beggar floated on his crutch or gourd, the general rode his fan, the lady stood on her lotus leaf, and the rest each used their own treasure, and the whole company sailed out over the waves.

In many versions the crossing led to trouble: the son of the Dragon King of the sea seized one of the treasures, and a battle followed between the immortals and the dragons, which only ended through the mediation of a higher power. But the image of the crossing itself became a proverb: when the Eight Immortals cross the sea, each shows his own powers.
lesson: A team does not need everyone to work the same way. Let each member reach the goal with the skills they have, as long as everyone arrives.
people: The Eight Immortals
source: Ming dynasty drama and the novel Journey to the East (Dongyou ji) by Wu Yuantai
caveat: Details such as each immortal's vehicle and the battle with the dragons vary between versions.

title: The Valladolid Debate on the Indians
text:
By 1550 Spanish conquest in the Americas had brought enslavement, forced labor and mass death to Indigenous peoples. Bartolome de las Casas, a former settler and slaveholder who had become a Dominican friar, had spent decades denouncing these abuses. His protests helped persuade Emperor Charles V to take a remarkable step: he suspended new conquests and convened a panel of theologians and jurists at Valladolid, in Spain, to decide whether the wars were just.

The case for conquest was made by Juan Gines de Sepulveda, a respected scholar who drew on Aristotle. He argued that the Indians were by nature inferior, natural slaves, and that war to subject them and Christianize them was justified.

Las Casas answered for days, reading from a long Latin treatise. He argued that the peoples of the Americas were fully rational human beings with their own societies, laws and arts, that they could only be won to Christianity by peaceful persuasion, and that the conquest was robbery and murder. The sessions continued in 1551.

The judges never issued a clear verdict, and conquest resumed. But the debate became a landmark: an empire had formally asked whether its own conquests were just.
lesson: Stand up for the humanity of others, even when your own side profits from denying it. Moral arguments can change history slowly even when they lose the day.
people: Bartolome de las Casas, Juan Gines de Sepulveda, Charles V
source: Bartolome de las Casas, Apologia (In Defense of the Indians); Domingo de Soto, summary of the disputation (1552)

title: Mori Motonari and the Three Arrows
text:
Mori Motonari was a minor lord in Aki province, in western Japan, who rose during the age of civil wars to rule most of the Chugoku region. He had three adult sons by his principal wife. The eldest, Takamoto, was his heir. The two younger ones he placed as heirs of other powerful families, the Kikkawa and the Kobayakawa, binding those clans to the Mori.

In 1557 Motonari wrote his three sons a long letter of fourteen articles, which survives. In it he urged them again and again to stay united for the sake of the Mori house, to support one another and never let any quarrel come between them, since their fortunes depended on each other.

Later tradition turned this letter into a famous scene. Motonari, it is said, gave each of his sons a single arrow and asked them to break it, which they did easily. Then he handed them three arrows bound together, which none could break. As long as the three stood together, he told them, no one could destroy them. The story resembles Aesop's fable of the bundle of sticks, and it is almost certainly a legend: Takamoto died years before his father.

The three brothers did largely stay loyal to one another, and the Mori survived the wars. Today the Hiroshima football club is called Sanfrecce, from the Japanese word for three and the Italian for arrows.
lesson: Siblings who stand together are far harder to break than any one alone. Unity has to be asked for, explained and renewed, not assumed.
people: Mori Motonari, Mori Takamoto, Kikkawa Motoharu, Kobayakawa Takakage
source: Mori Motonari, Letter of Admonition to Three Sons (Sanshi Kyokunjo, 1557); later tradition
caveat: The letter is genuine, but the scene with the arrows is a later legend.

title: Montaigne and La Boetie
text:
In about 1558, at a large public gathering in Bordeaux, Michel de Montaigne met Etienne de La Boetie. Both were young magistrates in the city's parliament. La Boetie, a few years older, was already known as a brilliant writer; as a student he had written a daring essay against tyranny, the Discourse on Voluntary Servitude. Montaigne says they had heard of each other before and that they were so taken with each other at that first meeting that from then on nothing was as close to either of them as the other.

Their friendship lasted only about four years. In August 1563 La Boetie fell ill with a fever and died at the age of thirty two, with Montaigne at his bedside. Montaigne wrote a long letter to his father describing his friend's last days.

Years later, when he retired to write his Essays, Montaigne devoted a chapter to friendship. He wrote that ordinary friendships are acquaintances held together by some interest, but in theirs two souls had blended so completely that the seam could not be found. If someone pressed him to say why he loved La Boetie, he could only answer: "Because it was he, because it was I." He also saw to it that his friend's writings were published.
lesson: The deepest friendships cannot be reduced to reasons or usefulness. When you find one, value it while you have it, because time together is never as long as you expect.
people: Michel de Montaigne, Etienne de La Boetie
source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, Book I, chapter 28, "Of Friendship"; Montaigne, letter to his father on La Boetie's death (1563)

title: Nobunaga's Gamble at Okehazama
text:
In the summer of 1560 Imagawa Yoshimoto, one of the most powerful lords of eastern Japan, marched west into Owari province with a large army, commonly estimated at around twenty-five thousand men. Owari belonged to Oda Nobunaga, a young lord of 26 whom many considered reckless. He had perhaps two or three thousand men to oppose the invasion, and his border forts were falling.

Nobunaga's retainer Ota Gyuichi, who wrote his life, describes the morning. Nobunaga refused advice to shut himself up in his castle. Before dawn he danced and sang lines from the play Atsumori about the brevity of life, armed himself, ate standing up, and rode out with only a handful of followers, collecting troops on the way.

Yoshimoto, pleased with his victories at the forts, had halted his headquarters near a hill called Okehazama to rest. His army was spread out over the countryside. Early in the afternoon a violent rainstorm swept the area. As it cleared, Nobunaga's men charged straight into Yoshimoto's headquarters. The Imagawa guards, caught off guard, scattered, and Yoshimoto himself was cut down and killed.

With its leader dead, the Imagawa army fell back and the house never recovered. Nobunaga's reputation was made. One of Yoshimoto's vassals, the young Matsudaira Motoyasu, later known as Tokugawa Ieyasu, broke away and soon became Nobunaga's ally.
lesson: A small force cannot win everywhere, but it can win at one decisive point. Strike where the opponent is complacent, and at the moment he least expects it.
people: Oda Nobunaga, Imagawa Yoshimoto, Tokugawa Ieyasu
source: Ota Gyuichi, Shincho Koki (Chronicle of Lord Nobunaga)
caveat: The size of both armies is uncertain, and historians debate whether Nobunaga attacked frontally or by the flanking surprise of popular tradition.

title: Hai Rui Buys a Coffin Before Criticizing the Emperor
text:
By 1566 the Jiajing Emperor of the Ming dynasty had ruled China for more than forty years. For much of that time he had withdrawn from government, rarely holding court, absorbed in Daoist rituals meant to bring him immortality, while officials governed in his name and corruption spread.

Hai Rui was a minor official in the Ministry of Revenue, known for strict honesty. He wrote a memorial to the emperor criticizing him directly: for neglecting the state, for his superstitions, for his treatment of his family and ministers, and for the suffering of the people. He wrote that the realm had long thought the emperor in the wrong.

According to the official History of Ming, before submitting it he bought a coffin, said farewell to his wife and children, and waited for punishment, expecting to be executed.

The emperor read the memorial, threw it to the ground and ordered Hai Rui arrested before he could escape. A eunuch told him that Hai Rui was known for his foolish stubbornness, had already bought his coffin, that his servants had fled, and that he would not run. The emperor picked up the memorial and read it again and again. Hai Rui was imprisoned, but the emperor died months later, and Hai Rui was released and restored to office.
lesson: Honest criticism of those above you may cost a great deal. Decide in advance what you are willing to pay, and then say what is true.
people: Hai Rui, Jiajing Emperor
source: Ming Shi (History of Ming), Biography of Hai Rui; Hai Rui, Memorial on Public Order (Zhi An Shu)

title: Uesugi Kenshin Sends Salt to His Enemy
text:
In 16th century Japan, Uesugi Kenshin and Takeda Shingen were the most famous rivals of the Warring States period. They fought each other again and again at Kawanakajima without either winning a final victory.

According to a tradition recorded in the Edo period, around 1567 or 1568 the Imagawa and Hojo clans, who had turned against Takeda, cut off the supply of salt to his mountain province of Kai. Kai had no coast, and without salt its people would suffer. Kenshin's province of Echigo lay on the sea. He was urged to join the blockade and weaken his great enemy.

Kenshin refused. In the story he declares that he fights Shingen with bows and swords, not with rice and salt, and he allowed salt to flow to Kai at fair prices. Some versions add that Shingen sent him a fine sword in thanks.

The tale gave Japanese the expression "sending salt to the enemy," still used for helping a rival in trouble. When Shingen died in 1573, Kenshin is said to have wept for the loss of so worthy an opponent.
lesson: Compete hard with your rivals, but do not win by making innocent people suffer. How you fight says as much about you as whether you win.
people: Uesugi Kenshin, Takeda Shingen
location: Echigo and Kai provinces (modern Niigata and Yamanashi, Japan)
source: Edo-period tradition and later popular histories of the Sengoku period
caveat: The episode is not attested in contemporary documents and is generally treated as legend.

title: Ieyasu's Portrait of Defeat
text:
In January 1573 (late 1572 in the Japanese calendar of the time), the young warlord Tokugawa Ieyasu rode out of his castle at Hamamatsu to fight the much stronger army of Takeda Shingen at Mikatagahara. It was a disaster. His army was routed, many of his retainers died covering his escape, and he barely made it back to the castle.

According to a well-known tradition, Ieyasu then had a painter make a portrait of him as he looked that day: hunched on a stool, one leg drawn up, his face twisted and exhausted with fear and defeat. He kept it, the story goes, as a reminder of his rashness and of what overconfidence had cost him, so that he would never repeat the mistake.

The painting known as the shikami portrait, the "grimacing portrait", survives in the Tokugawa Art Museum in Nagoya. Ieyasu himself went on to win at Sekigahara in 1600 and to found the Tokugawa shogunate, which governed Japan for more than two and a half centuries. He became known for patience and caution, the opposite of the young man at Mikatagahara.
lesson: Keep an honest reminder of your worst mistake where you can see it. Remembering defeat is a good guard against arrogance.
people: Tokugawa Ieyasu, Takeda Shingen
source: Tokugawa family tradition; the shikami portrait, Tokugawa Art Museum, Nagoya
caveat: Recent research suggests the link between the portrait and Mikatagahara was made long after Ieyasu's time, so the story may be modern legend.

title: Ishida Mitsunari's Three Cups of Tea
text:
A favorite Japanese legend tells how Ishida Mitsunari, later one of the most powerful administrators of 16th century Japan, first came to the notice of his lord. Toyotomi Hideyoshi, then governing the castle town of Nagahama in Omi province, was out hawking on a hot day. Thirsty, he stopped at a Buddhist temple and asked for tea. A boy serving at the temple, young Sakichi, brought it.

The first time, the boy brought a large bowl of lukewarm tea, which Hideyoshi drank down at once. He asked for another. This time the boy brought a smaller cup of hotter tea. When Hideyoshi asked for a third, the boy brought a small cup of very hot, strong tea, to be sipped and savored.

Hideyoshi understood what the boy had done. He had judged the needs of a parched man first, then of a man whose thirst was eased, then of a man who could enjoy the tea. Impressed by such attention, Hideyoshi took the boy into his service. As Ishida Mitsunari he rose to become one of Hideyoshi's most trusted officials.
lesson: Pay attention to what the other person actually needs at this moment, not what is easiest for you to give. That kind of care is noticed.
people: Ishida Mitsunari, Toyotomi Hideyoshi
source: Edo-period anecdote collections about Toyotomi Hideyoshi and his retainers
caveat: The story is a legend with no contemporary evidence, and it is told with variations.

title: The Venetian Arsenal Builds a Galley in a Day
text:
The Arsenal of Venice was one of the largest industrial sites in pre-industrial Europe: a walled complex of shipyards, ropewalks, foundries and warehouses where thousands of state-employed workers, the arsenalotti, built and fitted out the Republic's war galleys. Dante had already used its boiling pitch and busy shipwrights as an image of hell's activity in the Inferno.

Its secret was organization. Hulls were built in large numbers from standardized parts and stored ready to be finished. In 1436 the Spanish traveler Pero Tafur described how, at the Arsenal's exit, a galley was towed along a channel past a row of windows, and from each window workers handed out what it needed: cordage, arms, oars, provisions. By the end of the line it was ready for sea, and he saw ten galleys fitted out this way in a matter of hours.

The most famous story comes from July 1574, when King Henry III of France visited Venice on his way home from Poland. According to Venetian accounts, the arsenalotti began assembling a galley from prepared parts when the king sat down to a banquet, and had it complete and launched before he rose from the table.

Whatever the exact timing, the Arsenal could produce and outfit war galleys at a pace no rival yard could match. In emergencies, such as the war leading up to Lepanto in 1571, it turned out dozens of galleys within months.
lesson: Speed comes from preparation and organization more than from heroic effort. Standard parts, clear stations and well-drilled people can do in hours what improvisation does in months.
people: The arsenalotti of Venice, Henry III of France, Pero Tafur
source: Frederic C. Lane, Venetian Ships and Shipbuilders of the Renaissance (1934); Pero Tafur, Andancas e viajes (c. 1454)
caveat: The galley built during a single banquet is a celebrated story whose exact timing is probably embellished.

title: Akbar's House of Worship
text:
In 1575 the Mughal emperor Akbar built a hall at his new capital, Fatehpur Sikri, called the Ibadat Khana, or House of Worship. At first it hosted Thursday evening discussions among Sunni Muslim scholars. The debates soon grew bitter, as learned men quarreled and insulted each other in front of the emperor, and Akbar became disillusioned with their pride.

Over the following years he opened the discussions to others. Shia Muslims, Sufis, Hindu pandits, Jain monks, Zoroastrian priests and Jews took part, and in 1580 Jesuit missionaries arrived from Goa at his invitation. Akbar, who could not read, listened for hours, questioned each side and made them answer each other.

His court historian Abul Fazl describes this as a search for truth wherever it could be found. The orthodox historian Badauni, who disapproved, complained that the emperor was drifting from Islam. Both agree on what happened.

The debates helped shape Akbar's policy of sulh-i kul, or peace with all. He had already abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims in 1564 and the tax on Hindu pilgrims. He appointed Hindus to high office and ruled one of the most diverse empires of his age with relative tolerance.
lesson: Listen seriously to people who believe differently from you, and make them hear each other. Understanding grows from honest exchange, not from surrounding yourself with agreement.
people: Akbar, Abul Fazl, Abd al-Qadir Badauni
source: Abul Fazl, Akbarnama; Abd al-Qadir Badauni, Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh

title: Birbal's Khichdi
text:
On a bitter winter day, the emperor Akbar wondered aloud whether anyone would stand all night in icy water for money. He announced a reward for any man who could do it. A poor man came forward, stood through the night in a freezing lake, and in the morning came to the court to claim his prize.

Akbar asked him how he had endured the cold. The man answered that he had kept his eyes on a lamp burning far away in a window of the palace. At once the emperor declared that the lamp had warmed him, so he had not really met the challenge, and sent him away without the reward.

Birbal, Akbar's witty minister, said nothing. The next day he did not come to court. The emperor sent for him and was told that Birbal was cooking khichdi, a dish of rice and lentils, and would come when it was ready. Hours passed. At last Akbar went to see for himself. He found Birbal sitting beside a small fire, with the pot hanging from a branch high above the flames.

When Akbar laughed and asked how food could cook so far from the fire, Birbal asked how a man in a lake could be warmed by a lamp half a mile away. Akbar understood, called back the poor man and paid him in full.
lesson: If you find yourself searching for a technicality to avoid paying what you owe, apply the same reasoning to yourself. When someone shows you the flaw, have the grace to correct it.
people: Akbar, Birbal, a poor man
source: Akbar and Birbal folk tales
caveat: Birbal was a real minister at Akbar's court, but the witty tales about him are folklore, not historical records.

title: Birbal Shortens the Line
text:
The emperor Akbar liked to test the wits of his courtiers with puzzles. One day he took a piece of chalk and drew a straight line across the floor of the court. Then he turned to the assembled nobles and set the challenge: make this line shorter, but without erasing any part of it, and without touching it at all.

The courtiers stared at the line. They walked around it, conferred in low voices, and tried to think of some trick. To make a line shorter, surely you had to rub out part of it. One after another they admitted that it could not be done.

Then Akbar turned to Birbal, his favorite minister, known for his quick mind. Birbal said nothing. He picked up the chalk, bent down, and drew a second line next to the first one, parallel to it and much longer.

Then he stepped back. The emperor's line had not been touched, and not a speck of it had been erased. But beside the new line it was now plainly the shorter of the two. Akbar laughed and praised him, and the courtiers had to admit that Birbal had solved it.
lesson: You do not always have to cut down a rival or a problem to change how it looks. Sometimes the best move is to build something bigger beside it.
people: Akbar, Birbal, the courtiers
source: Akbar and Birbal tales
caveat: The Akbar and Birbal stories are popular folklore attached to two historical figures, not recorded events.

title: Sir Philip Sidney's Cup of Water
text:
Sir Philip Sidney was the model of the English gentleman of his age: poet, courtier, diplomat and soldier. In 1586 he was serving with the English army helping the Dutch against Spain. On September 22, at a skirmish outside Zutphen, he rode into action without his thigh armor and was struck by a musket ball above the knee.

His friend and biographer Fulke Greville tells what happened as he was carried back from the field, thirsty from loss of blood. Someone brought him a bottle of drink, traditionally remembered as water. As he raised it to his mouth he saw a dying foot soldier being carried past, who looked longingly at it. Sidney handed the water to the man before drinking any himself, saying, "Thy necessity is yet greater than mine."

The wound became infected, and Sidney died at Arnhem about three weeks later, at the age of thirty one. England gave him a grand state funeral in London, and the story of the water became one of the best remembered acts of chivalry in English history.
lesson: Real kindness sometimes means giving up what you badly need to someone whose need is greater. It is noticed most when it costs the most.
people: Sir Philip Sidney
source: Fulke Greville, The Life of the Renowned Sir Philip Sidney (written c. 1610, published 1652)
caveat: The story comes only from Greville, writing about twenty five years later, and cannot be confirmed by other witnesses.

title: Elizabeth at Tilbury
text:
In the summer of 1588 the Spanish Armada sailed up the English Channel. Its plan was to escort a Spanish army from the Netherlands across to England. By early August the Armada had been driven past into the North Sea, but no one in England knew whether it would return, and an invasion from Flanders was still feared.

English troops were gathered at Tilbury, on the Thames east of London. Against the advice of those worried for her safety, Queen Elizabeth I went there and rode among the soldiers.

The text of her speech that has come down to us was recorded by Leonel Sharp, a chaplain who was present, in a letter published decades later. In it she says that she has been warned to beware of armed crowds for fear of treachery, but that she does not desire to live distrusting her faithful people. She has come, she says, resolved to live or die among them. Then the famous words: "I know I have the body of a weak and feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king, and of a king of England too."

The invasion never came, and the speech became part of England's memory of the Armada.
lesson: Words carry weight when you stand where the danger is. Showing up in person tells people you share their risk.
people: Elizabeth I, Leonel Sharp
source: Leonel Sharp's letter to the Duke of Buckingham, published in Cabala (1654)
caveat: The text survives only through Sharp's later version, so the exact wording is uncertain.

title: Hideyoshi Orders His Tea Master to Die
text:
Sen no Rikyu was the most influential tea master in sixteenth-century Japan. He shaped the wabi style of the tea ceremony: small rustic rooms, plain rough bowls, and an aesthetic of quiet simplicity. Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the warlord who unified Japan, made him his chief tea master and a trusted confidant. Hideyoshi also had a portable tea room covered in gold, the opposite of everything Rikyu's taste stood for.

In early 1591 Hideyoshi suddenly turned against him. One charge was that Rikyu had placed a wooden statue of himself in the upper story of the gate he had paid to restore at the Daitokuji temple in Kyoto, so that anyone entering, including Hideyoshi, passed beneath his feet. Another was that he had sold tea utensils at inflated prices. Hideyoshi exiled him to Sakai, then called him back to Kyoto and ordered him to commit seppuku. The statue was taken down and displayed at a place of execution.

Rikyu died in the spring of 1591, at about sixty-nine. Hideyoshi later is said to have regretted it, and Rikyu's descendants founded the tea schools that still exist today.
lesson: A leader who cannot tolerate an independent voice near him may destroy the very person whose judgment he most needed.
people: Sen no Rikyu, Toyotomi Hideyoshi
source: Contemporary diaries and letters; later Japanese histories of the tea ceremony
caveat: Hideyoshi's real reasons are unknown; historians propose political rivalry, aesthetic conflict and court intrigue.

title: The Pilgrims of the Journey to the West
text:
In Wu Cheng'en's great novel, the monk Tang Sanzang was sent from China to India to bring back Buddhist scriptures. He was gentle, devout and almost helpless, so the bodhisattva Guanyin gave him companions, each a former troublemaker working off a punishment.

Sun Wukong, the Monkey King, was brilliant and brave, able to cover a vast distance in one somersault and change into seventy-two forms, but he was also arrogant and quick to kill. Zhu Bajie, the Pig, was strong but greedy, lazy and always ready to give up and go home. Sha Wujing, the quiet former river monster, carried the luggage and kept the peace. A dragon prince, turned into a white horse, carried the monk.

They quarreled constantly. Bajie stirred up the master against Monkey. Once Tang Sanzang, unable to see through a shapeshifting demon, sent Monkey away in anger, and the group nearly came to ruin until he was brought back. Yet each member was needed. Monkey saw through disguises, Bajie fought in the water, Sha held the group together, and the monk's steadiness gave them a purpose.

After eighty-one ordeals they reached the West, received the scriptures and carried them home.
lesson: A team does not need members who get along easily. It needs members whose different strengths fit the task, and a shared purpose strong enough to survive their quarrels.
people: Tang Sanzang, Sun Wukong, Zhu Bajie, Sha Wujing
source: Wu Cheng'en (attributed), Journey to the West (Xiyou ji)

title: Matteo Ricci Writes On Friendship
text:
The Italian Jesuit Matteo Ricci reached China in 1582 and spent years in the south learning the language and the classics. He found that Chinese scholars valued learning and good conduct above everything, and that friendship between scholars was one of the five basic human relationships in Confucian thought. In 1595 he gave up the robes of a Buddhist monk he had first worn and dressed as a Confucian scholar instead.

That year, in the city of Nanchang, Ricci was invited to the court of a local prince of the imperial family, who asked him what people in the West thought about friendship. In answer Ricci wrote a little book in Chinese, the Jiaoyou lun, or Treatise on Friendship. It collected about a hundred short sayings on friendship drawn from Greek and Roman writers and Christian authors, rendered in polished Chinese. It opened with the idea that a friend is not another but half of oneself, a second self.

The book was copied and printed again and again, and won Ricci admiration among Chinese literati. It opened doors for him that preaching could not have opened. Ricci eventually reached Beijing, where he lived until his death in 1610.
lesson: To earn trust in another culture or group, start from what they already value and show that you share it. Common ground opens doors that argument cannot.
people: Matteo Ricci
source: Matteo Ricci, Jiaoyou lun (Treatise on Friendship, 1595); Timothy Billings, trans., On Friendship: One Hundred Maxims for a Chinese Prince (2009)

title: Romeo and Juliet
text:
In Verona, two noble families, the Montagues and the Capulets, had been feuding for so long that no one remembered how it started. Their servants brawled in the streets, and the Prince warned that the next fight would cost lives.

Romeo, a young Montague, slipped into a Capulet party and fell in love with Juliet, the Capulets' thirteen-year-old daughter. Only afterward did each learn the other's name. That night, under her balcony, they declared their love, and the next day Friar Laurence married them in secret, hoping the match might end the feud.

Within hours Juliet's cousin Tybalt killed Romeo's friend Mercutio, and Romeo, enraged, killed Tybalt. He was banished. Juliet's parents, knowing nothing of the marriage, ordered her to marry Count Paris at once and threatened to throw her out if she refused.

The friar gave Juliet a potion that would make her seem dead for two days, and sent word to Romeo. The message never reached him. Hearing only that Juliet was dead, Romeo bought poison, went to her tomb and drank it beside her. Juliet woke, found him dead, and stabbed herself with his dagger.

Over the bodies of their children, the two fathers finally clasped hands and ended the feud.
lesson: Quarrels between families do not stay with the people who start them. Children inherit them and pay for them. End the feud before they must.
people: Romeo, Juliet, the Montagues and Capulets, Friar Laurence, Tybalt
location: Verona, Italy (play written in London, England)
source: William Shakespeare, Romeo and Juliet

title: Portia and the Pound of Flesh
text:
To help his friend Bassanio, the Venetian merchant Antonio borrowed three thousand ducats from the moneylender Shylock, who hated him. The terms were strange: if the money was not repaid on time, Shylock could cut a pound of flesh from Antonio's body. Antonio's ships were lost at sea, he could not pay, and Shylock took him to court before the Duke of Venice to claim his bond.

Bassanio's new wife, Portia, came to the court disguised as a young doctor of law. She first appealed to Shylock to show mercy. He refused. Bassanio offered to repay the money many times over. Shylock refused that too. He wanted only what the contract gave him. Portia agreed that the bond was valid and that Venetian law could not set it aside. Shylock sharpened his knife.

Then Portia stopped him. The bond, she said, gave him a pound of flesh, but not a single drop of blood. If he shed even one drop of a Christian's blood in taking it, his lands and goods would be confiscated. And he must cut exactly one pound, no more and no less, or he would die.

Shylock, defeated, asked for his money instead and was refused. Portia then turned the law against him further, and he left the court stripped of his fortune and forced to convert. Antonio was saved.
lesson: If the other side insists on the letter of an agreement, read the letter more carefully than they did. Precise terms cut both ways.
people: Portia, Shylock, Antonio, Bassanio, the Duke of Venice
source: William Shakespeare, The Merchant of Venice, Act 4, Scene 1
caveat: The play's treatment of Shylock reflects the antisemitism of its time and is read critically today.

title: "I Still Have Twelve Ships"
text:
In 1597 Japan invaded Korea for the second time. The Korean admiral Yi Sun-sin, who had defeated the Japanese at sea during the first invasion, had been falsely accused, arrested, tortured and demoted to the rank of a common soldier. His replacement, Won Gyun, led the Korean fleet to disaster at Chilcheollyang in the summer of 1597. Almost the entire fleet was destroyed.

The court hastily restored Yi to command. He found only about a dozen warships left. King Seonjo, judging the navy finished, suggested that Yi abandon the sea and join the land forces. Yi replied in a report to the court that he still had twelve ships, and that as long as he lived, the enemy would not dare to look down on Korea's navy.

In October 1597, with thirteen ships, he met a Japanese fleet of more than a hundred and thirty warships at the Myeongnyang Strait, a narrow channel with violent tidal currents. He chose the place because the strait limited how many enemy ships could engage at once. Yi's flagship held the line almost alone at first. By the end of the day dozens of Japanese ships had been sunk or damaged, and Yi had lost none.
lesson: Do not let what you have lost define you. Count what you still have, choose ground where it counts, and commit.
people: Yi Sun-sin, King Seonjo
location: Myeongnyang Strait, South Jeolla (modern South Korea)
source: Yi Sun-sin, War Diary (Nanjung Ilgi); Annals of the Joseon Dynasty; Yi Bun, Biography of Yi Sun-sin
caveat: Japanese losses at Myeongnyang are uncertain, and Korean and Japanese sources give different figures.

title: We Few, We Happy Few
text:
In Shakespeare's play, King Henry V of England had invaded France, and by the morning of the battle of Agincourt in 1415 his army was sick, hungry and badly outnumbered by the French. In the English camp, the Earl of Westmoreland wished aloud that they had even ten thousand more of the men sitting idle back in England.

The king overheard and disagreed. If they were going to die, he said, they were enough for their country to lose. If they were going to live, the fewer men, the greater each one's share of honor. He did not wish for one man more. In fact, he ordered that any soldier who had no stomach for the fight should be allowed to leave, with a passport and money for his journey. He did not want to die in the company of anyone who feared to die alongside him.

That day, he reminded them, was the feast of Saint Crispin. Those who fought and came home safe would stand tall whenever the day was named, show their scars to their neighbors, and be remembered as long as the story was told. "We few, we happy few, we band of brothers," he said, for whoever shed his blood with him that day would be his brother, however humble his birth.

The English army went into battle, and in the play it won.
lesson: Shared hardship can turn a group into a band of brothers when the leader stands with them as an equal. Give people a reason to be proud of being few rather than wishing for more.
people: King Henry V, the Earl of Westmoreland, the English army
location: London, England (play set at Agincourt, France)
source: William Shakespeare, Henry V, Act 4, Scene 3
caveat: The speech is Shakespeare's invention, not a record of what Henry said at the real battle.

title: King Henry Walks Among His Soldiers
text:
In Shakespeare's Henry V, the English army lies outnumbered and exhausted on the night before the battle of Agincourt. The king borrows a cloak from old Sir Thomas Erpingham and walks through the camp in disguise.

He falls into conversation with three common soldiers, John Bates, Alexander Court and Michael Williams. Bates says the king may be brave, but he would rather be up to his neck in the Thames than here. Henry, posing as an ordinary soldier, says he would die happily in the king's company, since his cause is just. Williams answers that this is more than they know. And if the cause is not good, the king himself has a heavy reckoning to make, when all the legs and arms and heads chopped off in battle join together at the last day and cry out.

Henry argues that each soldier's soul is his own, and the king is not responsible for every man's sins. But the words strike home. Henry and Williams quarrel and exchange gloves, promising to settle it after the battle.

Alone, Henry speaks of the burden of kingship: everything is laid on the king. What does he have that ordinary men lack, except ceremony? He envies the peasant who sleeps soundly. After the victory, he reveals himself to Williams and has his glove filled with crowns.
lesson: Listening to the people you lead, without your title in the room, tells you what reports never will. Take what you hear seriously, including the hard part about your responsibility for them.
people: Henry V, Michael Williams, John Bates, Alexander Court, Sir Thomas Erpingham
source: William Shakespeare, Henry V, Act 4, Scene 1 and Scene 8

title: Antony's Funeral Speech
text:
After Caesar was assassinated, Brutus spoke first to the Roman crowd. He explained that he had loved Caesar, but loved Rome more, and had killed him because he was ambitious. The crowd cheered Brutus. He then allowed Mark Antony to speak at the funeral, on condition that Antony not blame the conspirators.

Antony began by agreeing. He had come, he said, to bury Caesar, not to praise him. Brutus said Caesar was ambitious, and Brutus was an honorable man. Then he reminded them of things they knew: Caesar had filled Rome's treasury with ransoms, had wept when the poor cried, and had three times refused a crown. Each time, he repeated that Brutus was an honorable man, until the words began to sound like an accusation.

He mentioned Caesar's will, then said he should not read it, because it would inflame them. The crowd demanded it. Instead he came down among them, held up Caesar's bloodied cloak, and showed them the tears made by each dagger, including the one by Brutus, whom Caesar had loved. Then he uncovered the body.

Only then did he read the will, which left money to every citizen and Caesar's gardens to the public. The crowd broke into a riot, set out to burn the conspirators' houses, and Brutus and Cassius fled the city.
lesson: People are moved more by what they work out for themselves than by what they are told. Concede the surface, then let facts and curiosity carry them to your conclusion.
people: Mark Antony, Brutus, the Roman crowd
source: William Shakespeare, Julius Caesar, Act 3, Scene 2

title: The Turncoat at Sekigahara
text:
On 21 October 1600 the two great coalitions of Japan met in a valley at Sekigahara. The Eastern Army was led by Tokugawa Ieyasu. The Western Army was organized by Ishida Mitsunari in the name of the young heir of the late ruler Toyotomi Hideyoshi. On paper the Western side held strong positions on the hills around the valley.

One of those hills, Mount Matsuo, was held by Kobayakawa Hideaki, a young lord with a large force who was related by adoption to the Toyotomi. But Ieyasu had been in secret contact with him for weeks, and Hideaki had agreed to change sides. Ieyasu had made similar arrangements with other Western commanders.

When the battle began in the morning fog, Hideaki did not move. For hours the fighting was hard and indecisive while he watched from his hill. According to a well-known tradition, Ieyasu, angry and impatient, had his troops fire at Mount Matsuo to force a decision. Around midday Hideaki finally came down, not against Ieyasu but against the flank of the Western commander Otani Yoshitsugu. Other Western units then turned as well.

The Western Army collapsed within hours. Ishida Mitsunari was captured and executed. In 1603 Ieyasu became shogun, founding a dynasty that ruled Japan for over 250 years. The battle was won before it began, in the negotiations of the previous weeks.
lesson: Many contests are decided before they start, by the commitments secured in advance. Know who is really on your side, and work on the waverers early.
people: Tokugawa Ieyasu, Kobayakawa Hideaki, Ishida Mitsunari, Otani Yoshitsugu
source: Japanese chronicles of the battle; Anthony J. Bryant, Sekigahara 1600 (1995)
caveat: The story that Ieyasu fired on Kobayakawa's position to force his hand is questioned by some modern historians.

title: Prince Salim Rebels Against Akbar
text:
The Mughal emperor Akbar long had no surviving son. According to tradition, he visited the Sufi saint Salim Chishti at Sikri to ask for his blessing, and when a son was born in 1569, he named him Salim after the saint and later built a new capital, Fatehpur Sikri, at the saint's village.

Salim was raised as heir, but as he grew older, his father lived on and showed no sign of handing over power. Salim drank heavily and grew impatient. In 1600, while Akbar was campaigning in the Deccan, Salim seized the fort at Allahabad and set up his own court there, behaving as an independent king.

The worst blow came in 1602. Akbar's closest friend and adviser, the historian Abul Fazl, was returning to court when he was ambushed and killed by a chieftain acting on Salim's orders. Akbar was devastated. Salim himself admitted the deed years later in his memoirs, saying he believed Abul Fazl was turning his father against him.

The women of the family worked to heal the breach. Akbar's senior wife, Salima Sultan Begum, went to Allahabad and brought Salim back to court, and father and son were reconciled, though further quarrels followed. When Akbar lay dying at Agra in October 1605, he recognized Salim as his heir. Salim took the throne as Jahangir.
lesson: A child's impatience for power can wound a parent deeply, yet families can still find their way back. Peacemakers within a family are often its unsung heroes.
people: Akbar, Salim (Jahangir), Abul Fazl, Salima Sultan Begum
source: Jahangir, Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri (Memoirs of Jahangir), trans. Rogers and Beveridge; Abul Fazl, Akbarnama

title: Othello and Iago
text:
Othello, a Moorish general in the service of Venice, had secretly married Desdemona, a senator's daughter, who loved him for the dangers he had passed. His ensign Iago, resentful that Othello had promoted Michael Cassio over him, set out to destroy them all, while appearing to be the most honest man in the army.

Iago worked by suggestion. He got Cassio drunk and disgraced, then urged him to ask Desdemona to plead for him. Meanwhile he dropped hints to Othello: how close Cassio and Desdemona seemed, how she had deceived her own father. He never accused outright; he let Othello's imagination do the work. When Desdemona innocently pleaded for Cassio, every word looked like proof.

Then Iago's wife Emilia found a handkerchief Othello had given Desdemona as his first gift, and gave it to her husband. Iago planted it in Cassio's room and let Othello see Cassio with it. Othello, consumed by jealousy, no longer trusted his wife's denials, only Iago's lies.

That night Othello smothered Desdemona in her bed. Emilia, discovering the murder, revealed the truth about the handkerchief, and Iago killed her. Othello understood too late that he had believed a liar over the woman who loved him. He called himself one who loved not wisely but too well, and stabbed himself, while Iago was led away to torture, refusing to say another word.
lesson: Be careful whose suggestions you let shape your view of the people closest to you. Before acting on suspicion, ask them directly.
people: Othello, Iago, Desdemona, Cassio, Emilia
source: William Shakespeare, Othello

title: Don Quixote and the Windmills
text:
Don Quixote, a country gentleman who had read so many tales of chivalry that he believed himself a knight errant, rode out across the plains of La Mancha with his squire, Sancho Panza. As they went, they came in sight of thirty or forty windmills standing on the plain.

Don Quixote's eyes lit up. Fortune, he declared, was guiding them better than they could have wished. There before them were monstrous giants, and he meant to fight them all and take their spoils. Defeating them would be a service to God.

Sancho asked what giants he meant. Those over there, said the knight, with the long arms. Sancho pointed out that they were windmills, and what looked like arms were their sails, which turned in the wind and drove the millstones.

Don Quixote replied that Sancho clearly knew nothing of adventures, and if he was afraid, he could stand aside and pray. Then he spurred his horse, Rocinante, and charged at the nearest windmill, lance leveled. Just then the wind rose and the sails began to turn. His lance pierced a sail, which swung up and shattered it, and flung horse and rider rolling across the field.

Sancho found him badly bruised. Even then, Don Quixote insisted that an enchanter had turned the giants into windmills to rob him of his victory.
lesson: Check that the enemy you are charging is real. If everyone around you sees a windmill, at least pause before you lower your lance.
people: Don Quixote, Sancho Panza
source: Miguel de Cervantes, Don Quixote, Part I, Chapter 8

title: King Lear Divides His Kingdom
text:
Lear, the aging king of Britain, decided to divide his kingdom among his three daughters and retire. But first he wanted a public show. Each daughter was to declare how much she loved him, and the one who loved him most would receive the largest share.

Goneril, the eldest, said she loved him more than eyesight, space or liberty. Regan claimed she loved him even more. Lear rewarded both. Then he turned to his youngest and favorite, Cordelia. Asked what she could say to win a richer third, she answered, "Nothing, my lord." She would not flatter. She loved him, she said, as a daughter should, no more and no less, and when she married, half her love would go to her husband.

Furious, Lear disowned her and split her share between her sisters. When the Earl of Kent protested, Lear banished him too. Cordelia left to marry the King of France, who took her without a dowry.

Once they held the kingdom, Goneril and Regan stripped their father of his knights, his dignity and his home, and shut the door on him in a storm. Lear, raving, wandered the heath half mad. Cordelia came back with an army to rescue him, and they were reconciled in tears. But her army was defeated. Cordelia was hanged in prison, and Lear died over her body.
lesson: Do not mistake flattery for love. The person who tells you an uncomfortable truth may be the one who cares for you most.
people: Lear, Goneril, Regan, Cordelia, the Earl of Kent
location: Ancient Britain (play written in London, England)
