source: William Shakespeare, King Lear

title: Macbeth's Ambition
text:
Returning from victory in battle, the Scottish general Macbeth and his friend Banquo meet three witches. They hail Macbeth as the future king, and tell Banquo that his descendants will be kings. Macbeth writes to his wife, and Lady Macbeth, fearing he is too full of the milk of human kindness, pushes him to act. When King Duncan stays at their castle, Macbeth murders him in his sleep and takes the crown.

The first crime does not make him safe. It makes him afraid. Remembering the prophecy for Banquo, he hires murderers to kill his friend and his son Fleance. Banquo dies, but Fleance escapes, and at a banquet Macbeth sees Banquo's ghost in his own seat. When the thane Macduff flees to England, Macbeth has his wife and children slaughtered.

Scotland turns against him. Lady Macbeth, tormented, walks in her sleep trying to wash invisible blood from her hands, and dies. Macbeth, hollowed out, says that life is a tale told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, signifying nothing. The witches had promised that no man born of woman could harm him, but Macduff, who was cut from his mother's womb, meets him in battle and kills him. Duncan's son Malcolm becomes king.
lesson: A position won by wrongdoing has to be protected by more of it, and each step makes the next one easier. The safest moment to stop is before the first compromise.
people: Macbeth, Lady Macbeth, Banquo, Duncan, Macduff
source: William Shakespeare, Macbeth

title: The King James Bible Committees
text:
In January 1604 King James I met church leaders at Hampton Court Palace. The Puritan scholar John Rainolds suggested a new English translation of the Bible, and the king, who disliked the popular Geneva Bible and its notes, agreed.

About fifty scholars were divided into six companies, two each at Westminster, Oxford and Cambridge, and each company was given a section of the Bible. Archbishop Richard Bancroft issued a set of rules. The translators were to follow the existing Bishops' Bible where it was accurate, keep familiar church words, and add no marginal notes except to explain Hebrew or Greek.

The rules also set out a system of review. Each member of a company translated the same chapters on his own. The company then met to compare versions and agree on one. Each finished book was sent to the other companies for comment, and disagreements were settled at a general meeting. In 1610 a small committee met in London to review the whole text.

The translators borrowed heavily from earlier versions, above all William Tyndale's. Their preface, written by Miles Smith, said they had not set out to make a new translation, but to make a good one better. The King James Version appeared in 1611. Its language, much of it inherited from Tyndale and polished by the committees, shaped English prose for centuries.
lesson: A committee can produce excellent work when it has clear rules, independent drafts and real review. Structure the process so that every draft gets tested by fresh eyes.
people: King James I, John Rainolds, Richard Bancroft, Lancelot Andrewes, Miles Smith
location: Westminster, Oxford and Cambridge, England, United Kingdom
source: 'The Translators to the Reader', preface to the King James Bible (1611); Adam Nicolson, Power and Glory (2003)

title: Sancho Panza Governs Barataria
text:
In the second part of Don Quixote, a duke and duchess entertain themselves by making Sancho Panza, Don Quixote's simple, illiterate squire, governor of an "island" called Barataria, really a town on their estate. They expect him to make a fool of himself.

He surprises everyone. In one case, an old man swore he had repaid a debt of ten gold crowns, handing his walking stick to the lender to hold while he took the oath. Sancho noticed the stick, had it broken open, and found the ten crowns inside. In another, a woman accused a herdsman of assault and was awarded his purse, and when he tried to take it back from her she fought him off with such strength that Sancho concluded she could easily have defended herself the first time, and gave the purse back. He issued sensible ordinances on prices, wine and beggars.

The pranks did not stop. A court doctor took away every dish before Sancho could eat it, and on the seventh night of his rule he was woken by a staged invasion, strapped between two shields and trampled. The next morning he went to the stable, embraced his donkey, and resigned. He had come into the governorship without a penny, he said, and he was leaving without one, which few governors could say.
lesson: Good judgment often comes from paying attention, common sense and honesty more than from rank or education. And knowing when to walk away from a position is part of handling it well.
people: Sancho Panza, the Duke and Duchess, Doctor Pedro Recio
source: Miguel de Cervantes, Don Quixote, Part II, Chapters 45 to 53

title: Kepler Defends His Mother Against Witchcraft
text:
In 1615, in the small town of Leonberg in Wurttemberg, a neighbor named Ursula Reinbold accused Katharina Kepler, a widow of about seventy, of poisoning her with a potion. Katharina was known as a sharp-tongued woman who made herbal remedies. Accusations multiplied, and she was formally charged with witchcraft. In that region and era, such charges could end in torture and burning.

Her son was Johannes Kepler, imperial mathematician, the astronomer who had discovered that the planets move in ellipses. He was then living in Linz, in Austria, working on his astronomy. He put much of it aside to defend her. He studied the law, wrote long legal arguments refuting each accusation, and traveled to Wurttemberg to be at her side.

In August 1620 Katharina was arrested and held in chains for about fourteen months. In September 1621 the court ordered her to be taken to the torture chamber, shown the instruments and threatened with their use, in the hope that she would confess. She refused, saying they could do what they liked but she had nothing to confess. In October 1621, thanks largely to her son's defense, she was released.

Katharina died about six months later. Kepler returned to his work and in 1627 published the Rudolphine Tables, the most accurate planetary tables of his time.
lesson: Some causes are worth more than our career, and a parent in danger is one of them. Standing by family when the whole town turns against them takes real courage.
people: Johannes Kepler, Katharina Kepler, Ursula Reinbold
source: Trial records (Kepler's defense briefs); Ulinka Rublack, The Astronomer and the Witch (2015)

title: The Mayflower Compact
text:
In November 1620, after more than two months at sea, the Mayflower reached Cape Cod. Its passengers held a patent to settle in the territory of the Virginia Company, far to the south, but bad weather and dangerous shoals forced them to stay where they were. That raised a problem. Outside the area of their patent, no one had legal authority over the colony.

The passengers were a mixed group: religious Separatists from England and the Netherlands, and others recruited for the venture whom the Separatists called "strangers." William Bradford, later the colony's governor, wrote in Of Plymouth Plantation that some of the strangers made discontented and mutinous speeches, saying that once ashore they would use their own liberty, since no one had power to command them.

Before anyone landed, on 11 November by the calendar they used, forty-one men signed a short agreement. They combined themselves, it said, into a "civil body politic," and promised to make and obey just and equal laws for the general good of the colony. They then chose John Carver as their governor.

The first winter was brutal, and about half the colonists died. But the colony held together. The compact remained the basis of Plymouth's government, and later generations saw it as an early example of people agreeing to govern themselves by consent.
lesson: A group heading into uncertainty should agree on its rules before trouble starts. A simple shared commitment can keep a mixed team from splitting apart.
people: William Bradford, John Carver, Mayflower passengers
source: The Mayflower Compact (1620); William Bradford, Of Plymouth Plantation, book 2

title: Squanto Teaches the Pilgrims to Plant
text:
Tisquantum, known to the English as Squanto, came from the Patuxet people on the coast of what is now Massachusetts. In 1614 an English captain, Thomas Hunt, kidnapped him and other men and sold them as slaves in Spain. Squanto escaped to England, learned English, and finally returned home in 1619 only to find his whole village dead from an epidemic.

In the winter of 1620 to 1621 the Pilgrims settled on that same empty site and named it Plymouth. About half of them died before spring. In March 1621 a Native man named Samoset walked into the settlement, and soon after brought Squanto, who could speak to them in their own language.

William Bradford, the colony's governor, describes what followed in Of Plymouth Plantation. Squanto helped arrange a peace treaty with Massasoit, leader of the Wampanoag. He showed the colonists how to plant corn with fish to fertilize it, where to catch fish and how to find other food, and he guided and interpreted for them. Bradford called him a special instrument sent by God for their good. Squanto's own position was complicated, and he also used his role to build influence for himself. He died of a fever in 1622.
lesson: Help can come from the person you least expect, even one with every reason to resent you. Be open to it, and remember who carried you through your first hard season.
people: Tisquantum (Squanto), Massasoit, William Bradford, Samoset
source: William Bradford, Of Plymouth Plantation, Book 2, years 1621 and 1622

title: Nzinga Refuses to Sit on the Floor
text:
In 1622 the kingdom of Ndongo, in what is now Angola, was being ravaged by Portuguese troops and their allies from the colony at Luanda. Its king, Ngola Mbandi, sent his sister Nzinga to Luanda to negotiate peace with the new Portuguese governor, Joao Correia de Sousa.

The Capuchin missionary Antonio Cavazzi, who later knew Nzinga, recorded what tradition said happened at the audience. When Nzinga entered, she found that the governor sat on a chair, while for her there was only a mat or cushion on the floor, the position of a subject. Nzinga did not protest. She signaled to one of her attendants, who knelt on all fours, and Nzinga sat on the woman's back for the whole meeting, level with the governor.

She then negotiated as an equal. She argued that Ndongo was a sovereign kingdom, not a conquered people, and that an ally was worth more to Portugal than a subject. She reached a peace agreement that included the removal of a Portuguese fort built on Ndongo land. While in Luanda she was baptized, taking the name Ana de Sousa. The Portuguese did not keep the treaty, but Nzinga went on to rule Ndongo and Matamba and resisted Portugal for decades.
lesson: The setting of a negotiation often defines the roles before anyone speaks. Refuse a position that makes you smaller, calmly, before the talking starts.
people: Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba, Joao Correia de Sousa, Ngola Mbandi
source: Giovanni Antonio Cavazzi da Montecuccolo, Istorica descrizione de' tre regni Congo, Matamba et Angola (1687); Linda Heywood, Njinga of Angola (2017)
caveat: The chair episode is known from later accounts and may have been embellished.

title: The Vasa Sinks on Its Maiden Voyage
text:
In the 1620s King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden, at war in the Baltic, ordered a great new warship for his navy. The Vasa was built in Stockholm under the Dutch shipwright Henrik Hybertsson, who died before it was finished. The king followed the work closely and approved its size and armament. It was given two full gun decks with heavy cannon, an unusual and ambitious design, and was richly decorated with carved sculptures.

Before it sailed, Admiral Klas Fleming had a stability test carried out: thirty men ran back and forth across the deck together. After three runs the ship was rolling so heavily that the test was stopped. Nobody, it seems, knew how to fix the problem, and the king, away at war, was pressing for the ship to be ready. The test results did not stop the launch.

On 10 August 1628 the Vasa set sail from Stockholm harbor in front of crowds. After sailing about 1,300 meters, a gust of wind heeled it over. Water poured in through the open lower gunports, and the ship sank in minutes. Some thirty people died.

An inquiry was held. The captain, the crew and the builders were questioned, and each testified that they had followed instructions. In the end no one was punished. In 1961 the remarkably preserved ship was raised, and it is now one of Sweden's most visited museums.
lesson: When everyone sees a problem but no one feels able to stop the project, the whole team fails together. Make it safe to halt a launch when a test goes wrong.
people: Gustavus Adolphus, Henrik Hybertsson, Klas Fleming
source: Records of the 1628 inquiry; Vasa Museum research publications, e.g. Fred Hocker, Vasa (2011)

title: Shah Jahan Builds a Tomb for Mumtaz Mahal
text:
Arjumand Banu Begum married Prince Khurram, the future Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, in 1612. When he took the throne in 1628, she received the title Mumtaz Mahal, "chosen one of the palace." She was his constant companion and adviser, and traveled with him even on military campaigns, giving birth to fourteen children.

In 1631 she was with him on a campaign in the Deccan. In June, at Burhanpur, she gave birth to their fourteenth child, a daughter, and died soon afterwards. The court histories describe the emperor's grief as overwhelming: he went into mourning, gave up music and fine clothes for a time, and the whole court mourned with him.

Shah Jahan resolved to build her a tomb unlike any other. Her body was moved to Agra, and in the following years a white marble mausoleum rose on the bank of the Yamuna river, with gardens, a mosque and a guest house. Thousands of artisans and laborers worked on it, using marble from Makrana and stones from across Asia. The main tomb was finished around 1643 and the whole complex about ten years later.

Shah Jahan's last years were sad. In 1658 his son Aurangzeb seized the throne and confined him in the Agra fort, from which he could see the Taj Mahal across the river. When he died in 1666 he was buried beside her.
lesson: Grief for someone we love can be turned into something that lasts and gives beauty to others. Love is often measured best by what we build in its memory.
people: Shah Jahan, Mumtaz Mahal
source: Abdul Hamid Lahori, Padshahnama; Ebba Koch, The Complete Taj Mahal (2006)

title: Galileo Puts the Pope's Words in a Fool's Mouth
text:
Cardinal Maffeo Barberini was an admirer of Galileo Galilei and once wrote a Latin poem in his praise. In 1623 Barberini became Pope Urban VIII. Galileo visited Rome and came away believing he could write about the Copernican idea that the Earth moves around the Sun, as long as he treated it as a hypothesis and gave the opposing view a fair hearing. The Pope asked that the book include one of his own favorite arguments: that God, being all powerful, could produce the same effects in ways human reason cannot discover.

The Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems appeared in 1632. It was written as a conversation among three characters. The defender of the old Earth centered view was named Simplicio, and he came off badly throughout. At the very end of the book, the Pope's argument was given to Simplicio.

Urban VIII's enemies were quick to say he had been mocked, and the Pope felt betrayed. He let the Inquisition take up the case. In 1633 Galileo was tried, forced to abjure, and sentenced to house arrest, which lasted until his death in 1642.
lesson: Never ridicule the person whose support you depend on, even indirectly. A patron who feels mocked can become a far more dangerous opponent than one who simply disagreed.
people: Galileo Galilei, Pope Urban VIII
source: Galileo Galilei, Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (1632); trial documents in Maurice A. Finocchiaro, The Galileo Affair (1989)
caveat: Historians debate how much the Simplicio passage itself, as opposed to Church politics and the Thirty Years War, drove Urban's decision.

title: Galileo and His Daughter Maria Celeste
text:
Galileo Galilei never married, but he had three children with Marina Gamba. His two daughters, being illegitimate, had little chance of a good marriage, and when they were young girls he placed them in the convent of San Matteo at Arcetri, near Florence. The elder, Virginia, took the name Suor Maria Celeste.

She was intelligent, devoted and practical. From 1623 she wrote to her father regularly, and 124 of her letters survive, though his replies are lost. She made him candied fruit and medicines, mended and washed his collars, and worried about his health. He sent the poor convent food and wine and helped it with money and favors. In 1631 he rented a villa near the convent to be close to her.

In 1633 Galileo was tried in Rome by the Inquisition for his support of the idea that the earth moves around the sun. He was forced to recant and was sentenced to house arrest, with the penance of reciting the seven penitential psalms every week for three years. Maria Celeste wrote to him with comfort and news, and obtained permission to say the psalms for him herself.

In December 1633 he was allowed to return to his villa at Arcetri. They had only a few months together. In April 1634 she fell ill and died, at thirty-three. Galileo wrote to a friend of his immense sadness and that he felt her continually calling him.
lesson: A child's love can sustain a parent through disgrace when the world turns away. The small, practical care we give each other often matters most.
people: Galileo Galilei, Maria Celeste (Virginia Galilei)
source: Letters of Suor Maria Celeste to Galileo; Dava Sobel, Galileo's Daughter (1999)

title: The Shogun's System of Alternate Attendance
text:
After the Tokugawa won control of Japan in the early 1600s, the shoguns faced a basic problem: around two hundred and fifty regional lords, the daimyo, still had their own lands, revenues and samurai. Several had fought against the Tokugawa only a generation before.

In 1635 the third shogun, Tokugawa Iemitsu, revised the Laws for the Military Houses and made a practice that had grown up informally into a formal obligation, known as sankin kotai, alternate attendance. Most daimyo had to spend every other year in the shogun's capital of Edo and the alternate year in their home domains. Their wives and heirs had to live in Edo permanently.

The system worked in several ways at once. The families in Edo were in effect hostages. The lords had to maintain grand residences in the capital, and travel to and from it in large processions that matched their rank, sometimes with thousands of retainers. These costs consumed a large share of each domain's income, leaving less money for armies or plots. And lords who spent half their lives at the shogun's court were drawn into its culture and rivalries rather than building power at home.

The system lasted more than two centuries, a period with no major civil war. It also had side effects nobody planned: roads, inns and trade along the highways flourished, and Edo grew into one of the largest cities in the world.
lesson: You can tame rivals not only with force but by shaping their obligations, so that their resources and attention are absorbed by the system itself.
people: Tokugawa Iemitsu, the daimyo
source: Buke Shohatto (Laws for the Military Houses), revision of 1635; Constantine Vaporis, Tour of Duty (2008)

title: Roger Williams Learns the Narragansett Language
text:
Roger Williams was an English minister in the Massachusetts Bay Colony who held views the colony's leaders found dangerous. He said the state should not punish religious belief, and he argued that the king's charter could not give the colonists land that belonged to the Native peoples: it had to be fairly bought from them. In late 1635 he was banished. In January 1636, warned he might be shipped back to England, he fled south through the winter snow.

Williams had spent years trading with the Wampanoag and Narragansett peoples and had learned their language. They sheltered him through that winter. In the spring the Narragansett sachems Canonicus and Miantonomi granted him land at the head of Narragansett Bay. He named the settlement Providence and opened it to people of any religion.

In 1643 Williams published A Key into the Language of America, a phrasebook and description of Narragansett life. In it he often praised their hospitality and courtesy, and he challenged the English to see that they were not superior. He served many times as a go-between between the colonists and the Native nations.
lesson: Learn the language of the people you live among and deal with them fairly. Trust is built by understanding and honest dealing, not by claims of superiority.
people: Roger Williams, Canonicus, Miantonomi
source: Roger Williams, A Key into the Language of America (1643); Williams's letters

title: The Dutch Tulip Mania
text:
In the 1630s tulips were a luxury in the Dutch Republic. Bulbs with streaked, flamed petals, caused, as later science showed, by a virus, were especially prized, and the rarest varieties, such as Semper Augustus, were valued at sums that could buy a house.

In the winter of 1636 to 1637 trading spread beyond wealthy collectors. In taverns in Haarlem and other towns, people bought and sold contracts for bulbs that were still in the ground and would not be delivered until summer. Prices for even ordinary varieties climbed rapidly within weeks, and many buyers planned to resell before delivery.

In early February 1637, at an auction in Haarlem, buyers failed to show up at the expected prices. Confidence collapsed within days across the country. Many contracts could not be honored, and the courts generally declined to enforce them. Towns eventually allowed buyers to settle by paying a small fraction of the agreed price.

For two centuries the episode served as a warning about speculative madness, especially after Charles Mackay's popular 1841 book. The historian Anne Goldgar, working through archives, found a more modest story: the trade involved a limited circle of merchants and artisans, and she found no wave of bankruptcies or ruin of the Dutch economy. The shock was real, but it was mainly a crisis of trust.
lesson: When prices rise because everyone expects to sell to someone else, the floor can vanish overnight. Also be wary of famous cautionary tales that grew in the retelling.
people: Dutch tulip traders, Anne Goldgar
location: Haarlem and other towns of the Dutch Republic (Netherlands)
source: Anne Goldgar, Tulipmania: Money, Honor, and Knowledge in the Dutch Golden Age (2007); contemporary pamphlets
caveat: The scale of the mania and its economic damage were greatly exaggerated in popular accounts such as Mackay's.

title: Jijabai Raises Shivaji
text:
Jijabai was the daughter of a Maratha noble, Lakhuji Jadhav, and the wife of Shahaji Bhosale, a commander who served the sultans of the Deccan. Shahaji spent most of his career far away in the south, in the service of Bijapur, and lived there with another wife. Jijabai raised their younger son, Shivaji, born around 1630, largely on her own.

In the late 1630s she settled with the boy in Pune, on Shahaji's estate. The town had been ravaged by war. With the help of the administrator Dadoji Konddev, she rebuilt it and had the land brought back under cultivation. Maratha tradition remembers her telling Shivaji the stories of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata, of heroes who fought injustice, and teaching him to see himself as the protector of his people and their faith rather than as the servant of foreign sultans.

Shivaji grew up among the hill people of the region and began, as a teenager, to seize forts in the Sahyadri hills. Over the following decades he built an independent Maratha kingdom. Jijabai remained his adviser, and the chronicles describe her as managing affairs when he was away or in danger.

In June 1674 Shivaji was crowned king at Raigad fort. Jijabai lived to see it. She died less than two weeks later.
lesson: The stories a parent tells and the values she lives by can shape a child's whole idea of who he is. Upbringing is the first school of leadership.
people: Jijabai, Shivaji, Shahaji Bhosale, Dadoji Konddev
source: Maratha chronicles (bakhars); Jadunath Sarkar, Shivaji and His Times (1919)
caveat: Much of what is told about Jijabai's teaching comes from later Maratha chronicles and tradition.

title: Shivaji Sends Back the Governor's Daughter-in-Law
text:
Shivaji Bhosale, founder of the Maratha state in western India, spent his early career seizing forts and towns from the Sultanate of Bijapur. Maratha tradition tells of an episode from around 1657, when his commander Abaji Sondev captured the wealthy town of Kalyan, near modern Mumbai.

Among the spoils, the story goes, the commander brought back the young and beautiful daughter-in-law of the defeated governor, and presented her to Shivaji as a prize, expecting to please him.

Shivaji was angry with his officer. In the best known version he looked at the frightened woman and said that if his own mother had been as beautiful as she was, he too would have been handsome. He addressed her as a mother, gave her clothes and gifts, and had her escorted back to her family with full honor. He also made it a rule that women captured in war were not to be harmed.

The story is told in Maharashtra to this day as an example of Shivaji's respect for women, including the women of his enemies, and it is often shown in plays and paintings.
lesson: How you treat the defenseless among your opponents reveals your real character. Power over someone is a test, not a prize.
people: Shivaji Bhosale, Abaji Sondev
source: Maratha tradition and later bakhar chronicles
caveat: The episode comes from later tradition and is not confirmed by contemporary records, though Shivaji's orders protecting women are mentioned by other sources.

title: The Sons of Shah Jahan Fight for the Throne
text:
In September 1657 the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan fell seriously ill in Delhi, and rumors spread that he had died. He had four sons, each governing a part of the empire. His eldest and favorite, Dara Shikoh, a liberal-minded scholar, was at court beside him. In Bengal, Shah Shuja proclaimed himself emperor. In Gujarat, Murad Bakhsh did the same. In the Deccan, Aurangzeb, a seasoned soldier, allied himself with Murad and marched north.

Shah Jahan recovered, but it was too late to stop the war. Aurangzeb and Murad defeated an imperial army in April 1658 and Dara himself at Samugarh in May. Aurangzeb then besieged his father in the Agra fort and cut off its water from the river, forcing him to surrender. Shah Jahan spent his last eight years as a prisoner in the fort, cared for by his daughter Jahanara.

Aurangzeb turned on his ally next. He had Murad arrested at a feast and later executed. Dara was defeated again, betrayed and brought to Delhi in 1659, where he was paraded through the streets on a filthy elephant before being put to death. The French physician Francois Bernier, who was in Delhi, described the crowds weeping. Shuja fled to Arakan and disappeared.

Aurangzeb ruled for nearly fifty years. The pattern did not end with him: his own eldest son, who had briefly gone over to Shuja, spent the rest of his life in prison.
lesson: When a family's inheritance is a prize to be seized, it can destroy the family itself. Clear succession and fairness among children prevent wars that love alone cannot.
people: Aurangzeb, Dara Shikoh, Shah Shuja, Murad Bakhsh, Shah Jahan, Jahanara
source: Francois Bernier, Travels in the Mogul Empire (1670); Jadunath Sarkar, History of Aurangzib, vols. 1 to 2

title: Shivaji's Escape From Agra
text:
In 1665, after a Mughal army under Jai Singh pressed him hard, the Maratha leader Shivaji agreed to the Treaty of Purandar, giving up many forts. Jai Singh then persuaded him to travel north to the court of the emperor Aurangzeb at Agra, with assurances of his safety.

Shivaji arrived with his young son Sambhaji in May 1666, around the time of the emperor's birthday celebrations. At the audience he was placed among nobles of lower rank than he expected. Accounts agree that he showed his anger openly in the hall. Soon he found himself under house arrest, his residence surrounded by guards, while the court debated what to do with him.

Shivaji did not try to force his way out. He sent most of his men home, which reduced suspicion, and declared himself ill. He began sending large baskets of sweets and food out of the house as gifts to holy men and nobles, and the guards grew used to checking them less and less. In August 1666, according to the traditional account, Shivaji and Sambhaji slipped out hidden in the baskets, while a servant lay in Shivaji's bed with only his hand and ring showing. The escape was discovered only hours later.

Shivaji traveled back to the Deccan in disguise, leaving Sambhaji hidden with trusted people at Mathura, and eventually reached his own lands safely. Within a few years he recovered the forts he had surrendered, and in 1674 he was crowned king.
lesson: When force is impossible, patience and routine can be your tools. Let watchers grow used to a pattern, then use it.
people: Shivaji, Sambhaji, Aurangzeb, Jai Singh
source: Jadunath Sarkar, Shivaji and His Times (1919); Mughal and Maratha chronicles
caveat: The details of the escape, including the baskets, come from traditional accounts and are not certain.

title: The Oak and the Reed
text:
On the bank of a river stood a great oak, with a trunk so thick that it had survived many winters. Near its roots grew a slender reed. The oak looked down on the reed with pity. The smallest breeze, it said, made the reed bow and tremble, while the oak stood firm and held its head high against the strongest winds.

The reed answered that it was not as frightened of the wind as the oak imagined. It bent, but it did not break.

That night a violent storm came down the valley. The wind roared and the rain lashed the trees. The reed bent low, almost to the water, and let the gusts pass over it. The oak refused to give way. It stood straight and resisted with all its strength.

The storm grew stronger still. At last, with a terrible crack, the oak was torn up by the roots and thrown down across the riverbank. When morning came and the wind died away, the reed straightened up again and stood exactly where it had stood before, beside the fallen giant.
lesson: Rigid strength can be the very thing that breaks you. In a crisis, the ability to bend, adapt and wait out the storm is often worth more than the will to stand firm.
people: An oak, a reed
source: Jean de La Fontaine, Fables, Book I, Fable 22 (Le Chene et le Roseau), after Aesop
caveat: In Aesop's older version the oak is uprooted first and then asks the reeds how they survived; the conversation before the storm is La Fontaine's.

title: The Dragon with Many Heads and the Dragon with Many Tails
text:
In La Fontaine's fable, an envoy of the Ottoman sultan was at the court of the Holy Roman Emperor, and the Germans there were boasting about their empire's power. Their emperor, one of them said, had so many princes and lords under him, each with an army of his own, that he could field more troops than any other ruler.

The envoy answered with a story. He had once seen, he said, a dragon with a hundred heads trying to pass through a hedge. Each head wanted to go its own way. One head pushed through here and another there, and the body was held back. The whole creature got stuck, and it could not get through at all.

Then, he said, he had seen another dragon, with only one head but a hundred tails. That head chose a gap in the hedge, went through, and the body and every one of the hundred tails followed easily behind it.

The envoy's point was clear. The Germans' empire was the first dragon. His own master's empire, with a single head to command it, was the second.
lesson: Many strong members do not make a strong team if each one wants to lead in a different direction. Agree on who decides, and a large group can move through a narrow gap.
people: An envoy of the sultan, German courtiers
location: France (story set at the imperial court)
source: Jean de La Fontaine, Fables, Book I, The Dragon with Many Heads and the Dragon with Many Tails, 1668

title: Mitsui's Cash and Fixed Prices
text:
In 1673 Mitsui Takatoshi, a merchant from Matsusaka, opened a kimono fabric shop called Echigoya in Edo, the city that is now Tokyo. The trade was dominated by established houses that served wealthy customers in a particular way. Clerks carried samples to clients' homes, prices were bargained case by case, and goods were sold on credit, with bills settled once or twice a year. The system was slow and costly, and the merchants built the risk of unpaid debts into their prices.

Takatoshi turned this around. Customers came to the shop, where prices were set and displayed, with no haggling and no credit: payment in cash on the spot. Because he was not carrying debts for months, he could charge less. He also sold cloth cut to whatever length a customer wanted, so people of modest means could buy what they needed rather than a whole bolt.

The established merchants were hostile and tried to obstruct him, but customers flocked to Echigoya. Its trade grew rapidly, and in the 1680s Takatoshi moved to a larger site and added a money exchange business that later served the shogunate. The shop became the ancestor of the Mitsukoshi department store, and the family business grew into the Mitsui group.
lesson: Look at the hidden costs and frictions everyone in your field accepts as normal. Removing them for the customer can be a more powerful advantage than a better product.
people: Mitsui Takatoshi
source: Mitsui corporate histories; Charles David Sheldon, The Rise of the Merchant Class in Tokugawa Japan (1958)
caveat: Sources differ on whether the cash and fixed price policy began at the opening in 1673 or was formalized a few years later.

title: The Bear and the Garden Lover
text:
A bear lived alone in the mountains, and after a while solitude began to depress him. Not far away lived an old man who loved his garden but was lonely too, since flowers make poor conversation. One morning the two met on a path. Nervous as he was, the old man invited the bear to his home, and soon they were fast friends.

They suited each other well. The bear said little and spent his days hunting, bringing game home for them both. His chief task, as he saw it, was to keep the flies off his friend while the old man slept.

One day, as the old man was sound asleep, a fly landed on the tip of his nose. The bear chased it away, but it came back. He chased it again, and again it landed. The bear grew angry. "I will get you this time," he thought. He picked up a heavy paving stone and hurled it with all his strength.

He killed the fly. He also crushed his friend's skull.

La Fontaine ends: nothing is as dangerous as an ignorant friend. A wise enemy would be better.
lesson: Good intentions are not enough; help must be fitted to the real need. Be wary of zealous helpers who lack judgment, and check that your own help does not do harm.
people: A bear, an old gardener
source: Jean de La Fontaine, Fables, Book VIII, Fable 10

title: The Coach and the Fly
text:
On a steep, sandy road, in the full heat of the sun, six strong horses were struggling to drag a heavy coach uphill. The passengers, a woman, a monk and some old men, had all climbed out to lighten the load. The horses were sweating and exhausted.

A fly arrived. It buzzed around the horses and stung one, then another, as though urging them on. It landed on the shaft, then on the coachman's nose. Whenever the coach moved forward a little, the fly took the credit. It zipped back and forth like a sergeant on a battlefield, and it complained loudly that it alone was doing everything, while the others were no help at all. The monk was saying his prayers, and the woman was singing. What a time to sing!

At last, after a great struggle, the horses reached the top of the hill. The fly settled down, satisfied. Now, it said, let us take a breath. I have worked so hard to get you all up here. So, horses, pay me for my trouble.

La Fontaine adds that there are people like this everywhere, who bustle around other people's work, make themselves seem indispensable, and are only a nuisance.
lesson: Busy noise near a task is not the same as doing it. Notice who is actually pulling the load, and be wary of the one who complains loudest and claims the credit.
people: A fly, six horses, a coachman, passengers
source: Jean de La Fontaine, Fables, Book VII, The Coach and the Fly (Le Coche et la Mouche), 1678

title: The Milkmaid and the Pot of Milk
text:
Perrette set off for the town market with a pot of milk balanced on her head, on a cushion. She had dressed lightly and worn flat shoes so she could walk fast, and as she walked, she counted up her future.

With the money for the milk, she would buy a hundred eggs. The eggs would hatch into chicks; with care, she could raise three broods. The fox would have to be clever indeed to leave her too few to buy a pig. A pig costs little to fatten, and she would sell it for good money. With that she would buy a cow and a calf, and she could already see the calf frisking among the flock.

At that thought Perrette gave a little jump of joy. The pot fell from her head, and the milk ran out onto the road. Goodbye calf, cow, pig and chicks. She went home to explain herself to her husband, at the risk of a beating.

La Fontaine adds that everyone builds castles in the air like this, the wise as well as the foolish. He admits that he does it himself, and is a great king in his dreams, until some accident brings him back to what he really is.
lesson: Plan for the future, but keep your eyes on the step in front of you. Celebrating gains you have not secured is the surest way to lose them.
people: Perrette the milkmaid
source: Jean de La Fontaine, Fables, Book VII (La Laitiere et le pot au lait); older versions in the Panchatantra
caveat: Fable numbering within Book VII differs between editions.

title: The Animals Sick of the Plague
text:
A plague swept through the animal kingdom. Not all died, but all were stricken. The lion called a council and proposed a remedy: heaven was punishing them for their sins, so the guiltiest among them should be sacrificed to appease it. To set an example, he would confess first. He had eaten many sheep, which had never done him any harm, and once or twice even the shepherd.

The fox hurried to reassure him. Eating sheep, that foolish rabble, was no sin, and it was an honor for them. As for the shepherd, he deserved it for claiming power over the animals. The courtiers applauded. Then the tiger, the bear and the other powerful beasts confessed their own deeds, and each was found to be practically a saint.

Last came the donkey. He admitted that once, passing a monks' meadow, hungry and tempted, he had eaten a strip of grass the width of his tongue. He had no right to it, he said. The assembly cried out against him. A wolf with some learning made a speech proving that this cursed animal was the source of all their troubles. Eating someone else's grass was a hideous crime. The donkey was put to death.

La Fontaine closes by saying that depending on whether you are powerful or wretched, the judgments of the court will make you white or black.
lesson: When an organization looks for someone to blame, notice whether the standard depends on the rank of the person judged. A fair process judges the act, not the actor.
people: The lion, the fox, the wolf, the donkey
source: Jean de La Fontaine, Fables, Book VII, Fable 1 (Les Animaux malades de la peste)

title: The Two Friends
text:
La Fontaine sets this fable in the faraway land of Monomotapa, where, he says, two true friends once lived. Whatever one owned belonged to the other.

One night, while everyone was asleep, one of the friends jumped out of bed in alarm, ran through the dark streets to his friend's house and woke the servants. The friend in bed was astonished. He got up, took his purse and his sword, and went to meet his visitor.

"You never run about at this hour," he said. "You are a man who values his sleep. Something must have happened. Have you lost money gambling? Here is my purse. Have you quarreled with someone? Here is my sword, and I will go with you. Or are you lonely tonight? Here is a beautiful slave girl; I can send her to you."

"No," said his friend, "it is none of that. I thank you for all of it. But I fell asleep and dreamed that you looked sad. I was afraid it might be true, and I could not rest. That bad dream is why I came running."

Which of the two loved the other more, La Fontaine asks, and leaves the question to the reader.
lesson: Good friends pay attention and come before they are called. Offer help freely, and do not wait for someone you love to ask.
people: Two friends of Monomotapa
source: Jean de La Fontaine, Fables, Book VIII, Fable 11

title: The Monkey and the Cat
text:
Bertrand the monkey and Raton the cat lived in the same house and shared the same master. They were a pair of rascals, and nothing in the house was safe from them.

One day they found some chestnuts roasting in the fireplace. Bertrand wanted them badly, but he had no intention of burning his own fingers. So he turned to the cat with his best flattery. Brother, he said, this is the day to show your talent. With paws as quick as yours, you could have those chestnuts out in no time. If I had your gifts, they would already be ours.

Raton was flattered. He reached into the ashes carefully, drew back his paw, reached in again, and flicked out one chestnut, then another, then a third. Each time he did, Bertrand gobbled the chestnut up.

Then a servant girl came in, and the two thieves ran off. Raton, La Fontaine says, was not very pleased. He had burned his paws, and Bertrand had eaten every chestnut.
lesson: Be wary of a partner who praises your skill just when there is a risky job to do. Check who takes the burns and who eats the chestnuts.
people: Bertrand the monkey, Raton the cat
source: Jean de La Fontaine, Fables, Book IX, The Monkey and the Cat (Le Singe et le Chat), 1679

title: Bankei and the Thief
text:
When the Zen master Bankei held his weeks of meditation retreat, pupils came from all over Japan to attend. During one of these gatherings, a pupil was caught stealing. The matter was reported to Bankei, with the request that the culprit be expelled. Bankei ignored the case.

Later the same pupil was caught stealing again, and again Bankei paid no attention. This angered the other pupils. They drew up a petition asking for the thief to be dismissed and declaring that if he was not, they would all leave together.

Bankei read the petition and called everyone before him. "You are wise brothers," he told them. "You know what is right and what is not right. You may go somewhere else to study if you wish, but this poor brother does not even know right from wrong. Who will teach him if I do not? I am going to keep him here even if all the rest of you leave."

Tears poured down the face of the brother who had stolen. All his desire to steal had vanished.
lesson: It is easy to remove the person who causes trouble and harder to help them change. Before you give up on someone, ask whether anyone else will ever teach them.
people: Bankei Yotaku, his pupils, a thieving student
source: 101 Zen Stories, compiled by Nyogen Senzaki and Paul Reps (1919), Right and Wrong

title: William Penn's Treaty Under the Elm
text:
In 1681 King Charles II granted William Penn, a Quaker, a vast territory in America to repay a debt owed to Penn's father. Penn named it Pennsylvania and planned it as a "holy experiment" in religious freedom. Unlike many colonizers, he held that the land belonged to the Lenape people who lived there, and that it should be bought from them, not simply taken.

According to tradition, in late 1682 Penn met Lenape leaders, among them the chief Tamanend, under a great elm tree at Shackamaxon, on the Delaware River near what became Philadelphia. There, the story goes, they made a treaty of friendship, promising to live in peace for as long as the rivers flowed and the sun shone.

No written text of such a treaty survives, and historians think the tradition may combine several agreements. But Penn did deal with the Lenape fairly by the standards of his time, and Pennsylvania had no war with them for decades. Voltaire praised it as the only treaty never sworn to and never broken, and Benjamin West's famous painting made the scene an American icon.

After Penn's death his sons cheated the Lenape in the Walking Purchase of 1737, and the peace broke down.
lesson: Fair dealing with neighbors can keep the peace for generations. Trust built over years can be destroyed in one dishonest bargain.
people: William Penn, Tamanend
source: Pennsylvania tradition; Voltaire, Letters on the English (1733), letter 4
caveat: No document of the treaty survives, and its details are traditional.

title: Peter the Great Works in a Dutch Shipyard
text:
In 1697 Tsar Peter I of Russia, then twenty-five years old, sent a large diplomatic mission, the Grand Embassy, to western Europe. Officially he was not part of it. He traveled incognito, under the name Peter Mikhailov, as a junior member. His real aim was to learn how western countries built ships and ran navies, which Russia lacked.

In August 1697 he went to Zaandam, a shipbuilding town in the Netherlands, and stayed in a small wooden house, which is preserved today. He worked in the yards for about a week before crowds of curious onlookers, who had soon worked out who he was, made it impossible.

He moved to Amsterdam, where he worked for about four months in the shipyard of the Dutch East India Company, taking part in building a frigate from the keel up, using the tools of a carpenter himself. He also visited workshops, hospitals and museums. He then went to England and studied at the royal dockyard at Deptford.

Peter returned to Russia with hundreds of recruited foreign specialists. He built a navy, founded Saint Petersburg in 1703 as a port on the Baltic, and pushed through sweeping reforms.
lesson: To change how others work, first learn the work yourself. Knowledge gained with your own hands earns respect and makes better decisions.
people: Peter I of Russia
source: Accounts of the Grand Embassy; Dutch records at Zaandam and Amsterdam

title: The Crane Wife
text:
A poor, lonely young man found a crane lying in the snow with an arrow through its wing. He pulled the arrow out, cleaned the wound and let the bird fly away.

Not long after, on a snowy night, a beautiful young woman knocked at his door, asking for shelter. She stayed, and before long they were married. They were very poor, so she offered to weave cloth for him to sell. She had only one condition: while she was weaving, he must never look into the room.

She shut herself in for days. When she came out, pale and thin, she carried a bolt of cloth so beautiful that it sold for a great price. The money ran out, and he asked her to weave again. She did, and grew thinner still. Encouraged by the money, or by neighbors who saw a chance to get rich, he asked a third time.

This time curiosity got the better of him. He slid the door open a crack and saw not his wife but a crane at the loom, plucking out its own feathers and weaving them into the cloth.

The crane saw him too. She came out, told him that she was the bird he had saved and that now that he had seen her true form she could not stay, then flew away and never came back.
lesson: Trust in a marriage rests on keeping promises, including the small ones about privacy. And asking a loved one to give more and more can use them up.
people: A poor man, his wife who is a crane
source: Japanese folktale (Tsuru Nyobo, The Crane Wife); a related tale is Tsuru no Ongaeshi
caveat: The tale exists in many regional versions, and in some the grateful crane comes to an old couple as a daughter rather than a wife.

title: The Straw Hats for the Jizo
text:
A poor old couple lived in a mountain village in Japan. On the last day of the year they had nothing in the house with which to celebrate the New Year, not even a few rice cakes. So the old man took five straw hats that he had woven and set out through the snow to sell them in town.

Nobody in the market wanted to buy hats. As evening came on, the old man trudged home with all five, the snow falling ever thicker.

On the way he passed a row of six stone Jizo statues standing by the road, the guardian figures that watch over travelers and children. Their heads and shoulders were covered with snow. The old man felt sorry for them. He brushed off the snow and tied a straw hat on each one. When he came to the sixth, there was no hat left, so he took off his own head cloth and tied it on the last statue.

At home he told his wife what he had done, and instead of scolding him, she said he had done well. They went to bed hungry. In the night they heard voices singing and something heavy being dragged through the snow. In the morning they found rice, rice cakes, vegetables and treasures piled at their door, and six Jizo, wearing hats, walking away into the distance.
lesson: The kindness that matters most is often given when you have little to spare. Small gestures to those who cannot repay you are never wasted.
people: A poor old couple, six Jizo statues
source: Japanese folktale (Kasa Jizo)

title: Momotaro the Peach Boy
text:
An old woman was washing clothes in a river when an enormous peach came floating toward her. She carried it home to her husband, and when they cut it open, a baby boy stepped out. The childless couple named him Momotaro, Peach Boy, and raised him. He grew very strong.

When he was grown, Momotaro announced that he would go to Onigashima, the island of the ogres, who had been raiding the land. His mother gave him millet dumplings for the road.

On the way he met a dog, who asked for a dumpling. Momotaro gave him one, and the dog joined him. Then a monkey asked, received a dumpling, and joined. Then a pheasant did the same.

They crossed the sea to the island, where the ogres' fortress had a great gate. The pheasant flew over the walls to scout and then pecked at the ogres' eyes. The monkey climbed the wall and opened the gate from inside. The dog bit at their legs, and Momotaro fought their chief. The ogres were beaten and surrendered, giving up the treasure they had stolen, and Momotaro and his companions brought it home to the old couple.
lesson: Sharing what you have is a good way to build a team. Allies with different abilities, each playing to strength, can take on what none could face alone.
people: Momotaro, a dog, a monkey, a pheasant
date: Japanese folk tradition, recorded from the Edo period
source: Japanese folktale (Momotaro)

title: The Battle of the Monkey and the Crab
text:
A crab found a rice ball, and a monkey found a persimmon seed. The monkey talked the crab into trading, pointing out that a seed would grow into a tree that would give fruit for years. The crab planted the seed and cared for it, and in time it became a tree covered with persimmons.

The crab could not climb, so the monkey offered to pick the fruit. Up in the tree, he ate the ripe ones himself and threw a hard green persimmon down at the crab, wounding her so badly that she died. In some versions she is only injured.

The crab's children wanted justice, but they were small, and the monkey was big and strong. So they asked for help, and a chestnut, a bee, a heavy rice mortar and a lump of cow dung joined them. While the monkey was out, they slipped into his house and each took a position.

When the monkey came home and sat by the hearth to warm himself, the chestnut burst out of the fire and burned him. He ran for water, and the bee stung him. He fled, slipped on the cow dung by the door, and fell, and the mortar dropped from the roof onto him. The crabs had their revenge.
lesson: Small allies who each contribute one exact ability, placed at the right moment, can bring down someone much stronger. Plan the whole sequence, not only your own part.
people: The crab and her children, a chestnut, a bee, a mortar, cow dung, the monkey
date: Japanese folk tradition, recorded from the Edo period
source: Japanese folktale (Saru Kani Gassen)
caveat: The allies and the exact sequence differ between versions.

title: The Tongue Cut Sparrow
text:
A kind old man in Japan kept a little sparrow that he loved and fed every day. His wife, however, was mean and greedy. One day, while the old man was out, the sparrow pecked at some rice starch she had made for her laundry. In a rage she seized the bird, cut its tongue with scissors and drove it away.

When the old man came home and heard what had happened, he was heartbroken. He went out to search for his sparrow, calling for it through the hills and bamboo groves. At last he found the sparrows' home deep in a bamboo forest. His sparrow welcomed him joyfully, and the sparrows feasted him and danced for him.

When he rose to leave, they offered him a parting gift: a large basket or a small one. The old man said he was old and the road was long, and chose the small one. At home he opened it and found it full of gold, silk and treasure.

His wife at once set off for the sparrows' house and demanded a gift. Offered the same choice, she seized the large basket. She could not wait to see what it held and opened it on the way home. Out came demons, snakes and monsters, and she fled in terror, or in some versions died of fright.
lesson: Kindness and modesty tend to be repaid, and greed tends to choose its own punishment. Take only what you need, and treat small creatures gently.
people: An old man, his wife, a sparrow
source: Japanese folktale (Shita-kiri Suzume)

title: Mokusen's Hand
text:
Mokusen Hiki was a Zen teacher who lived in a temple in the province of Tamba. One of his followers came to him with a complaint about his wife: she was terribly stingy. She hoarded everything and would not spend or give anything away.

Mokusen went to visit the woman. When she came in, he held up his fist in front of her face, clenched tight.

"What do you mean by that?" she asked, surprised.

"Suppose my hand were always like this," he said. "What would you call it?"

"Deformed," she answered.

Then he opened his hand flat and held it out in front of her. "Suppose it were always like this. What then?"

"Another kind of deformity," she said.

"If you understand that much," said Mokusen, "you are a good wife." Then he left.

After his visit, the story says, the woman helped her husband to give as well as to save.
lesson: A household needs both saving and giving. Either one practiced all the time, with no room for the other, becomes a kind of deformity.
people: Mokusen Hiki, a disciple, the disciple's wife
source: Nyogen Senzaki and Paul Reps, 101 Zen Stories (1919), Mokusen's Hand

title: The Forty-Seven Ronin
text:
In the spring of 1701, inside the shogun's castle at Edo, the young lord Asano Naganori of Ako drew his sword and wounded Kira Yoshinaka, a senior court official. Drawing a blade in the castle was a grave crime. Asano was ordered to commit suicide the same day, his domain was confiscated, and his samurai became ronin, masterless men. Kira was not punished.

Asano's chief retainer, Oishi Kuranosuke, first tried to have the house restored under Asano's brother. When that failed, he and a group of former retainers committed themselves to avenging their lord. They scattered, took humble work, and waited, so that Kira's guards would lower their watch. Later tradition says Oishi lived a dissolute life in Kyoto to throw off suspicion.

On a snowy night at the end of 1702 by the Japanese calendar (early 1703 in ours), forty-seven of them stormed Kira's mansion in Edo. They found him hiding, killed him, and carried his head to their lord's grave at Sengaku-ji temple. Then they turned themselves in to the authorities.

The shogunate debated what to do with men who had broken the law out of loyalty. In early 1703 it ordered the forty-six who had surrendered to commit seppuku, which they did. They were buried beside Asano at Sengaku-ji, where visitors still burn incense at their graves. Their story became the basis of Chushingura, one of Japan's most performed plays.
lesson: A group that shares one purpose can stay united for years without visible progress. Patience and discretion are often what make collective commitment succeed.
people: Oishi Kuranosuke, Asano Naganori, Kira Yoshinaka, the Ako ronin
source: Contemporary records of the Ako incident; Takeda Izumo and others, Kanadehon Chushingura (1748)
caveat: Many details popular today, such as Oishi's feigned debauchery, come from later drama rather than contemporary records.

title: Bhai Kanhaiya Gives Water to Both Sides
text:
Sikh tradition remembers Bhai Kanhaiya, a devoted follower of Guru Gobind Singh, as a water carrier. During the battles around the Sikh stronghold of Anandpur, in the early 1700s, he went among the wounded with a leather water bag, giving drink to the injured and dying.

Some Sikh soldiers noticed that he gave water to wounded Mughal and hill soldiers as well as to their own men, and that some of those he revived went back to fight. They complained to the Guru that Kanhaiya was helping the enemy.

Guru Gobind Singh called him and asked if this was true. According to the tradition, Kanhaiya replied that he saw no friend or enemy on the field. He saw only the Guru's face in every man who cried out for water. The Guru was pleased. He gave Kanhaiya a balm and told him to dress the wounds of the injured as well as give them water.

Sikhs see Bhai Kanhaiya as an example of selfless service, and some describe him as a forerunner of the idea later embodied by the Red Cross. Sikh volunteer groups that serve all victims of war and disaster honor his name.
lesson: Compassion for someone in pain need not ask which side they are on. Helping without distinction is the purest form of service.
people: Bhai Kanhaiya, Guru Gobind Singh
source: Sikh tradition, recorded in later Sikh histories and sakhis (traditional stories)
caveat: The episode comes from Sikh tradition and is not documented in contemporary records.

title: Newton, Leibniz and the War Over Calculus
text:
Isaac Newton worked out his method of "fluxions," the core of calculus, in the 1660s but published little of it for decades. Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz developed his own version independently in the 1670s and published it first, in 1684, with a notation so convenient that much of it is still used today.

For years the two were polite. Then, around 1699, followers of Newton began to hint that Leibniz had stolen the idea after seeing Newton's papers. Leibniz's supporters answered with hints of their own. In 1711 Leibniz appealed to the Royal Society in London to clear his name.

Newton was President of the Royal Society. He appointed a committee, supplied the documents and secretly wrote much of its report himself. In 1712 the Society published it as the Commercium Epistolicum, which found in Newton's favor. Newton then reviewed it anonymously, praising its conclusions. Leibniz died in 1716, largely neglected.

Historians now agree that both men discovered calculus independently. The feud split European mathematics: British mathematicians clung to Newton's notation out of loyalty and fell behind the Continent for about a century.
lesson: A feud over credit can damage not just the rivals but everyone around them. When you have real power in a dispute, use it fairly, not to judge your own case.
people: Isaac Newton, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
source: Royal Society, Commercium Epistolicum (1712); A. Rupert Hall, Philosophers at War (1980)

title: Morgiana and the Forty Thieves
text:
Ali Baba, a poor woodcutter, saw forty thieves open a cave in a rock with the words "Open, Sesame" and helped himself to some of their gold. His greedy brother Cassim went to the cave, forgot the password on the way out, and was killed by the thieves. Ali Baba secretly brought his body home, and the family's clever slave girl, Morgiana, arranged for a cobbler to be led there blindfolded to sew it together, so the death could pass as natural.

The thieves knew someone else had their secret. One of them found the cobbler, had himself led to the house, and marked its door with chalk. Morgiana noticed the mark and put the same mark on every door in the street. That night the thieves could not tell which house it was. A second thief marked the door with red chalk, and again she marked all the neighbors' doors.

Then the captain came himself, disguised as an oil merchant, with mules carrying large jars. One held oil; in the others hid his men. Going to fetch oil for a lamp, Morgiana heard a voice from a jar and discovered the plot. She boiled oil and poured it into each jar, killing the men inside. The captain escaped, but later returned in disguise as a guest. Morgiana recognized him, performed a dance with a dagger, and killed him. Ali Baba gave her her freedom and married her to his son.
lesson: Watchfulness beats numbers. Notice the small signs others miss, and answer a clever move with one that makes it useless.
people: Morgiana, Ali Baba, Cassim, the captain of the thieves
location: Persia, in the story; published in France
source: Antoine Galland, Les Mille et une nuits, volume 11 (1717)
caveat: No Arabic manuscript of this tale predates Galland's French version, which he wrote down from a story told to him by Hanna Diyab.

title: Lady Mary Montagu Inoculates Her Children
text:
Lady Mary Wortley Montagu knew smallpox firsthand. Her brother died of it, and in 1715 she caught it herself; she survived, but her face was scarred and she lost her eyelashes. The next year her husband was appointed British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, and she went with him to Constantinople.

There she discovered a practice unknown in England. In a letter of 1717, she described how old women, at gatherings in the autumn, scratched open a vein and placed a little matter from a smallpox sore into the wound. The children who received it fell mildly ill for a few days and were then protected for life. She wrote that she was patriotic enough to try to bring the practice into fashion in England.

In March 1718 she had her five-year-old son, Edward, inoculated in Constantinople, with the help of the embassy surgeon, Charles Maitland, and an old Greek woman. He recovered well.

Back in London, during a smallpox epidemic in 1721, she had Maitland inoculate her young daughter, this time in the presence of court physicians. The demonstration attracted attention. Experiments followed on prisoners and orphans, and in 1722 the Princess of Wales had two of her own daughters inoculated. Many doctors and clergymen attacked Lady Mary, but inoculation spread, and decades later it prepared the ground for Edward Jenner's safer vaccine.
lesson: A parent's courage to try something new for a child can benefit many other families. Watching carefully how others solve a problem can bring home a better answer.
people: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, Edward Wortley Montagu, Charles Maitland
source: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, Turkish Embassy Letters, letter to Sarah Chiswell (1 April 1717); Isobel Grundy, Lady Mary Wortley Montagu (1999)

title: The Pirates' Articles
text:
Bartholomew Roberts, a Welsh sailor forced into piracy when his ship was captured in 1719, became one of the most successful pirates of his age, taking hundreds of ships off Africa, Brazil and the Caribbean. His crew was large and drawn from many places. To keep it working together, they lived under a written set of articles that each man signed or swore to.

The book A General History of the Pyrates, published in 1724 under the name Captain Charles Johnson, reproduces Roberts's articles. Every man had a vote in affairs of importance and an equal right to fresh food and drink when captured. Gambling for money was forbidden. Lights and candles had to be out at eight at night. Each man had to keep his weapons clean and ready. Fighting among the crew on board was banned; quarrels had to be settled ashore, by duel. A man who deserted his post in battle could be killed or marooned.

Shares of plunder were set in advance: the captain and quartermaster received two shares, a few officers one and a half or one and a quarter, and everyone else one. A man who lost a limb in service received a fixed compensation from the common fund. The musicians had the Sabbath off.

Roberts was killed in battle with a British warship off the coast of Africa in February 1722. Many of his crew were tried and hanged.
lesson: Even outlaws need fair shares, clear rules and a voice for every member to work together. Agreements made in the open are what hold a team together.
people: Bartholomew Roberts and his crew
location: Atlantic Ocean, West Africa and the Caribbean
source: Captain Charles Johnson, A General History of the Robberies and Murders of the Most Notorious Pyrates (1724), chapter on Bartholomew Roberts
caveat: The author 'Charles Johnson' is unidentified, and some details of his book may be embellished.

title: Isaac Newton and the South Sea Bubble
text:
In 1720 the South Sea Company took over a large part of the British national debt in exchange for its own shares and promises of trade profits that never really existed. Its share price rose from around 128 pounds in January to about 1,000 pounds by late June, pulling all of London into a frenzy of speculation, then collapsed in the autumn.

Isaac Newton, then Master of the Mint and one of the most admired minds in Europe, held South Sea stock. Records studied by historians, notably the economist Andrew Odlyzko, show that he sold much of it in the spring of 1720 at a large profit. Then, as prices kept soaring and others grew rich, he bought back in during the summer, near the top, at much higher prices. When the bubble burst in the autumn, he lost heavily.

Anecdotes recorded after his death, some of them collected by Joseph Spence, say the loss came to about twenty thousand pounds, a fortune at the time, and attribute to Newton a famous remark: that he could calculate the motions of the heavenly bodies, but not the madness of people. The remark may be embellished, but the pattern of his trades is documented.
lesson: Being right early can tempt you back in when you see others profiting. Intelligence does not protect against crowd psychology, so set your rules before the frenzy, not during it.
people: Isaac Newton
source: Andrew Odlyzko (2019). Newton's financial misadventures in the South Sea Bubble. Notes and Records of the Royal Society, 73(1); Joseph Spence, Anecdotes
caveat: The famous quote about the madness of people is first recorded long after Newton's death and may be apocryphal.

title: Franklin Borrows a Book From a Rival
text:
In 1736 Benjamin Franklin was chosen clerk of the Pennsylvania Assembly, a post that also brought him profitable printing work for the province. The next year, when he was proposed again, a new member of the House made a long speech against him. Franklin noted that the man was wealthy, educated and likely to become influential, so his hostility was a real problem.

Franklin decided not to flatter him. Instead, he heard that the man owned a very scarce and curious book, and he wrote him a note asking to borrow it for a few days. The rival sent it at once. Franklin returned it about a week later with another note thanking him warmly for the favor.

The next time they met in the House, the man spoke to Franklin for the first time, and with great civility. In his Autobiography Franklin says the man was ready to serve him on every occasion afterward, and that they became great friends until the man's death. Franklin explained it with an old maxim: he who has once done you a kindness will be more ready to do you another than he whom you yourself have obliged.
lesson: To soften a cold or hostile colleague, try asking for a small, genuine favor and thanking them sincerely. People tend to like those they have helped.
people: Benjamin Franklin
source: Benjamin Franklin, Autobiography, Part III

title: Maria Theresa Before the Hungarian Diet
text:
In 1740 the emperor Charles VI died, leaving his Habsburg lands to his twenty-three-year-old daughter, Maria Theresa. Almost immediately, Prussia invaded the rich province of Silesia, and France, Bavaria and Saxony moved against her. Her treasury was empty and her army weak. Her inheritance looked likely to be carved up.

She turned to Hungary, whose nobles had a long history of resisting Habsburg rule. On September 11, 1741, she appeared before the Hungarian Diet at Pressburg, now Bratislava. Speaking in Latin, the language of the Diet, she told them that her kingdom and her person were in danger, that she was abandoned by all, and that she placed herself in the hands of their loyalty and courage. Contemporary reports say she was in tears.

The nobles responded with a shout that became famous: "Vitam et sanguinem", their lives and blood for their king, Maria Theresa, using the title she held as crowned ruler of Hungary.

The Diet voted to raise troops. Behind the scene there had also been hard bargaining, and she confirmed Hungarian privileges, including the nobles' freedom from taxation. The Hungarian forces helped her hold her throne through the War of the Austrian Succession.
lesson: In a crisis, an honest appeal to people's honor and loyalty can win support that pressure never would, especially when backed by real concessions.
people: Maria Theresa
source: Contemporary reports from the Diet of Pressburg; records of the Hungarian Diet of 1741
caveat: The popular image of her holding up her infant son Joseph during this speech is an embellishment, since he was presented at a later session.

title: The Miller of Sanssouci
text:
In the 1740s Frederick the Great of Prussia built his summer palace, Sanssouci, on a hill at Potsdam. Close to it stood a windmill, which still stands there today in rebuilt form.

According to a famous story, the king was annoyed by the mill, its noise or the way it spoiled his view, and offered to buy it so it could be torn down. The miller refused to sell the mill his family had worked. The king lost patience and reminded the miller that he could simply take it without paying. The miller answered that he could, if there were no judges in Berlin. In the story, the king was pleased by this faith in Prussian justice and let the mill stand.

The tale spread across Europe, especially after the French writer Andrieux turned it into a verse tale in 1797, and the miller's reply became a proverb for the rule of law.

There is an irony behind it. In the real case of a miller named Arnold in 1779, Frederick overruled the courts, believing they had wronged a poor miller, and had the judges arrested and imprisoned.
lesson: Power is most trustworthy when it accepts the same rules as everyone else. A leader who respects limits on himself earns lasting authority.
people: Frederick the Great
source: Prussian popular tradition; Francois Andrieux, Le Meunier de Sans-Souci (1797)
caveat: There is no reliable evidence that the conversation took place; it is a legend that grew around a real mill.

title: The Gates of Paradise
text:
A soldier named Nobushige came to the Zen master Hakuin and asked him, "Is there really a paradise and a hell?"

"Who are you?" asked Hakuin.

"I am a samurai," the warrior replied.

"You, a soldier!" exclaimed Hakuin. "What kind of ruler would have you as his guard? Your face looks like that of a beggar."

Nobushige became so angry that he began to draw his sword. Hakuin went on: "So you have a sword! Your weapon is probably much too dull to cut off my head."

As Nobushige pulled out his blade, Hakuin said, "Here open the gates of hell!"

At these words the samurai understood what the master had done. He put his sword back in its sheath and bowed.

"Here open the gates of paradise," said Hakuin.
lesson: Anger can take you somewhere terrible in a few seconds, and noticing it can bring you back just as fast. Catch the moment before you act.
people: Hakuin, the samurai Nobushige
source: Nyogen Senzaki and Paul Reps, 101 Zen Stories (1919)
caveat: This is a traditional anecdote attached to Hakuin, and similar versions are told of other masters.

title: Is That So?
text:
The Zen master Hakuin was praised by his neighbors as a man of pure life. A pretty girl whose parents kept a food shop nearby discovered she was pregnant. Her parents were furious and demanded to know who the father was. At first she would not say, but under pressure she named Hakuin.

In great anger the parents went to the master. All he said was, "Is that so?"

When the child was born, they brought it to Hakuin. By then he had lost his reputation, which did not seem to trouble him. He took good care of the baby, getting milk and everything else it needed from his neighbors.

A year later the girl could stand it no longer. She told her parents the truth: the real father was a young man who worked in the fish market. Her mother and father went straight to Hakuin, asked his forgiveness, apologized at length, and asked for the child back.

Hakuin was willing. In handing the child over, all he said was, "Is that so?"
lesson: Do the right thing in front of you even when you are misjudged. A calm heart does not need other people's opinion to stay steady.
people: Hakuin, a village girl and her parents
source: Nyogen Senzaki and Paul Reps, 101 Zen Stories (1919)
caveat: This is a traditional anecdote about the historical Hakuin and is not documented in his own writings.

title: The Encyclopedie
text:
In 1747 a group of Paris publishers, who had planned simply to translate an English reference work, gave the job of editing it to two men: the writer Denis Diderot and the mathematician Jean le Rond d'Alembert. They turned it into something far more ambitious, a complete survey of human knowledge, the sciences, the trades and the arts, written in a spirit of reason and open inquiry.

The first volume appeared in 1751. Contributors included Voltaire, Rousseau, Montesquieu and many specialists, physicians and craftsmen, some of them anonymous. Diderot visited workshops to learn how trades actually worked, and the volumes of engraved plates showed tools and processes in precise detail.

The work soon ran into trouble. In 1752 the royal government suspended it. In 1759 its privilege to publish was revoked and the Pope condemned it. D'Alembert withdrew, exhausted by the attacks. Diderot carried on almost alone, with the tireless help of the Chevalier Louis de Jaucourt, who wrote thousands of articles himself. The director of the book trade, Malesherbes, is said to have warned Diderot of a raid and hidden the manuscripts in his own house. Diderot later discovered that his own publisher had secretly cut passages from proofs to avoid trouble, and he was furious.

The remaining text volumes were printed quietly and released together in 1765, and the last plates came out in 1772. The finished work ran to seventeen volumes of text and eleven of plates.
lesson: A long collective project survives setbacks when a core of committed people keeps going. One or two persistent members can carry a team through years of opposition.
people: Denis Diderot, Jean le Rond d'Alembert, Louis de Jaucourt, Malesherbes
source: Encyclopedie, ou dictionnaire raisonne des sciences, des arts et des metiers (1751 to 1772); Philipp Blom, Enlightening the World (2004)

title: Samuel Johnson's Letter to Lord Chesterfield
text:
In 1747 Samuel Johnson, a poor and little known London writer, published the plan for a great Dictionary of the English Language and addressed it to the Earl of Chesterfield, a famous man of taste who might act as his patron. Chesterfield gave him ten pounds and little else. Johnson later said he had waited in the earl's outer rooms and been turned away from his door.

For the next seven years Johnson worked on the dictionary almost alone, with a few hired copyists, in poverty. In late 1754, when the dictionary was about to appear, Chesterfield published two essays in a magazine praising the coming work and recommending Johnson as its author, apparently hoping to receive the dedication.

On February 7, 1755, Johnson wrote him a letter. He reminded him of the seven years he had waited and worked without one act of assistance. "Is not a Patron, my Lord," he asked, "one who looks with unconcern on a man struggling for life in the water, and when he has reached ground encumbers him with help?" The notice the earl had now chosen to take, he wrote, had come too late for him to enjoy it.

The Dictionary appeared that April, with no dedication. Boswell later published the letter in his Life of Johnson.
lesson: Support is worth most when it is needed, not after someone has succeeded without you. Offer help at the start, or do not expect gratitude at the end.
people: Samuel Johnson, Philip Stanhope, 4th Earl of Chesterfield
source: Samuel Johnson, letter to the Earl of Chesterfield, February 7, 1755, in James Boswell, The Life of Samuel Johnson (1791)

title: Leopold Mozart Takes His Children on Tour
text:
Leopold Mozart was a violinist and composer at the court of the Archbishop of Salzburg and the author of a respected violin method. When he realized how gifted his two children were, his daughter Maria Anna, called Nannerl, and his son Wolfgang, he devoted himself to their training and their careers.

In June 1763, when Wolfgang was seven and Nannerl twelve, the whole family set out on a tour that lasted three and a half years. They traveled by coach through Munich, Mannheim, Brussels and Paris, where they played at Versailles, and on to London, where they stayed more than a year and Wolfgang met Johann Christian Bach. The children played for kings and paying audiences. Wolfgang performed tricks such as playing on a keyboard covered with a cloth, and wrote his first symphonies.

Leopold's long letters home to his landlord in Salzburg, Lorenz Hagenauer, record the money, the illnesses and the triumphs. In The Hague, in 1765, first Nannerl and then Wolfgang fell dangerously ill, and Nannerl was given the last rites. Both recovered, and the family returned to Salzburg in November 1766.

Leopold gave up much of his own career for his son. The bond was close but heavy. When Wolfgang, as a grown man, settled in Vienna and married Constanze Weber against his father's wishes, their relationship cooled, though they kept writing until Leopold's death in 1787.
lesson: Investing everything in a gifted child can open the world to them. But a parent's ambition must eventually give way to the child's own life.
people: Leopold Mozart, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Nannerl Mozart
location: Salzburg, Austria; Paris, France; London, UK; The Hague, Netherlands
source: The Letters of Mozart and His Family, trans. Emily Anderson (1938)

title: Wedgwood Makes Queen's Ware
text:
