In the 1760s Josiah Wedgwood was a successful potter in Staffordshire, making a refined cream-colored earthenware. In 1765 he received an order for a tea service from Queen Charlotte, wife of George III. He executed it with great care and then asked permission to call his cream ware Queen's Ware and to style himself Potter to Her Majesty. Both were granted.

Wedgwood understood what this meant. In his letters to his business partner Thomas Bentley, he wrote repeatedly about how fashion flowed downward: if the court and the great families adopted his wares, the middle classes would want them too. He sought aristocratic patrons, gave them special designs, and advertised the connections.

He also changed how pottery was sold. He opened showrooms in London where fashionable customers could see whole table services elegantly displayed, and he rearranged the displays regularly to keep people coming back. He produced catalogues, offered sets in many patterns, guaranteed replacement of goods broken in transit, and in some cases offered money back to dissatisfied customers. When he made a huge service for Catherine the Great of Russia in the early 1770s, decorated with views of British scenes, he first displayed it in London, drawing crowds.

Queen's Ware became the standard tableware of middle-class Britain and was exported across Europe and America. Wedgwood became one of the richest manufacturers of his age.
lesson: Endorsement from people others admire can turn a product into an aspiration. How something is shown and sold can matter as much as how it is made.
people: Josiah Wedgwood, Thomas Bentley, Queen Charlotte
source: Josiah Wedgwood's letters to Thomas Bentley; Neil McKendrick, Josiah Wedgwood: An Eighteenth-Century Entrepreneur in Salesmanship and Marketing Techniques, Economic History Review (1960); Brian Dolan, Josiah Wedgwood (2004)

title: Rousseau Turns on His Benefactor Hume
text:
In 1765 Jean-Jacques Rousseau was hounded out of France and Switzerland for his writings on religion. The Scottish philosopher David Hume, then the most celebrated British man of letters, offered to help. In January 1766 he brought Rousseau to England, found him a place to live, and quietly worked to obtain a pension for him from King George III.

Rousseau, already deeply suspicious by nature, came to believe the opposite of what was happening. A cruel joke made things worse: Horace Walpole wrote a mock letter from the King of Prussia ridiculing Rousseau, which circulated widely, and Rousseau suspected Hume was behind it. He grew convinced that Hume had brought him to England to dishonor him. In July 1766 he wrote Hume an enormous letter of accusation, listing every supposed sign of betrayal, including the way Hume had looked at him.

Hume was stunned and furious. Against the advice of some friends, he published his side of the correspondence as A Concise and Genuine Account of the Dispute. All of literary Europe took sides. Rousseau left England in 1767, and the two never reconciled.
lesson: Suspicion can twist even kindness into imagined betrayal. When you start reading every act as a plot against you, check your story before you act on it.
people: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, David Hume, Horace Walpole
source: David Hume, A Concise and Genuine Account of the Dispute between Mr. Hume and Mr. Rousseau (1766)

title: Uesugi Yozan Rescues a Bankrupt Domain
text:
In 1767 a teenager named Uesugi Harunori, later known as Yozan, became lord of the Yonezawa domain in northern Japan. He had been adopted into the Uesugi family from a smaller house. Yonezawa was crushed by debt, its population shrinking, and its leaders had seriously considered handing the domain back to the shogunate.

Yozan began with himself. He cut his own household spending sharply, wore cotton instead of silk, and ate plain meals. He then pushed reforms across the domain: planting mulberry for silk, lacquer trees and other crops, developing local weaving, opening new land, and reviving a domain school to train capable officials regardless of rank.

The reforms met resistance. In 1773 seven senior retainers petitioned against them. Yozan investigated, rejected the petition, and punished the leaders. Then he carried on.

When he retired in 1785 he gave his successor three principles: the domain belongs to the ancestors and descendants, not the lord; the people belong to the domain, not the lord; and the lord exists for the domain and its people. Yonezawa's finances recovered over the following decades, and Uchimura Kanzo later chose him as one of his Representative Men of Japan.
lesson: If you ask an organization to tighten its belt, start with your own. Reform is believed when the leader is the first to pay for it.
people: Uesugi Harunori (Yozan)
source: Yonezawa domain records; Uchimura Kanzo, Representative Men of Japan (1908)

title: Abigail Adams: "Remember the Ladies"
text:
John and Abigail Adams married in 1764 and spent much of their marriage apart. While John served in the Continental Congress in Philadelphia, Abigail ran the family farm at Braintree, Massachusetts, raised four children, dealt with tenants, debts and war shortages, and wrote him letters full of news, politics and argument. More than a thousand of their letters survive.

On 31 March 1776, as Congress moved toward independence, Abigail wrote to John: "in the new Code of Laws which I suppose it will be necessary for you to make I desire you would Remember the Ladies, and be more generous and favourable to them than your ancestors." She warned him not to put unlimited power into the hands of husbands, since "all Men would be tyrants if they could," and joked that the ladies would foment a rebellion of their own if they were ignored.

John replied on 14 April that he could only laugh at her "extraordinary Code of Laws," though he added that men knew better than to repeal their masculine systems, which in practice left them only the name of masters. Abigail did not let it go. She complained to her friend Mercy Otis Warren about his answer.

The marriage remained a partnership of two strong minds. John called her his "dearest friend" and relied on her judgment all his life, through his presidency and beyond. Her letter is still quoted as one of the earliest American appeals for women's rights.
lesson: The best partners challenge each other honestly, even on things they will not win at once. A marriage of minds is one in which both voices are heard.
people: Abigail Adams, John Adams
source: Adams Family Correspondence, vol. 1 (Massachusetts Historical Society); Abigail Adams to John Adams, 31 March 1776

title: Benjamin Franklin and His Loyalist Son
text:
William Franklin was Benjamin Franklin's son, born out of wedlock around 1730 and raised in his father's household. The two were close. William helped with his father's electrical experiments, traveled with him to London, and with his father's influence became royal governor of New Jersey in 1763.

When the American Revolution came, they chose opposite sides. Benjamin became one of the leaders of independence. William stayed loyal to the king. In 1776 he was arrested by the patriots and imprisoned in Connecticut in harsh conditions. His wife, Elizabeth, died in 1777 in New York while he was held; he was not allowed to see her. His father did not intervene. After his release in an exchange, William led loyalist forces in New York and then left for England in 1782.

In 1784 Benjamin wrote to him that nothing had ever hurt him so much as finding himself deserted in old age by his only son, and not only deserted but opposed in arms, in a cause in which his good name, fortune and life were at stake.

In 1785 the two met briefly in Southampton, England. They spent the time settling business. In his will Franklin left William very little, explaining that the part he had played against his father in the war accounted for it. William's son, Temple, whom Benjamin had raised, sided with his grandfather.
lesson: Political division can break even the closest family ties. When loyalties collide, decide early whether the relationship matters more than winning the argument.
people: Benjamin Franklin, William Franklin, William Temple Franklin
location: Philadelphia and New Jersey, USA; Southampton, England (UK)
source: Benjamin Franklin to William Franklin, 16 August 1784; Franklin's will (1788); Sheila L. Skemp, William Franklin (1990)

title: Washington Crosses the Delaware
text:
By December 1776 the American cause seemed close to collapse. George Washington's army had been driven out of New York and chased across New Jersey into Pennsylvania. It had shrunk to a few thousand ill-clothed men, and most of their enlistments would expire on 31 December. Thomas Paine wrote that these were the times that try men's souls.

Washington decided to strike before his army dissolved. Across the Delaware River, at Trenton, New Jersey, a garrison of Hessian soldiers under Colonel Johann Rall held an advanced post for the winter. On the night of 25 December, Washington took about 2,400 men across the icy river at McConkey's Ferry, in a storm of snow and sleet, with artillery hauled in boats. The crossing ran hours late, and two supporting columns failed to cross at all. Washington went ahead anyway.

The soldiers marched about nine miles through the storm and attacked Trenton from two directions early on the morning of 26 December. The Hessians, caught by surprise, tried to form up in the streets under American cannon fire. Rall was mortally wounded, and around nine hundred Hessians surrendered. The Americans lost only a handful of men.

A week later Washington won again at Princeton. The victories revived the morale of the army and the country, and enough soldiers agreed to stay on to keep the revolution alive.
lesson: At your lowest point, a well-chosen, limited success can restore belief. Pick a target you can actually win, and act before the moment passes.
people: George Washington, Johann Rall, Henry Knox
location: Delaware River and Trenton, New Jersey (USA)
source: Washington's letters and reports to Congress; David Hackett Fischer, Washington's Crossing (2004)

title: Washington Returns General Howe's Dog
text:
In the autumn of 1777 the British army under General William Howe captured Philadelphia, the American capital. On October 4 George Washington attacked part of Howe's forces at Germantown, just outside the city. The attack, fought in thick fog, ended in confusion and an American retreat.

Afterward, by tradition, American soldiers found a small dog wandering near the lines. Its collar bore the name of General Howe. Washington ordered it returned to its owner under a flag of truce, with a short note in the handwriting of his aide Alexander Hamilton.

The note survives among Washington's papers, dated October 6, 1777. It reads: "General Washington's compliments to General Howe. He does himself the pleasure to return him a Dog, which accidentally fell into his hands, and by the inscription on the Collar appears to belong to General Howe."

The war went on for six more years. But the two commanders, fighting each other in deadly earnest, had exchanged a moment of plain courtesy, and the note became one of the small, much loved documents of the Revolution.
lesson: Courtesy toward an opponent costs almost nothing and reveals a great deal about your character. You can fight hard and still behave decently.
people: George Washington, William Howe, Alexander Hamilton
source: George Washington to William Howe, October 6, 1777, The Papers of George Washington, Revolutionary War Series, vol. 11

title: Mozart Breaks the News of His Mother's Death
text:
In 1777 Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, then twenty-one, set out from Salzburg to find a better position than his post at the archbishop's court. His father, Leopold, could not get leave to go, so his mother, Anna Maria, went with him. They traveled to Munich, Mannheim and finally Paris.

Paris was a disappointment. Wolfgang went out all day looking for pupils and commissions, while his mother sat alone in dark, cold lodgings. In June 1778 she fell ill. Wolfgang cared for her as best he could and found a doctor. She died on 3 July 1778, with him beside her.

That night Wolfgang wrote two letters. To his father he wrote that his mother was very ill, that he had little hope but that everything was in God's hands, and filled the rest of the letter with news of his music. Then he wrote to a close family friend in Salzburg, the priest Abbe Joseph Bullinger, telling him the truth: his mother was dead. He asked Bullinger to prepare his father and sister gently for the news.

A few days later, on 9 July, Wolfgang wrote to his father again and told him plainly that his mother had died, consoling him with their faith and assuring him that he would look after himself. Leopold, however, came to blame his son in part for her death, and the reproach hung over their relationship.
lesson: Breaking terrible news gently, with someone close to support the listener, is an act of love. How we tell people hard truths matters almost as much as the truth itself.
people: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Anna Maria Mozart, Leopold Mozart, Joseph Bullinger
source: Mozart, letters of 3 July 1778 (to Leopold Mozart and to Abbe Bullinger) and 9 July 1778, in The Letters of Mozart and His Family, trans. Emily Anderson

title: The Montgolfier Brothers Send Up a Balloon
text:
Joseph-Michel and Jacques-Etienne Montgolfier were two of the sixteen children of a paper manufacturer in Annonay, in southern France. Joseph, the elder, was a restless inventor and dreamer with little head for business. Etienne, five years younger, had trained as an architect and was called home to run the family paper mill, which he did with skill.

In 1782 Joseph became convinced that a light bag filled with heated air could rise. He tested the idea with small envelopes of silk and paper, and brought his brother into the work. The two built ever larger balloons from cloth lined with paper, the product of their own mill. On 4 June 1783 they launched an unmanned balloon in the market square of Annonay before a crowd. It rose to a great height and came down more than a mile away.

The news reached Paris, and Etienne, the more polished of the two, went there to repeat the demonstration. On 19 September 1783, at Versailles, before King Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, a balloon lifted a sheep, a duck and a rooster, which landed safely. On 21 November 1783, a Montgolfier balloon carried two men, Jean-Francois Pilatre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes, over Paris in the first free flight of human beings. The king ennobled the brothers' father in recognition.
lesson: Partners with different gifts can achieve together what neither could alone. A dreamer needs an organizer, and an organizer needs a dream.
people: Joseph-Michel Montgolfier, Jacques-Etienne Montgolfier
source: Charles Coulston Gillispie, The Montgolfier Brothers and the Invention of Aviation (1983)

title: Washington's Spectacles at Newburgh
text:
In March 1783 the Continental Army was camped at Newburgh, New York, waiting for a peace treaty with Britain. The officers had gone unpaid for months, and Congress seemed unable to keep its promises of pensions. An anonymous letter circulated in camp urging the officers to defy Congress, and possibly to march on it, if their demands were not met. Washington forbade the meeting the letter proposed and called one of his own for March 15, where he was not expected to appear.

On March 15 George Washington unexpectedly walked into the meeting hall. He gave a prepared speech asking the officers not to stain the honor they had won and to trust Congress to do them justice. The room remained cold.

He then began to read a letter from a congressman. He stumbled over the words, took out a pair of spectacles that few of his officers had ever seen him wear, and said, according to accounts of those present, that he had grown gray in the service of his country and was now growing blind. Several officers were moved to tears.

After he left, the officers voted to reject the anonymous call and to express their confidence in Congress. The threat of a military coup dissolved.
lesson: Showing honestly what your service has cost you can move people more than argument. Credibility built over years is what makes such a moment work.
people: George Washington
source: Washington's address to the officers, March 15, 1783; accounts of officers present, including Samuel Shaw
caveat: The exact words about growing gray and blind differ slightly among the accounts of those present.

title: Washington Resigns His Commission
text:
By late 1783 the War of Independence was over and the last British troops had left New York. George Washington was the most admired man in the new United States, and he commanded the only national army. Many people at home and abroad assumed he would use that position to rule.

Instead he rode to Annapolis, Maryland, where the Continental Congress was then meeting. On December 23, 1783, he appeared before Congress in the Maryland State House. In a short speech he thanked his officers and the army, commended the country to God, and announced that he was retiring from public life. He then handed his commission, the document that had made him commander in chief in 1775, back to the president of Congress, Thomas Mifflin.

The journals of Congress record the ceremony. Witnesses described members and spectators in tears. Washington left the same day and reached his home at Mount Vernon on Christmas Eve.

His return to private life helped establish the principle that the army is subordinate to civilian government. He came back to public life only years later, through election.
lesson: Handing power back when you could keep it is one of the strongest ways to prove you deserved it. People trust the leader who is willing to leave.
people: George Washington, Thomas Mifflin
source: Journals of the Continental Congress, December 23, 1783; Washington's address to Congress on resigning his commission

title: Haydn's Words to Mozart's Father
text:
By 1785 Joseph Haydn was the most celebrated composer in Europe, and Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, twenty four years younger, was a rising star in Vienna. The two had become friends and sometimes played string quartets together. Mozart had studied Haydn's quartets closely and spent more than two years writing a set of six of his own, which cost him unusual effort.

In February 1785 Mozart's father Leopold came to visit his son in Vienna. On one evening Haydn came to hear three of the new quartets. Leopold described the scene in a letter to his daughter: Haydn turned to him and said, "Before God and as an honest man I tell you that your son is the greatest composer known to me either in person or by name." Haydn praised his taste and his deep knowledge of composition. For a father who had devoted his life to his son's career, it was an extraordinary moment.

That autumn Mozart published the six quartets with an affectionate dedication to Haydn, calling them his children and entrusting them to his friend's care. When Mozart died in 1791, Haydn, then in London, was deeply grieved.
lesson: Praise a younger talent generously, even one who might outshine you. Recognizing greatness in others is a sign of strength, not a loss of standing.
people: Joseph Haydn, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Leopold Mozart
source: Leopold Mozart, letter to Nannerl Mozart, February 16, 1785; Mozart, dedication of the six "Haydn" quartets (September 1, 1785)

title: Wedgwood's "Am I Not a Man and a Brother?"
text:
In May 1787 a small group in London, most of them Quakers along with Thomas Clarkson and Granville Sharp, founded the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade. They needed to persuade a British public that profited from slavery, and for whom enslaved Africans were mostly out of sight and out of mind.

The committee adopted a seal showing an African man kneeling in chains, hands raised, with the words "Am I Not a Man and a Brother?" Josiah Wedgwood, the great pottery manufacturer and a committee member, had his factory turn the design into small ceramic cameos, black figure on white, and sent them out free by the hundreds.

People began wearing them. Clarkson later wrote that the medallions were set in snuffboxes, bracelets and hairpins, and that ladies wore them as ornaments, so that fashion, usually confined to trivial things, was used in the cause of justice. Wedgwood sent a batch to Benjamin Franklin in Philadelphia, who replied that he believed it would be as effective as the best written pamphlet. The image spread on both sides of the Atlantic. Parliament abolished the British slave trade in 1807.
lesson: To change people's minds about how others should be treated, help them see the other as a person like themselves. A simple, human image can persuade where arguments fail.
people: Josiah Wedgwood, Thomas Clarkson, Benjamin Franklin
source: Thomas Clarkson, The History of the Rise, Progress and Accomplishment of the Abolition of the African Slave Trade (1808); Benjamin Franklin, letter to Josiah Wedgwood, May 15, 1788

title: Bligh's Open-Boat Voyage
text:
On April 28, 1789, near Tonga in the South Pacific, part of the crew of HMS Bounty mutinied under the master's mate Fletcher Christian. Lieutenant William Bligh, the ship's commander, had a sharp tongue and a temper that had worn on his men. The mutineers forced him and eighteen loyal men into the ship's launch, a boat about twenty-three feet long, with a little food and water, a compass and a quadrant, and set them adrift.

They landed first on the island of Tofua, where islanders attacked them and killed the quartermaster, John Norton. Bligh decided their only chance was to sail to the Dutch settlement at Kupang on Timor, more than three thousand nautical miles away.

He rationed food strictly, weighing out tiny portions of bread with a pair of coconut-shell scales and a pistol ball as the weight. He navigated largely from memory, through storms and rain, along the Great Barrier Reef and through the Torres Strait, and kept a careful log. He clashed with some of his men on the way.

After forty-seven days, on June 14, 1789, the launch reached Kupang. Every man who had left Tofua was still alive, though several later died of illness in the Dutch East Indies.
lesson: Leadership has many parts. You can fail badly at some, such as how you treat people, and still save lives through skill, discipline and refusal to give up.
people: William Bligh, Fletcher Christian, John Norton
location: From Tofua (Tonga) to Kupang, Timor (modern Indonesia)
source: William Bligh, A Narrative of the Mutiny on Board His Majesty's Ship Bounty (1790)

title: Do You Know What Hurts Me?
text:
Rabbi Moshe Leib of Sasov was a Hasidic master known for his tireless love of ordinary people. He used to say that he had learned what it means to love from a peasant.

He had stopped at a country inn, where two peasants were sitting at a table, drinking. They had both had a fair amount, and they were in the warm and sentimental mood that drink can bring.

One of them turned to the other. "Tell me," he said, "do you love me?"

"Of course I love you," said the other. "I love you very much."

The first man shook his head. "You say you love me," he said, "but you do not know what hurts me. If you really loved me, you would know."

The second man had no answer to that, and the two of them sat on in silence. But the rabbi, according to the story, understood. To love people, he concluded, is to know their needs and to bear the burden of their sorrow.
lesson: Saying you care is easy. Showing it means paying enough attention to know what hurts the people you love, and acting on that knowledge.
people: Rabbi Moshe Leib of Sasov, two peasants
source: Hasidic tradition, retold in Martin Buber, Tales of the Hasidim

title: Toussaint Louverture Leads the Haitian Revolution
text:
In August 1791 the enslaved people of Saint-Domingue, France's richest colony, rose in revolt. Among those who joined was Toussaint, a man in his late forties who had been born into slavery and later freed, who could read and had worked as a coachman and steward.

Toussaint, who took the name Louverture, trained his followers into a disciplined army. At first he fought alongside Spain against France. In 1794 the French Republic abolished slavery, and he changed sides. Over the next years he defeated the Spanish, forced a British invasion force to withdraw in 1798, and beat rival leaders within the colony. By 1801 he governed all of Hispaniola and issued a constitution that abolished slavery permanently and named him governor for life.

Napoleon then sent a large expedition under his brother-in-law Leclerc to restore French control. In June 1802 Toussaint was invited to a meeting, seized and shipped to France. As he was taken aboard, he reportedly said that in overthrowing him they had cut down only the trunk of the tree of liberty, which would grow again from roots that were many and deep.

He died in a prison in the Jura mountains in April 1803. Haiti declared independence on January 1, 1804.
lesson: Discipline, patience and a clear vision can build strength out of people the world has written off.
people: Toussaint Louverture, Charles Leclerc, Napoleon Bonaparte
location: Saint-Domingue (modern Haiti) and Fort de Joux, France
source: Toussaint's letters and the Constitution of 1801; C. L. R. James, The Black Jacobins (1938)

title: Goethe and Schiller Become Friends
text:
For years Johann Wolfgang von Goethe and Friedrich Schiller lived near each other in the small German duchy of Weimar and kept their distance. Goethe was the older, established poet, and Schiller resented his coolness. Their temperaments seemed opposite: Goethe trusted observation and nature, Schiller ideas and philosophy.

In July 1794, after a meeting of a natural science society in Jena, the two happened to leave together and fell into conversation. Goethe described his theory of the metamorphosis of plants and sketched a symbolic primal plant. Schiller listened and shook his head: that was not an experience, he said, but an idea. Goethe recalled being irritated, but the argument drew them together. A few weeks later Schiller wrote him a letter analyzing the nature of Goethe's mind with such insight that Goethe was won over.

For the next ten years they exchanged around a thousand letters, read each other's work, wrote satirical verses together and pushed each other forward. Schiller urged Goethe to return to Faust; Goethe encouraged Schiller's great plays, including Wallenstein and William Tell. When Schiller died in May 1805, Goethe wrote that he had lost a friend and with him half of his own existence.
lesson: Someone very different from you can become your best collaborator. Honest disagreement, taken seriously, can turn into mutual respect that makes both of you better.
people: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Friedrich Schiller
source: Goethe-Schiller correspondence (1794 to 1805); Goethe, "Gluckliches Ereignis" (A Fortunate Encounter, 1817)

title: Mary Shelley and the Mother She Never Knew
text:
Mary Wollstonecraft, author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, married the philosopher William Godwin in March 1797, when she was already expecting their child. On 30 August she gave birth to a daughter, Mary. The placenta did not come away properly, infection set in, and on 10 September 1797 Wollstonecraft died. Her daughter was eleven days old.

Godwin, grieving, wrote a frank memoir of his wife's life, including her love affairs and suicide attempts. It shocked the public and damaged her reputation for a century. He raised Mary and her older half-sister Fanny, and later remarried.

Mary grew up surrounded by her mother's books and legend. She read and reread her writings. Wollstonecraft was buried in the churchyard of St Pancras in London, and Mary went there often. Biographers record that she read and studied by her mother's grave. In 1814, at sixteen, it was there that she met in secret with the young poet Percy Bysshe Shelley, a disciple of her father. In July 1814 they ran away together to the continent, against her father's furious objections.

Four years later, in 1818, Mary Shelley published Frankenstein, a novel about a creature brought into the world and abandoned by its maker. Later she became the editor and keeper of Shelley's work. Her mother, whom she never knew, remained her guide.
lesson: A parent we never knew can still shape us through what she left behind. What we write and believe may become a child's inheritance.
people: Mary Wollstonecraft, Mary Shelley, William Godwin, Percy Bysshe Shelley
source: William Godwin, Memoirs of the Author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1798); Miranda Seymour, Mary Shelley (2000)

title: Anansi and Turtle Share a Meal
text:
Anansi the spider had just cooked a delicious pot of yams when Turtle arrived at his door, tired and hungry after a long walk. In Ashanti custom a visitor at mealtime must be fed, so Anansi had to invite him in. But he had no intention of sharing.

As Turtle reached for the food, Anansi stopped him. "Turtle, your hands are filthy from the road. Go to the river and wash them first." Turtle went down to the river and washed, but the path back was dusty, and since he walked on his hands, they were dirty again when he arrived. Anansi sent him back to wash a second time. When Turtle finally returned, walking on the grass to keep clean, the pot was empty. Anansi had eaten everything. Turtle said nothing but invited Anansi to dine at his home some day.

When Anansi came, Turtle's home was at the bottom of the river. Turtle swam down and began to eat. Anansi tried to dive but kept floating to the surface, so he filled the pockets of his jacket with stones and sank to the table.

Just as he reached for the food, Turtle said politely, "In my house we do not wear jackets at the table." Anansi took off his jacket, shot up to the surface, and watched from above as Turtle finished the meal.
lesson: If you treat a guest or partner unfairly through some clever rule, expect the same rules to be used on you. Generosity is cheaper than cleverness in the long run.
people: Anansi, Turtle
source: Ashanti (Akan) folk tradition of Anansi tales

title: Feathers in the Wind
text:
In a small town a man spread a story about the local rabbi. It was not true, but it was interesting, and it passed from mouth to mouth through the market and the houses until everyone had heard it.

After a while the man began to feel ashamed. He went to the rabbi, admitted what he had done, and asked how he could make amends. He was ready to do whatever penance was required.

The rabbi told him to take a feather pillow, carry it to the top of a hill, cut it open and shake the feathers out into the wind. Then he was to come back. The man thought this an easy penance. He did as he was told, watched the feathers swirl away over the roofs and fields, and returned to the rabbi, relieved.

"Now," said the rabbi, "go and gather up all the feathers."

The man protested that it was impossible. The wind had already carried them everywhere, over walls, into gardens and far across the fields. "Exactly," said the rabbi. "And that is how it is with the words you spread. You can ask forgiveness, but you can never gather them all back."
lesson: Think before repeating a story about someone. Once words are out, no apology can follow every place they reach.
people: A rabbi, a gossip
source: Jewish folk tradition, told of several Hasidic rabbis
caveat: The tale has no single original source and is attributed to various rabbis in different versions.

title: Stone Soup
text:
Some hungry travelers came to a village, tired and with nothing to eat. They knocked on doors, but every household said it had nothing to spare. Times were hard, and the villagers hid what little food they had.

So the travelers set a large pot on a fire in the middle of the village square, filled it with water, and dropped in a smooth stone. People came out to see what they were doing. Stone soup, the travelers explained. It was delicious, though it would be even better with a little salt. Someone fetched salt. And a few carrots would really bring out the flavor of the stone. A woman went and found some carrots. Perhaps an onion? A neighbor brought onions. One by one other villagers added cabbage, potatoes, a bit of meat, some barley.

At last the soup was ready, and it was thick and rich. The travelers and the whole village sat down together and ate their fill. The villagers marveled that a soup could be made from a stone, and the travelers, in some tellings, left the stone behind as a gift.
lesson: People who will not give to a plea will often add a little to something that is already underway. Start the pot, and invite everyone to contribute one thing.
people: Hungry travelers, villagers
source: European folktale (Stone Soup; Aarne-Thompson type 1548)

title: The Tortoise Who Called Himself All of You
text:
In an Igbo tale, known to many readers from Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart, the birds were invited to a great feast in the sky. It was a time of famine, and Tortoise, whose stomach was always his first thought, begged to come along. The birds did not trust him, but he spoke so sweetly that each bird gave him a feather, and with them he made a pair of wings.

On the way he told them that people invited to such a feast should take new names for the occasion. Each bird chose one. Tortoise chose "All of You."

When the feast was laid out, Tortoise asked their hosts for whom it had been prepared. "For all of you," they answered. "You see," said Tortoise to the birds, "the feast is for me." He ate the best of everything, and the birds got only the scraps. Furious, each bird took back its feather, leaving Tortoise stranded in the sky.

He begged Parrot to tell his wife to bring out all the soft things in the house so he could jump down safely. Parrot told her instead to bring out the hard things: hoes, machetes, spears and pots. Tortoise jumped, fell and crashed down so hard that his shell broke into pieces. A medicine man glued it back together, and that is why a tortoise's shell is not smooth.
lesson: Using the people who help you for your own gain may work once, but it leaves you alone when you need them most.
people: Tortoise, the birds, Parrot
source: Igbo folk tradition; retold in Chinua Achebe, Things Fall Apart (1958), Chapter 11

title: Real Prosperity
text:
A rich man came to the Zen master Sengai and asked him to write something that would bring continued prosperity to his family. He wanted a blessing that the family could treasure from one generation to the next.

Sengai took a large sheet of paper and wrote: "Father dies, son dies, grandson dies."

The rich man was furious. "I asked you to write something for the happiness of my family," he said. "Why do you make a joke of it?"

"I am not joking," Sengai answered. "If your son were to die before you, it would grieve you greatly. If your grandson died before your son, both of you would be heartbroken. If your family, generation after generation, passes away in the order I have written, it will be the natural course of life. I call that real prosperity."
lesson: The deepest good fortune a family can have is ordinary: that the old go before the young. Ordinary life in its natural order is worth being grateful for.
people: Sengai Gibon, a rich man
source: Nyogen Senzaki and Paul Reps, 101 Zen Stories (1919), Real Prosperity

title: Nelson Puts the Telescope to His Blind Eye
text:
On April 2, 1801, a British fleet attacked the Danish fleet and shore batteries at Copenhagen. Vice Admiral Horatio Nelson led the attacking squadron into the narrow channel, while the commander in chief, Admiral Sir Hyde Parker, watched from farther away with the heavier ships.

The fighting was fierce, and several British ships ran aground. Parker, unable to see clearly how the battle was going, hoisted signal 39, ordering the fleet to discontinue the action.

Colonel William Stewart, who was beside Nelson on his flagship, wrote an account of what happened next. Nelson was told of the signal and asked whether his own signal for close action was still flying. He ordered it kept up. Then he turned to his flag captain, Thomas Foley, and said he had only one eye and had a right to be blind sometimes. He raised his telescope to his blind eye and said he really did not see the signal.

Nelson kept fighting. Within a few hours the Danish line was largely silenced, and Nelson negotiated a truce. He was later made a viscount.
lesson: The person closest to the problem often sees it best. Know the purpose behind an order well enough to judge when following it would defeat it.
people: Horatio Nelson, Sir Hyde Parker, Thomas Foley, William Stewart
source: Colonel William Stewart's account, printed in Clarke and M'Arthur, The Life of Admiral Lord Nelson (1809); Robert Southey, The Life of Nelson
caveat: Some historians think Parker meant the signal as permission to withdraw at Nelson's discretion, and that the telescope scene was partly a joke.

title: The Louisiana Purchase
text:
In 1802 the United States learned that Spain had secretly returned the vast Louisiana territory to France and that Spanish officials had closed New Orleans to American trade. Farmers west of the Appalachians shipped their goods down the Mississippi through that port. President Thomas Jefferson sent Robert Livingston and then James Monroe to Paris to try to buy New Orleans and some land on the river.

Napoleon's plans had changed. His army sent to retake Saint-Domingue, the base for a new French empire in America, had been destroyed by the Haitian revolution and yellow fever. War with Britain was about to resume, and Louisiana could not be defended. In April 1803, to Livingston's astonishment, the French minister offered to sell not just New Orleans but all of Louisiana.

The American envoys had no authority for such a purchase, but they did not let the chance pass. They agreed to a price of 60 million francs plus the assumption of certain claims, about 15 million dollars in total. The treaty, dated 30 April 1803, roughly doubled the size of the United States. Livingston is reported to have said that it was the noblest work of their whole lives.

Jefferson had doubts about whether the Constitution allowed such an acquisition, but he set them aside, and the Senate approved the treaty that autumn.
lesson: Pay attention to the other side's situation, not just your own request. When they need to sell, a much larger deal may be possible than the one you came for.
people: Thomas Jefferson, Robert Livingston, James Monroe, Napoleon Bonaparte, Talleyrand, Francois Barbe-Marbois
source: Treaty between the United States and the French Republic (1803); diplomatic correspondence of Livingston and Monroe

title: Hamilton and Burr at Weehawken
text:
Alexander Hamilton and Aaron Burr had been rivals in New York law and politics for fifteen years. Hamilton distrusted Burr deeply and said so often, in letters and conversation. In 1800 he helped deny Burr the presidency, and in 1804 he opposed Burr's campaign for governor of New York, which Burr lost badly.

That spring a newspaper published a letter by a Dr. Charles Cooper, who claimed Hamilton had expressed at a dinner a "despicable opinion" of Burr. Burr, his career collapsing, wrote to Hamilton demanding that he acknowledge or deny it. Hamilton replied that he could not be held responsible for every inference others drew from his words. Letters went back and forth through their seconds, each more rigid. Neither would back down.

At dawn on July 11, 1804, the two men met on the dueling ground at Weehawken, New Jersey, across the Hudson from New York, the same area where Hamilton's eldest son Philip had been killed in a duel three years earlier. Burr's shot struck Hamilton in the abdomen. He died the next day. Burr, the sitting Vice President, was indicted for murder and his political career never recovered.
lesson: An insult left to fester, combined with pride that cannot back down, can destroy both sides. Find a way to clear the air before honor makes retreat impossible.
people: Alexander Hamilton, Aaron Burr
source: Hamilton-Burr correspondence of June 1804, The Papers of Alexander Hamilton, vol. 26; Ron Chernow, Alexander Hamilton (2004)

title: Napoleon Gives Up the Pratzen Heights
text:
In late November 1805 Napoleon's army was deep in Moravia, far from France, facing a combined Russian and Austrian army under the eyes of Tsar Alexander I and Emperor Francis II. Napoleon wanted a decisive battle before more enemy forces arrived, and he set out to make the allies attack him on ground of his choosing.

He acted as if he was weak and anxious. He asked for an armistice and talks, and treated the tsar's envoy in a way that suggested he feared battle. He gave up the commanding Pratzen Heights, in the center of the battlefield, and kept his right wing, toward the south, deliberately thin, while Marshal Davout's corps was hurrying from Vienna by forced marches to reinforce it. The allied staff concluded that the French right was vulnerable and could be turned, cutting Napoleon off from Vienna.

On the morning of 2 December 1805 the allies did exactly that. Column after column marched down from the Pratzen Heights to attack the French right, where Davout's arriving troops held them. As the heights emptied, Marshal Soult's corps, hidden in the fog in the valley below, climbed the slope and seized them as the sun broke through. The allied army was cut in two, and its southern wing was trapped and driven back against frozen ponds.

Austria made peace within weeks, and the Russians withdrew. Austerlitz became Napoleon's most celebrated victory.
lesson: Showing weakness at the right point can invite an opponent into the move you have prepared for. Make the attractive option the one that serves you.
people: Napoleon Bonaparte, Louis-Nicolas Davout, Jean-de-Dieu Soult, Alexander I, Mikhail Kutuzov
location: Austerlitz (modern Slavkov u Brna, Czech Republic)
source: Napoleon's 30th Bulletin of the Grande Armee (1805); David Chandler, The Campaigns of Napoleon (1966)

title: Napoleon Cannot Refuse Jenner
text:
In 1796 the English country doctor Edward Jenner showed that inoculation with cowpox could protect people against smallpox, one of the deadliest diseases of the age. Vaccination spread quickly across Europe, including France. Napoleon Bonaparte admired it and had his soldiers vaccinated.

When war between Britain and France resumed in 1803, Napoleon ordered the detention of British civilians who happened to be in France, and many British prisoners were held there for years. Their families appealed to Jenner, whose name was respected throughout Europe, and he wrote to the French authorities asking for the release of several of them.

According to Jenner's early biographer John Baron, one petition was presented to Napoleon, who was about to reject it. Then the Empress Josephine mentioned the name of the man who had signed it. Napoleon stopped and said, "Ah, Jenner, I can refuse nothing to that man." The prisoners were released. Jenner was able to secure the freedom of a number of British detainees this way, at a time when the two nations were at war.
lesson: Good done for everyone earns trust and goodwill even among opponents. A reputation for serving people beyond your own side can open doors that are closed to everyone else.
people: Edward Jenner, Napoleon Bonaparte, Josephine Bonaparte
source: John Baron, The Life of Edward Jenner (1827 to 1838)
caveat: Napoleon's exact words and the role of Josephine come from Jenner's admiring biographer and cannot be confirmed.

title: The Corps of Discovery Votes on Winter Camp
text:
By late November 1805 the Lewis and Clark expedition had reached the mouth of the Columbia River, after a year and a half of travel from St. Louis. Rain fell almost without pause, their clothes were rotting, and they had to decide where to spend the winter before starting home in spring.

The captains could simply have given an order. Instead, on 24 November, they put the question to the whole party. William Clark wrote down each person's choice in his journal: whether to stay on the north side of the river, cross to the south side and look for a site, or go back upstream.

Two names on that list stand out. York, Clark's enslaved servant, voted with the rest, at a time when he would have had no vote anywhere in the United States. Sacagawea, the Shoshone woman traveling with her husband and infant son, was also asked. Clark recorded her view under the nickname "Janey": she favored a place where there were plenty of "Potas", the wapato roots the party relied on for food.

Most of the party wanted to cross to the south side and examine the country there. They did, and in December they built Fort Clatsop near present-day Astoria, Oregon. They spent a hard, wet winter there and set out for home in March 1806.
lesson: Asking everyone, including those usually left out, makes a hard decision a shared one. People endure a tough plan better when they had a voice in choosing it.
people: Meriwether Lewis, William Clark, York, Sacagawea
location: Mouth of the Columbia River, Washington and Oregon, USA
source: The Journals of the Lewis and Clark Expedition, William Clark's entry for 24 November 1805 (ed. Gary Moulton)

title: Sacagawea Finds Her Brother
text:
Sacagawea was a Lemhi Shoshone girl captured by a Hidatsa raiding party around 1800 and taken far east to the villages on the Missouri River. There she became one of the wives of a French Canadian trader, Toussaint Charbonneau. In 1804 the American explorers Meriwether Lewis and William Clark hired Charbonneau as an interpreter, partly because Sacagawea could speak Shoshone. She joined the expedition in April 1805 with her infant son on her back.

The explorers needed horses to cross the Rocky Mountains, and the Shoshone were the people who had them. In August 1805, near the Continental Divide, Lewis met a Shoshone band and persuaded its chief, Cameahwait, to come back with him to meet Clark's party. On 17 August, as they met, Sacagawea began to dance and suck her fingers, a sign that these were her own people. During the council that followed she recognized Cameahwait as her brother. The account Nicholas Biddle later prepared from the expedition's records says she jumped up, ran to him, threw her blanket over him and wept.

The reunion helped the expedition get the horses and the guide it needed. Lewis wrote that the meeting was very affecting. Sacagawea learned that most of her family had died, though she found the son of a sister, whom she adopted. Then she continued west with the expedition to the Pacific.
lesson: Family ties can open doors that no amount of negotiation can. Keeping connection with where we came from can matter at the moment we least expect.
people: Sacagawea, Cameahwait, Meriwether Lewis, William Clark
location: Camp Fortunate, near Lemhi Pass, Montana, USA
source: The Journals of the Lewis and Clark Expedition, entries for 17 August 1805; Nicholas Biddle, History of the Expedition under the Command of Captains Lewis and Clark (1814)
caveat: Accounts disagree on details of Sacagawea's later life, but the reunion itself is recorded in the expedition journals.

title: The Secret Lines of Torres Vedras
text:
In October 1809 Lord Wellington (he became a duke only in 1814), commanding the British and Portuguese forces in Portugal, expected a much larger French army to invade again. He gave secret orders to his chief engineer, Richard Fletcher, to fortify the hills north of Lisbon. Over the next year thousands of Portuguese laborers built lines of forts, redoubts, ditches and dammed rivers across the peninsula between the Atlantic and the Tagus. Few people outside the project, including in London, understood their scale.

In 1810 Marshal Andre Massena invaded Portugal. Wellington fought a delaying action at Bussaco and then withdrew south. At the same time the Portuguese authorities ordered the countryside in front of the French cleared: crops gathered or destroyed, mills disabled, people moved behind the lines.

In October 1810 Massena arrived before Torres Vedras and found a barrier he had not known existed. He probed it, judged it too strong to attack, and after a month in front of it fell back to Santarem, hoping the British would weaken first. Instead his own army starved in the stripped land, while Wellington's troops were supplied by sea. In March 1811 Massena retreated to Spain, having lost many thousands of men to hunger and disease without fighting a major battle at the lines.
lesson: Quiet preparation done long before it is needed can decide a contest. Pick a position the opponent cannot afford to attack and let time and logistics work for you.
people: Arthur Wellesley, Viscount Wellington, Richard Fletcher, Andre Massena
source: The Dispatches of Field Marshal the Duke of Wellington; Charles Oman, A History of the Peninsular War, vols. 3 and 4

title: The Quartet
text:
A mischievous monkey, a donkey, a goat and a clumsy bear decided to form a string quartet. They got hold of music and instruments, a pair of violins, a viola and a cello, and sat down in a meadow under a lime tree to charm the world with their art.

They began to play, and the noise was dreadful. They stopped. The monkey had an idea: the trouble must be how they were sitting. The bear with the cello should face the viola, and the first violin should sit across from the second. They rearranged themselves and began again. It was just as bad.

They argued and moved their seats again and again. Then the donkey announced that he had the answer: they should all sit in a row. They tried that, and the noise did not improve.

At last they noticed a nightingale in the tree and asked him to settle the matter. How should they sit to play well? The nightingale answered that to be musicians, one needs skill and a finer ear than theirs. And you, my friends, however you sit, he said, you still will not be musicians.
lesson: Reorganizing a team cannot replace the skills it lacks. Before changing the structure again, ask whether the people have what the work requires.
people: A monkey, a donkey, a goat, a bear, a nightingale
source: Ivan Krylov, Fables (Basni), The Quartet (Kvartet), 1811

title: The Brave Little Tailor
text:
A little tailor swatted the flies on his jam bread and killed seven at one blow. Delighted, he stitched a belt reading "Seven at One Blow" and set out to see the world.

On a mountain he met a giant who read the belt and assumed it meant seven men. The giant squeezed a stone until water ran out; the tailor squeezed a soft cheese he had in his pocket until whey dripped. The giant threw a stone so high it was hard to see; the tailor threw a bird, which flew away and never came down. The giant carried a tree trunk; the tailor offered to carry the branches and simply rode on them. Invited to sleep in the giants' cave, he found the bed too big and lay in a corner, so when a giant smashed the bed with an iron bar in the night, the tailor survived, and the giants fled in terror when they saw him in the morning.

His fame reached the king, who promised him half the kingdom and his daughter if he killed two giants terrorizing the forest. The tailor climbed a tree above the sleeping giants and dropped stones on one, then the other. Each thought the other had hit him, and they fought until both were dead.

After more tasks, the tailor married the princess and became king.
lesson: Strength is only one kind of power. Reputation, nerve and a clear reading of an opponent's temper can let a small player win against much bigger ones.
people: The tailor, the giants, the king
source: Brothers Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmarchen, No. 20

title: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, Partners for Life
text:
Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm were born a year apart, in 1785 and 1786, in Hanau. When their father died in 1796, the family fell into poverty, and as the eldest sons they took responsibility for their mother and younger siblings. They studied law at Marburg and became fascinated by old German literature.

From 1806 they began collecting folk tales, from books and from storytellers such as Dorothea Viehmann, a tailor's wife who sold produce at market and knew dozens of stories. In December 1812 they published the first volume of Children's and Household Tales. Wilhelm, the gentler stylist, kept revising the tales through seven editions until 1857, while Jacob devoted himself more to the history of language, describing the regular sound shifts of the Germanic languages that are still called Grimm's law.

The brothers lived and worked together nearly all their lives. When Wilhelm married Dorothea Wild in 1825, Jacob, who never married, simply lived on in their household. In 1837 both lost their professorships at Gottingen because they joined five colleagues in protesting against the King of Hanover's abolition of the constitution. In 1841 they moved to Berlin, where they carried on the vast German Dictionary they had begun together in 1838.

Wilhelm died in 1859 and Jacob in 1863, still working on the letter F. Scholars finished the dictionary in 1961.
lesson: Siblings who keep working side by side can build something neither could finish alone. A shared life's project is a powerful bond.
people: Jacob Grimm, Wilhelm Grimm, Dorothea Viehmann
source: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmarchen (1812 to 1857); Jack Zipes, The Brothers Grimm (1988)

title: Cat and Mouse in Partnership
text:
A cat persuaded a mouse to set up house with her. To prepare for winter they bought a pot of fat, and after some thought they hid it in the safest place they knew: under the altar of the church, where nobody would dare take anything.

Before long the cat began to long for the fat. She told the mouse that a cousin had asked her to be godmother at a christening, and she went out. She went straight to the church and licked the top off the fat. When she came home, the mouse asked the baby's name. Top-off, said the cat.

Soon she was invited to another christening, she said, and this time she ate half the pot. The baby was called Half-done. The third time she finished it, and the name she gave was All-gone. The mouse thought these were very strange names, but she trusted her partner.

When winter came and food was scarce, the mouse suggested they go and fetch their store. They went to the church and found the pot empty. Suddenly the mouse understood everything, and she began to say so. The cat told her to be quiet or she would eat her too. But the words were already on the mouse's lips. The cat sprang on her, seized her and swallowed her.
lesson: Shared resources need shared oversight. If a partner's explanations keep getting stranger, check the store before it is gone and before you are the only one left trusting.
people: A cat, a mouse
source: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmarchen, No. 2, Cat and Mouse in Partnership

title: The Fisherman and His Wife
text:
A poor fisherman lived with his wife Ilsebill in a miserable hovel by the sea. One day he caught a great flounder, which spoke to him: it was an enchanted prince, it said, and begged to be let go. The fisherman released it at once.

When he told his wife, she asked whether he had wished for anything. He had not. She sent him back to ask the fish for a little cottage. He went reluctantly, called the flounder, and the wish was granted. Soon the cottage was not enough. She sent him back for a stone castle, then to make her king, then emperor, then pope. Each time the fisherman went unwillingly, and each time the sea looked darker and more troubled, but each time the flounder said, "Go home, she already is."

Every evening the wife lay awake, unable to sleep for wanting more. At last, watching the sunrise, she declared that she wanted to be like God, so that she could make the sun and moon rise.

The fisherman went out into a raging storm, with waves as high as church towers, and shouted the wish to the flounder. "Go home," it said. "She is sitting in her old hovel again." And there they are still sitting to this day.
lesson: Wanting more is natural, but a household that is never satisfied can lose everything it already had. Learn to recognize enough.
people: The fisherman, his wife Ilsebill, the flounder
source: Brothers Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmarchen, No. 19 (Von dem Fischer un syner Fru), from Philipp Otto Runge's Low German version

title: The Old Man and His Grandson
text:
There was once a very old man whose eyes had grown dim, whose ears were dull and whose knees trembled. When he sat at the table he could hardly hold his spoon. He spilled soup on the tablecloth, and some of it ran out of his mouth.

His son and his son's wife were disgusted. They made him sit in the corner behind the stove and gave him his food in an earthenware bowl, and not even enough of it. He sat there looking at the table with tears in his eyes.

One day his trembling hands could not hold the bowl, and it fell and broke. The young wife scolded him. He said nothing but only sighed. They bought him a wooden bowl for a few coins, and he had to eat from that.

Some time later the parents saw their little son, four years old, sitting on the floor gathering bits of wood together. "What are you doing?" his father asked. "I am making a little trough," the child answered, "for Father and Mother to eat out of when I am big."

The man and his wife looked at each other and began to cry. They brought the old grandfather back to the table at once, and from then on he always ate with them, and they said nothing if he spilled a little.
lesson: Children are watching how we treat our parents, and they are learning how to treat us. Patience with the old is also a lesson for the young.
people: An old grandfather, his son and daughter-in-law, their child
source: Brothers Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmarchen, No. 78 (Der alte Grossvater und der Enkel)

title: The Six Swans
text:
A king who had lost his way in a forest was rescued by a witch, on condition that he marry her daughter. He did, but he feared her, and he hid his six sons and one daughter, children of his first marriage, in a lonely castle. The new queen found out. She sewed six small white shirts with a spell in them, threw them over the boys, and they turned into swans and flew away.

The sister went in search of them. She learned that to break the spell she must not speak or laugh for six years, and must sew six shirts for them out of starwort flowers. If she said one word, all her work would be lost.

She sat in a tree and sewed. A king out hunting found her, fell in love with her and married her, though she never spoke. His mother hated the silent young queen. When she bore a child, the mother-in-law took it away, smeared the queen's mouth with blood and accused her of eating it. Two more times this happened. The queen could not defend herself without breaking her silence, and she was sentenced to be burned.

On the day of the fire, the six years ended. Six swans flew down. She threw the shirts over them and her brothers stood there as men, though the youngest kept a swan's wing where one sleeve was unfinished. Then at last she spoke, and told the king the truth.
lesson: Some of the most important things we do for family are slow, unseen and misunderstood. Keep faith with the work even when you cannot explain it.
people: A sister, her six brothers, the king, his mother
source: Brothers Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmarchen, No. 49 (Die sechs Schwane)

title: The Straw, the Coal and the Bean
text:
An old woman in a village was cooking a dish of beans. To get the fire going quickly, she lit it with a handful of straw. As she poured the beans into the pot, one bean slipped to the floor beside a piece of straw, and a moment later a glowing coal jumped out of the fire and landed next to them.

The three had each narrowly escaped death, so they decided to stay together and travel to a foreign country. Soon they came to a small brook with no bridge. The straw had an idea. It would lay itself across the water, and the others could walk over on it.

The coal, which was hot-tempered, went first and tripped boldly onto the straw. But halfway across, it heard the water rushing below. It grew frightened and stopped, and stood there unable to go forward or back. The straw caught fire under it, burned through and broke apart. The coal hissed into the water and went out.

The bean, still on the bank, laughed so hard at the sight that it burst. A wandering tailor who was resting by the brook took pity on it and sewed it up. He only had black thread, and that, the story says, is why beans have a black seam.
lesson: A shared plan can fail because one member freezes halfway through. Once a team commits to a crossing, hesitation in the middle is often worse than either going on or turning back.
people: A straw, a coal, a bean, a tailor
source: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmarchen, No. 18, The Straw, the Coal and the Bean

title: The Wolf and the Seven Young Kids
text:
A mother goat had seven young kids. One day she had to go into the forest for food, and she warned them: do not open the door to the wolf. You will know him by his rough voice and his black feet.

Soon there was a knock. "Open up, children, your mother is back," said a rough voice. The kids refused: their mother's voice was soft. The wolf went and ate a lump of chalk to soften his voice. When he came back, he put a black paw on the windowsill, and again they refused. He made a baker spread dough on his paw and a miller dust it with white flour. The third time, his voice was soft and his paw was white, and the kids opened the door.

The wolf swallowed six of them, one after another. Only the youngest, hiding in the clock case, escaped. The wolf lay down in the meadow and fell asleep.

When the mother returned, the youngest told her everything. She found the wolf snoring, cut open his belly with scissors, and out jumped all six kids alive, for in his greed he had swallowed them whole. They filled his belly with stones and sewed it up. When the wolf woke, thirsty, he went to the well, leaned over, and the stones pulled him in.
lesson: Warnings only protect children if they remember them under pressure. Teach the reasons behind the rules, because a clever threat will look different each time.
people: The mother goat, her seven kids, the wolf
source: Brothers Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmarchen, No. 5 (Der Wolf und die sieben jungen Geisslein)

title: Hansel and Gretel
text:
At the edge of a great forest lived a poor woodcutter with his wife and his two children, Hansel and Gretel. When famine came, the wife persuaded her husband to take the children deep into the woods and leave them there, so that there would be fewer mouths to feed.

Hansel overheard. That night he slipped out and filled his pockets with white pebbles, and as they walked into the forest the next day he dropped them along the way. When the children were abandoned, they waited until the moon rose and followed the shining pebbles home. The second time, the door was locked and Hansel could only drop crumbs of bread. The birds ate them, and the children were lost.

After three days they found a little house made of bread with a roof of cake and windows of sugar. An old woman welcomed them in. She was a witch who ate children. She locked Hansel in a stable to fatten him and made Gretel work. When she decided to bake Hansel, she told Gretel to crawl into the oven to test the heat. Gretel said she did not know how; the witch leaned in to show her, and Gretel pushed her in and slammed the door.

Gretel freed her brother. They filled their pockets with the witch's pearls and jewels and found their way home. The wife had died, and their father, who had not had a happy hour since leaving them, wept for joy.
lesson: Siblings who keep their heads and look out for each other can get through what neither could manage alone.
people: Hansel, Gretel, their father, their mother (later stepmother), the witch
source: Brothers Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmarchen, No. 15 (Hansel und Gretel)
caveat: In the 1812 first edition the woman is the children's own mother; the Grimms made her a stepmother in later editions.

title: Adams and Jefferson Begin Writing Again
text:
John Adams and Thomas Jefferson had worked side by side in the American Revolution and as diplomats in Europe, and they had become close friends. Party politics in the 1790s drove them apart. In the bitter election of 1800 Jefferson defeated Adams for the presidency, and Adams left Washington early on the morning of Jefferson's inauguration. For more than ten years the two men did not write to each other.

Their mutual friend Benjamin Rush, the Philadelphia physician, worked patiently to bring them together. He wrote to each of them, urging reconciliation, and even told Adams of a dream in which the two old friends renewed their correspondence.

On January 1, 1812, Adams sent Jefferson a short, friendly letter. Jefferson answered warmly. Over the next fourteen years they exchanged well over a hundred letters about politics, religion, books, old age and the meaning of the Revolution.

Both men died on the same day, July 4, 1826, the fiftieth anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. Adams's last words were reportedly that Jefferson still survived. Jefferson had died a few hours earlier.
lesson: A friendship broken by a quarrel can often be saved by a patient go-between and one short first letter. Someone has to write it.
people: John Adams, Thomas Jefferson, Benjamin Rush
location: Quincy, Massachusetts, and Monticello, Virginia, USA
source: Lester J. Cappon, ed., The Adams-Jefferson Letters (1959)
caveat: Adams's last words come from family recollection and are not certain.

title: Kutuzov Gives Up Moscow
text:
On 7 September 1812 the Russian army under Mikhail Kutuzov fought Napoleon's Grande Armee at Borodino, west of Moscow. It was one of the bloodiest days of the century, and both armies were badly mauled. Napoleon held the field, and the road to Moscow lay open.

A week later Kutuzov held a council of war in a peasant's hut at the village of Fili. Several generals wanted to fight again in front of the city. Kutuzov decided otherwise: as long as the army existed, Russia could still win the war; if the army was destroyed defending Moscow, both would be lost. He ordered the retreat through the city, and most of the inhabitants left with it.

Napoleon entered Moscow on 14 September and found it nearly empty. Fires broke out that night and burned much of the city, widely believed to have been set on Russian orders. Napoleon waited for Tsar Alexander to ask for peace. No answer came. Meanwhile Kutuzov moved his army south to Tarutino, where it rested, received reinforcements and covered the rich southern provinces.

In mid October, with winter approaching and supplies failing, Napoleon left Moscow. Blocked from the southern route, he retreated along the devastated road he had come by, harried by Kutuzov's army and Cossacks. Only a small fraction of the Grande Armee left Russia.
lesson: Do not confuse the symbol with the thing that actually decides the outcome. Giving up what looks most important can preserve what really is.
people: Mikhail Kutuzov, Napoleon Bonaparte, Alexander I
source: Dominic Lieven, Russia Against Napoleon (2009); Carl von Clausewitz, The Campaign of 1812 in Russia

title: Elizabeth Fry in Newgate Prison
text:
In 1813 Elizabeth Fry, a Quaker mother of a large family in London, was taken to see the women's section of Newgate Prison. She found some three hundred women and their children crowded into a few rooms, sleeping on the floor in filthy straw, cooking, washing and eating in the same space. Some had been convicted, others were waiting for trial. Visitors were warned that the women were wild and dangerous.

Fry brought clothes, and returned in earnest in 1816. She asked the women what they wanted for their children and, with their agreement, started a school inside the prison, choosing one of the prisoners as teacher. In 1817 she and other Quaker women founded an association to help the women prisoners. They brought in work, sewing and knitting that could be sold, read the Bible aloud, and drew up rules that the prisoners themselves agreed to, with monitors chosen from among them.

Officials were astonished at the change in behavior. In 1818 Fry described her work to a committee of the House of Commons, a rare role for a woman at the time. Her methods spread to prisons across Britain and Europe.
lesson: Treat people as capable of change and give them a say in their own improvement. Respect and responsibility often achieve more than control and contempt.
people: Elizabeth Fry
source: Memoir of the Life of Elizabeth Fry, edited by her daughters (1847); Report from the Select Committee on the Prisons within the City of London (1818)

title: Demyan's Fish Soup
text:
Demyan had invited his neighbor Foka to dinner and served him a pot of fish soup, the clear Russian ukha. It was very good soup, and Demyan was very proud of it.

"Come, dear friend, have another plate," he said. "Just look at it, a fine bream, and here are the giblets, and a bit of sturgeon. Eat, eat, do me the favor." Foka had already eaten one plate. He ate a second. Demyan filled it again. "Another spoonful, neighbor, it is made just for you. Wife, come and bow to our guest so he will eat more."

Poor Foka was sweating. He had eaten three plates and could not swallow another drop, but he did not want to offend his host. Demyan kept talking, kept praising, kept filling the plate, and would not hear a refusal.

At last Foka could bear no more. He seized his belt and his hat, jumped up, and fled out of the house without a word of goodbye. And from that day on he never set foot in Demyan's house again.

Krylov aimed the fable at a writer who forces his works on his listeners, but in Russian "Demyan's soup" has become a phrase for any kindness pressed on someone until it becomes a burden.
lesson: Generosity should serve the other person, not your own wish to be thanked. When someone says they have had enough, believe them.
people: Demyan, his neighbor Foka
source: Ivan Krylov, Fables, Demyan's Fish Soup (Demyanova ukha)

title: The Swan, the Pike and the Crayfish
text:
Ivan Krylov opens this fable with a warning: when partners are not in agreement, things go badly for them, and nothing comes of their work but trouble.

One day a swan, a pike and a crayfish decided to pull a cart loaded with goods. They harnessed themselves to it, all three together, and set to work with great effort. They strained and pulled with all their might. The load was not especially heavy, and with three strong animals pulling, the job should have been easy.

But the cart did not move an inch. The swan pulled upward, toward the clouds. The pike pulled toward the water. The crayfish, as crayfish do, crawled backward. Each was working hard, and each was sure the others were to blame.

Who was right and who was wrong, Krylov remarks, is not for us to judge. All that is known is that the cart is still standing there to this day.
lesson: Effort is wasted when a team pulls in different directions. Before working harder, make sure everyone agrees where the cart is going.
people: A swan, a pike, a crayfish
source: Ivan Krylov, Fables (Basni), The Swan, the Pike and the Crayfish (Lebed, Shchuka i Rak), 1814

title: The Little Shroud
text:
A mother had a little boy of seven who was so lovely that no one could look at him without liking him, and she loved him more than anything in the world. Suddenly he fell ill and died, and she could not be comforted. She wept for him day and night.

Soon after he was buried, the child began to appear at night in the places where he used to sit and play. When his mother wept, he wept too, and when morning came he vanished.

As his mother went on weeping without end, the child came one night in the little white shroud he had been buried in, with the wreath of flowers on his head. He sat on her bed and said, "Oh, Mother, stop crying, or I cannot fall asleep in my coffin. My shroud never dries, because of all your tears that fall on it."

The mother was shocked, and from then on she stopped weeping. The next night the child came again, holding a little candle, and said, "Look, Mother, my shroud is almost dry now, and I can rest in my grave." Then she gave her sorrow to God and bore it quietly and patiently. The child never came again, and slept in his little bed under the earth.
lesson: Love for someone we have lost can, in time, take the form of letting them rest. Moving through grief is not a betrayal of the one we mourn.
people: A mother, her dead child
source: Brothers Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmarchen, No. 109 (Das Totenhemdchen)

title: Napoleon Faces the Royal Troops at Laffrey
text:
In February 1815 Napoleon escaped from exile on the island of Elba and landed in southern France with about a thousand men. He marched north through the Alps toward Grenoble, avoiding the main roads where royalist troops waited.

On March 7, near the village of Laffrey, his way was blocked by a battalion of the 5th Line Infantry Regiment, sent by the royalist government to stop him. Their muskets were loaded. Napoleon's small force could not have fought its way through, and a single volley could have ended his return.

According to accounts of the scene, Napoleon ordered his own men to lower their weapons and walked forward alone toward the soldiers, wearing his familiar gray greatcoat. Within range, he stopped, and called out to the soldiers of the 5th that he was their emperor. He opened his coat and said that if any of them wanted to kill his emperor, here he was.

The soldiers did not fire. They broke ranks, shouting "Vive l'Empereur!", and went over to him. Regiment after regiment followed. On March 20 Napoleon entered Paris without a battle. The Hundred Days ended at Waterloo in June.
lesson: Facing people directly, and openly accepting the risk, can win them over when force or argument would fail.
people: Napoleon Bonaparte
source: Contemporary accounts of the Return from Elba, including memoirs of officers present
caveat: The exact words Napoleon used vary between accounts.

title: Shaka and the Buffalo Horns
text:
In the early 19th century the Zulu were a small chiefdom in what is now KwaZulu-Natal. Shaka kaSenzangakhona, who took power around 1816, had served in the army of Dingiswayo of the Mthethwa and built on military practices already developing in the region.

According to oral traditions and the accounts of the first European traders at his court, Henry Francis Fynn and Nathaniel Isaacs, Shaka reorganized warfare in several ways. He organized men by age into regiments that lived in military settlements and trained together. He favored a short, broad-bladed stabbing spear for close combat over throwing spears, used with a large cowhide shield. Tradition says he made his warriors go barefoot to move faster over rough ground.

The best-known reform is the battle formation called the buffalo horns. A strong central body, the chest, engaged the enemy head on. Two faster wings, the horns, ran out to surround the enemy's flanks and close behind it. A reserve, the loins, waited behind the chest, often seated with their backs to the fight so they would not get excited too early.

Within about a decade Shaka's warfare and conquests turned the Zulu into the dominant power in the region. The buffalo horns formation was still used by Zulu armies in 1879, when it overwhelmed the British camp at Isandlwana.
lesson: Lasting advantage comes from combining training, organization and tactics into one system. A small group can outgrow larger rivals by working differently, not just harder.
people: Shaka kaSenzangakhona, Dingiswayo
source: Henry Francis Fynn, The Diary of Henry Francis Fynn; Nathaniel Isaacs, Travels and Adventures in Eastern Africa (1836); Zulu oral traditions in the James Stuart Archive
caveat: Historians debate how many of these innovations Shaka actually originated, since the colonial sources tended to exaggerate his role.

title: The Bremen Town Musicians
text:
A donkey had worked for his master for many years, but now he was old and weak, and he learned that his master meant to get rid of him. So he ran away and set off for the city of Bremen, where he thought he could become a town musician.

On the road he met an old hunting dog whose master was going to kill him because he could no longer hunt. Then a cat who was going to be drowned because she could no longer catch mice. Then a rooster crowing his heart out because he was going to be made into soup. To each the donkey said: come with us to Bremen, you will find something better than death.

That night, in the forest, they saw a lit house. Inside a band of robbers sat at a table full of food. The animals made a plan. The donkey put his front hooves on the window sill, the dog jumped on his back, the cat climbed on the dog, and the rooster perched on the cat. Then all four made their music at once: braying, barking, meowing and crowing. They crashed through the window, and the terrified robbers fled into the woods.

When one robber crept back in the dark, the cat scratched him, the dog bit him, the donkey kicked him, and the rooster screamed. The robbers never returned, and the four friends liked the house so much that they stayed there.
lesson: People the world has written off can still be formidable together. Combine what each one has left, and use it at the same moment.
people: A donkey, a dog, a cat, a rooster, robbers
source: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmarchen, No. 27, The Bremen Town Musicians

title: The Four Skillful Brothers
text:
A poor man sent his four sons out into the world to learn a trade. After four years they came home. One had become a master thief, one an astronomer, one a huntsman and one a tailor whose magic needle could sew anything.

Their father tested them. The astronomer looked up into a tree and said there was a bird's nest with five eggs at the top. The thief climbed up and took the eggs from under the sitting bird without her noticing. The huntsman set the eggs on a table and broke all five with a single shot. The tailor sewed the shells back together, and when the chicks hatched, each had only a thin red line around its neck.

Soon afterward a dragon carried off the king's daughter, and the king promised her hand to whoever rescued her. The astronomer found her through his telescope, sitting on a rock far out at sea, with the dragon asleep with its head in her lap. The brothers sailed there, and the thief stole her out from under the dragon's head. On the way back the dragon woke and flew after them. The huntsman shot it through the heart, but the falling body smashed their boat. The tailor quickly sewed the planks together, and they all came safely home.

Then they quarreled over who had earned the princess. The king decided that since each had an equal claim, none of them would marry her. Instead he gave each brother a share of his kingdom as a reward.
lesson: Some tasks need every skill on the team, in sequence, and no one can claim the whole success. Arguing over sole credit can cost the prize everyone earned together.
people: Four brothers (a thief, an astronomer, a huntsman, a tailor), a king's daughter, a dragon
