source: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmarchen, No. 129, The Four Skillful Brothers

title: Frederick Douglass Remembers His Mother
text:
Frederick Douglass was born into slavery in Talbot County, Maryland, around 1818. In the first chapter of his autobiography, published in 1845, he described how he and his mother were separated when he was a baby, as was common, he said, in that part of Maryland: children were taken from their mothers to blunt the natural bond between them.

His mother, Harriet Bailey, was hired out to a farmer about twelve miles away. Douglass wrote that he saw her only four or five times in his life, and always at night. After a full day's work in the fields, she would walk the twelve miles on foot to see him, lie down with him and get him to sleep. Before he woke in the morning, she was gone, because she had to be back in the field at sunrise, and a slave not there in time could be whipped.

She died when he was about seven. He was not allowed to be with her during her illness or at her burial. He wrote that he received the news of her death with much the same feelings as he would the death of a stranger, because he had hardly known her.

In a later autobiography, written ten years after, Douglass added one more memory of her standing up for him against a cruel cook, and wrote that he learned only later that his mother had been able to read.
lesson: Love can find a way even under brutal conditions, sometimes at enormous personal cost. The effort a parent makes to be present is never wasted.
people: Frederick Douglass, Harriet Bailey
source: Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (1845), chapter 1; My Bondage and My Freedom (1855)

title: The Moon Cannot Be Stolen
text:
Ryokan, a Zen master and poet, lived the simplest kind of life in a little hut at the foot of a mountain. He owned almost nothing.

One evening, while Ryokan was out, a thief broke into the hut, only to find that there was nothing in it worth taking. As he was searching, Ryokan came home and caught him.

Instead of shouting for help, Ryokan spoke to him kindly. "You may have come a long way to visit me," he said, "and you should not go home empty-handed. Please take my clothes as a gift." He took off the clothes he was wearing and held them out.

The thief was bewildered. He took the clothes and slunk away into the night.

Ryokan sat down naked by his door and looked up at the moon, which was shining brightly over the mountain. "Poor fellow," he murmured. "I wish I could have given him this beautiful moon."
lesson: Meeting someone's worst moment with generosity instead of anger can unsettle them more than punishment. What matters most to you can never be taken anyway.
people: Ryokan, a thief
source: Nyogen Senzaki and Paul Reps, 101 Zen Stories (1919)
caveat: This is a traditional anecdote about the historical poet monk Ryokan, not a documented event.

title: Sequoyah and His Daughter Prove the Cherokee Script
text:
Sequoyah was a Cherokee silversmith who could neither read nor write English. He had seen white Americans read marks on paper and became convinced that his own people could have what he called talking leaves. Around 1809 he began trying to create a way of writing Cherokee. For years neighbors thought he was wasting his time, or worse, practicing witchcraft.

His first attempts used a symbol for every word, which proved unworkable. He then realized that Cherokee could be broken into a limited number of syllables. By about 1821 he had created a syllabary of some eighty-five characters, one for each sound.

According to accounts gathered by later writers, he taught the system to his young daughter, Ayoka, and the two demonstrated it to Cherokee leaders. Sequoyah was sent out of the room while the men dictated words to Ayoka, who wrote them down. Then he came back and read them aloud. Or, in other versions, the roles were reversed. Either way, the leaders were persuaded that the marks carried speech.

The script spread with astonishing speed. Because it fit the language so closely, Cherokee speakers could learn it in days. Within a few years a large part of the Cherokee Nation could read and write, and in 1828 the Cherokee Phoenix, a bilingual newspaper, began publication.
lesson: A child who learns first can help a parent prove an idea to the world. Patience in the face of mockery can turn a private project into a gift to a whole people.
people: Sequoyah (George Gist), Ayoka
location: Cherokee Nation (modern Tennessee, Alabama and Arkansas, USA)
source: Grant Foreman, Sequoyah (1938); accounts collected by later biographers and Cherokee histories
caveat: Details of the demonstration with Ayoka vary between accounts and come from later tradition.

title: The Rothschilds and the Five Arrows
text:
Mayer Amschel Rothschild grew up in the crowded Jewish quarter of Frankfurt, the Judengasse, where Jews lived under harsh restrictions. Starting as a dealer in rare coins, he built a trading and banking business and became agent to the Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel.

He had five sons, and he sent them out across Europe. Amschel stayed in Frankfurt, Salomon went to Vienna, Nathan to London, Carl to Naples and James to Paris. The brothers wrote to each other constantly, often in Hebrew script, and lent money, moved gold and shared information across borders in a way no single bank could. In his will of 1812, Mayer ordered that the business stay in the hands of his sons and their male heirs, and urged them to remain united.

In 1822 the Austrian emperor made the five brothers barons. Their coat of arms showed a hand holding five arrows, one for each brother, with the motto Concordia, Integritas, Industria: unity, integrity, diligence. Family tradition connects the arrows to the ancient story, told by Plutarch, of a Scythian king who showed his sons that a bundle of arrows could not be broken although each single arrow could.

For much of the nineteenth century the Rothschild houses, working together, were the most powerful bank in the world.
lesson: A family that spreads out but keeps faith with one another can be stronger than any single member. Unity is a decision renewed by constant contact, not a feeling.
people: Mayer Amschel Rothschild, Amschel, Salomon, Nathan, Carl and James Rothschild
location: Frankfurt, Germany; Vienna; London; Naples; Paris
source: Niall Ferguson, The House of Rothschild: Money's Prophets 1798 to 1848 (1998); Rothschild Archive, coat of arms of 1822
caveat: The deathbed arrow scene sometimes told of Mayer Amschel is family legend; the arms and the will are documented.

title: San Martin Steps Aside at Guayaquil
text:
By 1822 Jose de San Martin had led an army across the Andes, freed Chile and taken Lima, where he ruled as Protector of Peru. But Spanish armies still held the Peruvian highlands, and his forces were not strong enough to finish the war alone. In the north, Simon Bolivar had freed Venezuela, Colombia and now Ecuador.

The two liberators met at Guayaquil, in what is now Ecuador, on July 26 and 27, 1822. They talked in private and no record of the conversation was kept. Historians believe San Martin hoped for military help and that the two men disagreed about the future form of government, Bolivar favoring a republic and San Martin a constitutional monarchy.

Whatever was said, San Martin drew his own conclusion. He returned to Lima, and on September 20, 1822, before the first Congress of Peru, he resigned all his powers. He left Peru that night, went to Chile and Argentina, and later to Europe, where he lived quietly for the rest of his life. Bolivar's armies completed the liberation of Peru in 1824.
lesson: Sometimes the best thing a leader can do for the cause is to step aside so that someone else can finish it.
people: Jose de San Martin, Simon Bolivar
source: San Martin's letters and proclamation on leaving Peru; standard histories of South American independence
caveat: What was said at Guayaquil is unknown, and a letter attributed to San Martin explaining his reasons is of disputed authenticity.

title: Humphry Davy Opposes Faraday
text:
In 1812 Michael Faraday, a young bookbinder's apprentice in London with almost no schooling, attended lectures by Sir Humphry Davy, the most famous chemist in Britain. He wrote out his notes, bound them and sent them to Davy, asking for work. In 1813 Davy hired him as a laboratory assistant at the Royal Institution and soon took him on a long tour of Europe. Faraday learned fast.

By the early 1820s the assistant was making discoveries of his own: the first electric motor in 1821 and, in 1823, the liquefaction of chlorine. Davy, who had suggested the chlorine experiment, felt Faraday did not give him enough credit.

In 1823 friends nominated Faraday for Fellowship of the Royal Society. Davy was its President, and he opposed the election. He told Faraday to take down the certificate. Faraday replied that he had not put it up and could not take it down; his proposers had. In January 1824 Faraday was elected, with a single vote against him.

Faraday never spoke ill of his old patron. He went on to become one of the greatest experimental scientists in history.
lesson: Be glad when someone you trained begins to surpass you. A mentor's envy can turn a proud achievement into a sour rivalry.
people: Humphry Davy, Michael Faraday
location: Royal Institution and Royal Society, London, England
source: Faraday's correspondence; Henry Bence Jones, The Life and Letters of Faraday (1870)
caveat: Some details, such as the single vote against, rest on later accounts, and Davy's motives are interpreted differently by historians.

title: Moshoeshoe Spares His Grandfather's Killers
text:
In the 1820s southern Africa was torn by the wars and migrations known as the Lifaqane, or Difaqane. Whole communities were scattered, crops were destroyed, and some starving groups turned to cannibalism. In 1824 Moshoeshoe, a young Basotho chief, led his people to the flat-topped mountain of Thaba Bosiu, which became his stronghold. On the way, his aged grandfather Peete was captured by a band of cannibals and eaten.

Moshoeshoe's followers wanted revenge. The French missionary Eugene Casalis, who lived among the Basotho from 1833 and knew Moshoeshoe well, reported what the chief decided instead. When the cannibals were in his power, Moshoeshoe refused to kill them. He gave them cattle and land so they could live by farming and herding rather than by eating people. According to the tradition, he said they had become the living graves of his grandfather, and he would not disturb a grave.

Former enemies and refugees of many origins settled under his protection. From these scattered people Moshoeshoe built the Basotho nation, which became the kingdom of Lesotho, and he is honored there as its founder.
lesson: Mercy toward people who have done terrible harm can sometimes accomplish what revenge cannot. Turning enemies into neighbors is how lasting peace is built.
people: Moshoeshoe I, Peete
source: Eugene Casalis, The Basutos (1861); later Basotho oral histories
caveat: The chief's exact words and some details come from oral tradition recorded years later.

title: Darwin and FitzRoy Aboard the Beagle
text:
In 1831 Captain Robert FitzRoy, twenty six years old, was preparing HMS Beagle for a long survey voyage around South America. Commanding a ship meant isolation, and FitzRoy wanted a gentleman companion to share his meals and conversation. The post went to Charles Darwin, a twenty two year old graduate with a passion for natural history. The voyage lasted almost five years.

The two lived at close quarters and admired each other, but they also clashed. FitzRoy had a fierce temper. Darwin later recalled a quarrel in Brazil over slavery: FitzRoy said slaves he had asked had told him they were happy, and Darwin asked what such an answer was worth in front of their master. FitzRoy exploded and said they could not live together. Within hours he apologized.

After the voyage their paths split. Darwin's observations led him to evolution. FitzRoy, a devout believer, came to regret that his ship had carried the man who wrote On the Origin of Species, and spoke against it. He went on to found official weather forecasting in Britain. Worn down by overwork and disappointment, he took his own life in 1865. Darwin contributed to a fund for his family.
lesson: Close companions can drift apart when their beliefs collide. Disagreement need not erase gratitude for what you shared.
people: Charles Darwin, Robert FitzRoy
location: HMS Beagle, South America, and England
source: Charles Darwin, Journal of Researches (The Voyage of the Beagle, 1839); Darwin, Autobiography; Darwin's correspondence

title: The Emperor's New Clothes
text:
An emperor cared about nothing so much as fine clothes. Two swindlers came to his city, claiming to be weavers of a marvelous cloth. Not only was it beautiful, they said, but it had a special property: it was invisible to anyone who was unfit for his position or hopelessly stupid.

The emperor paid them handsomely, and they set up empty looms and pretended to work. He sent his honest old minister to inspect. The minister saw nothing, but he did not dare say so, in case it meant he was unfit for office, and he praised the colors and pattern. A second official did the same. Finally the emperor went himself. He saw nothing either, but since everyone around him admired the cloth, he admired it too.

On the day of the great procession, the swindlers pretended to dress him, and he walked through the streets under a canopy while the chamberlains held up a train that did not exist. The crowds cheered the beautiful clothes, because no one wanted to be thought a fool.

Then a small child said, "But he hasn't got anything on!" The words passed from person to person until the whole crowd was saying it. The emperor felt they were right, but he decided the procession must go on, and he walked even more proudly, with his chamberlains carrying the invisible train.
lesson: Groups can agree to a falsehood because each person fears looking foolish alone. Make it safe for someone to say the obvious, and say it yourself when you see it.
people: The emperor, two swindlers, ministers, a child
source: Hans Christian Andersen, The Emperor's New Clothes (Keiserens nye Klaeder), 1837

title: Grace Darling Rows Out into the Storm
text:
Grace Darling was the daughter of William Darling, keeper of the Longstone lighthouse on the Farne Islands off the coast of Northumberland. She grew up on the bare rock, helping her father keep the light.

Early on 7 September 1838, the steamship Forfarshire, bound from Hull to Dundee with engine trouble, was driven onto Big Harcar, a rock near the lighthouse, and broke in two. Many passengers were swept away. At first light Grace, then twenty-two, saw survivors clinging to the rock. The sea was too rough for the lifeboat from the mainland to set out at once.

Grace and her father launched their small rowing boat, a coble, and rowed about a mile along a sheltered route to the rock. William climbed onto it while Grace held the boat steady in the waves. They took off a woman and four men and brought them back to the lighthouse. Then William and two of the rescued crewmen went back for the remaining four. In all, nine people were saved.

The rescue made Grace famous across Britain. Gifts, letters and requests for locks of her hair poured in, and Queen Victoria sent money. Grace found the attention hard to bear. She died of tuberculosis in 1842, at twenty-six, and is buried at Bamburgh.
lesson: Courage is often shared: one person rows, another holds steady. Families that face danger side by side can do what neither could alone.
people: Grace Darling, William Darling
source: Contemporary newspaper reports; William Darling's lighthouse journal; Jessica Mitford, Grace Had an English Heart (1988)
caveat: Accounts differ on how much of the rowing Grace did, and the fame that followed added romantic details.

title: Captain Whitfield and John Manjiro
text:
In January 1841 a fourteen year old fisherman's boy named Manjiro and four companions were blown out to sea off the coast of Tosa, in Japan. They were wrecked on the uninhabited island of Torishima and survived for months on birds and rainwater. In June an American whaling ship, the John Howland, captained by William Whitfield of Fairhaven, Massachusetts, spotted them and took them aboard.

Japan was then closed to the outside world, and returning castaways risked death. Whitfield left the older men in Hawaii, but Manjiro, bright and curious, wanted to go with him. The captain took him home to Fairhaven, treated him as a son, and sent him to school, where he learned English, mathematics and navigation. The boy, called John Mung by the Americans, later sailed on whalers himself and earned money in the California Gold Rush.

In 1851 he managed to return to Japan. After long questioning by officials he was made a samurai and became a valued interpreter and teacher of English and navigation, helping Japan in its first dealings with the United States. His and Whitfield's descendants kept in touch for generations.
lesson: Kindness to a stranger far from home can change a life and build bridges far beyond it. Treat the outsider in your care as you would your own.
people: Nakahama Manjiro, William Whitfield
location: Torishima, Japan, and Fairhaven, Massachusetts, USA
source: Manjiro's account to Japanese officials (Hyoson Kiryaku, 1852); Emily V. Warinner, Voyager to Destiny (1956)

title: Fanny Mendelssohn's Song and Queen Victoria
text:
Fanny Mendelssohn was born in 1805, four years before her brother Felix. Both were musical prodigies, taught by the same teachers in Berlin. But their father, Abraham, wrote to Fanny in 1820 that music might become Felix's profession, while for her it could only ever be an ornament. A woman of her class was not expected to publish or perform in public.

Fanny kept composing: hundreds of songs and piano pieces, chamber music and choral works. Felix admired her and asked her opinion of his own work. Yet he too discouraged her from publishing. Instead, a few of her songs appeared in his early collections under his own name.

In 1842 Felix visited Queen Victoria and Prince Albert at Buckingham Palace. The queen offered to sing one of his songs and chose "Italien," which she loved. Felix wrote home that he had to confess that the song was actually by his sister. Victoria then sang one of his own, and sang it well.

Fanny married the painter Wilhelm Hensel, who encouraged her, and she hosted famous Sunday concerts at the family home in Berlin. In 1846, at forty, she finally began to publish under her own name. In May 1847 she died suddenly of a stroke while rehearsing. Felix, devastated, died six months later.
lesson: Talent kept hidden by family expectations is a loss to everyone. Encouraging a person to claim her own work is a gift we can give while there is still time.
people: Fanny Mendelssohn Hensel, Felix Mendelssohn, Abraham Mendelssohn, Queen Victoria
source: Felix Mendelssohn, letter to his mother, 19 July 1842; R. Larry Todd, Fanny Hensel: The Other Mendelssohn (2010)

title: The Overcoat
text:
Akaky Akakievich was a humble copying clerk in a government department in St. Petersburg. He loved copying and asked for nothing else. His colleagues mocked him and he barely noticed. His one problem was his overcoat, which had worn so thin that the bitter wind went straight through it. The tailor Petrovich declared it beyond repair. A new coat would cost about eighty rubles.

For months Akaky saved. He gave up his evening tea, did without candles and walked on tiptoe to spare his boots. At last the new coat was made, with a cat fur collar, and he wore it to the office as if it were a festival. That same night, crossing a dark square on his way home from a party, he was attacked by thieves who stripped the coat from his back.

The police were useless. Someone advised him to seek help from a certain Important Person, a man recently promoted who loved to show his authority. Akaky came at a moment when the Important Person had an old friend visiting and wanted to impress him. Instead of listening, he shouted at the clerk for his impertinence in coming directly to him, stamping his foot until Akaky nearly fainted.

Akaky went home through a blizzard, caught a fever and died within days. Afterward, the city was haunted by a ghost who pulled the coats off passersby, until one night he seized the Important Person's own coat.
lesson: To someone with little power, a moment of your attention can matter enormously. Never use a person in need as an audience for your own importance.
people: Akaky Akakievich, the Important Person, Petrovich the tailor
source: Nikolai Gogol, The Overcoat, 1842

title: Taras Bulba on Comradeship
text:
In Nikolai Gogol's novel, the old Cossack colonel Taras Bulba led his men in a campaign against the Poles. The Cossacks were besieging the city of Dubno, and things were going badly. Many of their number had left to pursue a raiding party of Tatars who had attacked their home camp, and those who remained were expecting a hard battle against a strong enemy.

Before the fighting, Taras gave his men a speech about what bound them together. A father loves his child, he said, and a mother loves her child, and a child loves father and mother. But even a beast loves its young. To be kin by the soul and not by blood was something only a human being could do. Such brotherhood had existed in other lands, he told them, but nowhere as it existed among the Cossacks. He asked them to stand together and to show what Cossack comradeship meant.

The Cossacks, moved by his words, went into the battle. They fought hard, and many of them fell, among them old friends of Taras. In the end Taras himself lost both of his sons in the war: Andriy, who had gone over to the Poles and whom Taras killed with his own hand, and Ostap, who was captured and executed by the enemy.
lesson: Bonds chosen through shared struggle can be as strong as family ties. A leader who names what holds a group together can help it stand in the hardest hour.
people: Taras Bulba, the Cossacks, his sons Ostap and Andriy
location: Russian Empire (novel set in Ukraine and Poland)
source: Nikolai Gogol, Taras Bulba (1842 edition), chapter 9

title: The Nightingale
text:
The Emperor of China learned from a book that the most wonderful thing in his realm was a nightingale that sang in the forest by the sea. No one at court had heard of it. At last a poor girl from the kitchen led the courtiers to the bird, and it came to the palace and sang. The Emperor wept with emotion and kept the nightingale at court.

Then a gift arrived from the Emperor of Japan: an artificial nightingale covered with diamonds, rubies and sapphires, which sang one waltz perfectly every time it was wound. The court adored it. It never tired and was always predictable. While everyone admired it, the real nightingale flew back to the forest, and it was banished from the empire.

One day the mechanical bird broke with a whirr. The watchmaker could repair it only enough for it to be played once a year. Five years later the Emperor fell gravely ill. He lay alone while Death sat on his chest, and he begged the golden bird to sing, but there was no one to wind it.

Suddenly the living nightingale appeared at the window and sang. Death listened, longed for his garden, and drifted away. The nightingale promised to come back and sing to the Emperor about the good and the evil kept hidden from him. When the servants came in to see their dead Emperor, he stood up and said good morning.
lesson: Polished, predictable reports are comfortable, but they cannot tell you what you need to hear. Keep the honest voices close, even if they do not perform on command.
people: The Emperor of China, the nightingale, the kitchen girl
source: Hans Christian Andersen, The Nightingale (Nattergalen), 1843

title: Old Fezziwig's Ball
text:
In A Christmas Carol, the Ghost of Christmas Past takes Ebenezer Scrooge back to the warehouse where he served his apprenticeship as a young man. There sits his old master, Fezziwig, a kindly old gentleman in a Welsh wig.

It is seven o'clock on Christmas Eve. Fezziwig calls out cheerfully to young Scrooge and his fellow apprentice Dick Wilkins: no more work tonight. The shutters go up, the floor is swept, the lamps are trimmed, and the warehouse turns into a ballroom. A fiddler arrives. In come Mrs. Fezziwig and the three Miss Fezziwigs, their young admirers, all the young people employed in the business, the housemaid, the baker, the cook. There is dancing, cake, roast, mince pies and plenty of beer, and Fezziwig and his wife dance with such energy that they seem to shine. At eleven the ball breaks up, and the Fezziwigs shake hands with every guest at the door.

The Ghost remarks that it was a small matter: Fezziwig spent only a few pounds. Scrooge, heated, defends him. His master had the power to make them happy or unhappy, to make their work light or burdensome, a pleasure or a toil. That power lay in words and looks and small things, and the happiness he gave was as great as if it had cost a fortune.

Then Scrooge falls quiet. He says he would like to say a word or two to his own clerk just now.
lesson: As someone's boss, you shape a large part of their daily happiness, mostly through small things that cost little. Use that power generously.
people: Mr. Fezziwig, young Ebenezer Scrooge, Dick Wilkins, the Ghost of Christmas Past
source: Charles Dickens, A Christmas Carol, Stave 2

title: Scrooge's Christmas
text:
Ebenezer Scrooge was a hard, grasping old moneylender in London. On Christmas Eve he turned away his cheerful nephew Fred's invitation to dinner, refused gentlemen collecting for the poor, and grudged his clerk, Bob Cratchit, both an extra lump of coal and the day off. Christmas, he said, was humbug.

That night the ghost of his dead partner, Jacob Marley, appeared in chains forged by his own greed and warned that three spirits would visit him. The Ghost of Christmas Past showed Scrooge the lonely boy he had been, the happy apprentice at Fezziwig's dances, and the young woman who had left him because he loved money more. The Ghost of Christmas Present took him to the Cratchits' small, happy feast, where Tiny Tim, a crippled little boy, said, "God bless us, every one," and the spirit warned that the child would die if nothing changed. The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come showed him a dead man whom nobody mourned, his belongings sold off by servants, the Cratchit home grieving for Tim, and finally a neglected gravestone with Scrooge's own name.

Scrooge woke on Christmas morning, alive and weeping with joy. He sent the biggest turkey in the shop to the Cratchits, gave generously to the poor, and went to dinner at Fred's. The next day he raised Bob's salary. He became a second father to Tiny Tim, who did not die, and as good a friend and master as the old city knew.
lesson: It is never too late to change how you treat the people around you. Generosity done today is worth more than regret later.
people: Ebenezer Scrooge, Bob Cratchit, Tiny Tim, Fred
source: Charles Dickens, A Christmas Carol (1843)

title: The Hare and the Hedgehog
text:
On a fine Sunday morning, a hedgehog went out to look at his turnip field and met a hare. The hare, who thought very well of himself, mocked the hedgehog's short crooked legs. Stung, the hedgehog challenged him to a race and bet him a gold coin and a bottle of brandy that he would win. The hare laughed and agreed.

The hedgehog went home first, he said, for breakfast. There he told his wife to come with him to the field. Hedgehogs look so alike that no one could tell husband and wife apart. He placed her at the far end of a furrow and went back to the near end, where the hare was waiting.

The hare ran down his furrow like the wind. The hedgehog went a few steps and then sat still. When the hare reached the far end, the hedgehog's wife rose up from the other furrow and called out that she was already there.

The hare could not believe it. He demanded another run and raced back. At the other end, the hedgehog popped up: already here. The hare ran again and again, seventy three times, and each time a hedgehog was waiting. On the seventy fourth run he collapsed and died. The hedgehog took the gold coin and the brandy home, and lived happily with his wife.
lesson: Do not accept a contest on your opponent's terms when you can set the terms yourself. And never assume that the one who looks slow has no plan.
people: A hedgehog, his wife, a hare
source: Brothers Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmarchen, No. 187, from a Low German tale published by Wilhelm Schroder

title: The Snow Queen
text:
A wicked troll once made a mirror that shrank everything good and beautiful and magnified everything ugly. It shattered, and its tiny splinters flew all over the world. Kai, a boy who loved his neighbor and playmate Gerda, got one splinter in his eye and another in his heart. At once he turned cold and mocking. He laughed at Gerda, mimicked old people and found fault with everything.

One winter day the Snow Queen swept him up in her great white sleigh and carried him off to her palace in the far north. Everyone said he was dead. Gerda refused to believe it and set off alone to find him.

Her journey was long. She was held by an old woman with an enchanted garden, helped by a prince and princess, captured by robbers and freed by a wild robber girl, who gave her a reindeer to carry her north. A wise Finnish woman said she could give Gerda no greater power than she already had: her own pure, loving heart.

In the Snow Queen's empty hall of ice Gerda found Kai, blue with cold, trying to arrange pieces of ice into the word Eternity. He did not even know her. Gerda threw her arms around him and wept, and her hot tears ran into his chest and melted the ice in his heart and the splinter with it. Then Kai burst into tears too, and the splinter washed out of his eye. Together they went home, and found that they had grown up, though they were still children at heart.
lesson: When someone you love turns cold, patient and faithful love can sometimes reach them where argument cannot. Do not give up on people too soon.
people: Gerda, Kai, the Snow Queen
source: Hans Christian Andersen, The Snow Queen (1844)

title: The Rochdale Pioneers
text:
In the 1840s Rochdale, a mill town near Manchester, was suffering. Flannel weavers had lost a strike, wages were low, and shopkeepers often sold adulterated food at high prices and on credit that trapped families in debt. Earlier attempts at cooperative shops in Britain had mostly failed.

A group of working men, many of them weavers, formed the Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers. Over most of a year they saved a pound each, a large sum for them, some paying in a few pence a week. With the small capital that resulted, on 21 December 1844 they opened a shop on Toad Lane with a meager stock of butter, sugar, flour, oatmeal and candles. Local accounts say boys jeered at them through the window.

What made the Rochdale Pioneers different was their set of rules. Membership was open to anyone. Each member had one vote, regardless of how much capital he held. Goods were sold for cash only, at market prices, and were pure and honestly weighed. Profits were returned to members in proportion to how much they had bought. Part of the surplus was set aside for education.

The shop survived and grew. Within a few decades the society had many branches and thousands of members, and its rules, known as the Rochdale Principles, became the model for the cooperative movement around the world.
lesson: Ordinary people who pool their resources under fair, clear rules can build something lasting. Good rules matter as much as good intentions.
people: Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers
source: George Jacob Holyoake, The History of the Rochdale Pioneers (1857)

title: All for One, One for All
text:
In Alexandre Dumas's novel, young d'Artagnan arrived in Paris from Gascony in 1625, hoping to join the king's musketeers. On his first morning he managed to offend three musketeers in turn, Athos, Porthos and Aramis, and he agreed to fight each of them in a duel that same day, one after the other, at the same place.

When they had all gathered and Athos and d'Artagnan crossed swords, a patrol of Cardinal Richelieu's guards arrived to arrest them, since dueling was forbidden. The three musketeers were outnumbered, five to three. D'Artagnan had to choose a side, and he chose them. The four fought together and beat the guards. From that day the four were inseparable.

Their friendship was tested again and again. When they rode to England to recover the queen's diamond studs before the cardinal could expose her, they were ambushed one by one along the road. Porthos was left behind after a duel, Aramis was wounded, Athos was trapped in a fight at an inn. Each sacrifice kept d'Artagnan moving, until he reached London with only his servant and brought the studs back in time.

Their motto was a promise each made to the others: all for one, one for all.
lesson: Friends who commit to each other completely can achieve what none could alone. Sometimes being a good teammate means taking the blow so another can carry the mission forward.
people: D'Artagnan, Athos, Porthos, Aramis
source: Alexandre Dumas, The Three Musketeers (Les Trois Mousquetaires), 1844

title: The Bronte Sisters Publish as Men
text:
Charlotte, Emily and Anne Bronte grew up in the parsonage at Haworth, on the Yorkshire moors, with their father, a clergyman, and their brother Branwell. Their mother and two older sisters died when they were children. Shut in among the moors, the children invented imaginary kingdoms and wrote tiny books about them.

In the autumn of 1845, Charlotte came upon a notebook of Emily's poems. Emily was furious that her privacy had been invaded, but Charlotte was convinced the poems were remarkable, and Anne then shyly offered her own. In 1846 the three published a volume together, paying the costs themselves. They chose the names Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell, keeping their own initials. Charlotte later explained that they did not want to be judged with the prejudice reserved for women writers. The book sold two copies.

They were not discouraged. Each had been writing a novel. In 1847 Charlotte's Jane Eyre became a sensation, and Emily's Wuthering Heights and Anne's Agnes Grey followed. Critics speculated that the Bells were one man. In 1848 Charlotte and Anne traveled to London to prove to their publisher that they were separate people.

Their success was short. Branwell died in September 1848, Emily in December, and Anne the following May. Charlotte's friend Elizabeth Gaskell told their story in her biography of 1857.
lesson: Siblings who believe in each other's talent can push one another past discouragement. A first failure is often only the first draft of a success.
people: Charlotte Bronte, Emily Bronte, Anne Bronte
source: Charlotte Bronte, Biographical Notice of Ellis and Acton Bell (1850); Elizabeth Gaskell, The Life of Charlotte Bronte (1857)

title: Elizabeth Barrett Elopes with Robert Browning
text:
In the 1840s Elizabeth Barrett was one of the most famous poets in England, and also an invalid who rarely left her room at 50 Wimpole Street in London. Her father, Edward Moulton-Barrett, a wealthy and domineering man, did not allow any of his children to marry.

In January 1845 the younger poet Robert Browning wrote to her: "I love your verses with all my heart, dear Miss Barrett," adding that he loved her too. She answered, and a correspondence began that grew into nearly six hundred letters. In May 1845 he visited her for the first time, and after that came regularly, always when her father was out. They fell in love and knew that he would never consent.

On 12 September 1846 Elizabeth, forty, slipped out of the house with her maid and married Robert at St Marylebone Church. She returned home as if nothing had happened. A week later she left for good, taking her maid and her dog, Flush, and the couple traveled to Italy.

Her father disinherited her and never spoke to her again. He returned her letters unopened. In Italy, her health improved remarkably. In 1849, at forty-three, she gave birth to a son. The couple settled in Florence. In 1850 she published Sonnets from the Portuguese, the love poems she had written to Robert during their courtship, and other works followed. She died in his arms in 1861.
lesson: A parent's control can drive a child to choose love over family, at a lasting cost to both. Love that is forbidden instead of understood is love lost.
people: Elizabeth Barrett Browning, Robert Browning, Edward Moulton-Barrett
source: The Letters of Robert Browning and Elizabeth Barrett Barrett, 1845 to 1846 (1899); Margaret Forster, Elizabeth Barrett Browning (1988)

title: Who Survived the Donner Party
text:
In the spring of 1846, a group of emigrant families left Illinois and the Midwest for California. On bad advice they took an untested shortcut, the Hastings Cutoff, which cost them weeks. By late October they were trapped by early snow in the Sierra Nevada, near what is now Donner Lake. Of the eighty-seven people in the group, nearly half died over the winter from cold, starvation and exhaustion, and some survivors resorted to eating the dead.

Nearly a century and a half later, the anthropologist Donald Grayson examined who lived and who died. His study, published in 1990, found a strong pattern. Age and sex mattered: young children and the elderly died at high rates, and women survived better than men. But one of the clearest factors was family. People traveling with large family groups were much more likely to survive than those traveling alone. Most of the young single men, the teamsters and hired hands who had joined the group without relatives, died.

Grayson suggested a reason. Family members shared food, warmth and care with one another when there was not enough for everyone. Someone alone in the snow had no one whose survival was bound up with his own. The Reed family, for example, lost no members, while many of the solitary men were among the first to die.
lesson: In a crisis, the people bound to us matter more than strength. Building and keeping close ties is a form of survival, not only of comfort.
people: Donner Party members; Donald K. Grayson
source: Donald K. Grayson (1990). Donner Party deaths: A demographic assessment. Journal of Anthropological Research, 46(3), 223 to 242
caveat: The exact numbers vary slightly between accounts because membership of the party is counted in different ways.

title: The Story of a Mother
text:
A mother sat by her sick little child through a winter night. An old man came in to warm himself. She dozed for a moment, and when she woke, the old man and her child were gone. The old man was Death.

She ran out into the snow to follow. Night, sitting in the snow, would show her the way only if the mother sang all the songs she had sung to her child. A thornbush would show her only if she warmed it against her breast, and she pressed it so close that the thorns drew blood. A lake would carry her across only if she gave it her eyes, and she wept them out into the water. An old woman who kept Death's greenhouse wanted her long black hair, and she gave it, taking the old woman's white hair in exchange.

In the greenhouse, where every human life grew as a plant, she found her child's small crocus by its heartbeat. When Death arrived, she seized two other flowers and threatened to tear them up unless he gave her child back. Death asked if she would make another mother as unhappy as she was. He returned her eyes, and showed her in a well the two possible futures for her child: one full of happiness, one full of misery and fear.

Not knowing which was her child's, she fell to her knees and prayed not to be heard if she asked against God's will. Death then carried her child away to the unknown land.
lesson: Love will give almost anything for a child. But sometimes the last act of love is to accept what we cannot control.
people: A mother, Death, Night, an old woman
source: Hans Christian Andersen, The Story of a Mother (Historien om en Moder), 1847

title: The Choctaw Gift to Starving Ireland
text:
In the early 1830s the United States government forced the Choctaw Nation off its homelands in Mississippi and marched its people west to Indian Territory, in what is now Oklahoma. Thousands died of exposure, hunger and disease on the way, on one of the routes later remembered as the Trail of Tears.

Fifteen years later, news reached them of another catastrophe. In Ireland the potato crop had failed again and again, and hundreds of thousands of people were dying of hunger and disease. In March 1847 Choctaw people gathered at a meeting in Skullyville, in Indian Territory, and took up a collection for Irish famine relief. They raised 170 dollars, a considerable sum for a community that had little, and sent it on through a relief committee.

The gift was reported in American newspapers at the time and then largely forgotten outside the two peoples. In Ireland it was never fully forgotten. In 2017 the town of Midleton in County Cork unveiled a large steel sculpture called Kindred Spirits, a ring of tall eagle feathers, to honor the Choctaw donation, and Irish leaders, among them President Mary Robinson in 1995, have visited the Choctaw Nation to give thanks.
lesson: Those who have suffered can be the quickest to recognize suffering in others. Giving from little, to strangers far away, creates bonds that last generations.
people: Choctaw Nation
source: Arkansas Intelligencer and other contemporary American newspaper reports (1847); records of famine relief committees

title: Semmelweis Was Right and Still Lost
text:
In the 1840s, at the Vienna General Hospital, the young Hungarian doctor Ignaz Semmelweis was troubled by a puzzle. Women giving birth in the clinic run by doctors and medical students died of childbed fever far more often than those in the clinic run by midwives. In 1847 a colleague cut his finger during an autopsy and died with the same symptoms. Semmelweis concluded that doctors coming from the dissecting room were carrying something from corpses to the mothers.

He ordered everyone to wash their hands in a chlorinated lime solution before examining patients. Deaths in his clinic fell sharply, to roughly the level of the midwives' clinic.

But Semmelweis was slow to publish, and he could not explain the mechanism, since germ theory did not yet exist. Many senior doctors resisted the idea that they themselves were killing patients. His appointment in Vienna was not renewed, and he moved to Pest. When he finally published his book in 1861 and critics dismissed it, he wrote open letters calling his opponents ignorant and murderers. The insults made enemies, not converts. In 1865 he was committed to an asylum and died there two weeks later. Only after Pasteur and Lister did his work win acceptance.
lesson: Being right is not enough to change minds. If you need others to adopt your idea, explain it patiently and give them a way to change without being humiliated.
people: Ignaz Semmelweis
location: Vienna, Austria, and Pest (modern Budapest, Hungary)
source: Ignaz Semmelweis, The Etiology, Concept and Prophylaxis of Childbed Fever (1861); Sherwin B. Nuland, The Doctors' Plague (2003)
caveat: Historians note that his rejection had several causes, including the lack of a theory to explain his results, so his abrasiveness was only part of the story.

title: Savitribai and Jyotirao Phule Open a School for Girls
text:
Jyotirao Phule was born in 1827 in Pune into a family of the Mali caste, gardeners, who were low in the caste hierarchy. He was married at thirteen to Savitribai, who was about nine and could not read. Jyotirao taught her at home, and she then trained as a teacher.

In 1848 the couple opened a school for girls in Pune, in a house called Bhide Wada. It was one of the first schools for girls run by Indians, and Savitribai became its teacher, perhaps the first woman teacher of her kind in India. They also opened their classes to children of the castes considered untouchable.

Many in the city were outraged. According to accounts handed down about her, as Savitribai walked to school people insulted her and threw mud, dung and stones at her. She carried a second sari in her bag and changed when she arrived. Under pressure from the community, Jyotirao's father made the couple leave the family home. They kept going. By the early 1850s they were running several schools.

The couple went on together to fight caste discrimination and child marriage, opened a home for widows and their infants, and adopted a widow's son. Jyotirao died in 1890. Savitribai, a poet as well as a teacher, died in 1897 of plague, caught while caring for patients during an epidemic.
lesson: A husband and wife united by a cause can face down a whole society. Sharing knowledge with the people closest to us can be the start of a revolution.
people: Savitribai Phule, Jyotirao Phule
source: Rosalind O'Hanlon, Caste, Conflict and Ideology (1985); Jyotirao Phule's writings
caveat: Some details, such as the stones and the second sari, come from later biographies and tradition.

title: Lemminkainen's Mother
text:
Lemminkainen, a reckless and boastful young hero, went to the cold northern land of Pohjola to win a bride. To earn her, he was given dangerous tasks, the last of which was to shoot the swan of Tuonela, the river of the dead. On its bank an old blind cowherd, whom he had once insulted, was waiting for him. He struck Lemminkainen with a water snake, and the young man fell into the river. The son of Tuoni, god of the dead, cut his body into pieces and threw them into the black water.

At home, Lemminkainen had left a comb with his mother, saying that if it ever began to bleed, misfortune had come to him. One day blood dripped from the comb. His mother set off at once, searching across the world, asking the trees, the road and the moon. At last the sun told her where her son lay.

She had the smith Ilmarinen forge her a huge copper rake with a long handle. She waded into the river of death and raked it again and again, bringing up his shirt, his stockings, his hat, and then piece after piece of his body. She fitted them together, bone to bone, vein to vein, and sang charms over them.

Still he lay lifeless. She sent a bee to fetch magical honey from beyond the ninth heaven and anointed him with it. Lemminkainen woke. His mother led him home.
lesson: A parent's love can be more stubborn than any danger. Even when a child brings trouble on himself, the persistence of those who love him can bring him back.
people: Lemminkainen, his mother, the blind cowherd, Ilmarinen
source: Elias Lonnrot, Kalevala (1849 edition), Runos 14 and 15

title: It Could Always Be Worse
text:
A Yiddish folk tale tells of a poor man who lived in a one-room hut with his wife, his mother and his many children. The house was so crowded and noisy that he could not bear it. The children fought, his wife and mother quarreled, and there was no peace anywhere. At his wits' end, he went to the rabbi for advice.

The rabbi asked whether he had any animals. A few chickens, the man said, a rooster, a goose, a goat and a cow. "Take the chickens, the rooster and the goose into the house with you," said the rabbi. The man was puzzled but did as he was told. Now the hut was worse than ever, full of clucking and crowing and honking.

He went back to the rabbi, who told him to bring in the goat. When he came back again, the rabbi told him to bring in the cow as well. Each time the poor man came back more desperate. The house was chaos: animals underfoot, feathers in the soup, nowhere to sleep.

At last the rabbi said: "Go home and let all the animals out of the house." The man did. That night his family slept peacefully. The hut seemed quiet and spacious. He went back to the rabbi and thanked him: life had never been so sweet.
lesson: A crowded, noisy home can feel unbearable until we remember how much worse it could be. Gratitude often depends on what we compare our life with.
people: A poor man, his family, a rabbi
source: Yiddish folk tradition; retold by Margot Zemach, It Could Always Be Worse (1976)

title: The Underground Railroad
text:
Before the American Civil War, thousands of enslaved people escaped from the South to the free states and Canada. Many were helped along the way by an informal network that came to be called the Underground Railroad. It had no headquarters and no membership list. It was made up of free Black communities, formerly enslaved people, Quakers and other white abolitionists, each of whom usually knew only the next few links in the chain. The secrecy protected everyone.

In Philadelphia, William Still, a free Black clerk with the Pennsylvania Anti-Slavery Society, helped run the city's Vigilance Committee, which sheltered, fed and moved fugitives onward. Against all caution, he kept written records of the people he helped, their names, where they came from and how they escaped, hiding the notes so they could one day reunite families. One of the people he interviewed turned out to be his own brother, whom his mother had been forced to leave behind in slavery decades earlier.

Still's records include Henry "Box" Brown, who had himself shipped from Richmond to Philadelphia in a wooden crate in 1849, and the many trips of Harriet Tubman, who returned south again and again to guide others out.

After the war, in 1872, Still published his notes as The Underground Rail Road, one of the few detailed records of how the network actually worked, told largely through the stories of the people who escaped.
lesson: A loose network of people who each do their part, and trust the next person, can achieve what no single hero could. Small, reliable links make a strong chain.
people: William Still, Harriet Tubman, Henry "Box" Brown, Vigilance Committee members
location: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and routes across the eastern USA and Canada
source: William Still, The Underground Rail Road (1872); Eric Foner, Gateway to Freedom (2015)

title: Charles Darwin Loses His Daughter Annie
text:
Anne Elizabeth Darwin, called Annie, was the second child and eldest daughter of Charles and Emma Darwin. She was lively and affectionate, and her father adored her. In 1850, at nine, she began to fall ill with a fever and sickness that would not go away.

In March 1851 Darwin took her to Malvern for the water cure of Dr James Gully, which he had tried himself. She seemed to improve, then grew worse. Darwin hurried back to her side, while Emma, heavily pregnant, stayed at home at Down House. For days he sat with her and wrote anxious letters to Emma describing every change. Annie died on 23 April 1851, at the age of ten. Darwin was too distraught to stay for the funeral.

A week later he wrote a private memorial of her, describing her joy, her tenderness and the way she used to fling herself into his arms. "We have lost the joy of the household, and the solace of our old age," he wrote. "She must have known how we loved her."

Darwin's biographers believe the loss did much to end what remained of his Christian faith, since he could no longer reconcile her death with a loving God. Emma kept a small box of Annie's things. Generations later, his great-great-grandson Randal Keynes used it as the starting point of a book about the family.
lesson: Grief for a child can reshape everything we believe. Writing down what we loved about someone can help us keep them.
people: Charles Darwin, Emma Darwin, Annie Darwin
location: Malvern and Down House, Kent, England (UK)
source: Charles Darwin, memorial of Anne Elizabeth Darwin (30 April 1851), Darwin Correspondence Project; Randal Keynes, Annie's Box (2001)
caveat: How far Annie's death, rather than his scientific work, ended Darwin's faith is a matter of interpretation.

title: Ahab's Obsession
text:
The whaling ship Pequod sailed from Nantucket on what its owners and crew believed was an ordinary voyage for whale oil. Its captain, Ahab, stayed hidden in his cabin for days. When he finally appeared on deck, walking on a leg made of whale bone, he gathered the crew and nailed a gold doubloon to the mainmast. It would go to the first man to sight the white whale, Moby Dick, the whale that had taken his leg.

Ahab had the crew swear to hunt the white whale to the death, and in the excitement they cheered. Only the first mate, Starbuck, objected. He had come to hunt whales for profit, he said, not his captain's vengeance on a dumb animal, and to be enraged with a dumb thing seemed blasphemous. Ahab overrode him.

As the voyage went on, Ahab grew more consumed. He destroyed his navigation instrument. When the captain of another ship, the Rachel, begged for help searching for his lost son, Ahab refused. Starbuck once stood outside Ahab's cabin with a loaded musket, thinking of killing him to save the crew, and could not do it.

They found the whale. For three days Ahab chased it. On the third day the whale rammed and sank the Pequod, and Ahab, caught by his own harpoon line, was dragged under. Only the narrator, Ishmael, survived, floating on a coffin until the Rachel picked him up.
lesson: When a leader's personal goal quietly replaces the shared one, everyone pays for it. Watch for that in yourself, and do not let enthusiasm in the moment commit your people to someone else's obsession.
people: Captain Ahab, Starbuck, Ishmael, the crew of the Pequod
source: Herman Melville, Moby-Dick; or, The Whale, 1851

title: Bartleby, the Scrivener
text:
The narrator is a comfortable, elderly lawyer with chambers on Wall Street, where he employs copyists to make handwritten copies of legal documents. Business is growing, so he hires a new one: Bartleby, pale, neat and silent. At first Bartleby copies enormous amounts, day and night, though mechanically and without cheer.

Then one day, asked to help check a copy against the original, Bartleby answers mildly: "I would prefer not to." The lawyer is stunned. Soon Bartleby prefers not to check anything, then not to run errands, and finally not to copy at all. He simply stands looking out the window at a blank brick wall. The lawyer discovers he has been living in the office.

The lawyer tries everything. He reasons, offers money, and orders him to leave. Bartleby prefers not to. Unable to bring himself to throw out a helpless man, the lawyer finally moves his own offices instead. The new tenants have Bartleby removed. When the lawyer visits, he offers to take Bartleby into his own home, and Bartleby prefers not to. He is taken to the Tombs prison as a vagrant.

There he refuses to eat and dies. Afterward the lawyer hears a rumor that Bartleby once worked in the Dead Letter Office in Washington, sorting letters meant for people who had died. "Ah Bartleby! Ah humanity!"
lesson: Some problems at work are really human crises that rules and incentives cannot reach. You may not be able to fix them, but you can still see the person and refuse to treat them as just a problem.
people: The lawyer narrator, Bartleby, Turkey, Nippers, Ginger Nut
source: Herman Melville, Bartleby, the Scrivener: A Story of Wall Street, 1853

title: Perry's Black Ships
text:
For more than two centuries Tokugawa Japan had strictly limited contact with the outside world, allowing only Dutch and Chinese traders at Nagasaki. Foreign ships that tried to open relations had been turned away.

In July 1853 Commodore Matthew Perry of the United States Navy sailed into Edo Bay with four warships, two of them steam frigates belching black smoke. The Japanese called them the black ships. Perry refused orders to go to Nagasaki. He insisted on delivering a letter from President Millard Fillmore asking for trade, coaling stations and protection for shipwrecked sailors, and he made clear that he would deliver it in person or by force if necessary. Japanese officials received the letter at Kurihama. Perry announced that he would return the next year for an answer and sailed away.

The shogunate was divided and alarmed. Its coastal defenses were no match for the guns of steam warships, and it knew what had happened to China in the Opium War. It took the unusual step of consulting the daimyo, which weakened its authority.

Perry came back in February 1854 with a larger squadron. He brought gifts including a miniature steam railway and a telegraph. On 31 March 1854 the Treaty of Kanagawa was signed, opening the ports of Shimoda and Hakodate to American ships. No shots had been fired, but the episode set off the crisis that ended the shogunate fourteen years later.
lesson: A credible display of strength, combined with clear demands and time to think, can bring an opponent to the table without a fight. It may also unsettle more than you intended.
people: Matthew C. Perry, Tokugawa shogunate, Abe Masahiro
source: Narrative of the Expedition of an American Squadron to the China Seas and Japan (1856), compiled under Perry's supervision

title: Robert Schumann Announces Brahms
text:
On September 30, 1853, a shy, fair haired young pianist of twenty knocked at the door of Robert and Clara Schumann in Dusseldorf. Johannes Brahms came from a poor family in Hamburg, had earned money playing piano from an early age, and was almost unknown. He carried a letter of introduction from the violinist Joseph Joachim.

Brahms sat down and began to play one of his own piano sonatas. Robert Schumann soon stopped him and called Clara in to hear it from the start. That evening Robert noted in his diary a visit from Brahms, "a genius." For the next weeks Brahms was almost part of the household.

Schumann had not written for his old music journal in years. On October 28, 1853, he published an article titled "Neue Bahnen" (New Paths), announcing Brahms as the young man destined to give the highest expression to the age, one who had sprung forth fully armed. It made Brahms famous overnight, and placed a heavy expectation on him.

A few months later Robert suffered a breakdown and was confined to an asylum. Brahms stayed close, helping Clara and the children. His friendship with Clara lasted until her death in 1896.
lesson: If you see real talent in someone unknown, say so publicly and back it with your name. A single act of recognition can change the course of a life.
people: Robert Schumann, Johannes Brahms, Clara Schumann, Joseph Joachim
source: Robert Schumann, "Neue Bahnen," Neue Zeitschrift fur Musik, October 28, 1853; Robert Schumann's household diaries

title: The Charge of the Light Brigade
text:
On 25 October 1854, during the Battle of Balaclava in the Crimean War, the British commander Lord Raglan watched from the heights as Russian troops began hauling away British guns from captured redoubts. He sent an order to his cavalry commander, Lord Lucan, telling the cavalry to advance rapidly to the front and try to prevent the enemy carrying away the guns.

Lucan was in the valley below and could not see what Raglan saw. The order was carried by Captain Louis Nolan, an impatient cavalry officer who despised Lucan. When Lucan asked what guns were meant, Nolan, according to witnesses, waved his arm toward the end of the valley and said, "There, my lord, is your enemy, there are your guns." At the end of that valley stood a Russian battery, with more guns and riflemen on the slopes on both sides.

Lucan passed the order to the commander of the Light Brigade, Lord Cardigan, his brother-in-law, whom he loathed. The two men barely spoke. Cardigan questioned the order, Lucan said it was Raglan's, and Cardigan led about 670 men down the valley. Nolan rode out across the front of the brigade, perhaps trying to redirect it, and was killed by a shell.

The brigade reached the guns and was shattered. More than a hundred men were killed and many more wounded or captured. Watching, the French general Pierre Bosquet is said to have remarked: "It is magnificent, but it is not war."
lesson: Vague orders, poor communication and feuding leaders can destroy a brave team. Make sure instructions are clear and that people who must work together can talk to each other.
people: Lord Raglan, Lord Lucan, Lord Cardigan, Captain Louis Nolan
source: Cecil Woodham-Smith, The Reason Why (1953); contemporary accounts including William Howard Russell's dispatches to The Times

title: Clara Schumann Holds Her Family Together
text:
Clara Wieck was a celebrated concert pianist from her childhood. In 1840, after a court battle against her own father, she married the composer Robert Schumann. They had eight children, and she kept performing while raising them, often championing her husband's music.

In February 1854 Robert, tormented by mental illness, threw himself into the Rhine. He was rescued and, at his own request, taken to an asylum at Endenich near Bonn. Clara was pregnant with their eighth child. The doctors kept her from visiting him for more than two years; she saw him again only in July 1856, in the last days before he died. The young Johannes Brahms, who had become a close friend of the family, helped look after the household during these years.

With seven children to support, Clara went back to the concert stage. For four decades she toured Germany, the rest of Europe and England, earning the family's living and making her husband's works known. She also edited his compositions, and from 1878 taught at the conservatory in Frankfurt.

Her family life brought more sorrow. A son spent his life in an asylum, a daughter and two more sons died before her, and she took in the children of her son Ferdinand. Her diaries record exhaustion and grief, but also her determination to work. She died in 1896, one of the great musicians of her century.
lesson: When disaster strikes a family, steady work can be both a living and a refuge. Resilience is often less a feeling than a daily choice to keep going.
people: Clara Schumann, Robert Schumann, Johannes Brahms
source: Clara Schumann's diaries and letters; Nancy B. Reich, Clara Schumann: The Artist and the Woman (1985)

title: John Snow and the Broad Street Pump
text:
At the end of August 1854 cholera exploded in Soho, London. Snow later wrote that there were more than five hundred fatal attacks within about ten days around Broad Street. Most doctors believed cholera spread through bad air, or miasma. The physician John Snow suspected that it spread through contaminated water.

Snow went door to door collecting the addresses of the dead and plotted them on a map. The deaths clustered around the public water pump on Broad Street. He also studied the exceptions. A nearby workhouse with its own well had few cases. Workers at a local brewery, who drank beer and water from the brewery's own well, were largely spared. A widow living far away in Hampstead died of cholera, and Snow found that she had liked the taste of Broad Street water so much that she had it brought to her by cart.

On 7 September Snow presented his findings to the local Board of Guardians. They were skeptical but agreed to act, and the next day the pump handle was removed. The epidemic, already declining as people fled, faded out. Snow published his analysis in the second edition of On the Mode of Communication of Cholera in 1855. The miasma theory held on for years, but his map became a founding document of epidemiology.
lesson: When everyone agrees on a cause, look at where the cases actually are, and pay special attention to the exceptions. They often test the theory best.
people: John Snow, Henry Whitehead
source: John Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, 2nd ed. (1855)
caveat: The epidemic was already in decline when the handle was removed, so the action itself did not end it.

title: Florence Nightingale at Scutari
text:
In November 1854, during the Crimean War, Florence Nightingale arrived at the British army's Barrack Hospital at Scutari, across the Bosphorus from Constantinople, with a group of thirty-eight nurses. She found wounded and sick soldiers lying in filth, without enough beds, blankets, clean linen, food or basic supplies. Many more men were dying of disease than of wounds.

She met resistance from army doctors at first, but she organized. Using private funds, she bought supplies, set up kitchens and a laundry, and insisted on cleanliness. At night she made rounds of the wards with a lamp, which made her famous in Britain.

Deaths remained extremely high through the winter. In March 1855 the government sent a Sanitary Commission, which cleaned out the sewers and improved ventilation, and the death rate fell sharply.

After the war Nightingale worked with the statistician William Farr on the army's records. The analysis showed that most deaths had come from preventable disease caused by poor sanitation. She presented the data in striking diagrams and used them to push for a Royal Commission on army health, which led to lasting reforms in military hospitals and in nursing.
lesson: Measure what is really happening and show it clearly. Good data, honestly read, can force change that pleading cannot.
people: Florence Nightingale, William Farr
source: Nightingale's reports and letters; Notes on Matters Affecting the Health of the British Army (1858); Report of the Royal Commission on the Sanitary State of the Army (1858)
caveat: The fall in deaths at Scutari owed more to the Sanitary Commission than to nursing, as Nightingale's own later analysis recognized.

title: Harriet Tubman Goes Back for Her Family
text:
Harriet Tubman escaped from slavery in Dorchester County, Maryland, in 1849, walking north to Philadelphia. She later said that when she crossed into freedom she felt like she was in heaven, but she was a stranger in a strange land, because her family was still in slavery. She decided to bring them out.

In 1850 she helped her niece and the niece's two children escape after they had been put up for sale. In 1851 she returned for her husband, John, only to find he had married another woman and would not come. She brought out others instead.

At Christmas 1854 she came back for three of her brothers, who were about to be sold. They hid near their parents' cabin. According to her biographer Sarah Bradford, their father brought them food but kept his eyes covered, so that if he were questioned, he could truthfully say he had not seen them. Their mother was not told, because it was feared she would cry out.

In 1857, learning that her father was in danger of arrest for helping fugitives, Tubman returned for her aged parents. Unable to walk far, they rode in a makeshift cart she arranged. She took them all the way to St. Catharines, in Canada. The abolitionist William Still, who kept records of fugitives passing through Philadelphia, noted several of these escapes. In all, Tubman made about thirteen trips and freed some seventy people, many of them her own relatives.
lesson: Personal freedom can feel incomplete while those we love remain in danger. Going back for others is the truest test of what we have gained.
people: Harriet Tubman, Ben and Rit Ross, her brothers
location: Dorchester County, Maryland, USA, and St. Catharines, Ontario, Canada
source: Sarah Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869); William Still, The Underground Railroad (1872); Kate Clifford Larson, Bound for the Promised Land (2004)

title: Lucy Stone and Henry Blackwell's Marriage Protest
text:
Lucy Stone was one of the best known American speakers for the abolition of slavery and for women's rights. She had long said she would never marry, because the law at the time gave a husband control over his wife's property, earnings, children and even her person. Henry Blackwell, a businessman and abolitionist, courted her for two years and promised that their marriage would be a partnership of equals.

They married on 1 May 1855 at her family home in West Brookfield, Massachusetts. The minister, Thomas Wentworth Higginson, was a fellow reformer. Before the ceremony, Lucy and Henry read aloud a protest they had written together. While declaring their affection for each other, they protested against the laws that gave the husband custody of the wife's person, the exclusive control and guardianship of their children, and ownership of her property, and that made a married woman's legal existence disappear into her husband's. Henry renounced the rights the law gave him.

Higginson sent the protest to the newspapers, and it was widely reprinted. Lucy Stone also kept her own name after marriage, almost unheard of at the time. Women who later followed her example were called "Lucy Stoners."

The couple worked side by side for women's suffrage for the rest of their lives. In 1870 they founded the Woman's Journal, which their daughter, Alice Stone Blackwell, later edited.
lesson: A marriage can begin with a public promise of equality. Partners who name the unfair rules around them are better placed to live differently.
people: Lucy Stone, Henry Blackwell, Thomas Wentworth Higginson
source: Marriage of Lucy Stone under Protest (1855), published in the Worcester Spy and the Liberator; Andrea Moore Kerr, Lucy Stone (1992)

title: Maui Fishes Up the Land
text:
The Maori tell that the demigod Maui wanted to go fishing with his older brothers, but they refused to take him. So he hid in the bottom of their canoe, and when they were far out at sea, he revealed himself. They were angry, but by then it was too late to turn back.

Maui made them paddle farther than they had ever gone. Then he took out a magic fishhook made from the jawbone of his ancestor. His brothers would not give him bait, so he struck his own nose and smeared the hook with his blood. He let it down into the deep, and soon it caught on something vast. Chanting, Maui hauled it up: an enormous fish, so large it was a whole land.

Before he left, Maui told his brothers not to touch the fish until he had gone to make an offering to the gods and returned. But as soon as he was gone, the brothers began cutting it up and eating it. The fish writhed and thrashed under their knives. That, the story says, is why the North Island of New Zealand, Te Ika a Maui, the Fish of Maui, is full of mountains and valleys instead of being flat.
lesson: A team that breaks the agreed plan as soon as the leader looks away can spoil what it has won together. Discipline matters most just after success.
people: Maui, his brothers
source: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology (1855), The Legend of Maui

title: Tane Separates Sky and Earth
text:
In the Maori account, Rangi the Sky Father and Papa the Earth Mother once lay locked together in a close embrace. Their many children were born and lived between them, crowded in a cramped darkness where no light could reach.

The children grew tired of the darkness and began to discuss what to do. Tumatauenga, the fierce one, wanted to kill their parents. Tane Mahuta, father of the forests and birds, said it was better to separate them: let the sky stand far above, and let the earth remain close below as their nursing mother. All the brothers agreed except Tawhirimatea, father of the winds and storms.

One by one the brothers tried to push their parents apart. Rongo tried, then Tangaroa, then Haumia, then Tu. None could. Last came Tane. He placed his head against his mother Earth and his feet against his father Sky, and slowly, steadily, he pushed. Rangi and Papa cried out in grief at being torn apart. But Tane did not stop until the Sky was lifted high above.

Light flooded in for the first time, and the world could grow. Still the parents grieve: Rangi's tears fall as rain and dew, and Papa's sighs rise up as mist. And Tawhirimatea, angry at what his brothers had done, followed his father into the sky and still makes war on them with storms.
lesson: Children need room to grow, even when making it hurts the parents who hold them close. Separation can be an act of love on both sides.
people: Rangi (Ranginui), Papa (Papatuanuku), Tane Mahuta, Tawhirimatea, Tumatauenga
source: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology (1855), The Children of Heaven and Earth

title: Darwin, Wallace and the Shared Discovery
text:
Charles Darwin had worked on his theory of evolution by natural selection for twenty years without publishing it. In June 1858 a letter arrived at his house in Kent from Alfred Russel Wallace, a young naturalist collecting specimens in the Malay Archipelago. Enclosed was a short essay setting out almost exactly the same idea. Darwin was stunned. He wrote to his friend Charles Lyell that he had never seen a more striking coincidence, and that he would rather burn his whole book than have anyone think he had behaved in a paltry spirit.

Lyell and the botanist Joseph Hooker found a solution. On July 1, 1858, they presented Wallace's essay together with extracts from Darwin's earlier writings at the Linnean Society of London. Neither author was there: Wallace was on the other side of the world, and Darwin was mourning his baby son.

Wallace could easily have felt cheated. Instead he was generous for the rest of his life. He insisted the theory was Darwin's and in 1889 titled his own book on it Darwinism. Darwin later helped secure Wallace a government pension, and Wallace was a pallbearer at Darwin's funeral in 1882.
lesson: When credit could be disputed, choose generosity over grievance. Rivals who share honor fairly can end up as friends and allies instead of enemies.
people: Charles Darwin, Alfred Russel Wallace, Charles Lyell, Joseph Hooker
location: Down House, Kent, and Linnean Society, London, England
source: Darwin and Wallace, "On the Tendency of Species to form Varieties," Journal of the Proceedings of the Linnean Society, Zoology 3 (1858); Alfred Russel Wallace, Darwinism (1889)

title: The Rani of Jhansi
text:
Lakshmibai married Gangadhar Rao, the raja of Jhansi in central India. Shortly before he died in 1853 the couple adopted a boy as heir. The British East India Company refused to recognize the adoption and annexed Jhansi under the "doctrine of lapse". The widowed Rani was pensioned off.

In 1857 a great rebellion spread across northern India. In Jhansi, mutinous soldiers killed British officers and civilians. The Rani took control of the state and organized its defense. In March 1858 a British force under Sir Hugh Rose besieged the city. The Rani directed the defense from the fort, and the city held out for about two weeks before it was stormed. She escaped at night with a small escort.

She joined the rebel leader Tatya Tope, and together they seized the fortress of Gwalior. In June 1858, fighting at the head of her cavalry near Gwalior, she was killed. She was in her twenties.

Rose is reported to have called her the bravest and best of the rebel military leaders. In India she became a lasting symbol of resistance.
lesson: Courage and capacity in a crisis do not wait for title or permission. Lead with what you have when the moment demands it.
people: Rani Lakshmibai, Sir Hugh Rose, Tatya Tope
source: British military reports, including Sir Hugh Rose's dispatches; Indian histories of the 1857 rebellion
caveat: Some popular details, such as her escape with her son tied to her back, and her exact role in the 1857 killings at Jhansi, are disputed.

title: "Tutti Fratelli" at Solferino
text:
On 24 June 1859 the armies of France and Piedmont-Sardinia fought the Austrian army near the village of Solferino in northern Italy. It was one of the largest battles of the century, and by evening tens of thousands of men lay dead or wounded. The armies' medical services were completely overwhelmed.

A Swiss businessman, Henry Dunant, arrived that evening. He had come hoping to see Napoleon III about a business venture in Algeria. Instead he found himself in the nearby town of Castiglione delle Stiviere, where thousands of wounded soldiers had been carried into churches, houses and streets, many lying without water, food or care.

Dunant began organizing help. He gathered local women and girls to wash wounds, bring water and food, write letters for the dying and simply sit with them. He bought supplies with his own money and set up makeshift care in the main church. The women tended French, Italian and Austrian soldiers alike. In his account, Dunant reports that they repeated, "Tutti fratelli," all are brothers.

Back in Geneva, he wrote A Memory of Solferino, published in 1862, proposing that every country form volunteer relief societies in peacetime, ready to aid the wounded in war, and that nations agree to protect them. In 1863 a committee of five Geneva citizens, including Dunant, founded what became the International Committee of the Red Cross. The first Geneva Convention followed in 1864. In 1901 Dunant shared the first Nobel Peace Prize.
lesson: Volunteers who care for everyone in need, regardless of side, can start something far larger than themselves. Organized compassion lasts longer than individual pity.
people: Henry Dunant, the women of Castiglione delle Stiviere
location: Solferino and Castiglione delle Stiviere, Lombardy, Italy
source: Henry Dunant, A Memory of Solferino (Un souvenir de Solferino, 1862)

title: Grace Bedell Tells Lincoln to Grow a Beard
text:
In October 1860, a few weeks before the presidential election, an eleven year old girl in Westfield, New York, named Grace Bedell wrote to the Republican candidate, Abraham Lincoln. She had seen his picture and thought his face was very thin. If he let his whiskers grow, she wrote, he would look a great deal better, and since all the ladies liked whiskers, they would tease their husbands to vote for him.

Lincoln answered her himself on October 19. He said he had no daughter, only three sons, and asked whether people would not think it a piece of silly affectation if he began wearing whiskers now, having never worn any. But soon afterward he stopped shaving.

In February 1861 the new President's train to Washington stopped at Westfield. Lincoln told the crowd that he had a correspondent there and asked for Grace Bedell. She was brought forward, and he stepped down from the platform, told her he had let his whiskers grow for her, and kissed her. He became the first American president to wear a beard.
lesson: Take seriously the advice of people who seem to have no standing to give it. Respect shown to a child, or to anyone small, is long remembered.
people: Abraham Lincoln, Grace Bedell
location: Westfield, New York, and Springfield, Illinois, USA
source: Grace Bedell, letter to Abraham Lincoln, October 15, 1860; Lincoln, letter to Grace Bedell, October 19, 1860, Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln, vol. 4

title: Morozko
text:
An old man lived with his second wife, her daughter and his own daughter. The stepmother loved her own girl and hated the stepdaughter, who did all the work of the house without complaint. At last the stepmother ordered the old man to take his daughter into the forest in the depth of winter and leave her there. Afraid of his wife, he obeyed, and left his daughter under a fir tree in the snow.

As she sat shivering, Morozko, the Frost, came leaping through the trees, cracking and snapping. "Are you warm, maiden?" he asked. "Warm, Father Frost," she answered gently, though she was freezing. He came lower and the cold grew fiercer, and he asked again. Again she answered kindly. Pleased by her patience and good manners, he wrapped her in furs and blankets and gave her a chest full of rich gifts.
