The next day the stepmother sent the old man to bring back the body. He came home with his daughter alive, dressed in finery, with the chest of treasure.

The stepmother at once sent her own daughter out to the same place. When Morozko asked if she was warm, she answered rudely, complaining about the cold and demanding gifts. Morozko froze her stiff. The mother waited for her daughter to come home rich, and the old man brought back only her body.
lesson: Patience and courtesy under hardship tend to be rewarded, and favoritism in a family harms the favored child as well as the neglected one.
people: A stepdaughter, her father, her stepmother, Morozko (Father Frost)
source: Alexander Afanasyev, Russian Folk Tales (Narodnye russkie skazki), Morozko

title: Vasilisa the Beautiful
text:
When Vasilisa was eight, her mother lay dying. She called the girl to her bed and gave her a tiny wooden doll. "Keep it with you always and show it to no one," she said. "If trouble comes, give it a little food and ask its advice." Then she blessed her daughter and died.

Her father remarried a widow with two daughters, and the three of them were cruel to Vasilisa, piling on work to make her ugly and thin. But each night Vasilisa fed the doll, and the doll comforted her and did her chores while she rested.

One evening the stepmother let every fire and candle in the house go out and sent Vasilisa to the witch Baba Yaga, in the deep forest, to bring back light. Baba Yaga lived in a hut on chicken legs behind a fence of bones. She set the girl impossible tasks: cleaning, cooking, sorting good grain from black. Each night the doll did them.

At last Baba Yaga asked how she managed it all. "My mother's blessing helps me," Vasilisa said. The witch wanted no blessed person in her house. She pushed her out and gave her a skull with burning eyes on a stick to light her way. When Vasilisa reached home, the skull's eyes stared at the stepmother and her daughters and burned them to ashes. Vasilisa later married the tsar.
lesson: What a parent gives in love and teaching can keep guiding a child long after the parent is gone. Pass on blessings that will travel.
people: Vasilisa, her mother, her stepmother and stepsisters, Baba Yaga
source: Alexander Afanasyev, Russian Folk Tales (Narodnye russkie skazki), Vasilisa the Beautiful

title: Muddy Road
text:
Two Zen monks, Tanzan and Ekido, were once walking together along a road that heavy rain had turned to deep mud. The downpour was still coming down.

At a bend in the road they came upon a lovely young woman in a silk kimono and sash. She stood at the edge of a stretch of mud, unable to cross without ruining her clothes.

"Come on, girl," said Tanzan at once. He lifted her in his arms, carried her over the mud and set her down on the other side. Then the two monks walked on.

Ekido did not say a word for the rest of the day. That night, when they had reached a temple where they could lodge, he could no longer restrain himself. "We monks do not go near women," he burst out, "especially not young and lovely ones. It is dangerous. Why did you do that?"

"I left the girl there," said Tanzan. "Are you still carrying her?"
lesson: Grievances and judgments you keep turning over in your mind weigh more than the event itself. Help when help is needed, then put it down.
people: Tanzan, Ekido, a girl in a kimono
source: Nyogen Senzaki and Paul Reps, 101 Zen Stories (1919)

title: What the Old Man Does Is Always Right
text:
An old peasant couple owned little except a horse. One day the wife suggested that her husband take the horse to the market in town and exchange it for something more useful. "Whatever you do will be right," she said.

On the road he met a man with a cow and traded the horse for it. Then he traded the cow for a sheep, the sheep for a fat goose, the goose for a hen, and finally the hen for a sack of rotten apples.

At the inn, two rich Englishmen heard his story and laughed. His wife would surely give him a beating, they said. The old man said she would give him a kiss. They bet him a bushel of gold coins against his sack of apples and went home with him to see.

As he told her each trade, the wife was delighted. A cow meant milk, butter and cheese. A sheep was even better: wool and sheep's milk. A goose meant a goose to roast. A hen would lay eggs and hatch chickens. And the rotten apples? Only that morning a neighbor's wife had refused to lend her even one rotten apple; now she could lend her a whole sack. She gave her husband a kiss.

The Englishmen paid the bushel of gold without complaint. A wife who believed her husband always did right, they said, was worth the money.
lesson: Meeting a partner's mistakes with good humor rather than blame can be worth more than any trade. A household rich in trust has wealth of its own.
people: An old peasant, his wife, two Englishmen
source: Hans Christian Andersen, What the Old Man Does Is Always Right (Hvad Fatter gjor, det er altid det Rigtige), 1861

title: Queen Victoria Mourns Prince Albert
text:
Queen Victoria married her cousin, Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, in 1840. They had nine children. Albert became her closest adviser, her private secretary in all but name, and the organizer of the Great Exhibition of 1851. She depended on him completely.

In late 1861 Albert, overworked and in poor health, was distressed to learn that their eldest son, the Prince of Wales, had had an affair with an actress. He traveled to Cambridge to speak with his son, walking with him in the rain. Soon afterwards he fell ill with what his doctors diagnosed as typhoid fever. He died at Windsor Castle on 14 December 1861, at forty-two. Victoria never fully forgave her son, whom she partly blamed.

Victoria was forty-two too. She wore black for the rest of her life, nearly forty years. For years she withdrew from public life, and newspapers and politicians grew impatient with her absence. She had Albert's rooms kept as they had been, with his clothes laid out and hot water brought each morning. She raised monuments to him across the country, among them the Albert Memorial and the Royal Albert Hall in London.

In her letters she wrote of being cut off from her husband, and in old age she still marked the anniversary of his death. She lived until 1901, the longest reign in British history until then.
lesson: Grief for a spouse can last a lifetime and shape everything after. Mourning deeply is natural, but those still living, including our children, need us too.
people: Queen Victoria, Prince Albert, Albert Edward, Prince of Wales
source: The Letters of Queen Victoria; Stanley Weintraub, Uncrowned King: The Life of Prince Albert (1997)
caveat: Modern historians debate whether Albert died of typhoid or of a chronic illness such as Crohn's disease.

title: Lincoln Waits for a Victory
text:
By the summer of 1862 Abraham Lincoln had decided to declare the freedom of slaves in the states in rebellion. On 22 July he read a draft of the proclamation to his cabinet. He made clear that he had made up his mind on the policy and wanted advice only on details.

Secretary of State William Seward raised an objection about timing. The Union army had just suffered a string of defeats in Virginia. Lincoln later told the painter Francis Carpenter what Seward had argued: that issued at such a moment, the proclamation might be seen as the act of an exhausted government, a cry for help, or, in Lincoln's recollection of Seward's phrase, as "our last shriek, on the retreat". Better to wait and issue it on the back of a military success. Lincoln said the argument struck him with great force, and he put the draft away.

The wait was longer than he hoped. In August the Union lost again at the Second Battle of Bull Run. Then, on 17 September 1862, Union forces stopped Robert E. Lee's invasion of Maryland at Antietam. It was not a crushing victory, but it was enough. Five days later Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, and the final proclamation took effect on 1 January 1863. The new war aim made it much harder for Britain and France to support the Confederacy.
lesson: The same message can read as strength or desperation depending on when it arrives. Choose your moment so that a bold decision looks like confidence.
people: Abraham Lincoln, William Seward
source: Francis B. Carpenter, Six Months at the White House with Abraham Lincoln (1866); Doris Kearns Goodwin, Team of Rivals (2005)

title: The Bishop's Candlesticks
text:
Jean Valjean had served nineteen years in the galleys, five for stealing a loaf of bread for his sister's starving children and the rest for trying to escape. When he was finally released, his yellow passport marked him as a dangerous ex-convict. In the town of Digne every inn turned him away, and even a dog kennel would not have him.

At last he knocked at the door of the bishop, Monseigneur Myriel. The bishop welcomed him as a guest, called him monsieur, sat him at his table and served him by the light of two silver candlesticks, using the silver plates he kept for company. In the night Valjean, hardened by years of brutality, stole the silver plates and fled.

In the morning gendarmes brought him back. They had caught him with the silver. The bishop greeted Valjean warmly. "I am glad to see you. But I gave you the candlesticks too. They are silver like the rest. Why did you not take them with the plates?" The gendarmes released him. The bishop gave him the candlesticks and said quietly that he must not forget his promise to use the silver to become an honest man. "Jean Valjean, my brother, you no longer belong to evil, but to good. I am buying your soul."

Valjean had made no such promise. Shaken, he left the town and wandered in turmoil, and after one last petty theft that horrified him, he broke down weeping. He went on to live an honest life, and he kept the candlesticks until he died.
lesson: Mercy offered where punishment is expected can change a person in ways punishment rarely does. Treat people as who they could become.
people: Bishop Myriel, Jean Valjean
source: Victor Hugo, Les Miserables (1862), Part One, Book Two

title: Lincoln Appoints the Man Who Snubbed Him
text:
In 1855 Abraham Lincoln, then a lawyer in Illinois, was hired for a major patent case, McCormick v. Manny, to be heard in Cincinnati. He prepared carefully. But the defense team also included Edwin Stanton, a prominent attorney from Pittsburgh, who treated the lanky lawyer from the prairie with contempt. Lincoln was pushed aside, his brief was never used, and by later accounts Stanton refused to work with him. Lincoln went home hurt.

Seven years later Lincoln was President and the War Department was in disarray under Simon Cameron. In January 1862 Lincoln chose as the new Secretary of War the same Edwin Stanton, a Democrat who had also been a sharp critic of his administration. Lincoln judged that Stanton's energy, honesty and organizing ability mattered more than the old insult.

Stanton was hard, abrasive and often clashed with the President, but he ran the war effort with great force, and over the years he came to respect and love Lincoln. He was at Lincoln's bedside when he died in April 1865.
lesson: When choosing people for an important job, weigh what they can do, not how they once treated you. Setting aside a personal slight can win you a capable and loyal ally.
people: Abraham Lincoln, Edwin Stanton
location: Cincinnati, Ohio, and Washington, D.C., USA
source: Doris Kearns Goodwin, Team of Rivals (2005); Benjamin P. Thomas and Harold M. Hyman, Stanton (1962)
caveat: Some of the harshest words attributed to Stanton in 1855 come from later recollections and may be embellished.

title: Lincoln Loses His Son Willie
text:
William Wallace Lincoln, called Willie, was the third son of Abraham and Mary Lincoln. Bright, gentle and lively, he was ten when the family moved into the White House in 1861, and he and his younger brother Tad ran wild through its corridors.

In early February 1862, Willie fell ill with a fever, probably typhoid from the contaminated water supply. While he lay sick, the Lincolns held a large evening reception, and his parents kept slipping upstairs to see him. Tad fell ill too. Willie grew steadily worse and died on 20 February 1862.

Elizabeth Keckley, Mary Lincoln's dressmaker and friend, who was present, later recorded the president's grief as he looked at the boy's face. Lincoln said that his poor boy had been too good for this earth, that God had called him home, and that it was hard, hard to have him die. Keckley wrote that she had never seen a man so bowed down by grief.

All this happened in the middle of the Civil War, while Lincoln was directing the Union's armies. He went back to his work. Mary was overwhelmed and stopped appearing in public for months; she never again entered the room where Willie died. When Lincoln was assassinated three years later, Willie's coffin was placed on the funeral train beside his father's, and they were buried together in Springfield, Illinois.
lesson: Leaders carry private grief alongside public duty, and so do ordinary people at work. Remember that others may be bearing losses we cannot see.
people: Abraham Lincoln, Mary Todd Lincoln, Willie Lincoln, Tad Lincoln, Elizabeth Keckley
location: The White House, Washington, D.C., USA
source: Elizabeth Keckley, Behind the Scenes (1868), chapter 7; Michael Burlingame, Abraham Lincoln: A Life (2008)

title: Chamberlain at Little Round Top
text:
On July 2, 1863, the second day of the Battle of Gettysburg, the 20th Maine Infantry, about 385 men under Colonel Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain, a former college professor, was placed at the far left end of the Union line on the rocky slope of Little Round Top. Their brigade commander, Colonel Strong Vincent, told Chamberlain to hold the position at all costs. If it fell, the whole Union flank could be turned.

Confederate regiments, led by the 15th Alabama under Colonel William Oates, attacked up the hill again and again. Chamberlain stretched and bent his line to keep from being outflanked. Casualties mounted, and his men began running out of ammunition.

With another attack coming and no ammunition to stop it, Chamberlain ordered a bayonet charge. The left wing of the regiment swung forward like a door, down the slope into the attackers. The exhausted Confederates broke, and many were captured.

The Union left held. Chamberlain was later awarded the Medal of Honor for his actions that day.
lesson: When you are out of good options, a bold decision made quickly can be safer than waiting. Doing nothing is also a choice.
people: Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain, the 20th Maine, William Oates, Strong Vincent
location: Little Round Top, Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, USA
source: Official reports of the 20th Maine and the 15th Alabama; Chamberlain's later accounts
caveat: Later popular accounts, partly based on Chamberlain's own writings, may overstate the 20th Maine's role, and other officers claimed credit for starting the charge.

title: The Enormous Turnip
text:
An old man planted a turnip, and it grew and grew until it was enormous. When it was time to harvest, the old man took hold of the leaves and pulled. He pulled and pulled, but the turnip did not move.

He called the old woman. She took hold of the old man, and the old man took hold of the turnip, and they pulled and pulled, but they could not pull it up.

The old woman called their granddaughter. The granddaughter took hold of the old woman, the old woman of the old man, the old man of the turnip. They pulled and pulled, and still nothing.

The granddaughter called the dog. The dog took hold of the granddaughter, and they all pulled together, but the turnip stayed in the ground. The dog called the cat, and the cat joined the line, and they pulled once more without success.

Finally the cat called the mouse. The mouse took hold of the cat, the cat of the dog, the dog of the granddaughter, the granddaughter of the old woman, the old woman of the old man, and the old man of the turnip. They pulled and pulled, and out came the turnip.
lesson: Big tasks often succeed only when everyone adds a share, and the last small contribution can make the difference. Keep calling in help, and never scorn the smallest helper.
people: Grandfather, grandmother, granddaughter, dog, cat, mouse
source: Alexander Afanasyev, Russian Folk Tales (Narodnye russkie skazki), The Turnip (Repka)

title: Lee Takes the Blame at Gettysburg
text:
On July 3, 1863, the third day of the Battle of Gettysburg, General Robert E. Lee ordered a massive frontal assault on the center of the Union line. About twelve thousand Confederate soldiers, in what became known as Pickett's Charge, marched across nearly a mile of open fields under artillery and rifle fire. The attack failed, and about half of them were killed, wounded or captured.

Arthur Fremantle, a British army officer who was traveling with the Confederate army as an observer, watched what happened next and recorded it in his account published that same year. Lee rode out alone to meet the shattered troops as they streamed back, encouraging them and telling them to rally. When a distraught brigade commander, Cadmus Wilcox, came up to report the state of his men, Fremantle heard Lee tell him not to mind: all this had been his own fault, it was he who had lost the fight, and Wilcox must help him out of it as best he could.

The army retreated to Virginia. In August, Lee wrote to Jefferson Davis offering to resign his command. Davis refused, and Lee led the army until the end of the war.
lesson: When a decision you made fails, say so plainly and first. Taking the blame yourself keeps your people's trust when it is most fragile.
people: Robert E. Lee, Arthur Fremantle, Cadmus Wilcox
source: Arthur J. L. Fremantle, Three Months in the Southern States (1863); Lee's letter to Jefferson Davis, August 8, 1863

title: Lincoln's Letter to General Hooker
text:
In January 1863, after the Union defeat at Fredericksburg, Abraham Lincoln removed Ambrose Burnside from command of the Army of the Potomac and gave the post to Joseph Hooker. Hooker was a capable, aggressive general, but he had openly criticized Burnside and undermined him, and he had been heard saying that the country needed a dictator.

On January 26 Lincoln wrote to Hooker. He began by saying he had appointed him for good reasons, but that there were things about him he was not satisfied with. He listed his strengths frankly: Lincoln believed him a brave and skillful soldier, who kept politics out of his profession and had confidence in himself. Ambition within reasonable bounds did good rather than harm. But under Burnside, Lincoln wrote, Hooker had taken counsel of his ambition and thwarted his commander, doing a great wrong to the country and to an honorable brother officer.

Then came the famous lines: "Only those generals who gain successes, can set up dictators. What I now ask of you is military success, and I will risk the dictatorship." He closed by telling him to beware of rashness, but to go forward with energy and sleepless vigilance and give the country victories.

Hooker was defeated at Chancellorsville that May.
lesson: Tell people plainly what you value in them and what worries you, in the same conversation. Clear expectations respect both the person and the task.
people: Abraham Lincoln, Joseph Hooker
source: Lincoln to Joseph Hooker, January 26, 1863, Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln, Volume 6

title: The Letter Lincoln Never Sent
text:
In early July 1863 the Union army under General George Meade beat Robert E. Lee at Gettysburg. Lee retreated south, but heavy rains swelled the Potomac River and trapped his battered army on the Maryland side. In Washington, Abraham Lincoln waited for Meade to strike the final blow. Meade hesitated, held councils of war, and on the night of July 13 Lee slipped across the river.

Lincoln was bitterly disappointed. On July 14 he sat down and wrote Meade a letter. He told the general that he did not believe Meade appreciated "the magnitude of the misfortune involved in Lee's escape," that the war could have been ended, and that he was distressed beyond measure by it.

Then Lincoln put the letter away. It was found among his papers, with an endorsement in his hand noting it was never sent or signed. Meade, who had already offered to resign after hearing of the President's displeasure, stayed in command of the Army of the Potomac until the end of the war. Lincoln had written out his anger in full, and in the end kept the general he still needed.
lesson: When you are furious, write the letter if it helps, then wait before sending it. Ask whether it will fix anything or only cost you someone you still need.
people: Abraham Lincoln, George Meade
source: Abraham Lincoln, letter to George G. Meade, July 14, 1863 (unsent), Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln, ed. Roy P. Basler, vol. 6

title: Harriet Tubman Leads the Combahee River Raid
text:
Harriet Tubman had escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849 and then returned again and again to guide others north. During the Civil War she went to the Union-held coast of South Carolina, where she worked as a nurse and organized a network of scouts among formerly enslaved people who knew the rivers and plantations of the area.

In the night of June 1 to 2, 1863, three Union gunboats carrying black soldiers of the 2nd South Carolina Volunteers, under Colonel James Montgomery, steamed up the Combahee River. Tubman went with them as a guide. Her scouts had located where Confederate mines lay in the river and where the troops were posted.

The soldiers landed, burned plantations and rice mills, and destroyed a pontoon bridge. When the boat whistles blew, enslaved people came running from the fields toward the river, carrying children, pots and animals. More than seven hundred were taken aboard and freed. Many of the men later joined the Union army.

Newspapers reported the raid and noted the role of a black woman. Tubman later spent decades petitioning the government for a pension for her wartime service.
lesson: Knowledge of the ground and the trust of the people on it can matter more than rank. Lead from what you know best.
people: Harriet Tubman, James Montgomery
source: Union army reports; Wisconsin State Journal and Commonwealth reports, 1863; Sarah Bradford, Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869)

title: Grant's Terms at Appomattox
text:
On April 9, 1865, after four years of war and a final week of retreat, Robert E. Lee met Ulysses S. Grant in the parlor of Wilmer McLean's house at Appomattox Court House, Virginia, to surrender the Army of Northern Virginia.

Grant wrote the terms himself, at a small table. In his Personal Memoirs he says he did not know what he would write until he began. The officers and men were to be paroled, give their word not to fight again, and go home, not to be disturbed by United States authority as long as they kept their parole and obeyed the laws. Officers could keep their side arms, horses and baggage. When Lee mentioned that many of his cavalrymen and gunners owned their horses, Grant agreed that any man claiming a horse or mule could take it home to work his farm. He also arranged rations for Lee's hungry soldiers.

When Union troops began firing salutes to celebrate, Grant ordered them stopped. He wrote that the Confederates were now their prisoners and that he did not want to exult over their downfall. Lee told Grant the terms would have a very happy effect on his army.
lesson: When you win, how you treat the people who lost shapes everything that follows. Generosity at the right moment costs little and builds peace.
people: Ulysses S. Grant, Robert E. Lee
source: Ulysses S. Grant, Personal Memoirs, chapter 67; Grant's letter of terms to Lee, April 9, 1865

title: Ryoma Brokers the Satsuma-Choshu Alliance
text:
In the 1860s two powerful southwestern domains of Japan, Satsuma and Choshu, both wanted to change a shogunate that seemed helpless before the Western powers. But they hated each other. In 1864 Satsuma troops had helped drive Choshu forces out of Kyoto in bloody fighting, and Choshu men wore sandals with the word Satsuma written on them so they could tread on it.

Sakamoto Ryoma, a former samurai of the Tosa domain who had left his lord to work for national reform, saw that neither domain could defeat the shogunate alone. With his ally Nakaoka Shintaro he worked to bring them together. He found a practical first step: Choshu, under threat of attack by the shogunate, could not buy modern weapons openly, so Ryoma's trading company arranged for Western rifles and a ship to be bought in Satsuma's name and passed on to Choshu.

In March 1866 (the first month of the old Japanese calendar), in Kyoto, Ryoma brought together Saigo Takamori of Satsuma and Kido Takayoshi of Choshu. For days both sides waited for the other to propose terms first, out of pride. Ryoma confronted Saigo, and an agreement was reached. Kido wrote out its six points and asked Ryoma to endorse it, which Ryoma did on the back of the document.

That summer Choshu defeated the shogunate's punitive expedition. In 1868 Satsuma and Choshu forces led the coup and war that restored imperial rule. Ryoma did not see it: he was assassinated in Kyoto in December 1867.
lesson: Former enemies can become the most powerful partners when they share a larger goal. A trusted go-between and a practical first step can break a deadlock of pride.
people: Sakamoto Ryoma, Saigo Takamori, Kido Takayoshi, Nakaoka Shintaro
source: Marius Jansen, Sakamoto Ryoma and the Meiji Restoration (1961)
caveat: Some details, including the sandals and Ryoma's confrontation with Saigo, come from later traditional accounts.

title: Seward Buys Alaska
text:
After the Crimean War, Russia saw its colony in North America, Russian America, as a burden. It was far from St. Petersburg, made little money, and would be almost impossible to defend against Britain, whose Canadian territory lay next door. Russia preferred to sell it to the United States rather than see it fall to the British.

In March 1867 the Russian minister in Washington, Eduard de Stoeckl, opened talks with Secretary of State William Seward, a keen believer in American expansion. They worked quickly, and the treaty was signed in the early hours of 30 March 1867. The price was 7.2 million dollars, roughly two cents an acre, for about 586,000 square miles.

The purchase drew mockery from some newspapers and politicians, who called Alaska Seward's Folly or Seward's Icebox and asked what anyone would do with a land of ice. But the Senate approved the treaty by a large majority, helped by the influential senator Charles Sumner, and in October 1867 the American flag was raised at Sitka.

The doubters were proved wrong. Gold was found in the region in the 1880s and 1890s, the fisheries and timber were rich, and in 1968 huge oil reserves were discovered at Prudhoe Bay. Alaska's strategic position also became important in the Second World War and the Cold War. It became a state in 1959.
lesson: Some opportunities look foolish at the time because their value lies far in the future. Judge a long-term purchase by what it could become, not by its current use.
people: William Seward, Eduard de Stoeckl, Charles Sumner, Alexander II
source: Treaty concerning the Cession of the Russian Possessions in North America (1867); contemporary press
caveat: Historians note that the press mockery was less widespread than legend suggests, since many newspapers supported the purchase.

title: The Christmas Breakfast
text:
It was Christmas morning during the Civil War. The four March sisters, Meg, Jo, Beth and Amy, lived with their mother, whom they called Marmee, in genteel poverty while their father served as an army chaplain. The night before, they had grumbled about having no presents, and then decided to spend their little bit of money on gifts for their mother instead.

They came down to a breakfast table laid with hot muffins and buckwheat cakes, cream and bread, the best meal they had seen in a long time. Before they could start, their mother came in from outside. Not far away, she told them, lay a poor woman, Mrs. Hummel, with a newborn baby and six children huddled in one bed to keep from freezing, with no fire and nothing to eat. Would they give them their breakfast as a Christmas present?

There was a moment of silence. The girls were very hungry. Then Jo said, "I'm so glad you came before we began!" and the others agreed.

They carried the food through the snow to the bare, miserable room where the Hummels lived. They made a fire, fed the children and wrapped them up, laughing at the German children's attempts at English. That day they had bread and milk for their own breakfast, but none of them thought it a bad bargain. That evening a surprise feast of ice cream and cake arrived from their rich old neighbor, Mr. Laurence, who had heard what they had done.
lesson: Giving something up together can make a family's holiday richer than receiving. Let children share in the giving, not only watch it.
people: Meg, Jo, Beth and Amy March, Marmee, the Hummel family, Mr. Laurence
source: Louisa May Alcott, Little Women (1868), Chapter 2, A Merry Christmas

title: Kutuzov's Council at Fili
text:
In War and Peace, after the bloody battle of Borodino in 1812, the Russian army falls back to the village of Fili, just outside Moscow. Napoleon's army is approaching. Field Marshal Kutuzov calls his generals to a council of war in the best room of a peasant's hut. The peasant's six year old granddaughter, Malasha, has been forgotten on the big stove, and she watches everything from there.

The generals argue. General Bennigsen insists that Moscow, the holy ancient capital, must be defended, and others propose plans for fighting in front of the city. Kutuzov listens, sitting heavily in a corner, his eyes half closed. In Tolstoy's account he sees the question differently: whether to risk losing the army by fighting, or to lose Moscow without a battle.

At last he speaks. He says that by the authority entrusted to him by his sovereign and his country, he orders a retreat. The generals leave quietly, as if from a funeral.

Alone that night, Kutuzov cannot sleep. He asks himself when the decision that Moscow would be abandoned was really made. Yet he also swears that the French will pay for it, and that he will make them eat horseflesh. In the novel, the retreat preserves the army, and Napoleon's capture of an empty Moscow becomes the beginning of his ruin.
lesson: A leader sometimes has to make the decision no one in the room wants, and take its weight alone. Saving what matters most may require giving up what looks most important.
people: Mikhail Kutuzov, General Bennigsen, Malasha
location: Russia (novel set at Fili near Moscow, 1812)
source: Leo Tolstoy, War and Peace, Volume III, Part 3, Chapters 3 to 4
caveat: The council at Fili was a real event of September 1812, but Tolstoy's scene, including the child on the stove, is a novelist's dramatization.

title: Tushin's Battery
text:
In War and Peace, Tolstoy describes the battle of Schongrabern in 1805, where a small Russian rearguard under Prince Bagration had to hold off the French. In the middle of the line stood a battery of four guns commanded by Captain Tushin, a small, shy, awkward officer with a pipe, whom his superiors barely noticed.

In the confusion of the battle, Tushin's battery was simply forgotten. No infantry covered it. Nobody told him what to do. So he decided for himself to fire on the village of Schongrabern in front of him, and the village caught fire. The flames and the steady fire of his guns slowed the French advance, and the French, seeing so much resistance, assumed a large force was there.

Tushin's gunners worked under heavy fire, losing men and horses, while Tushin, half dreaming, imagined his guns as living creatures and himself as a giant hurling cannonballs. His men loved him. When at last Prince Andrei rode up with orders to withdraw, he found them still firing, and he helped bring the guns away.

That evening, at Bagration's headquarters, a staff officer complained that Tushin had abandoned two guns. Tushin stood there tongue-tied, unable to defend himself. It was Prince Andrei who spoke up: the day's success, he said, was owed above all to Tushin's battery and its men.
lesson: The people who decide a result are often the quiet ones doing their job without being seen. Make sure the credit reaches them, and speak up when it does not.
people: Captain Tushin, his gunners, Prince Andrei Bolkonsky, Prince Bagration
source: Leo Tolstoy, War and Peace, Volume I, Part 2, chapters 20 to 21
caveat: Schongrabern was a real battle, but Tushin and his role are Tolstoy's fiction.

title: The Crews of the Transcontinental Railroad
text:
In the 1860s two companies raced to link the eastern United States with California by rail. The Union Pacific built west from Omaha, largely with Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans. The Central Pacific built east from Sacramento, straight into the granite of the Sierra Nevada.

The Central Pacific could not find enough workers. In 1865, against the doubts of its construction boss James Strobridge, it hired a crew of Chinese laborers. They proved so effective that the company recruited thousands more, many directly from southern China, until they made up most of its workforce. They worked in gangs with their own cooks, drank boiled tea, and blasted tunnels through solid rock, through winters when snow buried camps and avalanches swept men away. They were paid less than white workers. In 1867 thousands of them went on strike for equal pay and hours; the company cut off their supplies and the strike collapsed within about a week.

As the lines converged in Utah in 1869, a Central Pacific crew laid ten miles of track in a single day, a record.

On 10 May 1869 the two lines met at Promontory Summit, and a golden spike was driven to celebrate. In the most famous photograph of the day, the Chinese workers who had built most of the western line are hard to find.
lesson: Great achievements rest on teams whose work is easily forgotten. Notice who actually did the work, and make sure they are counted and credited.
people: Central Pacific Chinese workers, Union Pacific crews, Charles Crocker, James Strobridge
location: Sierra Nevada, California, to Promontory Summit, Utah, USA
source: Gordon H. Chang, Ghosts of Gold Mountain (2019); Stephen E. Ambrose, Nothing Like It in the World (2000)

title: Bismarck Edits the Ems Dispatch
text:
In July 1870 France was alarmed that a Hohenzollern prince, a relative of the Prussian king, had been offered the Spanish throne. Under French pressure the candidacy was withdrawn. But the French government wanted more, and on 13 July its ambassador, Vincent Benedetti, approached King Wilhelm I of Prussia on the promenade at the spa town of Bad Ems. He asked for a guarantee that the candidacy would never be renewed. The king politely declined and later sent word that he had nothing more to say on the subject.

A report of the encounter was telegraphed to the Prussian chancellor, Otto von Bismarck, in Berlin, with permission to publish it. Bismarck believed a war with France was coming and that it would unite the German states behind Prussia, but only if France appeared to be the aggressor. In his memoirs he describes how, at dinner with the generals Moltke and Roon, he shortened the text. Without adding anything, he cut it so that it read as if the king had abruptly dismissed the ambassador and refused to see him again.

Bismarck wrote that the edited version would have the effect of a red rag on the Gallic bull. It was released to the press and foreign governments. In Paris, public opinion was outraged at the supposed insult, and on 19 July 1870 France declared war on Prussia. The southern German states joined Prussia. Within months France was defeated, and in January 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed.
lesson: Words can be shaped to provoke the reaction you want, so read official messages critically. A side that loses its temper can be maneuvered into the role of aggressor.
people: Otto von Bismarck, Wilhelm I, Vincent Benedetti, Napoleon III
source: Otto von Bismarck, Thoughts and Reminiscences (Gedanken und Erinnerungen), vol. 2
caveat: Bismarck wrote his memoirs decades later and may have dramatized his own role.

title: The Iwakura Mission
text:
In late 1871, only a few years after the Meiji Restoration, Japan's new government sent abroad an extraordinary delegation. It was led by Iwakura Tomomi, a senior court noble, with several of the country's most powerful leaders as deputies, including Okubo Toshimichi, Kido Takayoshi and the young Ito Hirobumi. Dozens of officials went with them, along with students who would stay abroad to study, among them a handful of young girls.

The mission had two aims. The first was to begin revising the unequal treaties that Western powers had forced on Japan. That failed quickly: in the United States the envoys found they were not ready to negotiate on equal terms. The second aim became the real work: to see how the Western world functioned and what Japan should learn.

For nearly two years the delegation traveled through the United States and Europe, visiting Britain, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany, Russia, Scandinavia, Italy, Austria and Switzerland. They divided their attention among constitutions, parliaments, schools, factories, shipyards, railways, banks, prisons and armies, and compared notes. The historian Kume Kunitake kept a detailed record, later published in five volumes.

The leaders returned in 1873 convinced that Japan needed above all to strengthen itself at home, building industry, education and modern institutions. They opposed a proposal to send an expedition against Korea and focused on reform. Many of the policies that transformed Meiji Japan grew from what they had seen together.
lesson: A team sent out to learn, and willing to share and compare what each member sees, can bring back what an organization needs. Learning together builds shared conviction.
people: Iwakura Tomomi, Okubo Toshimichi, Kido Takayoshi, Ito Hirobumi, Kume Kunitake
location: United States and Europe; Tokyo, Japan
source: Kume Kunitake, The Iwakura Embassy, 1871 to 1873: A True Account of the Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary's Journey of Observation through the United States and Europe (1878; English translation 2002)

title: God Sees the Truth, But Waits
text:
Ivan Aksionov, a cheerful young merchant of Vladimir, set out for the fair at Nizhny Novgorod although his wife had dreamed his hair had turned grey. At an inn on the way he shared a room with another merchant. Early in the morning he drove on, and later the police caught up with him. The other merchant had been found with his throat cut, and a bloody knife was in Aksionov's bag. He was flogged and sent to hard labor in Siberia.

He spent twenty-six years there. His hair turned white, he grew meek and prayed, and the other convicts respected him. Then a new prisoner arrived, Makar Semyonich, and from his talk Aksionov came to understand that this was the real murderer, who had planted the knife.

Soon after, Aksionov discovered Makar digging an escape tunnel under the bunks. When the guards found the tunnel, the governor questioned the prisoners, and Aksionov, who was known never to lie, was asked who had dug it. He could have destroyed Makar with one word. He said he would not tell.

That night Makar came to him in tears, confessed the murder, and begged forgiveness. Aksionov wept too, and said God would forgive him; perhaps he himself was a hundred times worse. At once his heart felt light. Makar confessed to the authorities. But when the order for Aksionov's release finally arrived, he was already dead.
lesson: Forgiving someone who has done you great wrong does not change the past, but it can free you from it. Do not wait for justice to make peace.
people: Ivan Aksionov, Makar Semyonich
source: Leo Tolstoy, God Sees the Truth, But Waits (1872)

title: Susi and Chuma Carry Livingstone Home
text:
On 1 May 1873, in the village of Chitambo in what is now Zambia, the Scottish missionary and explorer David Livingstone was found dead, kneeling by his bed. He had been searching for the source of the Nile and was worn out by years of illness.

His African companions, led by Abdullah Susi and James Chuma, who had traveled with him for years, decided that his body must be taken home. It was a dangerous choice. The journey to the coast was over a thousand miles through territory where carrying a corpse could provoke fear and hostility. They buried his heart under a tree at Chitambo, preserved the body with salt and by drying it in the sun, wrapped it, and enclosed it in a cylinder of bark covered with sailcloth.

For months the party, some sixty people, carried Livingstone's body, his journals and his instruments toward the Indian Ocean. On the way they met a British relief expedition whose leader urged them to bury the body in the interior. They refused and went on.

In February 1874 they reached Bagamoyo on the coast, and the body was shipped to England. Livingstone was buried in Westminster Abbey in April 1874. Susi and Chuma were later brought to England, where they helped Horace Waller prepare Livingstone's last journals for publication, and their account of the journey was printed with them.
lesson: A team's loyalty can carry a mission past its leader's death. Those who seem like followers are often the ones who finish the work.
people: Abdullah Susi, James Chuma, Jacob Wainwright, David Livingstone
source: Horace Waller, ed., The Last Journals of David Livingstone (1874)

title: The Castaways of the Mysterious Island
text:
In Jules Verne's novel, five prisoners of war escaped from besieged Richmond in 1865 during the American Civil War by stealing a balloon. A storm carried them far over the Pacific, and the balloon came down on an unknown island. They had almost nothing: the clothes they wore, a notebook, a watch, and a dog named Top.

They were the engineer Cyrus Smith, a man of great scientific knowledge; the journalist Gideon Spilett; the sailor Pencroft, practical and full of energy; Herbert, a teenage boy who knew natural history; and Neb, Smith's devoted companion. They decided to work as one.

When they had no matches, Smith made a lens from the glasses of two watches and lit a fire from the sun. Herbert identified plants and animals for food. Pencroft built boats. Together they made bricks and pottery, smelted iron, produced chemicals and explosives, and even built a telegraph line. Over the years they turned the island into a small, organized colony, helped from time to time by a mysterious protector who turned out to be Captain Nemo.

At last the island's volcano erupted and destroyed almost everything they had built. The colonists, clinging to the last rock above the sea, were rescued by a passing ship.
lesson: A group that pools its knowledge can build a great deal from almost nothing. Each person's skill becomes far more valuable when it is combined with the others'.
people: Cyrus Smith, Gideon Spilett, Pencroft, Herbert, Neb, Captain Nemo
location: France (novel set on a fictional Pacific island)
source: Jules Verne, The Mysterious Island (L'Ile mysterieuse), 1874 to 1875

title: The Peasant Marey
text:
In 1876 Dostoevsky recalled a day during his years as a convict in Siberia. It was Easter week, and the prisoners were drunk, brawling and singing obscene songs. Disgusted, he went out of the barracks, where a Polish political prisoner muttered to him in French that he hated these bandits. Dostoevsky went back in and lay on his bunk, and a memory from his childhood came to him.

He was nine years old, on his father's country estate in August. He had wandered into a birch wood when, in the silence, he thought he heard someone shout, "Wolf!" He ran screaming out of the wood to a peasant plowing in the field. It was Marey, one of his father's serfs, a man of about fifty.

Marey stopped his horse and held the trembling boy. "Christ be with you, cross yourself," he said. There was no wolf; the boy had imagined it. Marey smiled at him like a mother, gently touched the boy's quivering lip with a finger black with earth, and promised to watch over him as he walked home. Every few steps the boy looked back and saw Marey still standing there, watching.

Lying on the plank bunk, Dostoevsky climbed down and looked at the faces of the convicts around him. Suddenly the hatred was gone. Any of these shaven, branded men, he felt, might be Marey.
lesson: One stranger's gentleness can change how you see a whole group of people. Remember that those who seem hostile may carry the same tenderness inside.
people: Fyodor Dostoevsky as a boy, the serf Marey
location: Omsk prison camp and Darovoye estate (modern Russia)
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, A Writer's Diary (February 1876), The Peasant Marey

title: Tom Sawyer Whitewashes the Fence
text:
It was a bright Saturday morning, and Tom Sawyer had been punished by his Aunt Polly. Instead of playing, he had to whitewash thirty yards of board fence nine feet high. He looked at the endless wall, felt the whole day being swallowed, and sat down in despair. He thought of paying someone to do it, but all his worldly wealth would not buy even half an hour of freedom.

Then he had an idea. When his friend Ben Rogers came by, eating an apple and pretending to be a steamboat, Tom kept painting with the absorbed care of an artist. Ben teased him about having to work. Tom said he didn't see it as work. Did a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day? He stepped back to study the effect of a stroke and added a touch here and there. Ben watched, and begged to be allowed to try. Tom refused: Aunt Polly was very particular about this fence, and not one boy in a thousand could do it right. In the end Ben gave him his apple for the privilege.

Other boys came by all day, and each one stayed to paint. By afternoon Tom had a kite, a dead rat on a string, twelve marbles and a pile of other treasures, and the fence had three coats of whitewash. Tom had discovered, Twain says, that to make someone want a thing, you only need to make it hard to get.
lesson: How a task is framed changes how people feel about doing it. If you want willing effort, show why the work is worth doing, but stay honest, because people resent a trick once they see it.
people: Tom Sawyer, Ben Rogers, Aunt Polly
source: Mark Twain, The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Chapter 2

title: "I Will Fight No More Forever"
text:
In 1877 the United States government ordered the non-treaty bands of the Nez Perce to leave their homeland in the Wallowa Valley of Oregon and move to a reservation in Idaho. Shortly before the deadline, some young warriors killed several settlers, and the army attacked. Joseph, called Hinmatoowyalahtqit, was one of several band leaders.

For almost four months about seven hundred and fifty Nez Perce, most of them women, children and old people, retreated across Idaho, Wyoming and Montana, more than a thousand miles, fighting off pursuing army columns. They were heading for Canada.

At the Bear Paw Mountains in Montana, about forty miles from the border, Colonel Nelson Miles's troops caught and surrounded them. After a siege of several days in snow and cold, on October 5, 1877, Joseph surrendered. Lieutenant Charles Erskine Scott Wood recorded the message he said Joseph sent: that the chiefs were killed, the old men were dead, the little children were freezing, and his people had no blankets and no food. It ended: "From where the sun now stands I will fight no more forever."

The army's promise that they could return home was broken. The survivors were sent to Kansas and then Indian Territory.
lesson: When pride and the survival of the people you lead pull in different directions, choosing their survival is not defeat but responsibility.
people: Chief Joseph (Hinmatoowyalahtqit), Nelson Miles, Charles Erskine Scott Wood
source: Surrender speech as reported by Lt. Charles Erskine Scott Wood; army reports of the Nez Perce campaign
caveat: Wood later wrote the speech down and may have shaped its wording; whether Joseph spoke these exact words is debated.

title: Frederick Douglass Visits His Old Master
text:
Frederick Douglass was born into slavery in Maryland and escaped in 1838. In his writings he described Thomas Auld, his legal owner, as cruel and hypocritical, and in 1848 he published a stinging open letter to him. In 1846 British friends had bought Douglass's freedom from Auld's brother Hugh, to whom Thomas Auld had transferred him.

In June 1877, by then a famous orator and United States Marshal for the District of Columbia, Douglass returned to St. Michaels, Maryland. Thomas Auld, old and near death, had let it be known that he wished to see him, and Douglass went to his bedside. In Life and Times of Frederick Douglass he describes the meeting. Auld called him Marshal Douglass; Douglass asked to be called Frederick, as in the old days, and addressed him as Captain Auld. The old man wept, and Douglass was for a time too moved to speak. They talked frankly. Auld told him that in Douglass's place he would have run away too. Douglass also corrected one charge he had made in print about Auld's treatment of his grandmother, after learning he had been mistaken.

The visit was widely reported, and some critics thought Douglass had been too soft on a former slaveholder. In his account he made clear that his hatred of slavery had not changed. He now saw Auld, as he saw himself, as a victim of the circumstances of birth, law and custom.
lesson: You can make peace with a person without excusing the wrong he took part in. Forgiveness and moral clarity are not opposites.
people: Frederick Douglass, Thomas Auld
source: Frederick Douglass, Life and Times of Frederick Douglass (1881), Part 2, chapter on the visit to St. Michaels

title: Levin Mows with the Peasants
text:
In Anna Karenina, the landowner Konstantin Levin, restless and unhappy, decided one summer to go out and mow hay with the peasants on his own estate. He took a scythe and joined the line of mowers at dawn.

At first it went badly. He was out of practice, he swung too hard, and the rows he cut were ragged. An old peasant in the line showed him how to do it, and the young man behind him was pressing at his heels. Levin sweated and ached and was afraid he would have to give up in front of everyone. But he kept on, row after row, matching his pace to the man ahead.

Then something changed. As the day went on, there came moments when he stopped thinking about the scythe at all. It seemed to move by itself, and the whole line of men moved together in one rhythm. Those were the happiest moments. When he started thinking about what he was doing, the work grew hard again.

At midday he ate bread with the peasants and drank water from the stream. By evening they had mowed a large meadow that in the morning had looked impossible. Levin walked home tired and happier than he had been in a long time.
lesson: Hard work done in rhythm with others can become a source of joy. Learn from the people who already do it well, and match their pace before trying to set your own.
people: Konstantin Levin, the peasant mowers
source: Leo Tolstoy, Anna Karenina, Part III, chapters 4 to 6

title: The Beggar
text:
In one of his short prose poems, Turgenev describes walking along a street when an old beggar stopped him. The man was frail and pitiful: red, tearful eyes, blue lips, rough rags, filthy sores. Poverty had eaten him away. He held out his swollen, red, unwashed hand and moaned, asking for help.

The narrator began searching through his pockets. He found no purse, no watch, not even a handkerchief. He had taken nothing with him. And the beggar went on waiting, his outstretched hand trembling slightly.

Confused and ashamed, the narrator took the dirty, trembling hand in his own and pressed it warmly. "Do not be angry with me, brother," he said. "I have nothing with me, brother."

The beggar raised his inflamed eyes to him. His blue lips smiled, and he in turn squeezed the narrator's cold fingers. "Never mind, brother," he said. "Thank you for this as well. This too was a gift, brother."

And the narrator understood that he, too, had received a gift from his brother.
lesson: When you cannot give anything material, you can still give respect, warmth and your full attention. People feel that as a gift.
people: The narrator, a beggar
source: Ivan Turgenev, Poems in Prose (Senilia), The Beggar (1878)

title: The Sparrow
text:
Turgenev tells of walking back from hunting along an avenue in his garden, with his dog running ahead of him. Suddenly the dog slowed down and began creeping forward, as if it had scented game.

Looking along the path, he saw a young sparrow with yellow at the corners of its beak and down on its head. It had fallen from its nest, which the wind was shaking in the birches overhead. It sat motionless on the ground, its little wings helplessly spread.

The dog was approaching it slowly when an old sparrow dropped from a nearby tree like a stone, right in front of the dog's nose. All its feathers ruffled, distorted, with a desperate and pitiful chirping, it hopped twice toward the open, toothy jaws. It had flung itself down to save its young, to shield the chick with its own body. Its whole small body was trembling with terror and its voice was hoarse, but it would not move.

To the sparrow, the narrator says, the dog must have seemed a giant monster. Still it could not stay safe in its tree. The dog stopped and backed away. Turgenev called his dog off and walked away, filled with reverence for that small, heroic bird and its love, which he felt was stronger than death.
lesson: Love for a child can make the weakest creature fearless. Do not underestimate what a parent will face for the sake of their young.
people: The narrator, his dog, a mother sparrow, a fledgling
source: Ivan Turgenev, Poems in Prose (Senilia), The Sparrow (Vorobei), 1878

title: The Disaster at Isandlwana
text:
In January 1879 the British invaded the Zulu kingdom of King Cetshwayo. The main column under Lord Chelmsford camped below a rocky hill called Isandlwana. The British commanders were confident that their rifles and artillery would beat any Zulu attack, and their main fear was that the Zulu army would avoid battle.

The camp was not fortified. No wagon laager was formed and no trenches were dug, partly because the column expected to move on soon. Early on 22 January, reports came of Zulu forces to the southeast. Chelmsford took about half his column out to find and fight them, leaving the camp under Lieutenant Colonel Henry Pulleine, later joined by Colonel Anthony Durnford.

The main Zulu army, more than twenty thousand men, was in fact hidden in a valley a few miles away from the camp. Discovered by a British patrol, it attacked at once in the traditional formation, with horns sweeping around both flanks. The British firing line was spread too thin and far from the camp, and it was outflanked. Within a few hours the camp was overrun. About 1,300 men of the British force died, among the worst defeats the British army suffered at the hands of an indigenous force.

Chelmsford returned that evening to find the camp destroyed. The British won the war later in 1879, but Isandlwana shook the Empire's sense of invincibility.
lesson: Contempt for an opponent leads to skipped precautions and divided strength. Plan as if the other side is as capable as you are.
people: Lord Chelmsford, Henry Pulleine, Anthony Durnford, Cetshwayo
source: Proceedings of the Court of Inquiry into the loss of the camp at Isandlwana (1879); Ian Knight, Zulu Rising (2010)

title: The Volunteers Behind the Oxford English Dictionary
text:
In 1857 the Philological Society of London proposed a dictionary that would trace every English word through its history, with quotations showing how each was used over the centuries. No small staff could read enough books to do that. So the project relied on volunteers.

When James Murray, a Scottish schoolmaster and self-taught philologist, became editor in 1879, he issued a new appeal to English speakers across the world. Readers were asked to take books, note words that interested them, and copy each quotation onto a separate slip of paper with the word, the date, the author and the title. The slips poured in by the million. Murray built a corrugated iron shed he called the Scriptorium, lined with pigeonholes to sort them, first at Mill Hill School, where he taught, and later in the garden of his house in Oxford.

The readers were a varied crowd: clergymen, retired officers, housewives, scholars and amateurs. One of the most productive was William Chester Minor, an American former army surgeon confined to Broadmoor asylum after killing a man. From his cell he sent in many thousands of quotations, chosen to fill gaps the editors had listed.

The first section, covering A to Ant, came out in 1884. Murray died in 1915, having reached the letter T. Other editors finished the work, and the complete dictionary was published in 1928.
lesson: Thousands of small, well-organized contributions can build what no expert could build alone. Give volunteers a clear, simple format, and their work adds up.
people: James Murray, William Chester Minor, the volunteer readers
location: Mill Hill and Oxford, United Kingdom
source: K. M. Elisabeth Murray, Caught in the Web of Words (1977); Simon Winchester, The Professor and the Madman (1998)

title: Please Don't Throw Me in the Briar Patch
text:
These tales come from the African American storytelling of the South, written down and published by Joel Chandler Harris in 1880.

Brer Fox was tired of being outwitted by Brer Rabbit, so he made a figure out of tar, dressed it, and set it by the road. Brer Rabbit came along and greeted it politely. The tar baby said nothing. Offended, Brer Rabbit hit it, and his fist stuck. He hit it with the other fist, kicked it and butted it, until he was stuck fast all over. Then Brer Fox strolled out from the bushes, laughing.

Now Brer Fox debated aloud how to finish him off. He might roast him over a fire, hang him or drown him. Brer Rabbit said he did not care what Brer Fox did to him, so long as he did not throw him into the briar patch. Roast me, he said, hang me, drown me, skin me, but please, please do not fling me into that briar patch.

Brer Fox wanted to hurt Brer Rabbit as much as possible, so he grabbed him by the hind legs and threw him right into the middle of the thorns. There was a moment of silence. Then, from a log on the hill, Brer Rabbit called down that he had been born and raised in a briar patch, and skipped away.
lesson: When you are in a weak position, your opponent's eagerness to hurt you can become your exit. Think about what they believe you fear, and use it.
people: Brer Rabbit, Brer Fox
location: Southern United States (African American folk tradition)
source: Joel Chandler Harris, Uncle Remus: His Songs and His Sayings (1880), The Wonderful Tar-Baby Story and How Mr. Rabbit Was Too Sharp for Mr. Fox

title: The Grand Inquisitor
text:
In The Brothers Karamazov, Ivan Karamazov tells his younger brother Alyosha a story he has composed. It is set in Seville in the sixteenth century, at the height of the Inquisition, the day after a hundred heretics have been burned. Christ quietly appears among the people. They recognize him at once, crowd around him, and he heals a blind man and raises a dead child.

The Grand Inquisitor, a cardinal of nearly ninety, sees this and has him arrested. That night the old man visits the prisoner in his cell. He does most of the talking, and Christ says nothing.

The Inquisitor accuses him of having overestimated humanity. In the desert, Christ refused to turn stones into bread, to perform a miracle that would compel belief, and to take the kingdoms of the world. He wanted people to follow him freely. But freedom, says the Inquisitor, is an unbearable burden for most people. They want bread, miracle, mystery and authority. The Church has corrected his work: it has taken their freedom and given them certainty, and the people are grateful. Tomorrow, he says, the crowd will help burn Christ.

When he finishes, the prisoner rises, approaches and silently kisses the old man on his bloodless lips. The Inquisitor shudders, opens the door and tells him to go and never come back.
lesson: Taking decisions away from people can be presented as kindness. Be wary of any authority, including your own, that keeps people comfortable by keeping them from thinking for themselves.
people: The Grand Inquisitor, the prisoner (Christ), Ivan and Alyosha Karamazov
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book V, Chapter 5

title: The Onion
text:
In The Brothers Karamazov, Grushenka tells Alyosha a folk tale she heard as a child from an old peasant woman.

Once there was a very wicked woman, and when she died she had not left behind a single good deed. The devils seized her and threw her into the lake of fire. Her guardian angel stood by, trying to think of some good thing she had done that he could tell to God. At last he remembered: once she had pulled an onion from her garden and given it to a beggar woman.

God told the angel to take that same onion, hold it out to her in the lake, and let her grab it. If he could pull her out by it, she could go to paradise. If the onion broke, she would stay where she was.

The angel held out the onion, and the woman seized it. He began to pull, carefully, and she was nearly out when the other sinners in the lake saw what was happening and grabbed onto her, hoping to be pulled out too. The woman kicked at them. "It is me being pulled out, not you! It is my onion, not yours!" As soon as she said that, the onion broke. She fell back into the lake, where she is burning to this day, and the angel wept and went away.
lesson: One small kindness can be a lifeline. Do not ruin what good you have by refusing to share it with others who are reaching for the same hope.
people: Grushenka, Alyosha, a wicked woman, her guardian angel
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov (1880), Book VII, Chapter 3

title: Pasteur's Public Test at Pouilly-le-Fort
text:
In 1881 anthrax was killing large numbers of sheep and cattle in France. Louis Pasteur announced that he had developed a vaccine against it. Many veterinarians were skeptical, and one of them, Hippolyte Rossignol, challenged Pasteur to prove it in public. The test was to be held at a farm at Pouilly-le-Fort, near Melun, southeast of Paris.

Pasteur accepted, and with his assistants Emile Roux and Charles Chamberland he set up a demonstration designed to leave no doubt. Fifty sheep were divided into two groups, along with a few other animals, mostly cattle. In May 1881 half the animals received two doses of vaccine some days apart. On 31 May all of the animals, vaccinated and unvaccinated alike, were injected with a deadly dose of anthrax.

Pasteur had committed himself publicly to the result. On 2 June a crowd of farmers, officials, veterinarians and journalists gathered at the farm. The vaccinated sheep were alive and healthy. The unvaccinated sheep were dead or dying, and the rest died soon after. The result was reported throughout Europe, and demand for the vaccine quickly followed.

A century later, the historian Gerald Geison studied Pasteur's private notebooks. He found that the vaccine used at Pouilly-le-Fort had been prepared with a chemical method developed in Pasteur's lab by Chamberland and Roux, close to one used by a rival, Henri Toussaint, rather than the oxygen method Pasteur had implied in public.
lesson: A clear, public demonstration with a control group can persuade skeptics far better than argument. Be honest about how you got the result, because the details come out.
people: Louis Pasteur, Emile Roux, Charles Chamberland, Hippolyte Rossignol
source: Louis Pasteur, Chamberland and Roux, report to the Academy of Sciences (June 1881); Gerald L. Geison, The Private Science of Louis Pasteur (1995)
caveat: Geison's research showed Pasteur was not candid about the method used to make the vaccine.

title: What Men Live By
text:
Simon, a poor village shoemaker, went to town one winter to buy sheepskins for a coat. His customers would not pay their debts, so he spent the little he had on vodka and set off home grumbling. Near a roadside shrine he found a young man sitting naked in the cold. Simon was afraid and almost passed by, but his conscience turned him back. He put his own coat on the stranger and brought him home.

His wife Matrena was furious at a drunk husband bringing home another mouth to feed. But when she looked at the stranger, pity rose in her, and she gave him the last of their bread. At that moment the stranger smiled for the first time.

His name was Michael. He stayed and worked as Simon's apprentice, and he worked wonderfully. He smiled a second time when a rich gentleman ordered boots to last a year, and Michael made soft slippers instead, the kind used for the dead; the gentleman died that very day. Years later a woman came in with two little girls, one of them lame, and told how she had taken them in when their mother died. Michael smiled a third time.

Then he revealed that he was an angel, punished for refusing to take that mother's soul, and sent to earth to learn three truths. He had learned that love dwells in people, that no one is given to know what he truly needs, and that people live not by care for themselves but by love.
lesson: None of us gets through life by our own planning alone. We live because others choose to care for us, so do the same for those around you.
people: Simon the shoemaker, his wife Matrena, the angel Michael
source: Leo Tolstoy, What Men Live By (1881)

title: The Prince and the Pauper
text:
In Mark Twain's novel, two boys are born in London on the same day in the reign of Henry VIII. One is Edward Tudor, heir to the throne. The other is Tom Canty, a beggar's son from Offal Court. They look exactly alike. When Tom wanders up to the palace gate, Prince Edward invites him in, and for fun the two trade clothes. Before the prince can explain, the guards throw him out into the street in Tom's rags.

No one believes Edward is the prince. He is beaten by Tom's father, falls among thieves and beggars, and wanders the country. A discharged soldier, Miles Hendon, takes pity on the boy, thinks him mad, and protects him anyway. On the road Edward sees what the king's laws do to the poor: he is thrown into jail, meets two women who are burned at the stake for their religion, and hears of people hanged for stealing small things to eat. He promises himself that the law will change.

Meanwhile Henry VIII dies, and Tom is about to be crowned. At the very moment of the coronation, Edward pushes into the abbey. He proves who he is by revealing where the missing Great Seal is hidden; Tom has been using it to crack nuts. Crowned at last, Edward VI rules with mercy, rewards Tom and Miles Hendon, and often tells stories of what he saw on the road.
lesson: Rules look different from the receiving end. If you make decisions for others, find ways to experience what your choices are like for the people with the least power.
people: Edward Tudor (Edward VI), Tom Canty, Miles Hendon
source: Mark Twain, The Prince and the Pauper, 1881

title: Fat and Thin
text:
On a platform of the Nikolaevsky railway station two old school friends ran into each other. One was fat, freshly dined, smelling of sherry and orange blossom. The other was thin, loaded with bags and parcels, accompanied by his thin wife and his lanky son.

They embraced three times and stood with tears in their eyes. The thin man talked happily about their school days, introduced his family and told how life had gone. He was a collegiate assessor now, a modest civil service rank, and his wife gave music lessons. "And you, my dear friend, how far have you got?"

"I am a privy councillor," said the fat man. "I have two stars."

The thin man turned pale and went stiff. His face twisted into a broad, sugary smile. He seemed to shrink, and so did his bags and his family. "Your Excellency, I am very pleased," he stammered. "A friend, one might say, of my childhood, and now risen to such a height." His wife smiled, his son clicked his heels and dropped his cap.

"Come, come," the fat man said, frowning. "What is this tone? We were boys together. There is no need for this rank business." But the thin man only giggled and cringed further. The fat man felt sick. He turned away, gave the thin man his hand to say goodbye, and left.
lesson: Respect for rank can destroy real connection. Treat people the same whatever their title, and do not shrink yourself in front of status.
people: Two old school friends, the thin man's wife and son
source: Anton Chekhov, Fat and Thin (Tolstyi i tonkii, 1883)

title: Emily Roebling Finishes the Brooklyn Bridge
text:
John Augustus Roebling designed the Brooklyn Bridge, but he never saw it begun. In 1869, while surveying the site, his foot was crushed by a ferry against a piling, and he died of tetanus weeks later. His son Washington, an engineer and Civil War veteran, took over as chief engineer.

Washington worked inside the caissons, the huge pressurized chambers sunk to the river bottom for the foundations. In 1872 he was struck down by caisson disease, the bends. Partly paralyzed and in great pain, he could not visit the site. From a room in Brooklyn Heights he watched the work through a telescope.

His wife, Emily Warren Roebling, became his link to the project. She carried his instructions to the engineers, answered their questions, and dealt with officials and contractors. To do it, she studied stress analysis, cable construction and the strength of materials. For about eleven years she was so present on the project that many people believed she was the real engineer. When politicians tried to remove her husband in 1882, she defended him before the American Society of Civil Engineers.

The bridge opened on 24 May 1883. Emily Roebling was the first person to cross it by carriage, carrying a rooster as a sign of victory. A plaque on the bridge honors the three of them: John, Washington and Emily.
lesson: When illness strikes a family, the work does not have to die. Someone willing to learn what was never expected of her can carry it through.
people: Emily Warren Roebling, Washington Roebling, John A. Roebling
location: Brooklyn and New York City, USA
source: David McCullough, The Great Bridge (1972); Roebling family papers, Rutgers University

title: Pinocchio Finds Geppetto
text:
Pinocchio, the wooden puppet carved by the poor old woodworker Geppetto, had caused his father endless grief. He sold his schoolbook, ran off with a puppet theater, was cheated by a fox and a cat, and was turned into a donkey for running away to the Land of Toys. Meanwhile Geppetto, searching for his lost son, had set out to sea in a little boat and vanished.

At last Pinocchio, thrown into the sea, was swallowed by the Terrible Dogfish, a sea monster a kilometer long. Deep inside its belly he saw a faint light. There, at a table, sat an old man, white as snow, eating live fish. It was Geppetto, who had been swallowed two years before and had survived on the supplies of a ship the monster had also swallowed. Now the last candle was nearly burned out.

Pinocchio threw his arms around his father. While the old monster slept with its mouth open, he led Geppetto out along its tongue. Geppetto could not swim, so Pinocchio took him on his shoulders and swam with him toward land, until both were nearly exhausted and a friendly tuna carried them ashore.

From then on Pinocchio worked. For months he turned a water wheel for a farmer to earn a glass of milk a day for his frail father, and in the evenings he wove baskets. One morning he woke to find he was no longer a puppet but a real boy.
lesson: Children begin to grow up when they start caring for the parents who cared for them. That turn from receiving to giving is the real change.
people: Pinocchio, Geppetto
source: Carlo Collodi, The Adventures of Pinocchio (Le avventure di Pinocchio), 1883, Chapters 35 to 36

title: Chameleon
text:
Police inspector Ochumelov was crossing the market square in a new greatcoat when he heard a shout. A crowd had gathered around Khryukin, a goldsmith, who was holding up a bleeding finger. A small white puppy, trembling, sat on the ground nearby. The dog had bitten him.

Ochumelov took charge. He declared that dogs running loose would no longer be tolerated, that the owner would be fined and the animal destroyed. Then someone in the crowd said it looked like General Zhigalov's dog. Ochumelov suddenly felt hot, asked for help taking off his coat, and announced that Khryukin must have provoked the little thing, probably by jabbing a cigarette in its face.

A policeman then said the general had only pointer dogs. Ochumelov changed his mind again: this was a mongrel, a stray, and it should be put down. The policeman had second thoughts, and the inspector, now cold, put his coat back on and called the dog a delicate thoroughbred. This went back and forth until the general's cook happened by. The dog was not the general's, he said, but belonged to the general's brother, who had just come for a visit.

Ochumelov beamed, called the puppy a lively little thing, and let the cook take it. The crowd laughed at Khryukin, and Ochumelov, threatening the goldsmith that he would deal with him later, wrapped himself in his coat and walked on.
lesson: If your judgment of a case changes when you learn who is involved, you are not judging the case. Decide on the facts first, then find out whose interests are at stake.
people: Police inspector Ochumelov, Khryukin the goldsmith, a policeman, the general's cook
source: Anton Chekhov, Chameleon, 1884

title: The Necklace
text:
Mathilde Loisel was pretty and charming but married to a minor clerk in the Ministry of Education, and she felt she had been born for luxury. When her husband proudly brought home an invitation to a ministry ball, she wept because she had nothing to wear. He gave her the four hundred francs he had saved for a gun so she could buy a dress. Then she lamented that she had no jewels, so she borrowed a diamond necklace from her rich school friend, Madame Forestier.

At the ball she was a triumph. But when they got home, the necklace was gone. They searched everywhere and could not find it. Rather than confess to her friend, they found an identical necklace in a jeweler's shop for thirty-six thousand francs. Loisel spent his inheritance and borrowed the rest from moneylenders, and they returned it without a word.

Then came ten years of poverty. They dismissed their maid and moved to an attic. Mathilde scrubbed floors, carried water and haggled over every sou. Her husband worked evenings copying documents. Her hands grew red, her hair untidy, her looks gone.

When the last debt was paid, Mathilde met Madame Forestier on the Champs-Elysees, still young and lovely, and told her the whole story with some pride. Her friend was deeply moved and took her hands. "Oh, my poor Mathilde! But mine was paste. It was worth five hundred francs at most."
lesson: Pride that keeps you from telling a friend the truth can cost far more than the embarrassment of an honest word. Admit problems early.
people: Mathilde Loisel, her husband, Madame Forestier
source: Guy de Maupassant, The Necklace (La Parure, 1884)

title: All Right, Then, I'll Go to Hell
text:
Huck Finn had floated down the Mississippi on a raft with Jim, a man escaping from slavery. Now two swindlers traveling with them had sold Jim for forty dollars to a farmer named Phelps, who was holding him to collect a reward.

Huck had been raised to believe that helping a slave escape was a terrible sin, stealing someone's property, and that people who did it went to everlasting fire. Sick with guilt, he decided to do the right thing. He sat down and wrote a letter to Miss Watson, Jim's owner, telling her where Jim was. For the first time in his life, he felt washed clean of sin, and he thought he could pray now.

But he did not pray. He sat thinking about the trip down the river. He saw Jim before him, in daylight and at night, in moonlight and storms. He remembered Jim standing his watch on top of his own so Huck could sleep, how glad Jim was every time Huck came back, how he called him honey and petted him, and how he had said Huck was the best friend he had in the world, and the only one he had now.

Then he looked at the letter. He was trembling, because he had to choose between two things forever. He held his breath for a minute. "All right, then, I'll go to hell," he said, and tore it up. Then he set his mind on stealing Jim out of slavery.
lesson: Sometimes loyalty to a real person means going against what you were taught. Let what you know of someone's goodness count more than rules that treat them as less than human.
people: Huck Finn, Jim
source: Mark Twain, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (1884), Chapter 31

title: Sorrow
text:
Grigory Petrov, a turner known in his district as a master craftsman and also as the most worthless peasant there, was driving his sick old wife through a snowstorm to the hospital in town. She lay silent in the sledge. As he drove, he talked to her, to himself, to the doctor in his head, and he began to remember.

For forty years they had lived together, and in those forty years, he realized, he had been drunk, had quarreled with her and beaten her, and had never once shown her any tenderness. She had gone out begging bread for them and had been afraid of him the whole time. He began to plan how he would make it up to her: buy her a kerchief, treat her well, let her sit quietly at home.

He turned to look at her. The snow was not melting on her face. She was dead. And only now, too late, he felt how sorry he was for her.

He turned the sledge back toward home, but he lost the road in the storm and fell asleep in the snow. He woke in a hospital, with the doctor telling him his frozen hands and feet would have to be cut off. Grigory wanted to say something, to start his life over, but he could not.
lesson: Tenderness put off until later may never be given at all. Say and show the love you mean to your family now.
people: Grigory Petrov the turner, his wife, the doctor Pavel Ivanovich
source: Anton Chekhov, Sorrow (Gore), 1885

title: Little Girls Wiser Than Men
text:
It was an early Easter, and the snow was melting. Two little girls from neighboring houses, Malasha and Akulya, came out into the lane in their new holiday frocks and found a big puddle. They took off their shoes and started to wade, warning each other to be careful. But Malasha stepped down hard, and the water splashed all over Akulya's new frock.

Akulya ran crying to her mother, who came out and slapped Malasha. Malasha's mother rushed out to defend her daughter, and the two women began to shout at each other. Their husbands came out, then other neighbors, and soon half the village was in the lane, shoving and shouting, ready to fight. An old grandmother tried to calm them, reminding them it was Easter, but no one listened.

Meanwhile the two little girls had forgotten all about the frock. Akulya wiped it as well as she could, and the two of them were back at the puddle.
