They scratched a little channel with a chip of wood to let the water run off down the lane, and sent a stick sailing along it, right through the legs of the shouting crowd.

The old woman pointed at them. The children had already made up and were playing happily together, while the grown men and women were still fighting about them. The people looked, felt ashamed, laughed at themselves, and went home.
lesson: Children forgive and move on quickly, and adults can learn from them. Ask whether a quarrel is still about the original problem or only about pride.
people: Malasha, Akulya, their mothers, an old grandmother, the villagers
source: Leo Tolstoy, Little Girls Wiser Than Men (1885)

title: A Spark Neglected Burns the House
text:
Ivan Shcherbakov and his neighbor Gavrilo, called the Lame, had lived side by side for years in peace. Then one of Ivan's hens laid an egg in Gavrilo's yard. Ivan's daughter-in-law went to look for it and accused Gavrilo's family of taking it. Words flew between the women, then between the men. Gavrilo tore out a tuft of Ivan's beard, and Ivan's family struck back.

The quarrel grew year by year. There were lawsuits about the beard, about a broken cart, about anything that could be found. Ivan's old father, lying on the stove, kept begging his son to make peace before it was too late, but Ivan would not listen. At last Ivan got Gavrilo sentenced to a flogging, and Gavrilo muttered a threat about fire.

One night Ivan saw Gavrilo creeping by his shed with a burning wisp of straw. Instead of stamping out the flame, he ran after Gavrilo and seized him, but Gavrilo struck him on the head and knocked him senseless. When he came to, the fire had caught the thatch, and with the wind it spread until half the village was burned, Ivan's house among them.

His old father, carried out of the burning house, lay dying. He asked Ivan whose fault the fire was. Ivan admitted it was his own. The old man told him to say nothing about who had set it, and to forgive. Ivan obeyed. He never told, he made peace with Gavrilo, and the two families rebuilt and lived as good neighbors again.
lesson: Small grievances grow when pride keeps feeding them. Put out the spark of a quarrel early, while it costs only a little humility.
people: Ivan Shcherbakov, Gavrilo the Lame, Ivan's father
source: Leo Tolstoy, A Spark Neglected Burns the House (1885)

title: Where Love Is, God Is
text:
Martin Avdeitch was a shoemaker who lived in a basement room with one window onto the street. Through it he saw people's feet, and he knew many of them by their boots. His wife and children had all died, the last a little son, and Martin had fallen into despair until an old pilgrim told him to live for God. He began to read the Gospels every evening, and his heart grew lighter.

One night he dozed over the book and heard a voice: "Martin, look out into the street tomorrow, for I shall come."

The next day he kept looking out of the window. He saw old Stepanitch, a retired soldier, shoveling snow and shivering, and called him in for hot tea. Later he saw a young mother in thin summer clothes trying to shelter her baby from the cold. He brought her in, fed her, and gave her his old cloak and a little money. In the afternoon an old woman caught a boy stealing an apple from her basket and seized him by the hair. Martin went out, made peace between them, and paid for the apple, and the boy ended up helping the old woman carry her sack.

That evening Martin sat sadly with his Gospel, since the visitor had not come. Then he heard the voice ask whether he did not know him, and saw the soldier, the mother with her baby, and the old woman with the boy, each smiling. The book lay open at the words: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me."
lesson: The chances to do real good usually come through the ordinary people who pass your window each day. Pay attention to them.
people: Martin Avdeitch the cobbler, Stepanitch, a young mother, an apple seller and a boy
source: Leo Tolstoy, Where Love Is, God Is (1885)

title: Misery
text:
It was evening in Petersburg, and wet snow was falling. The cab driver Iona Potapov sat motionless on his sleigh, white with snow, his little mare equally still. That week his son had died, and he had not yet been able to talk about it to anyone.

An officer hired him. As they drove, Iona turned around and said, "My son, sir, died this week." "What did he die of?" asked the officer, and then told him to drive on and keep his eyes on the road. Later three noisy young men climbed in, arguing and cursing at him to go faster. Iona tried again to tell them about his son. One of them answered that we all must die, and told him to hurry up.

Iona looked at the crowds hurrying along the streets. Among all those thousands, was there not one who would listen? He went back to the cabmen's lodging house, where a young driver got up for a drink of water. Iona asked if he was thirsty and began, "My son died." But the young man had already covered his head and gone back to sleep.

It was too early to bed. Iona went out to the stable, where his mare stood munching hay. "Are you eating?" he asked her. "Suppose you had a foal, and that foal died. You would be sorry, would you not?" The mare munched and breathed on her master's hands. And Iona told her everything.
lesson: Someone grieving often needs nothing more than a person willing to listen. Take a moment to hear people out, even strangers.
people: Iona Potapov the cab driver
source: Anton Chekhov, Misery (Toska, 1886)

title: Vanka
text:
Vanka Zhukov, a boy of nine, had been sent three months earlier to Moscow as an apprentice to the shoemaker Alyakhin. On Christmas Eve, while his master and the workmen were at church, he took out a crumpled sheet of paper and a rusty pen and began a letter to his grandfather, Konstantin Makaritch, a night watchman on a country estate.

He wrote that he had no father and no mother, that his grandfather was all he had. His master had pulled him by the hair into the yard and thrashed him for falling asleep while rocking the baby. The mistress had poked him in the face with a herring. There was nothing to eat but bread in the morning and porridge at night. "Dear grandfather, for God's sake take me away from here, home to the village."

Between lines he remembered his grandfather: his laughter, the frosty nights, the dogs, going with him to cut a Christmas tree, the young lady at the big house who had taught him to read.

He folded the letter and addressed the envelope: "To grandfather in the village." Then, after a moment's thought, he added the name: "Konstantin Makaritch." He ran out and dropped it in the post box, and that night he fell asleep happy, dreaming of his grandfather reading his letter to the cook by the stove.
lesson: A child sent away to work or to cope alone still needs home more than anything. Make sure the children in your life know where to reach you.
people: Vanka Zhukov, his grandfather Konstantin Makaritch
source: Anton Chekhov, Vanka, 1886

title: The Candle
text:
On an estate in the days of serfdom, the owner hired a steward named Michael Semyonovich who treated the peasants with relentless cruelty. He worked them without rest, fined them, and had them flogged for the smallest fault. The peasants hated him and began talking among themselves about killing him.

Then he ordered them to plow his fields on Easter Sunday, the greatest holy day of the year. The peasants were furious, and the talk of murder grew louder. One man, Peter Mikhyeev, refused to join in. Killing a man, he said, was a far worse sin than working on a holy day, and the evil would fall on whoever did it.

On Easter Peter went out to plow as ordered. He fixed a lighted wax candle to his plow, the kind lit in church at Easter, and plowed singing the Easter hymn. All day the candle never went out.

When the steward heard about it, he was shaken. He went pale and said that Peter had beaten him. Soon afterward he fell from his horse and was killed. The peasants were freed from him without having to take his life.
lesson: Cruelty from those in charge invites hatred and revenge. One person's quiet refusal to answer evil with evil can do more to break that cycle than violence.
people: Michael Semyonovich the steward, Peter Mikhyeev
source: Leo Tolstoy, The Candle, 1886

title: How Much Land Does a Man Need?
text:
Pahom was a Russian peasant who said that if only he had enough land, he would not fear the Devil himself. The Devil heard him, and took him at his word.

Pahom bought a little land, then more. He moved to a bigger farm near the Volga and prospered, but it never felt like enough. Then a traveler told him about the Bashkirs, a people on the steppe who would sell their land cheaply. Pahom went to them. Their chief named a strange price: one thousand rubles a day. For that sum, Pahom could have all the land he could walk around between sunrise and sunset. But if he did not return to his starting point by sunset, he would lose his money.

At dawn Pahom set off with a spade, marking his corners as he went. The land was good everywhere, and he kept going a little farther to include one more meadow, one more hollow. By afternoon he realized he was very far from the start. He turned back and walked, then ran, his heart pounding, as the sun sank toward the horizon.

He reached the starting point just as the sun went down, and the Bashkirs cheered. But Pahom fell forward and lay dead. His servant took the spade and dug him a grave. Six feet from his head to his heels was all he needed.
lesson: Decide in advance what enough looks like. Without a limit you set yourself, every gain just becomes a reason to go a little farther than you can afford.
people: Pahom, the Bashkir chief
source: Leo Tolstoy, How Much Land Does a Man Need? (1886)

title: The Death of Ivan Ilyich
text:
Ivan Ilyich Golovin had lived a correct, comfortable life as a judge in St. Petersburg. His marriage to Praskovya Fyodorovna had cooled into irritation, but he had his work, his card games and his well furnished flat. While hanging curtains in the new apartment, he slipped and knocked his side against a window frame. The bruise seemed nothing, but a pain began that would not go away.

As he grew worse, his family and doctors kept up a lie: that he was merely ill and would get better if he followed the treatment. He knew he was dying, and their pretense tormented him. His wife and daughter went to the theater and talked of engagements while he lay in agony, and he felt utterly alone.

The only one who comforted him was Gerasim, a young peasant servant. Gerasim did not pretend. He cleaned up after him without disgust and sat for hours holding Ivan's legs on his shoulders, the only position that eased the pain. Everyone dies some day, he said plainly, so why should he not take a little trouble for a sick man?

In his last hours, after three days of screaming, Ivan felt his young son kiss his hand and saw his wife's tear-stained face. He felt sorry for them and wanted to release them. The fear of death left him. Where death had been, there was light.
lesson: When someone we love is dying, honest presence comforts far more than polite pretending. Sometimes the bravest care is simply not to lie.
people: Ivan Ilyich Golovin, his wife Praskovya Fyodorovna, his son Vasya, the servant Gerasim
source: Leo Tolstoy, The Death of Ivan Ilyich (Smert Ivana Ilyicha), 1886

title: The Lottery Ticket
text:
Ivan Dmitritch, a man of modest means who was quite content with his life, sat down on the sofa after supper with the newspaper. His wife Masha asked him to look for the lottery results. She had a ticket.

He found that the series number matched. Before checking the ticket number, he paused, enjoying the suspense. It might be seventy five thousand roubles. The two of them began to imagine.

Ivan pictured an estate in the country, lying in the sun, going abroad. Then he wondered: why should his wife go abroad? She would fuss, complain about trains, spend his money. He looked at her and found her old and plain, smelling of the kitchen. And her relations would come begging, those wretches.

Masha, meanwhile, had her own dreams, and he saw in her eyes that she too would grab the money and keep it from him. Each began to look at the other with hatred.

At last he checked the number. It was wrong. At once the hatred and the hopes vanished. But the room now seemed dark and small, the supper sat heavy, and the two of them were left bitter and sour with each other.
lesson: Sudden wealth, even imagined, can expose resentments that ordinary life keeps quiet. Contentment is easier to lose than to rebuild.
people: Ivan Dmitritch, his wife Masha
source: Anton Chekhov, The Lottery Ticket (Vyigryshny bilet), 1887

title: Anne Sullivan at the Water Pump
text:
Helen Keller lost her sight and hearing to an illness before she was two. By the age of six she was a wild, frustrated child in Tuscumbia, Alabama, who kicked, grabbed food from plates and threw tantrums her loving but helpless family could not control. In March 1887 a twenty year old teacher from the Perkins Institution in Boston, Anne Sullivan, herself partly blind, arrived to teach her.

Sullivan spelled words into Helen's hand with her fingers from the first day: d-o-l-l for a doll, c-a-k-e for cake. Helen copied the movements like a game but had no idea they were names. Sullivan insisted on table manners and fought long battles of will with her, but she never stopped spelling.

On April 5, 1887, Sullivan took Helen to the water pump in the garden. While one hand was under the cold stream, Sullivan spelled w-a-t-e-r into the other, again and again. Suddenly Helen stood still. In The Story of My Life she wrote that she knew then that the word meant the wonderful cool thing flowing over her hand. She touched the ground and demanded its name, then the pump, then her teacher. By evening she had learned many new words. Sullivan stayed at her side for almost fifty years.
lesson: Patience that keeps trying the same loving effort, day after day, can reach someone who seems unreachable. Breakthroughs often come after long stretches where nothing seems to work.
people: Anne Sullivan, Helen Keller
source: Helen Keller, The Story of My Life (1903), chapter 4, with Anne Sullivan's letters

title: The Man Who Would Be King
text:
Daniel Dravot and Peachey Carnehan were two loafers and former soldiers in British India. They signed a contract with each other to give up drink and women and go to Kafiristan, a remote land in the mountains beyond Afghanistan, where they meant to make themselves kings. They set off with twenty rifles disguised as a mad priest and his servant.

In Kafiristan they trained villagers to shoot and won battle after battle. The people took Dravot for a god, the son of Alexander the Great. By a stroke of luck, Dravot recognized local rituals as resembling Freemasonry, and he used the signs of the lodge to take command of the priests. He became king, and Carnehan his general. Dravot began to dream of a great kingdom, an empire to hand to the Queen.

Then he decided that a king needed a queen, and he insisted on marrying a local girl, against Carnehan's warnings and the priests' fear. At the ceremony the terrified bride bit him, and blood ran down his beard. A god does not bleed. The people rose against them. Dravot was made to walk onto a rope bridge over a gorge, the ropes were cut, and he fell. Carnehan was crucified between two pine trees and survived.

Months later, a crippled, half mad Carnehan reached the narrator's newspaper office carrying Dravot's head in a bag, still wearing its gold crown. He died soon afterward.
lesson: Authority built on an illusion lasts only while you remember it is an illusion. The moment you start believing your own legend and ignoring your partners' warnings, it begins to fall.
people: Daniel Dravot, Peachey Carnehan, the narrator
location: British India (story set in Kafiristan, modern Afghanistan)
source: Rudyard Kipling, The Man Who Would Be King, 1888

title: Theo van Gogh Keeps His Brother Painting
text:
Vincent van Gogh and his younger brother Theo began writing to each other in 1872, when Vincent was nineteen. Theo kept Vincent's letters, and more than six hundred of them survive. They are among the most moving records of an artist's life ever preserved.

Vincent failed as an art dealer, a teacher and a lay preacher before deciding, in 1880, to become a painter. From then on Theo, who worked for the Paris art dealers Goupil and Co., sent him money every month for the rest of his life. It paid for food, rent, paint and canvas. In return Vincent sent his work, which Theo kept and tried, almost entirely without success, to sell. The brothers lived together in Paris for two years, quarreling often; when Vincent left for Arles in 1888, the letters began again.

Theo's support was more than money. He believed in Vincent when no one else did, wrote to him about new art, and was the reader for whom Vincent explained his ideas about color and painting. When Theo's son was born in January 1890, he was named Vincent Willem after his uncle.

Vincent shot himself in July 1890 at Auvers-sur-Oise and died two days later, with Theo at his side. Theo died six months later. They are buried side by side at Auvers. Theo's widow, Jo van Gogh-Bonger, then devoted herself to publishing the letters and showing the paintings.
lesson: Steady faith in someone who is struggling can be worth more than any success. Quiet support, given month after month, may be what keeps another person's work alive.
people: Vincent van Gogh, Theo van Gogh, Jo van Gogh-Bonger
source: Vincent van Gogh, The Letters (Van Gogh Museum edition, 2009)
caveat: Most historians accept that Vincent shot himself, but a minority, notably his biographers Naifeh and Smith, have argued that the shot was fired by someone else.

title: Edison and the War of the Currents
text:
In the 1880s Thomas Edison's companies built the first electric lighting systems using direct current, or DC. DC worked well over short distances but lost power quickly along wires, so it needed a power station every mile or so. George Westinghouse backed a rival system, alternating current, or AC, whose voltage could be raised by transformers for long-distance transmission and lowered for use. In 1888 he bought the patents of the inventor Nikola Tesla on AC motors.

Edison, who had huge investments in DC, chose to fight AC as dangerous. His company published warnings about deaths from high-voltage AC lines. An electrical engineer named Harold Brown, assisted in Edison's laboratory, staged public demonstrations in which he killed animals with alternating current. Edison's allies also promoted the use of AC for the new electric chair in New York State, so that AC would be associated with death. In 1890 William Kemmler became the first man executed by electricity, in a botched and horrifying execution, using Westinghouse generators obtained without Westinghouse's consent.

The campaign won headlines but not the market. AC was cheaper to deliver over distance. In 1892 Edison's company merged into the new General Electric, which soon adopted AC as well. In 1893 Westinghouse lit the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago with AC, and he won the contract to generate power at Niagara Falls. AC became the standard for the world's power grids.
lesson: Fighting a better technology with fear may win a few battles but loses the war. When the economics turn against you, adapt instead of attacking.
people: Thomas Edison, George Westinghouse, Nikola Tesla, Harold P. Brown
source: Jill Jonnes, Empires of Light (2003); Thomas P. Hughes, Networks of Power (1983)

title: The Devoted Friend
text:
Little Hans was an honest fellow who grew the loveliest garden in the countryside. His dearest friend, as he believed, was the rich Miller. The Miller loved to say that real friends should have everything in common, and he never passed Hans's garden without filling a big basket with flowers or plums. He never gave anything in return.

In winter, when Hans had no flowers to sell and went hungry, the Miller did not visit. People in trouble should be left alone, he explained to his family, and anyway it might make Hans envious to see their warm kitchen. In spring he promised to give Hans his old broken wheelbarrow. From then on, he reminded Hans of this generosity every time he wanted something. Hans gave him a plank, carried his sack of flour to market, mended his barn roof and drove his sheep to the mountain, while his own garden went to weeds.

One stormy night the Miller knocked at Hans's door. His son had fallen from a ladder, and someone must fetch the doctor. He would not lend his new lantern in case it was lost. Hans went out into the dark and rain, found the doctor, and on the way home lost his path on the moor and drowned in a deep pool.

At the funeral the Miller walked at the head of the procession as Hans's best friend. Afterward he remarked that Hans's death was a great loss to him, because he had as good as given him his wheelbarrow and now did not know what to do with it.
lesson: Judge a friendship by what is done, not by what is said about it. If one side always takes, it is not friendship, so do not be that side.
people: Little Hans, the Miller
source: Oscar Wilde, The Devoted Friend, in The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1888)

title: The Selfish Giant
text:
Every afternoon after school the children played in the Giant's garden. It was large and lovely, with soft grass, flowers like stars and twelve peach trees. Then the Giant came home from a seven-year visit to his friend the Cornish ogre. Seeing the children, he shouted them away, built a high wall around the garden and put up a sign: Trespassers Will Be Prosecuted.

Spring came to the rest of the country, but not to the Giant's garden. Snow and Frost moved in, the North Wind came to stay, and the Hail rattled on the roof. Summer and autumn passed it by.

One morning the Giant heard a bird singing. The children had crept in through a hole in the wall, and in every tree sat a child, and the trees had burst into blossom. Only in one corner was it still winter, where a tiny boy stood crying because he could not reach the branches. The Giant's heart melted. He went down, lifted the boy into the tree, which flowered at once, and the boy kissed him. The Giant knocked down the wall and gave the garden to the children.

The little boy never came back, though the Giant longed for him. Years later, when the Giant was old, he saw him one winter morning under a tree white with blossom, with the marks of nails in his hands and feet. "You let me play once in your garden," the child said. "Today you shall come with me to my garden, which is Paradise." That afternoon the children found the Giant lying dead under the tree, covered with white blossoms.
lesson: Closing yourself off from others to protect what is yours leaves your life cold. Opening your door is what lets things grow.
people: The Giant, the children, a little boy
source: Oscar Wilde, The Selfish Giant, in The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1888)

title: The Mayo Brothers Build a Clinic
text:
William Worrall Mayo was an English-born doctor who settled in the small town of Rochester, Minnesota. His sons, William James and Charles Horace, grew up in his practice. As boys they rolled bandages, held lamps and helped at operations. Both studied medicine and came home to work with their father.

On 21 August 1883 a tornado tore through Rochester, killing dozens of people. There was no hospital, so the Mayos treated the injured in makeshift spaces, helped by the Sisters of Saint Francis. Afterward Mother Alfred Moes, the head of the order, proposed to build a hospital if Dr. Mayo would staff it. He thought the town too small, but she insisted. Saint Marys Hospital opened in 1889, with the Mayos as its doctors.

The brothers became famous surgeons. They worked as a team: while one operated at home, the other often traveled to learn new techniques from surgeons across America and Europe, then taught them to his brother. They invited other doctors to join them as partners and created one of the first group practices, in which specialists worked together on each patient.

In 1919 the brothers gave the bulk of their fortune to a nonprofit foundation, so that the clinic would serve patients and research rather than any family. They died within two months of each other in 1939. The Mayo Clinic still carries the family name.
lesson: A family's shared mission, and the willingness to share credit, can build something far larger than itself. Working as a team often starts at home.
people: William Worrall Mayo, William James Mayo, Charles Horace Mayo, Mother Alfred Moes
source: Helen Clapesattle, The Doctors Mayo (1941); Mayo Clinic historical records

title: The Origin of Strawberries
text:
The Cherokee tell that when the first man and the first woman had not been married long, they quarreled. The woman, angry, left the house and set off walking toward the east, toward the Sun, and she did not look back.

The man followed, grieving, but she kept far ahead and would not stop. The Sun took pity on him and asked if he was still angry with his wife. He said he was not. Would he like her to come back? Yes, he said, he would.

So the Sun made a patch of ripe huckleberries spring up along the path in front of the woman. She walked straight past without looking at them. Farther on the Sun put a clump of blackberries beside the way. She ignored those too. The Sun tried other fruits and trees, but nothing tempted her.

At last the Sun made a patch of strawberries grow, the first there had ever been, bright red and sweet. She stopped to pick a few. As she ate, she turned to face the west and began to think of her husband, and she found she could not go on. She sat down and gathered strawberries until he caught up with her. Then they went home together.
lesson: After a fight, walking away is easy, and stopping is the hard part. Something small and sweet, offered in time, can give both people room to turn around.
people: The first man, the first woman, the Sun
source: James Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee (Nineteenth Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, 1900), Origin of Strawberries

title: The Ertugrul Rescue and a Debt Repaid
text:
In September 1890 the Ottoman frigate Ertugrul was sailing home from a goodwill mission to Japan when a typhoon drove her onto the rocks off Oshima island, near Kushimoto in Wakayama. More than five hundred sailors died. The villagers of Oshima, poor fishing families, climbed down the cliffs in the storm to pull survivors from the sea. They carried them up, warmed them with their own bodies, and fed them their own scarce food, including their chickens. Sixty nine men survived, and Japanese warships carried them home to Istanbul.

In Turkey the story was taught in schools for generations. In Japan it was largely forgotten outside Kushimoto.

In March 1985, during the Iran-Iraq War, Saddam Hussein announced that after a 48 hour deadline any aircraft over Iran could be shot down. Foreign governments rushed to fly their citizens out of Tehran, but more than two hundred Japanese were stranded without seats. At Japan's request, Turkey sent Turkish Airlines planes, which flew the Japanese out shortly before the deadline. A Turkish diplomat later explained that Turkey had not forgotten the Ertugrul.
lesson: Kindness to strangers in distress is never wasted. It can be remembered and repaid by people you will never meet, long after you are gone.
people: Crew of the frigate Ertugrul, villagers of Oshima, Turkish Airlines crews
location: Kushimoto, Wakayama, Japan, and Tehran, Iran
source: Japanese and Turkish official accounts; contemporary press reports of the March 1985 evacuation from Tehran

title: The Dabbawalas of Mumbai
text:
Every working day in Mumbai, thousands of office workers eat a hot lunch cooked in their own homes that morning, delivered by the dabbawalas, "box carriers." The service traces its origins to 1890, when Mahadeo Havaji Bachche began delivering lunch to office workers in what was then Bombay.

The system works as a relay. In the morning a dabbawala collects tiffin boxes from homes in his area and carries them to the local railway station. There boxes are sorted by destination and loaded onto suburban trains in crates. At stations in the city center other dabbawalas unload, sort again, and deliver by bicycle, handcart or on foot to offices. After lunch the empty boxes travel back the same way.

Many dabbawalas have little formal schooling. Instead of addresses, each box carries a simple code of colors, letters and numbers on the lid that shows the origin station, the destination station, the building and the floor. Teams are small, each responsible for an area, and members cover for each other. Dabbawalas are members of their association rather than employees, share in its earnings, wear the same white cap, and follow strict rules about punctuality.

The network is often said to handle about two hundred thousand lunches a day, and late or lost boxes are rare. Business schools and visiting executives have studied it as a model of reliability built from simple tools and teamwork.
lesson: Reliability comes from a simple system run by a disciplined team. Clear codes, small groups with shared ownership and mutual cover can beat complex technology.
people: Mahadeo Havaji Bachche, Mumbai dabbawalas
source: Studies of the dabbawala system, e.g. Stefan Thomke, 'Mumbai's Models of Service Excellence', Harvard Business Review (November 2012)
caveat: The widely repeated claim of 'six sigma' accuracy (one error in millions) comes from a 1998 Forbes report and was never rigorously measured.

title: Kabuliwala
text:
Mini was five years old and could not stop talking. One day she called out to a tall Afghan fruit seller passing in the street, a man from Kabul with a bag of dried fruit on his back. Her father, a writer in Calcutta, was afraid she would be frightened of him. Instead, within days, the Kabuliwala, whose name was Rahamat, and the little girl were the best of friends, laughing at their private jokes. He came every day and brought her almonds and raisins.

One morning Rahamat was led away by the police, his clothes stained with blood. A man had owed him money and denied it, and in the quarrel Rahamat had stabbed him. He was sentenced to years in prison.

Mini grew up and forgot him. On the morning of her wedding, Rahamat appeared at the door, just released. He asked to see her. Her father, busy and uneasy, put him off. Rahamat turned to go, then offered a few raisins and almonds for Mini, and took out a crumpled piece of paper. On it was the smudged print of a small hand. He had a daughter of his own in Afghanistan, he explained, and he had carried this mark of her hand all those years.

The father's eyes filled. He called Mini in her bridal clothes. Rahamat saw that she was grown, and realized his own daughter must be too. The father gave him money from the wedding budget so he could go home to her, and cut back the wedding lights and band.
lesson: Parents everywhere share the same longing for their children. Seeing that in a stranger can turn suspicion into kindness.
people: Rahamat the Kabuliwala, Mini, her father
source: Rabindranath Tagore, Kabuliwala (1892)

title: Vivekananda Greets Chicago as Family
text:
In September 1893 the World's Parliament of Religions opened in Chicago, alongside the great World's Columbian Exposition. Speakers from many faiths gathered before an audience of several thousand. Among them was a young Hindu monk from India, Swami Vivekananda, almost unknown in America, who had arrived with little money and no official delegation behind him.

On the opening day, September 11, he had postponed his turn several times out of nervousness. When he finally rose in his orange robe and turban, he began with the words "Sisters and Brothers of America." Before he could go on, the audience rose to its feet and applauded for a long time.

His short speech that followed spoke of tolerance and universal acceptance. He said he was proud to belong to a religion that had sheltered persecuted refugees of other faiths, and quoted a Hindu hymn comparing the different paths people take to streams that all flow into the same sea.

Newspapers described him as one of the most impressive figures at the Parliament. He spent the next years lecturing in America and Britain and became one of the first teachers to bring Hindu philosophy to a broad Western audience.
lesson: Speak to strangers as members of your own family, and they often respond in kind. Warmth that comes before argument opens doors argument alone cannot.
people: Swami Vivekananda
source: John Henry Barrows, ed., The World's Parliament of Religions (1893); The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda, vol. 1

title: Kaa's Hunting
text:
In Kipling's Jungle Book, the Bandar-log, the monkey people, were noisy, boastful and leaderless. They always talked of great plans and never carried them out. One day they snatched the boy Mowgli and carried him off through the treetops to the Cold Lairs, a ruined city in the jungle.

As he was carried away, Mowgli called to Chil the kite, who flew to tell Baloo the bear and Bagheera the panther. They knew they could not handle the whole monkey horde alone, and the monkeys feared only one creature: Kaa, the great rock python. So, swallowing their pride, Baloo and Bagheera went to ask for his help, and Kaa agreed.

The three made their way to the Cold Lairs. In the moonlight, Bagheera attacked first, and the monkeys swarmed over him by the hundreds. Mowgli had been thrown into a summer house full of cobras, who left him alone after he gave the Snake People's master word. Baloo arrived and fought beside Bagheera. Then Kaa struck. He smashed through the wall of the summer house to free Mowgli, and the terrified monkeys fled to the walls.

At last Kaa began his hunger dance in the moonlight, swaying and coiling, until the monkeys, helpless and hypnotized, began to walk toward him. Baloo and Bagheera, also falling under the spell, had to be shaken awake. They led Mowgli home.
lesson: A small team that plans and brings in the right ally will beat a large, noisy crowd with no leader. Know what the opponent fears, and ask for help even when it costs you pride.
people: Mowgli, Baloo, Bagheera, Kaa, Chil the kite, the Bandar-log
location: England and the United States (story set in the jungles of central India)
source: Rudyard Kipling, The Jungle Book (1894), Kaa's Hunting

title: Nansen and Johansen Winter in a Stone Hut
text:
In March 1895 Fridtjof Nansen and Hjalmar Johansen left their ship Fram, which was drifting with the Arctic ice, and set out with dogs, sledges and kayaks to try for the North Pole. On 8 April they reached 86 degrees 14 minutes north, farther north than anyone before them, then turned back toward land.

The retreat took months. By late August they reached a barren island in Franz Josef Land, too late in the year to go on. They built a hut of stones and moss, roofed with walrus hides, barely big enough for two men lying down, and settled in for the polar night. They lived on walrus and polar bear meat, burned blubber for heat and light, and wore the same greasy clothes for nine months.

Nansen was a famous scientist and the expedition leader; Johansen was a reserve army officer. In Farthest North Nansen writes that through all of this they had continued to address each other with the formal Norwegian "De". On New Year's Eve, in their filthy hut, Nansen proposed that they drop it and use the familiar "du". They lived side by side through the whole winter without a serious quarrel.

In May 1896 they set off south again. In June, by pure chance, Nansen met the British explorer Frederick Jackson at Cape Flora, whose expedition took them home. Fram arrived in Norway a week after them.
lesson: Two people sharing hardship in a small space need patience and respect more than skill. Courtesy and small gestures keep a partnership intact through long strain.
people: Fridtjof Nansen, Hjalmar Johansen
location: Jackson Island, Franz Josef Land (modern Russia)
source: Fridtjof Nansen, Farthest North (1897)

title: Master and Man
text:
Vasili Brekhunov was a prosperous village merchant who measured everything in money. One winter evening he set out by sledge with his servant Nikita, a gentle, hardworking peasant he routinely underpaid, to close a deal on a forest before rival buyers could. A snowstorm was rising, but he would not wait.

They lost the road again and again and at last had to stop in an open field. Nikita settled into the sledge, resigned to whatever came. In the night Vasili, unable to sleep and terrified, mounted the horse and rode off alone, leaving Nikita to freeze. In the dark and the blowing snow he rode in a circle and ended up back at the sledge.

There he found Nikita nearly frozen. Something changed in Vasili. He opened his fur coat, lay down on top of his servant, and covered him with his own body and warmth. Lying there through the night, he felt a joy he had never known, and he thought that Nikita was alive, and so he himself was alive.

By morning, Vasili was dead. Nikita was found alive under him. He lost some toes to frostbite, but he lived for twenty more years.
lesson: Power over others is easy to treat as a source of profit. Its real meaning shows when the people who depend on you are in danger and you choose to shield them.
people: Vasili Andreevich Brekhunov, Nikita
source: Leo Tolstoy, Master and Man, 1895

title: Menelik's Victory at Adwa
text:
In 1889 Menelik II of Ethiopia signed the Treaty of Wuchale with Italy. The Amharic text said Ethiopia could use Italy for its foreign relations if it wished; the Italian text said it must. Italy used its version to claim a protectorate. Menelik rejected the claim, and in 1895 Italian forces from Eritrea advanced into northern Ethiopia.

Menelik had spent years preparing. He had imported large quantities of modern rifles and some artillery, and he had built alliances with regional rulers who had once been rivals. His wife, Empress Taytu, a firm opponent of any concession, commanded her own troops. When he called for mobilization, a very large army gathered and marched north, fighting the Italians at Amba Alage and besieging their fort at Mekele.

By late February 1896 the armies faced each other near Adwa. The Ethiopian force was several times larger, and both sides were short of supplies. Under pressure from Rome to win, the Italian commander, General Oreste Baratieri, decided to attack. On the night before 1 March his brigades advanced through the mountains with poor maps, lost touch with each other, and were destroyed one by one. Italy lost several thousand dead and many prisoners.

In the Treaty of Addis Ababa later that year, Italy recognized Ethiopia's full independence. Adwa became a symbol of resistance to colonialism across Africa.
lesson: Victory often goes to the side that prepared long before the battle: resources secured, allies united, and leaders agreed on what they will not concede.
people: Menelik II, Empress Taytu Betul, Oreste Baratieri
source: Raymond Jonas, The Battle of Adwa (2011); Harold Marcus, The Life and Times of Menelik II (1975)

title: The Open Boat
text:
Stephen Crane based this story on his own experience. In January 1897 the steamer he was on sank off the coast of Florida, and he spent more than a day in a small dinghy before reaching shore.

In the story, four men were left in a ten-foot boat on a rough sea after their ship went down: the injured captain, the cook, the oiler Billie, and a newspaper correspondent. The waves were so steep that every one of them threatened to swamp the boat. The cook bailed. The captain, unable to row, gave orders and kept their spirits up. The oiler and the correspondent took turns at the oars, changing places carefully so as not to tip the boat, rowing until they could hardly move.

They could see the shore and a lighthouse, but no one saw them, and the surf was too heavy to land. They spent a long night at sea, taking turns to row and sleep. Crane wrote that among the four grew a subtle brotherhood, a comradeship the correspondent felt was the best experience of his life.

The next morning they decided to take the boat through the surf. It overturned, and they swam for the beach. Rescuers on shore pulled the captain, the cook and the correspondent out alive. The oiler, the strongest of them, who had rowed the hardest, was found dead on the sand.
lesson: Shared danger can forge a deep bond in people who would otherwise have little in common. In a crisis, take turns, share the load, and keep each other going.
people: The captain, the cook, Billie the oiler, the correspondent
location: Off the coast of Florida, USA
source: Stephen Crane, The Open Boat (1897)

title: Suicide and Social Integration
text:
Suicide seems like the most personal of acts. In 1897, the French sociologist Emile Durkheim set out to show that it also has social causes. Working with official statistics from several European countries, he compared suicide rates across groups and over time.

He found that rates differed in consistent ways. Protestant regions had higher rates than Catholic ones, and Jewish communities lower still. Married people had lower rates than unmarried ones, and those with children lower than those without. Rates tended to fall during major political crises and wars, when people were drawn together.

Durkheim argued that what these patterns had in common was the degree to which people were integrated into a group and regulated by its norms. He described several types of suicide. Egoistic suicide arose when people were too weakly bound to family, religion or community. Altruistic suicide arose in the opposite case, when the group's claim on the individual was so strong that a person sacrificed themselves for it. Anomic suicide arose when sudden change, such as economic upheaval, disrupted the norms that gave people's lives order.

His work became a founding study of sociology, showing that social facts could be measured and explained.
lesson: Belonging to a group protects people. Pay attention to members who are drifting to the edges of the team, especially during times of upheaval.
people: Emile Durkheim
source: Durkheim, E. (1897). Le Suicide: Etude de sociologie. Felix Alcan.
caveat: Later scholars have criticized the quality of 19th century suicide statistics and the risk of drawing individual conclusions from group-level data, though the link between social integration and suicide remains widely studied.

title: The Burning of the Rice Fields
text:
In a story told by Lafcadio Hearn, an old man named Hamaguchi Gohei was the most respected man in a Japanese fishing village. His house stood on a high terrace above the bay, and from it he looked down on the village and the beach below. It was harvest time, and his rice stood stacked in the fields around his house, ready to bring in. Down by the shore the villagers were preparing for a festival.

One evening there was a long, slow earthquake. Hamaguchi, watching the sea, saw it suddenly run back from the shore, uncovering the sand far out. The villagers ran down onto the beach to stare at it. He understood that a great wave was coming and that there was no time to warn them.

He took a burning torch and set fire to his own rice stacks, one after another. The temple bell was rung, and seeing the fire on the hill, the villagers came running up to help, as was their duty. Hamaguchi stood over the burning harvest and would not let them put it out. Then he pointed to the sea. The wave struck, and the village below was swept away. But the people were on the hill.

Hamaguchi had made himself poor to save them. The grateful villagers rebuilt their homes and his, and while he still lived they built a shrine to him and worshipped his spirit as a living god.
lesson: Sometimes the only way to get people to move fast is to sacrifice something of your own that they can see. Act on the danger you can see before others recognize it.
people: Hamaguchi Gohei, the villagers
source: Lafcadio Hearn, A Living God, in Gleanings in Buddha-Fields (1897)
caveat: Hearn based the story on Hamaguchi Goryo and the 1854 tsunami in Hiro, Wakayama, where the real man burned rice straw to guide villagers to safety in the dark, as the tsunami was striking.

title: Harvey on the We're Here
text:
Harvey Cheyne was fifteen, the spoiled son of an American railroad millionaire, and he was insufferable to everyone on the ocean liner taking him to Europe. One day, seasick, he fell overboard off the Grand Banks of Newfoundland. A Portuguese fisherman named Manuel picked him out of the sea and brought him aboard the fishing schooner We're Here, from Gloucester, Massachusetts.

Harvey demanded that the captain, Disko Troop, take him straight to New York, promising his father would pay. Troop did not believe a word about the millionaire father and would not cut short the fishing season. When Harvey accused him of stealing the money he had lost overboard, Troop knocked him down. Then he offered Harvey a job as a ship's boy for ten dollars and a half a month.

With nothing else to do, Harvey took it. Dan, the captain's son, became his friend. Harvey learned to bait hooks, row a dory, clean and salt the cod, keep watch and take his share of every job, and the crew began to treat him as one of them. For the first time in his life he was valued for what he did.

At the end of the season the We're Here sailed home to Gloucester, and Harvey's parents came to fetch him. They found a different boy.
lesson: Respect in a team is earned by doing your share of the real work. Being needed by others can change a person more than any amount of comfort.
people: Harvey Cheyne, Disko Troop, Dan Troop, Manuel
location: England and the United States (novel set on the Grand Banks and in Gloucester, Massachusetts)
source: Rudyard Kipling, Captains Courageous (1897)

title: Empress Dowager Cixi and the Guangxu Emperor
text:
Cixi began as a concubine of the Xianfeng emperor of the Qing dynasty and became powerful as the mother of his only son. When that son, the Tongzhi emperor, died young in January 1875, without an heir, Cixi chose the next emperor herself. She picked her three-year-old nephew Zaitian, son of her own sister and an imperial prince. Choosing a small child, rather than an adult of the next generation, allowed her to go on ruling as regent.

The boy, who reigned as the Guangxu emperor, was taken from his parents and raised in the palace under her authority. He was taught to call her his royal father. He grew up nervous and sickly but intelligent, and keen on reform.

In 1889 Cixi formally handed power to him, though she kept a close watch. In 1898, after China's defeat by Japan, Guangxu launched a burst of reforms known as the Hundred Days. Conservative officials turned to Cixi. In September 1898 she took back control, executed several reformers and confined the emperor to a pavilion on an island in the palace lake. He remained a virtual prisoner for the rest of his life.

On 14 November 1908, Guangxu died at thirty-seven. Cixi died the following day. In 2008 scientific tests on his remains found a lethal dose of arsenic, suggesting that he was poisoned.
lesson: When family ties and power become entangled, a guardian can become a jailer. Raising a child to need us is not the same as raising them.
people: Empress Dowager Cixi, Guangxu Emperor (Zaitian)
location: Forbidden City and Zhongnanhai, Beijing, China
source: Jung Chang, Empress Dowager Cixi (2013); Qing court records; Chinese forensic report on the Guangxu emperor's remains (2008)
caveat: Who ordered the poisoning is unknown; suspects include Cixi and court officials.

title: Pierre and Marie Curie: A Marriage of Equals
text:
Maria Sklodowska came from Warsaw to Paris in 1891 to study physics, living on very little in a cold attic room. In 1894 she met Pierre Curie, a physicist already known for his work on crystals and magnetism. They married in July 1895. Instead of a wedding dress she wore a dark blue outfit she could use in the laboratory, and they spent their honeymoon touring France by bicycle.

For her doctoral research Marie chose the strange rays given off by uranium, discovered by Henri Becquerel. She found that the ore pitchblende was more active than its uranium could explain. Pierre put his own research aside to join her. In 1898 they announced two new elements, polonium, named after her homeland, and radium. To isolate radium they processed tons of pitchblende residue in a leaky shed at the School of Physics and Chemistry, Marie stirring boiling masses with an iron rod.

In 1903 the Nobel Committee at first planned to honor only Pierre and Becquerel. Pierre insisted that Marie be included, and the three shared the Physics prize. Three years later, in April 1906, Pierre was killed by a horse-drawn wagon on a Paris street. Marie took over his professorship at the Sorbonne, the first woman to teach there, and won a second Nobel Prize, in chemistry, in 1911. Their daughter Irene later won one too.
lesson: A partnership works best when each person's ability is fully recognized. Standing up for a partner's share of the credit is part of the work, not a favor.
people: Marie Curie, Pierre Curie
source: Marie Curie, Pierre Curie (1923); Eve Curie, Madame Curie (1937)

title: The Cyclists and the Fishing Reels
text:
Norman Triplett, a psychologist at Indiana University and a keen cycling fan, noticed something in the official racing records of the League of American Wheelmen. Riders who raced against the clock alone were slower than riders who had a pacer, and both were slower than riders in head-to-head races. Cyclists had theories about suction behind the pacer or worry while leading, but Triplett suspected that the presence of another rider itself spurred people on.

To test this, he built an apparatus with two fishing reels. Turning a reel drew a silk band around a loop, and a flag on the band showed progress. Triplett had about forty children wind the reel as fast as they could, sometimes alone and sometimes side by side with another child doing the same task.

Many children wound faster when competing with another child. Some did not change, and a few did worse, which Triplett put down to overexcitement. He published his findings in 1898, and the study is often cited as one of the first experiments in social psychology, an early look at how merely working next to others changes how we perform.
lesson: Working alongside others can lift your pace. If a task drags, try doing it next to someone who is working hard too.
people: Norman Triplett
source: Triplett, N. (1898). The dynamogenic factors in pacemaking and competition. American Journal of Psychology, 9(4), 507-533.
caveat: A modern statistical reanalysis of Triplett's data found the effect among the children weaker than textbooks often suggest.

title: The Man That Corrupted Hadleyburg
text:
Hadleyburg was famous for being the most honest and incorruptible town in the region. Its children were taught honesty from the cradle and kept far from temptation. One day the town offended a passing stranger, and he decided to take revenge on the whole place.

Years later he returned and left a heavy sack at the house of an old bank cashier, Edward Richards, with a note. It said the sack held gold worth about forty thousand dollars, meant as a reward for a Hadleyburg man who had once given the stranger twenty dollars and a piece of good advice. The man who could repeat the remark would get the gold.

Then the stranger sent letters to nineteen of the town's leading citizens. Each one was told privately the exact remark and was invited to claim the prize. None of them had given the money, but each of them sent in a claim.

At a great town meeting, the claims were opened one by one, and the leading citizens were exposed, in front of everyone, as liars and cheats. Richards was spared only because the man reading the claims quietly held his back. The sack turned out to hold gilded lead. Disgraced, the town changed its name and its motto.
lesson: A group that has never tested its virtue may find out all at once that it lacks it. Honesty that depends on never meeting temptation is not yet honesty.
people: Edward and Mary Richards, the nineteen leading citizens of Hadleyburg, the stranger
source: Mark Twain, The Man That Corrupted Hadleyburg (1899)

title: Anansi and the Pot of Wisdom
text:
In the stories of the Ashanti people of Ghana, Anansi the spider once gathered up all the wisdom in the world and sealed it in a pot. Now he would be the wisest of all creatures, and everyone would have to come to him for advice.

But he worried that someone might steal it. He decided to hide the pot at the top of a very tall tree, where no one could reach it. He tied the pot to the front of his body and began to climb. The pot hung between him and the trunk, bumping against the bark, and every time he tried to pull himself up, it got in his way. He slipped and tried again and slipped again.

His young son Ntikuma had been watching from the ground. Father, he called up, why not tie the pot on your back? Then you could hold the tree.

Anansi was furious. He had all the wisdom of the world in his pot, and a small child had seen what he had missed. In his anger he let the pot fall. It smashed on the ground, and the wisdom scattered in every direction. People came from everywhere and picked up pieces of it, and that is why wisdom is shared among everyone today.
lesson: Nobody holds all the good ideas, and keeping knowledge to yourself makes you less wise, not more. Listen to the person you least expect to help.
people: Anansi, his son Ntikuma
source: Ashanti (Akan) folk tradition, Ghana
caveat: Versions differ on details, such as whether the pot belonged to the sky god Nyame.

title: The First Fire
text:
In the Cherokee story recorded by James Mooney, at first there was no fire and the world was cold. Then the Thunders sent lightning, which set fire to the bottom of a hollow sycamore tree on an island. The animals could see the smoke rising, but the tree stood in water, and nobody knew how to reach it.

The animals held a council. Raven offered to go first, because he was large and strong. He flew over and landed on the tree, but the heat scorched his feathers black, and he came back without fire. Then the little Screech Owl went. As he looked down into the hollow, a blast of hot air nearly burned out his eyes, which are still red. The Hoot Owl and the Horned Owl tried next, and the smoke left white rings around their eyes. The black racer snake swam over and slipped in through a hole at the bottom, but he was scorched black. The great black snake climbed up the outside and fell in, and came out as black as the racer.

At last the Water Spider, small and furry, offered to go. She spun a thread and wove a tiny bowl, fastened it on her back, and ran across the water to the island. She brought back one live coal in her bowl, and that is how the people got fire.
lesson: When the strongest members of a team fail, the solution may come from the smallest one with the right idea. Give everyone a chance to try.
people: Raven, the owls, the snakes, the Water Spider
source: James Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee (1900), The First Fire

title: The Cow Tail Switch
text:
A West African tale tells of a hunter named Ogaloussa who went into the forest one day and did not come back. Weeks passed. His family went on with their lives, and his sons stopped speaking of him.

Then a son was born to his wife. When the child began to talk, his first words were, "Where is my father?" The eldest son said they should look for him. The brothers went into the forest and each used his own gift. One knew how to find the path, and he led them to the place where their father had been killed and only his bones remained. One knew how to put bones together, and he assembled the skeleton. One restored the sinews, another the blood, another the flesh, another the breath. At last Ogaloussa sat up and walked home with them.

Later Ogaloussa made a beautiful switch from a cow's tail, the finest object of its kind, and announced that he would give it to the son who had done the most to bring him back. The brothers each argued their case.

Ogaloussa gave it to the baby. A man is not truly dead, he said, until he is forgotten. The one who asked "Where is my father?" was the one who brought him home.
lesson: Remembering and asking after the absent is itself a form of care. In families, the one who keeps asking is often the one who holds everyone together.
people: Ogaloussa the hunter, his sons
source: Harold Courlander and George Herzog, The Cow-Tail Switch and Other West African Stories (1947)

title: Muskrat Brings Up the Earth
text:
In an Anishinaabe story, a great flood once covered the whole earth. Nanabozho, the spirit hero, floated on a log with the animals who had survived. There was no land anywhere, and they could not live on the water forever.

Nanabozho said that if someone could bring up a little earth from the bottom, he could make new land. The Loon, a fine diver, went first. He was gone a long time, but he came up gasping and empty. The Otter tried and failed. The Beaver, strong and proud, dove deep and stayed down longer than anyone, and he too came up with nothing, almost drowned.

Then the little Muskrat said he would try. Some of the bigger animals laughed. Muskrat dove anyway and was gone so long that they gave up hope. At last his body floated to the surface. He had died in the attempt, but in his small clenched paw was a lump of mud from the bottom.

The Turtle offered his back. Nanabozho spread the mud on the Turtle's shell, and it grew and grew until it became the land that some Anishinaabe still call Turtle Island. The animals honored Muskrat, and in many tellings Nanabozho breathed life back into him.
lesson: Persistence can matter more than size or reputation. Do not dismiss the quiet member who volunteers after the stars have failed.
people: Nanabozho, Loon, Otter, Beaver, Muskrat, Turtle
location: Great Lakes region (Canada and the United States)
source: Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) oral tradition, the earth diver story
caveat: The animals who try first and the ending differ between communities and tellers.

title: The Lion's Whisker
text:
An Ethiopian folk tale tells of a woman who married a widower with a young son. The boy grieved for his mother and would have nothing to do with his stepmother. He refused the food she cooked and turned away from her kindness. In despair, she went to a wise old man and asked him for a potion that would make the boy love her.

He said he could make one, but he needed a whisker from a living lion. The woman was terrified, but she wanted the boy's love badly enough to try.

She took meat out to where a lion lived and left it at a distance, then retreated. Day after day she returned, each time coming a little closer and staying a little longer. The lion grew used to her. In time it ate from near her feet, and finally it let her sit beside it. One day, as it lay quietly, she reached out and plucked a single whisker.

She ran with it to the wise man. He took it, looked at it, and threw it into the fire. She cried out in dismay. He told her she did not need a potion. She had approached a wild lion with patience, little by little, until it trusted her. If she approached the boy the same way, he too would come to her.
lesson: Trust from a hurt child cannot be forced or bought. It is won the slow way: small, steady steps, repeated until they are believed.
people: A stepmother, her stepson, a wise man, a lion
source: Ethiopian folktale; retold in Brent Ashabranner and Russell Davis, The Lion's Whisker: Tales of High Africa (1959)
caveat: Versions differ in details, and in some the woman is trying to win back a husband rather than a stepson.

title: Tiddalik the Frog
text:
In a story from the Gunai (Kurnai) people of Gippsland in southeastern Australia, there was once a giant frog called Tiddalik. One morning he woke up with an enormous thirst, and he began to drink. He drank the creeks, the billabongs and the rivers until there was no water left anywhere. His belly swelled like a hill, and all the other animals and plants began to die of thirst.

The animals met to decide what to do. Someone had the idea that if Tiddalik could be made to laugh, the water would spill out of him. So one after another they tried. The kookaburra told his funniest stories. Other animals pulled faces, danced and played tricks. Tiddalik only sat there, swollen and sulky, staring at them.

At last Nabunum the eel, who had come out of the dry mud, began to dance. He twisted and turned, wriggled himself into knots and untied them again. Tiddalik's mouth began to twitch. Then he burst out laughing, and as he laughed, the water poured out of him and filled the rivers and lakes again.
lesson: When one person holds what everyone needs, force may not work. A group that keeps trying different approaches, with patience and good humor, can still find the one that does.
people: Tiddalik, the animals, Nabunum the eel
source: Australian Aboriginal oral tradition of the Gunai (Kurnai) people
caveat: Widely known versions are modern retellings, and the animals involved vary.

title: Yaa Asantewaa Leads the War of the Golden Stool
text:
In 1896 the British occupied Kumasi, capital of the Asante kingdom in what is now Ghana, and exiled its king, Prempeh I. Asante resentment grew. In March 1900 the British governor, Sir Frederick Hodgson, made a speech in Kumasi demanding to be given the Golden Stool so that he could sit on it.

The Golden Stool was the most sacred object of the Asante nation, believed to hold its soul. No one, not even the king, sat on it. The demand was an outrage.

The chiefs met in secret to discuss what to do. Yaa Asantewaa, the queen mother of Ejisu, was present. According to Asante oral tradition, when some of the men hesitated she told them that if they would not fight, the women would, and that she would call upon her fellow women.

The Asante rose. Under her leadership forces besieged the British in the Kumasi fort for months. British reinforcements eventually broke the siege, and Yaa Asantewaa was captured in 1901 and exiled to the Seychelles, where she died in 1921. The Golden Stool was never handed over, and the British did not demand it again.
lesson: When others hesitate, a leader who names what is at stake and steps forward first can give everyone the courage to act.
people: Yaa Asantewaa, Sir Frederick Hodgson, Prempeh I
source: British colonial records of the Asante war of 1900; Asante oral history
caveat: Her famous speech to the chiefs is known through oral tradition, and its exact words vary between versions.

title: Iktomi and the Ducks
text:
In a Dakota tale retold by Zitkala-Sa, Iktomi the trickster was walking along the edge of a lake with a bundle of grass tied on his back. A flock of ducks called out to ask what he was carrying. Iktomi said it was a bundle of songs.

The ducks begged him to sing them some. Iktomi agreed. He built a lodge of grass on the shore, and all the ducks crowded inside. He would sing, he told them, and they must dance with their eyes shut tight.

The ducks danced with their eyes closed. As they circled past him, Iktomi reached out, grabbed one, and wrung its neck, then another, still singing. The ducks heard nothing but the song and kept dancing.

Finally a little duck opened one eye a crack. He saw what was happening and screamed for the others to run, because Iktomi was killing them. The survivors fled out of the lodge and into the water.

Iktomi roasted his catch anyway. But while the ducks were cooking, he climbed a tree to stop two branches from creaking and got himself stuck between them, and a pack of wolves came by and ate every duck, leaving him only the bones.
lesson: A group that follows orders with its eyes shut can be picked off one at a time. Value the member who looks and speaks up, even if it means breaking ranks.
people: Iktomi, the ducks
location: Dakota lands, northern Great Plains, United States
source: Zitkala-Sa, Old Indian Legends (1901), Iktomi and the Ducks

title: Captain MacWhirr in the Typhoon
text:
Captain MacWhirr of the steamer Nan-Shan was a man of so little imagination that his crew thought him dull. He read facts, not ideas, and took everything literally. On one voyage in the China Sea, carrying about two hundred Chinese laborers returning home with their savings in camphorwood chests, the barometer began to fall faster than anyone had seen.

His first mate, Jukes, suggested changing course to put the ship's head to the swell and run around the storm, as the books advised. MacWhirr refused. Steering away would make them late, and the storm might go anywhere. He would not go around a gale. The way to get through it was to face it.

The typhoon struck with stunning force. The bridge was smashed, the boats were torn away, and Jukes, clinging on beside the captain, felt the end was near. Below, the laborers' chests broke open, their silver dollars spilled across the hold, and the men fought each other in the darkness. MacWhirr sent Jukes and the crew down to stop the fighting, gather up the money and lash the men safely in place. He held the ship steady through the eye of the storm and the second blow.

The Nan-Shan reached port battered but afloat. Since no one could tell whose dollars were whose, MacWhirr divided the money equally among the laborers. Jukes wrote to a friend, grudgingly, that the captain had got out of it very well for such a stupid man.
lesson: In a crisis, steady attention to the next necessary task often matters more than brilliance. Face the problem, protect people, and solve fairness questions in a way everyone can accept.
people: Captain MacWhirr, Jukes, the crew of the Nan-Shan
location: England (story set in the China Sea)
source: Joseph Conrad, Typhoon, 1902

title: Buck and the Sled Team
text:
In Jack London's novel, Buck, a big dog stolen from a California ranch, was sold into a sled team in the Yukon during the Klondike gold rush. The team carried mail for two French Canadian couriers, Francois and Perrault, and its lead dog was Spitz, a hard, experienced fighter who kept order with his teeth.

Buck learned the work quickly and came to hate Spitz. Instead of challenging him openly, he began to undermine him, stepping in to protect dogs that Spitz was punishing. Discipline broke down. The other dogs grew lazy and quarrelsome, the team stopped pulling together, and the sled slowed. Fights broke out constantly.

At last Buck and Spitz fought to the death in the snow, and Buck won. The next morning Francois tried to put another dog in the lead, but Buck would not allow it, and finally the men gave him the place.

As leader Buck surprised them. He punished the slackers, broke up the fighting, and brought the team back into line. Every dog pulled its weight again. The team, now working as one, made a record run back to Skagway, covering the trail in fourteen days at an average of forty miles a day.
lesson: A team where members fight for position stops moving forward. A leader earns the role by restoring order and making everyone pull together, not just by winning the fight.
people: Buck, Spitz, Francois, Perrault, the sled dogs
location: United States (novel set in the Yukon, Canada)
source: Jack London, The Call of the Wild (1903), chapters 3 and 4

title: The Three Questions
text:
A king decided that he would never fail at anything if he knew three things: the right time to begin each task, the right people to listen to, and the most important thing to do. Learned men gave him conflicting answers, so he went in plain clothes to a hermit known for his wisdom.

The hermit was digging his garden beds and did not answer. Seeing that he was old and tired, the king took the spade and dug for him. Toward evening a bearded man ran out of the woods, holding his stomach, bleeding badly, and collapsed. The king washed and bandaged the wound and spent the night caring for him.

In the morning the stranger begged forgiveness. He was the king's enemy: the king had executed his brother and seized his property. He had come to ambush the king on his way back, and when the king did not return he had been recognized and wounded by the bodyguards. Now the king had saved his life. The king forgave him gladly and promised to return his property.

The hermit then gave the answers. The most important time is now, the only time we have power over. The most important person is whoever you are with. The most important task is to do that person good.
lesson: Long plans are useful, but you only ever act in the present, with the person in front of you. Give them your full attention and help, and many future problems will never arise.
people: A king, a hermit, a wounded man
source: Leo Tolstoy, Three Questions, 1903

title: The Wright Brothers Argue Their Way to Flight
text:
Wilbur and Orville Wright never married. They lived together in their father's house in Dayton, Ohio, ran a bicycle shop together, and from 1899 worked together on the problem of flight. Their father, Milton, a bishop of the United Brethren Church, had brought home a toy helicopter when they were boys, and their sister Katharine kept the household going and later managed much of their correspondence.

The brothers were famous among their few employees for their arguments. Charlie Taylor, their mechanic, remembered them shouting at each other in the shop. Yet the arguments were a method. One would take a position, the other would attack it, and sometimes they would switch sides. When their glider of 1901 performed badly, they built a wind tunnel and tested some two hundred wing shapes, and discovered that the published lift tables everyone relied on were wrong.

On 17 December 1903, at Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville made the first powered, controlled flight, lasting twelve seconds. Wilbur had won the coin toss three days earlier but stalled on takeoff. That day they flew four times, taking turns. Wilbur said later that they had lived together, played together, worked together and thought together. They shared credit and held their patents jointly.
lesson: Close partners do not need to agree to work well together. Honest argument between people who trust each other can find what polite agreement misses.
people: Wilbur Wright, Orville Wright, Milton Wright, Katharine Wright
location: Dayton, Ohio and Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, USA
source: The Papers of Wilbur and Orville Wright, ed. Marvin W. McFarland (1953); David McCullough, The Wright Brothers (2015)

title: The Gift of the Magi
text:
On Christmas Eve, Della Dillingham Young counted her money three times. One dollar and eighty seven cents, saved a penny at a time by bargaining with the grocer and the butcher. It was all she had to buy a present for her husband Jim, who earned twenty dollars a week. She flopped down on the shabby couch and cried.

The young couple had two treasures. One was Jim's gold watch, which had been his father's and his grandfather's. The other was Della's hair, long and shining, falling below her knees. Della put on her old brown jacket and hat and went to a shop that bought hair. She sold it for twenty dollars. Then she searched the stores and found the perfect gift: a simple platinum chain for Jim's watch. It cost twenty one dollars.

When Jim came home and saw her short curls, he stood frozen, staring. She begged him not to be angry; her hair would grow back. He drew a package from his coat. Inside was a set of beautiful tortoise shell combs, with jeweled rims, that she had longed for in a shop window for ages. She held them to her heart. Then she showed him the watch chain.

Jim lay down on the couch, put his hands behind his head and smiled. He had sold the watch to buy her combs.
lesson: The worth of a gift lies in what the giver was willing to give up. Couples who sacrifice for each other are already rich.
people: Jim and Della Dillingham Young
source: O. Henry, The Gift of the Magi (first published in the New York Sunday World, 1905)

title: Togo at Tsushima
text:
In 1904 Japan went to war with Russia over Korea and Manchuria. Japan's navy had bottled up the Russian Pacific squadron at Port Arthur. Russia sent its Baltic Fleet, under Admiral Zinovy Rozhestvensky, on an extraordinary voyage of about eighteen thousand miles around Africa to the Far East. The voyage took more than seven months, and by the time the fleet arrived its crews were exhausted and the ships fouled with growth.

Admiral Togo Heihachiro waited for it with a fleet that had trained, repaired and rested. He placed his ships near the Korea Strait, which Rozhestvensky would probably use to reach Vladivostok. On 27 May 1905 Japanese scouts sighted the Russian fleet in the strait of Tsushima. As battle began, Togo hoisted a signal saying that the rise or fall of the empire depended on this battle and that every man should do his utmost.

Togo turned his battle line across the head of the Russian column, so that his ships could bring their guns to bear while the Russians could not answer fully. His faster ships, with better gunnery, concentrated fire on the leading Russian battleships. Over that afternoon and the following night and day, almost the whole Russian fleet was sunk, captured or interned. Rozhestvensky himself was wounded and captured. Japan lost three torpedo boats.

The battle ended Russia's hopes in the war, and a peace treaty was signed at Portsmouth, New Hampshire, in September 1905.
lesson: Readiness and position often matter more than size. Let the other side bear the costs of coming to you, and be fully prepared when it arrives.
people: Togo Heihachiro, Zinovy Rozhestvensky
source: Official naval histories of the Russo-Japanese War; Richard Hough, The Fleet That Had to Die (1958)

title: The Kellogg Brothers Fall Out over Corn Flakes
text:
John Harvey Kellogg was a famous doctor who ran the Battle Creek Sanitarium in Michigan, a health resort that promoted vegetarian food, exercise and abstinence. His younger brother, Will Keith Kellogg, worked for him for about twenty-five years as bookkeeper, manager and general helper, for modest pay and little recognition.

In the 1890s, while looking for digestible foods for the patients, the brothers developed a process for making flakes from boiled wheat, and later from corn. The flakes were a success with patients, and Will saw that they could be sold to the whole country. John was not interested in mass marketing, and he objected to Will's plan to add sugar, which he considered unhealthy.

In 1906 Will struck out on his own and founded the company that became Kellogg's, putting his signature on every box. The brothers then fought for years in court over who had the right to use the family name on cereal. Will won.

They never truly reconciled. According to family accounts and later biographers, near the end of his life John wrote his brother a long letter of apology, but it was held back by a secretary and Will did not see it until after John's death in 1943. Will, by then nearly blind, had given most of his fortune to the W. K. Kellogg Foundation, devoted to children's health and education.
lesson: Brothers who cannot agree on a shared enterprise may lose each other along with it. Say what needs saying while the other person can still hear it.
people: John Harvey Kellogg, Will Keith Kellogg
source: Howard Markel, The Kelloggs: The Battling Brothers of Battle Creek (2017)
caveat: The story of the undelivered letter comes from family accounts and is not fully documented.

title: Guessing the Weight of the Ox
text:
In 1906, the scientist Francis Galton, then in his eighties, visited the West of England Fat Stock and Poultry Exhibition in Plymouth. At the fair, a fat ox was on display, and visitors could buy a ticket for sixpence and write down their guess of its weight once it had been slaughtered and dressed. The best guesses won prizes.

Galton was skeptical of the judgment of ordinary people, and he saw an opportunity to test it. After the contest, he borrowed the tickets. Some were illegible, but around 800 were usable. Some came from butchers and farmers, but many came from people with no particular expertise.

He arranged the estimates in order and took the middle one, the median, as the voice of the people. It was 1,207 pounds. The ox's actual dressed weight was 1,198 pounds. The crowd's middle estimate was off by less than one percent.

Galton published his result in the journal Nature in 1907, under the title Vox Populi. He noted, somewhat to his surprise, that the collective judgment was more trustworthy than might have been expected.
lesson: Many independent guesses, pooled, can beat most experts. When estimating, collect separate judgments before people discuss and combine them.
people: Francis Galton
source: Galton, F. (1907). Vox populi. Nature, 75, 450-451.

title: The Last Leaf
text:
Two young women artists, Sue and Johnsy, shared a studio in a shabby corner of Greenwich Village. In November pneumonia swept the neighborhood, and Johnsy fell gravely ill. The doctor told Sue that her friend had perhaps one chance in ten, and that chance depended on whether she wanted to live.

Johnsy lay staring out of the window at an old ivy vine on the brick wall opposite, counting its leaves as the wind tore them off. When the last one fell, she told Sue, she would die too.

Downstairs lived Behrman, an old painter who had failed at art for forty years, drank too much, and was always going to paint his masterpiece. Sue told him about Johnsy's fancy. He scoffed at it, but he was upset. That night a cold rain and a howling wind beat against the house.

In the morning Johnsy asked Sue to raise the shade. One ivy leaf still clung to the vine. It was there all that day, and through another stormy night. Johnsy grew ashamed of wanting to die, asked for soup, and began to recover.

Then Sue told her the news. Behrman had died of pneumonia after only two days of illness. On the morning of the storm he had been found soaked through, with a lantern, a ladder, brushes and green and yellow paint. On the night the last leaf fell, he had painted it on the wall. It was his masterpiece.
lesson: A quiet act of care for a neighbor can give someone the strength to keep going. The greatest work of your life may be something done for one person.
people: Johnsy, Sue, old Behrman
location: Greenwich Village, New York City, USA
source: O. Henry, The Last Leaf, in The Trimmed Lamp (1907)

title: The Ransom of Red Chief
text:
Sam and Bill, two small time crooks, needed money for a land swindle. In a sleepy Alabama town they kidnapped the ten year old son of Ebenezer Dorset, a prosperous citizen, and hid him in a cave in the hills. They planned to ask two thousand dollars for his return.

The boy was delighted. He announced that he was Red Chief, terror of the plains, and that Bill was his captive. He kept them awake all night with war whoops, tried to scalp Bill at daybreak, dropped a hot potato down his back, hit him with a stone from a sling, and rode him like a horse for what Bill claimed was ninety miles. He had no intention of going home.
