By the second day Bill was a wreck. Sam lowered the ransom demand to fifteen hundred dollars and sent the letter. Dorset's reply was polite. He thought their demands a little high, and made a counter offer: if they brought Johnny home and paid him two hundred and fifty dollars in cash, he would agree to take the boy off their hands. They had better come at night, he added, because the neighbors believed the boy was lost and he could not answer for what they might do.

The kidnappers paid. At midnight they handed over the screaming boy, and while his father held him, they ran for the Canadian border.
lesson: A plan built on what you assume the other side values can collapse when you learn what they actually value. Know your counterpart before you set terms.
people: Sam, Bill Driscoll, Johnny Dorset, Ebenezer Dorset
source: O. Henry, The Ransom of Red Chief (1907; collected in Whirligigs, 1910)

title: To Build a Fire
text:
On a gray winter morning in the Yukon, a man set out alone along a frozen creek to join his companions at a mining camp. It was his first winter in the north. It was far colder than he knew: when he spat, the spit crackled in the air before it hit the snow. A big husky dog trotted with him. The dog's instinct told it that this was no time to travel, but it followed.

An old timer at Sulphur Creek had warned the man that no one should travel alone in the Klondike when it was colder than fifty below. The man had laughed at that. He was alert and capable, and he would be in camp by six.

Then he broke through thin ice over a hidden spring and soaked his legs to the knees. He knew what to do: build a fire and dry his feet. He built it under a spruce tree and it caught. But the tree's boughs were heavy with snow, and the heat and his movements shook them. The snow slid down and put the fire out.

His fingers were now numb and useless. He lit all his matches at once, burning his hands, but the second fire failed. He tried to kill the dog to warm his hands in its body and could not hold it. He ran until he collapsed. As he froze, he admitted that the old timer had been right. The dog waited, then went on toward the camp.
lesson: Confidence is no substitute for experience. When someone who has survived the conditions gives you a rule, follow it, especially when it seems overcautious.
people: A man, his dog, the old timer from Sulphur Creek
source: Jack London, To Build a Fire (1908)

title: Retaking Toad Hall
text:
In Kenneth Grahame's The Wind in the Willows, the vain and reckless Toad was sent to prison for stealing a motorcar. While he was away, the weasels and stoats from the Wild Wood moved into his grand house, Toad Hall, and took it over. When Toad escaped and came home, they drove him off with a gun.

Toad wanted to charge in at once. His friends had a better plan. Badger revealed that he knew a secret underground passage, which ran from the riverbank right up into the butler's pantry of Toad Hall. And he had learned that the weasels were holding a banquet the next night to celebrate the Chief Weasel's birthday, when they would all be gathered in the dining hall, eating and drinking and off their guard.

Each friend took a job. Rat laid out a sword, a cudgel, pistols and a policeman's truncheon for each of them. Mole disguised himself as a washerwoman and went to the house, where he spread a rumor that a huge force was coming to attack from the river and the woods. The worried weasels sent their guards out to the edges of the grounds.

The next night the four friends crept through the tunnel, burst into the dining hall with sticks swinging and Badger roaring, and drove every weasel and stoat out of the house. Toad Hall was Toad's again.
lesson: Friends who plan together, each taking a part that suits them, can recover what one person's folly lost. Prepare carefully, and let the quiet ones do their share.
people: Badger, Rat, Mole, Toad
source: Kenneth Grahame, The Wind in the Willows (1908), chapters 11 and 12

title: Raven Steals the Light
text:
In the beginning, the Tlingit say, the world was dark. A rich and powerful chief who lived at the head of the Nass River kept the stars, the moon and the daylight shut up in boxes in his house, and guarded them jealously. Raven wanted the light, but he could not take it by force, so he found a way into the chief's family.

The chief had a daughter. Raven turned himself into a tiny hemlock needle and floated in her drinking water. She swallowed it without noticing, became pregnant, and in time gave birth to a baby boy. It was Raven.

The chief doted on his grandson. The child cried and cried, pointing at the boxes hanging on the walls. To quiet him, the grandfather gave him the bag of stars to play with. The child let them go up through the smoke hole, and they scattered across the sky. Then he cried for the moon, and after a long time the old man gave him that too, and it went up into the sky as well.

At last he cried for the box that held the daylight. When the chief finally gave it to him, Raven turned back into a bird, took the box, and flew out through the smoke hole. Later he opened it, and daylight spread over the whole world.
lesson: When a door is closed to force, find a way to become part of the household. Patience and access can win what open confrontation never would.
people: Raven, the chief who kept the light, his daughter
location: Southeast Alaska (USA) and the Nass River (British Columbia, Canada)
source: John R. Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909)
caveat: Many versions exist among Tlingit, Haida, Tsimshian and other Northwest Coast peoples, and details vary between tellers.

title: Shackleton Gives Wild His Only Biscuit
text:
In January 1909 Ernest Shackleton and three companions, Frank Wild, Eric Marshall and Jameson Adams, were man-hauling their sledge back across the Antarctic ice after turning around less than a hundred miles from the South Pole. They had cut their rations to the bone to stretch the food between depots, and every man was starving.

Wild fell ill with dysentery and could barely keep going. On 31 January, at breakfast, Shackleton pushed his own single biscuit onto Wild and insisted he eat it. It was the one solid piece of food each man got that morning, and Shackleton would march all day without it.

Wild recorded the moment in his diary that night. He wrote that he did not suppose anyone else in the world could fully realize how much generosity and sympathy that act showed, and added: "I DO by God I shall never forget it. Thousands of pounds would not have bought that one biscuit."

He did not forget. Wild went south with Shackleton again on the Endurance expedition as his second in command, and it was Wild who held twenty-two men together on Elephant Island in 1916 while Shackleton sailed for help. He was with Shackleton on his last expedition too, and took command of it when Shackleton died aboard ship in 1922.
lesson: People remember who looked after them when it cost something. A small sacrifice at the right moment can earn a loyalty that no salary or title can buy.
people: Ernest Shackleton, Frank Wild
source: Frank Wild, diary of the Nimrod expedition, 31 January 1909 (Scott Polar Research Institute); quoted in Roland Huntford, Shackleton (1985)

title: Degania, the First Kibbutz
text:
In 1909 a small group of young Jewish immigrants from the Russian Empire was hired to work a farm at Umm Juni, on the southern shore of the Sea of Galilee, then part of the Ottoman Empire. They had come with ideals of returning to the land and living by their own labor. After a year of working under managers, they asked to run the farm themselves, collectively.

In 1910 the group, ten men and two women, founded Degania. They decided that everything would be shared. No one owned private property; work was organized together; income went into a common fund; and decisions were made at a general meeting where every member had a voice. They called it a kvutza, a group.

Life was hard. The land was hot, malaria was common, food was scarce, and the farm faced attacks. The members argued constantly about how to run things. The women had to fight for their place: at first they were expected to cook and wash, and they insisted on working in the fields and the dairy too. Joseph Baratz, one of the founders, later described these early years in his memoir, A Village by the Jordan.

Degania survived. It became the model for hundreds of kibbutzim, collective communities that played a large role in building the state of Israel. One of its first children, Moshe Dayan, was born there in 1915.
lesson: A small group sharing everything needs constant talking, fairness and the willingness to change roles. Equality has to be practiced, not just declared.
people: Joseph Baratz, Miriam Baratz, founders of Degania
location: Degania Alef, near the Sea of Galilee, Israel
source: Joseph Baratz, A Village by the Jordan (1954); kibbutz histories

title: Leo and Sofia Tolstoy: A Marriage That Made and Broke
text:
In September 1862, Leo Tolstoy, thirty-four, married Sofia Behrs, eighteen. Before the wedding he gave her his diaries to read, with their record of his past affairs, believing that honesty required it. She was deeply shocked and never quite forgot.

The early years of the marriage were productive. Sofia ran the estate at Yasnaya Polyana, bore thirteen children, of whom several died young, and became her husband's indispensable assistant. She copied out the manuscripts of War and Peace by hand, deciphering his crowded corrections, again and again, by candlelight. Anna Karenina followed.

From around 1880, Tolstoy underwent a religious crisis. He began preaching simplicity, chastity and the renunciation of property, and wanted to give up the copyrights on his works. Sofia, who had to provide for the family, fought him. His disciple Vladimir Chertkov gained more and more influence over him, and Sofia grew jealous and desperate. Both kept diaries, and each read the other's, which made things worse.

In 1910 Tolstoy signed a secret will leaving his copyrights to the public. In the night of 28 October, at eighty-two, he slipped out of the house and left. He fell ill on the train and died at the small station of Astapovo. Sofia hurried there, but she was kept from his bedside until he was no longer conscious.
lesson: A partnership that produced great work can still collapse if each partner stops trying to understand the other. Honesty without care can wound as deeply as lies.
people: Leo Tolstoy, Sofia Tolstaya, Vladimir Chertkov
source: The Diaries of Sofia Tolstoy, trans. Cathy Porter (1985); Tolstoy's diaries; A. N. Wilson, Tolstoy (1988)

title: Amundsen and Scott Race to the Pole
text:
In 1910 two expeditions set out for the South Pole. The British party was led by Robert Falcon Scott. The Norwegian Roald Amundsen had announced he was going to the Arctic, then, after news that Americans had reached the North Pole, he secretly turned south and informed Scott by telegram that he was heading for Antarctica.

The two men prepared differently. Amundsen had spent years in the Arctic, including two winters with the Netsilik Inuit, from whom he learned to use dogs, to dress in loose fur clothing and to travel efficiently. He took expert skiers and dog drivers and nearly a hundred dogs, planning to kill some along the way to feed the others and the men. He laid depots of food and marked them with lines of flags across his route so they could be found in poor visibility.

Scott relied on a mix of motor sledges, Siberian ponies, some dogs and, in the end, men pulling sledges themselves. The motor sledges broke down and the ponies suffered in the cold and had to be shot.

Amundsen's party of five reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911 and returned safely. Scott's party of five reached it on 17 January 1912 and found the Norwegian tent. On the long march back, slowed by illness, injury, short rations and severe cold, all five died. Scott's last diary entries were found with his body months later.
lesson: Preparation that borrows the best knowledge of those who know the terrain beats courage and effort alone. Choose methods proven in the conditions you will face.
people: Roald Amundsen, Robert Falcon Scott
source: Roald Amundsen, The South Pole (1912); Scott's Last Expedition: The Journals (1913); Roland Huntford, Scott and Amundsen (1979)
caveat: Historians still debate how much of Scott's failure was due to his choices and how much to unusually severe weather on the return march.

title: Einstein Writes to Marie Curie
text:
In the autumn of 1911 Marie Curie was the most famous woman scientist in the world. In early November she attended the first Solvay Conference in Brussels with Albert Einstein and other leading physicists. While she was there, the Paris press broke the story of her relationship with the physicist Paul Langevin, who was married. Newspapers attacked her as a foreign homewrecker, crowds gathered outside her house, and the scandal turned ugly.

In the middle of it she learned she had won her second Nobel Prize, in chemistry. A member of the Swedish Academy wrote suggesting she stay away from the ceremony.

On November 23, 1911, Einstein, who had admired her mind and character at the conference, wrote her a short letter. He told her he was angry at the base way the public was dealing with her, and urged her simply not to read the trash being written about her, but to leave it to the people it was made for. He added that he and others were grateful to have people like her among them.

Curie went to Stockholm in December and accepted the prize in person.
lesson: A word of support to someone being publicly humiliated means more than any praise in good times. Write it, even if you think you have nothing important to say.
people: Albert Einstein, Marie Curie
source: Albert Einstein, letter to Marie Curie, November 23, 1911, The Collected Papers of Albert Einstein, vol. 8

title: Gandhi and His Eldest Son Harilal
text:
Harilal was the eldest of Mohandas Gandhi's four sons, born in 1888. He grew up partly in South Africa while his father led the Indian community's struggle there. Harilal joined the campaigns and went to jail several times, earning the nickname "Chhota Gandhi," little Gandhi.

But father and son clashed. Harilal wanted a formal education and to study law in England, as his father had. Gandhi, who had turned against Western schooling and personal ambition, refused, and twice gave an opportunity to study in England to others instead. Harilal also married young, against his father's wishes. In 1911 he broke away, leaving South Africa, and later broke openly with his father.

His life went from failure to failure. His business ventures collapsed, his wife died in the 1918 influenza epidemic, and he struggled with alcohol and debt. In 1936 he converted to Islam and took the name Abdullah, a step that pained his parents, though he later returned to Hinduism. His mother Kasturba pleaded with him in a public letter to give up drink.

Gandhi wrote to and about his son with a mixture of love, sternness and regret, and admitted that he might have failed him. Harilal outlived his father by only a few months. He died, ill and poor, in a Bombay hospital in June 1948.
lesson: A parent devoted to great causes must not forget the child at home. Principles applied to a son without listening to him can cost the relationship.
people: Mohandas Gandhi, Harilal Gandhi, Kasturba Gandhi
source: Chandulal Bhagubhai Dalal, Harilal Gandhi: A Life (2007); Gandhi's collected letters; Rajmohan Gandhi, Mohandas (2006)

title: The Iron Law of Oligarchy
text:
In the early twentieth century the German Social Democratic Party was the largest and best organized socialist movement in Europe. It was committed to democracy and equality, and its members elected their leaders. The young sociologist Robert Michels, who had himself been active in socialist politics, set out to study how such parties and their allied trade unions actually worked.

What he found troubled him. As the organizations grew, they needed full-time officials, specialists and spokesmen. These leaders gained knowledge, skills, contacts and control over the party's newspapers and money that ordinary members lacked. Most members had little time or interest to follow party affairs closely and tended to defer to the experts. Once in office, leaders often stayed for many years, and their priority shifted toward preserving the organization and their own positions rather than pursuing its radical goals.

In his 1911 book Michels argued that this was not a failing of particular people but a tendency of all large organizations, even those founded on democratic ideals. He summed it up in a phrase that became famous: "Who says organization, says oligarchy." He called it the iron law of oligarchy.
lesson: Every organization tends to concentrate power in a few hands over time. Build in term limits, transparency and real ways for members to hold leaders to account.
people: Robert Michels
source: Michels, R. (1911). Zur Soziologie des Parteiwesens in der modernen Demokratie. Klinkhardt. English translation: Political Parties (1915).
caveat: Later research found organizations that resisted the tendency for long periods, so most scholars treat it as a strong tendency rather than an iron law.

title: Noguchi Hideyo and His Mother's Letter
text:
Noguchi Hideyo was born in 1876 into a poor farming family in Inawashiro, in northern Japan. When he was a baby, he fell into the open hearth while his mother, Shika, was working outside, and his left hand was badly burned, the fingers fused together. Shika blamed herself all her life. As a teenager he had an operation that partly restored the use of his hand, and the experience made him decide to become a doctor.

He qualified in medicine and in 1900 went to the United States. At the Rockefeller Institute in New York he became famous for his research, especially on syphilis, and was nominated several times for the Nobel Prize. He did not come home.

Shika had never been taught to read or write, but she taught herself as an adult. In 1912 she wrote to her son a letter in a clumsy hand, with many mistakes, begging him to come back. She wrote that she was waiting and that she wanted to see him, and asked him to come home soon, again and again. The letter is preserved and displayed at the Noguchi Hideyo Memorial Museum.

In 1915 Noguchi returned to Japan for the only time, and spent time travelling with his mother. She died in 1918. He died ten years later in Accra, in Africa, of yellow fever, the disease he had gone there to study.
lesson: Success far from home can make us forget those waiting for us. A visit we keep postponing may be the one that matters most.
people: Noguchi Hideyo, Noguchi Shika
location: Inawashiro, Fukushima, Japan, and New York, USA
source: Letter of Noguchi Shika (1912), Noguchi Hideyo Memorial Museum; Isabel R. Plesset, Noguchi and His Patrons (1980)
caveat: Some of Noguchi's scientific claims were later shown to be wrong.

title: Oates Walks Out into the Blizzard
text:
Robert Falcon Scott's party of five reached the South Pole on 17 January 1912 and found that Roald Amundsen had beaten them by about a month. On the long march back, things went wrong. Edgar Evans weakened and died in February. The weather was colder than expected, fuel at the depots ran short, and the men grew weaker.

Lawrence Oates, an army cavalry officer, suffered worst. His feet were badly frostbitten and turning gangrenous, and he could barely walk. Every day he slowed the others, and he knew it. Scott wrote that Oates asked them to leave him in his sleeping bag, and that they refused.

In mid March, during a blizzard, Oates woke in the tent and, according to Scott's journal, said, "I am just going outside and may be some time." He went out and did not come back. Scott added: "We knew that poor Oates was walking to his death, but though we tried to dissuade him, we knew it was the act of a brave man and an English gentleman."

The remaining three, Scott, Edward Wilson and Henry Bowers, struggled on until another blizzard pinned them in their tent about 11 miles from a large supply depot. They died there near the end of March. A search party found the tent and Scott's journal in November 1912. Oates's body was never found; the searchers raised a cairn near where he was thought to have died.
lesson: Some team members carry burdens quietly to protect the others. Notice what people give up for the group, and never take it for granted.
people: Lawrence Oates, Robert Falcon Scott, Edward Wilson, Henry Bowers
source: Robert Falcon Scott, journal of the Terra Nova expedition (published as Scott's Last Expedition, 1913)

title: Hardy Opens a Letter From Madras
text:
In January 1913 G. H. Hardy, one of the leading mathematicians in England, received a letter at Trinity College, Cambridge, from a clerk in the Madras Port Trust in India. The writer, Srinivasa Ramanujan, explained that he had no university degree but had been working on mathematics on his own. Enclosed were pages of formulas and theorems, many stated without proof. Ramanujan had already written to other Cambridge mathematicians, who had not taken him seriously.

Hardy nearly put the letter aside as the work of a crank. That evening he went over it with his colleague J. E. Littlewood. Some of the results were known; some were wrong; but others were unlike anything they had ever seen. Hardy later wrote that they must be true, because if they were not, no one would have had the imagination to invent them.

Hardy replied at once and worked to bring Ramanujan to Cambridge, which he did in 1914. For five years the two collaborated on work that changed number theory. Ramanujan was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1918. Ill, he returned to India in 1919 and died the next year at thirty two. Hardy called their collaboration the one romantic incident of his life.
lesson: Take seriously the work of people who lack credentials or connections. Looking twice at something unusual can uncover talent that others dismissed.
people: Srinivasa Ramanujan, G. H. Hardy, J. E. Littlewood
location: Cambridge, England, and Madras (modern Chennai), India
source: G. H. Hardy, Ramanujan: Twelve Lectures on Subjects Suggested by His Life and Work (1940); Robert Kanigel, The Man Who Knew Infinity (1991)

title: Pulling on a Rope Together
text:
Maximilien Ringelmann was a French agricultural engineer interested in how to get the most work out of people, horses and machines. In experiments he reported in 1913, he had men pull on a rope attached to a gauge, first alone and then in groups. The group total rose as people were added, but far less than the sum of their separate efforts. The more people on the rope, the less each one seemed to contribute.

Ringelmann's finding could have two causes: people slacking off, or simple coordination problems, since many people never pull at exactly the same moment or in exactly the same direction. In 1974 Alan Ingham and colleagues at the University of Massachusetts set out to separate the two.

They rebuilt the rope task and added a trick. Participants were blindfolded and told that others were pulling behind them, when in fact the others were confederates who only pretended. With no coordination to lose, any drop in force had to come from reduced effort. It did. People pulled less hard when they believed others were pulling with them, with most of the drop appearing once one or two others were added.

The decline that Ringelmann saw was not only clumsy teamwork. Part of it was motivation quietly leaking away in a crowd.
lesson: Adding people to a task does not add their full effort. Keep groups small enough that each person feels their pull matters.
people: Maximilien Ringelmann; Alan Ingham, George Levinger, James Graves, Vaughn Peckham
location: France; University of Massachusetts, Amherst, USA
source: Ringelmann, M. (1913). Recherches sur les moteurs animes: Travail de l'homme. Annales de l'Institut National Agronomique. Ingham, A. G., Levinger, G., Graves, J., and Peckham, V. (1974). The Ringelmann effect: Studies of group size and group performance. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 10.

title: The Christmas Truce of 1914
text:
By December 1914 the war that was supposed to be over by Christmas had settled into lines of muddy, freezing trenches across Belgium and France. In places the British and German lines were only a few dozen meters apart.

On Christmas Eve, along stretches of the front in Flanders, British soldiers saw small Christmas trees with candles appear on the German parapets and heard the Germans singing carols. The British answered with their own. Men began shouting greetings across no man's land. At dawn on Christmas Day, in many sectors, soldiers climbed out of the trenches unarmed and walked toward each other.

Their letters home describe what followed. They shook hands, exchanged cigarettes, chocolate, buttons and souvenirs, showed each other photographs of their families and took pictures together. Both sides used the quiet to bury their dead lying between the lines, sometimes in joint services. In some places men kicked a football around. In some sectors the truce lasted days.

It was never official, and commanders on both sides disapproved. Orders went out to prevent any repeat, and later Christmases saw no truce on that scale. The war went on for nearly four more years.
lesson: Even deep enmity hides a shared humanity that can surface when people meet face to face. Remember that those on the other side are people too.
people: British and German soldiers on the Western Front
location: Western Front, Flanders (Belgium) and northern France
source: Soldiers' letters and diaries; Malcolm Brown and Shirley Seaton, Christmas Truce (1984)
caveat: The truce was patchy and did not happen everywhere, and reports of organized football matches are less certain than the fraternization itself.

title: Marie Curie's Mobile X-Ray Cars
text:
When the First World War broke out in 1914, Marie Curie was the most famous scientist in France, with two Nobel Prizes. She soon saw that X-rays could save soldiers' lives by showing surgeons where bullets and shrapnel lay and where bones were broken, but that the army had very little radiology equipment, and almost none near the front.

She set out to fix this herself. Using donated cars and money, she had vehicles fitted with X-ray machines and with generators driven by the car's engine, so they could work where there was no electricity. Soldiers nicknamed them "petites Curies". She learned to drive, studied anatomy, and went to field hospitals near the front to operate the equipment, often with her teenage daughter Irene.

She also trained women as X-ray technicians, since there were not enough qualified men, and helped set up radiology rooms in hospitals. By the end of the war, according to standard accounts, about twenty mobile units and some two hundred fixed installations had been set up through her work. Over a million examinations of wounded soldiers are estimated to have been made.

After the war she described this work in a book, La radiologie et la guerre.
lesson: When you see what is needed and no one is providing it, use your skills and your name to build it yourself.
people: Marie Curie, Irene Curie
source: Marie Curie, La radiologie et la guerre (1921); Eve Curie, Madame Curie (1937)
caveat: The number of examinations is an estimate and varies between sources.

title: Henry Ford's Five Dollar Day
text:
By 1913 Ford's Highland Park plant near Detroit was running the new moving assembly line, and the work was fast, repetitive and exhausting. Workers quit in huge numbers. The company had to hire several times its workforce each year to keep the line staffed, and every new man had to be trained.

On 5 January 1914 Henry Ford and his business manager James Couzens announced a plan that shocked industry: a minimum of five dollars for an eight-hour day, roughly double the usual wage for such work, paid as a share of profits to qualifying workers. The next day thousands of men gathered at the plant gates in the winter cold hoping to be hired, and on one day the crowd grew so large that police turned fire hoses on it.

The extra pay came with conditions. To qualify, workers had to meet standards of conduct and home life checked by the company's Sociological Department, a paternalism many found intrusive. But turnover fell sharply and productivity rose. Ford later wrote in My Life and Work that paying five dollars a day for an eight-hour day was one of the finest cost-cutting moves the company ever made. Better-paid workers could also afford to buy the cars they built, which Ford liked to point out.
lesson: Paying people well can be a strategy rather than a cost, if it reduces turnover and raises commitment. Count the hidden expense of constantly replacing people.
people: Henry Ford, James Couzens
source: Henry Ford with Samuel Crowther, My Life and Work (1922), chapter 10; contemporary press reports

title: Gandhi's Sandals for General Smuts
text:
For years in South Africa, Mohandas Gandhi led the Indian community's campaigns of civil disobedience against discriminatory laws. His chief opponent in government was General Jan Smuts, who more than once had him jailed. Gandhi never treated Smuts as an enemy. He negotiated with him patiently, kept his word, and in January 1914 suspended a planned march rather than take advantage of a railway strike that was troubling the government.

The two men finally reached an agreement in 1914, and Gandhi prepared to leave for India. Before he sailed, he sent Smuts a gift: a pair of leather sandals he had made himself while in prison.

Smuts kept them. In 1939, for Gandhi's seventieth birthday, he wrote an essay for a commemorative volume. He said he had worn the sandals for many summers, "even though I may feel that I am not worthy to stand in the shoes of so great a man." He also wrote that it had been his fate to be the antagonist of a man for whom, even then, he had the highest respect.
lesson: You can oppose someone firmly and still treat them with courtesy and good faith. Respect shown to an opponent is often returned, sometimes decades later.
people: Mohandas Gandhi, Jan Smuts
source: Jan Christiaan Smuts, "Gandhi's Political Method," in Mahatma Gandhi: Essays and Reflections on His Life and Work, ed. S. Radhakrishnan (1939)

title: "I Am Not Ordering You to Attack"
text:
On the morning of April 25, 1915, Australian and New Zealand troops landed on the Gallipoli peninsula as part of the Allied attempt to force the Dardanelles and knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war. They pushed inland toward the high ridges that commanded the whole area.

Mustafa Kemal, then a lieutenant colonel commanding the Ottoman 19th Division in reserve, went forward to see for himself. By his own later account, he met a group of Ottoman soldiers retreating from the heights because they had run out of ammunition, with the enemy following. He ordered them to fix bayonets and lie down facing the enemy, which made the advancing troops pause and take cover. Then he brought up his 57th Infantry Regiment.

As he sent them into the attack, he recalled telling them: "I am not ordering you to attack. I am ordering you to die. In the time it takes us to die, other troops and commanders can come and take our places."

The 57th Regiment was almost entirely destroyed, but the counterattacks held the heights, and the Allies never broke through. The campaign ended with their evacuation in January 1916. The Turkish army has never formed another 57th Regiment.
lesson: In a crisis, being honest about what a task will cost, and why it matters, can hold people together better than false reassurance.
people: Mustafa Kemal (Ataturk), the 57th Infantry Regiment
source: Mustafa Kemal's later account of the Anafartalar and Ariburnu battles, recorded in his memoirs and interviews
caveat: The order is known from Mustafa Kemal's own later recollection rather than from a written order of the day.

title: The Silent Evacuation of Gallipoli
text:
By late 1915 the Allied campaign on the Gallipoli peninsula had failed. Australian, New Zealand, British and other troops clung to narrow beachheads at Anzac Cove, Suvla Bay and Cape Helles, often only a few meters from the Ottoman trenches. When London decided to withdraw, some commanders feared that pulling out under the enemy's eyes could cost a large share of the force.

At Anzac the plan was largely drawn up by the Australian staff officer Brudenell White. Weeks beforehand, the troops held "silent" periods in which they stopped firing for long stretches, so the Turks grew used to quiet trenches. Then, over a series of nights in December, men were taken off in stages while those remaining kept up normal activity. Paths were marked, boots were muffled with sacking, and each man had a precise time and route to the beach.

The last groups left in the early hours of 20 December. To cover their departure, some rigged rifles to fire by themselves. The best known device, credited to Lance Corporal William Scurry, used water dripping from one tin into another until the weight pulled the trigger, so shots kept sounding from empty trenches after the men had gone.

Tens of thousands of men left Anzac and Suvla with almost no casualties, and Helles was evacuated just as cleanly in January 1916. It was the most successful operation of the entire campaign.
lesson: Careful planning, rehearsal and discipline across a whole team can turn a dangerous retreat into a success. Every person knowing their exact part is what keeps a plan silent.
people: Brudenell White, William Scurry, ANZAC and British forces
location: Anzac Cove, Suvla Bay and Cape Helles, Gallipoli peninsula, Turkey
source: C. E. W. Bean, The Official History of Australia in the War of 1914 to 1918, vol. 2 (1924)

title: The Metamorphosis
text:
Gregor Samsa, a traveling salesman, woke one morning to find himself transformed into a huge insect. His first worry was not his new body but that he would miss his train and lose his job. For years he had worked at a job he hated to pay off his parents' debts and support the family, and he had dreamed of sending his sister Grete to study the violin.

When the family saw him, his mother fainted and his father drove him back into his room with a stick. At first Grete brought him food and cleaned his room. But the family soon had to find work themselves: the father as a bank messenger, the mother sewing, Grete as a shop girl. They took in lodgers. Gregor's room became a storeroom for junk.

Once, when Gregor came out, his father pelted him with apples. One lodged in his back and rotted there. When Gregor crept out to listen to Grete playing the violin for the lodgers, they saw him and gave notice. Grete told her parents that they must get rid of it. That thing could not be Gregor, she said; if it were, he would have gone away on his own.

That night Gregor died, thinking of his family with tenderness. The next morning the family took the day off, rode a tram into the country, and noticed with pleasure that Grete had grown into a pretty young woman ready to marry.
lesson: A family member is worth more than what he or she provides. Pay attention if your love for someone depends on how useful they are to you.
people: Gregor Samsa, his parents, his sister Grete
source: Franz Kafka, The Metamorphosis (Die Verwandlung), 1915

title: The Endurance Crew All Come Home
text:
In January 1915 Ernest Shackleton's ship Endurance froze into the pack ice of the Weddell Sea, short of the Antarctic coast where he had meant to land and cross the continent on foot. For ten months the ice carried the ship north. Then it crushed her, and in November 1915 she sank. Twenty-eight men were left on drifting floes with three small boats and whatever they had dragged off the wreck.

Shackleton changed the goal from crossing Antarctica to bringing every man home. He kept routines going, shared the same rations as everyone, and put the men most likely to grumble in his own tent so their moods would not spread. When there were too few warm fur sleeping bags to go round, lots were drawn, and according to Alfred Lansing's account the draw was quietly arranged so that Shackleton and his senior men got the thinner woolen ones.

In April 1916 the floes broke up and the men rowed to Elephant Island, their first solid ground in well over a year. It was far from any shipping route, so Shackleton took five men in the lifeboat James Caird across some 800 miles of the Southern Ocean to South Georgia. He, Frank Worsley and Tom Crean then crossed the island's unmapped mountains on foot to reach the whaling station at Stromness.

On Elephant Island, Frank Wild kept the remaining twenty-two men fed, busy and hopeful through four months of waiting. After three failed attempts through the ice, Shackleton returned on the Chilean tug Yelcho on 30 August 1916. Every man of the Endurance party was alive.
lesson: In a long crisis, the team's spirit is a survival resource. Share the hardship visibly, keep routines, and keep difficult moods close where you can manage them.
people: Ernest Shackleton, Frank Wild, Frank Worsley, Tom Crean
location: Weddell Sea, Elephant Island and South Georgia, Antarctica
source: Ernest Shackleton, South (1919); Alfred Lansing, Endurance (1959)
caveat: The expedition's Ross Sea party on the other side of the continent lost three men; the 'all came home' record applies to the Endurance party.

title: Panch Parmeshwar
text:
Jumman Shaikh and Algu Chaudhari were the closest of friends in their village in northern India. Jumman's elderly aunt had signed her property over to him on the promise that he would look after her. Once he had it, he and his wife made her life miserable. At last she called a panchayat, the village council, to settle the matter. To Jumman's delight, she asked Algu to serve as the head judge.

Algu was reluctant. The aunt asked him whether he would refuse to speak the truth for fear of losing a friend. Seated as the judge, Algu examined the case honestly and ruled against Jumman: he must give his aunt a monthly allowance or return her property. Jumman was furious, and the friendship ended. He waited for his revenge.

Some time later Algu sold one of his bullocks to a carter, Samjhu Sahu, on credit. Samjhu worked the animal mercilessly until it dropped dead, then refused to pay. Algu took the dispute to the panchayat, and Samjhu chose Jumman as head judge, sure that he would punish his old friend.

But once Jumman sat in the judge's seat, he felt its weight. He set aside his grudge and ruled that Samjhu must pay. Algu embraced him, and Jumman understood that the voice of the panch is the voice of God.
lesson: When you are given the role of judge, your loyalties and grudges must step outside the room. People accept hard decisions from someone they know will be fair even to a friend.
people: Jumman Shaikh, Algu Chaudhari, Jumman's aunt, Samjhu Sahu
source: Premchand, Panch Parmeshwar, 1916

title: Learning to Be Silent
text:
Four students of the Tendai school of Buddhism, who were close friends, made a vow together. For seven days they would keep complete silence as part of their meditation.

On the first day all four sat quietly. That night, as it grew dark and the oil lamps began to grow dim, one of the students could not help himself. He told a servant to fix the lamps.

The second student was surprised to hear the first one speak. He reminded him that they were not supposed to say a word.

The third student turned to the other two. Why are you two talking? he asked them.

The fourth student then remarked, with some satisfaction, that he was the only one who had not spoken.

And so, within the first day, all four had broken their vow, each one in the act of noticing someone else.
lesson: Be careful when you rush to correct a teammate, since you may be breaking the same rule while you do it. Keeping your own commitment does more good than policing others.
people: Four Tendai students
source: Nyogen Senzaki and Paul Reps, 101 Zen Stories (1919), Learning to Be Silent

title: Walt and Roy Disney: Dreamer and Banker
text:
Roy Disney was eight years older than his brother Walt. In 1923, when Walt arrived in Los Angeles with almost nothing after his first animation company in Kansas City went bankrupt, Roy was there recovering from tuberculosis. In October that year the two founded the Disney Brothers Studio. Walt supplied the ideas and the drive; Roy handled the money, the contracts and the banks.

The pattern held for forty years. When Walt decided to make a full-length animated feature, Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, the industry called it Disney's folly, and costs ran far over budget. Roy went to the banks again and again to keep the project alive. It opened in 1937 and was a huge success. When Walt dreamed up Disneyland in the 1950s, Roy at first doubted it, then found the financing, partly through a deal with a television network.

The brothers argued often and fiercely, and at times barely spoke. Yet each knew he needed the other.

Walt died in December 1966. Roy, already in his seventies and planning to retire, stayed on to build Walt's last project, a vast resort in Florida. He insisted it be called Walt Disney World, so that people would always know it was his brother's dream. It opened in October 1971. Roy died two months later.
lesson: One person dreams and another makes it possible, and both are needed. Disagreeing fiercely does not have to break a partnership built on respect.
people: Walt Disney, Roy O. Disney
location: Los Angeles, California, and Orlando, Florida, USA
source: Neal Gabler, Walt Disney: The Triumph of the American Imagination (2006); Bob Thomas, Building a Company: Roy O. Disney (1998)

title: The Lights at the Hawthorne Works
text:
From 1924 to 1932 researchers studied workers at Western Electric's Hawthorne Works near Chicago, a huge factory making telephone equipment. The first experiments asked a simple question: does better lighting raise output? The puzzling answer was that output seemed to rise both when the lights were turned up and when they were turned down, as if being studied mattered more than the light itself.

Later phases went further. A small group of women assembling telephone relays was moved to a separate test room, where researchers changed rest breaks and hours and talked with them often. Output generally rose over the years. In another room, the Bank Wiring study, observers found that a group of men quietly enforced their own idea of a fair day's work and pressured anyone who produced too much or too little.

Elton Mayo, Fritz Roethlisberger and William Dickson concluded that attention, informal groups and social relations shaped productivity as much as pay and physical conditions. The work helped launch the human relations movement in management, and the term "Hawthorne effect" came to mean people changing their behavior because they are observed.
lesson: People at work respond to how they are treated and to the norms of their group, not only to pay and conditions. Notice the informal rules your team actually lives by.
people: Fritz Roethlisberger, William Dickson, Elton Mayo
location: Western Electric Hawthorne Works, Cicero, Illinois, USA
source: Roethlisberger, F. J., and Dickson, W. J. (1939). Management and the Worker. Harvard University Press.
caveat: Reanalysis of the surviving lighting data by Steven Levitt and John List (2011) found the famous effect much weaker than the legend, and the relay room results had other explanations.

title: Einstein and Bohr Argue for Thirty Years
text:
Albert Einstein and Niels Bohr met in Berlin in 1920 and liked each other at once. Einstein wrote to Bohr afterward that few people had ever given him such joy simply by being present.

Then quantum mechanics divided them. Bohr believed the new theory was complete: at the smallest scale, nature was governed by probability, and some questions had no definite answer until a measurement was made. Einstein could not accept that physics would end with chance.

At the Solvay Conference in Brussels in 1927, the debate became legendary. At breakfast Einstein would propose a clever thought experiment that seemed to break the theory. Bohr would worry over it all day, and by dinner he usually had an answer. In 1930 Einstein proposed a box that released light at a precise moment. Bohr spent a sleepless night and then showed that Einstein's own theory of general relativity saved quantum mechanics.

The argument never ended. In 1949 Bohr wrote a long, warm essay describing their discussions. They remained friends until Einstein died in 1955. When Bohr died in 1962, the last drawing on the blackboard in his study was reportedly a sketch of Einstein's light box.
lesson: You can disagree with someone deeply and for years while keeping respect and affection. A worthy opponent sharpens your thinking more than an easy ally.
people: Albert Einstein, Niels Bohr
source: Niels Bohr, "Discussion with Einstein on Epistemological Problems in Atomic Physics," in Albert Einstein: Philosopher-Scientist, ed. P. A. Schilpp (1949)

title: Anansi Buys the Sky God's Stories
text:
Long ago all stories belonged to Nyame, the sky god. Anansi the spider went up to him and asked to buy them. Nyame laughed: great and wealthy towns had tried and failed. But he named a price. Anansi must bring him the python, the leopard, the hornets and Mmoatia, the fairy. Anansi agreed.

For the python, Anansi cut a palm branch and walked past the python's home arguing loudly with his wife about whether the python was longer than the branch. The python, overhearing, offered to settle it and stretched out along the branch. Anansi said he would tie him to it to measure him properly, and tied him fast.

For the hornets, he filled a gourd with water, poured some over their nest and the rest over himself, and called out that it was raining. He invited them to shelter in an empty gourd, and when they flew in, he plugged it.

For the leopard, he dug a pit across its path and covered it. The leopard fell in, and Anansi caught it. For Mmoatia, he carved a doll, covered it with sticky gum and set a dish of mashed yams before it. The fairy ate the yams, and when the doll did not answer her thanks, she struck it and stuck fast.

Anansi carried all four to Nyame, who kept his word. From that day, the stories have been called Anansi's stories.
lesson: When you lack strength, study each obstacle separately and use its own habits against it. A different tactic for each problem beats one blunt approach.
people: Kwaku Anansi, Nyame the sky god, the python, the leopard, the hornets, Mmoatia
source: R. S. Rattray, Akan-Ashanti Folk-Tales (1930)
caveat: The tale exists in many versions, and the details of how each creature is caught differ between tellers.

title: Gandhi's Salt March
text:
By early 1930 the Indian National Congress had declared the goal of full independence from Britain, and Gandhi was asked to lead a new campaign of civil disobedience. Colleagues expected a dramatic target. Gandhi chose salt.

British law gave the government a monopoly on making and selling salt and taxed it. Many in Congress thought the issue too small. But salt was needed by everyone, rich and poor, Hindu and Muslim, in every region, and making it from seawater was something anyone could do. Breaking the law would be simple, visible and hard to portray as violent.

On 12 March 1930 Gandhi set out from his ashram at Sabarmati, near Ahmedabad, with 78 followers. He walked about 240 miles to the coastal village of Dandi, speaking in villages along the way, as crowds and the world press followed. On 6 April he picked up a lump of natural salt from the shore, symbolically breaking the law.

Across India, people began making and selling salt illegally. Tens of thousands were arrested, Gandhi among them in May. At the Dharasana salt works, unarmed volunteers marched in rows to be beaten by police without resisting, and the American reporter Webb Miller's account reached readers around the world. In 1931 the viceroy, Lord Irwin, negotiated directly with Gandhi, and the British government invited him to a conference in London.
lesson: Pick a cause that everyone shares and an action that anyone can take. A simple, concrete symbol can unite more people than an abstract demand.
people: Mohandas Gandhi, Lord Irwin, Webb Miller
source: Contemporary press reports; Gandhi's letter to Lord Irwin (2 March 1930); Judith Brown, Gandhi: Prisoner of Hope (1989)

title: Nehru Teaches His Daughter from Prison
text:
Jawaharlal Nehru, a leader of India's independence movement, spent long years in British prisons. His only child, Indira, grew up seeing him rarely. In 1928, when she was ten and at school in Mussoorie, he wrote her a series of letters about the history of the earth, early humans and the first civilizations, later published as Letters from a Father to His Daughter.

On 26 October 1930, Indira's thirteenth birthday, Nehru was in Naini Central Prison near Allahabad. He wrote to her that he could not send her a present from jail, so he would send her letters instead, things of the mind and spirit that prison walls could not stop. That letter began a long series. Over the next three years, in prison after prison, without a library and relying largely on his notes and memory, he wrote her nearly two hundred letters telling the story of the world: ancient China and India, Greece and Rome, the rise of Islam, Europe's revolutions, empires and the struggle of colonized peoples.

The letters were published in 1934 as Glimpses of World History, and the book became a classic in India. Indira went on to become India's first woman prime minister.
lesson: Distance does not end a parent's role. Even far away, we can teach, share what we love and stay present in a child's mind.
people: Jawaharlal Nehru, Indira Gandhi
source: Jawaharlal Nehru, Glimpses of World History (1934); Letters from a Father to His Daughter (1929)

title: The Bodyline Series
text:
By 1932 the Australian batsman Don Bradman was scoring runs at a rate never seen before, and England's cricketers had no answer to him. Before the 1932 to 1933 tour of Australia, England's captain, Douglas Jardine, developed a plan with his fast bowlers, above all Harold Larwood of Nottinghamshire.

The tactic, then called leg theory and soon nicknamed bodyline by the press, was to bowl very fast, short balls that reared up at the batsman's body and head, with most fielders packed close on the leg side to catch any defensive shot. There were no helmets. Batsmen had to choose between being hit and offering catches.

It worked on the field. Bradman's average for the series fell to about 57, high for anyone else but around half of his usual level, and England won the series four games to one. But it caused an uproar. In the third Test at Adelaide, the Australian captain Bill Woodfull was struck over the heart and the wicketkeeper Bert Oldfield suffered a fractured skull from a Larwood ball. When the England manager Pelham Warner visited the dressing room, Woodfull was reported as saying that there were two teams out there, one trying to play cricket and the other not. The Australian Board of Control cabled London calling the bowling unsportsmanlike, and the dispute reached political leaders of both countries.

The laws of cricket were later changed to limit such bowling. Larwood never played for England again after the tour.
lesson: A tactic that wins within the rules but breaks the spirit of the game can cost more than the victory is worth. Consider how others will see your methods, not just whether they work.
people: Douglas Jardine, Harold Larwood, Don Bradman, Bill Woodfull
source: Contemporary press reports; Wisden Cricketers' Almanack; David Frith, Bodyline Autopsy (2002)

title: Konosuke Matsushita's 250-Year Mission
text:
Konosuke Matsushita founded his electrical goods company in Osaka in 1918, making plug sockets with his wife and brother-in-law. By the early 1930s it was a growing business, but he was searching for a deeper reason for it to exist.

On May 5, 1932, he gathered his employees and announced what he called the company's true mission. A manufacturer's purpose, he said, was to overcome poverty by producing goods as abundant and cheap as tap water, which people take freely from the street without anyone objecting. The company would pursue that goal over 250 years, divided into ten periods of twenty-five years each. The current generation would work through the first period, and their successors would carry the work forward.

Matsushita later wrote that the employees responded with great excitement, and that many came forward to speak about their commitment. The company counted 1932 as the first year of its founding mission.

The firm, later known as Panasonic, became one of the largest electronics makers in the world. Matsushita's "tap water philosophy" and the idea of a mission beyond profit became central to how Japanese management was discussed.
lesson: People work harder for a purpose that outlasts them than for a profit target. Give them a reason that is worth handing on.
people: Konosuke Matsushita
source: Panasonic corporate history; Konosuke Matsushita, Quest for Prosperity (1988)

title: The Moving Point of Light
text:
In the mid-1930s, at Columbia University, the young Turkish psychologist Muzafer Sherif used a quirk of human vision. In a completely dark room, a small, fixed point of light seems to drift, because the eye has nothing to anchor it. This is called the autokinetic effect. How far the light appears to move is pure guesswork.

Sherif asked people to estimate, again and again, how many inches the light moved. Alone, each person soon settled on a personal range of answers, and these ranges differed widely from one person to the next. Then he brought people into the dark room in twos and threes and had them call out their estimates in turn.

Over a few sessions, the estimates within each group drew together until the group shared a common range, its own norm for a movement that did not actually exist. Different groups settled on different norms. Most striking of all, when people who had formed a norm in a group were later tested alone, they kept using the group's figure rather than returning to their original answers.

Sherif concluded that when reality is unclear, people build shared frames of reference together, and those frames then live on inside each member.
lesson: Where facts are fuzzy, a team quietly invents its own standards. Check which of your group's habits rest on evidence and which only rest on having been repeated together.
people: Muzafer Sherif
source: Sherif, M. (1935). A study of some social factors in perception. Archives of Psychology.

title: The Washington Eight Win in Berlin
text:
The University of Washington crew that went to the 1936 Berlin Olympics was made up largely of the sons of loggers, farmers and fishermen, young men working their way through college in the Depression. One of them, Joe Rantz, had been left to fend for himself as a teenager when his family moved away without him.

Coach Al Ulbrickson spent seasons shuffling rowers until he found a combination that moved as one. Their boat, the Husky Clipper, was built by George Pocock, an English boatbuilder who also coached them in technique. Pocock taught that a crew wins when all eight oars catch and release in perfect rhythm, a feeling rowers call swing, and that a man has to trust the others completely to find it.

The final at Grunau on 14 August was stacked against them. They had drawn the most exposed lane, their stroke, Don Hume, was sick, and they did not hear the start, so they began well behind. Coxswain Bobby Moch kept the stroke rate low for most of the race, then called for more and more in the final stretch, with Hume barely able to see. In front of a crowd that included Hitler, they caught Italy and Germany and crossed the line first, by about six tenths of a second.

None of the nine was a famous athlete, and most had not rowed before college. Together, they won Olympic gold.
lesson: Some results come only when everyone trusts the others enough to stop pulling alone. Look for rhythm and trust in a team, not just raw strength.
people: Joe Rantz, Al Ulbrickson, George Pocock, Bobby Moch, Don Hume
source: Daniel James Brown, The Boys in the Boat (2013); official report of the 1936 Olympic Games

title: Haile Selassie Addresses the League of Nations
text:
In October 1935 Fascist Italy invaded Ethiopia, one of the few independent African states and a member of the League of Nations. The League condemned the invasion but imposed only limited sanctions, leaving out oil. The Italian forces used aircraft to spray mustard gas on soldiers and civilians. In May 1936 Addis Ababa fell, and Emperor Haile Selassie went into exile.

On June 30, 1936, he addressed the League's Assembly in Geneva. When he came to the rostrum, a group of Italian journalists in the gallery began whistling and shouting abuse, and they were removed.

Speaking in Amharic, the emperor described in detail how the gas had been sprayed from planes over the land, killing people and animals and poisoning the waters. He reminded the members of the promises of collective security in the League's covenant, on which his country had relied. What was at stake, he said, was not only Ethiopia, but collective security, the very existence of the League, and the value of promises made to small states. He asked what reply he should take back to his people.

Within days the League voted to lift its sanctions on Italy. Three years later Europe was at war. Haile Selassie returned to Addis Ababa in 1941.
lesson: Speaking the truth plainly in defeat can preserve your dignity and your cause, even when the powerful choose not to listen.
people: Haile Selassie
source: League of Nations, Official Journal, Records of the Assembly, 1936; text of Haile Selassie's speech

title: Jesse Owens and Luz Long in Berlin
text:
At the Berlin Olympics in August 1936, staged by the Nazi regime as a display of Aryan supremacy, the American sprinter Jesse Owens entered the long jump. In qualifying he fouled on his first two attempts and was one jump from elimination.

In the version Owens told for decades afterward, the German jumper Luz Long came over, introduced himself and suggested that Owens mark a spot well before the takeoff board and jump from there to be safe. Owens qualified easily. In the final the two fought a duel; Owens won with 8.06 meters and Long took silver. Long was the first to congratulate him, and the two walked arm in arm around the stadium in front of the German crowd.

They wrote to each other after the Games. Long was killed in Sicily in 1943 while serving in the German army. According to Owens, Long had written asking him, if he died, to look up his son and tell him about his father. Owens later met the son, Kai, and remained close to the Long family. Long was posthumously awarded the Pierre de Coubertin Medal for sportsmanship.
lesson: Treat a rival as a fellow human being, whatever the politics around you. Sportsmanship and friendship across a hostile divide can outlast the regimes that tried to forbid them.
people: Jesse Owens, Luz Long
source: Jesse Owens with Paul Neimark, The Jesse Owens Story (1970); Jeremy Schaap, Triumph (2007)
caveat: The advice during qualifying comes only from Owens's later accounts and has been questioned; the friendship and the embrace after the final are well attested.

title: Sakichi Toyoda Backs His Son's Dream of Cars
text:
Sakichi Toyoda, the son of a carpenter in a farming village near Nagoya, spent his life improving the loom. He watched his mother and the village women weaving by hand and resolved to make their work easier. After decades of experiment, in 1924 he produced the Type G automatic loom, which changed shuttles without stopping and halted itself the moment a thread broke, so that one worker could watch many machines. That idea, a machine that stops when something goes wrong, later became a pillar of the Toyota production system.

His son Kiichiro studied mechanical engineering at Tokyo Imperial University and became fascinated by automobiles, which Japan was then importing from America. In 1929 the British firm Platt Brothers bought the patent rights to the Toyoda loom. According to the company's history, Sakichi gave the proceeds to Kiichiro to develop cars, encouraging him to serve his country through the automobile as he himself had through the loom.

Sakichi died in 1930. Kiichiro set up an automobile department inside the family's loom company in 1933, studied and took apart foreign cars, and built prototypes. In 1937 the department became an independent company, the Toyota Motor Company. The loom maker's son had founded what would one day become one of the largest carmakers in the world.
lesson: A parent's greatest gift can be the freedom and support to pursue a different dream. Blessing a child's new path can carry the family's work further than repeating it.
people: Sakichi Toyoda, Kiichiro Toyoda
source: Toyota Motor Corporation, Toyota: A History of the First 50 Years (1988); Toyota 75 Years history
caveat: Sakichi's exact words to Kiichiro come from company tradition, and the share of patent money used for cars is debated.

title: Eighty Years of Harvard Men
text:
In 1938, with funding from the businessman W. T. Grant, the Harvard physician Arlie Bock began following a group of 268 healthy Harvard undergraduates, the so-called Grant Study. The idea was to learn what helps people thrive, not just what makes them sick. The men were examined, interviewed and surveyed again and again for the rest of their lives. Their records were later combined with those of a second study, begun by Sheldon and Eleanor Glueck, of several hundred boys from poor neighborhoods of inner-city Boston.

The psychiatrist George Vaillant directed the study for over three decades, and Robert Waldinger later took it over and extended it to the participants' children. Researchers looked at careers, marriages, health, drinking, mood and much else as the men aged.

The finding they emphasized most was about relationships. The warmth of men's relationships, with parents in childhood, with spouses and with friends, predicted their health and happiness in old age better than social class, intelligence or wealth did. Men who were more satisfied in their relationships at age 50 were healthier at 80. Vaillant summed it up by saying that what mattered most in life was relationships with other people.
lesson: Over a lifetime, the quality of your relationships matters more for health and happiness than money or status. Invest in them steadily, not only when there is time.
people: Arlie Bock, George Vaillant, Robert Waldinger and colleagues
source: Vaillant, G. E. (2012). Triumphs of Experience: The Men of the Harvard Grant Study. Harvard University Press. See also Waldinger, R., and Schulz, M. (2023). The Good Life. Simon and Schuster.
caveat: The original samples were all men and almost all white, and the findings are correlational.

title: The Codebreakers of Bletchley Park
text:
In August 1939 Britain's Government Code and Cypher School moved to Bletchley Park, a country house north of London, to attack the German Enigma cipher. Just weeks before, Polish cryptanalysts had handed their British and French allies everything they had learned about Enigma, including how they had reconstructed the machine.

The people recruited to Bletchley were an unusual mix: mathematicians such as Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman, linguists and classicists, chess champions like Hugh Alexander and Stuart Milner-Barry, and later people who could finish a newspaper crossword fast. Turing and Welchman designed the bombe, an electromechanical machine that tested possible Enigma settings, and thousands of young women, many from the Women's Royal Naval Service, ran the machines day and night. By the end of the war the staff numbered in the thousands, and most of them were women.

The work was organized in huts, each with its own task, passing material along like a factory line. When shortages of staff and typists slowed them in October 1941, Turing, Welchman, Alexander and Milner-Barry wrote directly to Winston Churchill. He ordered that they be given all they needed, marking the note "Action this day."

Bletchley's intelligence, code-named Ultra, helped the Allies fight the U-boats in the Atlantic, follow German moves in North Africa and plan D-Day. Engineer Tommy Flowers of the Post Office research station at Dollis Hill built Colossus for Bletchley to break a different German cipher. Nearly all of them kept the secret for some thirty years.
lesson: Hard problems yield to mixed teams. Bring together people with very different skills, give them a shared goal and the tools they need, and protect them from bureaucracy.
people: Alan Turing, Gordon Welchman, Hugh Alexander, Stuart Milner-Barry, Tommy Flowers, Joan Clarke
source: F. H. Hinsley et al., British Intelligence in the Second World War (1979 to 1990); F. H. Hinsley and Alan Stripp, eds., Codebreakers (1993)
caveat: Estimates that Ultra shortened the war by about two years come from Hinsley and are debated.

title: Three Ways to Lead a Boys' Club
text:
In the late 1930s Kurt Lewin and his students Ronald Lippitt and Ralph White formed small after-school clubs of ten and eleven year old boys in Iowa. The boys made masks, painted and built things. Adult leaders were trained to lead in one of three styles, and they rotated between clubs so that personality did not explain the results.

The autocratic leader decided everything, handed out tasks step by step and praised or criticized without explaining why. The democratic leader let the group discuss and choose its projects and offered options and reasons. The laissez-faire leader stayed friendly but passive and left the boys to themselves.

The differences were striking. Under autocratic leaders, groups either became apathetic or showed much more hostility, often taking it out on a scapegoat. Work went on while the leader was in the room, but when he stepped out, it largely stopped. Under democratic leaders the boys were friendlier, more creative and kept working when the leader left. The laissez-faire groups got the least done. Most boys said they preferred the democratic leader.
lesson: Control can keep people busy while you watch. Involving them in decisions keeps them working when you are not there.
people: Kurt Lewin, Ronald Lippitt, Ralph White
location: University of Iowa, Iowa City, USA
source: Lewin, K., Lippitt, R., and White, R. K. (1939). Patterns of aggressive behavior in experimentally created 'social climates.' Journal of Social Psychology, 10(2), 271-299.
caveat: The groups were few and small, so the results are best read as a vivid early demonstration rather than a precise measurement.

title: Nicholas Winton's Scrapbook
text:
In December 1938 Nicholas Winton, a 29 year old London stockbroker, cancelled a skiing holiday to visit a friend in Prague who was helping refugees. Germany had just taken the Sudetenland, and families who had fled the Nazis were crowded into camps around the city. Winton saw that Jewish children were in particular danger and that no one was organizing to get them out of Czechoslovakia.

Back in London, working from his home after office hours with his mother and a small team, he registered children, found British families willing to take them, raised the required guarantees and fought the Home Office for permits. Colleagues in Prague, including Trevor Chadwick, organized the departures. Between March and August 1939 trains carried 669 children to Britain. The largest transport, set for September 1, was cancelled when war broke out, and almost none of those children survived.

Winton told almost no one. In 1988 his wife found a scrapbook in their attic with lists and photographs of the children. It led to a BBC television program in which Winton, sitting in the audience, discovered that the people around him were the children he had saved, now grown. He was knighted in 2003 and died in 2015, aged 106.
lesson: Doing good quietly, without seeking credit, can still change hundreds of lives. When you see a need nobody is meeting, start where you are with what you have.
people: Nicholas Winton, Trevor Chadwick, Grete Winton
location: Prague, Czech Republic, and London, England
source: Winton's scrapbook and records; BBC, That's Life! (February 1988); Barbara Winton, If It's Not Impossible (2014)

title: Churchill Refuses to Negotiate
text:
Winston Churchill became British prime minister on May 10, 1940, the day Germany attacked France and the Low Countries. Within two weeks the French front had collapsed and most of the British army was trapped at Dunkirk. It seemed possible that it would be lost entirely.

In the small War Cabinet, Foreign Secretary Lord Halifax argued that Britain should at least explore whether Mussolini's Italy might mediate terms with Hitler, while Britain still had something to bargain with. For several days, from May 25 to 28, the debate went back and forth. Churchill's position in his own party was not yet secure.

On the afternoon of May 28 Churchill met the wider group of ministers outside the War Cabinet and spoke to them frankly about the situation. According to the diary of Hugh Dalton, who was present, he told them that he had wondered whether it was his duty to consider negotiating, but had concluded that any terms would make Britain a slave state. He said that if this long island story of theirs was to end at last, let it end only when each of them lay choking in his own blood upon the ground.

The ministers cheered and crowded around him. Churchill reported their reaction to the War Cabinet, and the idea of negotiation was dropped.
lesson: In the darkest moment, a leader who states plainly what is at stake and what he will not give up can give doubters the courage to hold on.
people: Winston Churchill, Lord Halifax, Hugh Dalton
source: War Cabinet minutes, May 1940; Hugh Dalton's diary, May 28, 1940

title: The Little Ships of Dunkirk
text:
In late May 1940 the German advance had trapped the British Expeditionary Force and many French troops against the coast at Dunkirk. The Admiralty launched Operation Dynamo to bring them home across the Channel. The problem was that the beaches shelved gently, and big ships could not get close enough to take men off.

The call went out for small craft. Pleasure cruisers, fishing boats, lifeboats, ferries, barges and private motor yachts were gathered from the Thames and the south coast ports. Many were crewed by naval reservists, others by their own owners and fishermen who refused to hand them over. They crossed under air attack, ran in to the beaches, and ferried soldiers out to the destroyers and transports waiting offshore, trip after trip.

Hundreds of these little ships took part, and a good number were sunk or wrecked. Most of the troops actually left from the harbor's long stone mole aboard destroyers and larger vessels, but the small boats made the beach evacuation possible and carried many thousands themselves.

When the operation ended on 4 June, about 338,000 Allied soldiers had been brought to England, far more than the few tens of thousands planners had hoped for. Churchill warned Parliament that "wars are not won by evacuations." But the army that would fight on had been saved, by a navy working alongside a flotilla of civilians.
lesson: Large institutions often succeed only when ordinary people step in with what they have. A big effort can be made of many small, willing contributions.
people: Bertram Ramsay, civilian boat owners and crews, Royal Navy
location: Dunkirk, France, and the English Channel
source: Walter Lord, The Miracle of Dunkirk (1982); Winston Churchill, speech to the House of Commons, 4 June 1940
caveat: Popular memory overstates the little ships' share: most soldiers were lifted from the harbor mole by destroyers and larger ships.

title: King Haakon Refuses the German Demands
text:
Early on April 9, 1940, Germany invaded Norway. The royal family, the government and members of parliament escaped from Oslo by train just ahead of the German forces, heading north into the interior. That same day the Norwegian fascist Vidkun Quisling declared himself prime minister on the radio.

On April 10 the German envoy, Curt Brauer, met King Haakon VII at Elverum and demanded that he appoint a government headed by Quisling. Haakon's powers as a constitutional monarch were limited, and he said he could not answer without consulting his ministers.

That evening he met the cabinet at Nybergsund. He told them that he could not appoint Quisling, a man he knew had no support among the people, and that if the government decided to accept the German demands, he would abdicate rather than be part of it. The ministers, who had been uncertain, unanimously backed him. The answer to Germany was no.

The next day German bombers attacked Nybergsund, and the king and crown prince sheltered in the snowy woods. After two months of fighting, Haakon and the government left for Britain in June 1940 and led the resistance from exile. He returned to Norway on June 7, 1945.
lesson: Even when your formal power is small, refusing to lend your name to injustice can stiffen everyone around you.
people: Haakon VII of Norway, Curt Brauer, Vidkun Quisling
source: Norwegian government records; contemporary accounts and later memoirs of ministers present

title: Sugihara Writes Visas Day and Night
text:
In the summer of 1940 Chiune Sugihara was the Japanese vice consul in Kaunas, Lithuania. The Soviet Union was occupying the country, and Jewish refugees from Poland and Lithuania were desperate to escape before the Nazis or the Soviets closed every door. Hundreds gathered outside the Japanese consulate asking for transit visas through Japan. Many held papers for the Dutch colony of Curacao, provided by the Dutch consul Jan Zwartendijk.

Sugihara cabled Tokyo three times for permission to issue the visas. Each time he was told not to give them to people without proper funds and final destinations. After discussing it with his wife Yukiko, he decided to disobey. For weeks, from late July to the end of August, he wrote visas by hand for many hours a day, often for whole families on a single visa. When the consulate was closed and he had to leave, he kept writing and signing papers until his train pulled out.

Thousands of refugees crossed the Soviet Union to Vladivostok, sailed to Japan and later reached Shanghai, the Americas and elsewhere. After the war Sugihara left the foreign service. In 1985 Yad Vashem recognized him as Righteous Among the Nations.
lesson: Rules exist to serve people, not to excuse us from helping them. One person's choice to act, at real personal cost, can save more lives than they will ever know.
people: Chiune Sugihara, Yukiko Sugihara
source: Yad Vashem, Righteous Among the Nations file on Chiune Sugihara; Hillel Levine, In Search of Sugihara (1996)
caveat: Estimates of the number saved vary widely, usually given as about 2,000 visas and up to 6,000 people, and the circumstances of his leaving the foreign ministry are debated.

title: The Tall Glass and the Wide Glass
text:
In Geneva in the 1930s and 1940s, the Swiss psychologist Jean Piaget and his collaborator Alina Szeminska sat with children of different ages and presented them with deceptively simple puzzles. In the best known, a child watched as two identical glasses were filled with the same amount of liquid. The child agreed that both held the same.

Then, in front of the child, the researcher poured the liquid from one glass into a taller, thinner one, and asked: is there the same amount to drink in both, or does one have more? Most children of four or five said the tall glass now had more, because the liquid came up higher. Some said it had less, because it was thinner. The pouring had happened right before their eyes, yet the appearance won.

Older children, usually from around six or seven, answered differently and with confidence: it is the same, because nothing was added or taken away, or because it is taller but thinner, or because you could pour it back. Piaget called this understanding conservation and found the same pattern with rows of counters spread out or pushed together, and with balls of clay rolled into sausages.

Piaget concluded that young children do not simply know less than adults; they reason in a different way.
lesson: When a child gives an answer that seems silly, they may be reasoning in a different way rather than not trying. Ask how they see it before correcting them.
people: Jean Piaget, Alina Szeminska
source: Piaget, J., and Szeminska, A. (1941). La genese du nombre chez l'enfant. Neuchatel: Delachaux et Niestle. English translation: The Child's Conception of Number (1952).
caveat: Later researchers found that young children often succeed when the task is made more natural or the questions less confusing, so Piaget probably underestimated what they can understand.

title: The Village That Hid Refugees
text:
Le Chambon-sur-Lignon is a village on a high, cold plateau in south-central France, home to a Protestant community descended from the persecuted Huguenots. When France fell in 1940, its pastor, Andre Trocme, and his assistant Edouard Theis preached that Christians must resist evil, but only with what they called the weapons of the spirit.

During the war the village and the surrounding plateau sheltered refugees, many of them Jewish children whose parents had been deported. They were hidden in homes, farms, boarding houses and schools. Villagers forged identity papers and ration cards, and some guided refugees across the mountains to Switzerland. Magda Trocme, the pastor's wife, opened her door to anyone who knocked. In his study of the village, the philosopher Philip Hallie wrote that she said the first refugee simply needed to come in, and she did not think further than that.

In 1942 a Vichy minister visited and was handed a letter from the village's youth saying they would hide Jews no matter what. When officials demanded a list of the Jews in the village, Trocme refused. In 1943 he and Theis were arrested and held for several weeks. Trocme's cousin Daniel, who ran a children's home there, was later deported and died at Majdanek.

The plateau is credited with saving thousands of people. In 1990 Yad Vashem honored the community as a whole as Righteous Among the Nations.
lesson: Shared values make individual courage easier. When a whole community quietly agrees on what is right, each person's risky act feels less alone.
people: Andre and Magda Trocme, Edouard Theis, Daniel Trocme, villagers of the plateau
source: Philip Hallie, Lest Innocent Blood Be Shed (1979); Yad Vashem, Righteous Among the Nations records
caveat: Estimates of the number of people sheltered vary widely, from about 3,000 to 5,000.

title: The Water Shortage That Revealed Midway
text:
In the spring of 1942 US Navy codebreakers at Station Hypo in Pearl Harbor, led by Commander Joseph Rochefort, were reading parts of the main Japanese naval code. They could see that Japan was preparing a major operation against a target referred to as AF.
