Rochefort's team believed AF was Midway Atoll, but others in Washington thought it might be somewhere else, such as Hawaii, the Aleutians or the US west coast. Admiral Chester Nimitz, with only a few carriers left, needed to know where to place them.

To settle the question, the codebreakers devised a test. The garrison on Midway was instructed, through a secure undersea cable, to send a radio message in plain language reporting that its water distillation plant had broken down. Soon afterward the codebreakers read a Japanese message reporting that AF was short of water.

With the target confirmed, and with further decrypts indicating the timing, Nimitz placed his three carriers northeast of Midway, waiting for the Japanese fleet. On 4 June 1942 American aircraft fatally damaged four Japanese fleet carriers, the core of the force that had attacked Pearl Harbor, while the Americans lost the carrier Yorktown. Japan's naval offensive in the Pacific never recovered.
lesson: When you are unsure what someone's words mean, design a small test that forces the answer. Confirming one key fact can change how you deploy everything else.
people: Joseph Rochefort, Chester Nimitz, Edwin Layton, Jasper Holmes
location: Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, and Midway Atoll (USA)
source: Edwin T. Layton, And I Was There (1985); W. J. Holmes, Double-Edged Secrets (1979); Gordon Prange, Miracle at Midway (1982)

title: The Navajo Code Talkers
text:
In 1942 the US Marine Corps needed a way to send battlefield messages by radio that the Japanese could not read, and that could be sent and decoded faster than with cipher machines. Philip Johnston, a civil engineer who had grown up on the Navajo reservation as a missionary's son, suggested the Navajo language, which was unwritten, very complex and spoken by almost no outsiders.

The first group of twenty-nine Navajo recruits built the code themselves. They chose Navajo words for military terms: a dive bomber was a chicken hawk, a submarine an iron fish, a tank a tortoise. For other words, each letter of the English alphabet had several Navajo words. Then they memorized it all; nothing was carried in writing in combat. Many of these men had gone to government boarding schools where they had been punished for speaking Navajo.

The program grew to several hundred code talkers, who served with Marine units across the Pacific. At Iwo Jima in 1945, according to the signal officer Major Howard Connor, six code talkers worked around the clock during the first two days and sent more than 800 messages without error. He later said that without the Navajos the Marines would never have taken the island.

The code was never broken. It stayed classified until 1968, so the code talkers could not speak of their work for years. In 2001 the original twenty-nine received the Congressional Gold Medal.
lesson: A team gains its edge from differences others overlook. Knowledge and skills that seem marginal can become the team's greatest strength.
people: Navajo Marines, Philip Johnston, Howard Connor
location: Pacific theater, including Iwo Jima, Japan
source: US Marine Corps records; Sally McClain, Navajo Weapon (1994)

title: Irena Sendler and the Children in the Jars
text:
Irena Sendler was a social worker for the city of Warsaw when the Germans sealed hundreds of thousands of Jews inside the Warsaw Ghetto in 1940. Her job gave her a pass to enter the ghetto to check for contagious diseases. She and her colleagues used it to bring in food and medicine, and then to bring children out.

She worked with Zegota, the underground Council to Aid Jews founded in late 1942, and in 1943 became head of its children's section. Children were smuggled out through the courthouse on the ghetto edge, through sewers, in ambulances, hidden in boxes or under tram seats. They were given false Christian names and placed with Polish families, in convents and in orphanages. Sendler kept coded lists of their real names so they could one day be reunited with their families, and hid the lists in jars buried in a friend's garden.

In October 1943 the Gestapo arrested her. She was tortured, but did not betray the network, and she was sentenced to death. Zegota bribed a guard, who let her escape on the way to execution. She continued her work under a false name. Yad Vashem honored her in 1965, though she remained little known in the wider world until the 2000s.
lesson: Ordinary jobs can become instruments of great courage. Use whatever access and skills you have to protect those who cannot protect themselves.
people: Irena Sendler, Zegota
source: Yad Vashem, Righteous Among the Nations file on Irena Sendler; Anna Mieszkowska, Irena Sendler: Mother of the Children of the Holocaust (2010)
caveat: The often cited figure of 2,500 children saved by her network is disputed by some historians, who think the real number was lower.

title: Denmark Ferries Its Jews to Sweden
text:
Germany occupied Denmark in 1940 but for years left much of its government in place, and the country's roughly 7,500 Jews were not deported. In late September 1943 that changed: Berlin ordered a roundup for the night of 1 to 2 October.

Georg Duckwitz, a German diplomat in Copenhagen, leaked the plan to Danish Social Democrat leaders. The warning spread fast. On 29 September, the eve of the Jewish New Year, Rabbi Marcus Melchior told his congregation to leave their homes and hide. Over the following days, ordinary Danes took Jewish neighbors and strangers into their apartments, summer houses, churches and hospitals. Doctors admitted people under false names. Students, policemen and resistance members guided them toward the coast.

From fishing villages along the Oresund, fishermen carried them across the narrow strait to neutral Sweden, mostly at night, hidden in holds and under nets. Sweden publicly announced it would take them in. Some fishermen charged high fares, especially at first, and others took people for little or nothing. Within about three weeks, some 7,000 Jews and several hundred non-Jewish relatives had reached Sweden.

The German raids caught fewer than 500, who were sent to the Theresienstadt camp. Danish officials kept pressing for their welfare, and most of them survived the war. Altogether, more than nine in ten of Denmark's Jews were saved.
lesson: When many ordinary people act quickly and together, even a powerful threat can be defeated. Collective courage spreads when the first few act.
people: Georg Duckwitz, Rabbi Marcus Melchior, Danish citizens and fishermen
location: Copenhagen and the Oresund coast, Denmark, and Sweden
source: Bo Lidegaard, Countrymen (2013); Yad Vashem, The Rescue of Danish Jewry

title: Henry Ford and His Son Edsel
text:
Edsel Ford was the only child of Henry and Clara Ford. In 1919, at twenty-five, he became president of the Ford Motor Company. On paper he ran the firm; in practice his father kept control of every important decision.

Edsel had taste and a modern mind. He wanted Ford to offer more stylish cars, hydraulic brakes and new engines, as General Motors was doing with great success. Henry, who believed the Model T was all anyone needed, resisted for years while Ford lost market share. Edsel pushed through the purchase of the Lincoln company in 1922 and shaped the design of the Model A in 1927, but his father often overruled or humiliated him in front of others. Henry gave great power to Harry Bennett, the head of the company's security department, who undermined Edsel at every turn. Henry seemed to think his son was too soft and needed toughening.

Edsel worked under this strain for more than twenty years. He also became a generous supporter of the arts, funding Diego Rivera's murals at the Detroit Institute of Arts. In May 1943 he died of stomach cancer at forty-nine. Henry, nearly eighty, took back the presidency. Two years later, Edsel's widow Eleanor and Henry's wife Clara forced him to hand the company to Edsel's son, Henry Ford II.
lesson: A parent who cannot let go can crush the very successor he chose. Giving real responsibility means accepting decisions we would not have made.
people: Henry Ford, Edsel Ford, Clara Ford, Eleanor Ford, Harry Bennett
source: Douglas Brinkley, Wheels for the World (2003); Allan Nevins and Frank Hill, Ford (1954 to 1963)

title: Lectures or Group Decision
text:
During World War II, meat was rationed in the United States, and the government wanted families to eat cuts that were nutritious and available but unpopular, such as beef hearts, kidneys and sweetbreads. Kurt Lewin, a German emigre psychologist then at the University of Iowa, ran a study to find the best way to change these habits.

He worked with groups of women volunteers who ran their households. Some groups heard an attractive lecture by an expert explaining the nutritional value of these meats, the wartime need, and giving recipes. Other groups of similar size were given the same information by a leader, but instead of listening to a lecture, they discussed it among themselves. At the end, they were asked to indicate, by raising their hands, whether they intended to try serving one of these meats.

Later follow-up showed a striking difference. Only about 3 percent of women who heard a lecture reported serving one of the meats. Among those who took part in the discussion and group decision, about 32 percent did.

Lewin concluded that changing habits is easier when people decide together, as a group, than when they are told what to do as individuals.
lesson: People change more when they decide together than when they are lectured. Give your team the facts, then let them discuss and commit as a group.
people: Kurt Lewin
location: University of Iowa, Iowa City, Iowa, USA
source: Lewin, K. (1947). Group decision and social change. In T. M. Newcomb and E. L. Hartley (Eds.), Readings in Social Psychology. Henry Holt.
caveat: The groups were small and the study was loosely controlled, so public commitment and other factors may have contributed to the effect.

title: The Bennington Women
text:
In the 1930s, Bennington College in Vermont was a new, small college for women. Most students came from wealthy, politically conservative families, but many of the faculty and older students were liberal, and the campus was alive with discussion of the New Deal, the Spanish Civil War and other public issues.

Theodore Newcomb, a social psychologist on the faculty, surveyed nearly all the students repeatedly from 1935 to 1939 to track their political and social attitudes. He found a steady shift. Freshmen tended to share their parents' conservative views, but with each year at Bennington, students became more liberal. In the 1936 presidential election, most first-year students favored the Republican candidate, Alf Landon, while most juniors and seniors favored Franklin Roosevelt or candidates further to the left.

The shift was strongest among students who were most involved in campus life and who looked to the college community as their reference group. Students who stayed closely tied to their families, or who were isolated on campus, changed less.

Newcomb and his colleagues later followed up with the same women in the 1960s and again decades after that. Many had kept their liberal views, often supported by husbands and friends who shared them.
lesson: People take on the views of the group they most want to belong to, and those views can last a lifetime. Choose your communities with care.
people: Theodore Newcomb
source: Newcomb, T. M. (1943). Personality and Social Change: Attitude Formation in a Student Community. Dryden Press.

title: Operation Mincemeat
text:
In early 1943, after victory in North Africa, the Allies planned to invade Sicily. The target was so obvious that Winston Churchill reportedly said anyone but a fool would know it. British intelligence officers Ewen Montagu and Charles Cholmondeley developed an idea to make the Germans doubt it.

They obtained the body of Glyndwr Michael, a homeless Welshman who had died after swallowing rat poison, and turned him into a fictional officer, Major William Martin of the Royal Marines. They gave him a uniform, identity papers, and a carefully built private life: love letters and a photograph from a fiancee, a bank overdraft letter, theater ticket stubs. Chained to him was a briefcase holding personal letters between senior British generals that hinted, as if casually, that the Allies would land in Greece and Sardinia and only pretend to aim at Sicily.

On 30 April 1943 the submarine HMS Seraph released the body into the sea off Huelva, on the coast of neutral Spain, where a German agent was known to be active. The body washed ashore and was found by a fisherman. As the British hoped, Spanish officials allowed the Germans to see the documents, which reached Berlin and were judged genuine.

German forces were reinforced in Greece and Sardinia, among them a panzer division sent to Greece. When the Allies landed in Sicily on 10 July 1943, the defense was weaker than it would otherwise have been. The real identity of Major Martin was officially revealed only in 1996.
lesson: A convincing story is built from many small, ordinary details. People believe most readily what flatters their own judgment and seems to have been discovered by themselves.
people: Ewen Montagu, Charles Cholmondeley, Glyndwr Michael
source: Ewen Montagu, The Man Who Never Was (1953); Ben Macintyre, Operation Mincemeat (2010)
caveat: The exact military impact on the Sicily landings is debated by historians.

title: Kelly Johnson's Skunk Works
text:
In June 1943 the US Army Air Forces, alarmed by reports of German jet fighters, asked the Lockheed Aircraft Corporation to design an American jet fighter around a British engine. Lockheed's chief research engineer, Clarence "Kelly" Johnson, promised a prototype in 180 days.

He was given a small team of engineers and mechanics and set them up apart from the rest of the company in a makeshift shop near the Burbank wind tunnel, partly walled with engine crates and covered with a rented circus tent. They worked long hours under strict secrecy. Johnson cut paperwork to a minimum, kept the designers close to the people building the plane, and made decisions on the spot.

The prototype, the XP-80, was ready in 143 days, ahead of schedule. It became the P-80 Shooting Star, America's first operational jet fighter.

The shop got its name from a comic strip. In Al Capp's Li'l Abner there was a "Skonk Works," a smelly backwoods factory, and one of the engineers began answering the phone with that name. It stuck as Skunk Works. The same group later built the U-2 and SR-71 spy planes. Johnson eventually set down his methods in a short list of rules, starting with giving the program manager real authority and keeping the number of people involved small.
lesson: A small, trusted team with authority and few layers between idea and execution can outpace a large organization. Protect such teams from bureaucracy.
people: Clarence "Kelly" Johnson, Lockheed engineers and mechanics
source: Kelly Johnson with Maggie Smith, Kelly: More Than My Share of It All (1985); Ben Rich and Leo Janos, Skunk Works (1994)

title: The German Pilot Who Let a Bomber Go
text:
On December 20, 1943, an American B-17 bomber nicknamed Ye Olde Pub, piloted by 21 year old Charles Brown, was badly shot up over Bremen, Germany. One engine was dead, much of the tail was shot away, one crewman was dead and several were wounded. It limped west alone.

A German fighter pilot, Franz Stigler, took off to finish it. Pulling up behind the bomber, he saw the shattered fuselage and the wounded men inside and the dead tail gunner, and he did not fire. He later said that shooting them would have been like shooting a man in a parachute. Instead he flew close alongside, tried to signal Brown to land in Germany or fly to neutral Sweden, and finally escorted the bomber past German flak positions over the coast. Then he saluted and turned away. Brown nursed the plane back to England.

Neither man spoke of it for decades. In 1990 Brown, searching for the German pilot, placed a notice in a newsletter for former fighter pilots. Stigler, then living in Canada, answered. They met, became close friends, and both died in 2008.
lesson: Mercy toward someone who is helpless, even when you are told he is your enemy, keeps you human. It can also create a bond that outlives the conflict itself.
people: Franz Stigler, Charles Brown
location: Over northern Germany and the North Sea coast
source: Adam Makos with Larry Alexander, A Higher Call (2012); interviews with both men

title: Abraham Wald and the Missing Bullet Holes
text:
During the Second World War the mathematician Abraham Wald worked for the Statistical Research Group at Columbia University, a team of scientists solving practical problems for the US military. One question concerned bombers. Armor protected planes from enemy fire, but it was heavy, so it could only be added where it would help most.

The popular version of the story runs like this. Military officers looked at the bombers returning from missions and noted where they had been hit. Bullet holes were common on the wings and fuselage and much rarer on the engines. The natural conclusion was to add armor where the holes were. Wald pointed out the flaw: the planes being examined were the ones that came back. Holes in the fuselage showed where a plane could be hit and still return. The missing holes on the engines showed where hits brought planes down, since those planes never returned to be counted. The armor should go where the surviving planes had no holes.

Wald's actual memoranda, written in 1943, were more technical. They developed mathematical methods to estimate how vulnerable different parts of an aircraft were, using damage on returning planes and correcting for the planes that were lost. But the core insight is the same, and it has become the classic illustration of survivorship bias: drawing conclusions only from the cases that made it through a filter.
lesson: Before drawing a lesson from the winners, ask what happened to those who did not make it into your sample. The missing cases may tell you the most.
people: Abraham Wald, Statistical Research Group
source: Abraham Wald, A Method of Estimating Plane Vulnerability Based on Damage of Survivors (Statistical Research Group memoranda, 1943; reprinted by the Center for Naval Analyses, 1980); Marc Mangel and Francisco Samaniego (1984), Journal of the American Statistical Association, 79(386)
caveat: The popular story of officers wanting to armor the holes is a simplification; Wald's work was a statistical method rather than a single dramatic recommendation.

title: The Bowling Scores of the Norton Street Gang
text:
In the late 1930s the young sociologist William Foote Whyte moved into the North End of Boston, a poor Italian American neighborhood he called Cornerville, and lived there for several years. He became friends with a group of young men who hung around a street corner and whom he called the Nortons. Their leader was a man he called Doc.

The Nortons often went bowling on Saturday nights, and bowling scores became a matter of pride. Whyte noticed a curious pattern. Over time, the members' scores tended to line up with their rank in the group. Doc and his close lieutenants usually bowled well, while low-status members did poorly, even when some of them were capable bowlers who performed much better when they played with others.

When a low-ranking member started to beat higher-ranking ones, the group heckled him and reminded him of his place, and his game soon fell apart. At a prize match the gang organized, the final standings came out almost exactly in the order of the group's hierarchy. Whyte concluded that confidence and performance were shaped by a person's position in the group and the expectations of the others.
lesson: How well people perform depends partly on where they stand in the group and what others expect of them. Leaders can lift or sink someone simply through their confidence in them.
people: William Foote Whyte
source: Whyte, W. F. (1943). Street Corner Society: The Social Structure of an Italian Slum. University of Chicago Press.
caveat: It is an ethnography of one group described by a single observer, so it is a rich case rather than a measured result.

title: Forty-Four Juvenile Thieves
text:
In the late 1930s, a young psychiatrist named John Bowlby worked at the London Child Guidance Clinic. Among the children referred to him were many who had been caught stealing. He studied 44 of them in detail, interviewing the children and their parents and building up a picture of each family's history, and compared them with a group of children at the clinic who had problems but did not steal.

One group among the thieves stood out. Bowlby described them as "affectionless": they seemed unable to form warm bonds and showed little guilt or feeling for others. When he looked at their histories, most of these children had gone through long separations from their mothers or main caregivers in their early years, because of illness, hospital stays or being moved between homes. Such separations were much rarer in the comparison group.

Bowlby published the study in 1944. It was a small clinical sample without a modern control design, and he later acknowledged its limits. But it set him on the path that led to attachment theory, his reports for the World Health Organization, and changes in how hospitals treated young children, such as allowing parents to visit and stay.
lesson: Early separations and broken bonds can leave marks that show up years later as behavior. When a child acts out, it is worth asking what happened to their connections.
people: John Bowlby
location: London Child Guidance Clinic, London, UK
source: Bowlby, J. (1944). Forty-four juvenile thieves: Their characters and home-life. International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, 25, 19-53 and 107-128.
caveat: The study relied on a small clinical sample and retrospective reports, so it showed an association rather than proving that separation caused the behavior.

title: Eisenhower's Note in Case of Failure
text:
On June 5, 1944, General Dwight D. Eisenhower had already given the order for the Allied invasion of Normandy, after postponing it once because of bad weather. Thousands of ships and aircraft were moving. Nothing more could be changed, and no one knew whether the landings would succeed.

That day he wrote a short note in pencil, to be released if the invasion failed. It said that the landings had failed to gain a satisfactory foothold and that he had withdrawn the troops. It said his decision to attack at that time and place had been based on the best information available, and that the soldiers, airmen and sailors had done all that bravery and devotion to duty could do. It ended: "If any blame or fault attaches to the attempt it is mine alone."

In the draft he first wrote that the troops "have been withdrawn", then crossed it out and wrote "I have withdrawn" instead. He also misdated the note July 5.

The landings succeeded, and the note was never needed. He later gave it to his naval aide, Harry Butcher, and it is now kept at the Eisenhower Presidential Library.
lesson: Before you know how a decision turns out, be ready to own it completely. Credit can be shared; responsibility should not be.
people: Dwight D. Eisenhower, Harry Butcher
source: Eisenhower's handwritten note, Eisenhower Presidential Library, Abilene, Kansas

title: Operation Fortitude
text:
As the Allies prepared to invade northern France in 1944, they faced a basic problem: the Germans knew an invasion was coming. The question was where. The shortest crossing was to the Pas de Calais, and German commanders expected the main blow there. The Allies planned to land in Normandy instead.

Operation Fortitude was built to keep the Germans believing what they already believed. Planners invented a whole army group, the First United States Army Group, supposedly based in southeast England opposite Calais and commanded by George Patton, whom the Germans regarded as the Allies' most dangerous general. Its existence was signaled through fake radio traffic, some dummy equipment and planted references. Most importantly, MI5's Double Cross system controlled the German spy network in Britain: every German agent there had been caught or turned. Double agents, above all Juan Pujol, code-named Garbo, fed Berlin a steady stream of convincing reports. A separate deception, Fortitude North, suggested an invasion of Norway.

After the Normandy landings on 6 June 1944, Garbo reported that they were only a diversion and that the real attack would come at Calais. German commanders took this seriously, and strong forces of the 15th Army stayed in the Pas de Calais for weeks, waiting for an attack that never came, while the Allies built up their beachhead in Normandy.
lesson: The easiest deception confirms what the other side already expects. Control the sources your opponent trusts, and let him reach the wrong conclusion himself.
people: Juan Pujol (Garbo), George S. Patton, the London Controlling Section and MI5
source: Roger Hesketh, Fortitude: The D-Day Deception Campaign (official history, published 1999); Ben Macintyre, Double Cross (2012)
caveat: Historians debate how much of the visual deception, such as dummy tanks, the Germans actually saw; the double agents carried most of the weight.

title: Raoul Wallenberg in Budapest
text:
In the spring and summer of 1944 hundreds of thousands of Hungarian Jews were deported to Auschwitz. In July, Raoul Wallenberg, a young Swedish businessman with no diplomatic experience, arrived in Budapest as a secretary at the Swedish legation. His mission, backed by the American War Refugee Board, was to save as many of the remaining Jews as he could.

He worked by improvising within the bureaucracy. He designed an official-looking Swedish protective passport, the Schutz-Pass, in blue and yellow with the Swedish crown, and issued thousands of them. He rented buildings around the city, hung Swedish flags on them and declared them Swedish territory, sheltering people inside. He bribed, bluffed and threatened Hungarian and German officials, and recruited hundreds of staff.

When the Arrow Cross took power in October and deportations and death marches resumed, Wallenberg went to railway stations and to the marching columns himself, handing out passes and pulling people out by insisting they were under Swedish protection.

In January 1945, as the Soviet army took Budapest, he was detained by Soviet officials and disappeared. The Soviet Union later claimed he died in a Moscow prison in 1947. The exact number of people he saved is uncertain, but it is counted in the thousands at least.
lesson: Creativity and nerve inside an existing system can achieve what direct force cannot. Use every tool your position gives you.
people: Raoul Wallenberg
source: Swedish Foreign Ministry records; Yad Vashem; reports of the US War Refugee Board
caveat: Estimates of the number of people he saved vary widely, and the circumstances of his death remain unresolved.

title: "Guts Enough Not to Fight Back"
text:
In 1945 no black player had appeared in major league baseball for more than sixty years. Branch Rickey, president of the Brooklyn Dodgers, set out to change that, and he chose Jackie Robinson, a former UCLA star and Army officer then playing in the Negro Leagues.

On August 28, 1945, Rickey met Robinson in his Brooklyn office. According to both men's later accounts, Rickey spent hours acting out what Robinson would face: insults from opposing players, racist taunts from crowds, hotel clerks refusing him rooms, umpires against him, pitchers throwing at his head. Robinson, who had been court-martialed and acquitted in the Army for refusing to move to the back of a bus, asked if Rickey was looking for a player who was afraid to fight back. Rickey answered, in the words Robinson later recorded, that he was looking for a ballplayer with guts enough not to fight back.

Robinson agreed to absorb the abuse without retaliating, at least at first. He played for Montreal in 1946 and joined the Dodgers on April 15, 1947. He endured everything Rickey had predicted, and more. He was named Rookie of the Year in 1947 and the league's Most Valuable Player in 1949. After his first years he spoke out freely.
lesson: Restraint under provocation, chosen for a larger goal, is a form of strength. Sometimes the hardest thing a leader does is not react.
people: Branch Rickey, Jackie Robinson
source: Jackie Robinson, I Never Had It Made (1972); Branch Rickey's accounts

title: Babies Fed but Not Held
text:
In the 1940s, the Austrian-born psychoanalyst Rene Spitz, working in New York, compared babies growing up in two institutions. One was a foundling home where infants were kept clean, well fed and protected from infection, but where a handful of nurses cared for many babies. Infants spent long hours alone in cots, sometimes with sheets hung over the sides, seeing little but the ceiling.

The other was a nursery attached to a prison for women, where the babies were cared for daily by their own mothers, with help from staff. The physical setting was no better, yet the babies there were held, played with and talked to.

Spitz followed both groups with developmental tests and films. Babies in the nursery developed normally. In the foundling home, development scores fell steeply over the first year. Many babies became withdrawn, stopped responding to people and were unusually vulnerable to disease, and the death rate there was strikingly high despite the good hygiene. Spitz called the condition "hospitalism."

His films of listless, unresponsive infants shocked audiences and, together with Bowlby's work, pushed orphanages and hospitals toward more personal care and family placement.
lesson: Clean, safe and fed is not the same as cared for. Attention, play and a familiar face are basic needs for small children, not extras.
people: Rene Spitz
location: New York, USA (Spitz's base; the two institutions were not named)
source: Spitz, R. A. (1945). Hospitalism: An inquiry into the genesis of psychiatric conditions in early childhood. Psychoanalytic Study of the Child, 1, 53-74.
caveat: Spitz's methods were criticized at the time for small samples and unclear comparisons, though later research broadly confirmed the harm of severe institutional neglect.

title: Amul and the Dairy Cooperative
text:
In the 1940s dairy farmers in the Kaira district of Gujarat, India, had to sell their milk to a private dairy that held a contract to supply Bombay and paid them whatever it chose. Many owned only one or two buffaloes and had no bargaining power. Encouraged by the nationalist leader Vallabhbhai Patel, a local farmer and freedom fighter, Tribhuvandas Patel, organized them. In 1946 the farmers refused to supply the private dairy and formed their own cooperative union at Anand, starting with just two village societies.

In 1949 a young engineer named Verghese Kurien was posted to a government creamery in Anand. He did not want to be there and planned to leave, but Tribhuvandas persuaded him to stay and help the cooperative. Kurien stayed for the rest of his career. With his colleague H. M. Dalaya, he developed a way to make milk powder from buffalo milk, which experts had said could not be done, letting the cooperative process its surplus.

The structure was simple: farmers belonged to village societies, which owned the district union, which owned the processing plant. Farmers were paid fairly and regularly, according to the quantity and fat content of their milk. The brand name Amul was adopted in the 1950s.

The model spread to other districts. From 1970, under Operation Flood, led by Kurien's National Dairy Development Board, it was copied across India, which went on to become the world's largest milk producer.
lesson: Small producers who join together on fair rules can compete with powerful companies. Ownership by the members keeps the team's interests aligned.
people: Verghese Kurien, Tribhuvandas Patel, Vallabhbhai Patel, H. M. Dalaya
source: Verghese Kurien, I Too Had a Dream (2005)

title: The Transistor Team at Bell Labs
text:
After the Second World War, Bell Telephone Laboratories set up a solid-state physics group to find a replacement for the vacuum tube, which was bulky, hot and unreliable. William Shockley led it. Two of its members made a remarkable pair: John Bardeen, a quiet theorist, and Walter Brattain, a skilled experimentalist who could build almost anything.

Working closely, with Bardeen suggesting what to try and Brattain building it, they spent months chasing problems at the surface of semiconductor crystals. In December 1947 Brattain pressed two gold contacts, very close together, onto a piece of germanium. A small signal going in came out amplified. It was the first transistor, and they showed it to Bell Labs management on 23 December.

Shockley had not been part of the final breakthrough, and he was stung. Over the next weeks, working largely alone, he worked out a different and better design, the junction transistor, which became the basis of later devices. But he began to shut Bardeen and Brattain out of his work, and the group soured. In publicity photographs Shockley appeared at the center, seated at the apparatus. Bardeen left Bell Labs in 1951 for the University of Illinois.

In 1956 the three men shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for the transistor. By then they were no longer working together. Bardeen went on to win a second Nobel, for superconductivity, with a new team.
lesson: Collaboration can produce breakthroughs that no one would reach alone. Rivalry over credit can wreck the same team, so share recognition generously.
people: John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, William Shockley
location: Bell Telephone Laboratories, Murray Hill, New Jersey, USA
source: Michael Riordan and Lillian Hoddeson, Crystal Fire: The Birth of the Information Age (1997)

title: The Kon-Tiki Raft Voyage
text:
The Norwegian Thor Heyerdahl believed that people from South America could have reached Polynesia in prehistoric times on balsa rafts. Experts told him such a raft would sink or fall apart. In 1947 he decided to prove it could be done.

He and five companions, four Norwegians and one Swede, built a raft of nine balsa logs lashed together with hemp rope, copying early Spanish descriptions of Peruvian rafts, with a small bamboo cabin and a square sail. They left Callao, Peru, on 28 April 1947. Each man had a role. Herman Watzinger, an engineer, took weather and current measurements. Knut Haugland and Torstein Raaby, radio operators who had served in the wartime resistance, kept contact with amateur radio stations. Erik Hesselberg navigated. Bengt Danielsson, the Swede, looked after the stores. Everyone took turns at the steering oar and on watch.

Heyerdahl's book describes the six men living for over three months on a deck the size of a small room, eating flying fish that landed on board at night, joking, and keeping strict watches. When Watzinger fell overboard and the raft could not turn back, Haugland jumped in with a line and the others hauled both men back.

After 101 days and some 4,300 miles (about 6,900 km), the raft was driven onto the reef of Raroia in the Tuamotu Islands on 7 August. All six men survived and waded ashore.
lesson: Small crews in close quarters hold together through clear roles, shared routines and humor. Make sure everyone knows their job and trusts the others to do theirs.
people: Thor Heyerdahl, Herman Watzinger, Erik Hesselberg, Knut Haugland, Torstein Raaby, Bengt Danielsson
location: Pacific Ocean, from Callao, Peru, to Raroia, French Polynesia
source: Thor Heyerdahl, The Kon-Tiki Expedition (1948)
caveat: The voyage proved the crossing was possible, but most scholars reject Heyerdahl's theory that Polynesia was settled mainly from South America.

title: The Marshall Plan
text:
Two years after the end of the Second World War, much of Europe was still in ruins. The winter of 1946 to 1947 was brutally cold, food and coal were short, trade had collapsed, and Communist parties were gaining strength in France and Italy. American officials feared that economic misery would push Western Europe toward the Soviet Union.

On 5 June 1947, at Harvard University's commencement, Secretary of State George Marshall gave a short speech proposing American help for European recovery. He said the policy was directed not against any country or doctrine but against hunger, poverty, desperation and chaos. He also insisted that the Europeans themselves should take the initiative and agree on a joint program. The offer was open to all European countries, including the Soviet Union and the countries of Eastern Europe, and also to the defeated Germans.

Britain and France quickly organized a conference. The Soviet foreign minister, Vyacheslav Molotov, attended, then walked out, and Moscow forced Eastern European governments to refuse. Sixteen Western European countries took part. In April 1948 Congress passed the European Recovery Program, and over about four years the United States provided roughly thirteen billion dollars in grants and loans, much of it as goods.

Western European production recovered strongly, trade revived, and the cooperation the plan required laid early foundations for European integration. West Germany, a recent enemy, became a partner. Marshall received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1953.
lesson: Helping a former rival recover can serve your own long-term interests better than leaving him weak. Generosity with conditions that encourage cooperation can build lasting alliances.
people: George C. Marshall, Harry S. Truman, Vyacheslav Molotov
source: George C. Marshall, Harvard commencement address (5 June 1947); Benn Steil, The Marshall Plan (2018)
caveat: Economists debate how much of Europe's recovery was due to the aid itself rather than to policy reforms and cooperation it encouraged.

title: Otto Frank Reads His Daughter's Diary
text:
In July 1942 Otto Frank, a German Jewish businessman who had moved his family to Amsterdam, took his wife and two daughters into hiding in a secret annex behind his company's offices. Four other people joined them. Office employees, among them Miep Gies, brought them food and news for more than two years. On 4 August 1944 the hiding place was discovered and all eight were arrested and deported.

Otto was the only one of the eight to survive. He was liberated at Auschwitz in January 1945 and made his way back to Amsterdam. There, in the summer of 1945, he learned that his daughters, Margot and Anne, had died in the camp of Bergen-Belsen.

After the arrest, Miep Gies had gathered up the notebooks and loose pages of Anne's diary from the floor of the annex and locked them away, hoping to return them to her. Now she gave them to Otto. He began reading, and he was overwhelmed. He later said he had not known the depth of his daughter's thoughts and feelings, and that he realized how little a parent may really know a child.

Anne had hoped to publish a book about the annex after the war, and had begun revising her diary for that purpose. Otto decided to fulfill her wish. In June 1947 the diary was published in Dutch as Het Achterhuis, The Secret Annex. Otto spent the rest of his life answering readers' letters and promoting her message.
lesson: Our children may have inner lives deeper than we imagine, so it is worth listening while we can. Honoring a loved one's wish can carry their voice far beyond their life.
people: Otto Frank, Anne Frank, Margot Frank, Miep Gies
source: Anne Frank, Het Achterhuis (1947); Miep Gies with Alison Leslie Gold, Anne Frank Remembered (1987); Anne Frank House archives

title: Pee Wee Reese Puts an Arm Around Robinson
text:
In 1947 Jackie Robinson broke the color line in Major League Baseball with the Brooklyn Dodgers. He faced abuse from crowds, opposing players and even some teammates, a few of whom had circulated a petition against playing with him. Dodgers shortstop Pee Wee Reese, a Southerner from Louisville, Kentucky, refused to sign it.

According to the story told by Robinson, teammates and later writers, during a game on the road, with fans jeering and opposing players shouting slurs, Reese walked over from shortstop, stood next to Robinson and put his arm around his shoulders. He said nothing, or nothing anyone remembered. The message to the crowd was plain: this man is my teammate.

Robinson later credited Reese with helping him survive that first season. The two played together for years and remained friends. In 2005 a statue of the two men in that pose was unveiled outside the minor league ballpark in Brooklyn.
lesson: When someone is being singled out, a simple, public sign that you stand with them can change how others treat them. It costs little and may be remembered for a lifetime.
people: Pee Wee Reese, Jackie Robinson
source: Jackie Robinson, I Never Had It Made (1972); Jonathan Eig, Opening Day (2007)
caveat: The date, city and even details of the gesture are disputed, and some historians doubt it happened in the form usually told.

title: The Berlin Airlift
text:
In June 1948 the Soviet Union cut all road, rail and canal routes into the western sectors of Berlin, leaving about two million people with weeks of food and coal. The Western allies decided to supply the city entirely by air, something many experts thought impossible.

At first the airlift was improvised. At the end of July the American general William Tunner, who had run the wartime airlift over the Himalayas, took command. On 13 August, a day of bad weather later called Black Friday, planes stacked up over Tempelhof airport, circling in the clouds while crews on the ground tangled with crashed and blocked aircraft. Tunner, caught in the stack himself, turned the operation into an assembly line. Planes flew in strict corridors at fixed altitudes and intervals. A pilot who missed his landing did not try again; he flew straight back to base with his load so that the stream behind him was never disrupted. Ground crews and German workers unloaded aircraft in minutes.

The pace kept rising. Berliners themselves, many of them women, built a new airfield at Tegel in about three months. On 16 April 1949 the airlift made an Easter parade of nearly 1,400 flights in twenty-four hours, almost one a minute.

The Soviets lifted the blockade in May 1949. By the time the airlift ended that autumn, the American, British and allied crews had flown in more than two million tons of supplies. Dozens of airmen died in crashes.
lesson: Huge efforts succeed through relentless coordination: clear rules, steady rhythm and everyone knowing exactly where they fit. Discipline in the system beats heroics.
people: Lucius Clay, William Tunner, allied aircrews, Berliners
source: William H. Tunner, Over the Hump (1964); US Air Force historical studies of the Berlin Airlift

title: The Pajama Factory Experiment
text:
At the Harwood pajama factory in Virginia, managers often had to change how jobs were done as styles and methods changed. Each time, output dropped, complaints rose and many workers quit. The personnel manager Lester Coch and the psychologist John French decided to test whether the way a change was introduced made a difference.

When the next set of small job changes came, they handled groups of workers in different ways. One group was simply told what the new method and piece rate would be, as usual. Another group chose representatives who helped study the job and design the new method. In two further groups, every worker took part in the discussion and planning.

The group that was simply told showed the familiar pattern: output fell and stayed low, there was open hostility toward management, and several workers left within weeks. The groups that took part recovered quickly and soon exceeded their old output, with the fully involved groups doing best. Later, the members of the first group were moved to another new job, this time with full participation, and they too recovered quickly.
lesson: Resistance to change is often a reaction to being left out. Involve the people affected in shaping the change, and they will help make it work.
people: Lester Coch, John French
location: Harwood Manufacturing Corporation, Marion, Virginia, USA
source: Coch, L., and French, J. R. P. (1948). Overcoming resistance to change. Human Relations, 1(4), 512-532.

title: The Dassler Brothers Split a Town in Two
text:
In 1924 Adolf and Rudolf Dassler founded a shoe company in their small Bavarian hometown of Herzogenaurach. Adolf, known as Adi, was the quiet craftsman who designed the shoes; Rudolf was the outgoing salesman. Their spiked running shoes became famous when Jesse Owens wore them at the Berlin Olympics of 1936.

During the Second World War the brothers and their wives, who lived in the same house, grew bitter toward one another. Rudolf was drafted, and later came to believe that Adi had a hand in it. After the war Rudolf was held by the Americans and suspected his brother had denounced him. The details of who said what are disputed, but the resentment was real and lasting.

In 1948 they split the company. Rudolf set up his own firm on the other side of the little Aurach river, which became Puma. Adi named his business after himself: Adidas. The two companies became fierce rivals, and the town divided with them. Workers of each firm used different bakeries, pubs and shops, and Herzogenaurach was nicknamed "the town of bent necks" because people looked at your shoes before speaking to you.

The brothers never reconciled. When they died, Rudolf in 1974 and Adi in 1978, they were buried in the same cemetery, at opposite ends. Only in 2009 did employees of the two companies play a friendly football match together.
lesson: A family quarrel left unresolved can outlive everyone in it and divide whole communities. Repair is easiest early, before pride hardens into identity.
people: Adolf Dassler, Rudolf Dassler
source: Barbara Smit, Sneaker Wars (2008); company histories of Adidas and Puma
caveat: The exact causes of the brothers' quarrel are disputed and partly based on family accounts.

title: Gail Halvorsen, the Candy Bomber
text:
In June 1948 the Soviet Union blockaded West Berlin, cutting road and rail links. The Western Allies answered with the Berlin Airlift, flying in food, coal and supplies around the clock. Lieutenant Gail Halvorsen was an American transport pilot flying into Tempelhof airport. Only three years earlier, Americans had been bombing the city.

One day in July 1948 he went to the airport fence and talked with a group of German children. He was struck that they asked for nothing. He had only two sticks of gum, and he broke them and passed them through the wire. The children shared the pieces and passed around the wrappers to smell them. Halvorsen promised to drop candy from his plane the next day. They asked how they would know his plane. He said he would wiggle his wings.

He and his crew tied candy to tiny parachutes made of handkerchiefs and dropped them on approach. Soon children waited daily for "Uncle Wiggly Wings." When his superiors found out, they made it an official operation, called Little Vittles, and American children and candy makers sent supplies. By the end of the airlift, crews had dropped tons of candy over Berlin.
lesson: A small kindness, especially to children, can change how a former enemy sees you. Notice the people at the fence, and give what you have.
people: Gail Halvorsen
source: Gail S. Halvorsen, The Berlin Candy Bomber (1990); US Air Force historical records of the Berlin Airlift

title: Seretse and Ruth Khama Defy Two Governments
text:
Seretse Khama was the heir to the chieftainship of the Bamangwato, the largest people of the British protectorate of Bechuanaland. While studying law in London after the Second World War, he met Ruth Williams, an English office clerk. They married in September 1948.

The marriage set off a crisis. Seretse's uncle, Tshekedi Khama, who had ruled as regent during his youth, opposed it. Next door, South Africa had just elected the National Party, which was building apartheid and soon outlawed mixed marriages. South Africa and Southern Rhodesia pressed Britain not to accept a chief with a white wife. Britain depended on South Africa for gold and uranium. A British judicial inquiry found that Seretse was fit to rule, but the government kept its report secret. In 1950 it banished him from his own country.

Ruth stood by him. Their first child, Jacqueline, was born in Serowe while the dispute raged, and the couple spent the exile years in England. The Bamangwato repeatedly asked for his return. In 1956 Seretse and Ruth were allowed back, after he renounced his claim to the chieftainship.

He entered politics instead. When Bechuanaland became independent as Botswana in 1966, Seretse Khama was elected its first president, and he was knighted the same year. Ruth became the First Lady. Their son Ian Khama later became president too.
lesson: A marriage can hold firm against pressure from governments as well as families. What others forbid may become, with patience, the foundation of a new life.
people: Seretse Khama, Ruth Williams Khama, Tshekedi Khama
source: Susan Williams, Colour Bar: The Triumph of Seretse Khama and His Nation (2006); British government records

title: Why Soldiers Kept Fighting
text:
By the last months of World War II in Europe, Germany was clearly losing. Yet many German army units kept fighting stubbornly. Allied propaganda tried to persuade them to surrender with arguments about the hopelessness of the war and the evils of Nazism, with limited success.

Edward Shils and Morris Janowitz worked in the Psychological Warfare Division of the Allied command. They interviewed German prisoners of war and studied captured documents to understand what held German units together and what made them fall apart.

They concluded that for most ordinary soldiers, Nazi ideology and political arguments mattered surprisingly little. What kept a man fighting was his small unit, his primary group: the comrades he lived and fought beside, and the junior officers and sergeants who looked after them. As long as the squad stayed intact, met his basic needs and remained a source of respect and protection, he fought on. Units tended to collapse when this group broke down, through heavy losses, isolation or the loss of trusted leaders, or when soldiers became more concerned with their own families' survival at home. Propaganda worked best when it addressed these personal concerns rather than politics.
lesson: People commit to those beside them more than to abstract causes. Protect the small, stable groups in which loyalty actually lives.
people: Edward Shils, Morris Janowitz
source: Shils, E. A., and Janowitz, M. (1948). Cohesion and disintegration in the Wehrmacht in World War II. Public Opinion Quarterly, 12(2), 280-315.
caveat: Later historians, notably Omer Bartov, argued that Nazi ideology played a larger role, especially on the Eastern Front, than these interviews suggested.

title: The American Soldier and Relative Deprivation
text:
During World War II, the US Army created a Research Branch staffed by social scientists, led by sociologist Samuel Stouffer. They surveyed hundreds of thousands of American soldiers about their attitudes, morale and experiences. After the war, Stouffer and his colleagues published the results in a series of volumes called The American Soldier.

One finding puzzled them. In the Army Air Forces, promotion was fast and common. In the Military Police, it was slow and rare. Yet Air Forces men were more critical of the promotion system and more likely to say a capable soldier had a poor chance of advancing, while Military Police men were more satisfied with their chances.

The researchers explained this by what they called relative deprivation. People judged their situation not by an absolute standard but by comparing themselves with others around them. A soldier in the Air Forces who had not been promoted saw many of his peers moving up and felt left behind. A military policeman who had not been promoted saw that most of his peers had not been either. Similar comparisons appeared elsewhere in the surveys, for example in how married and single men felt about being drafted.
lesson: Satisfaction depends on comparison with nearby peers. When rewarding a team, consider how people will see their outcome next to their colleagues', not only its size.
people: Samuel Stouffer, Edward Suchman, Leland DeVinney, Shirley Star, Robin Williams
source: Stouffer, S. A., Suchman, E. A., DeVinney, L. C., Star, S. A., and Williams, R. M. (1949). The American Soldier: Adjustment During Army Life. Princeton University Press.

title: Two Kinds of Leader in a Group
text:
Around 1950 the Harvard sociologist Robert Freed Bales built a room where small groups of students met to discuss and solve problems while trained observers watched through a one-way mirror. He developed a system for classifying every act in a conversation into categories such as giving suggestions, giving opinions, asking for information, agreeing, joking, showing tension or disagreeing.

Coding thousands of interactions, Bales saw that groups had to handle two kinds of demand at once. One was the task itself: proposing ideas, organizing and pushing toward a decision. The other was social and emotional: easing tension, encouraging others and holding the group together after disagreements.

In later analyses with Philip Slater, Bales found that these two roles were often filled by different people. Members tended to name one person as having the best ideas and doing the most to guide the discussion, and often a different person as the one they liked best. The task leader's push tended to create friction, and a well-liked member helped repair it. Groups seemed to work best when both functions were covered.
lesson: A team needs someone driving the work and someone holding people together. If you are the driver, value and support the person who mends relationships.
people: Robert Freed Bales; Philip Slater (later work)
source: Bales, R. F. (1950). Interaction Process Analysis: A Method for the Study of Small Groups. Addison-Wesley.
caveat: The clear split between the two roles was found mostly in groups of strangers; in established teams one person sometimes does both.

title: Friendship and the Staircase
text:
After the Second World War, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology housed married veteran students and their families in two complexes called Westgate and Westgate West. Couples were assigned apartments more or less as they came free, so they had no say in who their neighbors would be. For the social psychologists Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter and Kurt Back, this was a natural experiment.

They asked residents which three people in the housing project they saw most often socially. The answers followed the floor plan with striking regularity. People named their next-door neighbors far more often than those two doors away, and those two doors away more than people at the end of the hall. Friendships across floors were rarer still.

Small details of architecture mattered. Residents whose apartments sat near the foot of a staircase or beside the mailboxes, where others passed every day, were chosen as friends more often than people in quieter spots on the same floor. Friendship, the researchers concluded, grows from the countless small encounters that physical layout makes likely, not only from shared interests or personality.
lesson: Friendships grow from repeated casual contact. If you want closer ties with someone, put yourself on their daily path and give small encounters a chance to add up.
people: Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter, Kurt Back
location: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, USA
source: Festinger, L., Schachter, S., and Back, K. (1950). Social Pressures in Informal Groups: A Study of Human Factors in Housing. Harper.

title: The Warm or Cold Guest Lecturer
text:
In 1950 the psychologist Harold Kelley ran a simple study in classes at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Students were told that their regular instructor was away and that a guest would lead the session. Before he arrived, they were handed a short written note about him: his background, his teaching experience and a few traits.

Half the students got a note describing the guest as "a rather cold person, industrious, critical, practical, and determined." The other half got the same note with one change: "a very warm person." Then the guest came in and led a twenty-minute discussion, the same for everyone.

Afterward the students rated him. Those who had read "warm" saw him as more considerate, informal, sociable, popular, humorous and humane than those who had read "cold," although both groups had watched the same man doing the same things. The single word also changed behavior: Kelley noted that more of the students who expected a warm instructor took part in the discussion than of those who expected a cold one. One word in an introduction had shaped both the impression and the interaction that followed.
lesson: A single word said about someone before you meet can color everything you see. Be careful what labels you pass on, and hold the ones you receive lightly.
people: Harold Kelley
location: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, USA
source: Kelley, H. H. (1950). The warm-cold variable in first impressions of persons. Journal of Personality, 18(4), 431-439.

title: The Lines on the Card
text:
In the early 1950s, Solomon Asch invited male students at Swarthmore College to what he called a test of visual judgment. Seated around a table with seven or eight other young men, each student looked at a card with one line on it and a second card with three lines of different lengths. The task was simply to say aloud which of the three matched the first. The answers were obvious.

What the real participant did not know was that everyone else at the table was working for Asch. On most rounds, after a couple of honest answers, they all calmly named the same wrong line. The participant, seated near the end, had to choose between his own eyes and a unanimous group.

About a third of all answers on these critical rounds went along with the wrong majority, and roughly three out of four participants yielded at least once. About a quarter never gave in. Many who conformed later said they had doubted their own judgment, while others knew the group was wrong but did not want to stand out.

Then Asch changed one thing. When a single other person at the table gave the correct answer, conformity collapsed to a small fraction of its former level. One ally was enough to make independence easy.
lesson: If you see a meeting drifting toward an answer you think is wrong, speak up early. A single dissenting voice frees others to say what they really see.
people: Solomon Asch
source: Asch, S. E. (1956). Studies of independence and conformity: I. A minority of one against a unanimous majority. Psychological Monographs, 70(9).
caveat: Later replications in other countries and decades have often found lower conformity than Asch did, though the effect has not disappeared.

title: Who Said It, and the Sleeper Effect
text:
In 1951 Carl Hovland and Walter Weiss of Yale University asked how much the reputation of a source affects persuasion, and how long the effect lasts. They gave students printed articles on several topics, such as whether antihistamine drugs should be sold without a prescription and whether a practical atomic-powered submarine could be built soon.

Each article was presented as coming either from a highly trusted source or from a doubtful one. For the submarine article, for example, the trusted source was the physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer and the doubtful one was Pravda, the Soviet newspaper. The articles themselves were identical. The researchers measured opinions before reading, right after, and again four weeks later.

Right after reading, the trusted sources changed opinions much more than the doubtful ones, even though the arguments were the same. But four weeks later, the gap had largely closed. People who had read the trusted source had drifted back somewhat, while those who had read the doubtful source had moved further toward the message. Over time, people seemed to remember what they had read but forget, or stop connecting it with, where it came from. Hovland and his colleagues had earlier named this delayed rise in persuasion the sleeper effect.
lesson: People remember messages longer than they remember who sent them. Check the source when you hear something, because later you will only remember the claim.
people: Carl Hovland, Walter Weiss
source: Hovland, C. I., and Weiss, W. (1951). The influence of source credibility on communication effectiveness. Public Opinion Quarterly, 15(4), 635-650.
caveat: Later research found the sleeper effect is fragile and appears only under specific conditions.

title: Wheel, Chain and Circle
text:
Does it matter who can talk to whom in a team? Harold Leavitt, at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, built an experiment to find out. Groups of five people sat at a table divided by partitions, so they could not see each other. They could communicate only by passing written notes through slots, and the researcher controlled which slots were open.

This created different communication networks. In the wheel, one person in the center could exchange notes with all four others, who could not talk to each other. In the chain, messages had to pass along a line. In the circle, each person could talk to two neighbors, and no one was in the middle.

Each person received a card with several symbols, and the group's task was to find the one symbol that all five cards had in common. Groups solved the problem many times in a row.

The wheel, the most centralized network, was fastest and made the fewest errors, and the person in the center quickly became the recognized leader. The circle was slower and made more mistakes, and no clear leader emerged. But members of the circle enjoyed the task more. In the wheel, the person at the center was satisfied, while those at the edges were not.
lesson: Centralizing communication makes simple work fast but leaves people on the edges disengaged. Decide how much speed you need versus how involved everyone should feel.
people: Harold Leavitt
location: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, USA
source: Leavitt, H. J. (1951). Some effects of certain communication patterns on group performance. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 46(1), 38-50.
caveat: Later work found that centralized networks lose their advantage on complex problems, where the person at the center becomes overloaded.

title: Truman Fires MacArthur
text:
In 1950 and 1951 General Douglas MacArthur commanded United Nations forces in Korea. After Chinese armies entered the war, President Harry Truman decided to seek a limited war and eventually a negotiated settlement, not an expansion into China. MacArthur disagreed and said so in public, repeatedly, in statements and letters that contradicted the administration's policy.

In March 1951 he issued his own ultimatum to the Chinese commanders, undercutting a peace initiative Truman was preparing. In early April a Republican congressman, Joseph Martin, read aloud in the House a letter from MacArthur criticizing the policy and ending with the phrase that there was no substitute for victory.

On April 11, 1951, Truman relieved MacArthur of command, with the backing of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. The decision was hugely unpopular. MacArthur returned to ticker-tape parades and addressed Congress, and Truman's approval rating fell to historic lows.

In the Senate hearings that followed, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs, Omar Bradley, defended the decision, arguing that MacArthur's strategy would mean the wrong war, at the wrong place, at the wrong time, with the wrong enemy. Civilian control over the military held.
lesson: Some decisions protect principles that matter more than your popularity. Make them clearly and accept the cost.
people: Harry S. Truman, Douglas MacArthur, Omar Bradley
source: Truman's statement of April 11, 1951; Truman, Memoirs, Volume 2; Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations Committee hearings (1951)

title: Hillary and Tenzing Reach the Summit Together
text:
The 1953 British Everest expedition, led by John Hunt, was a large team effort. Hundreds of porters and a strong group of Sherpas carried supplies up through the Khumbu Icefall and the Western Cwm, while climbers took turns breaking trail and stocking camps higher on the mountain. On 26 May the first assault pair, Tom Bourdillon and Charles Evans, reached the South Summit but had to turn back, exhausted and with failing oxygen.

Three days later Edmund Hillary, a beekeeper from New Zealand, and Tenzing Norgay, the experienced Sherpa climber, left their tiny tent at about 27,900 feet. They passed the South Summit, climbed a steep rock and snow step on the ridge, and at about 11:30 in the morning of 29 May stood on the highest point on Earth. Hillary photographed Tenzing holding up his ice axe hung with flags. There is no summit photograph of Hillary.

Back in the world, the press and politicians kept asking one question: who stepped onto the top first? It became a nationalist quarrel in India and Nepal. For a time the two men simply said they had arrived together.

In his autobiography, Tiger of the Snows (1955), Tenzing settled it himself: Hillary had been slightly ahead, and Tenzing came up just after him. He added that it did not matter, because they had climbed as a team, roped together, and the summit belonged to both of them and to everyone who had carried them there.
lesson: Shared achievements rarely survive a fight over credit. Agree early that the win belongs to the whole team, and it stays a win.
people: Edmund Hillary, Tenzing Norgay, John Hunt
source: John Hunt, The Ascent of Everest (1953); Tenzing Norgay with James Ramsey Ullman, Tiger of the Snows (1955)

title: Hungary Beats England 6-3 at Wembley
text:
On 25 November 1953 England met Hungary at Wembley. England had never lost a home match to a team from outside the British Isles, and much of the English press expected the visitors to be taught a lesson. Hungary, the Olympic champions, had gone unbeaten for over three years under coach Gusztav Sebes.

The match was over as a contest within half an hour. Nandor Hidegkuti scored in the first minute. Wearing the number 9 shirt of a centre forward, he dropped back into midfield instead of staying up front, and England's centre half, used to marking a striker, did not know whether to follow him. Hungary's forwards and midfielders swapped positions constantly and passed the ball quickly in short combinations. Ferenc Puskas scored one goal after dragging the ball back with the sole of his boot, leaving England's captain Billy Wright sliding past him.

Hungary won 6 to 3, with Hidegkuti scoring three. The players had been drilled as a unit, many of them together at the same club, Honved, and they played a system in which every man understood the others' movements. England's players were skilled, but they played in fixed positions.

Six months later, in Budapest, Hungary beat England again, 7 to 1. The Wembley defeat forced English football to rethink its training, tactics and attitudes to the rest of the world.
lesson: A team whose members understand each other's movements can outplay individually strong opponents stuck in fixed roles. Flexible, shared systems beat rigid positions.
people: Ferenc Puskas, Nandor Hidegkuti, Gusztav Sebes, Billy Wright
source: Contemporary match reports; Jonathan Wilson, Inverting the Pyramid (2008)

title: The Belay on K2
text:
In the summer of 1953 an American expedition led by Charles Houston attempted K2, the world's second highest mountain, with eight climbers. By early August they were high on the mountain at their highest camp, ready for a summit push, when a storm pinned them in their tents for days.

Then one of the climbers, Art Gilkey, collapsed. Houston, a doctor, diagnosed blood clots in his leg, a condition likely to kill him at that altitude. The summit was forgotten. The team decided to try to get Gilkey down, wrapping him in a sleeping bag and a tent and lowering him down the steep slopes in the storm.

On 10 August, during the descent, one climber, George Bell, slipped. His rope partner was pulled off, and their rope tangled with others. Within seconds five men were falling down the slope toward a drop of thousands of feet. Above them, Pete Schoening was holding the rope attached to Gilkey, with his ice axe jammed behind a boulder. When the falling ropes caught on Gilkey's line, Schoening held on. The axe held, the rope held, and all six men stopped.

Shortly afterward, while the others pitched an emergency camp, Gilkey, anchored to the slope nearby, was swept away, most likely by an avalanche. The rest of the team, injured and exhausted, made it down the mountain alive. Schoening's ice axe is preserved in a museum.
lesson: A team roped together shares its fate. Abandoning the summit to save one member, and one person's steady grip, can keep everyone alive.
people: Pete Schoening, Charles Houston, Art Gilkey, George Bell, Robert Bates
source: Charles S. Houston and Robert H. Bates, K2: The Savage Mountain (1954)
caveat: It is not known for certain whether Gilkey was taken by an avalanche or freed himself to spare the others; most accounts favor the avalanche.

title: The Double Helix and Photo 51
text:
In the early 1950s several groups were racing to find the structure of DNA. At King's College London, Rosalind Franklin, an expert in X-ray crystallography, was producing the sharpest diffraction images of DNA anyone had taken. She and her student Raymond Gosling made the most famous of them, known as Photo 51, in 1952. Her relationship with her colleague Maurice Wilkins was poor: he assumed she had come to assist him, while she understood the DNA work to be her own.

In Cambridge, James Watson and Francis Crick were trying to build a model. Their first attempt, a three-stranded structure, was wrong, and Franklin pointed out its errors when they showed it to the King's group.

In January 1953 Wilkins showed Photo 51 to Watson without Franklin's knowledge. Its cross pattern told Watson at a glance that DNA was a helix. Crick also saw a research council report summarizing Franklin's measurements. Combining her data with their own model building and with Erwin Chargaff's rules on base ratios, Watson and Crick arrived at the double helix within weeks.

Their paper appeared in Nature on 25 April 1953, alongside papers from Wilkins's team and from Franklin and Gosling. Watson and Crick acknowledged only that they had been stimulated by a general knowledge of the King's group's unpublished results. Franklin died of cancer in 1958, at 37. In 1962 Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared the Nobel Prize, which is not awarded after death.
lesson: Big discoveries are almost always built from many people's work. Share data openly, ask before using a colleague's results, and give credit in full.
people: James Watson, Francis Crick, Rosalind Franklin, Maurice Wilkins, Raymond Gosling
location: King's College London and Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge, United Kingdom
source: James D. Watson, The Double Helix (1968); Brenda Maddox, Rosalind Franklin: The Dark Lady of DNA (2002); Watson and Crick, Nature 171 (1953)

title: The Four-Minute Mile with Pacers
text:
By 1954 the four-minute mile had become a famous barrier. Gunder Haegg of Sweden had run 4:01.4 in 1945, and nobody had gone faster since. Roger Bannister, a British medical student who trained in short sessions around his hospital work, believed it could be done, but not alone.

He planned the attempt with two friends and fellow runners, Chris Brasher and Chris Chataway, with advice from the coach Franz Stampfl. The idea was simple: Brasher would set the pace for the first two laps, Chataway would take over for the third, and Bannister would save himself for the final lap, running at even speed without having to think about the clock.

On 6 May 1954, at the Iffley Road track in Oxford, the wind was gusting so strongly that Bannister almost called it off. Minutes before the start it eased, and the three decided to go. Brasher led through two laps, with Bannister at one point shouting at him to go faster and Brasher ignoring him, sticking to the plan. Chataway took over and led through the bell. With about 300 yards left Bannister passed him and drove for the line, collapsing as he crossed it.

The announcer, Norris McWhirter, began reading out the time, and after the word "three" the rest was lost in the crowd's roar: 3:59.4. Bannister later stressed that the record had been a shared effort. About seven weeks later John Landy of Australia ran faster still.
lesson: Even a solo achievement often rests on a team. Ask for help with the parts others can carry, and trust the plan you made together when the moment gets hard.
people: Roger Bannister, Chris Brasher, Chris Chataway, Franz Stampfl
location: Iffley Road track, Oxford, United Kingdom
source: Roger Bannister, The Four-Minute Mile (1955)

title: The Founding of CERN
text:
After the Second World War, European physics was in ruins. Many of its best scientists had fled to the United States, and no single European country could afford the giant accelerators that modern nuclear physics required. A handful of scientists, among them the French physicist Louis de Broglie, Isidor Rabi of the United States, and Pierre Auger and Edoardo Amaldi in Europe, began arguing for a shared laboratory.

At a UNESCO conference in Florence in 1950, Rabi formally proposed that European countries pool their resources. Over the next three years diplomats and physicists hammered out the details. In 1952 a provisional council was created, whose French initials, CERN, became the name. A site was chosen at Meyrin, near Geneva in Switzerland.

The convention establishing the organization was signed in 1953 by twelve countries, among them nations that had been at war less than a decade before, including France, the United Kingdom and West Germany. It came into force on 29 September 1954, after enough governments had ratified it. The convention stated that the laboratory would have no concern with military work and that its results would be published or otherwise made generally available.

CERN's first accelerator started up in 1957. The laboratory grew into one of the world's leading centers of physics, with scientists from many nations working side by side. In 1989 a CERN researcher, Tim Berners-Lee, proposed the system that became the World Wide Web.
lesson: Former enemies can build something together when a shared goal is too big for any of them alone. Openness about results helps keep trust between partners.
people: Isidor Rabi, Louis de Broglie, Pierre Auger, Edoardo Amaldi
source: Convention for the Establishment of a European Organization for Nuclear Research (1953); Armin Hermann et al., History of CERN, vol. 1 (1987)

title: When Prophecy Fails
text:
In 1954, a woman near Chicago, called Marian Keech in the published study (her real name was Dorothy Martin), announced that she had received messages from beings on another planet. They warned that a great flood would destroy much of North America before dawn on December 21, and that true believers would be rescued by a flying saucer. A small group gathered around her. Some quit their jobs, gave away possessions or broke with family.

Leon Festinger, Henry Riecken and Stanley Schachter, then at the University of Minnesota, saw a chance to test an idea. They predicted that if believers were deeply committed and had social support, a failed prophecy would not end their faith but would push them to seek new converts. They and their assistants joined the group, posing as believers.

On the night of December 20, the members waited at Keech's house for the saucer. Midnight passed, and nothing happened. In the early morning, Keech announced a new message: the group's faith had spread so much light that the world had been spared. The group, which had previously avoided publicity, began calling newspapers and seeking to spread its message. Believers who had waited alone, away from the others, were more likely to lose faith.
lesson: A committed group facing evidence that it was wrong may double down rather than reconsider. Build habits of admitting error before your team's identity depends on being right.
people: Leon Festinger, Henry Riecken, Stanley Schachter
source: Festinger, L., Riecken, H. W., and Schachter, S. (1956). When Prophecy Fails. University of Minnesota Press.
caveat: Later archival research has suggested that the observers influenced the group more than the book admits and that some members had sought publicity before the prophecy failed.

title: They Saw a Game
text:
On November 23, 1951, Princeton played Dartmouth in the last football game of the season. It was a rough game. Princeton's star player, Dick Kazmaier, left with a broken nose in the second quarter, and a Dartmouth player later left with a broken leg. Penalties piled up on both sides. Afterward the student newspapers of both colleges gave very different accounts of who was to blame.

The psychologists Albert Hastorf of Dartmouth and Hadley Cantril of Princeton saw an opportunity. They asked students at both universities questions about the game, and showed a film of it to groups of students from each school. While watching, each student marked every rule violation they saw, and whether it was flagrant or mild.

The two groups seemed to have watched different games. Princeton students saw the Dartmouth team commit more than twice as many infractions as their own team. Dartmouth students saw the two sides commit about equal numbers. Most Princeton students thought the game was rough and dirty and that Dartmouth had started it; many Dartmouth students thought it was rough but fair.

Hastorf and Cantril concluded that there was no single game that people simply observed. Each person selected and interpreted what they saw according to what mattered to them.
lesson: Loyalties shape what we literally see, not only how we judge it. When you disagree about the facts with someone on the other side, assume both views are colored.
people: Albert Hastorf, Hadley Cantril
location: Princeton University and Dartmouth College, USA
source: Hastorf, A. H., and Cantril, H. (1954). They saw a game: A case study. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 49(1), 129-134.

title: Clinical Versus Statistical Prediction
text:
In 1954 Paul Meehl, a psychologist at the University of Minnesota who was himself a practicing clinician, published a short book with an uncomfortable question at its heart. When professionals predict how people will turn out, are they better than a simple formula?

Meehl gathered the studies then available, about twenty of them, that compared two ways of making the same prediction. In one, trained experts such as psychologists, psychiatrists or counselors studied the case and used their judgment. In the other, a few pieces of information, such as test scores or past records, were combined by a fixed statistical rule. The outcomes predicted included success in school or training, parole violations and response to psychiatric treatment.
