The tickets were cards showing pictures of football players. Some participants chose their own card from a box; others were simply handed one by the experimenter. On the morning of the drawing, the experimenter went back to each participant and asked how much they would sell their ticket for, explaining that someone else wanted to buy in.

Every ticket had exactly the same chance of winning. Yet people who had picked their own card asked, on average, for more than four times as much money to give it up as people who had been handed a card.

In other studies in the same paper, Langer found that elements of skill, such as choice, familiarity, competition and active involvement, all increased people's confidence in winning games that were entirely random. People who drew cards against a nervous, awkward opponent bet more than those facing a confident one, although the game was pure chance. Langer argued that because skill and chance situations are often mixed in daily life, people carry the habits of skill into situations where they do not apply.
lesson: Making a choice, practicing or feeling involved can make random outcomes feel controllable. Before investing more, ask whether your actions actually change the odds or only your confidence.
people: Ellen Langer
source: Langer, E. J. (1975). The illusion of control. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 32(2), 311-328.

title: The Logging Trucks That Filled Up
text:
In the early 1970s Gary Latham, then working with a forest products company, studied the crews who drove logs from the woods to the mill. Each truck could legally carry a certain weight, but drivers usually loaded only about 60 percent of what was allowed, so the company was paying for many more trips than it needed.

The drivers were simply told to "do your best." Latham and James Baldes replaced that with a specific, hard goal: load each truck to 94 percent of the legal limit. There was no extra pay for reaching it, no punishment for missing it, and no threat to anyone's job. Drivers only received the target and could see how close they came.

Within a few months, average loads rose to above 90 percent of the legal maximum, and they stayed there for the rest of the study. Drivers began to compete informally with one another and to take pride in reaching the mark. The company estimated it saved a large sum it would otherwise have spent on additional trucks. The study became a classic example that goal setting works not only in the lab but in real jobs.
lesson: A clear target and visible progress can change performance even without new rewards. Before adding incentives, make sure people know exactly what good looks like.
people: Gary Latham, J. James Baldes
source: Latham, G. P., and Baldes, J. J. (1975). The 'practical significance' of Locke's theory of goal setting. Journal of Applied Psychology, 60(1), 122-124.

title: We Won, They Lost
text:
In the early 1970s, Robert Cialdini and his colleagues ran a series of field studies at seven American universities with major college football teams, including Arizona State, Notre Dame, Ohio State and Michigan. They wanted to see how people use the success of a group to which they only loosely belong.

In the first study, observers in introductory psychology classes counted how many students wore clothing with their university's name, team name or insignia on the Monday after each football game. More students wore school clothing after their team had won than after it had lost, and the bigger the win, the more they wore it.

In another study, researchers phoned students and asked them, among other questions, to describe the outcome of a recent game. When their team had won, students were much more likely to use the word we: we won. When it had lost, they more often distanced themselves: they lost. This tendency was strongest when the students had just been made to feel they had failed a test, suggesting that people reach for a winning group's glory most when their own image needs a boost.

Cialdini's team called this basking in reflected glory.
lesson: People rush to share in a team's wins and quietly step away from its losses. Notice who still says we when things go badly; that is real commitment.
people: Robert Cialdini, Richard Borden, Avril Thorne, Marcus Walker, Stephen Freeman, Lloyd Sloan
location: Seven universities in the United States
source: Cialdini, R. B., Borden, R. J., Thorne, A., Walker, M. R., Freeman, S., and Sloan, L. R. (1976). Basking in reflected glory: Three (football) field studies. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 34(3), 366-375.

title: Grameen Bank's Lending Groups
text:
In 1974 a famine struck Bangladesh. Muhammad Yunus, an economics professor at Chittagong University, felt that his theories had nothing to say to the starving people near his campus. He began visiting the nearby village of Jobra.

There he met women who made bamboo stools. They had to borrow money for materials from a trader who then bought the stools back at a price that left them almost nothing. In his book Banker to the Poor, Yunus says he made a list of people in the village caught in this trap: there were 42 of them, and together they needed only 27 dollars. He lent them the money himself.

Banks refused to lend to the poor without collateral, so Yunus began acting as guarantor, and he developed a system that relied on groups instead of property. Borrowers, most of them women, formed groups of five. Only two members would receive loans at first; the others got theirs only after the first ones had kept up repayments. Groups met weekly with bank workers, and members encouraged and supported each other. Repayment rates were high.

In 1983 a government ordinance made Grameen, "village" in Bengali, an independent bank, owned largely by its borrowers. The group model spread to many countries. In 2006 Yunus and the Grameen Bank shared the Nobel Peace Prize.
lesson: Small groups of peers who support and vouch for each other can unlock trust that formal rules cannot. Shared responsibility can stand in for collateral.
people: Muhammad Yunus
source: Muhammad Yunus, Banker to the Poor (1998)
caveat: Later randomized studies of microcredit found only modest average effects on poverty, and Yunus's early figures come from his own account.

title: Designing Work That Motivates
text:
In the 1970s the organizational psychologists Richard Hackman and Greg Oldham asked what makes a job itself motivating. They proposed that five features matter most: skill variety (using different skills), task identity (doing a whole, visible piece of work from start to finish), task significance (affecting other people), autonomy (freedom in how to do it) and feedback (knowing how well it is going).

According to their theory, these features create three key psychological states. People feel their work is meaningful, they feel responsible for the outcomes, and they know the results of their efforts. Those states, in turn, lead to stronger motivation, higher satisfaction and better work.

To test the idea, they surveyed several hundred employees working in dozens of different jobs in seven organizations, and also gathered ratings from supervisors and observers. Jobs that scored higher on the five features were linked to more internal motivation and satisfaction, and to some extent to better performance and less absence. The effects were strongest for people who wanted to grow in their work. The model became one of the most widely used tools for redesigning jobs.
lesson: Motivation is often built into the job, not added by speeches. Give people whole tasks, freedom in how to do them, a view of who benefits, and clear feedback.
people: J. Richard Hackman, Greg Oldham
source: Hackman, J. R., and Oldham, G. R. (1976). Motivation through the design of work: Test of a theory. Organizational Behavior and Human Performance, 16(2), 250-279.

title: The Hokule'a Sails to Tahiti
text:
By the 1970s many scholars believed that the Polynesian settlement of the Pacific had happened largely by accident, with canoes drifting to new islands. Hawaiians had lost the knowledge of how their ancestors navigated. In 1973 the anthropologist Ben Finney, the artist Herb Kane and the sailor Tommy Holmes founded the Polynesian Voyaging Society to test the question by sailing a traditional canoe to Tahiti without instruments.

They built Hokule'a, a double-hulled voyaging canoe about 19 meters long. But no Hawaiian could navigate it in the old way. They found Mau Piailug, a master navigator from the tiny island of Satawal in Micronesia, one of the last people trained in traditional wayfinding, who read the stars, the swells, the wind and the birds.

The canoe left Maui on 1 May 1976. The voyage was hard on the crew in more ways than one. Tensions grew between some of the Hawaiian crew members and the scientists, and there were quarrels and fights on board. Through it all Mau kept his course, guiding the canoe by stars and ocean swells across more than 4,000 kilometers of open sea.

On 4 June Hokule'a reached Papeete, where a huge crowd, reported at around 17,000 people, came out to greet it. Mau, upset by the conflict on board, flew home rather than sail back. He later returned to teach Hawaiian Nainoa Thompson, who revived the art for a new generation.
lesson: Reviving lost knowledge takes respect for the people who still hold it. A team's purpose can survive conflict, but healing it afterward matters for the next voyage.
people: Mau Piailug, Ben Finney, Herb Kane, Tommy Holmes, Nainoa Thompson
location: Pacific Ocean, from Maui, Hawaii, USA, to Papeete, Tahiti (French Polynesia)
source: Ben Finney, Hokule'a: The Way to Tahiti (1979)

title: Christmas Cards to Strangers
text:
In the 1970s, the sociologist Phillip Kunz of Brigham Young University tried a simple experiment around the holidays. With his colleague Michael Woolcott, he picked names of families he had never met from a city directory and mailed each of them a Christmas card. There was no letter of explanation and no way for the recipients to know who he was.

Then the replies came in. A sizable share of the strangers sent a card back, some with family photos or long handwritten notes about their year. Hardly anyone asked who this person was or why he had written. Receiving a card seemed to call for sending one, and that was enough.

The researchers also varied how the cards were signed, to suggest a sender of higher or lower social status, and found that this affected how many people answered. The title of their paper, "Season's greetings: From my status to yours," reflected that interest. But what made the study famous was the basic result: people returned a greeting to a total stranger almost by reflex, because a gift received feels like a gift owed.
lesson: Reciprocity runs deep and fast. A small, sincere gesture toward someone is often returned, which makes it one of the simplest ways to open or renew a connection.
people: Phillip Kunz, Michael Woolcott
location: Brigham Young University, Provo, Utah, USA
source: Kunz, P. R., and Woolcott, M. (1976). Season's greetings: From my status to yours. Social Science Research, 5(3), 269-278.
caveat: The exact response figures are reported differently in popular retellings, so they are left out here.

title: The Nursing Home Plants
text:
In the mid 1970s the psychologists Ellen Langer and Judith Rodin ran a field experiment in a Connecticut nursing home. The residents of two floors were similar in health and background. The administrator gave a short talk to each floor.

To one floor he stressed the residents' own responsibility. They could decide how their rooms were arranged, how to spend their time, and whether and when to complain about anything they disliked. Each resident was offered a small plant and told it was theirs to choose and to take care of. They could also choose which night to see a film. To the other floor, the talk stressed that the staff were there to take care of them. They were handed plants, told that the nurses would water them, and assigned a film night.

Three weeks later, residents on the responsibility floor were rated by nurses who did not know about the study as more alert and active, and they reported feeling happier. They attended more activities and took part more. In a follow-up eighteen months later, Rodin and Langer reported that fewer of the residents from the responsibility floor had died than from the comparison floor.
lesson: Doing everything for people can drain their vitality. Give the people you lead real choices and something of their own to be responsible for.
people: Ellen Langer, Judith Rodin
location: Arden House nursing home, Connecticut, USA
source: Langer, E. J., and Rodin, J. (1976). The effects of choice and enhanced personal responsibility for the aged: A field experiment in an institutional setting. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 34(2), 191-198.
caveat: The sample was small, and the mortality follow-up in particular involved few deaths, so that finding should be held loosely.

title: Knee-Deep in the Big Muddy
text:
In the mid 1970s Barry Staw asked business school students to play a financial executive at a fictional company whose profits had been falling. They read a case history and were told to allocate 10 million dollars of research and development money to one of two divisions, consumer products or industrial products.

Some students made this first choice themselves. Others were told that a previous executive had made it. Then all of them were shown what happened in the following years: in some versions the chosen division recovered, in others it continued to lose money. Finally, each student had to split a new budget of 20 million dollars between the two divisions.

The pattern was clear. Students who had personally chosen a division that then performed badly put the most money into it on the second round, more than students whose choice had worked out and more than those who had inherited a failing choice from someone else. Being responsible for a bad decision made people throw good money after bad, apparently to justify their earlier judgment. His title echoed a Pete Seeger protest song about a captain who keeps marching his men deeper into a river.
lesson: Owning a failing decision makes it harder to see clearly. Set review points in advance, and let someone without a stake judge whether to continue.
people: Barry Staw
source: Staw, B. M. (1976). Knee-deep in the big muddy: A study of escalating commitment to a chosen course of action. Organizational Behavior and Human Performance, 16(1), 27-44.

title: Scaffolding
text:
How does an adult best help a child learn something the child cannot yet do alone? In the early 1970s, David Wood, Jerome Bruner and Gail Ross studied this question with a puzzle and a careful tutor.

The puzzle was a set of interlocking wooden blocks that could be assembled into a pyramid, a task well beyond most three-year-olds and challenging for five-year-olds. Gail Ross worked one on one with children aged three, four and five. Her approach was deliberate. She first let the child try alone. When the child got stuck, she offered a spoken hint. If that did not work, she showed how to put two pieces together, then handed the task back. When the child succeeded at a step, she stepped back again.

Watching the sessions, the researchers identified what the tutor was doing. She kept the child interested, simplified the task by handling parts the child could not yet manage, kept the child pointed toward the goal, highlighted the important features, controlled frustration, and modeled solutions. They called this support scaffolding: a temporary structure that holds things up while building goes on and is removed as the child takes over.

The term spread widely through education and parenting, where it is still used to describe good teaching.
lesson: When helping someone learn, give just enough support to keep them moving, then step back as they gain control. Doing it for them teaches little.
people: David Wood, Jerome Bruner, Gail Ross
source: Wood, D., Bruner, J. S., and Ross, G. (1976). The role of tutoring in problem solving. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 17(2), 89-100.

title: Dick and Rick Hoyt Run Together
text:
Rick Hoyt was born in 1962 in Massachusetts with cerebral palsy, after the umbilical cord cut off oxygen to his brain at birth. He could not walk or speak. Doctors advised his parents to place him in an institution. Dick and Judy Hoyt refused. They were convinced he understood everything, and they raised him at home with his brothers.

In 1972 engineers at Tufts University built Rick a computer he could operate with movements of his head, letting him spell out words. Later he went to public school and eventually graduated from Boston University.

In 1977 Rick heard about a five-mile charity race for a young lacrosse player who had been paralyzed in an accident. He told his father he wanted to take part. Dick was not a runner, but he pushed Rick's wheelchair the whole way, and they finished nearly last. Afterward, Rick told his father that when they were running, he felt as if he was not disabled.

That changed both their lives. Team Hoyt went on to complete more than a thousand races together, including the Boston Marathon dozens of times and full Ironman triathlons, in which Dick swam towing Rick in a boat, cycled with him in a special seat and ran pushing his chair. Dick ran his last Boston Marathon with Rick in 2014, at seventy-three. He died in 2021, and Rick two years later.
lesson: A parent's love can turn a child's limits into a shared adventure. Ask what someone wants to do, not only what they cannot.
people: Dick Hoyt, Rick Hoyt
source: Dick Hoyt with Don Yaeger, Devoted: The Story of a Father's Love for His Son (2010); Boston Athletic Association records

title: Inside the Corporation Called Indsco
text:
In the 1970s the sociologist Rosabeth Moss Kanter spent several years studying a large American industrial company, which she called Indsco to protect its identity. She interviewed and observed managers, salespeople, secretaries and the wives of executives, and read company documents, to understand how life inside a big corporation shaped people.

Kanter argued that much of what people attributed to individual personality or to gender was really produced by the structure of their jobs. People whose jobs offered little chance of promotion tended to lower their aspirations, focus on friendships and complain, while those on promising paths became ambitious and engaged. Managers who lacked real power to get resources for their people tended to become controlling and petty.

Her best known analysis concerned what she called tokens: members of a group who make up a small minority, such as the few women among the company's sales force. Because they were so visible, every action was noticed and taken to represent their whole group. Differences between them and the majority were exaggerated, and they were pushed into stereotyped roles. Kanter argued that any minority in such a position would face the same pressures.
lesson: Before blaming people for how they behave, look at the position they hold: their opportunities, their power and whether they are the only one of their kind.
people: Rosabeth Moss Kanter
source: Kanter, R. M. (1977). Men and Women of the Corporation. Basic Books.
caveat: It is a case study of a single company, and later research found that men in token positions often do not face the same disadvantages as women.

title: Newborns Sticking Out Their Tongues
text:
In the 1970s, many psychologists followed Jean Piaget in believing that babies could not imitate facial expressions until near the end of their first year. Imitating a face is a hard problem: a baby can see the adult's face but cannot see its own, so it would have to link a seen movement with a felt one.

Andrew Meltzoff and M. Keith Moore at the University of Washington tested this with infants only 12 to 21 days old. An adult sat facing the baby and, in turn, stuck out his tongue, opened his mouth wide, pushed out his lips and slowly moved his fingers. The babies' faces were videotaped, and coders who did not know which gesture the adult had just made judged what each baby was doing.

The infants seemed to match the gestures more often than chance would predict: more tongue protrusion after seeing tongue protrusion, more mouth opening after seeing mouth opening. Meltzoff and Moore published the result in Science in 1977 and later reported similar findings with newborns only hours old.

The claim was exciting because it suggested that babies arrive ready to connect with other people, treating faces as something like their own from the very start.
lesson: Even the youngest babies are watching faces closely. Face-to-face play with an infant is not idle; it is the start of a conversation.
people: Andrew Meltzoff, M. Keith Moore
source: Meltzoff, A. N., and Moore, M. K. (1977). Imitation of facial and manual gestures by human neonates. Science, 198(4312), 75-78.
caveat: The finding is disputed: a large 2016 longitudinal study by Oostenbroek and colleagues found no reliable newborn imitation, though Meltzoff and others contest its methods.

title: The Quizmaster Advantage
text:
In 1977 Lee Ross, Teresa Amabile and Julia Steinmetz of Stanford University staged a quiz game. Pairs of students drew cards to decide their roles at random. One became the questioner, the other the contestant.

The questioner was asked to write ten challenging but fair general knowledge questions, drawing on any area they knew well, from a favorite book to their hobbies. The questioner then asked the contestant these questions aloud. Since each questioner could choose obscure topics they personally knew, contestants missed many of the answers.

Afterward, both participants rated the general knowledge of the questioner and of the contestant. Contestants rated questioners as far more knowledgeable than themselves. Observers who watched the game reached the same conclusion. Questioners, however, did not rate themselves as superior. Everyone knew the roles had been assigned by chance and that questioners had the huge advantage of choosing the questions, yet the contestants and observers still concluded that the person asking the questions was simply smarter.

The study showed how easily we mistake the advantages of a social role for qualities of the person who holds it, whether in a quiz, a job interview, or a meeting where one person sets the agenda.
lesson: The person asking the questions, setting the agenda or holding the title often seems smarter than they are. Judge people by what they know, not by the position they speak from.
people: Lee Ross, Teresa Amabile, Julia Steinmetz
source: Ross, L., Amabile, T. M., and Steinmetz, J. L. (1977). Social roles, social control, and biases in social-perception processes. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 35(7), 485-494.

title: Wearing the 'Eat at Joe's' Sign
text:
In 1977 Lee Ross, David Greene and Pamela House of Stanford University asked students a strange favor. Would they walk around campus for thirty minutes wearing a large sandwich board sign that read "Eat at Joe's"? Students were told they could learn something useful from the experience, but that they were free to refuse.

Some agreed and some refused. Then each was asked to estimate how many other students would make the same choice, and to describe the kind of person who would agree or refuse. Those who agreed to wear the sign estimated that most of their peers would also agree, on average around 60 percent. Those who refused estimated that only about a third would agree. Each group saw its own choice as the common and sensible one.

The students also judged people who would make the opposite choice more harshly, describing them in more extreme terms and attributing their choice to their personality. Ross and his colleagues found the same pattern with questionnaires about many other preferences and opinions. They called it the false consensus effect: we tend to believe our own choices and views are more widely shared than they are, and to see those who differ as odd.
lesson: Others are less like you than you assume. When someone makes a choice you would not, ask what they see before deciding something is wrong with them.
people: Lee Ross, David Greene, Pamela House
source: Ross, L., Greene, D., and House, P. (1977). The 'false consensus effect': An egocentric bias in social perception and attribution processes. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 13(3), 279-301.

title: Sadat Goes to Jerusalem
text:
In 1977 Egypt and Israel had fought four wars in less than thirty years. No Arab leader recognized Israel, and talks on a Middle East settlement were stuck in procedural arguments.

On 9 November 1977, in a speech to the Egyptian parliament, President Anwar Sadat said that he was ready to go to the ends of the earth for peace, even to the Knesset in Jerusalem. Many listeners took it as rhetoric. Israel's prime minister, Menachem Begin, responded with an official invitation. Ten days later, on 19 November, Sadat's plane landed at Ben Gurion airport, and the next day he addressed the Knesset. He did not soften his demands: Israeli withdrawal from the occupied territories and a solution for the Palestinians. But by coming in person he broke the taboo of direct recognition and changed the atmosphere completely.

Negotiations that followed were difficult and nearly failed. In September 1978 President Jimmy Carter brought Sadat and Begin to Camp David for thirteen days of talks, which produced the Camp David Accords. On 26 March 1979 Egypt and Israel signed a peace treaty, and Israel returned the Sinai Peninsula to Egypt in stages. Sadat and Begin shared the Nobel Peace Prize for 1978.

The gamble cost Sadat dearly in the Arab world. Egypt was suspended from the Arab League, and in October 1981 Sadat was assassinated by Islamist officers. The peace between Egypt and Israel has held.
lesson: A bold, personal gesture can break a deadlock that years of procedure could not. Be prepared to pay a price for it, and keep your substantive demands clear.
people: Anwar Sadat, Menachem Begin, Jimmy Carter
source: Sadat's speech to the Knesset (20 November 1977); Jimmy Carter, Keeping Faith (1982); Lawrence Wright, Thirteen Days in September (2014)

title: The Phone Call and the Photograph
text:
In 1977 Mark Snyder, Elizabeth Tanke and Ellen Berscheid of the University of Minnesota asked pairs of male and female students, who had never met, to get acquainted in a ten-minute phone conversation. Before the call, each man was handed a snapshot that he believed showed his partner. In fact the photo was of someone else, chosen to be either very attractive or quite unattractive. The women did not know about any photo.

Before talking, the men who expected an attractive partner predicted she would be sociable, poised, humorous and socially adept, while those who expected an unattractive partner predicted the opposite. Then the conversations were recorded.

Independent judges later listened only to the women's half of each conversation, knowing nothing about the photographs. They rated the women whose partners believed they were attractive as more friendly, likable and sociable, and as enjoying themselves more. The men who thought they were talking with a beauty had been warmer and more engaging, and the women had responded in kind. The men's belief had created the very behavior it expected. The researchers called it a self-fulfilling stereotype: our expectations of people can draw out of them the behavior that seems to confirm those expectations.
lesson: How you expect someone to be shapes how you treat them, and they respond in kind. Approach people expecting the best, and you will often see it.
people: Mark Snyder, Elizabeth Tanke, Ellen Berscheid
source: Snyder, M., Tanke, E. D., and Berscheid, E. (1977). Social perception and interpersonal behavior: On the self-fulfilling nature of social stereotypes. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 35(9), 656-666.

title: The Strange Situation
text:
Mary Ainsworth had watched mothers and babies at home, first in Uganda and then in Baltimore, taking careful notes on how mothers responded to crying, feeding and play. To compare children more systematically, she and her colleagues designed a short laboratory procedure for one-year-olds that became known as the Strange Situation.

A mother and her baby entered a playroom full of toys. A friendly stranger came in. Then the mother left for a few minutes, came back, left again, and returned once more. The researchers paid special attention not to how much the baby cried when she left, but to what happened when she came back.

Most babies, whom Ainsworth called securely attached, protested or missed their mother, greeted her warmly on her return, were soothed quickly and went back to play. Others seemed indifferent and avoided her when she returned. A third group was clingy and angry at once, seeking the mother yet resisting comfort. Later researchers added a fourth, disorganized pattern.

The home observations mattered most. Mothers who had responded sensitively and promptly to their babies' signals during the first year tended to have securely attached children. The babies had learned, from hundreds of small moments, whether care could be counted on.
lesson: A child's confidence is built from many ordinary moments in which you notice and respond. How you return after an absence matters as much as how you leave.
people: Mary Ainsworth, Mary Blehar, Everett Waters, Sally Wall
source: Ainsworth, M. D. S., Blehar, M. C., Waters, E., and Wall, S. (1978). Patterns of Attachment: A Psychological Study of the Strange Situation. Hillsdale, NJ: Erlbaum.

title: Lottery Winners and Accident Victims
text:
In the 1970s Philip Brickman, Dan Coates and Ronnie Janoff-Bulman interviewed three groups of people in Illinois. The first were recent winners of large prizes in the state lottery, sums ranging from fifty thousand dollars to a million. The second were people who had been paralyzed in accidents within the past year. The third were neighbors of the lottery winners, chosen as a comparison group.

All were asked how happy they were now, how happy they had been before, and how happy they expected to be in a couple of years. They also rated how much pleasure they got from everyday things, such as talking with a friend, watching television, eating breakfast, hearing a funny joke or getting a compliment.

The lottery winners were not significantly happier than the comparison group. And they took noticeably less pleasure in ordinary daily activities. The researchers suggested two reasons: once winning became the new standard, everyday pleasures looked smaller, and the thrill of the win itself faded with time. The accident victims rated their current happiness lower than the others, but still above the midpoint of the scale, higher than many people would have predicted.

The study became a classic illustration of hedonic adaptation: people adjust to good and bad fortune, returning to something near their usual level of happiness more than they expect. Later, larger studies found that some events, such as severe disability, do leave lasting effects, so adaptation is strong but not complete.
lesson: Do not bet your happiness on one big change, good or bad. People adapt to windfalls and to misfortune more than they expect, while daily pleasures and relationships keep mattering.
people: Philip Brickman, Dan Coates, Ronnie Janoff-Bulman
source: Brickman, P., Coates, D., and Janoff-Bulman, R. (1978). Lottery winners and accident victims: Is happiness relative? Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 36(8), 917-927.
caveat: The samples were small (a few dozen people per group), and later large studies found that adaptation to severe disability is often incomplete.

title: May I Use the Copier, Because...
text:
In the 1970s, the psychologist Ellen Langer and her colleagues Arthur Blank and Benzion Chanowitz ran a quiet experiment at a library copy machine at the City University of New York. A researcher waited until someone was about to make copies, then asked to cut in line. The wording was varied.

With a plain request ("Excuse me, I have five pages. May I use the Xerox machine?"), about 60 percent of people let the researcher go first. With a real reason ("because I'm in a rush"), about 94 percent agreed. The surprise came with a reason that contained no information at all: "May I use the Xerox machine, because I have to make copies?" Of course she had to make copies. Yet about 93 percent agreed, almost exactly as many as with the real reason.

The trick worked only when the stakes were small. When the researcher asked to copy twenty pages, the empty reason helped no more than no reason, while the real reason still did. Langer argued that for small requests people respond to the familiar shape of a request with "because" and do not really process what follows. When the cost goes up, they start paying attention.
lesson: Giving a reason makes people far more willing to help. For anything that matters, make it a real reason, since people stop accepting empty ones when the cost goes up.
people: Ellen Langer, Arthur Blank, Benzion Chanowitz
location: City University of New York, New York, USA
source: Langer, E., Blank, A., and Chanowitz, B. (1978). The mindlessness of ostensibly thoughtful action: The role of 'placebic' information in interpersonal interaction. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 36(6), 635-642.

title: The Still Face
text:
In the 1970s, the developmental psychologist Edward Tronick and his colleagues in Boston filmed young infants, only a few months old, playing face to face with their mothers. The mothers smiled, cooed and responded, and the babies smiled and babbled back in a kind of conversation.

Then the researchers asked the mothers to do something simple but hard: to keep facing the baby while holding their face completely still and expressionless, not responding to anything the baby did.

The babies noticed almost at once. They tried to get the conversation going again, smiling, cooing and reaching toward the mother. When that failed, they grew wary. Many turned away, slumped, lost control of their posture or began to cry. Some kept glancing back, as if checking whether the mother had returned. When the mothers resumed normal play, most babies recovered, though often with some lingering protest.

The still face procedure has since been repeated in many laboratories and cultures. It showed that even very young infants are not passive receivers of care. They actively take part in social exchanges, expect a response, and are thrown off balance when the person they rely on goes emotionally blank.
lesson: Being physically present is not the same as being there. A child, or anyone close to you, reads your face and feels it when you stop responding.
people: Edward Tronick, Heidelise Als, Lauren Adamson, Susan Wise, T. Berry Brazelton
location: Children's Hospital Medical Center and Harvard Medical School, Boston, USA
source: Tronick, E., Als, H., Adamson, L., Wise, S., and Brazelton, T. B. (1978). The infant's response to entrapment between contradictory messages in face-to-face interaction. Journal of the American Academy of Child Psychiatry, 17(1), 1-13.

title: United 173 Runs Out of Fuel
text:
On the evening of 28 December 1978, United Airlines Flight 173, a DC-8 with 189 people on board, was approaching Portland, Oregon. When the crew lowered the landing gear there was a loud thump and one of the indicator lights did not show that the gear was down and locked.

Captain Malburn McBroom put the plane into a holding pattern to work the problem and prepare the cabin for a possible emergency landing. For about an hour the crew circled near the airport. During that time the flight engineer and the first officer each mentioned the fuel situation, but in hesitant terms, and the captain remained absorbed in the landing gear and the cabin preparations. Neither pressed him forcefully, and he did not act on what they said.

At about 6:06 p.m. the engines began to flame out from fuel exhaustion. The plane came down in a wooded suburban area several miles short of the runway. Ten people died, including the flight engineer, and many more were injured. The landing gear, it turned out, had been down all along.

The National Transportation Safety Board found that the probable cause was the captain's failure to monitor the fuel and to respond to the crew's advisories, and that the other crew members had failed to make their concern clear. It recommended training that would teach crews to work together and speak up. United responded by building one of the first crew resource management programs in the industry.
lesson: Hinting at a danger is not the same as raising it. If you see the team heading for trouble, say so plainly and make sure the leader has heard you.
people: Malburn McBroom and the crew of United Airlines Flight 173
source: National Transportation Safety Board, Aircraft Accident Report NTSB-AAR-79-7 (1979)

title: Alameda County's Social Ties
text:
In 1965 researchers surveyed a large random sample of adults in Alameda County, California, the area around Oakland and Berkeley. Among many questions about health and habits, they asked about people's social lives: whether they were married, how many close friends and relatives they had and how often they saw them, whether they belonged to a church, and whether they took part in other groups.

Lisa Berkman and S. Leonard Syme of the University of California, Berkeley, then followed nearly seven thousand of these people for nine years, using death records to see who had died. They combined the answers into a social network index.

The people with the fewest social ties died at roughly two to three times the rate of those with the most ties, in every age group and for both men and women. The difference did not disappear when the researchers accounted for health status at the start of the study, income, smoking, drinking, weight and physical activity. Each kind of tie helped, and close ties such as marriage and friends mattered more than church or group membership, but different ties could partly make up for one another. This was one of the first large studies to show that social isolation itself is a risk to life.
lesson: Isolation is a health risk in its own right. Keeping several kinds of ties alive (family, friends and groups) protects you in ways diet and exercise alone cannot.
people: Lisa Berkman, S. Leonard Syme
source: Berkman, L. F., and Syme, S. L. (1979). Social networks, host resistance, and mortality: A nine-year follow-up study of Alameda County residents. American Journal of Epidemiology, 109(2), 186-204.
caveat: As an observational study, it shows a strong association but cannot by itself prove that social ties cause longer life.

title: Iacocca Takes a One-Dollar Salary
text:
In 1978 Henry Ford II fired Lee Iacocca as president of Ford. Within months Iacocca was running Chrysler, then the third-largest American carmaker, and he soon discovered it was close to bankruptcy. It was losing hundreds of millions of dollars, its cars were selling poorly, and its management was in disarray.

In 1979 Iacocca asked the federal government for loan guarantees, a highly controversial request. He also needed to ask suppliers, banks, the United Auto Workers union and Chrysler's own managers to accept painful cuts.

To make that request credible, he cut his own salary to one dollar a year. He wrote in his autobiography that he called it "equality of sacrifice": he could not ask others to give up money unless he went first. Senior executives took pay cuts, and the union accepted concessions in wages and benefits.

Congress passed the Chrysler loan guarantee act at the end of 1979, backing 1.5 billion dollars in loans. Chrysler launched new compact cars, returned to profit, and in 1983 repaid the guaranteed loans years ahead of schedule. Iacocca became one of the most famous businessmen in America.
lesson: If you need others to sacrifice, go first and make it visible. Shared hardship is accepted; imposed hardship is resented.
people: Lee Iacocca, Chrysler
source: Lee Iacocca, Iacocca: An Autobiography (1984); contemporary press reports
caveat: Iacocca also received large stock options, which later made him very rich, so his sacrifice was less total than the one-dollar figure suggests.

title: Prospect Theory: Why Losses Hurt More
text:
Classical economics assumed that people weigh choices by how much total wealth each option leaves them with. In the 1970s Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky tested that assumption with simple questions put to students and university staff, asking people to choose between sure things and gambles.

The answers showed a striking pattern. Offered a sure gain or a gamble with the same expected value, most people took the sure gain. But when the same choice was turned into losses, a sure loss against a gamble that might lose more or nothing at all, most people took the gamble. They were cautious when winning and willing to take risks to avoid losing.

Kahneman and Tversky concluded that people do not judge outcomes by final wealth. They judge them as gains or losses from a reference point, usually where they stand now or where they expected to be. And losses loom larger than gains: losing a sum of money hurts more than winning the same sum pleases. They also found that people overweight small probabilities and underweight outcomes that are merely probable compared with ones that are certain.

They published the model as prospect theory in Econometrica in 1979. It became one of the most cited papers in economics and the backbone of behavioral economics. In 2002 Kahneman received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for this work; Tversky had died in 1996.
lesson: When a choice feels painful, ask whether you are judging it against an arbitrary reference point. Taking big risks just to avoid admitting a small loss is often how a small loss becomes a large one.
people: Daniel Kahneman, Amos Tversky
location: Israel, Sweden and USA (student and faculty respondents)
source: Kahneman, D., and Tversky, A. (1979). Prospect theory: An analysis of decision under risk. Econometrica, 47(2), 263-291.

title: Many Hands Make Light the Work
text:
In the late 1970s, Bibb Latane, Kipling Williams and Stephen Harkins at Ohio State University asked students to make as much noise as they could. Wearing blindfolds and headphones that played loud noise, the students shouted or clapped alone, in pairs and in groups of six, while a meter measured the sound.

As in Ringelmann's rope experiment, groups produced less noise per person than individuals did. To check whether this was just sound waves cancelling or people getting in each other's way, the researchers added pseudo-groups. Participants believed others were shouting with them, but they were actually alone. Even so, each person shouted less when they thought others were joining in, and the more others they imagined, the less they put in.

The authors named this social loafing and compared it to a disease that weakens groups. In follow-up studies, the same team found a remedy. When people were told their individual output could be measured and identified, the loafing largely disappeared, even though they were still working in a group.
lesson: People ease off when their contribution disappears into the total. Make each person's part visible and recognizable, and effort comes back.
people: Bibb Latane, Kipling Williams, Stephen Harkins
source: Latane, B., Williams, K., and Harkins, S. (1979). Many hands make light the work: The causes and consequences of social loafing. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 37(6), 822-832.

title: Same Evidence, Stronger Beliefs
text:
In the late 1970s, Charles Lord, Lee Ross and Mark Lepper at Stanford University recruited students with strong opinions on capital punishment. Half believed the death penalty deterred murder; half believed it did not.

Each student read about two studies. One seemed to show that the death penalty deterred crime, comparing murder rates in states before and after it was adopted, or in neighboring states with and without it. The other seemed to show the opposite. The studies were invented by the researchers, and the methods were swapped between versions, so that each design supported deterrence for some readers and opposed it for others.

The students judged the study that supported their own view to be more convincing and better done. They picked apart the methods of the opposing study, finding flaws they ignored in the one they liked. And after reading the same mixed evidence, both groups reported that their original views had grown stronger. Instead of moving toward each other, the two sides moved further apart.

The researchers called this biased assimilation and attitude polarization. Later attempts to reproduce the polarization part, measured more directly, have found it weaker and less consistent, but the tendency to judge evidence by whether it agrees with us has been confirmed many times.
lesson: When you read research or news on a question you care about, apply the same standard to evidence you like and evidence you dislike. If you only find flaws on one side, that is a warning sign.
people: Charles Lord, Lee Ross, Mark Lepper
source: Lord, C. G., Ross, L., and Lepper, M. R. (1979). Biased assimilation and attitude polarization: The effects of prior theories on subsequently considered evidence. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 37(11), 2098-2109.
caveat: The polarization result relied on self-reported change in attitudes, and later studies measuring it directly found it weaker than the biased evaluation of evidence.

title: Who Does More of the Housework?
text:
In 1979 Michael Ross and Fiore Sicoly of the University of Waterloo in Canada asked married couples a simple set of questions, with each spouse answering separately. For a list of everyday activities, such as making breakfast, cleaning the house, shopping for groceries and caring for the children, each person estimated what share of the responsibility was theirs.

When the researchers added up the two spouses' estimates, the totals usually came to more than 100 percent. Each partner tended to believe they did more than their partner thought they did. This was true not only for pleasant or admirable contributions but also for negative ones, such as causing arguments. That suggested the bias was not just self-flattery.

Ross and Sicoly also asked people to recall specific examples of their own and their partner's contributions. Those who could remember more of their own contributions claimed a larger share. They argued that the root of the problem is memory. We witness every one of our own efforts, while we see only some of our partner's, and our own are easier to recall. Similar patterns appeared in other groups, including basketball players, whose memories of a game favored their own team's actions.
lesson: You probably notice your own contributions far more than other people's. Before arguing about who does more, assume you are missing some of what the other person does.
people: Michael Ross, Fiore Sicoly
source: Ross, M., and Sicoly, F. (1979). Egocentric biases in availability and attribution. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 37(3), 322-336.

title: Steve Jobs Visits Xerox PARC
text:
In the 1970s Xerox's Palo Alto Research Center, known as PARC, invented much of modern computing. Its researchers built the Alto, a personal computer with a graphical screen, windows, icons and a mouse, linked by Ethernet and printing on laser printers. Xerox headquarters, focused on copiers, struggled to see what to do with it.

In late 1979 Xerox's venture arm was allowed to invest in Apple before its stock offering. As part of the arrangement, Steve Jobs and a group of Apple engineers visited PARC and were shown the Alto and the Smalltalk environment. Some PARC researchers objected strongly to the demonstration. Jobs, by his own and others' accounts, was electrified by the graphical interface and returned to Apple convinced that this was the future of computing.

Apple hired several PARC people and built the ideas into the Lisa, released in 1983, and the Macintosh, in 1984, making them cheaper and simpler and adding its own inventions. Xerox did bring out a commercial machine, the Star, in 1981, but it was expensive, sold to offices and never caught on. The graphical interface that Xerox had invented became the basis of Apple's, and later Microsoft's, fortunes.
lesson: An invention is only as valuable as the vision for using it. Make sure the people who decide can see what your best ideas are good for.
people: Steve Jobs, Larry Tesler, Adele Goldberg, Xerox PARC
source: Michael Hiltzik, Dealers of Lightning (1999); Douglas K. Smith and Robert C. Alexander, Fumbling the Future (1988)
caveat: Accounts differ on how many visits there were and what exactly was shown, and Apple's interface work had begun before the visit.

title: Microsoft Keeps the Rights to DOS
text:
In 1980 IBM decided to enter the personal computer market quickly, using parts bought from outside suppliers. It approached a small company called Microsoft, run by Bill Gates and Paul Allen, for programming languages, and then also needed an operating system.

Microsoft did not have one. It obtained a system called 86-DOS from Seattle Computer Products, written by Tim Paterson, first under license and then outright, and adapted it for IBM. The crucial point was in the contract. Microsoft licensed the system to IBM, which shipped it as PC DOS, but did not sell it outright and kept the right to license it to other computer makers as MS-DOS.

IBM launched the PC in August 1981, and it quickly became the business standard. Because IBM had used off-the-shelf parts, other companies such as Compaq soon built compatible machines. Each of them needed an operating system that ran the same software, and they bought it from Microsoft. As the clone market grew, Microsoft's revenue grew with every machine sold by IBM's competitors, while IBM's own share of the market it had created steadily shrank. The operating system, not the hardware, became the center of the industry, and Microsoft became one of the most valuable companies in the world.
lesson: In any deal, look beyond the first payment to the rights you keep. A non-exclusive license can be worth far more than the sale itself.
people: Bill Gates, Paul Allen, Tim Paterson, IBM
location: Boca Raton, Florida, and Seattle, Washington (USA)
source: Paul Allen, Idea Man (2011); Paul Freiberger and Michael Swaine, Fire in the Valley

title: The Miracle on Ice
text:
In 1980 the Soviet Union had won the Olympic ice hockey gold four times running. Its players were seasoned professionals in all but name. The United States sent a team of college players and amateurs, picked and coached by Herb Brooks of the University of Minnesota. Many of them came from rival programs in Minnesota and Boston who had spent years fighting each other.

Brooks drove them hard and chose players for how they fit together, not just for talent. After a sloppy exhibition tie in Norway he kept them on the ice after the game, skating sprints from line to line until they could barely stand, to make them play for the team rather than for themselves. He gave them a fast, passing style borrowed partly from European hockey.

Two weeks before the Games, the Soviets beat the Americans 10 to 3 in an exhibition at Madison Square Garden. Then, on 22 February at Lake Placid, the two teams met in the medal round. The Soviets led three times. The Americans tied it each time, and midway through the third period captain Mike Eruzione scored to make it 4 to 3. Goalie Jim Craig held on for the last ten minutes under heavy pressure. As time ran out, broadcaster Al Michaels shouted, "Do you believe in miracles? Yes!"

Two days later the team came from behind again to beat Finland and win the gold medal.
lesson: A group chosen and trained to play for each other can beat a group of stronger individuals. Building the team is often worth more than collecting the stars.
people: Herb Brooks, Mike Eruzione, Jim Craig, the 1980 US Olympic hockey team
source: Contemporary reports; Wayne Coffey, The Boys of Winter (2005)

title: Solidarity at the Gdansk Shipyard
text:
In August 1980 the management of the Lenin Shipyard in Gdansk fired Anna Walentynowicz, a crane operator and independent union activist, a few months before she was due to retire. On 14 August the workers went on strike to demand her reinstatement and a pay rise. Lech Walesa, an electrician who had himself been fired for activism, climbed over the shipyard wall to join them and became the strike's leader.

Within two days management offered to meet the shipyard's demands, and Walesa announced that the strike was over. But workers from other factories and transport depots had walked out in support, and they feared they would be abandoned. Walentynowicz, Alina Pienkowska and other activists went to the gates and urged the shipyard workers to stay. Walesa reversed himself, and the strike continued as a solidarity strike.

Delegates from hundreds of workplaces formed an inter-factory strike committee in the shipyard and drew up a list of twenty-one demands, starting with the right to form free trade unions independent of the Communist Party. The gates were hung with flowers and pictures of the Pope, and the world's press gathered outside.

On 31 August the government signed the Gdansk Agreement, accepting independent unions for the first time in the Soviet bloc. Within months the new union, Solidarity, had about ten million members. It was banned under martial law in December 1981, but it survived underground and returned to lead Poland's peaceful transition in 1989.
lesson: A group is strongest when its members refuse to settle alone. Standing by the people who stood by you turns a local dispute into a movement.
people: Lech Walesa, Anna Walentynowicz, Alina Pienkowska, Gdansk shipyard workers
source: Gdansk Agreement (31 August 1980); Timothy Garton Ash, The Polish Revolution: Solidarity (1983)

title: Three Monks Have No Water to Drink
text:
A Chinese saying runs: one monk carries water by himself, two monks carry water together, three monks have no water to drink. The story behind it goes like this.

A young monk lived alone in a small temple on a hill. Each day he carried two buckets on a shoulder pole down to the river and back, filled the water jar, and tended the temple. Then a second monk arrived. Neither wanted to do more than the other, so they carried a single bucket between them, the pole across both their shoulders, each making sure the bucket hung exactly in the middle.

Then a third monk came. Now nobody would go. Each waited for one of the others, and each thought the job belonged to someone else. The water jar sat empty, and the three monks grew thirsty and sullen, reading their scriptures and ignoring one another.

In the well-known Chinese animated film of 1980 based on the saying, a mouse knocks over a candle one night and the temple catches fire. The three monks run for buckets, form a chain and put the fire out together. Afterward they build a pulley so the water comes up the hill with no argument over who carries it.
lesson: When a task belongs to everyone, it can end up belonging to no one. Assign clear responsibility, or design the work so that sharing it is natural.
people: Three monks
source: Chinese folk proverb; Three Monks (San ge heshang), Shanghai Animation Film Studio, 1980
caveat: The proverb is traditional, while the fire and the pulley come from the 1980 film version.

title: The Tit for Tat Tournament
text:
In the prisoner's dilemma, two players each choose to cooperate or defect. Each does better by defecting whatever the other does, yet if both defect, both end up worse off than if both had cooperated. When the game is played over and over by the same pair, what strategy works best?

Around 1980 the political scientist Robert Axelrod of the University of Michigan invited game theorists, economists, psychologists and computer scientists to submit computer programs that would play repeated prisoner's dilemmas against each other in a round-robin tournament. Fourteen strategies were entered in the first round, some of them elaborate. The winner was the shortest: Tit for Tat, submitted by the psychologist Anatol Rapoport. It cooperated on the first move and from then on simply copied whatever the other player had done on the previous move.

Axelrod published the results and ran a second tournament. This time 62 entries arrived, many designed specifically to beat Tit for Tat. It won again.

Analyzing the results, Axelrod identified what successful strategies had in common. They were nice, never the first to defect. They retaliated, so they could not be exploited. They were forgiving, returning to cooperation as soon as the other did. And they were clear, so others could quickly learn that cooperation paid. In a 1981 paper in Science with the biologist William Hamilton, he showed how such cooperation could evolve even among self-interested players, provided they were likely to meet again.
lesson: In long-term relationships, start by cooperating, respond firmly to bad faith, forgive quickly when the other side changes course, and be predictable so people know where they stand.
people: Robert Axelrod, William Hamilton, Anatol Rapoport
location: University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, USA
source: Axelrod, R., and Hamilton, W. D. (1981). The evolution of cooperation. Science, 211(4489), 1390-1396. Tournaments reported in Axelrod, R. (1980). Effective choice in the prisoner's dilemma. Journal of Conflict Resolution, 24(1), 3-25.
caveat: Later simulations with noise and errors found that more forgiving variants (such as Generous Tit for Tat) can do better than strict Tit for Tat.

title: Elaine's Electric Shocks
text:
Do people ever help purely for the sake of the other person, or always, in the end, to ease their own discomfort? In 1981 C. Daniel Batson and his colleagues at the University of Kansas designed an experiment to test this.

Female students watched, over what they believed was closed-circuit television, as another young woman named Elaine took part in a learning task in which she received mild electric shocks. In fact Elaine was a confederate and the scene was recorded. As the trials went on, Elaine reacted badly and explained that she had had a frightening experience with electricity as a child. The experimenter then asked the observer whether she would be willing to take Elaine's place for the rest of the session.

Two things were varied. Some observers were led to feel strong empathy for Elaine, for example by learning that she shared their values and interests. And some were told they could leave after watching just two trials, while others would have to watch all ten. If people helped only to escape the distress of watching, the easy exit should have reduced helping. That is what happened among low-empathy observers. But high-empathy observers offered to trade places at high rates even when they could easily have walked away.
lesson: Real empathy moves people to help even when looking away would be easier. Taking time to understand someone's situation is often the first step to caring for them.
people: C. Daniel Batson, Bruce Duncan, Paula Ackerman, Terese Buckley, Kimberly Birch
source: Batson, C. D., Duncan, B. D., Ackerman, P., Buckley, T., and Birch, K. (1981). Is empathic emotion a source of altruistic motivation? Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 40(2), 290-302.

title: When Arguments Matter
text:
In 1981 Richard Petty, John Cacioppo and Rachel Goldman tested when people are persuaded by good arguments and when they are persuaded by who is speaking. Their participants were students at the University of Missouri, who listened to a recorded message arguing that seniors should have to pass a comprehensive exam in their major in order to graduate.

Three things were varied. For some students, the message said the new exam policy would start the next year at their own university, so it would affect them directly. For others, it would start only in ten years, long after they had left. The arguments were either strong, backed by facts and figures, or weak, based on personal opinion and anecdotes. And the speaker was presented either as an expert, a commission on higher education chaired by a Princeton professor, or as a local high school class.

Students for whom the issue mattered personally were persuaded by strong arguments and unmoved by weak ones, almost regardless of who made them. Students for whom the issue was distant were swayed mostly by the prestige of the source and paid much less attention to the arguments. This became central evidence for the elaboration likelihood model, which holds that people think carefully about a message only when they are motivated and able to.
lesson: When the matter affects them, people judge the argument; when it does not, they judge the speaker. Make your case strong for those who care, and credible for those who do not.
people: Richard Petty, John Cacioppo, Rachel Goldman
source: Petty, R. E., Cacioppo, J. T., and Goldman, R. (1981). Personal involvement as a determinant of argument-based persuasion. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 41(5), 847-855.

title: Better Than Average Drivers
text:
In a short study published in 1981, the Swedish psychologist Ola Svenson asked groups of students in the United States and in Sweden a simple question: compared with the other people in this room, how skillful and how safe a driver are you?

Participants placed themselves on a scale by percentage, from the least skilled to the most skilled in the group. By definition, only half of any group can be above the median. Yet in the American group about 93 percent rated themselves as more skillful than the median driver, and about 88 percent rated themselves as safer. The Swedish students were more modest but still far from the logical limit: around 69 percent rated their skill above the median, and about 77 percent their safety.

The result became one of the best known illustrations of the better-than-average effect, a form of overconfidence in which most people believe they are above average in abilities they value. Later studies found similar patterns for many skills and traits, from getting along with others to ethics. They also found the effect is strongest for vague, self-defined qualities, where each person can define "good driving" in terms of what they happen to do well, and weaker for concrete, measurable skills.

Svenson noted that such self-assessments can make people feel less need for caution than their actual driving warrants.
lesson: If you feel sure you are better than most at something, look for objective feedback before relying on that feeling, especially where an error can hurt you or others.
people: Ola Svenson
source: Svenson, O. (1981). Are we all less risky and more skillful than our fellow drivers? Acta Psychologica, 47(2), 143-148.
caveat: The sample was small (students only), though the better-than-average effect has been found widely since.

title: An Apple Today or Two Tomorrow
text:
In 1981 the economist Richard Thaler published a short paper on a puzzle in how people value time. Standard economic theory assumed people discount future rewards at a steady rate: if waiting a month is worth a certain premium, waiting a year should be worth proportionally more, and preferences should not change as dates approach.

Thaler illustrated the problem with apples. Many people would prefer one apple today to two apples tomorrow. But almost nobody would prefer one apple in a year to two apples in a year and a day. The extra day of waiting is the same in both cases, yet it feels very different when it starts now.

He then asked students in the United States how much money they would need to receive later to make them indifferent to receiving 15 dollars right away. The typical answers were about 20 dollars in a month, 50 dollars in a year and 100 dollars in ten years. Converted to yearly interest rates, those answers imply enormous discounting over short delays and far milder discounting over long ones. Similar patterns appeared for larger sums and for losses, though people discounted large amounts and losses less steeply.

This pattern, later known as present bias or hyperbolic discounting, means that plans made in advance tend to unravel. From a distance, people choose patience; when the moment arrives, the immediate reward suddenly looms larger.
lesson: Your future self will feel the pull of the present more than you expect. Make important commitments in advance and remove easy chances to back out when the moment comes.
people: Richard Thaler
source: Thaler, R. (1981). Some empirical evidence on dynamic inconsistency. Economics Letters, 8(3), 201-207.

title: The Asian Disease Problem
text:
In a 1981 paper, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman asked university students in the United States and Canada to imagine that the country was preparing for an unusual disease expected to kill 600 people. Two programs had been proposed to fight it.

One group read the options in terms of lives saved. With Program A, 200 people would be saved. With Program B, there was a one-third chance that all 600 would be saved and a two-thirds chance that nobody would be saved. About 72 percent chose the sure option, Program A.

A second group read the same options described in terms of deaths. With Program C, 400 people would die. With Program D, there was a one-third chance that nobody would die and a two-thirds chance that all 600 would die. Now about 78 percent chose the gamble, Program D.

Programs A and C were identical, as were B and D. Only the wording had changed, from saving to dying. Yet the majority preference reversed. When the outcome was framed as a gain, people avoided risk; when it was framed as a loss, they embraced it. Tversky and Kahneman called this the framing effect and showed that it appeared even among people who, when shown both versions, agreed they ought to give the same answer. The finding has been replicated many times and is now a staple of decision research.
lesson: Before a decision, restate the options the other way around: as gains and as losses. If your preference flips, the wording, not the substance, was doing the choosing.
people: Amos Tversky, Daniel Kahneman
location: Stanford University, USA, and University of British Columbia, Canada
source: Tversky, A., and Kahneman, D. (1981). The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice. Science, 211(4481), 453-458.

title: Corinthian Democracy
text:
In the early 1980s Brazil was still ruled by a military government, and football clubs were run in an authoritarian way too. Players were often locked up in hotels for days before matches, a practice called concentracao, and had little say in their own lives.

In 1981 Corinthians, one of Sao Paulo's biggest clubs, was in trouble. A new club president appointed a young sociologist, Adilson Monteiro Alves, as director of football. With the team's leading players, especially the midfielder Socrates, a qualified doctor, the left back Wladimir and the young striker Casagrande, he began to share decisions. Everyone at the club, from the star players to the kit men, had one vote on questions such as training times, travel, signings and whether players should be confined before games. Concentracao was dropped for married players and became optional.

The team played freely and won. Corinthians took the Sao Paulo state championship in 1982 and 1983. Players wore shirts with the words Democracia Corinthiana, and before Brazil's 1982 elections they urged fans to vote. For the 1983 final the team walked out behind a banner reading "Win or lose, but always with democracy."

The experiment faded after 1984. Socrates had promised to stay in Brazil if Congress approved direct presidential elections; when the amendment failed, he left for Italy. But the movement became a symbol of Brazil's return to democracy, which came in 1985.
lesson: A team that decides together can be both freer and more successful. Giving people a real voice in their work often raises their commitment to it.
people: Socrates, Wladimir, Walter Casagrande, Adilson Monteiro Alves
source: Brazilian press reports; Socrates and Ricardo Gozzi, Democracia Corintiana: a utopia em jogo (2002)

title: Pygmalion Goes to Boot Camp
text:
In the early 1980s the organizational psychologist Dov Eden and his colleague Abraham Shani ran a field experiment in an Israel Defense Forces combat command course. Trainees were going through a fifteen week program, and four instructors were responsible for them.

Before the course began, the instructors were told that, based on test scores, ratings from earlier courses and evaluations, each trainee had been rated as having high, regular or unknown command potential. In fact the labels had been assigned at random. The trainees themselves were not told.

At the end of the course, the trainees labeled as high potential scored clearly higher on objective achievement tests in subjects such as combat tactics and navigation. They also reported more positive attitudes toward the course and a stronger wish to go on to further training. Their ratings of their instructors showed why: the instructors had, without realizing it, led them differently.

Eden and Shani concluded that a leader's expectations alone could change how much people learned and achieved. Eden spent much of his later career showing similar effects in other workplaces.
lesson: People tend to rise or sink to what their leader expects of them. Show genuine belief in your team's ability, and back it with real support and challenge.
people: Dov Eden, Abraham Shani
location: Israel Defense Forces training base, Israel
source: Eden, D., and Shani, A. B. (1982). Pygmalion goes to boot camp: Expectancy, leadership, and trainee performance. Journal of Applied Psychology, 67(2), 194-199.

title: The Ultimatum Game
text:
In 1982 the German economists Werner Guth, Rolf Schmittberger and Bernd Schwarze published an experiment that became one of the most studied games in economics.

Students at the University of Cologne were paired anonymously. One, the proposer, was given a sum of money and had to offer some share of it to the other, the responder. The responder could accept, and the money was divided as proposed, or reject, and then neither got anything. There was no negotiation and no second round.

Standard economic theory gives a clear answer. A responder who only cares about money should accept any offer above zero, since something beats nothing. Knowing this, a proposer should offer the smallest possible amount. That is not what happened. The most common offer was an even split, and many offers were close to it. And responders did reject low offers, giving up real money to deny the proposer an unfair gain. A week later, when the same students played again, behavior moved somewhat toward the theory, but fairness still mattered.

The ultimatum game has since been played thousands of times around the world, with higher stakes, in many cultures and in small-scale societies. Average offers vary between cultures, but the basic pattern holds nearly everywhere: people punish offers they see as unfair, and proposers who anticipate this offer more.
lesson: In any deal, the other side's sense of fairness is part of the math. An offer that is legally acceptable but feels insulting may cost you the whole agreement.
people: Werner Guth, Rolf Schmittberger, Bernd Schwarze
source: Guth, W., Schmittberger, R., and Schwarze, B. (1982). An experimental analysis of ultimatum bargaining. Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization, 3(4), 367-388.

title: The Decoy Option
text:
In 1982 Joel Huber, John Payne and Christopher Puto of Duke University published an experiment that challenged a basic assumption of choice theory: adding a new option to a menu should never increase the share of an option that was already there.

Students made choices between pairs of products in several categories, such as cars, restaurants, beers, lottery games and television sets. Each product was described on two attributes, for example a beer's price and its quality rating, or a car's mileage and its ride quality. In each pair, one option was better on one attribute and the other was better on the other, so there was a genuine trade-off.

Then the researchers added a third option, the decoy. It was designed to be clearly worse than one of the two original options, call it the target, on both attributes, while not clearly worse than the other. Almost nobody chose the decoy. But its presence changed choices between the other two: the target, the option that dominated the decoy, gained share. Next to an obviously inferior neighbor, it looked like the smart choice.

The authors called this the asymmetric dominance effect, now often called the decoy or attraction effect. It has been used in pricing ever since, as in a medium drink priced just below a large one. Some later studies found it weaker when options are shown in realistic formats, such as pictures, rather than numbers.
lesson: When one option looks clearly best, check whether it is only being compared with a deliberately weak alternative. Judge your top choices against each other, not against the filler.
people: Joel Huber, John Payne, Christopher Puto
location: Duke University, Durham, North Carolina, USA
source: Huber, J., Payne, J. W., and Puto, C. (1982). Adding asymmetrically dominated alternatives: Violations of regularity and the similarity hypothesis. Journal of Consumer Research, 9(1), 90-98.
caveat: Later studies (for example Frederick, Lee and Baskin, 2014) found the effect weaker or absent when options are presented perceptually rather than as numeric attributes.

title: The Coercion Trap
text:
At the Oregon Social Learning Center in Eugene, the psychologist Gerald Patterson and his colleagues spent years observing families of aggressive and hard-to-manage children, often in their own homes. Trained observers sat quietly in the living room and recorded, every few seconds, what each family member did and how the others responded.

Patterson saw the same sequence again and again. A parent asked a child to do something, like turning off the television. The child whined, argued or yelled. The parent, worn down, gave up. The child had just learned that being unpleasant works. But the parent had also learned something: giving in made the whining stop at once, which felt like relief.

The pattern could also run the other way. When the parent finally exploded and shouted, the child often complied, which taught the parent that yelling worked. Over thousands of such small exchanges, parent and child trained each other into longer and harsher conflicts. Patterson called it coercive family process and described it in a 1982 book of that name.

The insight was practical. His team developed parent management training, which teaches parents to give clear, calm instructions, follow through with mild and consistent consequences, and notice and reward good behavior. It became one of the best-supported treatments for children's conduct problems.
lesson: Giving in to whining and winning by yelling both teach bad habits. Calm, consistent follow-through and attention to good behavior break the cycle.
people: Gerald Patterson
location: Oregon Social Learning Center, Eugene, USA
source: Patterson, G. R. (1982). Coercive Family Process. Eugene, OR: Castalia.

title: Johnson and Johnson Pulls Tylenol
text:
In late September 1982 seven people in the Chicago area died after taking Extra-Strength Tylenol capsules. Someone had laced capsules with cyanide and put the bottles back on store shelves. Tylenol was then the best-selling painkiller in the United States, and the killer was never caught.

The company, led by chairman James Burke, did not know at first whether the poisoning had happened in its factories. It warned the public not to use Tylenol capsules, stopped advertising, worked openly with the police, the FBI and the press, and then recalled every bottle of Tylenol capsules in the country, around 31 million bottles, at a cost of about 100 million dollars. Burke appeared on television to explain what the company was doing. The poisoning turned out to have happened after the products left the factory.

Within weeks Johnson and Johnson reintroduced Tylenol in new triple-sealed, tamper-resistant packaging, and offered to swap capsules for tablets. Tylenol's market share collapsed after the deaths, but within about a year it had largely recovered. The response became a standard case in business schools.
lesson: In a crisis, protect the people who depend on you first and tell them the truth. Short-term cost spent on trust usually comes back.
people: James Burke, Johnson and Johnson
source: Contemporary press coverage; Harvard Business School case studies on the Tylenol crisis

title: The Children of Kauai
text:
In 1955, the psychologist Emmy Werner and her colleagues began a study of every child born that year on the Hawaiian island of Kauai, 698 in all. Most came from families of plantation workers of Japanese, Filipino, Hawaiian and other backgrounds. The researchers gathered information from before birth and then followed the children at ages one, two, ten and eighteen, and later into adulthood.

About a third of the children were considered at high risk. They had been born after a difficult pregnancy or birth and grew up in poverty, often with family conflict, divorce, or a parent with alcoholism or mental illness. Most of these children did develop serious learning or behavior problems by their teens.

But about one in three of the high-risk children did not. By eighteen they had grown into competent, caring young adults. Werner and Ruth Smith looked closely at what set them apart. These children tended to have easygoing temperaments that drew people to them. Above all, almost every one of them had at least one person who offered steady care and attention: a parent, a grandparent, an older sibling, an aunt, a teacher, or a neighbor.

Werner and Smith described the findings in the book Vulnerable but Invincible, and the study became a foundation of resilience research.
lesson: A single caring adult can change the course of a child's life. You may be that person for a child who is not your own.
people: Emmy Werner, Ruth Smith
source: Werner, E. E., and Smith, R. S. (1982). Vulnerable but Invincible: A Longitudinal Study of Resilient Children and Youth. New York: McGraw-Hill.

title: The Jar of Coins and the Winner's Curse
text:
In the early 1980s Max Bazerman and William Samuelson, then at Boston University, ran a simple auction in their MBA classes. They showed students a jar of coins, worth eight dollars, though the students did not know this, and auctioned it to the highest bidder. Students also wrote down their estimate of the jar's value. The procedure was repeated across many class sessions with jars of coins and of other small items.

On average, students underestimated the contents: the mean estimate was well below the true value. Yet the winning bids averaged above ten dollars.
