The winners lost money, around two dollars on average. The reason was not that the typical student overestimated. It was that the auction selected the person who had overestimated the most. Whoever won was, almost by definition, the bidder with the most optimistic error.

This phenomenon had been noticed in the 1970s by petroleum engineers, who saw oil companies winning drilling leases and then earning disappointing returns. They called it the winner's curse. Bazerman and Samuelson showed it in a controlled setting and found that it grew worse with more bidders and with more uncertainty about the value.

The title they chose captured the result: "I won the auction but don't want the prize."
lesson: When you win a bidding contest for something of uncertain value, ask why others valued it less. Bid as if winning means you were the most optimistic person in the room.
people: Max Bazerman, William Samuelson
source: Bazerman, M. H., and Samuelson, W. F. (1983). I won the auction but don't want the prize. Journal of Conflict Resolution, 27(4), 618-634.

title: John Paul II Visits the Man Who Shot Him
text:
On May 13, 1981, Pope John Paul II was riding through St. Peter's Square in Rome when a young Turkish gunman, Mehmet Ali Agca, fired at him. The Pope was hit in the abdomen and hand and lost a great deal of blood. He survived after hours of surgery. Agca was caught on the spot and sentenced to life imprisonment.

A few days after the shooting, from his hospital bed, the Pope asked people to pray for the brother who had shot him, whom he said he had sincerely forgiven.

On December 27, 1983, John Paul II went to Rebibbia prison in Rome and met Agca in his cell. Photographers recorded the two men sitting close together, the Pope holding Agca's hand as they spoke quietly for about twenty minutes. Afterward the Pope told reporters that what they had said would remain a secret between them, and that he had spoken to Agca as a brother he had pardoned.

The Pope kept in touch with Agca's family. In 2000 Italy pardoned Agca, with the Vatican's support, and sent him to Turkey to serve a sentence for an earlier murder.
lesson: Forgiveness is a choice that belongs to you, not to the person who hurt you. It can be offered without waiting for them to deserve it.
people: Pope John Paul II, Mehmet Ali Agca
source: Contemporary press reports and photographs of the prison visit (December 27 to 28, 1983); George Weigel, Witness to Hope (1999)

title: Dispensable Effort
text:
Social loafing research showed that people work less hard in groups. Norbert Kerr and Steven Bruun wanted to understand one reason why: people may hold back when they believe their effort will not change the group's result.

In their experiments, people worked in pairs or small groups on physically tiring tasks. The researchers varied the rule for how the group's score was calculated. Under one rule, the group's score was that of its best member, so only the strongest person really counted. Under another, the group's score was that of its weakest member, so the result depended on whoever did least well. Participants also learned how their ability compared with that of their partners.

Effort followed the rule closely. When the best member's score counted, the less able members, knowing their effort was unlikely to matter, reduced their effort. When the weakest member's score counted, it was the more able members who eased off, since the group's result would be limited by the weakest anyway. In each case, people slacked when they saw their own contribution as dispensable to the group's success.

Kerr and Bruun called these free-rider effects: people were not simply lazy but responding to whether their effort could actually make a difference.
lesson: People ease off when they think the result does not depend on them. Show each team member how their specific effort shapes the outcome.
people: Norbert Kerr, Steven Bruun
source: Kerr, N. L., and Bruun, S. E. (1983). Dispensability of member effort and group motivation losses: Free-rider effects. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 44(1), 78-94.

title: Stanislav Petrov Doubts the Alarm
text:
On the night of 26 September 1983, relations between the Soviet Union and the United States were at their worst in decades. Only weeks earlier the Soviets had shot down a Korean airliner. Lieutenant Colonel Stanislav Petrov was the duty officer at Serpukhov-15, a command center near Moscow that monitored the new Oko satellite system for warning of American missile launches.

Shortly after midnight the alarms went off. The system reported that a Minuteman missile had been launched from the United States, then more, up to five. The screens showed the warning in large letters. Petrov's task was to report to his superiors, who could then decide on a response within minutes.

Petrov judged that the alarm was probably false. He later explained his reasoning in interviews. An American first strike, he thought, would involve hundreds of missiles, not five. The satellite system was new and he did not fully trust it. And the ground radars, which would detect real missiles once they rose over the horizon, had shown nothing. He reported a system malfunction instead of an attack. Minutes passed, and no missiles arrived.

Investigation later showed that the satellites had mistaken sunlight reflecting off high clouds for the flare of rocket launches. Petrov received no reward at the time, and the incident remained secret until the 1990s, after which he was honored internationally.
lesson: Automated systems and alarms are tools, not oracles. When a signal does not fit what you know about the situation, check it before you act on it.
people: Stanislav Petrov
source: Stanislav Petrov's interviews (for example, BBC, 2013); David E. Hoffman, The Dead Hand (2009)
caveat: Some argue that Soviet procedure would have required further confirmation before any launch, so Petrov's call may not have been the only safeguard.

title: Why People Stay
text:
It seems obvious that people stay in relationships because they are happy in them. The social psychologist Caryl Rusbult thought that explanation was incomplete. People sometimes leave satisfying relationships and stay in unsatisfying ones. She proposed an investment model of commitment with three ingredients: how satisfied a person is, how good their alternatives look, and how much they have already put into the relationship that they would lose by leaving.

To test it, Rusbult followed college students in dating relationships over about seven months. Every few weeks they completed questionnaires about the rewards and costs of the relationship, how attractive their alternatives were, what they had invested in it, such as time, shared friends, memories and effort, and how committed they felt. At the end she checked who had stayed together and who had broken up.

Commitment grew when satisfaction rose, but also when investments accumulated and when alternatives came to seem less appealing. Commitment, in turn, predicted whether people stayed together better than satisfaction alone did.

The model became one of the most widely tested in relationship science. Rusbult and colleagues later used it to help explain why some people remain in abusive relationships: few alternatives and heavy investments can hold a person in place.
lesson: Commitment is built from what you invest and what you choose not to chase, not only from how happy you feel today. Feed the relationship you want to keep.
people: Caryl Rusbult
source: Rusbult, C. E. (1983). A longitudinal test of the investment model: The development (and deterioration) of satisfaction and commitment in heterosexual involvements. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 45(1), 101-117.

title: Linda the Bank Teller
text:
Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman wrote a short description of an imaginary woman. Linda was 31, single, outspoken and very bright. She had majored in philosophy, and as a student she had been deeply concerned with discrimination and social justice and had joined anti-nuclear demonstrations.

Participants then ranked several statements about Linda by how probable they were. Two of them mattered: "Linda is a bank teller" and "Linda is a bank teller and is active in the feminist movement."

Logic leaves no room for doubt here. Every feminist bank teller is a bank teller, so the combined statement can never be more likely than the single one. Yet in Tversky and Kahneman's studies, around 85 percent of the students ranked the feminist bank teller as more probable. The pattern held among graduate students with training in statistics, and it held when the two options were placed side by side.

The researchers called it the conjunction fallacy. The description of Linda matched the image of a feminist far better than the image of a bank teller, so people judged by resemblance instead of by probability. Adding a detail made the story more convincing while making it less likely. Later researchers argued about how much the wording of the problem contributed, and asking in terms of frequencies ("out of 100 women like Linda") reduced the error, but the basic effect has proved robust.
lesson: Each extra detail in a forecast or a plan makes it more vivid and less probable. When a scenario feels very convincing, count how many separate things must all come true for it to happen.
people: Amos Tversky, Daniel Kahneman
location: University of British Columbia, Canada, and Stanford University, USA
source: Tversky, A., and Kahneman, D. (1983). Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: The conjunction fallacy in probability judgment. Psychological Review, 90(4), 293-315.

title: Where Will Maxi Look for the Chocolate?
text:
At the University of Salzburg in Austria, Heinz Wimmer and Josef Perner wanted to know when children begin to understand that other people can believe something that is not true. They designed a short story acted out with toys.

A boy named Maxi helps his mother unpack the shopping and puts some chocolate in a blue cupboard. Then he goes out to play. While he is away, his mother takes the chocolate out, uses some for a cake, and puts the rest in a green cupboard. Maxi comes back, hungry for chocolate. The child listening to the story was asked a simple question: where will Maxi look for the chocolate?

The child knew where the chocolate really was. To answer correctly, they had to set aside their own knowledge and reason from Maxi's point of view: he did not see it moved, so he will look in the blue cupboard. The youngest children, around three and four, mostly pointed to the green cupboard, where the chocolate actually was. Between about four and six, more and more children gave the right answer, and most older children found it easy.

The false belief test became one of the most widely used tools in developmental psychology and in research on autism.
lesson: Understanding that others see the world differently from us is learned, not given. Help children practice it by asking what someone else knows and feels.
people: Heinz Wimmer, Josef Perner
source: Wimmer, H., and Perner, J. (1983). Beliefs about beliefs: Representation and constraining function of wrong beliefs in young children's understanding of deception. Cognition, 13(1), 103-128.
caveat: Some later studies using nonverbal methods suggest that infants may grasp false beliefs earlier than verbal tests show, though these results have been hard to replicate.

title: The NUMMI Plant
text:
General Motors' assembly plant in Fremont, California, was one of the worst in the company. By the early 1980s it was known for poor quality, high absenteeism, wildcat strikes and bitter relations between managers and the union. GM closed it in 1982.

In 1984 it reopened as New United Motor Manufacturing, Inc., or NUMMI, a joint venture between GM and Toyota. Toyota would run the plant using its production system. Remarkably, most of the hourly workforce was hired back from the old plant, members of the same United Auto Workers local, including some of the union leaders who had fought management hardest.

What changed was the system around them. Groups of workers were sent to Toyota's plants in Japan for training. Back in Fremont they worked in small teams with a team leader, helped design their own jobs and standards, and could pull the andon cord to stop the line when something went wrong. Managers were expected to help fix problems rather than assign blame.

Within a couple of years NUMMI's quality and productivity were close to those of Toyota's Japanese plants and far better than GM's other factories, and absenteeism had dropped sharply. Researchers at MIT and elsewhere studied it closely. GM, however, struggled for years to spread the lessons to its other plants. NUMMI closed in 2010, and the building became Tesla's Fremont factory.
lesson: Poor performance is often a property of the system, not the people. Change how a team is organized and treated, and the same people can do excellent work.
people: General Motors, Toyota, United Auto Workers, Fremont workers
source: John Shook, 'How to Change a Culture: Lessons from NUMMI', MIT Sloan Management Review 51(2) (2010); Paul S. Adler, 'Time-and-Motion Regained', Harvard Business Review (1993)

title: The Ski Trip You Already Paid For
text:
In the early 1980s, Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer of Ohio University studied why people keep investing in something because they have already paid for it.

In one questionnaire, students imagined they had bought a 100-dollar ticket for a weekend ski trip to Michigan and, later, a 50-dollar ticket for a trip to Wisconsin that they expected to enjoy more. Then they discovered both trips fell on the same weekend, and neither ticket could be sold or refunded. Which would they go on? More than half chose Michigan, the more expensive trip they expected to enjoy less. The money was gone either way, yet the larger sunk cost pulled them toward the worse weekend.

Arkes and Blumer then tested the idea in a real setting. People buying season tickets for the Ohio University theater were randomly sold them at full price or at one of two discounts. The researchers tracked attendance using the stubs. During the first half of the season, those who had paid full price attended more plays than those who had received a discount. Having paid more made people feel they had to get their money's worth, although the money spent could not be recovered either way. The difference faded later in the season.

The authors described this as the sunk cost effect: a tendency to continue an endeavor once money, effort or time has been invested, even when only future costs and benefits should matter.
lesson: When deciding whether to continue a project, course or purchase, ignore what you have already spent. Ask only which choice gives the best future from where you stand now.
people: Hal Arkes, Catherine Blumer
source: Arkes, H. R., and Blumer, C. (1985). The psychology of sunk cost. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 35(1), 124-140.

title: The Hot Hand
text:
Basketball players and fans widely believe in the "hot hand": after making a few shots in a row, a player is more likely to make the next one. In 1985 Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky decided to check.

They surveyed fans, who strongly endorsed the idea. Then they analyzed shooting records of the Philadelphia 76ers over a season, free throws by the Boston Celtics, and a controlled shooting experiment with players from Cornell University's teams. In the 76ers data, players were not more likely to score after a run of hits than after a run of misses. Streaks appeared about as often as one would expect from chance alone, given each player's overall shooting percentage.

The authors concluded that the hot hand was largely an illusion. People expect random sequences to alternate more than they really do, so when they see ordinary runs of success, they read meaning into them. The paper became a classic example of how people see patterns in randomness.

The story had a twist. In 2018 the economists Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo showed that the statistical method used in the original study had a subtle bias: in a finite sequence, looking at shots that follow a streak naturally underestimates the hit rate. Correcting for it, they found evidence of a modest hot hand in the original Cornell data. The debate now is mostly about its size, which appears smaller than fans believe.
lesson: Streaks happen naturally in random processes, so a run of success or failure is weak evidence on its own. Look at the longer record before concluding that someone is on fire or out of form.
people: Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone, Amos Tversky
location: Cornell University, Ithaca, and Stanford University, USA
source: Gilovich, T., Vallone, R., and Tversky, A. (1985). The hot hand in basketball: On the misperception of random sequences. Cognitive Psychology, 17(3), 295-314.
caveat: A 2018 reanalysis by Miller and Sanjurjo found a statistical bias in the original method and evidence for a real but modest hot hand.

title: The Romance of Leadership
text:
In 1985 James Meindl and his colleagues Sanford Ehrlich and Janet Dukerich suggested that people have a romantic view of leaders: they explain the successes and failures of organizations as the work of the person at the top, even when other causes are more important.

To test the idea, they ran several studies. In one, they counted how often articles in the Wall Street Journal about particular large companies mentioned leadership, and compared this with how those companies had performed. Leadership was mentioned more when performance was unusually good or unusually bad. In another, they looked at how often doctoral dissertations and business press articles focused on leadership over the years, and found that interest rose and fell with the economy.

In laboratory experiments, they gave people short descriptions of a company's results, along with a list of possible causes. When results were extreme, whether very good or very bad, participants put much more weight on the leader than when results were moderate. Meindl concluded that leadership is partly a story people use to make sense of events they find hard to explain.
lesson: Leaders get too much credit in good times and too much blame in bad times. Look honestly at what else drove the result before praising or firing the person in charge.
people: James Meindl, Sanford Ehrlich, Janet Dukerich
location: State University of New York at Buffalo, USA
source: Meindl, J. R., Ehrlich, S. B., and Dukerich, J. M. (1985). The romance of leadership. Administrative Science Quarterly, 30(1), 78-102.

title: The New Coke Fiasco
text:
In the early 1980s Coca-Cola was losing market share to Pepsi, whose advertising campaign, the Pepsi Challenge, showed ordinary people preferring Pepsi in blind sips. Coca-Cola's own research found the same thing: in sip tests, the sweeter Pepsi often won.

The company spent years developing a new, sweeter formula. In blind taste tests with roughly two hundred thousand people, the new recipe beat both old Coke and Pepsi. On 23 April 1985, chairman Roberto Goizueta announced that Coca-Cola was changing its formula, and the old one was taken off the market.

The reaction astonished the company. Tens of thousands of angry calls and letters poured in. People hoarded old Coke, a Seattle man organized a group called Old Cola Drinkers of America, and protesters poured the new drink into the streets. Many complainants said less about taste than about losing something that was part of their lives and of American identity. The taste tests had measured which drink people liked in one sip, not what they felt about the brand.

On 11 July 1985, less than three months after the launch, Coca-Cola announced that the original formula would return as Coca-Cola Classic. Sales of the old drink rose above their previous level, and the new formula slowly faded away.
lesson: Measuring the wrong thing can lead a careful process to a bad decision. Before changing something people love, ask what it means to them, not only how they rate it.
people: Roberto Goizueta, Donald Keough, Coca-Cola Company
source: Mark Pendergrast, For God, Country and Coca-Cola (1993); Thomas Oliver, The Real Coke, the Real Story (1986)

title: Mother's Face at the Visual Cliff
text:
The visual cliff is a sheet of strong glass laid over a checkered surface. On one side the pattern sits right under the glass; on the other it drops away, so that it looks as if the floor ends in a sudden fall. In the 1980s, James Sorce, Robert Emde, Joseph Campos and Mary Klinnert at the University of Denver used a version with a modest drop to ask how babies decide what to do when a situation is unclear.

One-year-olds were placed on the shallow side, with an attractive toy beyond the apparent drop and their mother standing on the far side. The drop was set at a height that made babies hesitate rather than refuse outright. As they reached the edge, most looked up at their mother's face.

The mothers had been trained to show a particular expression. When the mother looked happy, most of the babies crossed the glass to her. When she showed fear, none of them crossed. Other expressions, such as interest or anger, produced results in between.

The study became a classic demonstration of social referencing: when infants are uncertain, they look to a trusted adult and use that adult's emotion to decide whether to go ahead.
lesson: Children read your face to learn what is safe and what is dangerous. Your calm or your fear becomes theirs, so notice what you are showing them.
people: James Sorce, Robert Emde, Joseph Campos, Mary Klinnert
source: Sorce, J. F., Emde, R. N., Campos, J., and Klinnert, M. D. (1985). Maternal emotional signaling: Its effect on the visual cliff behavior of 1-year-olds. Developmental Psychology, 21(1), 195-200.

title: The Hidden Profile
text:
Groups are supposed to be wiser than individuals partly because members bring different information to the table. In 1985, Garold Stasser and William Titus at Miami University in Ohio tested whether groups actually use that information.

Students met in groups of four to choose the best of three fictional candidates for student body president. Each candidate came with a list of facts. In some groups, everyone received the full list. In others, the facts were split in a clever way: the information everyone shared made a weaker candidate look best, while the facts that pointed to the strongest candidate were scattered, each held by only one member. If the group pooled everything, the best choice became clear. This setup became known as a hidden profile.

With full information, groups usually picked the best candidate. With the hidden profile, they rarely did. Discussion dwelt on facts that everyone already knew, because those came up more often and were confirmed by others. Facts held by a single member were mentioned less, repeated less, and often never entered the conversation at all. Members also tended to argue for the candidate they had favored before the meeting, using the shared facts to support it.
lesson: Meetings tend to recycle what everyone already knows. Before deciding, ask each person directly for what only they know, and write it down where all can see it.
people: Garold Stasser, William Titus
source: Stasser, G., and Titus, W. (1985). Pooling of unshared information in group decision making: Biased information sampling during discussion. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 48(6), 1467-1478.

title: The Hostile Media Effect
text:
In September 1982, Lebanese Christian militiamen killed hundreds of Palestinian civilians in the Sabra and Shatila refugee camps near Beirut, in an area under Israeli military control. Television news covered the massacre and Israel's role extensively.

In 1985 Robert Vallone, Lee Ross and Mark Lepper of Stanford University showed students a selection of these network news segments. Some of the students were strongly pro-Israeli, some strongly pro-Arab, and some neutral. Everyone saw exactly the same footage.

Afterward, the two partisan groups each judged the coverage as biased, but in opposite directions. Pro-Israeli students saw the news as slanted against Israel; pro-Arab students saw it as slanted in Israel's favor. Each side remembered the segments as containing more references unfavorable to its own side. Each also believed that neutral viewers would be pushed toward the opposite camp. The more knowledgeable and strongly committed the viewers were, the more biased they found the reports.

The researchers called this the hostile media phenomenon. It helps explain why news organizations are often attacked as biased from both sides at once, and why even careful, balanced reporting rarely satisfies people who care deeply about an issue.
lesson: When you feel sure that coverage is unfair to your side, remember that the other side likely feels the same about the same report.
people: Robert Vallone, Lee Ross, Mark Lepper
source: Vallone, R. P., Ross, L., and Lepper, M. R. (1985). The hostile media phenomenon: Biased perception and perceptions of media bias in coverage of the Beirut massacre. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 49(3), 577-585.

title: But Wait, That's Not All
text:
Television salesmen have long used a familiar line: "But wait, there's more!" In 1986 the psychologist Jerry Burger of Santa Clara University tested whether the trick works and why.

At a campus bake sale, a table displayed cupcakes without price tags. When a customer asked about the price, the seller gave one of two answers. In the that's-not-all condition, the seller said the cupcakes cost 75 cents, then, before the customer could respond, added that the price included two cookies. In the control condition, the customer was shown the cupcake and two cookies together from the start and told the package cost 75 cents. The deal was identical. Only the order of presentation differed.

About 73 percent of customers in the that's-not-all condition bought, compared with about 40 percent in the control condition. In another version, the seller first said a cupcake cost one dollar twenty-five, then lowered the price to one dollar before the customer replied, which also sold more than simply asking for one dollar from the start. Burger suggested two forces at work: the improvement felt like a concession that people wanted to return, and the first price served as an anchor that made the final offer look better.
lesson: An offer that improves before you answer feels like a gift, even when it is the same deal. Judge the final offer on its own merits.
people: Jerry Burger
location: Santa Clara University, Santa Clara, USA
source: Burger, J. M. (1986). Increasing compliance by improving the deal: The that's-not-all technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 51(2), 277-283.

title: The Night Before Challenger
text:
On the evening of 27 January 1986, NASA and its contractor Morton Thiokol held a teleconference about the next morning's launch of the space shuttle Challenger. The forecast was for freezing temperatures at Cape Canaveral, far colder than any previous launch.

Thiokol engineers, among them Roger Boisjoly and Arnie Thompson, were alarmed. The joints of the solid rocket boosters were sealed by rubber O-rings, and earlier flights had shown erosion and soot getting past the seals, worst on a cold launch. The engineers argued that the rubber would stiffen in the cold and might not seal. Thiokol's first recommendation was not to launch below 53 degrees Fahrenheit.

NASA managers pushed back hard. One, Lawrence Mulloy, asked whether Thiokol wanted them to wait until April. Thiokol's managers asked for a private caucus. There, according to the Rogers Commission, senior vice president Jerald Mason told engineering vice president Robert Lund to "take off his engineering hat and put on his management hat." The managers then voted to approve the launch, without the engineers, and Thiokol reversed its recommendation.

The next morning, at about 36 degrees, Challenger lifted off. Seventy-three seconds later a booster joint failed and the shuttle broke apart, killing all seven crew members, including the schoolteacher Christa McAuliffe. The presidential commission concluded that the decision-making process itself had been flawed, and that the people who made the final call had not been told of the engineers' full concerns.
lesson: Expertise only protects a team if it is allowed to say no. When schedule pressure starts overruling the people closest to the risk, stop and listen.
people: Roger Boisjoly, Arnie Thompson, Jerald Mason, Robert Lund, Lawrence Mulloy
location: Kennedy Space Center, Florida, and Morton Thiokol, Utah, USA
source: Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident (Rogers Commission, 1986)

title: The Snow Shovel Price
text:
Economists often assume that businesses charge whatever the market will bear. In the mid-1980s Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch and Richard Thaler asked ordinary people whether they agreed. In telephone surveys of residents of Toronto and Vancouver, people were read short scenarios and asked whether the business behaved fairly.

The best known went like this: a hardware store has been selling snow shovels for 15 dollars. The morning after a large snowstorm, the store raises the price to 20 dollars. About 82 percent of respondents called this unfair. It was simply supply and demand, but people saw it as taking advantage of a sudden need.

Other scenarios revealed the rules people used. A company that cut wages by 7 percent in a time of unemployment and no inflation was judged unfair by most respondents. When the company instead gave a 5 percent raise while inflation was 12 percent, cutting real wages by about the same amount, only a minority objected. People judged changes against a reference point: they considered it fair for firms to protect their profits when their costs rose, but unfair to exploit shifts in demand to take what customers and workers saw as theirs. The researchers argued that firms that ignore these norms risk punishment from customers and employees.
lesson: People judge fairness by what they are used to and whether you seem to exploit their need. Raising prices or cutting pay can cost more in trust than it gains.
people: Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch, Richard Thaler
source: Kahneman, D., Knetsch, J. L., and Thaler, R. H. (1986). Fairness as a constraint on profit seeking: Entitlements in the market. American Economic Review, 76(4), 728-741.

title: Fire Commanders Who Do Not Compare Options
text:
In the mid-1980s the psychologist Gary Klein and his colleagues Roberta Calderwood and Anne Clinton-Cirocco set out to study how experienced fire commanders make life-and-death decisions under time pressure. They expected to find that commanders compared a few options and picked the best, as textbooks on decision making recommended.

They interviewed veteran fireground commanders in the United States about difficult incidents they had handled, going through each fire step by step and asking what the commanders had noticed and what they had considered at every decision point.

The commanders insisted they rarely compared options at all. In the large majority of decisions, they recognized the situation as a familiar type, and that recognition immediately suggested a reasonable course of action. Before acting, they often ran it forward in their minds, imagining how it would play out. If the mental simulation revealed a problem, they modified the plan or moved to the next option that came to mind. They did not lay out alternatives side by side.

Klein called this recognition-primed decision making. In a case Klein later retold in his book Sources of Power, a lieutenant ordered his crew out of a burning house because the fire felt wrong: too hot and too quiet. The floor collapsed soon after. The fire had been in the basement beneath them. The work launched the field of naturalistic decision making, the study of how experts actually decide in real settings.
lesson: Experience lets you recognize what a situation calls for and act quickly. Before you commit, run the plan forward in your mind, and if something feels off, take that signal seriously.
people: Gary Klein, Roberta Calderwood, Anne Clinton-Cirocco
source: Klein, G. A., Calderwood, R., and Clinton-Cirocco, A. (1986). Rapid decision making on the fire ground. Proceedings of the Human Factors Society 30th Annual Meeting.

title: Who Looks Like a Leader
text:
By the middle of the twentieth century, many researchers had concluded that personality traits had little to do with leadership. Influential reviews, including one by Richard Mann in 1959, found only weak and inconsistent links between traits and who became a leader.

In 1986 Robert Lord, Christy De Vader and George Alliger went back to the studies Mann had reviewed and reanalyzed them with modern statistical methods that correct for small samples and measurement error. They focused on a specific question: which traits predict whether a person is perceived as a leader by others in a group?

The corrected results told a different story. Intelligence was strongly related to being seen as a leader. Masculinity and dominance were also related, though less strongly. Lord and his colleagues argued that people carry mental prototypes of what a leader looks like, and they tend to grant leadership to those who match the prototype.

The authors were careful to note what they had and had not measured. Their analysis was about who is seen as a leader, not who actually makes groups perform better.
lesson: Groups tend to pick leaders who fit their picture of a leader. Separate that picture from the question of who will actually lead well.
people: Robert Lord, Christy De Vader, George Alliger
source: Lord, R. G., De Vader, C. L., and Alliger, G. M. (1986). A meta-analysis of the relation between personality traits and leadership perceptions: An application of validity generalization procedures. Journal of Applied Psychology, 71(3), 402-410.

title: Paul O'Neill Starts With Safety
text:
In 1987 Paul O'Neill, a former government official, became chief executive of Alcoa, the American aluminum giant. Investors expected a new CEO to talk about profits, costs and markets.

At his first big meeting with investors and analysts in New York, O'Neill instead began by pointing out the emergency exits in the room. Then he said he wanted to talk about worker safety. Aluminum plants were dangerous places, and he announced that his goal was to make Alcoa the safest company in America, aiming for zero injuries. Charles Duhigg, who told the story in The Power of Habit, reports that some investors left convinced the company was in trouble.

O'Neill required that any injury be reported to him within twenty-four hours, together with a plan to prevent it from happening again. To meet that demand, information had to flow quickly from the shop floor to the top, and managers and workers had to examine every process closely. The changes spread from safety into quality and efficiency.

Alcoa's injury rate fell sharply. By the time O'Neill left in 2000 to become Treasury Secretary, the company's profits and market value had grown many times over.
lesson: Pick one goal everyone can agree on and pursue it relentlessly. The habits it demands can change the whole organization.
people: Paul O'Neill, Alcoa
location: Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and New York, USA
source: Charles Duhigg, The Power of Habit (2012), chapter 4; O'Neill's speeches and interviews
caveat: How much of Alcoa's financial success came from the safety focus rather than market conditions is debated.

title: Brainstorming's Riddle
text:
In the 1950s, advertising executive Alex Osborn popularized brainstorming, claiming that a group following rules such as no criticism and quantity over quality would produce far more ideas than its members working alone. Research soon contradicted him. Again and again, groups produced fewer ideas than the same number of people working separately whose ideas were pooled afterward.

Michael Diehl and Wolfgang Stroebe at the University of Tubingen, in Germany, set out to solve the riddle of why. They tested three explanations: fear of being judged by others, people relaxing because others would contribute, and a simple practical problem they called production blocking. In a group, only one person can speak at a time, so others must wait, and while waiting they forget ideas or stop generating new ones.

In a series of experiments, they varied each factor. Evaluation fears and free riding made only small differences. Blocking made a big one. In one key test, people worked in separate rooms but could only speak their ideas when a light showed that no one else was talking. Even alone, they produced far fewer ideas, just like interacting groups. When blocking was removed, the gap largely disappeared.
lesson: Group brainstorming loses ideas while people wait their turn. Have everyone generate ideas alone first, then share and build on them together.
people: Michael Diehl, Wolfgang Stroebe
source: Diehl, M., and Stroebe, W. (1987). Productivity loss in brainstorming groups: Toward the solution of a riddle. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 53(3), 497-509.

title: Love as Attachment
text:
In the mid-1980s, Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver at the University of Denver wondered whether the attachment patterns Mary Ainsworth had seen in infants might also appear in adult romantic love. To find out, they placed a "love quiz" in the Rocky Mountain News, a Denver newspaper, and invited readers to mail in their answers. Hundreds did. They later repeated the study with university students.

The key question asked readers which of three short descriptions best fit their feelings in close relationships. One described finding it relatively easy to get close to others and not worrying much about being abandoned. Another described discomfort with closeness and difficulty trusting a partner. The third described wanting to get closer than partners seemed to want, and worrying that a partner did not really love them.

Most respondents chose the first, secure description; about a quarter chose the avoidant one and about a fifth the anxious one, proportions roughly similar to those found among infants. People in each group described their most important love relationship in distinctly different ways, and they also remembered their relationships with their parents differently.

The study launched the large field of adult attachment research.
lesson: The way you love as an adult often echoes what you learned about closeness as a child. Recognizing your pattern is the first step to changing it.
people: Cindy Hazan, Phillip Shaver
source: Hazan, C., and Shaver, P. (1987). Romantic love conceptualized as an attachment process. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 52(3), 511-524.
caveat: The original measure was a single self-report question, and later research treats attachment as a matter of degree on two dimensions rather than three fixed types.

title: Why Siblings Differ
text:
Parents of several children often marvel at how different their children are, despite the same house, the same parents and the same rules. In 1987, the behavioral geneticists Robert Plomin and Denise Daniels published a landmark review that took this puzzle seriously.

They gathered results from studies of twins, adopted children and ordinary families. One striking finding was that adopted children who grew up together in the same home, but shared no genes, ended up barely more similar in personality than strangers. Biological siblings were more alike, but mostly to the extent expected from the genes they share.

The implication was surprising. The parts of the environment that siblings share, such as family income, parents' education or the general atmosphere of the home, seemed to do little to make siblings alike in personality and many other traits. What mattered more was the nonshared environment: the experiences that differ for each child in the same family. These include being treated differently by parents, being older or younger, having different friends, teachers and illnesses, and chance events.

Plomin and Daniels argued that the important question was not how families differ from one another, but how each child in a family experiences a different family.
lesson: Each of your children lives in a different family, even under one roof. Pay attention to the distinct experience each child is having.
people: Robert Plomin, Denise Daniels
source: Plomin, R., and Daniels, D. (1987). Why are children in the same family so different from one another? Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 10(1), 1-16.
caveat: Later research has found it hard to identify specific nonshared experiences that explain much of the difference, and shared family environment matters more for some outcomes such as education.

title: The Midpoint Transition
text:
For years, textbooks described team development as a steady march through stages. In the 1980s, Connie Gersick followed eight real project teams from their first meeting to their deadline to see what actually happened. They ranged from student groups to working teams inside organizations, with deadlines from about a week to six months.

Gersick watched and recorded their meetings. She found that each team settled on a basic approach to its work very early, often in the first meeting, and then stuck with it for a long time, even when it was not working well.

Then, at almost exactly the halfway point of the time they had, each team went through a burst of change. Members seemed to realize that time was running short. They dropped old patterns, sought outside input, and adopted a new approach. This happened at the calendar midpoint regardless of whether the project lasted a week or six months. The team then worked steadily on that new plan until a final push near the deadline. Gersick called the pattern punctuated equilibrium, borrowing a term from evolutionary biology.
lesson: Teams lock in their approach early and rethink it around the halfway mark. Use the first meeting and the midpoint deliberately to review direction.
people: Connie Gersick
source: Gersick, C. J. G. (1988). Time and transition in work teams: Toward a new model of group development. Academy of Management Journal, 31(1), 9-41.

title: Shy From the Start
text:
Some toddlers walk into a room full of strangers and new toys and dive in. Others cling to a parent, fall silent and watch from a distance. The Harvard psychologist Jerome Kagan wanted to know whether such differences were passing moods or something deeper.

With J. Steven Reznick and Nancy Snidman, he selected toddlers who, in laboratory sessions with unfamiliar people, objects and situations, were consistently very timid, which they called behaviorally inhibited, or consistently bold and sociable, called uninhibited. The children were then seen again several times, up to about age seven.

The differences tended to persist. Many of the children who had been inhibited as toddlers were still quieter and more cautious with unfamiliar children and adults years later, while most uninhibited children stayed outgoing. The inhibited children also differed physiologically: on average they had higher and more stable heart rates and other signs of a more reactive stress system. Kagan concluded that part of shyness reflects an inborn temperament.

Yet the stability was far from complete. A good number of inhibited children became noticeably less shy over time. Kagan later suggested that parents who gently encouraged their wary children to face new situations, rather than shielding them from every discomfort, helped them change.
lesson: A shy child is not broken, and temperament is not destiny. Gentle, steady encouragement to try new things helps more than either pushing or overprotecting.
people: Jerome Kagan, J. Steven Reznick, Nancy Snidman
source: Kagan, J., Reznick, J. S., and Snidman, N. (1988). Biological bases of childhood shyness. Science, 240(4849), 167-171.

title: Lawrence Lemieux Leaves the Race
text:
At the 1988 Seoul Olympics, the sailing events were held off the port of Busan, South Korea. On September 24 a strong wind whipped up the sea. Lawrence Lemieux of Canada, sailing alone in the Finn class, was running second in his race and had a real chance at a medal.

On a nearby course, a two-man boat from Singapore in the 470 class had capsized in the rough water. One sailor, Joseph Chan, was injured and had been swept away from the boat, and his crewmate Siew Shaw Her was clinging to the hull. Rescue boats were busy with other boats in trouble.

Lemieux changed course. He sailed to the men, pulled the injured Chan out of the water, kept both men with him, and waited until a patrol boat arrived to take them. Then he went back to the race and finished well down the fleet.

The race jury, recognizing what he had done, gave him back the position he had held before the rescue. He finished eleventh overall. At a ceremony in Seoul, IOC President Juan Antonio Samaranch honored him with the Pierre de Coubertin Medal for sportsmanship.
lesson: When someone near you is in danger, your own goals can wait. No prize is worth more than helping a person who needs you right now.
people: Lawrence Lemieux, Joseph Chan, Siew Shaw Her
source: Official Report of the Games of the XXIVth Olympiad, Seoul 1988; contemporary press reports

title: Status Quo Bias
text:
In 1988 the economists William Samuelson and Richard Zeckhauser published a long study of a simple question: does it matter which option is presented as the one you already have?

In questionnaire experiments, they asked students to imagine they had inherited a large sum of money and had to choose how to invest it among several options, such as a moderate-risk company, a high-risk company, treasury bills and municipal bonds. Some participants simply chose. Others were told that the money was already invested in one of the options and that they could switch at no cost. Whichever option was described as the current holding was chosen far more often, whatever it happened to be.

They then looked at real decisions. When Harvard University added new health insurance plans for its staff, newly hired employees chose among all plans freely, while existing employees could switch but mostly stayed in the plan they already had, even when newcomers clearly preferred the new options. Similar patterns showed up in retirement plan choices.

Samuelson and Zeckhauser named the effect status quo bias. They traced it to several causes: the costs of thinking and switching, the regret people expect to feel if a change turns out badly, and the wish to stay consistent with past choices. The pattern helped explain why defaults have such strong effects in policy and business.
lesson: Review the arrangements you inherited, your plans, subscriptions and routines, as if you were choosing them today. Staying put is also a decision, and it deserves the same scrutiny as a change.
people: William Samuelson, Richard Zeckhauser
location: Boston University and Harvard University, USA
source: Samuelson, W., and Zeckhauser, R. (1988). Status quo bias in decision making. Journal of Risk and Uncertainty, 1(1), 7-59.

title: The Baltic Way Human Chain
text:
On 23 August 1989 it was fifty years since Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union had signed the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, whose secret protocol had assigned Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania to the Soviet sphere. The Soviet government still officially denied that the secret protocol existed.

The three countries' popular movements, the Estonian Popular Front, the Latvian Popular Front and Lithuania's Sajudis, decided to mark the anniversary together, with a human chain running from Tallinn through Riga to Vilnius. It would stretch about 675 kilometers, along roads through towns, forests and farmland, and it had to be unbroken.

The organizers divided the route into sections and assigned each to particular towns and districts, arranged buses and cars, and used radio broadcasts to direct people to gaps in the line. On the evening of 23 August, at the agreed time, about two million people, a large share of the three nations' population, joined hands for fifteen minutes. Families came with children; some held candles or flags, and in places flowers were laid for the victims of deportations.

Moscow condemned the event, but it was impossible to ignore. In December 1989 the Soviet Congress of People's Deputies formally acknowledged the secret protocol and declared it invalid. Lithuania declared its independence in March 1990, and all three countries were free by 1991.
lesson: Peaceful collective action needs careful coordination to have its effect. When people show up together, at once and in great numbers, they are hard to ignore.
people: People of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania; Popular Front of Estonia, Popular Front of Latvia, Sajudis
location: Tallinn, Estonia, to Riga, Latvia, to Vilnius, Lithuania
source: Contemporary reports; UNESCO Memory of the World register, The Baltic Way (2009)

title: The Marshmallow Test
text:
Starting in the late 1960s, Walter Mischel and his colleagues at Stanford University ran a simple experiment with preschoolers at the campus nursery school. A child sat at a table with a treat, often a marshmallow or a pretzel. The researcher explained that they were going to leave the room. If the child waited until the researcher came back, they would get two treats. If they could not wait, they could ring a bell and eat one right away.

Some children ate the treat almost at once. Others waited for many minutes. The most interesting finding was how they managed it. Children who succeeded often covered their eyes, sang, played with their hands, or imagined the marshmallow as a fluffy cloud rather than something tasty. Waiting was much easier when the treat was hidden than when it sat in plain view.

In a 1989 review in Science, Mischel, Yuichi Shoda and Monica Rodriguez summarized this work and reported that children who had waited longer were, years later, described by their parents as more competent adolescents and had higher SAT scores.

Those long-term links became famous. A 2018 study by Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan, using a larger and more diverse sample, found them much weaker once family background and early abilities were taken into account.
lesson: Self-control is less about willpower than about strategy. Help children, and yourself, by changing what is in view and what you think about while waiting.
people: Walter Mischel, Yuichi Shoda, Monica Rodriguez
location: Bing Nursery School, Stanford University, Stanford, USA
source: Mischel, W., Shoda, Y., and Rodriguez, M. L. (1989). Delay of gratification in children. Science, 244(4907), 933-938.
caveat: The follow-up samples were small, and a 2018 replication found the link between waiting time and later achievement much weaker after controlling for family background.

title: Imagining It Already Happened
text:
In 1989 Deborah Mitchell, J. Edward Russo and Nancy Pennington published a study on a small change in how people think about future events. They called it prospective hindsight: imagining that an event has already happened, then explaining why.

Participants read descriptions of possible future events and were asked to generate reasons why each might occur. For some, the event was presented as uncertain, something that might happen. For others, it was presented as if it had already occurred, with certainty, and they were asked to explain why it had happened. The situations were held otherwise constant.

People who imagined that the event had already happened produced more reasons, and their reasons tended to be more specific and more focused on particular causes, than those who considered the event merely possible. Treating the outcome as a fact seemed to free them to search their knowledge for explanations, rather than debating whether it would happen at all.

The psychologist Gary Klein later drew on this research to design a planning technique he called the premortem, described in a 2007 Harvard Business Review article. Before a project begins, the team imagines that it is a year later and the project has failed badly. Each member then writes down every reason they can think of for the failure. The exercise makes it easier, and socially safer, for people to voice doubts that would otherwise go unspoken, while there is still time to address them.
lesson: Before committing to a plan, imagine it has already failed and list every reason why. Treating failure as a fact makes risks easier to see and to discuss openly while you can still act.
people: Deborah Mitchell, J. Edward Russo, Nancy Pennington
source: Mitchell, D. J., Russo, J. E., and Pennington, N. (1989). Back to the future: Temporal perspective in the explanation of events. Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 2(1), 25-38.

title: United 232 at Sioux City
text:
On 19 July 1989 United Airlines Flight 232, a DC-10 flying from Denver to Chicago with 296 people aboard, suffered an explosive failure of its tail engine. Debris cut through all three hydraulic systems. The pilots had lost the normal use of their flight controls: no ailerons, no rudder, no elevators.

Captain Al Haynes, First Officer William Records and Flight Engineer Dudley Dvorak found that they could only steer by changing the thrust of the two remaining wing engines. A DC-10 training captain traveling as a passenger, Dennis Fitch, came forward to offer help. Haynes gave him the throttles, and Fitch knelt between the seats working them while the others handled the yoke, the radio and the checklists. For about forty minutes the four men shared information constantly, talked through every option, and nursed the plane toward Sioux City. When the controller cleared them to land on any runway, Haynes laughed and asked, "You want to be particular and make it a runway, huh?"

The plane hit the runway hard, broke apart and burst into flames. One hundred and twelve people died, but 184 survived, many helped by local emergency services that had rehearsed a similar disaster.

Investigators found that the crew had done remarkably well with an aircraft that was nearly impossible to fly. Haynes later credited his airline's crew resource management training, which had taught captains to draw on everyone in the cockpit rather than command alone.
lesson: In a crisis, a leader who shares the problem and uses everyone's skills gets far more than one who tries to carry it alone. Training to work together pays off when it matters most.
people: Al Haynes, Dennis Fitch, William Records, Dudley Dvorak
source: National Transportation Safety Board, Aircraft Accident Report NTSB/AAR-90/06 (1990)

title: Twins Reared Apart
text:
In 1979, Thomas Bouchard at the University of Minnesota read a newspaper story about identical twin brothers in Ohio, both named Jim, who had been adopted into different families as babies and had just met again at 39. He invited them to Minneapolis for testing, and soon the Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart was under way.

Over the following years, the team brought more than a hundred sets of twins and triplets who had been raised apart, from many countries, to Minneapolis for about a week of intensive testing. They underwent medical exams, intelligence tests, personality questionnaires and long interviews about their lives and interests. Identical twins, who share all their genes, could be compared with fraternal twins, who share about half.

In a 1990 paper in Science, Bouchard, David Lykken, Matt McGue, Nancy Segal and Auke Tellegen reported that identical twins raised in different homes were about as similar as identical twins raised together on many measures of personality, interests and social attitudes. On intelligence, they estimated that about 70 percent of the variation in their sample was associated with genetic differences.

The study was a major force in convincing psychologists that genes play a substantial role in human differences.
lesson: Children are not blank slates, and much of who they are comes with them. Parents shape a child, but they work with a nature that is already there.
people: Thomas Bouchard, David Lykken, Matt McGue, Nancy Segal, Auke Tellegen
source: Bouchard, T. J., Lykken, D. T., McGue, M., Segal, N. L., and Tellegen, A. (1990). Sources of human psychological differences: The Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart. Science, 250(4978), 223-228.
caveat: Many twins had some contact before testing and were raised in fairly similar homes, and heritability estimates apply to a population, not to any individual.

title: Litter in a Clean or Dirty Garage
text:
In 1990 Robert Cialdini, Raymond Reno and Carl Kallgren published a series of experiments on why people litter. In one, people returning to their cars in a parking garage found a large handbill tucked under the windshield wiper. The researchers watched whether they threw it on the ground.

The garage had been arranged in advance. Sometimes it was spotless; sometimes it was strewn with handbills, cigarette butts and candy wrappers. And as each person walked toward their car, a passing research assistant either simply walked by or dropped a handbill on the ground in plain view.

People littered more in the dirty garage than in the clean one: litter signaled that littering was what people did there. But the assistant's action changed things in an interesting way. In the dirty garage, seeing someone else litter drew attention to the mess and made people litter the most of all. In the clean garage, seeing someone drop a handbill made people litter the least, because the single piece of trash stood out as an exception against the clean floor.

Further studies showed that messages drawing attention to the norm, whether about what most people do or what most people approve of, could reduce littering, as long as people's attention was focused on the norm at the moment they acted.
lesson: People take cues from what others around them seem to do. Keep shared spaces in good order, and point out the good behavior that is common rather than the bad.
people: Robert Cialdini, Raymond Reno, Carl Kallgren
source: Cialdini, R. B., Reno, R. R., and Kallgren, C. A. (1990). A focus theory of normative conduct: Recycling the concept of norms to reduce littering in public places. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 58(6), 1015-1026.

title: The Pay Cut and the Missing Stock
text:
In the late 1980s a manufacturing company lost two large contracts and decided to cut pay by 15 percent for ten weeks at two of its three plants, rather than lay anyone off. The organizational psychologist Jerald Greenberg was able to study what happened next.

At one plant, the company president held a long meeting with the workers. He explained at length why the cut was necessary and that it would be temporary, expressed regret and answered their questions. At the second plant, a vice president announced the cut in a short meeting of about fifteen minutes, with little explanation and no expression of sympathy. The third plant had no pay cut and served as a comparison.

Greenberg tracked employee theft through the company's standard records of missing inventory. At the plant without a cut, theft stayed at its usual low level. At both pay cut plants it rose, but it rose far more at the plant where the cut had been announced curtly. More workers also quit there. When normal pay was restored, theft returned to its usual level.
lesson: Bad news delivered with honesty and respect causes far less damage than the same news delivered coldly. How you explain a decision is part of the decision.
people: Jerald Greenberg
location: Three plants of a US manufacturing company
source: Greenberg, J. (1990). Employee theft as a reaction to underpayment inequity: The hidden cost of pay cuts. Journal of Applied Psychology, 75(5), 561-568.

title: The Coffee Mugs and the Endowment Effect
text:
In the late 1980s, Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch and Richard Thaler ran a series of classroom markets, many of them at Cornell University. The goods were ordinary: coffee mugs bearing the university logo, the kind sold in the campus bookstore.

Half the students in a class were given a mug. The others were not. Then the researchers set up a simple market. Mug owners stated the lowest price at which they would sell, and the others stated the highest price they would pay. Since the mugs had been handed out at random, standard economics predicted that about half of them would change hands.

Far fewer trades happened. Owners typically asked for about twice as much as the buyers were willing to pay. The same pattern appeared with pens and other small items, and it did not disappear when the students had several rounds to learn how the market worked. The mere fact of owning the mug, for a few minutes, made it more valuable to its owner.

The researchers called this the endowment effect and linked it to loss aversion: giving up something you have feels like a loss, while acquiring the same thing feels like a smaller gain. Later studies debated how much depends on the exact procedure and on how experienced traders are, but the basic gap between selling and buying prices has been found many times.
lesson: When you hesitate to sell, cancel or give up something, ask whether you would buy it today at that price. If not, you may be paying only to avoid the feeling of losing it.
people: Daniel Kahneman, Jack Knetsch, Richard Thaler
source: Kahneman, D., Knetsch, J. L., and Thaler, R. H. (1990). Experimental tests of the endowment effect and the Coase theorem. Journal of Political Economy, 98(6), 1325-1348.
caveat: Later work (for example Plott and Zeiler, 2005) found that the gap shrinks under some experimental procedures, so its size depends on context.

title: Tapping a Song on the Table
text:
In 1990 Elizabeth Newton, a graduate student in psychology at Stanford University, carried out a simple experiment for her doctoral dissertation. She paired people up and gave them one of two roles: tapper or listener.

Each tapper received a list of well-known songs, such as "Happy Birthday" and the American national anthem. The task was to pick a song and tap out its rhythm with a knuckle on the table. The listener had to guess the song from the taps alone. Before hearing the listener's answer, the tapper predicted the chance that the listener would guess correctly.

Tappers expected listeners to get it right about half the time. In fact, over 120 songs, listeners identified only three. While tapping, the tappers heard the melody playing in their heads and could not imagine what the bare knocking sounded like without it. The listeners heard only a string of disconnected knocks. Many tappers were visibly frustrated that the listener could not recognize something so obvious. The study, later popularized by Chip and Dan Heath, became a classic illustration of what is called the curse of knowledge: once we know something, it is very hard to imagine not knowing it.
lesson: What is obvious to you because you know it is often unclear to others. When explaining, check what the listener actually hears, not what you hear in your head.
people: Elizabeth Newton
source: Newton, E. L. (1990). The rocky road from actions to intentions. Doctoral dissertation, Stanford University.
caveat: The study was an unpublished dissertation, and its figures are mostly known through later popular accounts.

title: Governing the Commons
text:
In 1968, ecologist Garrett Hardin popularized the tragedy of the commons: when many people share a resource such as a pasture, each has an incentive to overuse it, and the resource is ruined unless the state controls it or it is divided into private property. Political scientist Elinor Ostrom of Indiana University doubted that those were the only options.

She gathered detailed case studies of communities that had managed shared resources themselves, some for centuries. In the Swiss village of Torbel, residents had governed their alpine meadows and forests under rules dating back hundreds of years. In Valencia, Spain, farmers shared irrigation water through a system with its own water court. She also studied Japanese mountain villages, Philippine irrigation societies and fisheries and groundwater basins.

Ostrom found that successful commons shared certain features. Boundaries and membership were clear. Rules fit local conditions and were made largely by the users themselves. Users monitored each other, sanctions started mild and grew for repeat offenders, and there were cheap ways to resolve disputes. Failures tended to occur where these features were missing or where outside authorities overrode local rules. In 2009, she became the first woman to receive the Nobel Prize in economics.
lesson: Shared resources can be managed well by the people who use them, if they set clear rules together, watch each other fairly and settle disputes early.
people: Elinor Ostrom
location: Indiana University, Bloomington, USA (cases from Switzerland, Spain, Japan, the Philippines and elsewhere)
source: Ostrom, E. (1990). Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action. Cambridge University Press.

title: The Fixed-Pie Assumption
text:
In the late 1980s Leigh Thompson and Reid Hastie studied what negotiators believe about the other side, and how those beliefs shape the deals they reach. They set up simulated negotiations between pairs of students, such as a buyer and a seller of a car, covering several issues at once.

The cases were designed so that the two sides did not want opposite things on every issue. On some issues one side cared a lot and the other cared little, which allowed trades that would leave both better off. On at least one issue, both sides actually wanted the same outcome. The researchers asked negotiators, before and after bargaining, what they thought the other party wanted.

Most negotiators assumed that the other side's interests were directly opposed to their own on every issue, so that anything good for one meant equal loss for the other. Thompson and Hastie called this the fixed-pie perception. It formed early, often within the first few minutes, and it shaped the outcomes. Negotiators who held it reached worse joint agreements, missing trades that would have helped both. Some even settled on outcomes that were worse for both parties on the very issues where they agreed, because each assumed the other wanted the opposite and gave in on it as a concession.

Those who realized during the negotiation that interests could differ in importance reached much better agreements for both sides.
lesson: In a negotiation, do not assume the other side wants the opposite of you on everything. Ask what matters most to them, and share what matters most to you, to find trades that help both.
people: Leigh Thompson, Reid Hastie
source: Thompson, L., and Hastie, R. (1990). Social perception in negotiation. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 47(1), 98-123.

title: Why People Obey the Law
text:
In the mid 1980s the psychologist Tom Tyler asked a basic question: why do people follow the law? The usual answer was fear of punishment. Tyler suspected that something else mattered as much: whether people saw the authorities as legitimate.

He and his team interviewed about 1,500 randomly chosen residents of Chicago by telephone, asking about their views of the police and courts and about how often they broke everyday laws such as speeding, littering or shoplifting. Many had recently dealt with the police or courts themselves, for example after a traffic stop or a call for help. About a year later, many were interviewed again.

The results surprised many legal scholars. Whether people obeyed the law depended strongly on whether they saw the authorities as legitimate, more than on how likely they thought they were to be caught. And when people judged their own encounters with police or judges, what shaped their views most was not whether they won or lost, but whether the process had been fair: whether they had a chance to explain themselves, whether the officials were neutral and honest, and whether they were treated with dignity.
lesson: People accept even unwelcome decisions when they feel the process was fair and they were heard with respect. Fair procedures build the authority that force cannot.
people: Tom Tyler
source: Tyler, T. R. (1990). Why People Obey the Law. Yale University Press.

title: Divorce and Children
text:
By the late 1980s, divorce had become common in the United States, and the question of how it affects children was the subject of heated debate. Some studies found serious harm; others found almost none. In 1991, the sociologists Paul Amato and Bruce Keith brought order to the evidence with a meta-analysis that combined the results of 92 studies involving more than 13,000 children.

On average, children whose parents had divorced did somewhat worse than children in intact families on a range of measures: school achievement, conduct, psychological adjustment, self-esteem and relationships with others. But the differences were small, and many studies had found larger effects than the better-designed, more recent ones.

A key comparison concerned conflict. Children who lived in intact families with high levels of conflict between their parents had lower well-being than children of divorce. In other words, the fighting between parents seemed to matter at least as much as the separation itself. The quality of the child's relationship with both parents after the divorce, and the economic hardship that often followed, also made a difference.

The study helped shift attention from the question of whether parents divorce to how they handle conflict and care for their children, whether married or not.
lesson: Ongoing conflict between parents can hurt children as much as separation itself. Whether together or apart, keep children out of the battlefield.
people: Paul Amato, Bruce Keith
source: Amato, P. R., and Keith, B. (1991). Parental divorce and the well-being of children: A meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 110(1), 26-46.

title: Linus Torvalds Posts a Hobby Kernel
text:
On 25 August 1991 Linus Torvalds, a 21-year-old computer science student at the University of Helsinki, posted a message to an online discussion group for users of Minix, a small teaching operating system. He wrote that he was doing a free operating system, "just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu," for personal computers with Intel 386 processors. He asked people what features they would like to see.

He released the first version of the Linux kernel that September. Other programmers around the world began downloading it, testing it, finding bugs and sending back fixes and new code over the internet. Torvalds read the patches, accepted the good ones and released new versions often, sometimes several in a week. In 1992 he placed Linux under the GNU General Public License, which ensured that anyone could use and change the code, but that changes shared with others had to remain open too. Combined with tools from the GNU project, it became a complete free system.

The project had no company, no office and no contracts. Contributors came because the problems interested them and because their work was visible and credited. Torvalds acted as the final decision maker, later delegating whole areas to trusted maintainers.

By the end of the decade Linux ran large parts of the internet's servers. Today it runs most of the world's servers and supercomputers and, through Android, billions of phones.
lesson: Open collaboration among strangers can build work of the highest quality when contributions are visible, review is fast and someone keeps the whole coherent.
people: Linus Torvalds and Linux contributors
source: Linus Torvalds, Usenet post to comp.os.minix (25 August 1991); Linus Torvalds and David Diamond, Just for Fun (2001)

title: The Civil Servants of Whitehall
text:
The British civil service is a strict hierarchy, with clear grades from top administrators down to clerical and office support staff. Everyone in it has a job, a salary and access to free health care. That made it an ideal place for the epidemiologist Michael Marmot to ask whether a person's rank by itself was linked to health.

An earlier study of male civil servants, begun in 1967, had already shown that men in the lowest grades died at far higher rates than those at the top. In 1985 Marmot and his team began Whitehall II, enrolling more than 10,000 men and women aged 35 to 55 who worked in twenty London offices. They recorded their health, habits and working conditions and followed them for years.

The first report in 1991 found a clear step-by-step gradient: the lower the grade, the worse people's health, from heart disease to self-rated health. Smoking, diet and other risk factors explained only part of it. Later papers from the same study, published in the 1990s, showed that having little control over one's own work was one of the strongest contributors to the higher rate of heart disease in lower grades.
lesson: Lack of control over one's own work is not just unpleasant, it can damage health. Leaders who share decisions and autonomy protect their people.
people: Michael Marmot and colleagues
source: Marmot, M. G., Smith, G. D., Stansfeld, S., Patel, C., North, F., Head, J., White, I., Brunner, E., and Feeney, A. (1991). Health inequalities among British civil servants: The Whitehall II study. Lancet, 337(8754), 1387-1393.

title: Reactive Devaluation
text:
In the 1980s students at Stanford University campaigned for the university to sell its investments in companies doing business in apartheid-era South Africa. The university eventually announced a policy of partial divestment. Lee Ross and Constance Stillinger used the debate to study a barrier to resolving conflicts.

The researchers asked students to evaluate two possible plans: the partial divestment that the university had adopted, and an alternative plan that set a deadline for total divestment if conditions in South Africa did not improve. Some students were surveyed before the university announced its choice; others afterwards. Before the announcement, students rated the plans roughly according to their content. Once the university adopted partial divestment, students rated it less favorably than before, while the alternative plan, the one not offered, rose in their eyes. A proposal became less attractive simply because the other side had put it on the table.

In related studies by Ross and colleagues, Americans rated a nuclear arms reduction proposal less favorably when they were told it came from the Soviet leader than when told it came from the American president.

Ross and Stillinger called this reactive devaluation. In conflicts, people assume that anything their opponent offers must benefit the opponent, and therefore must be less valuable to them. Concessions lose value at the very moment they are offered, which can block agreements both sides would otherwise accept.
lesson: When an opponent offers a concession, judge it on its merits as if it came from a neutral party. Distrust of the source can make you reject a deal you would otherwise welcome.
people: Lee Ross, Constance Stillinger
source: Ross, L., and Stillinger, C. (1991). Barriers to conflict resolution. Negotiation Journal, 7(4), 389-404.

title: How a Couple Tells Its Story
text:
Kim Buehlman, John Gottman and Lynn Katz wanted to know whether the way a married couple talks about its own past could reveal where the marriage was heading. They asked couples raising young children a set of open questions in a relaxed interview: How did you meet? What attracted you to each other? What were the hard times, and how did you get through them? How has the marriage changed?

The researchers paid little attention to the facts of each story. Instead, they coded how it was told. Did the partners speak of each other with fondness and admiration, or with indifference and criticism? Did they say "we" and describe challenges they had faced together, or speak as two separate people? Did they look back on struggles with pride at getting through, or with disappointment and a sense that the marriage had not turned out as hoped? Was the story vivid and expansive, or vague and thin?

Three years later, the team checked which couples had divorced. The scores from the oral history interview alone predicted divorce with remarkable accuracy, reported at around 94 percent. Couples whose stories were full of disappointment and negativity were the ones who had split up.
lesson: Listen to how you tell the story of your relationship. Speaking with fondness and as a team keeps a bond strong; a story of disappointment is a warning.
people: Kim Buehlman, John Gottman, Lynn Katz
source: Buehlman, K. T., Gottman, J. M., and Katz, L. F. (1992). How a couple views their past predicts their future: Predicting divorce from an oral history interview. Journal of Family Psychology, 5(3-4), 295-318.
caveat: The sample was small and the high accuracy was not tested on a new group of couples, so the figure likely overstates real predictive power.

title: Derek Redmond and His Father Finish the Race
text:
Derek Redmond was one of Britain's best 400 meter runners, but injuries had haunted his career. At the 1988 Olympics in Seoul he had to pull out minutes before his first race with an Achilles tendon injury, and he went through many operations afterward.

At the Barcelona Olympics in 1992 he was in form. On 3 August he started the semifinal well. On the back straight, his right hamstring tore, and he fell to the track in agony. The medical staff came with a stretcher. Redmond waved them away. He got up and began hopping toward the finish line, determined to complete the race, while the other runners finished.

In the stands, his father, Jim Redmond, ran down, pushed past the security staff and came onto the track. He put his arm around his son. Derek, weeping, leaned on him, and Jim told him that they had started together and would finish together. With officials hesitating around them, father and son made their way down the home straight while the crowd of some 65,000 rose to its feet. Just before the line, Jim let go so that Derek could cross it alone.

Officially, because he had received help, Redmond was recorded as not finishing. The images of the moment became one of the best known in Olympic history. His career as a runner ended soon afterward.
lesson: When someone we love falls in public, standing beside them matters more than any result. Support at a moment of failure is remembered long after the medals.
people: Derek Redmond, Jim Redmond
source: Barcelona 1992 Olympic results; BBC and contemporary press reports; Derek Redmond's interviews
caveat: Accounts differ slightly on Jim Redmond's exact words.

title: Same Leader, Different Verdict
text:
In many experiments over the decades, researchers had given people descriptions or recordings of a leader at work and asked them to rate the leader. The trick was that the leader's behavior was identical, and only the leader's sex was varied, for example by changing the name on a written description or by using trained male and female actors.
