In 1992 Alice Eagly, Mona Makhijani and Bruce Klonsky combined the results of dozens of these studies in a meta-analysis. Overall, they found a small tendency to evaluate women leaders less favorably than men who behaved in exactly the same way.

The average was small, but the bias was much larger in some circumstances. Women were rated especially unfavorably when they led in an autocratic, directive style, which clashed with expectations that women be warm and collaborative. Men who led in the same autocratic style were not penalized to the same degree. Women were also judged more harshly in roles typically held by men, and when the people doing the rating were men.
lesson: People can judge identical behavior differently depending on who does it. When you evaluate leaders, check whether you would give the same verdict to someone of the other sex.
people: Alice Eagly, Mona Makhijani, Bruce Klonsky
source: Eagly, A. H., Makhijani, M. G., and Klonsky, B. G. (1992). Gender and the evaluation of leaders: A meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 111(1), 3-22.

title: Imran Khan's Cornered Tigers
text:
The 1992 Cricket World Cup was held in Australia and New Zealand. Pakistan, captained by thirty-nine-year-old Imran Khan, was playing without its leading fast bowler, Waqar Younis, who was injured, and Imran himself was playing with a painful shoulder.

After five matches Pakistan had won only one. Against England they had been bowled out for 74, and were saved from almost certain defeat only because rain washed out the game and gave them a point. Elimination looked likely.

Imran told his players to fight like a cornered tiger, the animal that is most dangerous when it has nowhere left to run, and he wore a T-shirt with a tiger on it to the toss. He kept faith in young players, including the twenty-two-year-old batsman Inzamam-ul-Haq.

Pakistan won its remaining group matches, against Australia, Sri Lanka and New Zealand, and slipped into the semi-finals. There they beat New Zealand, with Inzamam scoring a rapid 60. On March 25, 1992, at the Melbourne Cricket Ground, they beat England in the final by 22 runs. Imran top-scored with 72 and took the last wicket himself.
lesson: When your team is on the edge of failure, give them a clear image of who they can be and back them with your own effort.
people: Imran Khan, Inzamam-ul-Haq, Pakistan cricket team
source: 1992 Cricket World Cup match records; contemporary press reports
caveat: Imran was criticized after the final for a victory speech that focused on his cancer hospital project and did not mention his team.

title: Toddlers Comforting Their Mothers
text:
When does concern for others first appear in children? At the National Institute of Mental Health in the United States, Carolyn Zahn-Waxler, Marian Radke-Yarrow and their colleagues studied this question in the setting where it matters most: the home.

They followed children through the second year of life, starting at around thirteen to fifteen months. The mothers were trained to observe and record what happened whenever someone near their child was hurt, sad or upset, whether the child had caused it or simply witnessed it. In addition, researchers visited the homes, and from time to time the mother or the visitor would pretend to be in distress, for example bumping a knee and saying "ouch," or acting sad.

In the early months, children often just watched, or became upset themselves. Over the following year, their responses changed markedly. More and more often, they patted or hugged the person in distress, brought them a toy or a blanket, said kind words, or tried to fix the problem. They also showed signs of trying to understand what was wrong, looking back and forth between the person and the cause of the pain.

By their second birthday, many children were showing clear, if simple, empathy and comfort toward others.
lesson: Empathy begins very early and grows through daily life at home. When a toddler pats your arm after you get hurt, notice it and welcome it.
people: Carolyn Zahn-Waxler, Marian Radke-Yarrow and colleagues
location: National Institute of Mental Health, Bethesda, USA
source: Zahn-Waxler, C., Radke-Yarrow, M., Wagner, E., and Chapman, M. (1992). Development of concern for others. Developmental Psychology, 28(1), 126-136.

title: Half a Minute of Silent Video
text:
In 1993 Nalini Ambady and Robert Rosenthal of Harvard University asked how much people reveal in a few seconds of behavior. They used videotapes of college teaching fellows giving classes. From each tape they cut three ten-second clips, from the beginning, middle and end of a class, and removed the sound.

Students who had never seen these teachers watched the silent clips and rated them on traits such as confident, active, optimistic, warm, enthusiastic and likable. The researchers then compared these ratings with the evaluations the teachers had received from their own students at the end of the semester, after months of classes.

The match was remarkably strong. Judgments from thirty seconds of silent video predicted the end-of-term ratings well. When the clips were cut down further, to two-second slices, the predictions remained surprisingly good. A similar study with high school teachers found the same pattern. Ambady called these brief samples of behavior "thin slices." Gestures, posture, facial expression and energy communicated a great deal about how a teacher would be experienced, before a single word of content could be judged.
lesson: People read your manner within seconds, before they weigh your words. Warmth, energy and attention in how you show up shape how you are received.
people: Nalini Ambady, Robert Rosenthal
source: Ambady, N., and Rosenthal, R. (1993). Half a minute: Predicting teacher evaluations from thin slices of nonverbal behavior and physical attractiveness. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 64(3), 431-441.
caveat: The samples of teachers were small, and student evaluations themselves reflect impressions more than how much students learn.

title: Tightening the Iron Cage
text:
In the late 1980s, a small American manufacturer of circuit boards, which James Barker called ISE Communications, replaced its traditional hierarchy of supervisors with self-managing teams. Workers would now organize their own work, set their own schedules and hold each other accountable, guided by a shared statement of company values. Barker, a communication scholar, spent long periods at the plant observing meetings, interviewing workers and studying documents.

At first, the teams worked out their norms through discussion, grounded in shared values such as doing quality work and supporting each other. Over time, these norms hardened into formal rules. Teams set strict standards for attendance and punctuality and enforced them on each other, including on coworkers who had been friends. Members described the pressure from peers as much more intense than what they had felt under the old supervisors, because now their colleagues watched them all day and they felt they were letting the team down.

Barker called this concertive control: control that comes from workers themselves, based on shared values, rather than from managers. Borrowing an image from the sociologist Max Weber, he argued that removing the bosses had not freed the workers from the iron cage of bureaucratic control but had made it tighter.
lesson: Self-managed teams can police their members harder than any boss. Watch for peer pressure turning shared values into rigid rules.
people: James Barker
location: A small manufacturing company in the United States
source: Barker, J. R. (1993). Tightening the iron cage: Concertive control in self-managing teams. Administrative Science Quarterly, 38(3), 408-437.

title: Deliberate Practice
text:
In the late 1980s K. Anders Ericsson, Ralf Krampe and Clemens Tesch-Romer studied violin students at the Music Academy of West Berlin, a school that trained many top performers. With the help of the professors, they divided the students into three groups: the best violinists, likely to become international soloists; good violinists; and students training to become music teachers. They also interviewed violinists from professional orchestras.

The researchers asked the musicians to keep detailed diaries of their activities for a week and to estimate how much they had practiced alone at each age since they started. The groups did not differ in how much time they spent on music overall. What separated them was solitary, focused practice: working on specific weaknesses, with full concentration, usually following goals set by a teacher. By age 18, the best violinists had accumulated thousands of hours more of this kind of practice than the future teachers.

Ericsson called this deliberate practice: effortful activity designed specifically to improve performance, which is not inherently enjoyable. The best performers also slept more, including naps, which the authors linked to recovery from such demanding work. Ericsson argued that expert performance reflects long years of deliberate practice more than innate talent.

The study became famous, partly through popular books that turned it into a "10,000-hour rule," a phrase Ericsson himself disputed.
lesson: Improvement comes less from time spent than from focused practice on what you cannot yet do well, with clear goals and feedback. Plan it, protect it, and rest afterwards.
people: K. Anders Ericsson, Ralf Krampe, Clemens Tesch-Romer
location: Music Academy of West Berlin, Germany
source: Ericsson, K. A., Krampe, R. T., and Tesch-Romer, C. (1993). The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance. Psychological Review, 100(3), 363-406.
caveat: A 2014 meta-analysis (Macnamara, Hambrick and Oswald) found that practice explains only part of the differences in skill, so talent and other factors also matter.

title: Fixing Hubble's Flawed Mirror
text:
When the Hubble Space Telescope was launched in April 1990, it was meant to give the sharpest views of the universe ever seen. Within weeks, astronomers realized its images were blurred. The main mirror had been ground to the wrong shape. The error was tiny, about two microns at the edge, a small fraction of the width of a human hair, but enough to spoil the telescope's focus. An investigation traced it to a testing instrument that had been assembled slightly wrong.

Since the mirror could not be replaced in orbit, engineers designed corrections instead, like glasses for the telescope. A new camera was built with the correction in its own optics, and a device called COSTAR would place small corrective mirrors in front of the other instruments.

The repair mission, STS-61, flew on the shuttle Endeavour in December 1993. Its seven astronauts had rehearsed every step for months, including many hours underwater in giant pools that simulate weightlessness. In orbit, Claude Nicollier used the shuttle's robotic arm to capture the telescope, and two pairs of spacewalkers, Story Musgrave and Jeffrey Hoffman, Kathryn Thornton and Tom Akers, worked in turns over five long spacewalks, a record at the time. They installed the new camera and COSTAR, replaced solar panels and gyroscopes, and released Hubble again.

In January 1994 NASA released the first images after the repair. They were sharp. Hubble went on to become one of the most productive scientific instruments ever built.
lesson: Costly mistakes can be fixed when a team owns the problem and prepares thoroughly. Rehearsal turns a risky repair into a routine one.
people: Richard Covey, Story Musgrave, Jeffrey Hoffman, Kathryn Thornton, Tom Akers, Claude Nicollier, NASA engineers
location: Earth orbit, aboard Space Shuttle Endeavour
source: NASA mission reports for STS-61; The Hubble Space Telescope Optical Systems Failure Report (Allen Report, 1990)

title: The Longer Cold Water Trial
text:
In a study published in 1993, Daniel Kahneman, Barbara Fredrickson, Charles Schreiber and Donald Redelmeier asked volunteers to hold one hand in painfully cold water, at about 14 degrees Celsius, in two separate trials.

In the short trial, the hand stayed in the cold water for 60 seconds. In the long trial, it stayed for the same 60 seconds at 14 degrees, and then for 30 more seconds while the researchers quietly let slightly warmer water flow in, raising the temperature by about one degree. The water was still uncomfortable, but a bit less so. The long trial therefore contained everything in the short one, plus extra time in pain.

Afterwards, participants were told they would have to repeat one of the two trials and could choose which. About two thirds chose to repeat the long one. They preferred more total pain because its ending was less bad, and they remembered the long trial as less unpleasant overall.

The result fit what Kahneman called the peak-end rule: when we remember an experience, we judge it mainly by its most intense moment and by how it ended, and we largely ignore how long it lasted. A related study by Redelmeier and Kahneman found the same pattern in patients' memories of colonoscopies. The gap between the experiencing self and the remembering self became a central theme of Kahneman's later work.
lesson: People remember an experience by its high point and its ending more than its length. When you host, teach, treat or serve someone, put special care into how it ends.
people: Daniel Kahneman, Barbara Fredrickson, Charles Schreiber, Donald Redelmeier
source: Kahneman, D., Fredrickson, B. L., Schreiber, C. A., and Redelmeier, D. A. (1993). When more pain is preferred to less: Adding a better end. Psychological Science, 4(6), 401-405.

title: Everyone Thinks Everyone Else Drinks More
text:
In the early 1990s, Deborah Prentice and Dale Miller at Princeton University asked undergraduates two simple questions: how comfortable they personally felt with the drinking habits on campus, and how comfortable they thought the average Princeton student felt.

The students consistently believed that the average student was much more comfortable with heavy drinking than they themselves were. Since the average of their own answers was the actual average student, most of them were wrong about their peers. Each person privately had doubts but assumed everyone else was at ease. This is what social psychologists call pluralistic ignorance: a group in which most members privately reject a norm while wrongly believing that most others accept it.

The researchers followed some students over a semester and found that the misperception had consequences. Male students, in particular, gradually shifted their own attitudes toward what they believed the norm to be. Students who felt that they were out of step with their peers also reported feeling more alienated from the university.

Prentice and Miller suggested that norms like campus drinking can persist because everyone acts according to what they think others want, even when few actually want it.
lesson: A group's apparent consensus may be a shared misunderstanding. If you privately doubt a team norm, say so; others may have been waiting for someone to speak.
people: Deborah Prentice, Dale Miller
source: Prentice, D. A., and Miller, D. T. (1993). Pluralistic ignorance and alcohol use on campus: Some consequences of misperceiving the social norm. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 64(2), 243-256.

title: The Collapse at Mann Gulch
text:
On August 5, 1949, a crew of fifteen smokejumpers parachuted near a fire in Mann Gulch, in the mountains of Montana. They expected a routine fire they could contain by morning. Joined by a fire guard already on the ground, they followed their foreman, Wagner Dodge, down the gulch. Then the fire jumped across and raced uphill toward them through dry grass.

Dodge ordered the men to turn back and drop their heavy tools. With the fire gaining, he did something no one had seen before: he lit a fire in front of himself, let it burn a patch of grass, and lay down in the ashes. He called the others to join him. None did. Two men reached a gap in the ridge and survived. Dodge survived in his burned patch. Thirteen men died.

In 1993, organizational theorist Karl Weick reanalyzed the disaster, drawing on Norman Maclean's book Young Men and Fire. He argued that the crew suffered a collapse of sensemaking. Their picture of a small, routine fire fell apart, and with it their sense of who led and what each person's role was. Many of the men barely knew each other or Dodge. When the leader's strange order came, the group had no shared structure to hold it together.
lesson: Teams hold together through shared roles and a shared picture of what is happening. Build those in calm times, so that an odd but correct order can still be followed in a crisis.
people: Karl Weick; Wagner Dodge and the Mann Gulch crew
source: Weick, K. E. (1993). The collapse of sensemaking in organizations: The Mann Gulch disaster. Administrative Science Quarterly, 38(4), 628-652.

title: The Planning Fallacy
text:
Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky had coined the term planning fallacy in the late 1970s: the habit of underestimating how long a task will take, even when we know similar tasks have run late before. In 1994 Roger Buehler, Dale Griffin and Michael Ross put it to a careful test with university students in Canada.

In one study they asked senior students writing an honors thesis to predict when they would finish it. They also asked for a prediction if everything went as well as possible and one if everything went as badly as possible. On average the students expected to finish in about 34 days. Their worst case averaged about 49 days. In reality they took about 56 days on average, longer even than their own worst-case estimates. Fewer than a third finished by the time they had predicted.

Other studies in the paper showed why. When people forecast, they picture the specific steps of the task ahead and how it will go, a kind of best-case story. They rarely think about how long similar tasks took in the past, and when they do remember past delays, they explain them away as special circumstances that will not happen again. Asking people to connect their past experience to the current plan made their forecasts more realistic.

Observers, interestingly, were less optimistic about other people's tasks than the people themselves were.
lesson: When you estimate how long something will take, look up how long similar things took you before, and plan from that record rather than from your picture of the task going smoothly.
people: Roger Buehler, Dale Griffin, Michael Ross
location: Simon Fraser University and University of Waterloo, Canada
source: Buehler, R., Griffin, D., and Ross, M. (1994). Exploring the 'planning fallacy': Why people underestimate their task completion times. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 67(3), 366-381.

title: One Trader Brings Down Barings Bank
text:
Barings was the oldest merchant bank in London, founded in 1762, a bank that had helped finance the Louisiana Purchase and served the royal family. In the early 1990s it sent a young trader, Nick Leeson, to run its futures operation in Singapore.

Leeson was put in charge both of trading and of the back office that recorded and settled the trades. That meant there was no independent check on what he was doing. When he made losses, he hid them in a secret error account, number 88888, and made larger and larger bets on the Japanese stock market to win the money back. Meanwhile he reported large profits, and London sent him the cash he asked for, without anyone questioning how such low-risk trading could make so much.

In January 1995 the Kobe earthquake sent the Japanese market down, and Leeson's positions collapsed. He fled Singapore in February. The losses came to about 827 million pounds, more than the bank's entire capital. Barings was declared insolvent and was sold to the Dutch bank ING for one pound.

The Bank of England's report blamed serious failures of management and internal control at Barings, as well as Leeson's fraud.
lesson: Never let anyone check their own work, and question results that look too good. What you do not understand can ruin you.
people: Nick Leeson, Barings Bank
source: Bank of England, Report of the Board of Banking Supervision Inquiry into the Circumstances of the Collapse of Barings (July 1995)

title: Myopic Loss Aversion
text:
For most of the twentieth century, American stocks earned far higher returns than safe government bonds, several percentage points a year more on average. Economists called this gap the equity premium puzzle, because standard theories said investors would need to be implausibly afraid of risk to leave so much money on the table.

In 1995 Shlomo Benartzi and Richard Thaler offered an explanation built from two ideas. The first was loss aversion, from Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory: losses hurt roughly twice as much as equal gains please. The second was mental accounting: investors evaluate their portfolios at intervals, and each evaluation is felt as a gain or a loss.

Put together, these create what they called myopic loss aversion. Over a single day or month, stocks fall almost as often as they rise, so an investor who looks often experiences many painful losses and finds stocks unattractive. Over many years, stocks almost always come out ahead. Benartzi and Thaler calculated that the historical equity premium was just what one would expect if investors evaluated their portfolios about once a year.

Later experiments confirmed the idea. In a 1997 study by Thaler, Tversky, Kahneman and Schwartz, people who received frequent feedback on a simulated investment took less risk and earned less than those who received feedback rarely. Looking too often made investors more cautious and poorer.
lesson: For long-term goals, check your progress less often. Frequent glances at short-term ups and downs magnify losses in your mind and push you toward overly cautious, costly decisions.
people: Shlomo Benartzi, Richard Thaler
location: USA (analysis of historical US market data)
source: Benartzi, S., and Thaler, R. H. (1995). Myopic loss aversion and the equity premium puzzle. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 110(1), 73-92.

title: The Trust Game
text:
Economic theory long assumed that strangers who would never meet again had no reason to trust each other. In 1995 Joyce Berg, John Dickhaut and Kevin McCabe of the University of Minnesota designed a game to see what real people do.

Students were split into two rooms and paired anonymously, so no one ever learned who their partner was, and even the experimenters could not link choices to individuals. Each person in the first room received 10 dollars. They could keep it all or send any part of it to their partner in the other room. Whatever they sent was tripled on the way. The partner then decided how much, if any, of the tripled amount to send back.

A purely selfish partner would return nothing, and a sender who expected that would send nothing. That is not what happened. Nearly all senders sent some money, on average about half of their 10 dollars. Many receivers returned money too, some more than had been sent, though others kept everything. On average, senders got back about as much as they had sent, or slightly less. The game, now known as the trust game or investment game, became a standard tool for studying trust and reciprocity around the world.
lesson: Most people are willing to extend some trust to strangers, and many repay it. Trusting first is a risk, but it is often the only way to start something good.
people: Joyce Berg, John Dickhaut, Kevin McCabe
source: Berg, J., Dickhaut, J., and McCabe, K. (1995). Trust, reciprocity, and social history. Games and Economic Behavior, 10(1), 122-142.

title: Natural Frequencies
text:
A classic problem in medical reasoning goes like this. The probability that a woman of a certain age has breast cancer is 1 percent. If she has cancer, the probability that a mammogram is positive is 80 percent. If she does not, the probability of a positive result is still 9.6 percent. A woman tests positive. What is the chance she actually has cancer? The correct answer is only about 8 percent, but most people, including many doctors in earlier studies, guess far higher, often around 70 or 80 percent.

In 1995 the psychologists Gerd Gigerenzer and Ulrich Hoffrage argued that the difficulty lay less in people's minds than in the format of the information. Human beings, they reasoned, did not evolve to handle percentages and conditional probabilities, but they are used to counting cases as they encounter them.

They gave university students a set of such problems in two formats. One used probabilities as above. The other used natural frequencies: of 1,000 women, 10 have breast cancer; of these 10, 8 test positive; of the 990 without cancer, about 95 also test positive. Put that way, the answer becomes visible: 8 of the roughly 103 women who test positive actually have cancer. With probabilities, only about one in six students reasoned correctly. With natural frequencies, the share rose to almost half, with no training at all.

Gigerenzer later used this approach to teach doctors and judges to understand test results and risks.
lesson: When you explain or judge a risk, such as a test result, turn the percentages into counts: out of 1,000 people, how many have the condition, how many test positive, and how many of those are real cases.
people: Gerd Gigerenzer, Ulrich Hoffrage
source: Gigerenzer, G., and Hoffrage, U. (1995). How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: Frequency formats. Psychological Review, 102(4), 684-704.

title: The Words Children Hear
text:
In the 1960s, Betty Hart and Todd Risley ran a preschool program in Kansas City and were frustrated that its vocabulary gains faded. They decided to look at what happened at home, long before preschool.

They recruited 42 families with babies, ranging from professional families to families receiving welfare. Every month for about two and a half years, from before the children could talk until they were three, an observer spent an hour in each home recording everything said to and around the child. The researchers then transcribed and coded the tapes, a task that took years.

The differences were striking. Some parents talked with their children far more than others, used a richer vocabulary, asked more questions and gave more encouragement and fewer prohibitions. On average, children in professional families heard many more words per hour than children in families on welfare. The amount and quality of talk in the home predicted the children's vocabulary at age three and their language skills in later school years.

Hart and Risley extrapolated that by age four, some children would have heard about 30 million fewer words than others, a figure that became famous as the word gap and shaped many parenting programs.
lesson: Talking with a small child, not just near them, is one of the simplest gifts you can give. Narrate, ask, listen and answer.
people: Betty Hart, Todd Risley
source: Hart, B., and Risley, T. R. (1995). Meaningful Differences in the Everyday Experience of Young American Children. Baltimore: Paul H. Brookes.
caveat: The sample was small, and later studies (for example Sperry, Sperry and Miller, 2019) have disputed the size of the class gap, especially when speech by other family members is counted.

title: Navigating a Warship
text:
In the 1980s, cognitive scientist Edwin Hutchins spent time aboard a US Navy ship, which he called the Palau, observing how its crew navigated. When the ship moved through coastal waters, a team on the bridge had to determine its position at regular intervals. Sailors on each side of the ship took bearings on landmarks with special instruments and called them out over a phone. Another sailor recorded them, and a plotter used charts and tools to fix the ship's position and project its course.

Hutchins argued that no single person on the bridge knew where the ship was in a complete sense. The knowledge was produced by the whole system: the people, their instruments, the charts and the routines they followed. Some computations were built into the tools themselves, and the division of labor allowed the team to do what no individual could do alone.

He described one dramatic episode. As the ship was entering San Diego harbor, it suffered an engineering failure that cut power to some of the navigation equipment. The team had to make its calculations by hand. Under pressure and without a plan, the sailors gradually invented a new division of labor among themselves, and the ship came through safely.
lesson: Much of a team's intelligence lives in its tools, routines and shared work, not in any one head. Design those systems well, and they will carry the team through surprises.
people: Edwin Hutchins
source: Hutchins, E. (1995). Cognition in the Wild. MIT Press.

title: Training Together Builds Team Memory
text:
Should team members be trained individually or together? Diane Wei Liang, Richard Moreland and Linda Argote, at Carnegie Mellon University and the University of Pittsburgh, tested this with a hands-on task: assembling a transistor radio from a kit.

Participants were trained to build the radio either alone or in the groups of three that they would later work in. A week later, each group was asked to assemble the radio together, without instructions. The researchers measured how well the groups recalled the steps and how many errors their finished radios had.

Groups whose members had been trained together recalled more about how to build the radio and made fewer errors. Observing videotapes of the sessions, the researchers found that these groups showed more signs of what is called transactive memory: members knew who was good at what, trusted each other's knowledge, and coordinated smoothly. Each member specialized in part of the task, and the others relied on that.
lesson: Teams work better when members know who knows what. Train people together on the actual work, so they learn each other's strengths along with the task.
people: Diane Wei Liang, Richard Moreland, Linda Argote
location: Carnegie Mellon University and University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, USA
source: Liang, D. W., Moreland, R., and Argote, L. (1995). Group versus individual training and group performance: The mediating role of transactive memory. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 21(4), 384-393.

title: Aaron Feuerstein Keeps Paying His Workers
text:
On the night of December 11, 1995, a fire destroyed most of the Malden Mills textile plant in Lawrence and Methuen, Massachusetts. The family company made Polartec fleece and employed around three thousand people in a region that had already lost much of its industry. Its owner, Aaron Feuerstein, was seventy years old, and the insurance money would have let him close or move production somewhere cheaper.

Instead, a few days later, he announced that he would rebuild in Lawrence and that every worker would keep receiving full pay for the next thirty days. When the month ran out he extended it, and then extended it again. Workers received their wages and health benefits for months while the plant was rebuilt, at a cost to the company of millions of dollars.

The decision made Feuerstein a national figure. He was invited to the State of the Union address and praised by politicians and business writers. Most of the workers came back when the new plant opened.

The story did not end simply. The rebuilding left Malden Mills heavily in debt, and in 2001 the company filed for bankruptcy. Feuerstein lost control of it.
lesson: Loyalty to the people who depend on you can be right even when it is costly, but it is wise to count the cost honestly before you choose.
people: Aaron Feuerstein, Malden Mills
source: Contemporary press reports (Boston Globe, New York Times, CBS 60 Minutes)
caveat: Analysts disagree about how far the costly rebuilding and payroll decisions contributed to the company's later bankruptcy.

title: Mandela Invites His Prosecutor to Lunch
text:
In 1963 and 1964 Percy Yutar was the state prosecutor at the Rivonia Trial, where Nelson Mandela and his comrades were tried for sabotage and conspiracy against the apartheid state. Yutar prosecuted the case aggressively. The accused faced a possible death sentence, and Mandela and most of the others were sentenced to life imprisonment. Mandela remained in prison until 1990, twenty seven years after his arrest in 1962.

In 1994 Mandela became President of South Africa. In November 1995 he invited Yutar, by then an old man, to lunch at his official residence in Pretoria. The meal was kosher, out of respect for Yutar's Jewish faith. Afterward Yutar spoke to reporters about the President's kindness and said he had only been doing his duty under the law of the time.

The lunch was one of several deliberate gestures Mandela made that year toward former adversaries, including a visit to Betsie Verwoerd, widow of the architect of apartheid. Many people, including some of his own supporters, found them hard to accept. Mandela saw them as a way to show white South Africans that the new government would not seek revenge.
lesson: Reconciliation becomes believable when you reach out personally to the people who wronged you. Such gestures cost pride, but they can reassure a whole frightened community.
people: Nelson Mandela, Percy Yutar
source: Contemporary South African press reports (November 1995); Anthony Sampson, Mandela: The Authorized Biography (1999)

title: Mandela Wears the Springbok Jersey
text:
In 1995, a year after the end of apartheid, South Africa hosted the Rugby World Cup. Rugby was the sport of the white Afrikaner minority, and the green Springbok jersey was, for many black South Africans, a symbol of the old regime. Some in the African National Congress wanted the Springbok name and emblem dropped.

Nelson Mandela, now president, took the opposite view. He argued for keeping the name, met the team, and built a relationship with its captain, Francois Pienaar. The squad learned to sing Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika, which now stood beside the old anthem Die Stem as one of the country's two national anthems.

On June 24, 1995, South Africa played New Zealand in the final at Ellis Park in Johannesburg, before a mostly white crowd. Mandela walked onto the field wearing a Springbok jersey and cap, with Pienaar's number 6 on the back. The crowd began chanting his name.

South Africa won 15 to 12 in extra time. Mandela handed the trophy to Pienaar, who said afterward that the team had not had the support of 63,000 South Africans but of 43 million.
lesson: Reaching out to the people who fear you, through what they care about, can do more to build unity than any speech.
people: Nelson Mandela, Francois Pienaar
source: Contemporary press reports; John Carlin, Playing the Enemy (2008)

title: Why Silver Medalists Look Less Happy
text:
In the mid-1990s Victoria Husted Medvec, Scott Madey and Thomas Gilovich of Cornell University studied television footage of athletes at the 1992 Summer Olympics in Barcelona. They showed clips of silver and bronze medalists, captured at the moment the athletes learned their result and later on the medal stand, to students who knew little about sports and did not know who had placed where.

The students rated each athlete's expression on a scale from agony to ecstasy. On average, the bronze medalists looked happier than the silver medalists, both right after the competition and on the podium. In another part of the study, the researchers analyzed televised interviews and found that silver medalists talked more about what they had almost achieved, while bronze medalists talked more about having at least made it.

The explanation lay in what the athletes compared themselves with. The silver medalist, just short of first place, naturally thinks of the gold that slipped away. The bronze medalist, just above fourth place, thinks of how close they came to going home with nothing. The objectively better result produced the worse feeling.

The authors linked this to counterfactual thinking: our feelings about an outcome depend heavily on the alternatives that come to mind. A follow-up study of athletes at a regional athletic competition in New York found the same pattern.
lesson: How you feel about a result depends on what you compare it with. When you catch yourself dwelling on what you just missed, also consider what you just avoided.
people: Victoria Husted Medvec, Scott Madey, Thomas Gilovich
location: Cornell University, Ithaca, USA (footage of the 1992 Barcelona Olympics)
source: Medvec, V. H., Madey, S. F., and Gilovich, T. (1995). When less is more: Counterfactual thinking and satisfaction among Olympic medalists. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 69(4), 603-610.
caveat: Later work (McGraw, Mellers and Tetlock, 2005) found that athletes' prior expectations also shape their reactions, so the pattern does not always hold.

title: Guess Two Thirds of the Average
text:
John Maynard Keynes once compared the stock market to a newspaper beauty contest in which readers win by picking not the face they find prettiest, but the one they expect others to pick. In 1995 the economist Rosemarie Nagel published experiments that turned this idea into a simple game.

Groups of about fifteen to eighteen students in Germany were each asked to choose a number from 0 to 100. The winner was the person whose number came closest to a fraction, for example two thirds, of the group's average. The game was repeated four times, with the results announced after each round.

If everyone chose at random, the average would be around 50, so a smart player might guess about 33. But if everyone thought that way, the best answer would be about 22, and so on. Following this logic all the way leads to zero, the game's theoretical solution. Few players went that far. Nagel found clusters of first-round choices near 33 and 22, suggesting that most players reasoned one or two steps ahead and stopped. Some chose numbers with no clear reasoning. Over the repeated rounds, guesses fell steadily toward zero as players learned how others behaved.

Nagel's study launched a large body of research on how many steps of reasoning people actually perform. It showed that the winning answer is not the most logical one, but the one that correctly anticipates how deeply others think.
lesson: In any competitive situation, think about how others will actually reason, not how a perfectly logical player would. Being exactly one step ahead often beats being many steps ahead.
people: Rosemarie Nagel
source: Nagel, R. (1995). Unraveling in guessing games: An experimental study. American Economic Review, 85(5), 1313-1326.

title: Half a Team at Xerox
text:
In the early 1990s, Ruth Wageman studied customer service technicians at Xerox, the people who traveled to clients to repair copiers. Xerox was reorganizing them into teams, and the teams differed in how their work and their rewards were set up.

Some teams were designed so that technicians truly shared the work and were rewarded on team results. Others worked mostly as individuals with individual rewards. Many were hybrids, with some shared tasks, some individual ones, and a mix of team and individual rewards. Wageman, then at Harvard, studied about 150 of these teams, measuring how they operated and how well they performed on Xerox's service measures.

The clearly designed teams did well, whether they were fully interdependent or largely individual. The hybrid teams did worst. Members of mixed teams carried the costs of teamwork, such as coordination and meetings, without getting its benefits, and their groups showed poorer working processes and lower member satisfaction. The lesson Wageman drew was that half measures are risky: the way the work is organized and the way people are rewarded should point in the same direction.
lesson: Decide whether a group is really a team or a set of individuals, and design the work and the rewards to match. Halfway arrangements tend to get the worst of both.
people: Ruth Wageman
source: Wageman, R. (1995). Interdependence and group effectiveness. Administrative Science Quarterly, 40(1), 145-180.

title: The Units That Reported More Errors
text:
In the early 1990s Amy Edmondson, then a doctoral student at Harvard, joined a large study of medication errors in hospitals. Her task was to look at the nursing units involved and see whether the quality of their teamwork and leadership affected how many drug errors they made. She surveyed the staff of eight units in two hospitals, while medical researchers independently tracked the errors.

The data showed something unexpected. The units with the best leadership and the strongest working relationships did not have fewer errors. They appeared to have more. At first Edmondson thought the analysis was wrong. Then she considered a different explanation: perhaps the better units were not making more mistakes, but were more willing to report them.

To find out, a research assistant who did not know her hypothesis visited the units and observed how they worked. In some units, nurses said that mistakes were natural and talked about them openly. In others, nurses described being treated as if on trial when an error came to light, and admitting a mistake felt dangerous. The units where it felt safe to speak up were the ones with the higher reported error rates. The insight became the basis of Edmondson's later work on psychological safety.
lesson: A low count of reported problems may mean people are hiding them. Leaders who make it safe to admit mistakes see their problems early enough to fix them.
people: Amy Edmondson
source: Edmondson, A. C. (1996). Learning from mistakes is easier said than done: Group and organizational influences on the detection and correction of human error. Journal of Applied Behavioral Science, 32(1), 5-28.

title: Emotion Coaching Parents
text:
John Gottman, Lynn Katz and Carole Hooven wanted to know how parents' attitudes toward emotions shape their children. They studied families with young children, interviewing each parent at length about their own feelings and how they responded to their children's sadness and anger. They called this a parent's meta-emotion philosophy: their feelings about feelings.

Some parents tended to dismiss children's negative emotions. They distracted the child, minimized the problem, or wanted the feeling to pass quickly. Others were critical, punishing the child for showing anger or sadness. A third group, which the researchers called emotion coaching parents, did something different. They noticed even mild emotions in their children, saw them as a chance for closeness and teaching, helped the child put a name to the feeling, listened with empathy, and set limits on behavior while helping the child solve the problem.

The researchers followed the children for several years. Children whose parents practiced emotion coaching were better at calming themselves when upset, as shown even in measures of their physiology. By around age eight they also did better in school, got along better with other children and had fewer behavior problems.

Gottman later popularized these findings in his book Raising an Emotionally Intelligent Child.
lesson: A child's anger or sadness is a chance to connect and teach, not a problem to shut down. Name the feeling, empathize, and then help solve the problem.
people: John Gottman, Lynn Katz, Carole Hooven
source: Gottman, J. M., Katz, L. F., and Hooven, C. (1996). Parental meta-emotion philosophy and the emotional life of families: Theoretical models and preliminary data. Journal of Family Psychology, 10(3), 243-268.
caveat: The original sample was small and the results correlational, though later intervention studies of emotion coaching have reported encouraging results.

title: Seeing Your Partner a Little Better
text:
Sandra Murray, John Holmes and Dale Griffin, working at the University of Waterloo in Canada, wondered whether happy couples see each other accurately or through a slightly rosy lens. They recruited both dating and married couples and asked each person to rate themselves, their partner and their ideal partner on a long list of qualities, such as kind, understanding, patient, critical or lazy.

This allowed a clever comparison. The researchers could see how each person viewed their partner, and how that partner viewed themselves. If a woman rated her husband as more patient and understanding than he rated himself, she was seeing him through a positive illusion.

That is what many people did. They tended to see their partners more generously than the partners saw themselves, and their image of their partner resembled their image of an ideal partner. These positive illusions went along with greater satisfaction. People were happier when they idealized their partners, and also when they were idealized by them.

In a related follow-up, the same team found that dating couples who idealized each other more were more likely to stay together and to become more satisfied over time, as if being seen at one's best helped people live up to it.
lesson: Look at the people you love a little more generously than strict accuracy requires. Being seen at your best can help you become it.
people: Sandra Murray, John Holmes, Dale Griffin
source: Murray, S. L., Holmes, J. G., and Griffin, D. W. (1996). The benefits of positive illusions: Idealization and the construction of satisfaction in close relationships. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 70(1), 79-98.

title: Desmond Tutu and the Truth Commission
text:
When apartheid ended and Nelson Mandela became president in 1994, South Africa faced a hard question: what to do about decades of torture, killings and disappearances. Full trials could take forever and might tear the fragile country apart. A blanket amnesty would deny victims justice. Parliament chose a third way and created the Truth and Reconciliation Commission in 1995, with Archbishop Desmond Tutu as chairman.

From 1996 the commission held public hearings across the country, broadcast on radio and television. Thousands of victims and their families came forward to tell what had happened to them, often for the first time in public. At one early hearing Tutu himself put his head on the table and wept.

Perpetrators could apply for amnesty for politically motivated crimes, but only if they made full disclosure of what they had done. Police officers described in detail how they had tortured and killed activists, sometimes facing the families of their victims.

In October 1998 Tutu presented the commission's final report to Mandela. Tutu argued that there could be no future without forgiveness, but that forgiveness required the truth to be told first.
lesson: Reconciliation needs the truth to be told and heard before forgiveness can be real. Acknowledging what happened is the first step toward healing any broken relationship.
people: Desmond Tutu, Nelson Mandela
source: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of South Africa Report (1998); Desmond Tutu, No Future Without Forgiveness (1999)
caveat: The commission has been criticized because few perpetrators who were refused amnesty or did not apply were later prosecuted, and reparations to victims were limited.

title: Thirty-Six Questions to Closeness
text:
In the 1990s the psychologists Arthur Aron, Elaine Aron and their colleagues at the State University of New York at Stony Brook wanted to create closeness between strangers in the lab, so they could study it. Their tool was a list of thirty-six questions, divided into three sets of growing intimacy.

Pairs of students who had never met spent about forty-five minutes taking turns asking and answering the questions. The first set was light: whom would you want as a dinner guest, what would make a perfect day. The second went deeper, into treasured memories and what one valued most in a friendship. The last set asked for real vulnerability, such as when one had last cried in front of someone, or what one would most regret not having told someone if one died that evening. Other pairs spent the same time on small-talk questions.

At the end, pairs who had worked through the escalating questions reported feeling much closer to each other than the small-talk pairs. The key ingredients were that disclosure was mutual, gradual and sustained: each person took risks in turn, and each step went a bit deeper than the last. The procedure became widely known decades later through a newspaper essay about falling in love with it.
lesson: Closeness grows when two people open up a little more at each turn, and both take the risk. Ask questions that go one step deeper, and answer them yourself.
people: Arthur Aron, Edward Melinat, Elaine Aron, Robert Vallone, Renee Bator
location: State University of New York at Stony Brook, USA
source: Aron, A., Melinat, E., Aron, E. N., Vallone, R. D., and Bator, R. J. (1997). The experimental generation of interpersonal closeness: A procedure and some preliminary findings. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 23(4), 363-377.

title: Both Sides Think They Are Right
text:
Why do so many disputes end in costly lawsuits and strikes, when both sides would gain by settling? In a series of experiments during the 1990s, summarized in a 1997 article, Linda Babcock and George Loewenstein of Carnegie Mellon University pointed to a simple bias.

Pairs of participants were given the same materials from a real legal case in Texas, in which a motorcyclist had been hit by a car and was suing the driver for 100,000 dollars in damages. The materials included testimony, police reports and depositions. One participant was assigned to play the plaintiff, the other the defendant. Before negotiating, each privately predicted what the judge in the actual case had awarded, with a bonus for accuracy. Then they bargained, with costs mounting for every round without agreement. If they failed to settle, the judge's award was imposed.

Though both read the same facts, plaintiffs predicted much higher awards than defendants did. Each side recalled and weighed more heavily the facts that favored itself. The larger the gap in predictions within a pair, the more likely the pair was to reach an impasse.

In one variation, participants learned which role they would play only after reading the case. Their predictions converged, and impasses dropped sharply. In another, asking participants to write down the weaknesses of their own side's case reduced the bias, while merely explaining the bias to them did not help.
lesson: In any dispute, expect that your reading of the facts leans toward your side. Before negotiating, list the strongest points against your own position; it makes settlement more likely.
people: Linda Babcock, George Loewenstein
source: Babcock, L., and Loewenstein, G. (1997). Explaining bargaining impasse: The role of self-serving biases. Journal of Economic Perspectives, 11(1), 109-126.

title: New York Cab Drivers and the Daily Target
text:
New York City cab drivers in the late 1980s and early 1990s typically rented their cabs for a fixed fee per shift and then decided for themselves how long to drive. Some days were busy, with rain, conventions or holidays filling the cab; others were slow. A rational worker, economists reasoned, should drive longer on busy days, when each hour pays well, and go home early on slow ones.

Colin Camerer, Linda Babcock, George Loewenstein and Richard Thaler examined thousands of drivers' trip sheets, the logs of every fare, from several data sets. They found the opposite pattern, especially among less experienced drivers. On days when hourly earnings were high, many drivers quit early; on slow days, they drove longer.

The researchers proposed that drivers were working toward a daily income target, such as earning twice the lease fee, and quitting once they reached it. Taking each day separately, they called it working "one day at a time." Such narrow bracketing made sense as a simple rule of thumb that protected against quitting too early on bad days, but it cost the drivers money: by their estimate, working the same total hours but more of them on good days would have raised drivers' earnings noticeably.

The study became a classic of behavioral labor economics. It also became controversial. Using different data and methods, Henry Farber found that the decision to stop depended mainly on hours already worked, and that evidence for strong income targeting was weak.
lesson: When you set daily or weekly goals, notice whether a fixed target is making you stop exactly when effort pays best. Judge your effort over a longer stretch, not one day at a time.
people: Colin Camerer, Linda Babcock, George Loewenstein, Richard Thaler
source: Camerer, C., Babcock, L., Loewenstein, G., and Thaler, R. (1997). Labor supply of New York City cabdrivers: One day at a time. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 112(2), 407-441.
caveat: Later studies, notably by Henry Farber (2005, 2015), found little evidence of strong daily income targeting, so the result is disputed.

title: Paying a Town to Accept Nuclear Waste
text:
In the early 1990s the Swiss government was searching for a site to store low and medium level radioactive waste, and communities in central Switzerland were among the candidates. In 1993 the economists Bruno Frey and Felix Oberholzer-Gee surveyed residents of the area.

First, residents were asked whether they would accept a repository in their community if parliament decided to build it there. About half, a little over 50 percent, said yes, despite real fears about safety. Many explained that they saw it as a civic duty: the waste had to go somewhere, and someone had to accept it.

Then the researchers asked the same question with an added offer: the federal government would pay each resident a substantial sum of compensation every year. Standard economics predicts that money should increase acceptance. Instead, support fell to about 25 percent. Raising the amount offered did not bring it back up.

Frey and Oberholzer-Gee argued that the offer of money crowded out civic motivation. Accepting the facility for the common good felt honorable; accepting it in exchange for cash felt like a bribe, or suggested that the risks were greater than officials admitted. Once the decision was framed as a deal, people judged it as a deal, and many found the price too low. The study became a key example of motivation crowding, the idea that external rewards can weaken intrinsic or moral reasons for acting.
lesson: When asking people to bear a burden for a shared good, appeal first to their sense of duty and fairness. Offering money can turn a civic act into a bargain and make people less willing.
people: Bruno Frey, Felix Oberholzer-Gee
source: Frey, B. S., and Oberholzer-Gee, F. (1997). The cost of price incentives: An empirical analysis of motivation crowding-out. American Economic Review, 87(4), 746-755.
caveat: The findings come from survey answers about a hypothetical offer, not from observed behavior.

title: When, Where and How
text:
Most people know the gap between intending to do something and actually doing it. The German psychologist Peter Gollwitzer proposed a simple bridge: an implementation intention, a plan in the form "When situation X arises, I will do Y." In 1997 he and Veronika Brandstatter published studies testing it.

In one study, university students in Germany were asked, just before the Christmas holidays, to write a report about how they spent Christmas Eve and to send it in within two days of the holiday. Some students were also asked to write down exactly when and where during those two days they would write the report. The others received no such instruction.

The difference was large. Students who had formed a specific plan were far more likely to deliver the report on time, more than twice as often as those who had not. The plan took only a minute to make, yet it made the moment of action easier to recognize and to seize when it came.

Other studies in the paper showed that people with implementation intentions acted more promptly when the planned opportunity arrived. Over the following decades, hundreds of studies tested the technique for goals ranging from exercise and healthy eating to cancer screenings and voting. A 2006 meta-analysis by Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran found a medium to large effect on goal attainment.
lesson: Turn a vague goal into a specific if-then plan: when, where and how you will act. Deciding the moment in advance makes it much more likely that you will act when it arrives.
people: Peter Gollwitzer, Veronika Brandstatter
source: Gollwitzer, P. M., and Brandstatter, V. (1997). Implementation intentions and effective goal pursuit. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 73(1), 186-199.

title: Adverse Childhood Experiences
text:
In the 1980s, the physician Vincent Felitti ran a weight-loss program at Kaiser Permanente in San Diego. He was puzzled that some patients who were losing weight successfully dropped out. Talking with them, he heard surprisingly often about abuse in childhood. Weight, for some, seemed to be a kind of protection.

Together with Robert Anda of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Felitti designed a much larger study. In 1995 and 1996, adults coming to Kaiser's San Diego clinic for routine health checkups were sent a questionnaire about their childhoods, and more than 9,500 answered. It asked about seven kinds of adversity: psychological, physical and sexual abuse, and growing up with a household member who abused alcohol or drugs, was mentally ill, had been in prison, or with a mother who was treated violently.

These patients were mostly middle class, educated and insured. Even so, more than half reported at least one category of adversity, and about one in sixteen reported four or more. The more categories a person had experienced, the higher their rates of smoking, heavy drinking, drug use, depression, suicide attempts, and diseases such as heart disease, lung disease and cancer decades later.

The ACE study changed how many doctors, schools and courts think about childhood hardship and adult health.
lesson: What happens in a home echoes through a whole life. Protecting children from violence and chaos is also protecting the adults they will become.
people: Vincent Felitti, Robert Anda and colleagues
source: Felitti, V. J., Anda, R. F., Nordenberg, D., Williamson, D. F., Spitz, A. M., Edwards, V., Koss, M. P., and Marks, J. S. (1998). Relationship of childhood abuse and household dysfunction to many of the leading causes of death in adults: The Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACE) Study. American Journal of Preventive Medicine, 14(4), 245-258.
caveat: The data are retrospective and correlational, and researchers warn that an individual's ACE score cannot predict that person's future.

title: Immune Neglect
text:
In 1998 Daniel Gilbert, Elizabeth Pinel, Timothy Wilson, Stephen Blumberg and Thalia Wheatley published a series of studies on how well people predict their own emotional reactions to bad news.

In one study, they surveyed assistant professors at a large university about how happy they expected to be in the years after a tenure decision went for or against them. They also surveyed former assistant professors who had already been granted or denied tenure. The junior faculty expected to be considerably less happy for years if they were denied. But those who had actually been turned down were, on average, about as happy as those who had succeeded.

Similar gaps appeared elsewhere. Students predicted how they would feel some months after a romantic relationship ended, and those whose relationships had in fact ended were happier than predicted. Voters in a Texas governor's race expected their candidate's defeat to bother them for a month; a month later it bothered them much less than they had forecast. In a lab study, people rejected for a job by a single evaluator recovered faster than they expected.

The researchers called this immune neglect. People have a psychological immune system: they find silver linings, reinterpret events and move on. But they do not take this ability into account when they imagine the future, so they overestimate how long setbacks will hurt.
lesson: When you fear a setback, remember that you will likely adapt and recover faster than you now imagine. Do not let an exaggerated fear of disappointment keep you from trying.
people: Daniel Gilbert, Elizabeth Pinel, Timothy Wilson, Stephen Blumberg, Thalia Wheatley
location: University of Texas at Austin and other US universities, USA
source: Gilbert, D. T., Pinel, E. C., Wilson, T. D., Blumberg, S. J., and Wheatley, T. P. (1998). Immune neglect: A source of durability bias in affective forecasting. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 75(3), 617-638.

title: Newlyweds and Accepting Influence
text:
In the late 1980s and early 1990s, John Gottman and his colleagues at the University of Washington in Seattle invited 130 newlywed couples into their laboratory. Each couple was asked to discuss an ongoing disagreement in their marriage for about fifteen minutes while the researchers videotaped them and coded every expression and remark. The couples were then followed for six years.

The researchers expected to find that the happiest couples practiced active listening, the technique often taught in therapy, in which one partner paraphrases and validates the other's complaint. Instead, they found that it was rare among all couples, happy or not.

What did predict divorce was a pattern of escalating negativity. Marriages were in more danger when discussions began harshly, when negative remarks were met with even stronger negative remarks, and when couples failed to calm things down with humor or affection. One finding drew particular attention: husbands who refused to accept influence from their wives, answering a complaint by escalating rather than taking any part of it on board, were more likely to end up divorced.

In stable, happy couples, conflict still happened. But it was softened, and both partners let the other shape their decisions.
lesson: In any close relationship, let the other person change your mind sometimes. How a disagreement starts and whether you calm it down matter more than perfect listening technique.
people: John Gottman, James Coan, Sybil Carrere, Catherine Swanson
source: Gottman, J. M., Coan, J., Carrere, S., and Swanson, C. (1998). Predicting marital happiness and stability from newlywed interactions. Journal of Marriage and the Family, 60(1), 5-22.
caveat: Some statisticians have criticized Gottman's divorce predictions as fitted after the fact to the same sample rather than tested on new couples.

title: Hadza Grandmothers
text:
Humans are unusual among primates: women often live for decades after they stop being able to have children. The anthropologist Kristen Hawkes and her colleagues wondered why evolution would favor such long lives, and found a clue among the Hadza, hunter-gatherers living near Lake Eyasi in northern Tanzania.

Observing and measuring how Hadza women spent their days, the team noticed that older women were among the hardest workers in camp. They spent long hours gathering food, especially digging up deep tubers, a task too difficult for young children. Much of what they gathered went to their grandchildren and other young relatives.

The effect showed up in the children. When a mother had a new baby and could forage less, her weaned children's growth depended on how much time their grandmother spent gathering for them. A hardworking grandmother helped keep them well fed.

In a 1998 paper, Hawkes, James O'Connell, Nicholas Blurton Jones, Helen Alvarez and Eric Charnov proposed the grandmother hypothesis. In ancestral humans, they argued, older women who helped feed their grandchildren allowed their daughters to have babies more often, and their descendants thrived. Over many generations, this could have favored longer lifespans, and with them other features of human life, such as long childhoods.
lesson: Grandparents are not a footnote in family life; they may be part of why our species thrives. Draw them in and honor what they give.
people: Kristen Hawkes, James O'Connell, Nicholas Blurton Jones, Helen Alvarez, Eric Charnov
location: Hadza territory near Lake Eyasi, Tanzania
source: Hawkes, K., O'Connell, J. F., Blurton Jones, N. G., Alvarez, H., and Charnov, E. L. (1998). Grandmothering, menopause, and the evolution of human life histories. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 95(3), 1336-1339.
caveat: The grandmother hypothesis remains debated among anthropologists, and other explanations for long human lifespans have been proposed.

title: A Good Marriage and the End of Crime
text:
In the 1940s, the criminologists Sheldon and Eleanor Glueck at Harvard began following 500 boys from Boston who had been sent to reform schools for delinquency, along with 500 boys from similar neighborhoods who had not. They tracked the delinquent group into their thirties. Decades later, John Laub and Robert Sampson found the Gluecks' records in boxes in the basement of the Harvard Law School library and set out to analyze them with modern methods.

In a 1998 study with the statistician Daniel Nagin, they looked at how the former delinquents' offending changed over adulthood. Some men kept committing crimes; others gradually stopped. The researchers asked what life events went along with stopping.

Marriage stood out, but only a certain kind. It was not the wedding that mattered, but forming a good, cohesive marriage: one in which the man was attached to his wife and the bond was strong. Men who formed such marriages tended to reduce their offending, and the effect built up gradually over the years, as the relationship deepened and daily life changed. Weak marriages showed no such benefit.

Laub and Sampson argued that strong bonds give men something to lose, reshape their routines and connect them with new friends and family.
lesson: People can change at any age, especially when they have a strong bond to protect. A committed relationship can reshape a life over time.
people: John Laub, Daniel Nagin, Robert Sampson
source: Laub, J. H., Nagin, D. S., and Sampson, R. J. (1998). Trajectories of change in criminal offending: Good marriages and the desistance process. American Sociological Review, 63(2), 225-238.
caveat: The data were observational, so men who were already changing may have been more likely to form good marriages.

title: The Fall of Long-Term Capital Management
text:
Long-Term Capital Management was founded in 1994 by John Meriwether, a celebrated bond trader from Salomon Brothers. His partners included top traders and two of the most famous economists in finance, Myron Scholes and Robert Merton, who shared the Nobel Prize in economics in 1997. The fund bet on small price differences between related securities, expecting them to converge, and used sophisticated models built on historical data.

Because each bet earned very little, the fund borrowed heavily to make the returns worthwhile. At its peak, it held assets worth well over a hundred billion dollars on a capital base of under five billion, plus derivative positions with a far larger face value. For its first years returns were excellent, and banks competed to lend to it.

In August 1998 Russia defaulted on its debt. Investors around the world fled to the safest, most liquid assets. The price differences that LTCM had bet would narrow instead widened sharply, in many markets at once, a combination its models treated as extremely unlikely. Because of its leverage, the fund lost billions within weeks, and because everyone knew its positions were huge, it could not sell them without driving prices further against itself.

In September 1998, fearing a wider financial panic, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York brought together major banks, which put in about 3.6 billion dollars to take over the fund and wind it down in an orderly way. The original partners lost most of their own investments.
lesson: Models based on the past can fail exactly when it matters most. Leverage turns rare events into fatal ones, so leave a margin for being wrong.
people: John Meriwether, Myron Scholes, Robert Merton
source: Roger Lowenstein, When Genius Failed: The Rise and Fall of Long-Term Capital Management (2000)

title: Praise for Being Smart
text:
In a series of six studies published in 1998, Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck gave fifth-graders a set of moderately difficult puzzles. Afterward, every child was told they had done well. Then came one extra sentence that differed between groups. Some children were praised for their intelligence ("You must be smart at these problems"). Others were praised for their effort ("You must have worked hard at these problems"). A control group heard no extra comment.

Next the children were offered a choice of new problems: easy ones they would surely solve, or harder ones they could learn from. Most children praised for intelligence chose the easy, safe option. Most praised for effort chose the challenge.

Then all the children received a much harder set, on which nearly everyone did poorly. The children praised for intelligence enjoyed the task less, persisted less and, on a final set of ordinary problems, did worse than they had at the start. Those praised for effort held up better. When asked to write down their scores for other children, the intelligence-praised group was more likely to inflate them.

The studies became a foundation of Dweck's later work on fixed and growth mindsets.
lesson: Praise what a child did, the effort, strategy or persistence, rather than what they supposedly are. Labels like smart can make children afraid to fail.
people: Claudia Mueller, Carol Dweck
source: Mueller, C. M., and Dweck, C. S. (1998). Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 75(1), 33-52.
caveat: Later large-scale studies of growth mindset interventions have found much smaller effects than early laboratory work suggested.

title: The English and Romanian Adoptees
text:
In the early 1990s, many British families adopted children from Romanian orphanages, where conditions had been extremely poor. The child psychiatrist Michael Rutter and his team at the Institute of Psychiatry in London saw a rare chance to learn how far children can recover from severe early deprivation. They began following 111 Romanian children adopted into English homes before the age of two, and compared them with children born and adopted within Britain.

When they arrived, many of the Romanian children were badly underweight, small for their age and far behind in development. By age four, the picture had changed dramatically. Physical growth had largely caught up, and so had much of their cognitive development.

The age at adoption made a clear difference. Children who had left the orphanage before about six months of age did about as well as the British-born adoptees. Those adopted later had, on average, lower scores, even though they too had made large gains. The team kept following the children into adolescence and adulthood, and found that some difficulties linked to longer deprivation persisted for a minority.

The study showed both sides of the story: how resilient young children are when given a loving home, and how much time in deprivation can cost.
lesson: Love and a stable home can repair a great deal, and the sooner a child gets them the better. Never assume a child is beyond help.
people: Michael Rutter and the English and Romanian Adoptees (ERA) Study Team
source: Rutter, M., and the English and Romanian Adoptees (ERA) Study Team (1998). Developmental catch-up, and deficit, following adoption after severe global early privation. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 39(4), 465-476.

title: Does California Make You Happy?
text:
Many Americans picture California as a place where life is better, mostly because of the weather. In the late 1990s David Schkade and Daniel Kahneman tested whether Californians actually are happier and whether people elsewhere think they are.

They surveyed nearly 2,000 students at large universities in the Midwest (in Michigan and Ohio) and in Southern California. Students rated their own satisfaction with life overall and with specific aspects such as climate, job prospects, safety and cultural opportunities. Some were also asked to imagine a student similar to themselves living in the other region and rate that person's satisfaction.

Overall life satisfaction was the same in both regions. Californians were much happier with their climate, as expected, but it did not translate into a happier life. Yet both groups predicted that a student like themselves would be happier in California. When people thought about the difference between the regions, the obvious difference, the weather, came to mind and seemed decisive. In reality, everyday life in both places was dominated by things that were the same: studies, friends, money, plans for the future.

Schkade and Kahneman called this a focusing illusion. Kahneman later summed it up in one line: nothing in life is as important as you think it is while you are thinking about it.
lesson: When a single feature makes a change look wonderful, such as a new city, job or house, ask how much of your ordinary day it will really touch. Most of life stays the same.
people: David Schkade, Daniel Kahneman
location: Universities in the Midwest and Southern California, USA
source: Schkade, D. A., and Kahneman, D. (1998). Does living in California make people happy? A focusing illusion in judgments of life satisfaction. Psychological Science, 9(5), 340-346.

title: The Chameleon Effect
text:
In 1999 Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh of New York University published a set of experiments on how people unconsciously copy each other. In the first, students worked on a task of describing photographs with a partner who was actually a member of the research team. Some partners kept rubbing their faces; others kept shaking a foot. Hidden cameras recorded the participants, who began to rub their own faces or shake their own feet more, depending on which partner they were with. Almost none noticed doing it.

In the second experiment the roles were reversed. This time the research assistant quietly mirrored the participant's posture, gestures and mannerisms during the conversation, or simply behaved neutrally. Participants who had been mirrored liked the assistant more and said the interaction had gone more smoothly, without realizing they had been imitated.

A third study found that people who scored higher on a measure of perspective taking, the habit of trying to see things from others' viewpoints, mimicked others more. Chartrand and Bargh named the pattern the chameleon effect and suggested that this automatic mimicry acts as a kind of social glue, building rapport between people who interact.
lesson: People bond partly through small, unconscious echoes of each other's behavior. Paying real attention to someone tends to bring you into step with them naturally.
people: Tanya Chartrand, John Bargh
location: New York University, New York, USA
source: Chartrand, T. L., and Bargh, J. A. (1999). The chameleon effect: The perception-behavior link and social interaction. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 76(6), 893-910.

title: The Michelangelo Phenomenon
text:
Michelangelo is often credited with the idea that a statue already lies hidden in the block of stone, and the sculptor's task is to chip away whatever hides it. Stephen Drigotas, Caryl Rusbult and their colleagues borrowed the image to describe something that happens in close relationships.

Each person has an ideal self: the person they hope to become, with the skills, traits and goals they are reaching for. A partner can help or hinder that. The researchers proposed that when a partner sees you in a way that fits your ideal, and behaves toward you in ways that draw out those qualities, you gradually move toward that ideal self. They called this partner affirmation.

In a series of four studies with dating and married couples, the team measured how each partner perceived and treated the other, using both partners' reports and, in some studies, observers' ratings, and in some cases followed couples over time. Where partners affirmed each other's ideals, people reported more movement toward their ideal selves. That growth went along with greater well-being in the relationship and a better chance of staying together.

The idea suggested that good partners do not only accept each other; they help each other grow.
lesson: Get to know who your partner, child or friend is trying to become, and treat them as that person already. Your view of them can help shape them.
people: Stephen Drigotas, Caryl Rusbult, Jennifer Wieselquist, Sarah Whitton
source: Drigotas, S. M., Rusbult, C. E., Wieselquist, J., and Whitton, S. W. (1999). Close partner as sculptor of the ideal self: Behavioral affirmation and the Michelangelo phenomenon. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 77(2), 293-323.

title: Psychological Safety
text:
In the 1990s, Amy Edmondson, then a doctoral student at Harvard, studied 51 work teams in a manufacturing company that made office furniture. They ranged from sales and production teams to management groups. She combined surveys of team members, interviews and her own observations, and gathered ratings of each team's performance from managers and internal customers.

Her focus was a quality she called psychological safety: a shared belief in the team that it is safe to take interpersonal risks. In such teams, people do not expect to be embarrassed, rejected or punished for asking a question, admitting an error, asking for help or raising a concern.

Edmondson found that teams with higher psychological safety engaged more in what she called learning behavior. They sought feedback, discussed mistakes openly, asked for help and tried out new ideas. That learning behavior, in turn, was linked to better team performance. Team leaders who coached and were accessible tended to have safer teams. In interviews, members of low-safety teams described keeping quiet about problems and choosing not to ask questions so as not to look ignorant or incompetent.
lesson: Teams improve only when people can admit what they do not know. Make it normal to ask questions and report mistakes, starting with your own.
people: Amy Edmondson
location: A manufacturing company in the United States
source: Edmondson, A. (1999). Psychological safety and learning behavior in work teams. Administrative Science Quarterly, 44(2), 350-383.

title: Crew Resource Management
text:
In December 1978, United Airlines Flight 173 approached Portland, Oregon, with a landing gear warning light on. The captain circled for about an hour while the crew worked on the problem. The flight engineer and first officer mentioned the fuel situation, but only indirectly, and the captain did not act on it in time. The plane ran out of fuel and crashed short of the airport, killing ten people. Investigators found no mechanical failure that made the crash unavoidable. The problem lay in how the crew worked together.
