Accidents like this, and research showing that most crashes involved human error, led to a NASA workshop in 1979 and to training programs that became known as crew resource management. In 1999, Robert Helmreich, Ashleigh Merritt and John Wilhelm of the University of Texas reviewed how this training had evolved.

Early courses focused on personality and general psychology and drew resistance from pilots. Later versions concentrated on concrete skills: briefing the crew, inviting input, junior officers stating concerns clearly, and captains making it normal to be questioned. The newest generation framed the goal as error management: accepting that errors will happen and training crews to catch and correct them together.
lesson: In any team with a hierarchy, the person who sees the danger may not be the one in charge. Make it routine for juniors to speak plainly and for leaders to ask.
people: Robert Helmreich, Ashleigh Merritt, John Wilhelm
location: University of Texas at Austin, USA
source: Helmreich, R. L., Merritt, A. C., and Wilhelm, J. A. (1999). The evolution of crew resource management training in commercial aviation. International Journal of Aviation Psychology, 9(1), 19-32.

title: Unskilled and Unaware
text:
In 1999 Justin Kruger and David Dunning of Cornell University published a series of studies on how well people judge their own competence. Students took tests of humor (judging how funny jokes were, compared with ratings by professional comedians), logical reasoning and English grammar. Afterwards, each estimated their score and how they ranked compared with other students.

Most people thought they were above average, but the error was not evenly spread. Those who scored in the bottom quarter overestimated themselves the most. On the logical reasoning test, for example, students who on average performed around the 12th percentile believed they had done better than about two thirds of their peers. Top performers, in contrast, slightly underestimated their relative standing, because they assumed others found the test as easy as they did.

Kruger and Dunning argued that the skills needed to do a task well are often the same skills needed to recognize good performance. People who lack them suffer a double burden: they make mistakes and cannot see that they are mistakes. In one study, giving low scorers a short training in logic improved both their performance and their ability to judge it.

The pattern became famous as the Dunning-Kruger effect. Critics have since shown that part of it is a statistical artifact: when everyone tends to rate themselves above average, and self-ratings are imperfectly tied to actual scores, the lowest scorers will inevitably show the largest overestimates. The debate continues over how much remains beyond this.
lesson: Feeling confident is not evidence of being competent, especially in areas new to you. Seek honest feedback and outside measures, and learn enough to recognize what good work looks like.
people: Justin Kruger, David Dunning
source: Kruger, J., and Dunning, D. (1999). Unskilled and unaware of it: How difficulties in recognizing one's own incompetence lead to inflated self-assessments. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 77(6), 1121-1134.
caveat: Part of the pattern can be produced by regression to the mean and the general better-than-average effect, so its size beyond statistical artifact is debated.

title: When Accountability Makes Us Think
text:
Organizations often assume that making people answerable for their decisions will make those decisions better. In 1999 Jennifer Lerner and Philip Tetlock reviewed decades of experiments on accountability and found that the truth was more complicated.

Across the studies they examined, the effect of having to justify oneself depended on exactly how accountability worked. When people knew in advance what their audience thought, they tended to shift toward that view and tell the audience what it wanted to hear. When people had to justify a decision they had already made, they spent their effort defending it, and became more rigid. Accountability could even make some biases worse, by encouraging people to use every piece of information, including irrelevant information.

Accountability tended to produce careful, self-critical thinking under specific conditions. People had to know before they made up their minds that they would have to explain their reasoning, the audience's own views had to be unknown, and the audience had to be seen as well informed and interested in accuracy rather than in a particular outcome. Under those conditions, people considered more alternatives and anticipated more objections.
lesson: To get careful decisions, ask people to explain their reasoning before they decide, and do not reveal the answer you prefer.
people: Jennifer Lerner, Philip Tetlock
source: Lerner, J. S., and Tetlock, P. E. (1999). Accounting for the effects of accountability. Psychological Bulletin, 125(2), 255-275.

title: The Invisible Gorilla
text:
In 1999 Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris, then at Harvard University, filmed a short video of two teams of students passing basketballs, one team in white shirts and the other in black. Viewers were asked to count the passes made by the white team, a task that required close attention.

About halfway through the clip, something strange happened. In one version, a woman carrying an open umbrella walked through the game. In another, a person in a full gorilla suit walked into the middle of the players, stopped, faced the camera, thumped its chest and walked off.

After the video, the researchers asked whether viewers had noticed anything unusual. About half of them had not seen the gorilla at all. When they were shown the clip again, many could hardly believe they had missed it, and some suspected the researchers had switched tapes. The harder the counting task, the more people missed it.

Simons and Chabris used the study to illustrate inattentional blindness, a phenomenon earlier studied by Ulric Neisser and by Arien Mack and Irvin Rock: when our attention is focused on one task, we can fail to see something obvious that we are not looking for. Just as striking, people are confident that they would notice such things. The experiment has been repeated many times and became one of the best known demonstrations in psychology.
lesson: Focus has a price: what you are not looking for, you may not see at all. When much is at stake, ask someone with a different focus to look at the same situation.
people: Daniel Simons, Christopher Chabris
source: Simons, D. J., and Chabris, C. F. (1999). Gorillas in our midst: Sustained inattentional blindness for dynamic events. Perception, 28(9), 1059-1074.

title: Oscillating Through Grief
text:
For much of the twentieth century, a common view held that the bereaved must do "grief work": confront the loss directly and work through painful feelings, or risk trouble later. Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut, bereavement researchers at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, found that the evidence for this view was weaker than its popularity suggested, and that it did not fit what many grieving people actually did.

In 1999 they published the dual process model of coping with bereavement. They described two kinds of stress after a death. Loss-oriented coping deals with the loss itself: crying, yearning, looking at photographs, thinking about the person who died. Restoration-oriented coping deals with the life that remains: learning to handle the finances the spouse used to manage, building new routines, taking on new roles, and sometimes simply taking a break from grief by watching television or seeing friends.

The key idea was oscillation. Healthy grieving, they argued, does not mean staying in one mode. People move back and forth, sometimes within a single day, confronting the loss and then turning away from it. Too much of either can cause problems. The model has since become one of the most widely used frameworks in bereavement research and counseling.
lesson: When you or someone you love is grieving, it is fine to step away from sorrow to handle daily life or even enjoy a moment. Both belong to mourning.
people: Margaret Stroebe, Henk Schut
source: Stroebe, M., and Schut, H. (1999). The dual process model of coping with bereavement: Rationale and description. Death Studies, 23(3), 197-224.
caveat: This is a theoretical model built on earlier research rather than a single experiment, and evidence testing it directly is still limited.

title: Couples Tied Together on an Obstacle Course
text:
Many long relationships slip from early excitement into comfortable routine. Arthur Aron and his colleagues proposed that couples could recover some of the early spark by doing new and challenging things together, so that the excitement of the activity became linked with the partner.

After surveys suggested that couples who shared exciting activities were happier, the researchers tested the idea in the laboratory at the State University of New York at Stony Brook. Married couples first filled out questionnaires about their relationship. Then some couples were given a novel and mildly arousing task. Their wrists and ankles were bound together with Velcro straps, and they had to crawl on gym mats across the room and over a barrier, pushing a foam cylinder without using their hands or teeth, then turn around and come back, all against a time limit with a prize at stake. Other couples did a dull version: one partner slowly rolled a ball to the middle of the room while the other watched.

Afterward the couples again rated their relationship. Those who had stumbled, laughed and struggled through the obstacle course together reported a greater increase in relationship quality than those who had done the mundane task. Later experiments by the team found similar results.
lesson: Break routine together. Trying something new and a little challenging as a couple, or as a family, can renew a bond that has gone flat.
people: Arthur Aron, Christina Norman, Elaine Aron, Colin McKenna, Richard Heyman
location: State University of New York at Stony Brook, Stony Brook, USA
source: Aron, A., Norman, C. C., Aron, E. N., McKenna, C., and Heyman, R. E. (2000). Couples' shared participation in novel and arousing activities and experienced relationship quality. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 78(2), 273-284.

title: Trading Is Hazardous to Your Wealth
text:
In 2000 the finance professors Brad Barber and Terrance Odean, at the University of California, published a study of how ordinary people fared when they picked and traded stocks themselves. They obtained records from a large American discount brokerage covering more than 66,000 households from 1991 to 1996.

Over that period, the stock market as a whole returned roughly 17.9 percent a year. The average household earned about 16.4 percent after trading costs. That was respectable, but it trailed the market. The real difference showed up when Barber and Odean sorted households by how much they traded. The fifth of households that traded most turned over their portfolios more than twice a year, and they earned only about 11.4 percent a year after costs, far behind both the market and the households that traded least.

The stocks these active traders bought did not perform better than the ones they sold, at least not enough to cover the commissions and price spreads they paid for each trade. Their activity simply cost them money.

Barber and Odean argued that the most likely explanation was overconfidence: investors believed their information and judgment were better than they were, so they traded too often. In a follow-up study titled "Boys Will Be Boys," they found that men traded considerably more than women, and that the extra trading lowered men's returns more.
lesson: Activity is not the same as progress. If your decisions carry a cost each time you change course, make sure your confidence in each change is earned before you act on it.
people: Brad Barber, Terrance Odean
location: University of California, Davis, USA (data from a US discount brokerage)
source: Barber, B. M., and Odean, T. (2000). Trading is hazardous to your wealth: The common stock investment performance of individual investors. Journal of Finance, 55(2), 773-806.

title: The Embarrassing T-Shirt
text:
In 2000 Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Husted Medvec and Kenneth Savitsky of Cornell University published a study that many people find reassuring. Each participant was asked to put on a T-shirt with a large picture of the singer Barry Manilow, a choice that the students at the time considered deeply embarrassing. The participant was then sent into a room where several other students were already sitting and filling out questionnaires.

After a short time the participant was led out again and asked to estimate how many of the people in the room had noticed who was on the shirt. Participants guessed that about half of them had. When the researchers asked the people in the room, only about a quarter could say who was on the shirt.

In other studies, people similarly overestimated how much others noticed their contributions and mistakes in a group discussion. The researchers called this the spotlight effect. Because we are so keenly aware of our own appearance and actions, we assume others are watching them just as closely. In fact, other people are mostly busy with their own concerns, and our slips, bad hair days and awkward moments are far less visible than they feel.
lesson: Far fewer people notice your awkward moments than you think. Worry less about how you look in a moment, and act more freely.
people: Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Husted Medvec, Kenneth Savitsky
source: Gilovich, T., Medvec, V. H., and Savitsky, K. (2000). The spotlight effect in social judgment: An egocentric bias in estimates of the salience of one's own actions and appearance. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 78(2), 211-222.

title: A Fine Is a Price
text:
At day-care centers in the Israeli city of Haifa, parents sometimes came late to pick up their children, forcing a teacher to stay after closing time. In the late 1990s the economists Uri Gneezy and Aldo Rustichini ran a field experiment in ten of these private centers to see whether a fine would solve the problem.

For four weeks, they simply recorded how many parents arrived late. Then, in six of the centers, they introduced a fine of 10 shekels for any parent who was more than ten minutes late. The other four centers served as a comparison and changed nothing.

The result was the opposite of what the standard theory of deterrence predicts. In the centers with the fine, late arrivals increased, rising within a few weeks to about double their earlier level. In the comparison centers, lateness stayed about the same. After several months, the fine was removed. Lateness in those centers did not return to the original level; it stayed high.

Gneezy and Rustichini explained the result with the title of their paper: a fine is a price. Before, parents had seen lateness as a favor that imposed on the teachers, something to avoid out of guilt or respect. The fine turned it into a service for sale, and a cheap one. Once the social norm had been replaced by a market transaction, removing the price did not bring the old norm back.
lesson: Putting a price on behavior can replace a sense of obligation with a simple transaction. Before using fines or payments to change behavior, consider what moral reasons you might be crowding out.
people: Uri Gneezy, Aldo Rustichini
source: Gneezy, U., and Rustichini, A. (2000). A fine is a price. Journal of Legal Studies, 29(1), 1-17.

title: The Screen Behind the Audition
text:
Until the 1970s the top American symphony orchestras were almost entirely male, and their music directors had great personal discretion over who was hired. Starting in the 1970s and 1980s, many orchestras changed their audition rules. Candidates played behind a screen so that the jury could hear but not see them. Some orchestras even laid down a carpet so that the sound of footsteps would not reveal whether a candidate was wearing heels.

The economists Claudia Goldin and Cecilia Rouse wanted to know whether the screens had made a difference. They gathered audition records from several major orchestras, along with the orchestras' membership rosters over many years. Because some candidates auditioned both with and without screens at different times, they could compare how the same musicians fared under both systems.

Their estimates suggested that the screens increased the chance that a woman would advance from the early rounds of an audition and be hired in the end. They concluded that blind auditions could explain a meaningful share of the rise in the proportion of women in these orchestras, which grew from a small minority in 1970 to roughly a quarter by the mid 1990s.
lesson: If you want to judge people on their work alone, hide what should not matter. Simple changes to how you evaluate can remove biases you do not see in yourself.
people: Claudia Goldin, Cecilia Rouse
source: Goldin, C., and Rouse, C. (2000). Orchestrating impartiality: The impact of 'blind' auditions on female musicians. American Economic Review, 90(4), 715-741.
caveat: Later critics pointed out that many of the paper's estimates are statistically imprecise, so the size of the effect is uncertain even though the principle is widely accepted.

title: The Kohler Effect
text:
In the 1920s, the German psychologist Otto Kohler studied members of a rowing club doing a strength endurance exercise, curling a weight as many times as they could. He compared how long they lasted alone and in pairs, where the pair's result ended as soon as the weaker member gave up. He found that in some pairs, the weaker member lasted longer than he had alone, especially when the two partners differed moderately in ability.

For decades the finding was largely forgotten, overshadowed by research on social loafing. In 2000, Guido Hertel, Norbert Kerr and Lawrence Messe revived it in a series of experiments with modern controls.

Participants performed physically tiring persistence tasks, alone and in two-person teams. In some conditions, the team's score depended on the weaker member's performance, so that member was indispensable. These were compared with conditions in which the two members' scores were simply added together.

When the team's result depended on the weaker member, that person persisted noticeably longer than they did alone. This motivation gain, which the authors named the Kohler effect, was linked to the weaker member's sense that their effort was indispensable to the team and to comparisons with the more capable partner.
lesson: Being the weak link that the team depends on can bring out extra effort. Pair people with slightly stronger partners on tasks where each person's part truly counts.
people: Guido Hertel, Norbert Kerr, Lawrence Messe; Otto Kohler
source: Hertel, G., Kerr, N. L., and Messe, L. A. (2000). Motivation gains in performance groups: Paradigmatic and theoretical developments on the Kohler effect. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 79(4), 580-601.

title: Twenty-Four Jams or Six
text:
On two Saturdays at Draeger's, an upscale supermarket in Menlo Park, California, the psychologists Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper set up a tasting booth for a brand of jam. Through the day they switched the display back and forth. Sometimes it offered 24 flavors; sometimes only 6. Shoppers who stopped received a discount coupon for any jar of that brand.

The large display drew more attention: about 60 percent of passing shoppers stopped at it, against about 40 percent for the small one. But buying told a different story. Only about 3 percent of the people who stopped at the 24-jam table later bought a jar, while about 30 percent of those who saw just 6 flavors did.

In other studies in the same paper, students who chose from a small set of chocolates were more satisfied with their pick than those who chose from a large set, and students given a short list of essay topics were more likely to write the essay.

Published in 2000, the jam study became a famous example of choice overload: too many options can make people freeze or feel worse about what they pick. Later research was more cautious. A 2010 meta-analysis by Benjamin Scheibehenne and colleagues found that the average effect across many studies was close to zero, with overload appearing only under certain conditions, such as when options are hard to compare or people have no clear preferences.
lesson: When you offer choices, to customers, colleagues or yourself, make them easy to compare. If the options are many and similar, narrowing them down first can help people actually decide.
people: Sheena Iyengar, Mark Lepper
location: Draeger's supermarket, Menlo Park, California, USA
source: Iyengar, S. S., and Lepper, M. R. (2000). When choice is demotivating: Can one desire too much of a good thing? Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 79(6), 995-1006.
caveat: A 2010 meta-analysis (Scheibehenne, Greifeneder and Todd) found the average choice overload effect near zero, so it appears only under specific conditions.

title: The Windshield Installers of Safelite
text:
In the mid 1990s Safelite Glass, then the largest installer of car windshields in the United States, changed how it paid the workers who drove to customers and fitted the glass. Under the old system, installers were paid by the hour. Under the new one, they were paid a set amount for each windshield installed, with a guaranteed minimum so that no one would earn less than before.

The economist Edward Lazear, of Stanford, obtained detailed monthly records of each worker's output before and after the change, covering several thousand employees. Because the switch was rolled out across the company over about a year and a half, he could compare the same people under both systems.

Output per worker rose by about 44 percent. Lazear found that roughly half of this came from existing workers simply doing more once their effort was rewarded. The other half came from a change in who worked there: more productive workers were attracted to the company and stayed, while less productive ones were more likely to leave. Pay rose too, and the company's profits increased.
lesson: How you pay people shapes not only how hard they work but who chooses to work for you. Think about whom an incentive will attract as well as what it will reward.
people: Edward Lazear
source: Lazear, E. P. (2000). Performance pay and productivity. American Economic Review, 90(5), 1346-1361.
caveat: Installing windshields is easy to count and to check for quality, which is why piece rates worked so well here; in complex jobs they can backfire.

title: Bowling Alone
text:
In 1995 the political scientist Robert Putnam of Harvard published an essay with a striking image: more Americans were bowling than ever, but fewer were bowling in leagues. In 2000 he expanded it into the book Bowling Alone, drawing on surveys, membership records and other data covering several decades of American life.

Putnam documented a broad decline, starting around the 1960s and 1970s, in what he called social capital: the networks of relationships, trust and shared norms that let people cooperate. Membership in groups like parent-teacher associations, labor unions, fraternal clubs and civic organizations had fallen. People attended fewer public meetings, entertained friends at home less often, joined fewer picnics and card games, and reported trusting others less. Some forms of participation had grown, such as mailing-list organizations and self-help groups, but these often asked little more than writing a check.

He looked at several possible causes, including busier work lives, suburban sprawl and long commutes, and especially television, which kept people at home in the evening. The largest factor, he argued, was generational: the civic-minded generation that came of age around the Second World War was being replaced by generations that joined less. Putnam linked high social capital to better schools, safer neighborhoods, better health and more responsive government.
lesson: Community is built by showing up: joining, attending, hosting. Belonging to something beyond your home and work benefits you and everyone around you.
people: Robert Putnam
source: Putnam, R. D. (2000). Bowling Alone: The Collapse and Revival of American Community. Simon and Schuster.
caveat: Critics have disputed how steep the decline was and argued that new forms of association, including online ones, replaced some of what was lost.

title: The Baby and the Marriage
text:
The arrival of a first baby is a joy, but many couples find that their marriage becomes harder afterward. Alyson Shapiro, John Gottman and Sybil Carrere at the University of Washington wanted to know why some marriages weather the transition better than others.

They drew on a group of newlywed couples in the Seattle area whom Gottman's lab had been following since early in their marriages. Some of these couples had a first child over the next several years; others did not. Because the researchers had interviewed and observed the couples before any baby arrived, they could look for early signs that predicted what happened afterward.

Among the couples who became parents, about two-thirds of the wives reported a drop in marital satisfaction during the first years with the baby. The other third stayed stable or even grew happier. The couples who did not have children did not show the same decline over the same period.

What set the protected couples apart was visible before the birth. Husbands who expressed fondness and admiration for their wives, and who were aware of and interested in their wives' lives and the details of their world, predicted stable or rising satisfaction for the wives. Couples who described their lives as chaotic and out of control fared worse.
lesson: Before and after a baby arrives, keep showing fondness for your partner and stay curious about their inner world. That habit protects the marriage through hard years.
people: Alyson Shapiro, John Gottman, Sybil Carrere
source: Shapiro, A. F., Gottman, J. M., and Carrere, S. (2000). The baby and the marriage: Identifying factors that buffer against decline in marital satisfaction after the first baby arrives. Journal of Family Psychology, 14(1), 59-70.

title: The Cost of a Hostile Boss
text:
In 2000 the management researcher Bennett Tepper published a study of what he called abusive supervision: bosses who repeatedly ridicule, belittle, blame and give the silent treatment to their subordinates, without necessarily using physical aggression. He surveyed several hundred working adults in an American city and then surveyed them again about six months later.

At the first survey, participants described how often their supervisor engaged in such behavior. Six months later, Tepper checked who had left their jobs and asked those who remained about their attitudes and well-being.

Employees with more abusive supervisors were more likely to have quit. Those who stayed reported lower satisfaction with their jobs and their lives, less commitment to their organization, more depression, anxiety and emotional exhaustion, and more conflict between work and family life. The effects were stronger for people who felt they had few other job options, who were stuck with the abusive boss. Tepper found that a sense of being treated unfairly helped explain the damage.
lesson: A boss's contempt does not stay at the office: it follows people home. Treat everyone with basic respect, especially those who cannot easily leave.
people: Bennett Tepper
source: Tepper, B. J. (2000). Consequences of abusive supervision. Academy of Management Journal, 43(2), 178-190.

title: Polaroid and the Digital Camera
text:
Polaroid, founded by Edwin Land, built its fortune on instant photography: cameras that produced a finished print within minutes. Its business model, like that of many camera firms, relied on selling cameras at modest margins and earning profits on the film that customers bought again and again.

In 2000 Mary Tripsas and Giovanni Gavetti, then at Harvard Business School, published a detailed case study of how Polaroid responded to digital imaging from the early 1980s to the late 1990s. Based on company documents and interviews with managers and engineers, they showed that Polaroid was not slow to develop the technology. It invested heavily in digital imaging research and by the early 1990s had developed advanced image sensors and a high-resolution digital camera with strong technical performance.

The problem was not technical capability but the beliefs of senior managers. Leadership remained convinced that profits came from consumables, so a camera that needed no film was hard to fit into its plans. It also believed that customers would always want physical prints, and it judged new projects by whether they fit the instant photography business. Digital products were steered toward printing and toward markets that matched those assumptions. When digital cameras took off for consumers, Polaroid was not positioned to benefit.

Tripsas and Gavetti concluded that managers' mental models of how their business makes money can trap a company even when it holds the right technology. Polaroid filed for bankruptcy in 2001.
lesson: Owning a new capability is not enough if your beliefs about how you succeed stay the same. Regularly question the assumptions behind your business model, especially the ones that made you successful.
people: Mary Tripsas, Giovanni Gavetti
source: Tripsas, M., and Gavetti, G. (2000). Capabilities, cognition, and inertia: Evidence from digital imaging. Strategic Management Journal, 21(10-11), 1147-1161.

title: Who Should Make the First Offer?
text:
Negotiation folklore often advises letting the other side name a number first. In 2001 Adam Galinsky and Thomas Mussweiler put that advice to the test with MBA students at Northwestern University's Kellogg School of Management.

Students were paired as buyer and seller in a simulated negotiation over the sale of a pharmaceutical plant. Whoever made the first offer, buyer or seller, tended to end up with the better deal. The first offer worked as an anchor: the final agreed price was closely correlated with it. An ambitious opening number pulled the whole negotiation toward the side that made it.

The researchers then looked for ways to resist the anchor. In further studies, they asked the side receiving the first offer to focus on particular information before responding. Some were asked to think about the other side's alternatives to the deal and the lowest price the other side might accept. Others were asked to focus on their own target price, their ideal outcome. Either kind of focus, pointing attention to information inconsistent with the opponent's anchor, wiped out the advantage of the first mover. The final prices no longer tracked the first offer.

The authors concluded that making the first offer is often an advantage, especially when you are well prepared and the other side is not. But a negotiator who receives an extreme first offer can neutralize it by deliberately thinking about the facts that contradict it.
lesson: If you know the value of what is being negotiated, consider making the first, ambitious but defensible offer. If the other side opens first, refocus at once on your own target and their alternatives.
people: Adam Galinsky, Thomas Mussweiler
source: Galinsky, A. D., and Mussweiler, T. (2001). First offers as anchors: The role of perspective-taking and negotiator focus. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 81(4), 657-669.

title: Automatic Enrollment in Savings
text:
In the late 1990s a large American company changed one rule in its 401(k) retirement savings plan. Before, new employees had to sign up if they wanted to save. After the change, new employees were enrolled automatically, with a default of 3 percent of pay invested in a conservative money market fund, unless they chose otherwise.

The economists Brigitte Madrian and Dennis Shea compared workers hired just before and just after the switch. Among those hired under the old opt-in rule, fewer than 40 percent were participating at a comparable point in their tenure. Among those hired under automatic enrollment, participation was above 85 percent. The gains were largest among younger and lower-paid workers, the groups least likely to sign up on their own.

There was a catch. Most of the automatically enrolled employees stayed exactly where the default put them: at the 3 percent rate and in the money market fund, even though many of the earlier hires who had chosen for themselves saved more and invested in stocks. The default that brought people in also anchored how much and how they saved.

Madrian and Shea called their 2001 paper "The Power of Suggestion." Their findings helped persuade employers and lawmakers to adopt automatic enrollment, which was encouraged in the United States by the Pension Protection Act of 2006.
lesson: Inertia can work for you as well as against you. Set up good habits, savings and routines so they happen by default, and then check once in a while that the default still fits.
people: Brigitte Madrian, Dennis Shea
source: Madrian, B. C., and Shea, D. F. (2001). The power of suggestion: Inertia in 401(k) participation and savings behavior. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 116(4), 1149-1187.

title: Devil's Advocate or Real Dissent
text:
For decades, groups have been advised to fight groupthink by appointing a devil's advocate, someone told to argue against the prevailing view. Charlan Nemeth of the University of California, Berkeley, had spent years studying the creative effects of minority dissent, and she suspected that playacted disagreement was not the same as the real thing.

With Keith Brown and John Rogers, she ran an experiment in which small groups discussed a problem and had to reach a decision. Some groups included a member who genuinely disagreed with the majority view. Others included a member who argued the same opposing position but was openly playing devil's advocate.

Genuine dissent produced more and better thinking. Groups with an authentic dissenter generated more original ideas and considered a wider range of solutions. When the dissent was framed as a role, the majority often treated it as a game. Instead of reconsidering, they tended to come up with more reasons for their original view, so the devil's advocate sometimes ended up strengthening the very position it was meant to test.
lesson: Assigned critics are easy to dismiss. Seek out people who truly disagree with you and give them room to say so.
people: Charlan Nemeth, Keith Brown, John Rogers
source: Nemeth, C., Brown, K., and Rogers, J. (2001). Devil's advocate versus authentic dissent: Stimulating quantity and quality. European Journal of Social Psychology, 31(6), 707-720.

title: Self-Imposed Deadlines
text:
In 2002 Dan Ariely and Klaus Wertenbroch reported two studies on whether people who know they procrastinate will bind themselves with deadlines, and whether it works.

The first study took place in an executive education class at MIT. Students had to write three papers during the semester. In one section, the deadlines were fixed and evenly spaced. In another, students could set their own deadlines for each paper, as late as the last day of class, with a grade penalty for missing whatever date they chose. Rationally, there was no reason to set an early deadline: picking the last day kept every option open. Yet most students chose earlier, spaced deadlines, showing they knew they needed help against their own delays. Still, the students with evenly spaced deadlines set by the instructor earned better grades than those who set their own.

The second study tested this more cleanly. Participants were paid to proofread three long texts over three weeks, earning money for each error found and losing money for each day late. One group had evenly spaced deadlines, one set its own, and one had a single deadline at the end. The group with evenly spaced deadlines found the most errors, missed fewer deadlines and earned the most. The end-deadline group did worst, and the self-imposed group fell in between.

People recognized their tendency to procrastinate, but they did not set their deadlines as well as an outsider would.
lesson: If you tend to put things off, break the work into pieces with spaced deadlines, and consider letting someone else set or enforce them. Self-imposed limits help, but outside ones help more.
people: Dan Ariely, Klaus Wertenbroch
location: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, USA
source: Ariely, D., and Wertenbroch, K. (2002). Procrastination, deadlines, and performance: Self-control by precommitment. Psychological Science, 13(3), 219-224.

title: Resilience After Losing a Spouse
text:
Most studies of grief begin after a death, which makes it hard to know how people were doing before. George Bonanno and his colleagues found a way around this. A large study called Changing Lives of Older Couples had interviewed about 1,500 married people aged 65 and over in the Detroit area. Over the following years, some of them lost their husband or wife.

Bonanno's team examined about 200 of these widowed people, comparing their depression and well-being before the loss with measures taken six and eighteen months after it. That allowed them to trace distinct paths through bereavement.

The most common path, followed by close to half, was resilience. These people felt sadness and longing, but their depression stayed low throughout, and they continued functioning in their daily lives. Smaller groups showed what had long been assumed to be the usual pattern, grief that rose and then eased, or chronic grief that persisted. Another group had been depressed before the loss and remained so, and some who had been depressed in unhappy marriages actually improved after the spouse died.

Resilient widows and widowers were not cold or detached. They had generally had good marriages and missed their spouses. The study challenged the belief that the absence of intense distress means something is wrong.
lesson: There is no single right way to grieve. Steady functioning after a loss is common and healthy, not a sign of denial or lack of love.
people: George Bonanno, Camille Wortman, Darrin Lehman and colleagues
source: Bonanno, G. A., Wortman, C. B., Lehman, D. R., Tweed, R. G., Haring, M., Sonnega, J., Carr, D., and Nesse, R. M. (2002). Resilience to loss and chronic grief: A prospective study from preloss to 18-months postwidowhood. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 83(5), 1150-1164.

title: Paying to Punish Free Riders
text:
At the University of Zurich, economists Ernst Fehr and Simon Gachter had students play a public goods game for real money. In groups of four, each player received some money units and secretly decided how many to put into a common project. Whatever went in was multiplied and shared equally among all four. Everyone gained most if all contributed fully, but each individual earned more by keeping their own money and letting others pay.

The groups were reshuffled each round so that players never met the same partners twice. Without any way to respond, cooperation started at a moderate level and steadily fell, as people saw others holding back and cut their own contributions.

In another condition, after seeing what others had contributed, players could pay some of their own money to reduce the earnings of a free rider. Since partners changed every round, punishing could never bring the punisher any future gain. Yet many players did it, often heavily, and they reported anger at free riders. With punishment available, contributions rose and stayed high, and free riding collapsed.
lesson: Cooperation in a group needs a way to respond to people who take without giving. Fair, visible consequences protect those who do their share.
people: Ernst Fehr, Simon Gachter
source: Fehr, E., and Gachter, S. (2002). Altruistic punishment in humans. Nature, 415(6868), 137-140.
caveat: Later studies found that in some societies punishment is also aimed at cooperators, which can undermine cooperation instead of supporting it.

title: Family Routines and Rituals
text:
Family dinners, bedtime stories, Sunday visits to grandparents, the way a birthday is always celebrated: such habits seem too ordinary to study. In 2002, the psychologist Barbara Fiese, then at Syracuse University, and her colleagues set out to review what fifty years of research had found about them.

They drew a useful distinction. Routines are the practical, repeated tasks that keep a household running, such as who makes dinner and when children go to bed. They involve instrumental communication ("this is what needs to be done") and take little thought once established. Rituals are different. They carry symbolic meaning, say "this is who we are," and are often anticipated with pleasure and remembered long after. A routine dinner can become a ritual when it is a time the family reliably gathers and talks.

Across the studies they reviewed, regular routines and meaningful rituals were associated with a range of good outcomes: more competent parenting, better child health, including better management of chronic illnesses such as asthma, stronger academic achievement, and greater satisfaction in marriages. Disrupted routines, by contrast, often accompanied family stress.

The review helped bring attention to the quiet, repeated structure of family life as a source of stability.
lesson: Small repeated rituals, like a shared meal or a bedtime story, give a family structure and meaning. Protect a few of them even in busy seasons.
people: Barbara Fiese, Thomas Tomcho and colleagues
source: Fiese, B. H., Tomcho, T. J., Douglas, M., Josephs, K., Poltrock, S., and Baker, T. (2002). A review of 50 years of research on naturally occurring family routines and rituals: Cause for celebration? Journal of Family Psychology, 16(4), 381-390.
caveat: Most studies reviewed were correlational, so families that are already doing well may simply find it easier to keep routines.

title: Why Big Projects Run Over Budget
text:
In 2002 the Danish planning scholar Bent Flyvbjerg and his colleagues Mette Skamris Holm and Soren Buhl published the first large statistical study of cost overruns in public transport infrastructure. They gathered data on 258 projects, including roads, bridges, tunnels and railways, built in 20 countries on five continents over about 70 years.

Almost nine out of ten projects cost more than forecast. Rail projects were the worst, running on average about 45 percent over budget. Bridges and tunnels averaged around a third over, and roads around 20 percent. The overruns were found in every region studied, and, strikingly, they had not shrunk over time. Decades of experience, better methods and more data had not made the forecasts more accurate.

The authors argued that such a stable, one-sided pattern could not be explained by honest technical error, which should push estimates up as often as down and should improve with practice. They pointed instead to two forces: optimism on the part of planners, and what they called strategic misrepresentation, the deliberate understating of costs to get projects approved. In the title they put the question bluntly: error or lie?

Flyvbjerg later promoted reference class forecasting, a method that starts from the actual outcomes of similar past projects rather than from the details of the new plan, as a remedy.
lesson: For any large plan, compare your budget with what similar projects really cost, and be wary of estimates made by people who need the project approved.
people: Bent Flyvbjerg, Mette Skamris Holm, Soren Buhl
source: Flyvbjerg, B., Holm, M. S., and Buhl, S. (2002). Underestimating costs in public works projects: Error or lie? Journal of the American Planning Association, 68(3), 279-295.

title: Conditions for Great Teams
text:
J. Richard Hackman of Harvard spent decades studying teams in their natural habitats: airline cockpit crews, symphony orchestras, hospital teams, factory groups and many others. Again and again he saw managers try to fix a struggling team by coaching it in the moment or sending it on a team-building retreat, with little lasting effect.

In his 2002 book Leading Teams, Hackman argued that a team's success depends mostly on conditions set up before and around the work. He named five. It must be a real team, with clear membership, a shared task and enough stability to learn to work together. It needs a compelling direction, a purpose that is clear, challenging and important. It needs an enabling structure: a well designed task, the right size and mix of people, and clear norms of conduct. It needs a supportive organizational context that provides information, training and rewards for the team as a whole. And it benefits from expert coaching at the right moments, such as the start, the midpoint and the end of a piece of work.

Hackman found that when these conditions were in place, teams tended to manage themselves well. When they were missing, even talented members and skilled leaders struggled.
lesson: Before trying to fix a team's chemistry, check its setup. Clear membership, a purpose worth caring about and a well designed task do more than any pep talk.
people: J. Richard Hackman
source: Hackman, J. R. (2002). Leading Teams: Setting the Stage for Great Performances. Harvard Business School Press.

title: For Better or for Worse
text:
In the early 1970s, the psychologist E. Mavis Hetherington began a study of families with young children going through divorce, alongside similar families that stayed together. What began as a two-year project in Virginia grew into one of the longest studies of divorce ever done, eventually following around 1,400 families over three decades, including remarriages and stepfamilies.

Hetherington and her team used interviews, questionnaires and direct observation of family life. They saw how hard the first year or two after divorce often was: parents were stressed and less consistent, children were angry or anxious, and many families struggled with money and new routines.

In 2002, with the writer John Kelly, she summed up what the study had found in the book For Better or for Worse: Divorce Reconsidered. Her message cut against both optimistic and pessimistic stereotypes. About a quarter of the young people from divorced families had serious social, emotional or psychological problems, compared with about one in ten from families that stayed together, a real difference. But that meant that roughly three quarters of the children of divorce were doing reasonably well as adults, and many had grown more competent through their experiences.

The outcome depended heavily on what happened after the divorce: conflict between the parents, the quality of parenting, and the support children received.
lesson: Divorce raises risks for children but does not seal their fate. Calm co-parenting and steady, warm care after a separation make the biggest difference.
people: E. Mavis Hetherington, John Kelly
source: Hetherington, E. M., and Kelly, J. (2002). For Better or for Worse: Divorce Reconsidered. New York: W. W. Norton.

title: Specific Goals Beat Doing Your Best
text:
In 2002 the psychologists Edwin Locke and Gary Latham summarized more than thirty years of research on goal setting, much of it their own. The research covered hundreds of studies involving many thousands of people, in laboratories and in workplaces from logging crews to scientists, across several countries.

Their central finding was consistent. When people were given specific, difficult goals, they performed better than when they were given easy goals, vague goals, or the common instruction to "do your best." The harder the goal, as long as people accepted it and had the ability to reach it, the higher the performance.

They also mapped out why goals work. Goals direct attention toward what matters, raise effort, increase persistence and push people to search for better strategies. The effect was strongest when people received feedback on their progress and were committed to the goal, for example because it mattered to them or because they had a say in setting it. For very complex tasks that people were still learning, they found that goals to learn something often worked better than goals to reach a particular output.
lesson: Instead of asking people to do their best, agree on a clear and challenging target, give feedback along the way, and for new skills set learning goals first.
people: Edwin Locke, Gary Latham
location: University of Maryland, USA, and University of Toronto, Canada
source: Locke, E. A., and Latham, G. P. (2002). Building a practically useful theory of goal setting and task motivation: A 35-year odyssey. American Psychologist, 57(9), 705-717.

title: Dreaming Versus Expecting
text:
Popular advice often says that picturing success will help you achieve it. The psychologist Gabriele Oettingen, working in Germany, had doubts. In a 2002 paper with Doris Mayer, she separated two ways of thinking about the future: expectations, judgments of how likely success is based on past experience, and fantasies, pleasant images of the desired future that come to mind.

In one study, university graduates about to look for a job reported how likely they thought they were to find one, and also described the thoughts and images that came to them when they imagined their job search. Two years later the researchers followed up. Graduates with high expectations had done well. But those whose fantasies were the most positive, who pictured themselves sailing smoothly into an ideal job, had sent out fewer applications, received fewer offers and were earning less than those with more mixed or sober images.

Similar patterns appeared in other studies in the paper: among students hoping to start a relationship with someone they had a crush on, among students hoping to do well on an exam, and among patients recovering from hip replacement surgery. Positive expectations predicted more effort and better outcomes. Positive fantasies predicted less.

Oettingen argued that pleasant fantasies let the mind enjoy the goal in advance, which drains the energy needed to pursue it. She later developed a method called mental contrasting, which pairs the imagined goal with the obstacles in the way.
lesson: Enjoy imagining the goal, but do not stop there. Picture the main obstacle that stands in your way and plan how you will deal with it; that is what turns a dream into effort.
people: Gabriele Oettingen, Doris Mayer
source: Oettingen, G., and Mayer, D. (2002). The motivating function of thinking about the future: Expectations versus fantasies. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 83(5), 1198-1212.

title: The Bias Blind Spot
text:
In 2002 Emily Pronin, Daniel Lin and Lee Ross, working at Stanford University, published a set of studies on a curious asymmetry: people see bias in others much more easily than in themselves.

In one study, students read short descriptions of well-known biases, such as the tendency to take credit for success while blaming failure on circumstances, or to favor one's own group. For each, they rated how much they themselves showed the bias and how much the average American did. For nearly every bias, they rated themselves as less affected than the average person.

In another study, students took a test of social intelligence and were told, at random, that they had done well or poorly. Those told they had done poorly tended to judge the test as less valid, a classic self-serving response. Yet when the researchers then described this tendency to them, the students said it probably applied to others more than it had to them.

The researchers argued that people judge their own bias by looking inward. They search their thoughts and feelings, find no sense of being biased, and conclude they are objective. Other people's bias, by contrast, is judged from their behavior, where it is visible. The pattern came to be called the bias blind spot.
lesson: Introspection cannot reveal your own biases, because they do not feel like anything from the inside. Ask others to check your reasoning, and use checklists or outside views where it matters.
people: Emily Pronin, Daniel Lin, Lee Ross
source: Pronin, E., Lin, D. Y., and Ross, L. (2002). The bias blind spot: Perceptions of bias in self versus others. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 28(3), 369-381.

title: Maximizers and Satisficers
text:
The economist and psychologist Herbert Simon had argued in the 1950s that people often "satisfice": instead of searching for the best possible option, they settle on one that is good enough. In 2002 Barry Schwartz of Swarthmore College and colleagues, including Sonja Lyubomirsky and Darrin Lehman, asked what happens to people who do the opposite.

They built a questionnaire to measure the tendency to maximize, with statements such as "When I watch TV, I channel surf, often scanning through the available options even while attempting to watch one program" and "I never settle for second best." Well over a thousand people in the United States and Canada filled it out, along with measures of happiness, optimism, depression and regret.

People who scored high as maximizers reported less happiness, less optimism and less satisfaction with life, and more depression and regret, than satisficers. In follow-up studies, maximizers compared themselves with others more often and were more sensitive to how others were doing. In shopping, they considered more options and were more likely to imagine alternatives they had not chosen, which made them less pleased with what they bought.

Schwartz argued that in a world of abundant choice, holding out for the best can be a recipe for misery. A study he later coauthored on graduating students found that maximizers landed jobs with higher starting salaries but felt worse about the outcome than satisficers did.
lesson: For most choices, decide what good enough looks like before you start searching, take the first option that meets it, and stop comparing. Save maximizing for the few decisions that truly matter.
people: Barry Schwartz, Andrew Ward, John Monterosso, Sonja Lyubomirsky, Katherine White, Darrin Lehman
location: Swarthmore College, Pennsylvania, USA, and Canada
source: Schwartz, B., Ward, A., Monterosso, J., Lyubomirsky, S., White, K., and Lehman, D. R. (2002). Maximizing versus satisficing: Happiness is a matter of choice. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 83(5), 1178-1197.
caveat: The findings are correlational, and later work found the maximizing scale mixes high standards (fairly harmless) with exhaustive searching and decision difficulty (more harmful).

title: Mints with the Bill
text:
Restaurants often bring a mint or a piece of chocolate with the bill. In 2002 David Strohmetz, Bruce Rind, Reed Fisher and Michael Lynn published experiments testing whether this small gift changes how much diners tip.

In their studies, carried out in restaurants in the United States, servers delivered the bill in different ways, decided in advance for each table. Some diners got no candy. Some got one piece of chocolate per person with the check. Some got two pieces. In a fourth condition, the server first left one piece per person, started to walk away, then turned back and offered each diner a second piece, as if on a sudden personal impulse.

Tips rose with the gift. A single piece of candy raised them only slightly, about 3 percent. Two pieces raised them by about 14 percent. But the largest increase, about 23 percent, came when the server returned with the second piece. The diners received the same amount of chocolate in both two-piece conditions. What changed was the impression that the extra gift was personal, unexpected and meant for them, which turned a routine courtesy into a small act of kindness that diners wanted to repay.
lesson: How a kindness is given matters as much as what is given. A small gesture that feels personal and unexpected means more than a bigger routine one.
people: David Strohmetz, Bruce Rind, Reed Fisher, Michael Lynn
source: Strohmetz, D. B., Rind, B., Fisher, R., and Lynn, M. (2002). Sweetening the till: The use of candy to increase restaurant tipping. Journal of Applied Social Psychology, 32(2), 300-309.

title: Managers Who Bring Their Style Along
text:
Economists often treated corporate executives as interchangeable: put any capable manager in the same company and you should get roughly the same decisions. In 2003 Marianne Bertrand and Antoinette Schoar tested that view with a simple idea. They followed top managers who had moved between large American companies over several decades, and asked whether a manager's arrival changed a company's policies in a way that matched what that same manager had done before.

It did. Individual managers carried recognizable styles with them. Some consistently invested more, made more acquisitions, or took on more debt; others paid more dividends, held more cash or cut costs more aggressively. These personal differences explained a meaningful share of the variation in company policies, beyond what the company and the year would predict, and they were linked to differences in company performance.

The researchers also found that certain backgrounds predicted styles. For example, managers from older generations tended to be more conservative, while those with an MBA tended to follow more aggressive strategies.
lesson: A leader's personal habits and beliefs leave a lasting mark on an organization. Know your own style and its biases, and choose leaders whose style fits what you need.
people: Marianne Bertrand, Antoinette Schoar
source: Bertrand, M., and Schoar, A. (2003). Managing with style: The effect of managers on firm policies. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 118(4), 1169-1208.
caveat: Managers do not move between firms at random, so the results are strong evidence but not a perfect experiment.

title: Giving Help and Living Longer
text:
It is widely accepted that receiving support from others is good for health. In 2003 Stephanie Brown, Randolph Nesse, Amiram Vinokur and Dylan Smith of the University of Michigan asked whether giving support might matter too.

They used data from a study of older married couples in the Detroit area. At the start, the participants were asked how much practical help they gave to friends, relatives and neighbors, such as transportation, errands and childcare, and how much emotional support they gave to their spouse. They were also asked how much help they received. The researchers then followed them for five years and recorded who died.

People who reported giving more help were significantly less likely to die during those five years. The link remained after accounting for age, sex, health, income and many other factors. Receiving help, on the other hand, showed no protective link once these were considered. The authors suggested that the benefits of close relationships may come partly from what we give, not only from what we get. Contributing to others' lives may bring purpose and connection that are good for the giver's own health.
lesson: Helping others may be as good for you as being helped. Look for regular, practical ways to be useful to the people around you.
people: Stephanie Brown, Randolph Nesse, Amiram Vinokur, Dylan Smith
source: Brown, S. L., Nesse, R. M., Vinokur, A. D., and Smith, D. M. (2003). Providing social support may be more beneficial than receiving it: Results from a prospective study of mortality. Psychological Science, 14(4), 320-327.
caveat: The study is observational, so it cannot fully rule out that healthier people are simply more able to give help.

title: Left Out of a Game of Catch
text:
The psychologist Kipling Williams once found himself in a park, tossed a frisbee by two strangers who then went back to throwing it only to each other. He was surprised how bad it felt to be left out, and he turned the experience into a simple computer game called Cyberball, in which a player tosses a virtual ball with two others on screen.

In 2003 Naomi Eisenberger and Matthew Lieberman of the University of California, Los Angeles, together with Williams, used the game in a brain scanner. Each participant believed they were playing online with two other people, though the other players were run by the computer. In one round, the participant could only watch, supposedly because of a technical problem. In another, the participant was included in the game for a few throws, and then the two others threw the ball only to each other for the rest of the round.

Being excluded by strangers in a meaningless game left people feeling distressed and ignored, as they reported afterward. The brain scans showed increased activity in the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, a region also involved in the distress of physical pain, and the more upset people felt, the more active it was. Social rejection, the researchers suggested, may draw on some of the same alarm systems as bodily pain.
lesson: Even small exclusions hurt. Notice who is being left out of the conversation, the meeting or the game, and throw them the ball.
people: Naomi Eisenberger, Matthew Lieberman, Kipling Williams
location: University of California, Los Angeles, USA
source: Eisenberger, N. I., Lieberman, M. D., and Williams, K. D. (2003). Does rejection hurt? An fMRI study of social exclusion. Science, 302(5643), 290-292.
caveat: The brain imaging study was small, and the claim that social pain and physical pain share the same brain systems is debated, though the distress caused by exclusion is well replicated.

title: Do Defaults Save Lives?
text:
In 2003 Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein of Columbia University published a short paper in Science that compared organ donation consent across European countries. Some countries used an opt-in system: you were a donor only if you signed up. Others used an opt-out system: you were presumed to be a donor unless you registered a refusal.

The differences were enormous. In opt-in countries such as Germany, Denmark and the United Kingdom, effective consent rates ranged from about 4 percent to under 30 percent. In opt-out countries such as Austria, Belgium, France and Sweden, they ranged from about 86 percent to nearly 100 percent. Neighbors with similar cultures, such as Germany and Austria, sat at opposite ends.

Johnson and Goldstein also ran an online experiment. Asked whether they would be donors, participants who had to opt in agreed about 42 percent of the time. Those who had to opt out agreed about 82 percent of the time. Those forced to choose without any default agreed about 79 percent of the time.

The authors suggested several reasons: changing a default takes effort, a default can look like a recommendation from authorities, and it feels like the normal choice. Comparing actual donation rates, they found that opt-out countries had noticeably higher rates, though the gap was much smaller than the gap in consent, since families and medical systems also play a large role.
lesson: Whoever sets the default shapes most outcomes, because most people never change it. When you design a process for others, choose the default you would want them to end up with.
people: Eric Johnson, Daniel Goldstein
location: Columbia University, New York, USA (data from European countries)
source: Johnson, E. J., and Goldstein, D. (2003). Do defaults save lives? Science, 302(5649), 1338-1339.
caveat: Actual donation rates differ far less than consent rates, since families and hospital systems also decide outcomes.

title: Power Takes the Brakes Off
text:
In 2003 the psychologists Dacher Keltner, Deborah Gruenfeld and Cameron Anderson published an influential theory of how power changes people. They pulled together findings from many experiments and field studies on power, from children in classrooms to managers and animals in dominance hierarchies.

Their argument was that power switches on what psychologists call the approach system. People who hold power have more resources and fewer threats around them, so they tend to feel more positive emotions, notice rewards and opportunities, and act on their impulses. People with little power live with more threats and constraints, so their inhibition system is more active: they are more watchful, more anxious and more attentive to what others think and want.

The theory explained a range of observations. In studies they reviewed, people with more power spoke more freely, interrupted more, judged others more stereotypically and behaved in less inhibited, sometimes rude or socially inappropriate ways, such as eating more greedily from a shared plate. People with less power paid closer attention to others and read them more carefully. The paper became a foundation for a decade of research on what power does to the mind.
lesson: Gaining authority loosens your restraint and dulls your attention to others. The more power you hold, the more deliberately you must listen and check yourself.
people: Dacher Keltner, Deborah Gruenfeld, Cameron Anderson
source: Keltner, D., Gruenfeld, D. H., and Anderson, C. (2003). Power, approach, and inhibition. Psychological Review, 110(2), 265-284.
caveat: It is a theory built from a review of studies; some later findings on specific effects of power have replicated weakly.

title: Mandarin From a Person, Not a Screen
text:
Very young babies can tell apart the speech sounds of almost any language. By around their first birthday, they have become specialists, getting better at the sounds of their own language and worse at foreign ones. Patricia Kuhl and her colleagues at the University of Washington asked whether a short burst of exposure to a foreign language could keep that ability alive, and what kind of exposure would work.

They brought nine-month-old American babies from English-speaking homes into the lab for twelve short sessions over about four weeks. In each session, a native Mandarin speaker read books and played with toys while talking to the baby. A comparison group had the same kind of sessions in English.

Afterward, the babies were tested on a pair of Mandarin sounds that English does not distinguish. Infants who had played with the Mandarin speakers could tell the sounds apart about as well as babies of the same age growing up in Taiwan. The English group could not.

Then came the key test. Other American babies watched the same Mandarin speakers, saying the same things, on a video screen, or heard only the audio. These babies learned nothing measurable. The social presence of a real person seemed to be what made learning happen.
lesson: Small children learn language from people, not screens. Talking, reading and playing face to face does what no recording can.
people: Patricia Kuhl, Feng-Ming Tsao, Huei-Mei Liu
source: Kuhl, P. K., Tsao, F.-M., and Liu, H.-M. (2003). Foreign-language experience in infancy: Effects of short-term exposure and social interaction on phonetic learning. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 100(15), 9096-9101.

title: Unequal Childhoods
text:
The sociologist Annette Lareau wanted to see, in close detail, how social class shapes the daily lives of children. In the 1990s, she and her research assistants interviewed many families in a city and suburbs in the northeastern United States and then chose twelve families with children around nine and ten years old, Black and white, middle class, working class and poor, for intensive observation.

The researchers visited each family about twenty times, often for hours, riding along to soccer games and church, sitting through dinners and homework, and sometimes staying overnight.

Lareau found two broad cultural logics of child rearing. Middle-class parents practiced what she called concerted cultivation. Their children's days were filled with organized activities, parents reasoned and negotiated with them, and they encouraged children to question adults and speak up to doctors and teachers. These children gained a sense of entitlement that served them well in institutions, but families were often exhausted and siblings had little free time.

Working-class and poor parents practiced what she called the accomplishment of natural growth. They provided love, food and safety and then let children organize their own play, often with cousins and neighbors. Parents gave directives rather than reasons. These children were more independent and inventive with their time, but more often showed a sense of constraint when dealing with schools and officials.
lesson: Both structure and freedom give children something valuable. Teach children to speak up to institutions, and also leave them time to play on their own.
people: Annette Lareau
source: Lareau, A. (2003). Unequal Childhoods: Class, Race, and Family Life. Berkeley: University of California Press.
caveat: The study is based on a small number of families observed in depth, so its patterns are illustrative rather than statistically representative.

title: The Happiness Bump of Marriage
text:
Does getting married make people happier for good? Earlier surveys had found married people happier than single people, but that could simply mean happier people are more likely to marry. To track individuals over time, Richard Lucas, Andrew Clark, Yannis Georgellis and Ed Diener turned to the German Socio-Economic Panel, a survey that had asked the same people about their life satisfaction every year for fifteen years.

Among more than 24,000 people, they followed those who married during the study and those who lost a spouse. For the people who married, life satisfaction rose in the years leading up to the wedding and peaked around it. Then, on average, it drifted back to roughly where it had been before, within a couple of years. People seemed to adapt to marriage, as they adapt to many good things.

The average hid wide differences. Some people stayed happier long after marrying; others ended up less happy than before. Widowhood was different: satisfaction fell sharply, and on average people recovered only slowly and not completely, even years later.

The study added nuance to the idea that each person has a fixed happiness set point. Adaptation is common, but it is neither complete nor the same for everyone.
lesson: A wedding does not deliver lasting happiness by itself. What follows, the daily care of the relationship, decides whether the glow fades or grows.
people: Richard Lucas, Andrew Clark, Yannis Georgellis, Ed Diener
source: Lucas, R. E., Clark, A. E., Georgellis, Y., and Diener, E. (2003). Reexamining adaptation and the set point model of happiness: Reactions to changes in marital status. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 84(3), 527-539.

title: What Employees Do Not Tell the Boss
text:
In the early 2000s Frances Milliken, Elizabeth Morrison and Patricia Hewlin of New York University interviewed forty employees from a range of industries about times they had stayed silent at work. Most had full time jobs and some management experience.

The vast majority, around 85 percent, described at least one occasion when they had been aware of an issue or concern at work and had not raised it with their boss. The topics varied: problems with a colleague's or a supervisor's competence, concerns about pay, disagreement with company policies, suggestions for improving processes, and ethical issues.

When asked why they had kept quiet, the most common reason was fear of being seen negatively, for example labeled as a troublemaker or a complainer. Others worried about damaging a relationship, said speaking up would make no difference, feared retaliation, or did not want to embarrass others. Many said their impressions came from how their organization and particular managers had treated people who spoke up before.
lesson: Assume your people know about problems you do not. Ask them directly, and make sure no one is labeled a troublemaker for raising one.
people: Frances Milliken, Elizabeth Morrison, Patricia Hewlin
source: Milliken, F. J., Morrison, E. W., and Hewlin, P. F. (2003). An exploratory study of employee silence: Issues that employees don't communicate upward and why. Journal of Management Studies, 40(6), 1453-1476.
caveat: It was a small interview study, so the percentage is illustrative rather than precise.

title: The Mark of a Criminal Record
text:
In 2001 Devah Pager, a graduate student in sociology at the University of Wisconsin, sent pairs of young men to apply for real entry-level jobs in Milwaukee. The men were college students chosen to be similar in appearance and manner, and they were given matching fictional resumes. One pair was white and the other pair was Black.

Within each pair, the men took turns presenting a criminal record: a felony drug conviction and eighteen months in prison. Otherwise they applied in the same way to the same employers, in hundreds of applications in total, and the researchers recorded which applicants were called back.

Among white applicants, 34 percent without a record were called back, compared with 17 percent of those with a record. Among Black applicants, 14 percent without a record were called back, and only 5 percent of those with a record. A criminal record cut a man's chances roughly in half, and for Black applicants the effect was even larger. Most striking, white applicants with a prison record were called back at least as often as Black applicants with a clean record. Pager concluded that a criminal record, and race, act as powerful marks that close doors before an applicant can show what he can do.
lesson: Labels like a past record can close doors before a person can show who they are now. When you can, give people a chance to be judged on what they do today.
people: Devah Pager
source: Pager, D. (2003). The mark of a criminal record. American Journal of Sociology, 108(5), 937-975.

title: Penalty Kicks and Game Theory
text:
Game theory makes a clear prediction about contests like a soccer penalty kick. If the kicker always shot to the same side, the goalkeeper would learn it and dive there; if the keeper always dived one way, the kicker would shoot the other. The best strategy for each is to mix choices at random in such proportions that the opponent cannot gain by guessing, a solution known as minimax. In a real minimax equilibrium, a kicker's chance of scoring should be the same whichever side he picks, and his choices should show no predictable pattern over time.

These predictions had rarely been confirmed outside the laboratory, where people tend to alternate too often and make poor random choices. In 2003 Ignacio Palacios-Huerta, an economist at Brown University, analyzed over 1,400 penalty kicks taken in professional matches in several European leagues, mostly in the late 1990s.

He found that the professionals behaved almost exactly as the theory required. Scoring rates were statistically the same whether kickers aimed left or right, and so were goalkeepers' success rates whichever way they dived. And the sequence of each player's choices looked random: what a kicker did last time did not predict what he would do next.

The result was one of the first clean tests of minimax with real stakes. It showed that experienced professionals in a high-pressure contest had learned, without any formal theory, to be exactly as unpredictable as they needed to be.
lesson: In any contest where an opponent can learn your habits, predictability is a weakness. Vary your choices so the other side cannot profit from guessing them.
people: Ignacio Palacios-Huerta
location: Brown University, Providence, USA (kicks from European leagues)
source: Palacios-Huerta, I. (2003). Professionals play minimax. Review of Economic Studies, 70(2), 395-415.

title: Why Hospitals Don't Learn
text:
In the late 1990s and early 2000s, Anita Tucker shadowed nurses on their shifts in several American hospitals, recording every small problem that got in the way of their work. Together with Amy Edmondson, she analyzed what the nurses did when something went wrong.

The problems were mostly mundane: missing supplies, linens that had not been delivered, medications not ready, equipment that did not work, information missing from a chart. They happened constantly, often several times an hour, and they ate into time meant for patients.

The nurses were skilled at solving them. They borrowed linens from another unit, went to fetch medication themselves, or found a workaround and got on with caring for the patient. Tucker and Edmondson called this first-order problem solving. What the nurses rarely did was second-order problem solving: telling someone who could change the system, questioning why the problem kept happening, or working with other departments to fix its cause.

The researchers traced this to features of the organization: an ideal of the self-reliant nurse, managers who were rarely present, constant time pressure, and a lack of support for raising issues. Because every problem was quietly patched, the same problems came back every day, and the hospital never learned.
lesson: Heroic workarounds hide broken systems. When you fix the same problem twice, tell someone who can fix it for good.
people: Anita Tucker, Amy Edmondson
source: Tucker, A. L., and Edmondson, A. C. (2003). Why hospitals don't learn from failures: Organizational and psychological dynamics that inhibit system change. California Management Review, 45(2), 55-72.

title: Children and Marital Satisfaction
text:
Many couples expect children to bring them closer. Researchers had been studying the effect of children on marriage for decades, with mixed results. In 2003, Jean Twenge, W. Keith Campbell and Craig Foster combined the findings of nearly a hundred published studies, covering tens of thousands of people, in a meta-analysis.

On average, parents reported lower marital satisfaction than people without children. The difference was modest, but it was consistent, and it followed clear patterns. It was largest among mothers of infants, smaller among fathers, and it grew with the number of children. It was also larger among more affluent couples and in more recent generations, suggesting that the change was felt most by people who had grown used to freedom and an equal sharing of time before children arrived.

The researchers looked at possible reasons. Their analysis suggested that two factors mattered most: conflicts over roles, such as who does what at home now that there is so much more to do, and the loss of freedom, as parents found their time, sleep and spontaneity sharply reduced.

The study did not say that children make people unhappy. It described a specific strain on the couple relationship during the years of intensive care, one that partners can anticipate and work on together.
lesson: Expect children to strain a marriage, especially in the early years, and talk openly about roles and lost freedom. Naming the strain makes it easier to share.
people: Jean Twenge, W. Keith Campbell, Craig Foster
location: San Diego State University, San Diego, USA
source: Twenge, J. M., Campbell, W. K., and Foster, C. A. (2003). Parenthood and marital satisfaction: A meta-analytic review. Journal of Marriage and Family, 65(3), 574-583.

title: The Waitress Who Repeated the Order
text:
