source: Ariely, D., Kamenica, E., and Prelec, D. (2008). Man's search for meaning: The case of Legos. Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization, 67(3-4), 671-677.

title: Do You Know Where Your Grandparents Grew Up?
text:
At Emory University in Atlanta, the psychologists Marshall Duke and Robyn Fivush studied how families tell stories. Fivush had long been interested in how children learn to remember and narrate their lives, and the project included recording ordinary families talking at the dinner table.

Duke noticed something about the families that seemed to cope best: their children knew a lot about where they came from. To measure this, the team created a simple questionnaire called the Do You Know scale, with twenty yes or no questions. Do you know where your grandparents grew up? Do you know where your parents met? Do you know about an illness or something terrible that happened in your family? Do you know some of the lessons your parents learned from good or bad experiences?

In a 2008 report with Amber Lazarus, they described how children's scores related to standard measures of well-being. Children who knew more about their family's history tended to have higher self-esteem, a stronger sense of control over their lives, fewer behavior problems and better family functioning.

The researchers suggested that what helps is not the facts themselves but what they carry: a sense of belonging to something larger, and stories of a family that had ups and downs and kept going.
lesson: Tell your children the family stories, including the hard ones. Knowing that their people struggled and endured helps children face their own trouble.
people: Marshall Duke, Robyn Fivush, Amber Lazarus
source: Duke, M. P., Lazarus, A., and Fivush, R. (2008). Knowledge of family history as a clinically useful index of psychological well-being and prognosis: A brief report. Psychotherapy: Theory, Research, Practice, Training, 45(2), 268-272.
caveat: The study was a brief correlational report, so knowing family history may reflect close family communication rather than cause resilience by itself.

title: Spending Money on Others
text:
In 2008 Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin and Michael Norton published a short paper in Science asking whether how people spend money affects how happy they are. They started with a national survey of more than six hundred Americans. How much people spent on themselves did not predict their happiness, but how much they spent on gifts for others and on charity did.

They then followed employees at a company in Boston who received a profit-sharing bonus. Those who spent more of it on others reported being happier weeks later, regardless of the bonus size.

Finally, they ran an experiment at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver. In the morning, students were handed an envelope with either 5 or 20 dollars. Some were told to spend it on a bill, an expense or a gift for themselves by five o'clock. Others were told to spend it on a gift for someone else or a donation. That evening, those who had spent the money on others reported being happier than those who had spent it on themselves. The amount did not matter. Yet when other students were asked to predict the results, most expected spending on oneself, and more money, to bring more happiness.
lesson: Spending a little on someone else tends to lift your mood more than spending it on yourself. Even a small gift or treat for another person counts.
people: Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin, Michael Norton
location: University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada, and Boston, USA
source: Dunn, E. W., Aknin, L. B., and Norton, M. I. (2008). Spending money on others promotes happiness. Science, 319(5870), 1687-1688.
caveat: The experiment was small; later studies in many countries support the link, though its size varies.

title: Happiness Spreads Through Networks
text:
Since 1948 the Framingham Heart Study has followed residents of a town near Boston to learn about heart disease. Participants also listed relatives, close friends, neighbors and coworkers, often people who were in the study too. James Fowler and Nicholas Christakis realized that these records formed a map of a real social network, and that the study had also measured people's happiness.

In 2008 they analyzed data on nearly five thousand people from 1983 to 2003. Happy and unhappy people formed clusters in the network. More striking, happiness seemed to travel over time. A person whose friend living within a mile became happy was substantially more likely to become happy too, and the same held for next-door neighbors and for siblings who lived nearby. Coworkers showed no such effect. The association extended, more weakly, to the friend of a friend and even to the friend of a friend of a friend.

The researchers concluded that happiness is not only an individual matter but partly a property of groups, spreading through ties like a kind of contagion. The effect faded with physical distance and with time, suggesting that frequent face-to-face contact was part of how it worked.
lesson: Your mood affects people close to you and theirs affects yours. Spending time with cheerful people, and being one, may help a whole circle of friends.
people: James Fowler, Nicholas Christakis
source: Fowler, J. H., and Christakis, N. A. (2008). Dynamic spread of happiness in a large social network: Longitudinal analysis over 20 years in the Framingham Heart Study. BMJ, 337, a2338.
caveat: Critics argue that such network effects are hard to separate from people choosing similar friends and sharing the same surroundings, so the contagion claim remains debated.

title: Inside the Head of Your Opponent
text:
In 2008 Adam Galinsky, William Maddux, Debra Gilin and Judith White compared two ways of focusing on the other side in a negotiation. Perspective taking means thinking about what the other person wants and why, a mainly mental exercise. Empathy means feeling for the other person and connecting emotionally.

In one study, MBA students negotiated the sale of a gas station. The buyer's highest possible offer was lower than the seller's lowest acceptable price, so a simple deal on price was impossible. But the case contained hidden interests: the seller needed money for a trip and wanted a job afterwards, and the buyer needed someone to run the station. A creative deal, a lower price plus employment, could satisfy both. Before negotiating, buyers were asked either to imagine what the seller was thinking, to imagine what the seller was feeling, or were given no special instructions.

Buyers who took the seller's perspective were the most likely to discover the creative deal. Those who focused on the seller's feelings did better than the control group but not as well. In another study, about a job contract with several issues, perspective takers created more total value and also claimed more of it for themselves, while empathizers sometimes gave too much away.

The authors concluded that in negotiations it pays more to get inside the other side's head than inside their heart, though empathy has its own uses in building relationships.
lesson: Before a negotiation, take time to work out what the other side really needs and why. Understanding their interests reveals deals that a simple tug of war over price would miss.
people: Adam Galinsky, William Maddux, Debra Gilin, Judith White
source: Galinsky, A. D., Maddux, W. W., Gilin, D., and White, J. B. (2008). Why it pays to get inside the head of your opponent: The differential effects of perspective taking and empathy in negotiations. Psychological Science, 19(4), 378-384.

title: The Hotel Towel Cards
text:
Many hotels place cards in their bathrooms asking guests to reuse their towels to help the environment. In 2008 Noah Goldstein, Robert Cialdini and Vladas Griskevicius tested whether a different message would work better.

They worked with a hotel in Arizona over several months. In some rooms, the card carried the standard message urging guests to help save the environment by reusing their towels. In others, the card said that most guests at the hotel had reused their towels at least once during their stay, a fact drawn from an earlier study, and invited guests to join their fellow guests in helping to save the environment. Room attendants recorded whether guests reused at least one towel.

The social norm message did better. About 44 percent of guests who saw it reused towels, compared with about 35 percent of those who saw the environmental appeal. In a second study, the most effective message was the most specific: that most guests who had stayed in this very room had reused their towels. Guests responded more to what people in a situation like theirs were doing than to general appeals or to norms of broader groups such as citizens or men and women.
lesson: People follow what others like them actually do. If you want to encourage a behavior, show that it is already common, not that too few people do it.
people: Noah Goldstein, Robert Cialdini, Vladas Griskevicius
source: Goldstein, N. J., Cialdini, R. B., and Griskevicius, V. (2008). A room with a viewpoint: Using social norms to motivate environmental conservation in hotels. Journal of Consumer Research, 35(3), 472-482.
caveat: Later replication attempts found smaller or no effects, so the size of the effect in other hotels is uncertain.

title: Can Stars Take It with Them?
text:
Wall Street firms compete fiercely to hire star equity analysts, the people who research companies and advise investors. Each year, the magazine Institutional Investor publishes a ranking of the best analysts, which gave Boris Groysberg, Linda-Eling Lee and Ashish Nanda of Harvard Business School a measure of performance over time.

They followed more than a thousand ranked star analysts from the late 1980s through the mid-1990s and compared those who changed firms with those who stayed. If talent were purely personal, the movers should have performed as well after switching as before.

They did not. On average, stars who moved to a new firm saw their rankings fall, and the drop lasted for years. The researchers concluded that much of a star's performance depended on the old firm's resources, colleagues, research support and reputation.

There were important exceptions. Analysts who moved to firms with stronger capabilities fared better. And analysts who moved together with their team, taking their junior colleagues and assistants with them, did not suffer the same decline. What made a star shine turned out to be partly the team around them.
lesson: When you hire a star, you are not buying their team, systems or reputation. Hire whole working groups when you can, or give newcomers time to rebuild theirs.
people: Boris Groysberg, Linda-Eling Lee, Ashish Nanda
location: Wall Street investment firms, New York, USA
source: Groysberg, B., Lee, L.-E., and Nanda, A. (2008). Can they take it with them? The portability of star knowledge workers' performance. Management Science, 54(7), 1213-1230.

title: The Spreading of Disorder
text:
The broken windows theory holds that visible signs of disorder encourage further disorder and crime. In 2008, Kees Keizer, Siegwart Lindenberg and Linda Steg of the University of Groningen in the Netherlands tested this with a series of field experiments on the streets of their city.

In one, they hung flyers on the handlebars of bicycles parked in an alley next to a sign forbidding graffiti. When the wall was clean, about a third of cyclists threw the flyer on the ground. When the wall was covered in graffiti, more than two thirds did.

In another, they left an envelope hanging out of a mailbox, with a five-euro note clearly visible inside. When the mailbox was clean and the area tidy, about 13 percent of passersby took the envelope. When the mailbox was covered in graffiti, the share rose to 27 percent, and litter around it had a similar effect.

Other experiments showed similar patterns with fences, shopping carts and fireworks. Seeing that others had broken one rule made people more likely to break different rules. The authors argued that visible violations weaken people's sense that norms in general apply.
lesson: Small visible lapses in a shared space signal that rules no longer matter. Fix minor disorder quickly so it does not spread to bigger things.
people: Kees Keizer, Siegwart Lindenberg, Linda Steg
source: Keizer, K., Lindenberg, S., and Steg, L. (2008). The spreading of disorder. Science, 322(5908), 1681-1685.

title: Why Dominant People Get Heard
text:
It is well known that people with dominant personalities tend to gain influence in groups. In 2009 Cameron Anderson and Gavin Kilduff tested why. One explanation is that dominant people simply bully others into going along. The other is that they look more capable than they are.

In one study, students first completed a personality measure of dominance. They were then put into small groups to solve a set of math problems similar to those on graduate admissions tests, and the sessions were recorded. Afterward, group members rated each other's competence and influence, and outside observers rated the video.

Dominant individuals did become more influential, but not because they intimidated anyone. They spoke up first and offered more answers, and they behaved in ways that made them seem competent, which led both teammates and observers to see them as more able. Their actual math ability, measured separately, was no better than anyone else's. In a second study with a different task, the same pattern held: dominant people were seen as more competent even when they were not.
lesson: Confidence and speaking first are easily mistaken for competence. When choosing whom to follow or promote, look at track records, not only at who talks most.
people: Cameron Anderson, Gavin Kilduff
source: Anderson, C., and Kilduff, G. J. (2009). Why do dominant personalities attain influence in face-to-face groups? The competence-signaling effects of trait dominance. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 96(2), 491-503.

title: Large Stakes, Big Mistakes
text:
Many companies assume that the bigger the bonus, the better people will perform. In 2009 Dan Ariely, Uri Gneezy, George Loewenstein and Nina Mazar published a test of what happens when the stakes become very large.

Because large rewards are expensive, they ran their main experiment in rural India, near the city of Madurai, where modest sums of money in dollar terms meant a great deal. Participants played several games requiring concentration, memory, creativity or motor skill, such as remembering sequences of numbers, solving a puzzle under time pressure or throwing balls at a target. They were randomly offered small, medium or very large payments for reaching performance targets. The very large payment was roughly equal to several months of typical spending for people in the area.

Performance did not rise with the reward. People offered small and medium payments performed similarly, while those offered the very large payment performed worst on most of the tasks. In a separate study at MIT, larger rewards improved performance on a simple task of pressing keys, but hurt performance on a task requiring arithmetic. The authors concluded that very high stakes can make people choke.
lesson: Very high stakes can make people tense and worse at tasks that need careful thinking. Keep pressure in proportion, especially for skilled and creative work.
people: Dan Ariely, Uri Gneezy, George Loewenstein, Nina Mazar
location: Madurai, India, and Massachusetts Institute of Technology, USA
source: Ariely, D., Gneezy, U., Loewenstein, G., and Mazar, N. (2009). Large stakes and big mistakes. Review of Economic Studies, 76(2), 451-469.
caveat: The samples were modest in size, so the precise drop in performance should not be overstated.

title: The Surgical Safety Checklist
text:
In 2007 and 2008, a team led by Alex Haynes and Atul Gawande, working with the World Health Organization, tested a simple one-page checklist in eight hospitals in very different settings: Toronto, New Delhi, Amman, Auckland, Manila, Ifakara in Tanzania, London and Seattle.

The checklist had three short pauses. Before anesthesia, the team confirmed the patient's identity, the procedure and the risks. Before the first incision, everyone in the room introduced themselves by name and role, and the surgeon, anesthetist and nurses briefly went over what to expect. Before the patient left the room, they checked counts of instruments and sponges and discussed recovery.

The researchers compared thousands of operations before and after the checklist was introduced. The rate of major complications fell from about 11 percent to about 7 percent, and deaths after surgery fell from about 1.5 percent to about 0.8 percent. Improvements appeared in rich and poor hospitals alike. The researchers suggested that the gains came not only from catching specific errors but from changing how the team worked together, including the moment when every person in the room was named and invited to speak.
lesson: A short routine that makes everyone speak at the start of a task can save a team from its own silence. Introduce yourselves and say aloud what could go wrong.
people: Alex Haynes, Atul Gawande and colleagues
location: Eight hospitals in Canada, India, Jordan, New Zealand, the Philippines, Tanzania, the UK and the USA
source: Haynes, A. B., Weiser, T. G., Berry, W. R., Lipsitz, S. R., Breizat, A. H., Dellinger, E. P., et al. (2009). A surgical safety checklist to reduce morbidity and mortality in a global population. New England Journal of Medicine, 360(5), 491-499.
caveat: It was a before and after study without a control group, and some later evaluations, such as one in Ontario, found smaller or no improvements when checklists were mandated.

title: Fast Cashiers in the Next Lane
text:
Economists Alexandre Mas and Enrico Moretti, at the University of California, Berkeley, wanted to know whether working next to a productive colleague makes people work harder. They found an ideal setting in a national supermarket chain, which recorded every item every cashier scanned.

In the stores they studied, cashiers worked in shifts that were scheduled in ways that had nothing to do with who was fast or slow. That meant that at random moments, a cashier might find a particularly fast colleague arriving at a nearby register, or leaving. The researchers could then see how everyone else's speed changed.

When a highly productive cashier joined the shift, the others sped up. The effect was not small: an increase in the average productivity of coworkers was followed by a measurable increase in each cashier's own pace.

The arrangement of the registers revealed why. The speedup appeared only when the fast cashier was positioned where they could see the slower one working. Being observed by a fast colleague mattered, while seeing a fast colleague did not. The authors linked this to social pressure among coworkers who saw each other regularly.
lesson: Effort is contagious when people can see each other's work. Place your strongest performers where teammates notice them, and let good norms spread.
people: Alexandre Mas, Enrico Moretti
location: Stores of a national supermarket chain, USA
source: Mas, A., and Moretti, E. (2009). Peers at work. American Economic Review, 99(1), 112-145.

title: The Newcomer Who Is Different
text:
Katherine Phillips, Katie Liljenquist and Margaret Neale studied what happens when a newcomer joins a team. They recruited members of university fraternities and sororities and put them in groups of three from the same house to solve a murder mystery. Each member had some clues, and the group had to decide who the killer was.

After the trio had discussed the case for a while, a fourth person joined. In some groups, the newcomer was from the same fraternity or sorority as the others. In others, the newcomer was from a different house, a socially distinct outsider. The newcomer, like the others, had information and a view about the case.

Groups joined by an outsider were more likely to identify the right suspect than groups joined by an insider. Yet members of those groups found the discussion less pleasant, felt less confident in their decision and believed they had performed worse.

The researchers suggested that the outsider's mere presence made old members think harder: they could not assume agreement, so they examined their own reasoning more carefully and paid more attention to the evidence. The discomfort was part of what improved the result.
lesson: A team that feels comfortable is not always deciding well. Welcome people who are different from the group, and accept some friction as the price of better thinking.
people: Katherine Phillips, Katie Liljenquist, Margaret Neale
source: Phillips, K. W., Liljenquist, K. A., and Neale, M. A. (2009). Is the pain worth the gain? The advantages and liabilities of agreeing with socially distinct newcomers. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 35(3), 336-350.

title: Marching in Step
text:
Armies drill, congregations sing, and crowds chant together. Scott Wiltermuth and Chip Heath of Stanford University wondered whether moving in unison actually changes how people treat one another.

In one experiment, small groups of students walked around campus. Some were told to walk in step, others to walk normally. In another, participants wore headphones and listened to the Canadian national anthem. Some sang along together while others just read the words silently.

Afterward, the groups played economic games in which each person could keep money for themselves or contribute to a group outcome, and in which success depended on trusting others to cooperate. Groups that had walked, sung or moved in synchrony cooperated more than groups that had not. They also reported feeling more like part of a team.

The effect appeared even though the synchronous activities were brief and the people did not necessarily feel happier afterward. Acting in unison, the authors suggested, may be one of the old ways human groups have used to bind members together.
lesson: Shared rhythm builds shared purpose. Doing something together in time, even briefly, can make a group readier to cooperate.
people: Scott Wiltermuth, Chip Heath
source: Wiltermuth, S. S., and Heath, C. (2009). Synchrony and cooperation. Psychological Science, 20(1), 1-5.
caveat: Later research suggests the effect of synchrony on cooperation is real but smaller and less consistent than this first study implied.

title: The Power Pose That Did Not Hold
text:
In 2010 Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap reported a small experiment with a big promise. Participants held either expansive, open postures, such as leaning back with feet up on a desk, or closed, contracted postures, for about two minutes. Saliva samples were taken before and after.

According to the paper, people who struck the expansive poses showed a rise in testosterone and a drop in the stress hormone cortisol, felt more powerful and were more willing to take a gamble. The finding spread far beyond psychology. Cuddy's 2012 TED talk on power posing became one of the most watched talks ever, and many people began striking poses before interviews and presentations.

Then the evidence weakened. In 2015 a team led by Eva Ranehill ran a much larger replication and found no effect on hormones or risk taking, though people did report feeling slightly more powerful. In 2016 Dana Carney, the paper's first author, publicly stated that she no longer believed the effects were real and described problems in how the original data had been analyzed.
lesson: Be wary of quick tricks that promise instant confidence. Real authority grows from preparation, competence and practice.
people: Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy, Andy Yap
location: Columbia University and Harvard University, USA
source: Carney, D. R., Cuddy, A. J. C., and Yap, A. J. (2010). Power posing: Brief nonverbal displays affect neuroendocrine levels and risk tolerance. Psychological Science, 21(10), 1363-1368.
caveat: The hormone and risk taking effects failed to replicate and the first author disowned them; only a small effect on feeling powerful has some support.

title: How Behavior Spreads
text:
A common idea in network science is that information spreads fastest through networks with many long-range connections, linking distant parts of a community. Damon Centola, then at MIT, wondered whether behavior spreads the same way as information.

He created an online health community and recruited more than 1,500 participants. Without knowing it, they were placed in one of two kinds of networks. In clustered networks, each person's neighbors were also connected to each other, like a tight neighborhood. In random networks, each person had the same number of contacts, but they were scattered across the network, creating many shortcuts.

Participants did not see each other's names. They were given health buddies, and whenever a buddy signed up for an online health forum, participants received an email inviting them to join too.

The behavior spread further and faster in the clustered networks. People were much more likely to join when they received invitations from several of their buddies, which happened more often in the clustered networks, where contacts overlapped. A single invitation often was not enough. Centola concluded that for behaviors that involve some cost or uncertainty, people need reinforcement from multiple contacts before they act.
lesson: To change behavior in a team or community, concentrate efforts in tight clusters where people hear the same message from several peers, rather than spreading thinly.
people: Damon Centola
location: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, USA (online experiment)
source: Centola, D. (2010). The spread of behavior in an online social network experiment. Science, 329(5996), 1194-1197.

title: A Little Thanks Goes a Long Way
text:
In 2010 Adam Grant and Francesca Gino published four studies on why being thanked makes people more willing to help. Most were laboratory experiments in which students who had given feedback on a cover letter were then asked for more help. Those who had received a short note of thanks were far more likely to help again.

The final study took place in a university fundraising call center. Callers there phoned alumni to request donations, and their calls were tracked by the center's system. One day, the director of annual giving visited one group of callers and told them she was very grateful for their hard work and contributions to the university. A second group did not receive the visit.

During the following week, the callers who had been thanked made more than 50 percent more calls than before, while the other group's number of calls stayed about the same. In the lab studies, the researchers found the main reason: being thanked made people feel socially valued, which in turn made them willing to give more of themselves.
lesson: A sincere thank you costs nothing and tells people their effort is seen. Make it a habit, and say specifically what you value.
people: Adam Grant, Francesca Gino
location: A US university fundraising call center
source: Grant, A. M., and Gino, F. (2010). A little thanks goes a long way: Explaining why gratitude expressions motivate prosocial behavior. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 98(6), 946-955.
caveat: Francesca Gino was later found by Harvard to have falsified data in other papers; this paper was not among those retracted, but its results deserve some care.

title: Social Ties and Survival
text:
Doctors routinely ask about smoking, drinking and exercise. In 2010 Julianne Holt-Lunstad, Timothy Smith and J. Bradley Layton of Brigham Young University asked whether they should also ask about friends and family.

They gathered 148 studies that had measured people's social relationships and then followed them over time to see who died. Together the studies covered more than 300,000 people, mostly in North America and Europe, followed for an average of about seven years. Social relationships were measured in many ways: whether people were married, lived alone, belonged to groups, had others to rely on, or felt integrated in a social network.

Across all these studies, people with stronger social relationships had about a 50 percent greater likelihood of survival over the follow-up period than those with weaker ties. The link held across age, sex and initial health status. The authors noted that the size of the effect was comparable to quitting smoking and larger than that of well-known risks such as physical inactivity and obesity. Complex measures of social integration showed the strongest association, while simply living alone or not showed a weaker one.
lesson: Friendships and family ties are not a luxury but part of staying healthy. Treat time with the people close to you as seriously as exercise or sleep.
people: Julianne Holt-Lunstad, Timothy Smith, J. Bradley Layton
location: Brigham Young University, Provo, Utah, USA (meta-analysis of international studies)
source: Holt-Lunstad, J., Smith, T. B., and Layton, J. B. (2010). Social relationships and mortality risk: A meta-analytic review. PLoS Medicine, 7(7), e1000316.
caveat: The studies are observational, so the link shows association and cannot fully rule out that healthier people simply have more ties.

title: The Collective Intelligence of Groups
text:
Psychologists have long known that a person who does well on one kind of mental test tends to do well on others, the pattern behind the idea of general intelligence. In 2010, Anita Woolley, Christopher Chabris, Alex Pentland, Nada Hashmi and Thomas Malone, working at Carnegie Mellon, MIT and Union College, asked whether groups show something similar.

They brought hundreds of people into the lab in small groups and gave each group a range of tasks: brainstorming, solving visual puzzles, negotiating over limited resources, making moral judgments and planning a shopping trip, among others. Groups that did well on one task tended to do well on the others, suggesting a general factor the authors called collective intelligence.

What predicted it was not mainly the average intelligence of the members or the score of the smartest person. Groups did better when members took turns more evenly instead of being dominated by one or two speakers, and when members scored higher on a test of reading emotions from pictures of people's eyes. Groups with a larger share of women also did better, which the authors linked to the women's higher average scores on that social sensitivity test.
lesson: A team of bright people is not automatically a bright team. Share the airtime and pay attention to how others are feeling, and the whole group thinks better.
people: Anita Woolley, Christopher Chabris, Alex Pentland, Nada Hashmi, Thomas Malone
location: Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, and MIT, Cambridge, USA
source: Woolley, A. W., Chabris, C. F., Pentland, A., Hashmi, N., and Malone, T. W. (2010). Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups. Science, 330(6004), 686-688.
caveat: Later reanalyses and studies have debated how strong and general the collective intelligence factor is.

title: The Power of Small Wins
text:
Teresa Amabile of Harvard Business School and her husband and research partner Steven Kramer wanted to know what actually happens inside people's heads during an ordinary working day. They recruited 238 professionals working on creative projects in 26 teams across seven companies, and asked each of them to fill out a short diary survey by email every working day of their project, often for months.

The participants rated their mood, motivation and perceptions of their work, and described one event that stood out that day. In total the researchers collected nearly 12,000 diary entries.

When Amabile and Kramer compared the best and worst days, one factor stood out above all others. On days when people made progress in meaningful work, even a small step forward, their mood and motivation were most likely to be high. On the worst days, the most common event was a setback. Progress also fed creativity and productivity, so that good inner days and good work went together. Yet when the researchers surveyed hundreds of managers, very few ranked supporting progress as the top motivator.
lesson: The best thing a leader can do for morale is to clear the way for steady progress on meaningful work, and to remove the obstacles that cause setbacks.
people: Teresa Amabile, Steven Kramer
source: Amabile, T., and Kramer, S. (2011). The Progress Principle: Using Small Wins to Ignite Joy, Engagement, and Creativity at Work. Harvard Business Review Press.

title: Hungry Judges
text:
In 2011 Shai Danziger, Jonathan Levav and Liora Avnaim-Pesso published a study of more than 1,100 parole decisions made by eight experienced judges serving on parole boards in Israel over ten months. Each day the judges heard a series of requests from prisoners and took two food breaks, a morning snack and lunch, which split the day into three sessions.

The researchers plotted the share of favorable rulings across each session. At the start of a session, the judges granted about 65 percent of requests. As the session wore on, the rate fell steadily, approaching zero just before a break. After the break it jumped back to around 65 percent, then declined again. The authors suggested that repeated decisions wear down mental resources, so that tired judges fall back on the easier default, which is to deny parole.

The paper was widely cited as proof that legal rulings depend on what judges had for breakfast. Critics soon raised doubts. Keren Weinshall-Margel and John Shapard pointed out that the order of cases was not random: prisoners without lawyers, whose requests were more often denied, tended to be heard at the end of sessions. Later analyses, including simulations by Andreas Glockner, showed that if judges simply avoided starting a case they could not finish before the break, a similar pattern could arise without any fatigue at all.

The original authors defended their findings, but the size of the effect seems too large for mental fatigue alone.
lesson: Important judgments can be shaped by things that should not matter, like timing and order. Still, check how cases were sorted before blaming a striking pattern on the decision maker's state of mind.
people: Shai Danziger, Jonathan Levav, Liora Avnaim-Pesso
source: Danziger, S., Levav, J., and Avnaim-Pesso, L. (2011). Extraneous factors in judicial decisions. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 108(17), 6889-6892.
caveat: Critics showed that the ordering of cases (for example, unrepresented prisoners heard last) could produce much of the pattern, so the role of fatigue remains disputed.

title: Self-Control in Dunedin
text:
In 1972 and 1973, about a thousand babies were born in the city of Dunedin, New Zealand, who would become some of the most closely studied people in the world. The Dunedin Multidisciplinary Health and Development Study followed nearly all of them from birth into adulthood, with regular, detailed assessments.

In 2011, a team led by Terrie Moffitt and Avshalom Caspi used this data to ask how much childhood self-control matters. Between ages three and eleven, the children's self-control had been rated repeatedly by observers, parents, teachers and the children themselves: how impulsive they were, how easily they got frustrated, how well they could wait their turn and stick with tasks.

By age 32, childhood self-control predicted a remarkable range of outcomes. Children with less self-control were more likely as adults to have physical health problems, to be dependent on drugs or alcohol, to have money troubles and debts, to be single parents and to have criminal convictions. The relationship held along the whole range, not only for the most impulsive children, and it remained after accounting for intelligence and family social class.

The team also studied about 500 pairs of British twins and found that, within the same family, the sibling with lower self-control at age five fared worse by age twelve.
lesson: Self-control learned in childhood pays off across adult life. Helping a child practice patience and persistence is worth the daily effort.
people: Terrie Moffitt, Avshalom Caspi and colleagues
source: Moffitt, T. E., Arseneault, L., Belsky, D., et al. (2011). A gradient of childhood self-control predicts health, wealth, and public safety. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 108(7), 2693-2698.

title: Leaders Who Speak for Us
text:
In 2011 the social psychologists Alex Haslam, Stephen Reicher and Michael Platow pulled together two decades of their own and others' research into a book that challenged the idea of leadership as a set of personal traits. They argued that leadership is a relationship between leaders and followers inside a shared group.

Drawing on experiments, field studies and historical cases, they proposed that people follow leaders whom they see as "one of us," who embody what the group stands for. Leaders also gain influence when they are seen to act for the group rather than for themselves or for outsiders, when they help define what the group is and what it values, and when they turn that shared identity into concrete structures and achievements.

In experiments by Platow and colleagues, for example, leaders who acted in a way that served the group's interests were endorsed more strongly than leaders who seemed to serve themselves or another group, even when the second leaders behaved in otherwise similar ways. The authors argued that much of the charisma people attribute to great leaders reflects how well they represent and champion their group.
lesson: People follow leaders who stand for something they share. Lead by representing and building the group's identity, not by standing above it.
people: S. Alexander Haslam, Stephen Reicher, Michael Platow
source: Haslam, S. A., Reicher, S. D., and Platow, M. J. (2011). The New Psychology of Leadership: Identity, Influence and Power. Psychology Press.
caveat: It is a theoretical synthesis rather than a single study; the evidence comes from many smaller experiments and case analyses.

title: How Influence Spoils the Crowd
text:
The wisdom of crowds depends on people guessing independently, so that individual errors cancel out. In 2011, Jan Lorenz, Heiko Rauhut, Frank Schweitzer and Dirk Helbing at ETH Zurich tested what happens when people can see each other's answers.

They recruited 144 students and asked them factual questions with numerical answers, such as the population density of Switzerland or the length of its border with Italy. Each question was answered over five rounds, with a small payment for accuracy. Some participants received no information about others' answers between rounds. Others saw the average of everyone's previous estimates, or saw all of them.

Seeing others' answers changed the crowd in three ways. The estimates converged: the range of answers shrank, so the group lost the diversity that makes averaging work. The group's collective estimate did not become more accurate, and the true value often ended up outside the narrowed range. And participants became more confident in their answers even though they were no better.

The authors warned that the combination, reduced diversity and growing confidence without greater accuracy, could mislead decision makers who rely on a crowd's consensus.
lesson: A group that compares notes too early loses its independence. Collect people's estimates privately before anyone sees what others think.
people: Jan Lorenz, Heiko Rauhut, Frank Schweitzer, Dirk Helbing
source: Lorenz, J., Rauhut, H., Schweitzer, F., and Helbing, D. (2011). How social influence can undermine the wisdom of crowd effect. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 108(22), 9020-9025.

title: When Everyone Could See the Salaries
text:
In 2008 the Sacramento Bee newspaper launched a website where anyone could look up the salary of any California state employee, including the staff and faculty of the University of California. The economists David Card, Alexandre Mas, Enrico Moretti and Emmanuel Saez saw an opportunity for a natural experiment.

At several University of California campuses, they sent an email to a random selection of employees telling them about the website. Others received no such message. A few days later, the researchers surveyed employees in both groups about their job satisfaction and whether they were looking for a new job. They could also see what people actually earned compared with colleagues in their own department and occupation.

Learning about the website clearly increased the number of people who looked up colleagues' salaries. For employees paid below the median in their unit, finding out about the website lowered their job satisfaction and made them more likely to say they were looking for another job. For those paid above the median, there was no comparable increase in satisfaction. Knowing they earned more did not make people noticeably happier, but knowing they earned less made them unhappy.
lesson: People judge their pay against those around them, and falling short hurts more than being ahead helps. Make sure pay differences are ones you can explain and defend.
people: David Card, Alexandre Mas, Enrico Moretti, Emmanuel Saez
source: Card, D., Mas, A., Moretti, E., and Saez, E. (2012). Inequality at work: The effect of peer salaries on job satisfaction. American Economic Review, 102(6), 2981-3003.

title: The Cars That Did Not Stop
text:
In 2012 Paul Piff and his colleagues at Berkeley published seven studies on social class and ethics. The best known took place at street crossings in the San Francisco Bay Area. Observers stood at a busy four-way intersection and at a pedestrian crosswalk, coding the make, age and look of each car, and noting whether its driver cut in front of other cars or failed to yield to a pedestrian, as California law requires.

Drivers of the most expensive, high-status cars were more likely to cut off other drivers and to drive through the crosswalk while a person, actually a member of the research team, was waiting to cross. Drivers of the cheapest cars almost always stopped.

In laboratory studies, the team found that people who saw themselves as higher in class were more willing to lie in a negotiation, cheat in a game to win a prize, and even take candy meant for children. They also held more favorable attitudes toward greed. When lower-class participants were led to think about the benefits of greed, they too behaved less ethically. The authors argued that privilege and independence from others can weaken attention to the rules that protect them.
lesson: Status and resources can quietly convince people that the rules are for others. Those who rise should guard their own behavior most carefully.
people: Paul Piff and colleagues
location: San Francisco Bay Area, California, USA
source: Piff, P. K., Stancato, D. M., Cote, S., Mendoza-Denton, R., and Keltner, D. (2012). Higher social class predicts increased unethical behavior. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 109(11), 4086-4091.
caveat: Later replications, including a large Dutch survey study, found weak or opposite links between class and unethical behavior, so the result is not settled.

title: The Team Scaling Fallacy
text:
When a project is falling behind, managers often add people to it. Bradley Staats, Katherine Milkman and Craig Fox suspected that people systematically underestimate how much larger teams slow down because of the extra coordination they require.

In one study, they gave teams of two or four people the task of building the same figure out of Lego bricks. Before starting, each team estimated how long the job would take. The four-person teams took considerably longer than the pairs to finish, yet they had not expected to, and their estimates were much further off than those of the smaller teams.

The authors called this the team scaling fallacy: as a team grows, people increasingly underestimate the time and effort it will need, because they think of more hands adding more output without accounting for the growing costs of coordinating everyone. They noted that this bias may lead managers to create teams that are larger than they should be.
lesson: Adding people adds coordination costs that are easy to underestimate. Keep teams as small as the work allows, and pad estimates for large ones.
people: Bradley Staats, Katherine Milkman, Craig Fox
source: Staats, B. R., Milkman, K. L., and Fox, C. R. (2012). The team scaling fallacy: Underestimating the declining efficiency of larger teams. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 118(2), 132-142.

title: The Consultants in the Indian Mills
text:
Economists had long noticed that management practices and productivity go together, but it was hard to prove that better management actually caused better results. In 2008 a team led by Nicholas Bloom ran a real experiment with large cotton fabric firms near Mumbai.

The research team, working with an international consulting firm, offered free consulting to a randomly chosen group of plants. The advice focused on basic practices: keeping factories clean and organized, recording and fixing quality defects, tracking inventory, maintaining machines regularly and holding production meetings. A control group received only a brief diagnosis.

At the start, the plants were strikingly disorganized, with piles of yarn and garbage on the floors and stock left unrecorded. In the treated plants, quality defects fell sharply, inventory dropped and productivity rose by about 17 percent in the first year. Within three years, the treated firms had also opened more plants. When asked why they had not adopted such practices before, owners often said they had not known about them or had not believed they would pay off.
lesson: Many organizations lose a great deal simply by neglecting basic good practices. Before searching for a big new strategy, check whether the fundamentals are in place.
people: Nicholas Bloom, Benn Eifert, Aprajit Mahajan, David McKenzie, John Roberts
source: Bloom, N., Eifert, B., Mahajan, A., McKenzie, D., and Roberts, J. (2013). Does management matter? Evidence from India. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 128(1), 1-51.

title: Praise at Age One, Mindset at Seven
text:
Earlier laboratory studies by Carol Dweck and others suggested that the way adults praise children affects how they think about ability. Elizabeth Gunderson, Susan Levine and their colleagues at the University of Chicago wanted to know whether ordinary praise in everyday family life had lasting effects.

They visited the homes of 53 families in the Chicago area and filmed parents and their children going about normal activities for ninety minutes, when the children were about fourteen months old, then again at about twenty-six and thirty-eight months. The researchers coded every instance of praise. Process praise focused on effort or actions, such as "you worked hard" or "good throwing." Person praise focused on fixed qualities, such as "you're so smart" or "good girl."

Five years later, when the children were seven and eight, the team measured their attitudes: whether they preferred challenging tasks, and whether they believed that abilities like intelligence could be improved with effort.

The more of parents' praise had been process praise in those toddler years, the more the children later favored challenge and believed ability can grow. Boys had received more process praise than girls, and boys were correspondingly more likely to have these attitudes. Total praise and person praise did not predict the outcome in the same way.
lesson: Even with toddlers, praise what they do, how they try and what strategy they use. Those everyday words shape how a child will face challenges years later.
people: Elizabeth Gunderson, Sarah Gripshover, Carissa Romero, Carol Dweck, Susan Goldin-Meadow, Susan Levine
source: Gunderson, E. A., Gripshover, S. J., Romero, C., Dweck, C. S., Goldin-Meadow, S., and Levine, S. C. (2013). Parent praise to 1- to 3-year-olds predicts children's motivational frameworks 5 years later. Child Development, 84(5), 1526-1541.
caveat: The sample was small and the findings correlational, so other features of the families may explain part of the link.

title: The Broken Promise and the Marshmallow
text:
Celeste Kidd, Holly Palmeri and Richard Aslin at the University of Rochester added a twist to the classic marshmallow test. Kidd had once volunteered at a homeless shelter, where she noticed that children grabbed food immediately, for the sensible reason that anything left unclaimed could vanish.

The researchers gave children aged three to five an art project. Each child received a worn set of crayons and was told that if they waited, the researcher would bring a bigger, better set. For half the children, the researcher came back with the promised crayons. For the other half, she returned empty-handed and apologized. The same thing happened with a promise of nice stickers.

Then came the standard test: a marshmallow on the table, and the promise of a second one if the child waited. The difference was large. Children who had just experienced a reliable adult waited, on average, about four times longer than children whose adult had broken her promises. Many in the reliable group lasted the full fifteen minutes; few in the unreliable group did.

The study suggested that a child who eats the marshmallow quickly may not lack self-control at all. They may simply be making a reasonable judgment about whether the adults around them keep their word.
lesson: Children will only wait for a reward they believe in. If you want patience from others, start by keeping your promises.
people: Celeste Kidd, Holly Palmeri, Richard Aslin
source: Kidd, C., Palmeri, H., and Aslin, R. N. (2013). Rational snacking: Young children's decision-making on the marshmallow task is moderated by beliefs about environmental reliability. Cognition, 126(1), 109-114.
caveat: The study was small, with 28 children, though later work has supported the role of trust in children's waiting.

title: Sugarcane Farmers Before and After Harvest
text:
In 2013 Anandi Mani, Sendhil Mullainathan, Eldar Shafir and Jiaying Zhao published two studies in Science on how money worries affect thinking.

The first took place in a shopping mall in New Jersey. Participants were asked to imagine a financial problem, such as their car needing a repair, and to think about how they would handle it. For some the repair cost was modest; for others it was large. Then everyone took tests of reasoning and self-control. When the problem was easy, poorer and richer participants performed about equally. When it was hard, the poorer participants did markedly worse, as if thinking about a serious money problem had used up part of their mental capacity.

The second study took place among sugarcane farmers in Tamil Nadu, India. These farmers receive most of their income once a year, at harvest, so the same person is relatively poor before harvest and relatively well off afterwards. The researchers tested several hundred farmers in both periods. Before harvest, when many had pawned possessions and taken loans, the farmers scored noticeably worse on tests of reasoning and attention than they did after harvest. The difference could not be explained by nutrition, physical work or stress from the harvest itself, which the researchers checked.

The authors argued that poverty imposes a mental tax: scarcity captures attention and leaves less capacity for everything else. Later studies that tried to reproduce the effect with other groups and settings have had mixed results.
lesson: Financial stress or any acute scarcity drains attention you need for decisions. When you are under that pressure, simplify choices, use reminders and postpone big decisions if you can.
people: Anandi Mani, Sendhil Mullainathan, Eldar Shafir, Jiaying Zhao
location: New Jersey, USA, and Tamil Nadu, India
source: Mani, A., Mullainathan, S., Shafir, E., and Zhao, J. (2013). Poverty impedes cognitive function. Science, 341(6149), 976-980.
caveat: Some later replications (for example Carvalho, Meier and Wang, 2016, around paydays in the US) did not find the effect, so its generality is debated.

title: When Power Makes Others Speechless
text:
In 2013 Leigh Tost, Francesca Gino and Richard Larrick reported a series of studies on what happens to a team when its leader feels powerful. In laboratory experiments, teams worked on a problem in which each member held unique information, so that finding the best answer required everyone to share what they knew. Before the task, some leaders were made to feel powerful, for example by recalling a time they had held power over others.

Teams led by leaders who felt powerful did worse. The powerful leaders talked more and dominated the discussion, and other members spoke less and felt less free to contribute. Less information was shared, and the team's decisions suffered. A field survey of real teams found a similar pattern: when leaders reported feeling powerful, open communication was weaker and team performance lower.

The researchers also found a remedy. When leaders were reminded beforehand that every member had important information and that the team's success depended on everyone's input, the harmful effect largely disappeared.
lesson: Your sense of authority can silence the very people whose knowledge you need. Talk less, ask more, and remind yourself that every person brings something you lack.
people: Leigh Plunkett Tost, Francesca Gino, Richard Larrick
source: Tost, L. P., Gino, F., and Larrick, R. P. (2013). When power makes others speechless: The negative impact of leader power on team performance. Academy of Management Journal, 56(5), 1465-1486.
caveat: Francesca Gino was later found by Harvard to have falsified data in other papers; this paper was not among those retracted, but its results deserve some care.

title: Abecedarian Children Grow Up
text:
In the 1970s, the Abecedarian Project in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, enrolled infants born into disadvantaged families, most of them African American. Half were randomly chosen to receive an intensive program that began in the first months of life and continued until age five: full-day childcare focused on language, play and learning, along with nutrition and basic health care. The other half received nutritional supplements and the usual support available in the community.

Early reports focused on what the program did for intelligence and schooling. Children who took part had higher test scores and were more likely to attend college. But the researchers kept following them.

In 2014, a team led by Frances Campbell and the economist James Heckman published a study in Science looking at the participants' health in their mid-thirties. Doctors examined them, measured their blood pressure and weight and took blood samples. Those who had received the early childhood program had markedly lower risk of heart and metabolic disease than the control group. The differences were especially clear among the men, who had lower blood pressure and much less metabolic syndrome, a cluster of risk factors for heart disease and diabetes.

The study suggested that early care can shape not only learning but the body itself, decades later.
lesson: What a child receives in the first five years can protect health into middle age. Early care is one of the best long-term investments a family or a society can make.
people: Frances Campbell, Gabriella Conti, James Heckman and colleagues
source: Campbell, F., Conti, G., Heckman, J. J., Moon, S. H., Pinto, R., Pungello, E., and Pan, Y. (2014). Early childhood investments substantially boost adult health. Science, 343(6178), 1478-1485.
caveat: The health follow-up involved a small number of participants, so the precise sizes of the effects are uncertain.

title: Talking to Strangers on the Train
text:
Every morning, commuters in Chicago sit side by side on trains and buses in near total silence. Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder of the University of Chicago wondered whether this silence was really what people wanted.

In 2014 they published a set of field experiments. Researchers approached commuters on the platform and gave them one of three instructions: strike up a conversation with a stranger on the ride, keep to yourself, or commute as you normally would. Each person got a sealed survey to fill in at the end of the ride and mail back.

Those who had talked to a stranger reported the most pleasant commute, and they did not report getting less done. Yet when other commuters were asked to predict how each condition would feel, they expected the opposite: talking to a stranger would be the least pleasant option. Many believed others would not want to talk to them. The researchers found similar results with taxi passengers and in the lab, where people underestimated how interested strangers would be in talking. The silence on the train was not a shared preference, but a shared mistake that kept everyone apart.
lesson: Most strangers are more open to a friendly word than you expect. Next time you sit next to someone, try a short conversation; you will probably both enjoy it.
people: Nicholas Epley, Juliana Schroeder
source: Epley, N., and Schroeder, J. (2014). Mistakenly seeking solitude. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 143(5), 1980-1999.

title: Skin to Skin for Premature Babies
text:
Premature babies usually spend their first weeks in incubators, which keep them warm and safe but separate them from their parents' bodies. Kangaroo care, first promoted in Colombia in the late 1970s, offers an alternative: the baby, wearing only a diaper, is held upright against the parent's bare chest.

Ruth Feldman, a developmental psychologist and neuroscientist at Bar-Ilan University in Israel, and her colleagues Zehava Rosenthal and Arthur Eidelman studied its long-term effects. In a neonatal intensive care unit, mothers of 73 premature infants provided skin-to-skin contact for an hour a day over fourteen consecutive days. These babies were compared with 73 premature babies matched on factors such as birth weight and medical condition, who received standard incubator care.

The team then followed the children for ten years, assessing them seven times. At age ten, the children who had received kangaroo care showed more mature physiological regulation: better organized sleep, a more flexible heart rate pattern linked to calm and attention, and a healthier hormonal response to stress. They also performed better on tests of cognitive control, such as focusing attention and holding back impulses. Their mothers had been more sensitive in interactions with them during the early years.

Fourteen hours of touch in the first weeks of life were associated with differences a decade later.
lesson: Touch is a form of care with lasting power. Holding a baby close, skin to skin, does real work for the body and the mind.
people: Ruth Feldman, Zehava Rosenthal, Arthur Eidelman
source: Feldman, R., Rosenthal, Z., and Eidelman, A. I. (2014). Maternal-preterm skin-to-skin contact enhances child physiologic organization and cognitive control across the first 10 years of life. Biological Psychiatry, 75(1), 56-64.
caveat: Mothers were not randomly assigned to kangaroo care, so other differences between the groups may have played a role.

title: Diversity Deflates Bubbles
text:
Financial bubbles form when prices rise far above the real value of what is being traded. Sheen Levine and colleagues, including the sociologist David Stark, wanted to know whether the ethnic makeup of a market affects how prone it is to such bubbles.

They ran experimental markets in two very different places: Singapore and Kingsville, Texas. Participants with training in business or finance traded simulated stocks for real money. The value of the stocks could be calculated from the information everyone received. Each market was either ethnically homogeneous, made up of traders from the dominant local group, or diverse, including traders from other ethnic groups. During trading, they interacted only through bids and prices on their screens.

In both locations, prices in diverse markets stayed closer to the true value of the assets. In homogeneous markets, traders were more likely to accept inflated prices, bubbles grew larger, and they burst harder.

The authors argued that in homogeneous groups, people tended to trust that others' decisions were sensible and to follow them. In diverse groups, traders were more skeptical of others' choices and relied more on their own analysis, which kept prices more accurate.
lesson: Too much familiarity in a group invites blind trust in each other's judgment. Diverse colleagues keep everyone checking the facts.
people: Sheen Levine, Evan Apfelbaum, Mark Bernard, Valerie Bartelt, Edward Zajac, David Stark
source: Levine, S. S., Apfelbaum, E. P., Bernard, M., Bartelt, V. L., Zajac, E. J., and Stark, D. (2014). Ethnic diversity deflates price bubbles. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 111(52), 18524-18529.

title: Superforecasters
text:
In 2011 the US intelligence research agency IARPA launched a forecasting tournament. Several research teams competed to predict world events, such as whether a country would hold an election on schedule or whether a currency would fall below a certain level, with questions resolving within months. One team was the Good Judgment Project, led by Philip Tetlock and Barbara Mellers at the University of Pennsylvania, which recruited thousands of volunteer forecasters from the public.

The project used the tournament as an experiment. Forecasters were randomly assigned to conditions. Some received about an hour of training in probabilistic reasoning, covering ideas like starting from base rates and avoiding common biases. Some worked alone, while others worked in teams that could share information and debate. After each year, the top 2 percent of forecasters were grouped into elite teams of "superforecasters."

All three measures helped. Training improved accuracy, teamwork improved it further, and the superforecaster teams were the most accurate of all. Their predictions kept improving rather than falling back toward average, suggesting real skill rather than luck. By combining forecasts and giving more weight to the best performers, the Good Judgment Project beat the other competing teams by a wide margin, and the agency eventually concentrated its funding on it.

Mellers and colleagues reported these results in 2014. The best forecasters tended to be curious, open-minded, numerate and willing to update their estimates in small steps as news arrived.
lesson: Forecasting is a skill that improves with practice, feedback and a little training. Put numbers on your expectations, keep score, discuss with others and revise often in small steps.
people: Barbara Mellers, Philip Tetlock, Lyle Ungar, Jonathan Baron and colleagues
source: Mellers, B., Ungar, L., Baron, J., et al. (2014). Psychological strategies for winning a geopolitical forecasting tournament. Psychological Science, 25(5), 1106-1115.

title: The Barista and Your Mood
text:
Research on happiness usually focuses on close relationships. In 2014 Gillian Sandstrom and Elizabeth Dunn of the University of British Columbia looked at the people we barely know: classmates, neighbors, the person who makes our coffee.

In one set of studies, students tracked their interactions with classmates over a term, and adults counted their daily interactions with close friends and family and with more casual acquaintances. On days when people had more interactions than usual with weak ties, they reported being happier and feeling a greater sense of belonging, even after accounting for their contact with close ties.

In a related experiment published the same year, the researchers sent people into a busy Starbucks with one of two instructions. Some were told to be efficient: have the money ready and keep the exchange with the cashier brief. Others were told to have a genuine interaction: smile, make eye contact and have a short conversation. Those who had a genuine interaction left in a better mood and with a stronger sense of connection than those who had rushed through. They spent only a few moments longer, but those moments mattered.
lesson: Brief friendly exchanges with acquaintances and strangers lift your mood and sense of belonging. Smile and say a few real words to the people you pass every day.
people: Gillian Sandstrom, Elizabeth Dunn
location: University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada
source: Sandstrom, G. M., and Dunn, E. W. (2014). Social interactions and well-being: The surprising power of weak ties. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 40(7), 910-922. Also: Sandstrom, G. M., and Dunn, E. W. (2014). Is efficiency overrated? Minimal social interactions lead to belonging and positive affect. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 5(4), 437-442.

title: The Too-Much-Talent Effect
text:
Teams often try to sign as many stars as they can. Roderick Swaab, Adam Galinsky and their colleagues asked whether there can be too much of a good thing.

They first surveyed people, who generally believed that more top talent always makes a team better. Then they looked at sports data. In international football, they measured each national team's talent by the share of its players who played for elite clubs, and compared it with the team's results in World Cup qualifying. In professional basketball, they used measures of individual player quality and compared them with team records over multiple seasons. In baseball, where players depend less on each other during play, they did the same.

In football and basketball, adding top talent improved performance up to a point. Beyond that point, further stars brought no gain and appeared to harm results. In basketball, the authors linked this to a drop in coordination, such as fewer assists, as stars competed for the ball. In baseball, more talent simply kept helping.

The authors concluded that when team members must work closely together, too many stars can undermine coordination, as each expects to play the lead role.
lesson: Stacking a team with stars can backfire when the work requires close coordination. Make sure someone is happy to play the supporting roles.
people: Roderick Swaab, Michael Schaerer, Eric Anicich, Richard Ronay, Adam Galinsky
location: International football, the NBA and Major League Baseball
source: Swaab, R. I., Schaerer, M., Anicich, E. M., Ronay, R., and Galinsky, A. D. (2014). The too-much-talent effect: Team interdependence determines when more talent is too much or not enough. Psychological Science, 25(8), 1581-1591.
caveat: Later reanalyses with other data and methods have questioned whether extra talent actually hurts teams, rather than simply adding less.

title: Working From Home at Ctrip
text:
In 2010 the Chinese travel company Ctrip, which ran a large call center in Shanghai, wanted to know whether letting staff work from home would help or hurt. Its cofounder James Liang, then a doctoral student at Stanford, designed an experiment with the economist Nicholas Bloom.

Call center employees were invited to volunteer. Among the volunteers who had a suitable room at home and enough experience, those with even-numbered birthdays were allowed to work from home four days a week for nine months, while those with odd-numbered birthdays stayed in the office. Both groups used the same equipment and software and were paid in the same way.

The home workers performed about 13 percent better, mostly because they worked more minutes per shift, with fewer breaks and sick days, and partly because they handled more calls per minute in a quieter setting. Their quit rate was about half that of the office group. Yet when the experiment ended and Ctrip offered the option to all, about half of the home group chose to return to the office, many saying they felt lonely. Their promotion rate had also been lower given their performance.
lesson: Results, not presence, measure good work, but people still need contact and visibility. Offer flexibility, and keep remote people connected and in view.
people: Nicholas Bloom, James Liang, John Roberts, Zhichun Jenny Ying
source: Bloom, N., Liang, J., Roberts, J., and Ying, Z. J. (2015). Does working from home work? Evidence from a Chinese experiment. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 130(1), 165-218.
caveat: The jobs were simple, easily measured call center work, so the results may not transfer to tasks that need close collaboration.

title: Does Birth Order Shape Personality?
text:
Few beliefs about family are as popular as the idea that birth order shapes who we become: firstborns are responsible and bossy, middle children are diplomats, the youngest are charming rebels. Researchers had argued about it for a century, but many earlier studies compared people from different families or relied on siblings rating each other.

In 2015, Julia Rohrer, Boris Egloff and Stefan Schmukle at the University of Leipzig analyzed data from more than 20,000 people in three large national surveys from Germany, the United Kingdom and the United States. They looked at standard personality traits such as extraversion, emotional stability, agreeableness, conscientiousness and openness. Crucially, they compared not only people from different families but also brothers and sisters within the same family.

The result was clear. Birth order had no meaningful effect on extraversion, emotional stability, agreeableness or conscientiousness. The only consistent effect was on intellect: firstborns scored very slightly higher on intelligence tests and rated themselves slightly higher on intellect, a difference of about one or two IQ points between neighboring siblings, too small to notice in any individual family.

Around the same time, another large study by Damian and Roberts reached similar conclusions.
lesson: Do not let birth order write your children's script. Siblings differ, but not in the way family folklore says, so look at each child as they are.
people: Julia Rohrer, Boris Egloff, Stefan Schmukle
source: Rohrer, J. M., Egloff, B., and Schmukle, S. C. (2015). Examining the effects of birth order on personality. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 112(46), 14224-14229.

title: Moving to a Better Neighborhood
text:
In the mid-1990s, the United States government ran an experiment called Moving to Opportunity. In five cities, Baltimore, Boston, Chicago, Los Angeles and New York, families living in high-poverty public housing could sign up for a lottery. Some were offered vouchers to help pay rent, on condition that they move to a low-poverty neighborhood. Others received ordinary vouchers or nothing extra. Because the offers were random, the families could be fairly compared.

Earlier studies found that the moves improved adults' mental and physical health in some ways but did little for their earnings, and many concluded that neighborhoods did not matter much economically.

In 2016, the economists Raj Chetty, Nathaniel Hendren and Lawrence Katz looked again, this time at the children, using tax records to follow them into adulthood. The age at which a child moved turned out to matter greatly. Children whose families had moved to a lower-poverty neighborhood before they turned thirteen went on to earn substantially more in their mid-twenties than children in the control group, were more likely to attend college and less likely to become single parents. For children who moved as teenagers, there was no such gain, and possibly some harm.

The benefits seemed to grow with every year a child spent in the better environment.
lesson: Where a child grows up shapes their future, and the years of childhood add up. Decisions about home and neighborhood are among the biggest a family makes.
people: Raj Chetty, Nathaniel Hendren, Lawrence Katz
location: Baltimore, Boston, Chicago, Los Angeles and New York, USA
source: Chetty, R., Hendren, N., and Katz, L. F. (2016). The effects of exposure to better neighborhoods on children: New evidence from the Moving to Opportunity experiment. American Economic Review, 106(4), 855-902.

title: What Spanking Does
text:
For generations, many parents have believed that an occasional spanking teaches children to behave. Researchers had studied the question for decades, but critics argued that earlier reviews mixed spanking with harsher forms of physical abuse.

In 2016, Elizabeth Gershoff of the University of Texas at Austin and Andrew Grogan-Kaylor of the University of Michigan published new meta-analyses that focused narrowly on spanking, defined as hitting a child on the bottom or the limbs with an open hand. They combined the results of 75 studies covering more than 160,000 children.

The pattern was consistent. Spanking was linked to worse outcomes on most of the measures they examined, including more aggression, more antisocial behavior, more mental health problems, lower self-esteem, lower cognitive ability and poorer relationships between parent and child. Spanking was not linked to better behavior or greater compliance over time. The associations held in studies that followed children over time, and they looked similar to the associations found for physical abuse, only weaker.

The researchers also found that adults who had been spanked as children were more likely to support spanking their own children, suggesting how the practice passes from one generation to the next.
lesson: Spanking is linked to worse behavior, not better, across many studies. Clear limits, calm consequences and explanation are safer tools.
people: Elizabeth Gershoff, Andrew Grogan-Kaylor
location: University of Texas at Austin and University of Michigan, USA
source: Gershoff, E. T., and Grogan-Kaylor, A. (2016). Spanking and child outcomes: Old controversies and new meta-analyses. Journal of Family Psychology, 30(4), 453-469.
caveat: The studies were correlational, and some researchers argue that difficult behavior in children may partly cause spanking rather than only result from it.

title: The Liking Gap
text:
After talking with someone new, many people replay the conversation and worry: did I say too much, did they find me dull? In 2018 Erica Boothby, Gus Cooney, Gillian Sandstrom and Margaret Clark measured how accurate those worries are.

In the lab, pairs of strangers had short getting-acquainted conversations. Afterward each person rated how much they liked their partner and how much they thought their partner liked them. Again and again, people underestimated how much they were liked. Their partners had enjoyed them more than they believed. The researchers called this the liking gap. It appeared in conversations of different lengths, and among people in a personal development workshop who talked in small groups.

They also followed first-year students at Yale who had just been assigned to live together as suitemates. The students rated how much they liked each suitemate and how much they thought each suitemate liked them, several times over the academic year. The liking gap persisted for months, shrinking only slowly. The researchers suggested that people are so busy monitoring their own performance in a conversation that they miss the clear signs of warmth coming from the other side.
lesson: The other person probably liked you more than you think. Let that knowledge make you braver about following up, reaching out again and being yourself.
people: Erica Boothby, Gus Cooney, Gillian Sandstrom, Margaret Clark
location: Yale University, New Haven, USA, and other sites
source: Boothby, E. J., Cooney, G., Sandstrom, G. M., and Clark, M. S. (2018). The liking gap in conversations: Do people like us more than we think? Psychological Science, 29(11), 1742-1756.

title: A Quarter to Tip a Norm
text:
How big must a committed minority be to overturn an established social convention? In 2018, Damon Centola and his colleagues Joshua Becker, Devon Brackbill and Andrea Baronchelli tested this online.

Participants were placed in groups and paired repeatedly with random members of their group. In each round, both partners saw a picture of a face and had to type a name for it. They earned money when they gave the same name. Over many rounds, each group settled on a shared name, which became its convention.

The researchers then introduced a committed minority of confederates, who always used a different name no matter what others said. They varied the size of that minority across groups.

The result showed a clear threshold. When the committed minority made up less than about a quarter of the group, the established convention held. When it reached about a quarter, the new name spread and the whole group quickly switched. Below the threshold, the minority had little effect; above it, it won. The authors linked this to what each person saw in their recent interactions: once enough partners used the new name, people switched to it to coordinate.
lesson: Changing a group's habits does not require a majority, but it does require a committed core. Aim for roughly a quarter of the group acting consistently on the new norm.
people: Damon Centola, Joshua Becker, Devon Brackbill, Andrea Baronchelli
location: University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, USA (online experiment)
source: Centola, D., Becker, J., Brackbill, D., and Baronchelli, A. (2018). Experimental evidence for tipping points in social convention. Science, 360(6393), 1116-1119.
caveat: The quarter threshold was found in a simple naming game, and real norms with higher stakes or stronger beliefs may behave differently.

title: The Thank-You Letter You Never Sent
text:
Many people feel grateful to someone and never say so. In 2018 Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley of the University of Chicago looked at why.

They asked participants to write a short letter of gratitude to someone who had mattered to them, describing what that person had done and how it had affected them. Before the letters were delivered, the writers predicted how the recipients would feel: how surprised, how happy, and how awkward. Then the researchers contacted the recipients and asked how they actually felt.

The writers got it wrong in a consistent direction. They underestimated how surprised the recipients would be by the content, and how positive they would feel. They overestimated how awkward the recipients would feel. Recipients were often moved, and rarely uncomfortable. Writers also tended to worry about how well they had expressed themselves, focusing on finding the right words, while recipients focused on the warmth behind the letter. Because people expect thanks to land weaker and more awkwardly than it does, the researchers suggested, they hold back a simple act that would brighten someone's day and their own.
lesson: Thanks you never express does no good. Write the note or make the call; the other person will likely be happier and less awkward about it than you fear.
people: Amit Kumar, Nicholas Epley
source: Kumar, A., and Epley, N. (2018). Undervaluing gratitude: Expressers misunderstand the consequences of showing appreciation. Psychological Science, 29(9), 1423-1435.
